3
HANDHELD AND MOBILE
APPLICATIONS FOR THE GRID
The capability and utility of the system has been validated 
using handheld applications that have been developed for 
the Personal Java runtime environment on iPAQ Pocket 
PCs.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The clients we have developed can be run on any 
mobile device that supports Java.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Once installed users can 
use these applications irrespective of any underlying 
networks; wireless, wired or mobile.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
These clients were 
mainly developed for physicists and scientists to access and 
analyze data anytime on mobile devices (but of course are 
more generally applicable in other eScience applications).
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Later, considering the enormous size of data which is often 
required by scientists for analysis, we proposed to distribute 
storage and computation resources on the Grid.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In this way 
we maintained the ubiquitous access and analysis of data; 
we also saved low resource mobile devices from enormous 
storage and computation.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
However, these clients can be 
easily customized for any solution that requires heavy 
computation and storage from mobile devices.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
A description 
of the clients developed and the features offered by them for 
interactive analysis follows.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
3.1
Java Analysis Studio(JAS) & JASOnPDA
The Java Analysis Studio (JAS) has been developed at the 
Stanford Linear Accelerator (SLAC) [4].
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
JAS is a physics 
analysis tool used for analyzing data obtained from linear 
accelerators in the form of 1D-2D histograms as shown in 
figure 2.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Apart from 1D-2D analysis, JAS offers numerous 
other facilities, which include comparison of displayed 
histograms 
with 
predefined 
mathematical 
functions 
(Quadratic, Cubic, Gaussian, polynomial, Lorentzian etc), 
the fitting of these functions over the displayed histograms 
for statistical analysis (peak value, average value etc), and 
executing individual analyses code on selected datasets.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Figure 2: Java Analysis Studio (JAS) (above) running on a 
Desktop Machine.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
JASOnPDA [5] was our first application for the 
PocketPC.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
JASOnPDA is the scaled down version of Java 
Analysis Studio, especially designed for constrained 
handheld devices.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
JASOnPDA provides the essential 
analysis utilities of Java Analysis Studio on PocketPC 
devices, and was developed using J2SE v1.1.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
JASOnPDA 
allows mobile users to log on to the JClarens server using a 
certificate-based 
authentication 
procedure.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Once 
successfully authenticated, the user is allowed to access files 
stored at the server.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The remote browsing facility allows 
users to browse the directories served by JClarens and to 
look for desired ROOT files.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The selected ROOT [6] file is 
analyzed and a tree structure displays the hierarchy of 
objects in the ROOT file.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The user can move along the tree, 
selecting any object from the tree structure, and the selected 
object will be displayed in the form of 1D-2D Histograms in 
the display panel as shown in figure 3.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Figure 3: JASOnPDA running on a PDA showing features 
of histogram plotting, fitting, and statistics calculation.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In order to submit jobs to the Grid using JClarens, 
JASOnPDA allows users to select the file that will be used 
as the job’s executable.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
It also allows users to type in or to 
select a file that will be used as the submit file.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Once this has 
been carried out, the user can select the input files that will 
be used as the input for the jobs, and can finally submit the 
job.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
A notification is received when the job is successfully 
submitted, after which JASOnPDA periodically polls 
JClarens for the jobs’ status.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
As soon as the job is complete, 
a menu is displayed showing the files on which the job 
execution was successful.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The user can then select a 
particular file to get the resulting output of the job execution 
on that particular file.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In this way, users on handheld devices 
can submit jobs on compute farms, and at the same time, get 
back outputs of the job execution.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Statistical fitting features 
from JAS have also been ported.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The user can also view 
statistics information related to the histogram displayed on 
the screen.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Keeping in view the small screen size of the 
PocketPC, different viewing options are also provided.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
To overcome the issue of intermittent, unreliable 
connections during the transfer of large datasets and files, 
the downloading process for large files is carried out by 
dividing the size of the file into small chunks, and 
downloading those small file chunks in steps, rather than 
using a single connection to transfer the entire file.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
This 
allows us to checkpoint the file transfer process and to 
ensure that if there is a disconnection at any stage, the entire 


dataset is not lost, and downloading can be resumed from 
the latest checkpoint.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text: Recently, more features for extensibility have been added.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Interfaces have been exposed that allow users to write their 
own analysis classes for different file formats.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
This provides
users the flexibility to select the procedure by which their 
file will be analyzed and to have its contents displayed.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
To 
specify the class to be used for analysis, the user only has to 
give the name of the class in a simple properties file.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In this 
way, the user can easily plug in the classes that (s)he wants 
to use for handling new file formats and user-specific 
custom file formats.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
3.2
WWW Interactive Remote Event Display 
(WIRED) and WiredOnPDA
The WWW Interactive Remote Event Display (WIRED) 
[7] was a joint venture between Stanford Linear Accelerator 
(SLAC) and the European Organization for Nuclear 
Research (CERN).
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
WIRED is one of the first physics event 
displays written in Java for use on the World-Wide-Web.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
It 
provides a framework for writing event displays as shown in 
figure 4.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
It is in active use by the BaBar and GLAST 
experiments and the LCD detector study at SLAC.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Figure 4: WWW Interactive Remote Event Display running 
on a Desktop machine.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
WiredOnPDA is another of our analysis applications 
developed for PocketPC devices.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
As the name suggests, 
WiredOnPDA provides analysis features of the WWW 
Interactive Remote Event Display (WIRED) on a PocketPC
and is presented in figures 5 and 6.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
WiredOnPDA accesses 
data using JClarens in the same way as JASOnPDA.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Figure 5: Two views of WiredOnPDA displaying events 
from a HepRep2 file (left) and detector geometry (right).
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
As mentioned earlier, the user has to pass a security check 
by providing a valid certificate and key.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Once authenticated, 
the user can access the remote server and can select any 
HepRep2 event file placed on the server.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Figure 6: Two views of WiredOnPDA displaying event data 
and the structure of a HepRep2 file in separate panes.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Once the user selects a file from the JClarens server, the 
file is downloaded into the RAM and a SAX XML parser 
[8] parses the information stored in the file.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
“Drawables” are 
then extracted from the parsed data and are displayed in a
hierarchical tree structure in a WiredOnPDA tree panel.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
User can then select any “drawable” from the tree and it will 
be displayed in the display console.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Again, keeping in mind 
the small screen size of the PocketPC, various display 
options are provided in order to utilize the maximum screen 
space for event display.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
As shown in the screenshot figures, 
the application is provided with a tool bar that allows the 
user to scale, rotate or zoom the displayed event for 
improved analysis.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
WiredOnPDA also had some issues on its initial release, 
most of which were regarding performance.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The main 
reason for non-optimal performance was the poor parsing 
speed of the SAX parsers in PersonalJava.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Performance 
analysis has shown that the reason for this slow parsing is 
due to the differences in implementation of the PersonalJava 
virtual machine compared to the J2SE virtual machines.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
To 
address this issue various parsers were tried and tested 
including Xerces [9], Crimson [10], KXML [11] and Piccolo
[12].
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Piccolo has so far proved to be the fastest performer, 
with the best possible results amongst the parsers.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
3.3
Intermittent 
Connections 
and 
Data 
Transfer
Since wireless networks can be subject to intermittent 
network connection and loss of data during data transfer we 
have devised a mechanism to cater for interrupted 
connections which works as follows.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Applications keep a 
log of the files transferred and the number of bytes of the 
file that have been transferred.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Files were downloaded in N 
kilobyte chunks into a temporarily-created file, and every n 
kilobytes, the entry for the file was updated.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Once a file is 


totally transferred, the entry for the file was removed from 
the log, and the temporary file was deleted.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
If the connection 
was disconnected (such as when the timeout expired or the 
PDA itself detected a broken connection) the user simply 
has to wait until (s)he gets next connected and then tries to 
download that file again.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
However, since the extent of the 
file downloaded was saved in the temporary file and the 
number of correctly transferred bytes was stored in the log, 
the download can be restarted from that number of bytes.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
4
SERVER SIDE DESIGN
The server side relies mainly on the JClarens framework 
and the services provided by it.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
A detailed description of the 
clients is given in section 3.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Here we describe the overall 
design of the server-side Grid service host, how jobs are 
actually submitted to the Condor job scheduling system, and 
how they are managed.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
A modified version of Apache’s 
XML-RPC [13] classes is used to provide XML-RPC 
parsing and processing capabilities.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The XML-RPC server, 
encapsulated in a Java servlet, is responsible for processing 
incoming requests, for extracting information about what 
services and methods to invoke, and for writing out 
responses in XML.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In addition, we have also modified it to 
be able to write back responses directly in a binary form, to 
reduce overheads during binary file transfers.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The major components on the server side are detailed in 
the following sub-sections.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
4.1
Authentication and Authorization
Authentication and authorization of valid users and virtual 
organizations (VOs) is one of the most important 
requirements of any Grid-enabled system.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
JClarens carries 
out authentication using a GSI-based [14] security protocol.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The server and clients use X.509 certificates and RSA keys 
for authentication.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
A detailed description of Clarens 
authentication protocol is given in [2].
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Authorization is 
carried out using access control lists (ACLs) maintained in a 
database.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The database system available by default is 
MySQL [15], although any other DBMS can be easily 
plugged-in by providing a suitable JDBC driver, and by 
modifying the configuration settings in a properties file.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The database contains the distinguished names (DNs) or 
substrings of DNs that are allowed or denied access to 
various services.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
A set of methods is also available for 
manipulating these ACLs by system administrators.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Besides 
users’ DNs, the names of the VOs can also be used to 
configure access control for large groups of users or VOs.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
JClarens also provides data browsing, searching and 
downloading capabilities.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Using the “file” service, users can 
browse files, search for files using “wildcards”, and search 
within files.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
They can also download files and find out the 
validity of downloaded files using md5 hash values.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
4.2
Monitoring service
A prototype monitoring service has been developed which 
reports monitoring information to a central JClarens server, 
hereafter known as the resource broker.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The monitoring 
service gathers monitoring information using a companion 
End-host Monitoring Agent (EMA), a monitoring product is 
also currently being developed.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
EMA gathers information 
such as the CPU clock rate, CPU usage, Memory Usage and 
Last 1, 5 and 15-minute average load values.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
These 
parameters are used to calculate a “load coefficient”, which 
describes the load on a particular system in quantitative 
terms.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The coefficient is calculated using an empirical 
formula:
Coeff.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
= ((1-CPU_Usage/100)*-1*Clock_Rate) + ai Mi
Where CPU_Usage is the percentage of CPU power being 
used, Mi is the value of the i’th monitoring parameter and ai
is an experimentally determined weighting factor for the i’th 
monitoring parameter
Currently the monitoring parameters being used are the 
percentage of memory being used, the Disk I/O in Mbps, the 
average CPU load during the past one minute (Load1), and 
the number of currently executing processes.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Since CPU Usage indicates how much the CPU is being 
used, (1-CPU_Usage/100) in the first term shows the 
proportion of the CPU that is free.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In addition, because -1 is 
used as a factor in the term, the more the CPU is free, the 
lower is the value of the first term.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The second term in the 
formula indicates the load being added to a node because of 
other factors, like Disk I/O, memory I/O and other factors.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In this way, the lower the value of the coefficient for a node, 
the lower is the load on that node.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Every few seconds (10 by default), this coefficient value 
is sent to the resource broker as an XML-RPC call, where it 
is stored in a database, along with the URL of that particular 
server.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
This monitoring information is used at the time of 
job submission to decide where to forward jobs for 
execution.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In order to provide the resource broker more up-
to-date (and hence more accurate) monitoring information 
about a server, the interval after which the data is published 
to it can be decreased.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
However, this can result in the 
generation of more network traffic.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
To compensate, the 
network traffic can be reduced at the expense of updated 
monitoring information by increasing the interval after 
which the data is published.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Therefore, it is up to the 
administrator of each site to determine a threshold interval 
that can increase the accuracy of the information published 
and keep network traffic down to a manageable level.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
4.3
Job submission service
The job submission service is designed to submit jobs to 
the least loaded computer or a farm on the network (LAN or 
WAN).
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The job submission service receives requests for
submission of a job from handheld clients with the 
following parameters:
1)
The name of the job
2)
The binary code of the executable
3)
The submit file
4)
The name of the submit file
5)
The names of the input files
The handheld clients themselves do not provide the input 
files at present.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Instead the clients request the JClarens 


server for files available in its file publishing area and select 
the ones on which they wish to perform analysis.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
On receiving a job submission request (condorSubmit), 
the receiving JClarens server gets the minimum load 
coefficient reported by the other peer servers from the 
resource broker.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
It then forwards the job to the least loaded 
peer.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Note that the peer is basically a JClarens server 
running on another computer or on the head node of a 
compute farm.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
When a peer JClarens server receives a forwarded job 
submission request from another peer, it creates a temporary 
staging directory for Condor on the local hard disk (see 
figure 7).
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
It then generates a unique job ID for the request 
and creates a subdirectory in that folder with the same name 
as the job ID.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
A number of subdirectories are then created in 
the job’s particular subdirectory equal to the number of 
input files and the executable and the submit file are copied 
into each of the subdirectories, naming them the same as the 
file names in the request.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
If the forwarding peer is the local 
host itself, the server copies the file from the local file 
system to the appropriate subdirectory directly.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Otherwise, it 
downloads the file from the forwarding JClarens server 
using the “file.read” call.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Once the staging directories are prepared, JClarens 
submits the jobs to Condor by executing “condor_submit” 
calls on the submit file.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Condor submits jobs in logical 
groups called “clusters”.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
A mapping between the jobs 
themselves and the clusters to which the jobs have been 
submitted is also stored in a database.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Condor [16] then takes over the allocation of the 
individual jobs to different machines in the Condor pool and 
ensures that the jobs are completed and the results returned 
to the respective directories.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
While Condor executes the job 
on the pool, the client can repeatedly poll JClarens to check 
the status of its jobs.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Because only the job ID is required to 
check the status of a job, a very lightweight XML-RPC 
request has to be sent to the server to check the status of a 
job.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In case of successful submission, JClarens returns a 
unique ID generated for the job, and this is sent to the initial 
submitting client through the master JClarens.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
A table 
mapping the job ID with the peer where the job has been 
actually submitted is also updated.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
After that, the client uses 
this job ID to inspect the status of the job, or to retrieve its 
status at any later stage.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience
Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience
Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience
Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience
Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The Job is forwarded to the best available site;
6.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience
Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The User checks the status of jobs repeatedly, gets back 
outputs when desired etc.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Figure 7: An overview of the steps involved in submitting 
jobs and checking their status:
JClarens retrieves the status of a job with a particular ID 
by finding out the peer where the job with that ID has been 
submitted.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The execution of “condor_q” on that peer gives 
the status of all the jobs running on the machine.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The status 
of the jobs for that particular job ID is extracted by filtering 
out the clusters mapped to that job ID from the output of 
“condor_q”.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Once the job is complete, the handheld client can retrieve 
the outputs of all its jobs through JClarens.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Clients can look 
at all the output files produced during execution, and can 
download the desired output files.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In this way, a complex 
and time-consuming set of jobs can be rapidly executed on 
an underutilized Condor pool and its results displayed and 
visualized on the submitting handheld client.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
To provide fault tolerance and high availability, the 
system has been designed to be entirely self-healing.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Whenever a new JClarens server initiates and reports to the 
resource broker, the resource broker informs all the 
available servers of this new server.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In this way if at any 
stage the central JClarens resource broker goes down, one of 
the other servers detects this faulty condition automatically, 
and can establish itself as the central resource broker for all 
the other available servers.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In this way, it is ensured that the 
system is able to heal itself and remain available for the 
clients even if the central resource broker becomes 
inaccessible.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Using this architecture, even users on slow-processing 
PDAs connected to wireless networks can accomplish 
complex high end jobs.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
They can carry out remote 
processing of lengthy operations on powerful machines in 
the Condor pool.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
This allows even handheld devices to 
exploit the power of Grid computing.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
5
RELATED WORK
Mobile devices have hitherto not been used for launching 
and visualizing data intensive applications and jobs.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
For 
desktop machines, on the other hand, a variety of Grid


enabled physics analysis applications is available.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Some of 
these include JAS [4], ROOT [6] and WIRED [7].
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
As 
detailed earlier, JAS is used primarily for 1D and 2D 
graphical display of histogram data obtained from particle 
accelerators.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Along with graphical display, it also offers 
various mathematical functions to fit along the displayed 
data.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
WIRED was developed at CERN in collaboration with 
SLAC.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Wired uses XML based files for graphical rendering 
of events and sub component geometry information from 
various particle experiments.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Also developed at CERN, 
ROOT analyzes special format ROOT files in which data is 
arranged in a highly efficient, hierarchical structure.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Research is already being carried out to integrate the two 
groundbreaking fields of Grid computing and mobile 
computing 17].
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Even Java-enabled mobile phones have been 
targeted for possible integration with the Grid environment, 
in order to provide more computationally intensive features 
on mobile phones [18].
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Oracle and Vodafone announced a 
joint initiative to offer mobile Grid computing [25] in which 
they would offer enterprise customers integrated mobility 
solutions based on Oracle 10g and Vodafone Network 
Services.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Our Pocket PC based analysis applications are basically 
built around the Java Analysis Studio (JAS) and WWW 
Interactive Remote Event Display (WIRED) software, and 
have been optimized for the Personal Java [19] environment 
on the Pocket PC 2002.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
On the server side, JClarens is used 
to provide a framework on which Grid services are hosted to 
provide Grid authentication, job submission, job tracking, 
data access, and file browsing services.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Another direction 
that we have researched is in balancing mobile client load by 
using the JADE-LEAP [20] multi-agent system.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
In this
architecture mobile clients send agents along with job 
credentials to a central server which then locates a suitable 
site and dispatches the agent along with the job to that site.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
After execution the mobile client communicates with 
another agent residing in the client to transfer results.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
This 
approach has yielded useful input to the current research and 
the work continues in parallel with this effort.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The reader is 
refereed to [21] for further information on multi-mobile 
agents studies.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
[23] describe the disconnected operation 
service in mobile Grid computing.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
They discuss the 
intermittent connections but provide little information on the 
issues of the data intensive applications for the mobile 
devices.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Paul and Naian [24] describe an efficient 
checkpointing technique for mobile Grid computing systems 
and try to overcome the issues posed by the intermittent
connections.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
EC funded Akogrimo project [28] envisions 
that Grid services, pervasively available, should eventually 
meeting the needs of fixed, nomadic and mobile citizens in 
the ‘everywhere at every time in any context’ paradigm.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
But 
this project is in its initial phases and will take some time to 
see the results.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Chu and Humphrey [25] describe Mobile 
OGSI.NET which is created to promote resource sharing 
and collaboration that improves the user experience.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Mobile 
OGSI.NET extends an implementation of Grid computing, 
OGSI.NET, to mobile devices.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
This actually deploys the 
customized Grid toolkit on the mobile device but does not 
discuss the data handling and presentation issues on the
mobile devices.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Zhi Wang et al [27] describe the Grid for 
wireless and adhoc network.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
They actually test the 
applications on warless networks but do not take into 
consideration the Grid issues related to the mobile devices.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
6
CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
The analysis environment presented in this work has been
developed to contribute to eScience in general and the 
physics community in particular all around the world, to 
help them in their quest for ubiquitous access to data, over 
wired and wireless links.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
But it has yet to reach the high 
performance standards that are so easily achieved in the case 
of desktop PC-based applications.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The slow performance of 
handheld devices is a major barrier that has to be overcome 
to achieve true interactivity.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
However, the use of a 
distributed job execution and data analysis environment has 
enabled us to speed up our analysis applications to a great 
extent.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Even if a set of jobs is submitted on a standalone 
analysis server, users can get back the results of analysis on 
almost fifteen event files (each event stored in a 1MB file) 
in less than a minute, whereas a standalone PocketPC could 
not process more than three or four files per minute.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The distributed architecture of this model makes it unique 
as it enables mobile clients to analyze data which are too 
large for them to store or process.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
It shows that if merged, 
Grid computing and mobile computing could make use of 
the features provided by each technology to engender a new 
era of high resource consuming mobile applications.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
This 
can prove to be the first step towards enabling mobile 
devices to provide functionality and resources similar to 
desktop PCs.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Our PocketPC based applications were demonstrated in 
ITU Telecom World 2003 as a part of the “GRID-Enabled 
Physics Analysis” demonstration.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Also the JASOnPDA 
system was presented at the first Grid Analysis Environment 
(GAE) workshop at Caltech in June 2005, and attracted a 
great deal of attention, due to the fact that it was the first 
physics analysis application ported to the PDA.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
WiredOnPDA is expected to gain at least the same 
amount of attention as its predecessor.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Our work on this 
analysis environment, however, is far from over.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Already 
our current work proves that resource-constrained devices 
such as the PocketPC can be interfaced with the Grid, and 
can play a vital role in the realization of the idea of a Grid-
Enabled Analysis Environment (GAE).
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
This has clear 
implications to and application in other areas of Grid-based 
science analysis.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Mobile and ubiquitous computing has yet 
to reach a mature level, where it can compete with desktop 
PCs in the kind of applications it can offer.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The achievement 
of the above mentioned goals should prove to be a giant leap 
towards the attainment of this level of maturity.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
There are still some ideas that are yet to be implemented 
in this project.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
The most important of these is an even 
further decentralized architecture, where there is no master 
server at all.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Instead all the servers are true peers of each 
other and can get monitoring information from a 
decentralized source.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
We are currently working on 
developing a monitoring application that shows network 


monitoring information between the client and server and 
the client and other available servers or peer to peer (P2P) 
nodes.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
This application will provide data for some of the 
new features such as bandwidth utilization and data transfer 
rates.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Also, it will serve as a utility application by which 
users and network administrators can monitor network 
performance on their mobile handhelds.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
A self-organizing neural network (SONN [22]) can be 
introduced to learn usage and load patterns and thus 
schedule jobs more efficiently.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Another feature that is 
planned to be added is the ability to keep a catalogue of all 
files available in all the servers on the network, thereby 
allowing users to discover any dataset they require without 
prior knowledge of the server holding that dataset.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
One 
major advantage would be the ability to get job outputs back 
as soon as they are produced rather than having to retrieve 
them when the entire job is complete.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
This would be a major 
advance towards more interactivity.
title: Mobile Computing in Physics Analysis - An Indicator for eScience

text:
Further work on the 
handheld client side includes the extension of the analysis 
environment to run on PocketPC Phone Edition devices and 
to be able to use fast cellular networks such as GPRS, for 
data communication with the remote data servers, over the 
Internet.

Solving the Hamiltonian path problem with a
light-based computer
Mihai Oltean
Department of Computer Science,
Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science,
Babe¸s-Bolyai University, Kog˘alniceanu 1,
Cluj-Napoca, 400084, Romania.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
moltean@cs.ubbcluj.ro
www.cs.ubbcluj.ro/∼moltean
Abstract.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In this paper we suggest the use of light for performing use-
ful computations.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Namely, we propose a special computational device
which uses light rays for solving the Hamiltonian path problem on a di-
rected graph.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The device has a graph-like representation and the light
is traversing it by following the routes given by the connections between
nodes.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In each node the rays are uniquely marked so that they can be
easily identiﬁed.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
At the destination node we will search only for particu-
lar rays that have passed only once through each node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We show that the
proposed device can solve small and medium instances of the problem in
reasonable time.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
1
Introduction
Using light, instead of electric power, for performing computations is an exciting
idea whose applications can be already seen on the market.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This choice is mo-
tivated by the increasing number of real-world problems where the light-based
devices could perform better than electric-based counterparts.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Good examples
in this direction can be found in the ﬁeld of Optical Character Recognition [30].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Another interesting example is the n-point discrete Fourier transform which can
be performed in unit time by special light-based devices [12, 24].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In this paper we suggest a new way of performing computations by using
some properties of light.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The idea is used within a special device for solving the
Hamiltonian path problem.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The device, which is very simple, has a graph-like
structure.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In each node there are optical cables which are used to mark (delay)
the light which is passing through them.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Also, there are optical cables which
connect the nodes.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In each node the ray is
delayed by a certain amount of time and then is divided into several small rays
which are sent to the outgoing links.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
At the destination node we will search for a
particular ray which has passed exactly once through each node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This operation
can be done easily due to the special properties of the system which delays the
rays passing through a node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
2
The paper is organized as follows: Related work in the ﬁeld of optical comput-
ing is brieﬂy overviewed in section 2.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The Hamiltonian path problem is described
in section 3.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: The proposed device is presented in section 4.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Mathematical back-
ground of the labeling system is described in sections 4.2 - 4.5.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This part of the
paper shows how the rays can be marked so that we can easily distinguish them.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: The way in which the proposed device works is given in section 4.6.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
A list of
components required by the proposed device is given in section 4.7.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Suggestions for improving the device are given in
sections 4.11 and 4.12.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: Further work directions are suggested in section 5.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
2
Related work
Most of the major computational devices today are using electric power in order
to perform useful computations.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: Another idea is to use light instead of electrical power.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
It is hoped that optical
computing could advance computer architecture and can improve the speed of
data input and output by several orders of magnitude [9].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Many theoretical and practical light-based devices have been proposed for
dealing with various problems.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Optical computation has some advantages, one of
them being the fact that it can perform some operations faster than conventional
devices.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
An example is the n-point discrete Fourier transform computation which
can be performed in only unit time [12, 24].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: The quest for the light-based computers was started in 1929 by G.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Tauschek
who has obtained a patent on Optical Character Recognition (OCR) in Ger-
many, Next step was made by Handel who obtained a patent on OCR in USA
in 1933 (U.S.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Those devices were mechanical and used tem-
plates for matching the characters.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
A photodetector was placed so that when the
template and the character to be recognized were lined up for an exact match,
and a light was directed towards it, no light would reach the photodetector.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Since then, the ﬁeld of OCR has grown steadily and recently has become an um-
brella for multiple pattern recognition techniques (including Digital Character
Recognition).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
An important practical step was made by Intel researchers (see Figure 1)
who have developed the ﬁrst continuous wave all-silicon laser using a physical
property called the Raman Eﬀect [8, 23,25, 26].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The device could lead to such
practical applications as optical ampliﬁers, lasers, wavelength converters, and
new kinds of lossless optical devices.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Another solution comes from Lenslet [17] which has created a very fast pro-
cessor for vector-matrix multiplications (see Figure 2).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This processor can per-
form up to 8000 Giga Multiple-Accumulate instructions per second.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Lenslet tech-
nology has already been applied to data analysis using k−mean algorithm [19]
and video compression.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
A recent paper [27] introduces the idea of sorting by using some properties
of light.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The method called Rainbow Sort is based on the physical concepts
of refraction and dispersion.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
It is inspired by the observation that light that

traverses a prism is sorted by wavelength (see Figure 3).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
For implementing the
Rainbow Sort one need to perform the following steps:
– encode multiple wavelengths (representing the numbers to be sorted) into a
light ray,
– send the ray through a prism which will split the ray into n monochromatic
rays that are sorted by wavelength,
– read the output by using a special detector that receives the incoming rays.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: A stable version of the Rainbow Sort is proposed in [20].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Naughton (et al.) proposed and investigated [21, 28] a model called the con-
tinuous space machine which operates in discrete time-steps over a number of
two-dimensional complex-valued images of constant size and arbitrary spatial
resolution.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The (constant time) operations on images include Fourier transfor-
mation, multiplication, addition, thresholding, copying and scaling.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
There are also other devices which are taking into account the quantum
properties of light.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This idea has been used for solving the Traveling Salesman
Problem [5, 13] using a special purpose device.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
3
The Hamiltonian path problem
The description of the Hamiltonian Path problem (HPP) for a directed graph is
the following:
Given a directed graph G = (V, E) with |V | = n nodes and a start node
(vstart) and a stop node (vstop), the problem asks to compute is there is a simple
path, beginning with node vstart and ending with node vstop, containing all
nodes exactly once.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The output for this decision problem is either YES or NO
depending on whether the Hamiltonian path does exist or not.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
5
The Hamiltonian path problem arises in many real-word applications [3, 7].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: The problem belongs to the class of NP-complete problems [11].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
No polyno-
mial time algorithm is known for it.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
A small instance of this problem was also the ﬁrst problem solved using a
DNA computer [1].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4
The proposed device
Our idea is based on two properties of light:
– The speed of light has a limit.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The value of the limit is not very important
at this stage of explanation.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The speed will become important when we will
compute the size of the graphs that can be solved by our device (see section
4.9).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
What is important now is the fact that we can delay the ray by forcing
it to pass through an optical ﬁber cable of a certain length.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
– The ray can be easily divided into multiple rays of smaller intensity/power
by using some beam-splitters.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: Initially a light ray is sent to the start node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Generally speaking two opera-
tions must be performed when a ray passes through a node:
– The light ray is marked uniquely so that we know that it has passed through
that node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
– The ray is divided into a number of rays equal to the external degree of that
node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Each obtained ray is directed toward one of the nodes connected to
the current node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
At the destination node we will search only for particular rays that have
passed only once through each node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: This section deeply describes the proposed system.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
First step is to ﬁnd a way
to mark the signals which passes through nodes such that the interesting signals
can be easily identiﬁed at the destination node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The mathematical background
required for this operation is described in sections 4.1 - 4.5 and the physical
implementation of the labeling system is described in section 4.7.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.1
Labeling system
At the destination node we will wait for a particular ray which has passed
through all nodes of the graph exactly once.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This is why we need to ﬁnd a
way to label that particular ray so that it could be easily identiﬁed.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Actually we are interested in marking all rays which pass through a particular
node with a unique label, such that Hamiltonian path is uniquely identiﬁed at
the destination node (vstop).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In the solution proposed in this paper, the rays passing through a node are
marked by delaying them with a certain amount of time.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This delay can be easily
obtained by forcing the rays to pass through an optical ﬁber of a certain length.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
6
Roughly speaking, we will know if a certain ray has traversed a Hamiltonian path
only if its delay (at the destination node) is equal to the sum of delays of all
nodes in that graph.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We will also know the particular moment when the expected
ray (the one which has completed a Hamiltonian path) will arrive.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In this case
the only thing that we have to do is to ”listen” if there is a ﬂuctuation in the
intensity of the signal at that particular moment.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Due to the special properties
of the proposed system we know that no other ray will arrive, at the destination
node, at the moment when the Hamiltonian path ray has arrived.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: The delays, which are introduced by each node, cannot take any values.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
If
we would put random values for delays we might have diﬀerent rays (which are
not Hamiltonian paths) arriving, at the destination node, in the same time with
a ray representing a Hamiltonian path.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We need only the ray, which has traversed a Hamiltonian path, to arrive in
the destination node at the moment equal to the sum of delays of each node (the
moment when the ray has entered in the start node is considered moment 0).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Thus, the delaying system must have the following property:
Property of the delaying system
Let us denote by d1, d2, ..., dn the delays introduced by each node of the
graph.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
A correct set of values for this system must satisfy the condition:
d1 + d2 + ...
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
+ an · dn,
where ai (1 ≤i ≤n) are natural numbers (ai ≥0) and cannot be all 1 in the
same time.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Basicaly speaking ak tell us how many times the ray has passed through node
k.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Thus, if value ak is strictly greater than 1 it means that the ray has passed
at least twice through node k.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: Finding the appropriate labeling system was a three-step process.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
First of all
we have written a computer program which generates this numbers by using a
backtracking procedure [6].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Then we have extracted a general formula and we
have proved its correctness.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.2
Backtracking procedure
We also wanted to generate numbers such that the highest number in a system
is the smallest possible.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This will ensure that the network is constructed in an
eﬃcient way.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The labeling systems generated by our computer programs are
given in Table 1.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.3
Extracting the general formula
From Table 1 it can be easily seen that these numbers follow a general rule.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
For
a graph with n nodes one of the possible labeling systems is:
2n −2n−1,
2n −2n−2,


7

title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: The labeling system generated by our backtracking procedure.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
First column
contains the number of nodes of the graph.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The second column represents the labels
