title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Remarks
– The numbers in this set are also called Nialpdromes (sequence A023758
from The On-line Encyplopedia of Integer Numbers [29]).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
They are numbers
whose digits in base 2 are in nonincreasing order.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
– These numbers have been used in [16] for solving NP-complete problems in
the context of DNA computers [1],
– The delaying system described above has the advantage of being a general
one, but it also has a weakness: it is exponential.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.4
Proving the correctness
We have to prove that the property of delaying system (see section 4.1) holds
for this sequence of numbers.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Actually we have to prove that the equality:
2n −2n−1 + 2n −2n−2 + 2n −2n−3 + ...
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
+ an · (2n −20)
(1)
(where ai ≥0) is not possible unless all ai are equal to 1.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The left part of the equality is:
2n −2n−1 + 2n −2n−2 + 2n −2n−3 + ...
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
First of all we have to see that the equality does not hold if all ai numbers
are at least 1 and at least one number is strictly greater than 1.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
If this happens
the 2n term will be represented at least n times.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
But, it must be represented
only n −1 times (see above).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Thus, if at least one number ai is strictly greater than 1, it means that other
numbers aj must be 0.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We will prove that the equality (1) does not hold in this
case too.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
As discussed above, if one of the coeﬃcients is 0, at least one of the other
coeﬃcients must be strictly greater than 1.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
For instance, if a1 is set to 0, it
means that a2 must be set to 3 in order to compensate the missing 2n−1 term.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: This is a direct consequence of the fact that 2n−1 = 2 · 2n−2.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Of course, we also
have to take into account that 2n−2 must be represented once.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This is why we
have to set a2 to value 3.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
If a2 is also 0 we have to set a3 to value 7 (we need 4 · 2n−3 in order to
compensate the missing term 2n−1, we also need 2 · 2n−3 to compensate the
missing term 2n−2 and, of course, the term 2n−3 must be represented 1 time).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
As a general idea: if a particular term (2n−j) is missing (the corresponding
coeﬃcient aj is set to 0), it can be compensate by setting one of the next coef-
ﬁcients to a value of at least 3.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
But, a coeﬃcient set to 0 means that the term
2n is missing once, and by setting another coeﬃcient to at least 3 we will get
at least 2 extra representations for 2n.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This will mean that right part of the
equation (1) will be at least (n + 1) · 2n + 1.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
But, the left part of the equation is
only (n −1) · 2n + 1.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
With this we have shown that all ai(1 ≤i ≤n) must be 1 in order to have
equality in equation (1).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
For any other values of ai the equality (1) does not
hold.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.5
Proving the minimality
An important question is whether this system is the minimal possible (the
greatest number is the minimal possible).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We prove this by showing a counter-
example.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Let us suppose that there is another delaying system which is smaller than
the one described in section 4.3.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This means that the largest delay is smaller
than 2n −20.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We are not interested in the other (n −1) delays because the
largest one imposes the largest length for the cables.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: In this case the delaying system is {2, 3}.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: We will show that the largest delay cannot be smaller than 3.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
If it is smaller it should be 2 or 1 (actually it cannot be 1 because, in this
case, the other delay should be 0 and we do not allow this delay in our system).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: If the delay is 2 it means that the delay for the other node is 1.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The sum of the
delays is 3 which can be simply obtained by visiting 3 times the node with delay
1.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: This is in conﬂict with the property of the delaying system (see section 4.1).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
9
With this we have proved that the largest delay cannot be smaller than
2n −20.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.6
How the system works
An schematic example of a graph-like system is given in Figure 4.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: In the graph depicted in Figure 4 the light will enter in node 0.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
It will be
delayed with a certain amount of time and then it will be divided into 3 rays
which will be sent to nodes 1, 3 and 6.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In node 1 the ray will be delayed (with
the amount of time corresponding to node 1) and then it will be sent to nodes
2 and 3.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
One of the rays will be able to generate and Hamiltonian path (0, 1, 2,
3, 4, 5, 6).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: Note that there are also several cycles in the graph: 1, 3, 4 or 1, 2 or 2, 3.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: The cycles will make that some particular rays to be trapped within the system.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The rays which have passed once through the previously described cycle are not
considered Hamiltonian paths because the moments when they arrive, at the
destination node, are diﬀerent from the sum of delays introduced by each node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Because we are working with continuous signal we cannot expect to have dis-
crete output at the destination node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This means that rays arrival is notiﬁed by
ﬂuctuations in the intensity of the light.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
These ﬂuctuations will be transformed,
by the photodiode, in ﬂuctuations of the electric power which will be easily read
by the oscilloscope.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.7
Physical implementation of the labeling system
For implementing the proposed device we need the following components:
– a source of light (laser),
– Several beam-splitters for dividing light rays into multiple subrays.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
A stan-
dard beam-splitter is designed using a half-silvered mirror.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
For dividing a
ray into k subrays we need k −1 beam-splitters.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
An example on how to split
a ray in more than 2 subrays is given in Figure 5,
– A high speed photodiode for converting light rays into electrical power.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The
photodiode is placed in the destination node,
– A tool for detecting ﬂuctuations in the intensity of electric power generated
by the photodiode (oscilloscope),
– A set of optical ﬁber cables having certain lengths.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
These cables are used for
connecting nodes and for delaying the signals within nodes.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The length of
the cables must obey the rules described in section 4.1.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
A practical example
on how to compute their length is given in section 4.9.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.8
Complexity
This section answers a very important question: Why the proposed approach is
not a polynomial-time solution for the HPP?
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: A schematic representation of the proposed device.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: Start node is 0 and the destination node is 6.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In each
node the rays are delayed with a certain amount of time.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
At the destination node we
will have a photodiode and an oscilloscope.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
When a ray will arrive in the destination
node there will be a ﬂuctuation, in the light intensity, which could be measured by the
oscilloscope.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: The way in which a ray can be split into 3 sub-rays by using 2 beam-splitters.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
At the ﬁrst sight one may be tempted to say that the proposed approach
provides a solution in polynomial time to any instance of the HPP.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The reason
behind such claim is given by the ability of the proposed device to provide
output to any instance by traversing only once all nodes (O(n) complexity).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: This could mean that we have found a polynomial-time algorithm for the HPP.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
A direct consequence is obtaining solutions, in polynomial time, for all other
NP-Complete problems - since there is a polynomial reduction between them
[11].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
As can be seen from Table 1 the delay time
increases exponentially with the number of nodes.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Even if the ray has to traverse
only n nodes (resulting a complexity of O(n)), the total time required by the ray
to reach the destination node increases exponentially with the number of nodes.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
There are two direct consequences which are derived from here:
– The length of the optical ﬁbers, used for delaying the signals, increases ex-
ponentially with the number of nodes,
– The intensity of the signal decreases exponentially with the number of nodes
that are traversed.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: These two issues are discussed in sections 4.9 and 4.10.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.9
Problem size
We are interested in computing the size of the cables required to solve a certain
instance of the problem in a small amount of time.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This will give as a rough


12
indication on the size of the graphs that can be solved using our system in
reasonable time.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This size heavily depends on the accuracy of the measurement tools (response
time of the photodiode and the rise time of the oscilloscope).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The rise-time of the best oscilloscope available on the market is in the range
of picoseconds (10−12 seconds).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This means that we should not have two signals
that arrive at 2 consecutive moments at a diﬀerence smaller than 10−12 seconds.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Knowing that the speed of light is 3 · 108m/s we can easily compute the
minimal cable length that should be traversed by the ray in order to be delayed
with 10−12 seconds.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This value is the minimal delay that should be introduced by a node in order
to ensure that the diﬀerence between the moments when two consecutive signals
arrive at the destination node is greater or equal to the measurable unit of 10−12
seconds.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This will also ensure that we will be able to correctly identify whether
the signal has arrived in the destination node at a moment equal to the sum of
delays introduced by each node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
No other signals will arrive within a range of
10−12 seconds around that particular moment.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Once we have the length for that minimal delay is quite easy to compute the
length of the other cables that are used in order to induce a certain delay.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Recall from section 4.1, Table 1 that a graph with 5 nodes has the following
delaying system:
16, 24, 28, 30, 31.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
From the previous reasoning line we have deduced that the smaller indivisible
unit is 0.0003.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: So, we have to multiply these numbers by 0.0003.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
These numbers represent the length of the cables that must be used in graph’s
nodes in order to induce a certain delay.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Note that the delay introduced by the cables connecting the nodes was not
taken into account in this example.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The
cables connecting nodes can be set to have some length which must obey the
property of delaying system (see section 4.1).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Note that all cables must have the
same length.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In this case if we have a graph with 4 nodes the length of every
cable connecting the nodes must be set to 16 units (the shortest possible - in
order to reduce the costs).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The length of cables within the nodes should be 24,
28, 30 and 31 units.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: The largest length in this sequence is 0.00093 meters.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This length is not very
big, but for larger graphs the length of the cables within nodes can be a problem.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Once we have the length for that minimal delay is quite easy to compute the
maximal number of nodes that a graph can have in order to ﬁnd the Hamiltonian
path in one second.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We know the facts:
– the largest delay has the form 2n −1 (see equation 1),


13
– the distance traversed by light in 1 second is 3 · 108 meters,
– the shortest delay possible is 0.0003 meters.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We simply have to solve the equation:
2n · 0.0003 = 3 · 108
(2)
This number is about 40 nodes.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
However, the length of the optic ﬁbers used
for inducing the largest delay for this graph is huge: about 8 · 108 meters.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We
cannot expect to have such long cables for our experiments.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
However, shorter cables (of several hundreds of kilometers) are already avail-
able in the internet networks.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Assuming
that the longest cable that we have is about 300 kilometers we may solve in-
stances with about 26 nodes.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The amount of time required to obtain a solution
is about 10−6 seconds.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Note that the maximal number of nodes can be increased when the precision
of our measurement instruments (oscilloscope and photodiode) is increased.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: Also note that this diﬃculty is not speciﬁc to our system only.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Other major
unconventional computation paradigms, trying to solve NP-complete problems
share the same fate.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
For instance, a quantity of DNA equal to the mass of Earth
is required to solve HPP instances of 200 cities using DNA computers [14].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.10
Amplifying the signal
Beam splitters are used in our approach for dividing a ray in two or more subrays.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: Because of that, the intensity of the signal is decreasing.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In the worst case we
have an exponential decrease of the intensity.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
For instance, in a graph with n
nodes, each signal is divided (within each node) into n −1 signals.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Roughly
speaking, the intensity of the signal will decrease nn times.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This means that, at the destination node, we have to be able to detect very
small ﬂuctuations in the intensity of the signal.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
For this purpose we will use
a photomultiplier [10] which is an extremely sensitive detector of light in the
ultraviolet, visible and near infrared range.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This detector multiplies the signal
produced by incident light by as much as 108, from which even single photons
can be detected.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.11
Improving the device by reducing the speed of the signal
The speed of the light in optic ﬁbers is an important parameter in our device.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: The problem is that the light is too fast for our measurement tools.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We have
either to increase the precision of our measurement tools or to decrease the speed
of light.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
It is known that the speed of light traversing a cable is signiﬁcantly smaller
than the speed of light in the void space.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Commercially available cables have
limit the speed of the ray wave up to 60% from the original speed of light.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This
means that we can obtain the same delay by using a shorter cable.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
14
However, this method for reducing the speed of light is not enough for our
purpose.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: The order of magnitude is still the same.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This is why we have the
search for other methods for reducing that speed.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
A very interesting solution
was proposed in [15] which is able to reduce the speed of light by 7 orders of
magnitude and even to stop it [4, 18].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In [4] they succeeded in completely halting
light by directing it into a mass of hot rubidium gas, the atoms of which, behaved
like tiny mirrors, due to an interference pattern in two control beams.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: This could help our mechanism signiﬁcantly.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
However, how to use this idea for
our device is still an open question because of the complex equipment involved
in those experiments [15, 18].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
By reducing the speed of light by 7 orders of magnitude we can reduce the
size of the involved cables by a similar order (assuming that the precision of the
measurement tools is still the same).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This will help us to solve larger instances
of the problem.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.12
Improving the performance of the device for particular graphs
The labeling system proposed in section 4.1 is a general one.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
It can be used
for any kind of graph (with any number of nodes and arcs).
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We have shown
that this system has a big problem: the value of the involved numbers increase
exponentially with the number of nodes in the graph being solved.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
But, for particular graphs we can ﬁnd other labeling systems which are not
exponential.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
For example, the linear graph (see Figure 6 can be solved by our
device by using virtually no delays.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
In this case the moment when the signal
arrives in the destination node is equal to sum of delays introduced by the
cables connecting the nodes.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
No delays are required for the nodes of this graph
in order to ﬁnd a Hamiltonian path
Finding the optimal labeling system for a particular graph is an interesting
problem which will be investigated in the near future.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
4.13
Technical challenges
There are many technical challenges that must be solved when implementing the
proposed device.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Some of them are:


15
– Cutting the optic ﬁbers to an exact length with high precision.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Failing to
accomplish this task can lead to errors in detecting a ray which has passed
through each node once.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This is an essential step for solving
larger instances of the problem (see section 4.9),
– Finding cables long enough so that larger instances of the problem could
be solve.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This problem might have a simple solution: the internet networks
connecting the world cities.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
It is easy to ﬁnd cables of hundreds of kilometers
connecting distant cities.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This will help us to solve instance of more than
10 nodes.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
However, this solution introduces a diﬃculty too: cables of certain
lengths must be found or the system must be rescaled in order to ﬁt the
existing lengths.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
5
Conclusions and further work
The way in which light can be used for performing useful computations has been
suggested in this paper.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The techniques are based on the massive parallelism of
the light ray.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
It has been shown the way in which a light-based device can be used for
solving the Hamiltonian path problem.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Using the today technology we can build
a light-based device which can solve small and medium size instances in several
seconds.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Further work directions will be focused on:
– Implementing the proposed device,
– Finding optimal labeling systems for particular graphs.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This will reduce the
length of the involved cables signiﬁcantly,
– Our device cannot ﬁnd the Hamiltonian path.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
It can only say if this path ex-
ists or not.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text: If there are multiple paths we cannot distinguish them.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
However,
the HPP YES/NO decision problem is still a NP-complete problem [11].
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
We
are currently investigating a way to store the order of nodes so that we can
easily reconstruct the path,
– Finding other non-trivial problems which can be solved by using the pro-
posed device,
– Finding other ways to introduce delays in the system.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The current solution
requires cables that are too long and too expensive,
– Using other type of signals instead of light.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
Possible candidates are electric
power and sound,
– Finding other ways to implement the system of marking the signals which
pass through a particular node.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
This will be very useful because the cur-
rently suggested system, based on delays, is too time consuming.
title: arXiv:0708.1512v1  [cs.AR]  10 Aug 2007

text:
The other
properties of light can be used for this purpose: amplitude, wavelength, etc.

Computational performance of a parallelized
high-order spectral and mortar element
toolbox
Roland Bouﬀanais a,∗,1, Vincent Keller a, Ralf Gruber a,
Michel O.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

Deville a
aLaboratory of Computational Engineering,
´Ecole Polytechnique F´ed´erale de Lausanne,
STI – ISE – LIN, Station 9,
CH–1015 Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract
In this paper, a comprehensive performance review of a MPI-based high-order spec-
tral and mortar element method C++ toolbox is presented.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The focus is put on the
performance evaluation of several aspects with a particular emphasis on the paral-
lel eﬃciency.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The performance evaluation is analyzed and compared to predictions
given by a heuristic model, the so-called Γ model.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
A tailor-made CFD computation
benchmark case is introduced and used to carry out this review, stressing the par-
ticular interest for commodity clusters.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Conclusions are drawn from this extensive
series of analyses and modeling leading to speciﬁc recommendations concerning such
toolbox development and parallel implementation.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Key words: Spectral and mortar element method, C++ toolbox, MPI, scalability,
commodity clusters.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
1
Introduction
This paper provides a detailed performance evaluation of the C++ toolbox
named Speculoos (for Spectral Unstructured Elements Object-Oriented System).
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Email addresses: roland.bouffanais@epfl.ch (Roland Bouﬀanais),
vincent.keller@epfl.ch (Vincent Keller), ralf.gruber@epfl.ch (Ralf
Gruber), michel.deville@epfl.ch (Michel O.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text: 1 Supported by a Swiss National Science Foundation Grant No.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
200020–101707
Preprint submitted to Parallel Computing
25 October 2018


Speculoos is a spectral and mortar element analysis toolbox for the numer-
ical solution of partial diﬀerential equations and more particularly for solv-
ing incompressible unsteady ﬂuid ﬂow problems [1].
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The main architecture
choices and the parallel implementation were elaborated and implemented by
Van Kemenade and Dubois-P`elerin [2,3].
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Subsequently, Speculoos’ C++ code
has been growing up with additional layers enabling to tackle and simulate
more speciﬁc and arduous CFD problems: viscoelastic ﬂows by Fi´etier and
Deville [4–6], ﬂuid-structure interaction problems by Bodard and Deville [7],
large-eddy simulations of conﬁned turbulent ﬂows by Bouﬀanais et al.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
[8, 9]
and free-surface ﬂows by Bouﬀanais and Deville [10].
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
It is well known that spectral element methods are amenable easily to paral-
lelization as they are intrinsically a natural way of decomposing a geometrical
domain [11] and Chap.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The numerous references previously given and the ongoing simulations based
on Speculoos highlight the achieved versatility and ﬂexibility of this C++ tool-
box.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Nevertheless, ten years have passed between the ﬁrst version of Specu-
loos’ code and now, and tremendous changes have occurred at both hard-
ware and software levels: fast dual DDR memory, RISC architectures, 64-bit
memory addressing, compilers improvement, libraries optimization, libraries
parallelization, increase in inter-connecting switch performance, etc.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Back in 1995, Speculoos was commonly compiled and was running on HP, Sil-
icon Graphics workstations and also on the Swiss-Tx machine, a commodity-
technology based computer with enhanced interconnect link between proces-
sors [13].
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Currently most of the simulations based on Speculoos are compiled
and are running on commodity clusters.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The workstation world experienced
a technical revolution with the advent of ‘cheap’ RISC processors leading to
the ongoing impressive development of parallel architectures such as massively
parallel clusters and commodity clusters.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
As a matter of fact, Speculoos bene-
ﬁted from this fast technical evolution as it was originally developed as to run
in a single program, multiple data mode (SPMD) on a distributed-memory
computer.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The performance evaluations presented here are demonstrating the
correlation between the good performances measured with Speculoos and the
adequation of this code structure with the current hardware and software
evolutions in parallel computing.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
In Section 2 we introduce the numerical
context in which Speculoos was initiated, the software aspects related to its
implementation and the variable-size benchmark test case used for the perfor-
mance evaluation presented in the subsequent sections.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Section 3 is devoted to
the parallel performance analysis achieved on RISC-based commodity clusters.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text: Finally, in Section 4 we draw some conclusions on the results obtained.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
2


2
Speculoos numerical and software context
In this section, is gathered the necessary background information regarding the
numerical method—namely the spectral and mortar element method—, the
object-oriented concept and the parallel paradigm, essential roots embodied
in Speculoos.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The ﬁnal Section 2.3 introduces the simulation used throughout
this study as benchmark evaluation test case.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
2.1
Spectral and mortar element method
The spectral element method (SEM) is a high-order spatial discretization
method for the approximate Galerkin solution of partial diﬀerential equations
expressed in weak forms.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The SEM relies on expansions on Lagrangian inter-
polants bases used in conjunction with particular Gauss–Lobatto and Gauss–
Lobatto–Jacobi quadrature rules [14, 15].
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
As high-order ﬁnite element tech-
niques, the SEM can deal with arbitrary complex geometry where h-reﬁnement
is achieved by increasing the number of spectral elements and p-reﬁnement
by increasing the Lagrangian polynomial order within the elements.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
From a
high-order precision viewpoint, SEM is comparable to spectral methods as an
exponential rate-of-convergence is observed when smooth solutions to regular
problems are sought.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
C0-continuity across element interfaces requires the exact same interpolation
in each and every spectral element sharing a common interface.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The associ-
ated caveat to such conforming conﬁgurations is the over-reﬁnement meshing
generated in low-gradient zones.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The adopted remedy to such nuisance is a
technique developed by Bernardi et al.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
[16] referred to as the mortar ele-
ment method.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Mortars can be viewed as variational patches of the discontinu-
ous ﬁeld along the element interfaces.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
They relax the C0-continuity condition
while preserving exponential rate-of-convergence, and thus allow polynomial
nonconformities along element interfaces.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
2.2
Parallel implementation
The complexity and the size of the large three-dimensional problems tackled
by numericists in their simulations require top computational performance ac-
cessible from highly parallelized algorithms running on parallel architectures.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
As mentioned in [2], the implementation of concurrency in Speculoos was
based on the concept that concurrency is a painful implementation constraint
going against the high-level object-oriented programming concepts.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
As a mat-
ter of consequence, Speculoos parallelization was kept very low-level.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
In most
3

text:
From a computational viewpoint, systems discretized with a high-order spec-
tral element method rely mainly on optimized tensor-product operations tak-
ing place at the spectral element level.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The natural data distribution for high-
order spectral element methods is based on an elemental decomposition in
which the spectral elements are distributed to the processors available for the
run.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
It is worth noting that for very large computations, the number of spec-
tral elements can become relatively important as compared to the number of
processors available for the computation.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The design of Speculoos makes it
possible to have several elements sitting on a single processor.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Nodal values
on subdomain interface boundaries are stored redundantly on each proces-
sor corresponding to the spectral elements having this interface in common.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Moreover, this approach is consistent with the element-based storage scheme
which minimizes the inter-processor communications.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Inter-processor commu-
nication is completed by MPI instructions [17].
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
2.3
Benchmark evaluation test case description
As a common practice in performance evaluation, it is important to build
a tailor-made benchmark based on a numerical simulation corresponding to
a concrete situation.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Before proceeding to the ﬁrst step of our performance
evaluation, we have short-listed some key parameters that have the most sig-
niﬁcant impact on the performance of our toolbox: single-processor optimiza-
tion on the three computer architectures described in Table 1, single-processor
proﬁling analysis, parallel implementation and scalability (including speedup,
eﬃciency, communication times) and parallel implementation and processor
dispatching.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
A test case has been developed for this benchmark and for the parallel bench-
marking, see Sec.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
This test case belongs to the ﬁeld of CFD and consists
in solving the Navier–Stokes equations for a viscous Newtonian incompress-
ible ﬂuid.

Considering particular ﬂows, the governing Navier–Stokes equations (1)–(2)
are supplemented with appropriate boundary conditions for the ﬂuid velocity
u and/or for the local stress at the boundary.

For time-dependent problems,
a given divergence-free velocity ﬁeld is required as initial condition in the
internal ﬂuid domain.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
All our computations were carried out using two time integrators: the implicit
backward-diﬀerentiation formula (BDF) of order 2 for the treatment of the
Stokes operator and an extrapolation scheme (EX) [18,19] of same order for the
nonlinear convective term.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
One type of pressure decomposition mode, based
on a fractional-step method using pressure correction namely BP1-PC [20–22]
is used.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Speculoos uses a Legendre SEM [12, 14, 15] for the spatial discretization of
the Navier–Stokes equations.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
For the sake of simplicity the same polynomial
order has been chosen in the diﬀerent spatial directions (Nx = Ny = Nz = N).
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Moreover, to prevent any spurious oscillations in our Navier–Stokes compu-
tations, the choice of a staggered PN −PN−2 interpolation method for the
velocity and pressure respectively, has been made [12, 23].
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
As a consequence
of this choice of a staggered grid, the inner-element grid for the x-, y- and
z-component of the velocity ﬁeld is a Gauss–Lobatto–Legendre grid made up
with (N + 1)2 quadrature (nodal) points and the grid for the pressure is a
Gauss–Legendre grid made up with [(N −2) + 1]2 quadrature (nodal) points,
in each spectral element.

Conclusions
The extensive performance review presented in this paper for the high-order
spectral and mortar element method C++ toolbox, Speculoos, has shown that
13


good performances can be achieved even with relatively common internode
network communication systems, available software and hardware resources—
small commodity clusters with non-proprietary compilers installed on it.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
We can conclude that the main implementation choices made a decade ago re-
veal their promises.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Even though those choices could have been questionable
ten years ago, they are now in line with the current trend in computer ar-
chitecture developments with the generalization of commodity and massively
parallel clusters.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The parallel implementation of Speculoos based on MPI has shown to be
eﬃcient.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Reasonable scalability and eﬃciency can be achieved on commodity
clusters.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The results support the original choices made in Speculoos parallel
implementation by keeping it at a very low-level.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
One of the goal of this study was to estimate if Speculoos could run on a mas-
sively parallel computer architecture comprising thousands of computational
units, speciﬁcally on the IBM Blue Gene machine at EPFL with 4’096 dual
processor units.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The performance of one processor corresponds to approxi-
mately half of the performance of one processor on the Pleiades commodity
cluster.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text: Each Blue Gene node has 512 MB of main memory.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
A block with
4 × 4 × 4 elements and a polynomial degree of N = 8 in each space direction
takes 200 MB of main memory.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
In a ﬁrst step, one block per node will run on
one node.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Later, Speculoos will be modiﬁed to accommodate one block per
processor, i.e.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
A 4’096 blocks Speculoos case would oﬀer
the opportunity to run very accurate simulations of turbulent ﬂows with more
than half a billion of unknowns.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
Such a case would well scale on the IBM Blue
Gene solution.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
In fact, the point-to-point operations per node do not change
with the number of nodes.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The Gigabit-Ethernet network can well handle
the corresponding communications.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
The all-reduce operations scale logarith-
mically with the number of computational units.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
A special eﬃcient Fat Tree
network takes care of all multicast communications.
title: arXiv:0709.1024v1  [cs.DC]  7 Sep 2007

text:
As a consequence, large
Speculoos cases will perfectly scale on EPFL’s Blue Gene machine.

text:
JANUS: an FPGA-based System for High Performance Scientiﬁc
Computing
October 26, 2018
Abstract
This paper describes JANUS, a modular massively parallel and reconﬁgurable FPGA-based
computing system.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: Each JANUS module has a computational core and a host.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The computational
core is a 4x4 array of FPGA-based processing elements with nearest-neighbor data links.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Proces-
sors are also directly connected to an I/O node attached to the JANUS host, a conventional PC.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
JANUS is tailored for, but not limited to, the requirements of a class of hard scientiﬁc applications
characterized by regular code structure, unconventional data manipulation instructions and not too
large data-base size.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
We discuss the architecture of this conﬁgurable machine, and focus on its use
on Monte Carlo simulations of statistical mechanics.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
On this class of application JANUS achieves
impressive performances: in some cases one JANUS processing element outperfoms high-end PCs
by a factor ≃1000.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: We also discuss the role of JANUS on other classes of scientiﬁc applications.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
1
Overview
Several applications in computational physics, chemistry and biology are still far beyond the reach
of state-of-the-art computers, whenever following the evolution of even simple dynamics equations
responsible for very complex behavior requires inordinately long execution times.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
This is the case, for
instance, of Spin Glasses [3] (see later, for details): integration over conﬁguration space of a three-
dimensional lattice system of 503 sites, requiring up to 1013 Monte Carlo steps, is still an untreatable
task.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
One has to collect statistics for several copies of the system, say order 102, corresponding to about
1020 Monte Carlo spin updates (spins are the variables sitting at the lattice sites, see later).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: Extensive use of parallelism is the main avenue to boost computer performance.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The systems we are
interested in do have a very large degree of available parallelism.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Embarassingly parallel is the fact that
several copies of the system have to be simulated independently.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
State-of-the-art implementations on
traditional CPUs use this approach and reach average performances (usually measured in terms of the
spin update time) of ≃1 ns/spin when simulating > 100 copies at the same time, exploiting the SIMD
features available in many processors.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: The simulation program outlined above would take ≃104 years.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Even if we consider that simulations have to be performed for several values of the control parameters,
it is impossible to usefully deploy more than several dozens of CPU’s on one large-scale simulation.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
What is needed is to exploit the intrinsic parallelism of the simulation of each copy of the system to
shorten processing time.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
This problem is solved by the JANUS system, described in this paper, that exploits parallelism up
to the limits set by available hardware resources.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Each processor within JANUS is able to perform
the required 1013 Monte Carlo steps on one copy of the system in just several months, so the massive
system of 256 JANUS processors that we plan to deploy in spring 2008 makes the simulation program
outlined above possible in about one year time, a viable option on human timescales.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
JANUS is based on FPGAs for implementation simplicity and added ﬂexibility, so it is an example of
a reconﬁgurable architecture on which a high-performance application has been succesfully conﬁgured.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
It also turns out that JANUS, once its processing elements are conﬁgured for spin-glass simulations, has
several strong commonalities with many-core architectures (see e.g.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
[6]) that are clearly emerging as a
new trend in computer systems.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
So, JANUS can be seen by the physicist as a powerful simulation engine
and by the computer scientist as a succesful example of a massively many-core computing structure.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
This paper is structured as follows: in section 2, we review the computing needs of typical algorithms
of statistical mechanics simulations, deriving a set of architectural requirements.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
In section 3 we describe
the structure of the JANUS system, that we have architected trying to match in the most ﬂexible way
the requirements of section 2; in section 4 we describe the programming environment available to
1
arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008


the JANUS user, while section 5 describes the JANUS implementation of some class of spin-models,
showing aggressive exploitation of massive on-chip parallelism, enabled by high-bandwidth on-chip
memory structures.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: The paper ends with a short concluding section.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

parallelism, since E(si) for up to one half of all spins (arranged in a checkerboard scheme) can be
computed at the same time.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Up to one half of all operations implied by Listing 1 can be executed in
parallel, so all operations can be scheduled in two steps, if suﬃcient computing resources are available.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
This is also true when considering other Monte Carlo update scheme, as, for instance, in the Metropolis
algorithm.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Several other features of Listing 1 are shared by the applications we have in mind and are relevant
in this context:
• The code kernel has a regular structure, associated to regular loops.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
At each iteration the same
set of operations is performed on data stored at locations whose addresses can be predicted in
advance.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
• Data processing is associated to simple logical operations performed on bit-variables deﬁning the
spin variables, rather than on standard integer or ﬂoating-point arithmetics on long data words.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
• The data base associated to the computation is of the order of just a few bytes for each site (e.g.,
≃100 KBytes for a grid of 483 sites).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
We are interested in a parallel processing system able to deliver very high performance (order of
magnitudes more than possible with current PCs).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
This can be done if we are able to deploy a very
large fraction of the available parallelism available and to leverage on the other features discussed above.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: The structure has to be implemented using readily available technologies.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
From the architectural point
of view, our goal translates into two key features:
1.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
the processor must be conﬁgurable to perform exactly (and only) the subset of functions required
by the algorithm (and poorly supported by traditional architecture) so, for a given silicon budget,
the largest possible number of operations, exploiting the parallelism oﬀered by the algorithm, can
be performed.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
the performance made in principle possible by the previous point must be sustained by suﬃcient
memory bandwidth (as we will se later, in our target application we move from/to memory ≃4000
bits per clock cycle).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: This dictates the use of ﬁne grained on-chip memory structures.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
4


We make the choice of using latest generation FPGAs as the basic block of our system.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Their
reconﬁgurable structure matches point 1 above, and the availability of a large number of on-board
RAM blocks matches point 2.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: The system that we have deﬁned and built is described next.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
3
The JANUS architecture
JANUS builds on previous attempts made several years ago within the SUE project [8], with a much
wider application focus and much higher expected performances, made possible by a more ﬂexible design
and by recent progress in FPGA technology (for early ideas on JANUS, see [7]).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Figure 2: JANUS core: topology (left) and overview of the JANUS prototype implementation (right) with 16
SPs, the I/O module (IOP) and the JANUS host.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
3.1
Overall structure
JANUS is based on modules containing a computational core (the JANUS core) loosely connected to a
host system (the JANUS host) of one or more networked PCs (see Figure 2).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The JANUS core is based on:
• a 4 × 4 2-D grid of processing elements (each called SP) with nearest-neighbor links in both axis
(and periodic boundary conditions), making up the number-crunching kernel of the system;
• an IO-Processor (IOP) connected with all SPs and to the host.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: Both the SPs and the IOP are Xilinx Virtex4-LX200 FPGAs.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: Each SP processor contains uncommitted logic that can be conﬁgured at will by the IOP.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Once
conﬁgured, the SP is the main computational engine of the system.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Number crunching kernels are
allocated to one or more SPs.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
They run either as independent threads, ultimately reporting to the
JANUS host through the IOP or they run concurrently, sharing data, as appropriate, across the nearest-
neighbor links (in the current implementation each full-duplex link transfers four bytes per clock cycle
with negligible latency, i.e.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
A single task may execute on the complete core, or
up to 16 independent tasks may be allocated on the system.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
A major design decision has been that the
SPs have no memory apart from the one available on-chip (of the order of ≃0.5 MByte per processing
element).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: This choice constrains the class of problem that JANUS can handle.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
On the other hand, in
their quest for performance, applications can rely on the huge bandwidth and low latency made possible
by on-chip memory to feed all the cores conﬁgured onto the FPGA.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The IOP module controls the operation of all available SPs, merges and moves data to/from the
JANUS host on full-duplex IOP-SP point-to-point link transfering 2 bytes of data every clock cycle.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
A bank of staging memory is available, and the main communication channel uses 2 Gigabit-Ethernet
links (an USB port and a serial interface are available for debugging and test).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: The IOP FPGA is conﬁgured as a relatively stable control and I/O interface for the SPs.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
However
close to 70% of the available logical resources are left over, so more complex roles within large, multi-SP
applications are possible.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The IOP might act as a cross-bar switch for the array of SPs, supporting
complex patterns of data transfers or perform global operations on aggregated data sets.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
We also
plan to embed a standard microprocessor (e.g.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
MicroBlazeTM) in order to support more complex data
handling.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
In principle a slim Linux-like operating system might be supported, making the JANUS unit
an independent computer.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
5


Figure 3: A JANUS module (left) and the JANUS rack (right) with 16 JANUS modules and 8 JANUS hosts.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
3.2
IOP ﬁrmware
The current ﬁrmware conﬁguration of the Input/Output Processor (IOP) focuses on the implementation
of an interface between the SPs and the host.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The IOP is not a programmable processor with a standard
architecture: it basically allows streaming of data from the host to the appropriate destination (and
back), under the complete control of the JANUS host.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The IOP conﬁgured structure is naturally split in 2 segments:
• the IOlink block handles the I/O interfaces between IOP and the JANUS host (gigabit channels,
serial and USB ports).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Its supports the lower layers of the gigabit ethernet protocol, ensures data
integrity and provides a bandwidth close to the theoretical limit.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
• the multidev block contains a logical device associated to each hardware sub-system that may be
reached for control and/or data transfer: there is a memory interface for the staging memory, a
programming interface to conﬁgure the SPs, an SP interface to handle communication with the
SPs (after they are conﬁgured) and several service/debug interfaces.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The link between these two segments is the Stream Router that forwards the streams coming from
the IOlink to the appropriate device within the multidev according to a mask encoded in the stream.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: A block diagram of the IOP is shown in Figure 4.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Figure 4: Schematic logical representation of the IOP processor: on the left the IOlink that handles the I/O
interfaces between IOP and the JANUS host; on the right the devices of the multidev.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
As shown in Figure 4, the SP interface plays a special role in that it can be conﬁgured to perform
computing functions common to all the SPs involved in a given computational thread.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The IOP supports a low-level interface mechanism between the host computer and any conﬁgured
JANUS device ﬂexible enough to adapt to a conﬁgurable computer: basically the IOP handles so-called
6


data-worms: each worm is just a sequence of commands and data that is not interpreted by the IOP
but simply delivered to the conﬁgured device.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
3.3
System-level structure
The IOP and SP modules are engineered as small daughter-boards plugged onto a Processing Board
(PB).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: This implementation will allow to upgrade each component independently.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
We are already con-
sidering mid-term upgrades such as newer generation FPGAs for the SPs and more performing core-host
interfaces (using e.g.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Several JANUS modules can be grouped into a larger system: each core is packed in one standard
rack-mountable 19-inch box.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: Several cores and their associated hosts are placed in a standard rack.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
All
JANUS hosts are networked and connected to a supervisor host.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
End-users log onto the supervisor and
connect to one (or more) available JANUS modules.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
After a test period using prototype boards with Virtex4 LX160 FPGAs, we are at the moment testing
the ﬁrst complete JANUS system: 16 JANUS cores with 8 JANUS hosts assembled in a standard 19”
rack.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Three more JANUS cores with two JANUS hosts are also available for less compute-intensive
applications and for program development and test.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Pictures of a JANUS module and of the large
JANUS rack are shown in Figure 3.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: We plan to start physics simulations on these systems in spring 2008.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
4
Software Environment
Development of JANUS applications involves ﬁrmware design to conﬁgure the SPs, and the related host-
based software development.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Firmware development is performed by means of standard commercial
design tools, starting from HDL codes.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Handcrafting and optimizing a complex application for JANUS
is admittedly a complex and time consuming investment, justiﬁed in the statistical physics community
by huge rewards in term of performance.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
This trade-oﬀis not necessarily applicable in general; at this
stage, our project does not plans speciﬁc steps in the ﬁeld of making reconﬁgurable computing more
user friendly to the general users.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
We plan however to make available all the applications that will be
developed by the JANUS community in the form of a collection of tested ﬁrmware modules.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
We have developed a host-resident software environment able to cope with any SP-based ﬁrmware,
as long as the latter adheres to a model in which JANUS is a memory based coprocessing engine of
the host computer; user programs move their data onto the JANUS storage devices (FPGA embedded
memories), activates JANUS processing and, at the end of the computation, retrieve processed data.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
This model is supported by an host-resident execution and development environment that we call
JOS (JANUS Operating System).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
JOS runs on any Linux based PC and builds on a low-level C library,
based on standard Unix raw network sockets, implementing the protocol needed to communicate with
the IOP ﬁrmware on the Gbit ethernet link.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
For the application user, JOS consists of:
• A set of libraries with primitives to control IOP devices, written both in PERL and C (JOSlib)
• A multi-user environment for JANUS resource abstraction and concurrent jobs management
(josd)
• A set of SP ﬁrmwares for several scientiﬁc applications and the C libraries needed to control them
via the josd environment (jlib).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
josd is a background job running on the JANUS host, providing hardware abstraction and an easy
interface to user applications.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
It hides all details of the underlying structure of JANUS, mapping it to
the user as a simple grid of SPs.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
It interfaces to the user only via the Unix socket API, so high-level
applications may be written in virtually any language.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
For debugging and test, an interactive shell (JOSH), written in PERL and also based on (JOSlib)
oﬀers expert users complete access to all JANUS resources.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The JOSH interactive shell provides direct
access to JANUS resorces, allowing to communicate with the IOP and drive all its internal devices.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Whenever a new SP ﬁrmware is developed, new primitives to instruct the SP interface of the IOP are
added in JOSlib.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

Reconﬁguring JANUS for spin-system simulations
SP conﬁgurations for the simulation of three dimensional Ising spin models, deﬁned by a more general
version of Eq.

text:
1 (including the site-diluted case), as well as for the standard and glassy Potts model
Eq.

text: 3 have been already developed and tested and are discussed extensively in [11].
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: Consider the Metropolis Monte Carlo scheme discussed above.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Steps 1 and 3, that consume ran-
dom numbers, involve some 32-bit integer arithmetics (we choose the Parisi-Rapuano shift register
generator [9]).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: Step 2 involves logical (model speciﬁc) bitwise operations for each site.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
We divide the lattice in a checkerboard scheme, updating all black (white) spins simultaneously
and independently.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
In addition, when simulating disordered systems one usually has to deal with two
replicas (independent systems with same coupling conﬁgurations), so we can mix all black (white) sites
of one lattice system with the (white) black ones of its replica: spins on sites of one of the two resulting
artiﬁcial mixed replicas can be updated all simultaneously, with all their neighbors residing in the other
one.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Computations involved in step 2 can be programmed very eﬃciently on the basic logical operators of
the FPGA.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Several updating cells may be instantiated to operate in parallel, provided that the needed
bandwidth from and to spin and interaction conﬁgurations storage is guaranteed.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
FPGAs comes with
many embedded conﬁgurable memories (known as Block RAMs).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Each one has a natural 2D width
× depth structure and “stacking” some of them we arrange a 3D matrix of one bit variables.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Taking
z as the coordinate “inside” the memories, y as the index of “stacked” memories and x along their
width, an entire (xy) plane may be fetched and fed to update logic by simply addressing all memories
with the same z.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The total number of these memory structures depends on the model: we instantiate
two such structures (we have two checkerboard mixed replicas) for each bit needed to represent spin
variables, and one structure for each bit needed to represent couplings (1 for the Edwards-Anderson
and the disordered Potts models, 8 for random permutations in 4-states Glassy Potts model, and three
directions in 3D lattices must be considered).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Reminding the limit of two I/O operations on each Block
RAM per clock cycle, processing rate in which an entire plane of one of the two mixed replicas can be
updated at each clock cycle can be easily sustained, as to process the z plane we only need the same
z plane of the interaction memory structure, together with planes z −1, z and z + 1 of the neighbors
mixed lattice.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
So, we end up with a pipeline in which we fetch z + 1 from memory at the same time as
we write z −1.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
A number of update cells equal to the number of sites in a plane are implemented in conﬁgurable
logic.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Each cell receives an updating spin, its neighbors and a new random spin value as input, along
with all needed couplings, and computes an integer representations of the energy change.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The latter
becomes the pointer to a small (tipically not more than 13 values) look-up table containing transition
probabilities, also implemented in conﬁgurable logic as distributed RAM.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Considering the limit of
two I/O per clock, each look-up table can be shared by two update cells.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Transition probabilities
are represented as integers, so they can be immediately compared to random numbers to test for
acceptance in the Metropolis procedure.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
As discussed in [11], we implement the Parisi-Rapuano shift
register random number generator in a very eﬀective way, allowing for the generation of hundreds of
32-bit random numbers at each clock cycle.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Available on-chip memory limits Ising models to lattice sizes not larger than 963 and 4-states dis-
ordered Potts models to 883.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Available conﬁgurable logic limits the number of parallel updates to 1024
for Ising spin models and 512 for 4-states Potts models.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Table 1 summarize performances on one SP (in terms of the update time for a single spin) and
compares with high-end PCs.

text: Things are slightly more complicated for graph coloring.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Remember that no adjacent vertices can
be updated in parallel, using the Metropolis algorithm.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
One way to avoid this problem is to perform a
preliminary reordering of the graph vertices in P subsets of non adjacent vertices, and then updating
the elements of each P in parallel.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: It is possibile to do this in various ways, topological or not.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
This
reordering is in principle also a hard problem.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
It is however not a bottleneck in our case as we mainly
consider low-connectivity graphs, and we are only interested in reasonable (not necessarily optimal)
solutions.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
We perform graph reordering on a standard pc and then run an optimized parallel update routine
on JANUS.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
A challenging memory handling problem arises, as an irregular graph structure translates
into irregular memory access patterns.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: We assume that each vertex V has an index/address Vi (i.e.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
a “label” to localize it in the graph) and
a color Ci.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
We map the graph on two diﬀerent structures: a topological structure (TM) contanining

pointers to the neighbors of each vertex and a second structure (CM) storing current values for the
vertex colors.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: These structures are sketched in Figure 5, where each row represents one memory word.

Inside CM
a row stores the colors of P non-adjacent vertices.

text:
In the TM we store in the black rows the pointer to
each P vertex and in the gray columns the pointer of each vertex that is neighbor of the vertex in the
black row up.

In our preliminary tests we try to color with Q = 3 or 4 colors graphs of ≈16000 vertices with
average connectivity Cm = 4.

A high-end PC (Intel Core 2 Duo, 64 bit, 4 MB cache) updates one
vertex in 27ns, while JANUS does the same in ≈2.7ns.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Performances in this case are good but not
so impressive as in the previous models: irregular memory access and small on-chip memory are the
limiting factors.

title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: We now come to a comparison with conventional systems.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Traditional architectures have two bottle-
necks: it is impossible to generate many random numbers at the same time while logical manipulations
of independent bit-valued variables waste hardware resources.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Hence, the common trick to resort to
multi-spin coding (MSC) in which several (short) variables are mapped on one (long) machine word.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
In
an asynchronous scheme (AMSC) the variables mapped on each word are associated to diﬀerent copies
of the system.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
In this case the same random number can be used to control all updates performed in
parallel, boosting performance.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
On the other hand, as discussed earlier, we need to simulate eﬃciently
one (or a relatively small number of) system.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
In order to do so, synchronous schemes (SMSC) code in
each machine word more sites of the same system.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
In this case the bottleneck is the generation of many
random numbers (one for each mapped site; in the Metropolis case, the management of the probability
tables also becomes much more complex): performance is much lower.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: Performance comparison for all models is done in Table 1; In most cases performance is outstanding.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
It is striking to note the diﬀerence in performance for traditional architectures between Ising and Potts
models, i.e., between two diﬀerent but vastly similar systems.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
This is due to the fact that one resorts
to tricks to perform operations that are not supported by typical native instruction sets: in some cases
eﬀective tricks can be found in slightly diﬀerent situation the same trick may not work.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
This is the area where reconﬁgurability oﬀers a dramatic performance boost, as we setup data-
9


paths that use all available resources to perform exactly the required mix of operations required by
the algorithm.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Our most eﬀective handles are the limited complexity of the logic manipulation of the
spin-variables and the possibility to instance massively parallel random number generators.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Resources
are assigned to the two main task in a well balanced way.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The additional complexity of Potts models
respect to the Ising spin ones results in increasing connectivity between FPGA internal devices, but it
is completely taken up in increasing design ﬂow run times (especially placing and routing), that may
be considered equivalent to compilation time on standard computers.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
The more impressive boost obtained in FPGA respect to PCs is in the Glassy Potts case, as the need
of many bits to represent random permutations invalidates most of the beneﬁts of multi-spin coding
techniques.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Our level of performance is supported by the required memory access bandwidth, that we obtain by
a judicious data layout, supported in hardware by the ﬁne-grained memory structure within the FPGA.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Irregular access patterns is the main reason that makes the comparison between JANUS and PCs
less striking in the graph coloring problem.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
We try to escape this problem using multiple copies of the
system, but this is resource greedy, so we are hit by limited on-board memory size.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
In general this is a
reminder that memory bottlenecks are more and more a performance problem.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
6
Conclusions
In this paper we have described the JANUS computer, a parallel system that explores the potential for
performance of FPGAs on massively parallel algorithms.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text: We have tested JANUS performance on a class of applications relevant for statistical physics.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Our
results rest on instantiating available parallelism in an eﬃcient way on the logical resources of the
FPGA.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Fine-grained memory structures in turn provide the huge memory bandwidth required to sustain
performance.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
We considered a large but limited class of applications for which a careful handcrafting of the kernel
codes is required.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
Some more general lessons can be drawn:
• FPGAs can be conﬁgured to perform functions poorly done by traditional CPUs, with exceptional
performance rewards.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
• The main performance bottleneck is the amount of available on-chip memory: as long as the
simulation database can be stored on internal RAM blocks, enough bandwidth can be provided
to support performance.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
On the other hand, as soon as the database becomes so large that
(lower-bandwidth) external memory is needed, performance drops signiﬁcantly.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
• The problem is made more serious when access patterns are irregular (for graph coloring in our
case, but a common problem in many other cases).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
FPGA families oriented to high-performance
computing, with larger memories (at the expense of conﬁgurable logic) might be a partial solution
to the problem.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
It would be interesting to compare the performances of JANUS with those obtainable on commer-
cial multi-core chips, such as, for instance, the IBM Cell BE.
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
In principle one could estimate that
each SPE core has roughly the same performances as a traditional processors (clock frequencies are
approximately the same and the level of parallelism associated to SIMD instructions is the same).
title: arXiv:0710.3535v2  [cs.AR]  8 Apr 2008

text:
More
accurate evaluations require considerable additional studies, as in many cases it has been shown that
actual performances depend critically on the size of the system to be mapped on each SPE and on
the detailed pattern of communication among SPEs, between SPEs and their local storage and with
external memory.
