Keywords
Likelihood-free inference, curse of dimensionality, feed forward
neural networks, heteroscedasticity, coalescent models.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Abstract
Approximate Bayesian inference on the basis of summary statistics is well-
suited to complex problems for which the likelihood is either mathematically
or computationally intractable.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
However the methods that use rejection suf-
fer from the curse of dimensionality when the number of summary statistics
is increased.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Here we propose a machine-learning approach to the estimation
of the posterior density by introducing two innovations.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The new method
ﬁts a nonlinear conditional heteroscedastic regression of the parameter on
the summary statistics, and then adaptively improves estimation using im-
portance sampling.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The new algorithm is compared to the state-of-the-art
approximate Bayesian methods, and achieves considerable reduction of the
computational burden in two examples of inference in statistical genetics and
in a queueing model.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Keywords
: Approximate Bayesian computation | Conditional density es-
timation | Implicit statistical models | Importance sampling | non-linear re-
gression | indirect inference
2


1
Introduction
Making use of simulations to perform non-Bayesian inference in models for
which the likelihood is neither analytically solvable nor computationally
tractable has a well-established methodology that ﬁnds its roots at least
in the seminal papers of Diggle and Gratton (1984) and Gourieroux et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
This approach bypasses explicit likelihood functions by simulating
from an implicit statistical model – that is, a model deﬁned in term of a
stochastic generating mechanism.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In the Bayesian setting, there has been a growing interest in implicit
statistical models for demographic inference in population genetics (Marjo-
ram and Tavar´e 2006).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Statistical inference with population-genetic data
usually requires prior knowledge on genealogical trees.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
As the tree is usu-
ally considered as a nuisance parameter, Bayesian Monte Carlo is a natu-
ral approach to average over high-dimensional tree space.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Although many
likelihood-based methods have been proposed in this framework, these meth-
ods are restricted to particular demographic and genetic processes (Stephens
and Donnelly 2000; Wilson et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text: 2003; Kuhner 2006; Hey and Nielsen 2007).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Alternatively, likelihood-free methods, named approximate Bayesian compu-
tation (ABC) after Beaumont et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
(2002), have gained many advocates
in the recent years.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text: The principle of standard ABC (Tavar´e et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
2002) relies on the simulation of large
numbers of data sets using parameters drawn from the prior distribution.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
A
set of summary statistics is then calculated for each simulated sample, and
compared with the values for the observed sample.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Parameters that have
3


generated summary statistics close enough to the observed data are retained
to form an approximate sample from the posterior distribution.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Approximate Bayesian estimation algorithms – that were originally all
based on rejection algorithms – can be classiﬁed into three broad categories,
resembling the mainstream methods that are applied in standard computa-
tional Bayesian statistics (Gelman et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The ﬁrst class of methods
relies on the direct rejection algorithm as described in the previous paragraph
(Tavar´e et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The second class of algorithms
mimics Markov chain Monte Carlo methods (MCMC, Robert and Casella
2004), embedding simulations from the implicit model in the updating step
of the stochastic algorithm (Marjoram et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The MCMC-ABC algorithm takes into account the distance between the
simulated and the observed summary statistics into the Metropolis-Hastings
acceptance rule.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The third class of algorithms shares similarity with the re-
cently introduced sequential Monte Carlo samplers (SMC, Liu 2001).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The
main SMC-ABC algorithm combines ideas underlying rejection methods and
sequential importance sampling (Sisson et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Nevertheless, a severe limitation of rejection-based generative algorithms
arises when the dimensionality of the set of summary statistics increases.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Because the three classes of methods attempt to sample from a small mul-
tidimensional sphere around the observed summary statistics, all of them
suﬀer from the curse of dimensionality (see e.g.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
To
overcome this problem, Beaumont et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
(2002) allowed larger acceptance
4


rates in the rejection algorithm, ranging up to 20 percent of the simulated
values, and then performed local linear adjustment in order to correct for
the discrepancy between the simulated and the observed statistics.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Here,
we address the curse of dimensionality issue by adopting a machine learning
perspective constructing a functional relationship between the generated set
of summary statistics and the model parameters.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Assuming perfect construc-
tion, this relationship could ideally be utilized to produce samples from the
posterior distribution by exploiting information not restricted to a subset of
generated values, but to the extended set.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In the ﬁrst stage, our approach infers the functional relationship linking
the summary statistics to the model parameters by considering a ﬂexible non-
linear conditional heteroscedastic (NCH) model.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Flexible regression models,
like neural networks, are exploited to reduce dimension and to better account
for the correlation within the set of summary statistics.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In the second stage,
we introduce an adaptive version of the NCH (ANCH) algorithm using im-
portance sampling.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The rationale of the adaptive algorithm is to iteratively
limit the discrepancy between the sampling distribution and the posterior
distribution, which may be particularly useful when the prior distribution
is vague.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In two historical examples of demographic inference in population
genetics and in an example of a queueing process, we provide evidence that
the NCH and the ANCH algorithms reduce the computational burden when
compared to ABC with rejection and to ABC with local linear adjustment.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In ABC, we assume that there is a multidi-
mensional parameter of interest φ, and the observed value s of a set of sum-
mary statistics S is calculated for the data.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
To make statistical inference, a
rejection-sampling method generates random draws (φi, si) where φi is sam-
pled from the prior distribution, and si is measured from synthetic data,
simulated from a generative model with parameter φi.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

si, i = 1, .

A second change to the LocL ABC al-

The

run with a high acceptance rate, and adaptively builds a better approxima-

If the two empirical distributions obtained

again.

text:
3
Examples of implicit statistical models
In this section, we present three examples of implicit statistical models, two
of which have received considerable attention in population genetics, and
the last one has served to illustrate indirect inference (Gourieroux et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Using these examples, we performed an
empirical evaluation of the relative performance of three regression-based ap-
proximate Bayesian algorithms, the local linear regression model (LocL ABC
model), the non-linear conditional heteroscedastic model (NCH model), and
its adaptive implementation (ANCH model).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We used the R programming
language to implement the LocL, NCH and ANCH algorithms.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Least squares
adjustment for neural networks was implemented using the R package nnet
(R Core Team 2008).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Model choice for neural networks was based on a
Bayesian (or regularization) approach (Ripley 1996).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We used H = 4 hid-
12


den units and the weight-decay regularization parameter was set equal to
λ = 0.001.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Increasing the weight-decay parameter will increase the bias of
the estimator, but it will also decrease its variance.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
At this stage, cross-
validation might be a useful alternative approach to the choice of a FFNN
model, but the previous values for λ and H proved to work well in the exam-
ples considered here.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In the ANCH algorithm, the support of the conditional
density was estimated using a SVM ν-regression algorithm (ν = 0.005) as
implemented in the R package e1071 based on the public library libsvm
(Chang and Lin 2001).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
There has been tremendous in-
terest in simulation-based inference methods in evolutionary biology during
the last decade (Fu and Li 1997; Pritchard et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In these applications, the inference of demographic and genetic pa-
rameters depends on the so-called coalescent approximation which describes,
in a probabilistic fashion, the ancestry of genes represented in a sample.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Coa-
lescent models provide good examples of implicit statistical models for which
a straightforward stochastic generating mechanism exists, but the likelihood
is usually computationally intractable (see the Supplementary Material for
further information).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Given a set of n DNA sequences, the ﬁrst problem concerns
the estimation of the eﬀective mutation rate, θ > 0, under the inﬁnitely-
many-sites model.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In this model, mutations occur at rate θ at DNA sites
that have not been hit by mutation before.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
If a site is aﬀected by mutation,
13


it is said to be segregating in the sample.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In this example, the summary
statistic, s, is computed as the number of segregating sites.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Note that s is
not a suﬃcient statistic with respect to θ (Fu and Li 1993).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The generating
mechanism for s can be described as follows.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Simulate Ln, the length of the genealogical tree of the n sequences, as
the sum of independent exponential random variables of rate (j −1)/2,
j = 2, .
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text: Generate s according to a Poisson distribution of mean θLn/2.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The simulation of Ln can be derived from the formula Ln = Pn
j=2 jYj that
gives the total length of the tree as a function of the inter-coalescence times
denoted by Yj, j = 2, .
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The inter-coalescence times correspond to the
times during which the sample has j ancestors, j = 2, .
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In a wide range of models in population genetics, the inter-
coalescence times form independent random variables distributed according
to the exponential distributions of rate j(j −1)/2, j = 2, .
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
A more
detailed description of the coalescent process can be found in (Tavar´e 2004).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We computed the posterior distribution of the eﬀective mutation rate θ
given the observation of s = 10 segregating sites in a sample of n = 100 DNA
sequences.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The prior distribution for the parameter θ was taken to be the
exponential distribution of mean 50, which was meant to represent a vague
prior.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
An sample from the posterior distribution was obtained using a direct
rejection algorithm accepting only parameters that produced 10 segregating
sites exactly.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Ten millions of replicates were generated resulting in a sample
14


of size 39, 059 after rejection.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
For the ABC algorithms, we performed inference of the posterior distri-
bution using a total of 2,000 simulations of the bivariate vector (θ, s).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We
recorded the three quartiles and the 0.025 and 0.975 quantiles of the ap-
proximate posterior distributions computed by the three algorithms, and we
compared these 5 quantiles Qk, k=1,.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
,5, with the corresponding empirical
quantiles, Q0
k, obtained from the exact sample.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
For values of the tolerance
rate between 0 and 1 and for each quantile, Qk, the accuracy of each al-
gorithm was assessed by the relative median absolute error deﬁned as the
median of (Qk −Q0
k)/Q0
k computed over 150 runs.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In addition, we measured
the discrepancy between each approximate distribution and the empirical
posterior distribution using the sum of the RMAE’s over all quantiles.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In
the ANCH algorithm, the support was estimated as the range of the empir-
ical distribution – i.e., the (0, max) interval – obtained after a ﬁrst run.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
A
total of 1,000 replicates were used in the ﬁrst run and the tolerance rate,
denotes as Pδ, was set to 75%.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text: Comparisons with standard rejection algorithms were ﬁrst conducted.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We found that the posterior distribution obtained from the rejection meth-
ods deviated from the empirical posterior distribution signiﬁcantly for tol-
erance rates larger than 10% (Figure 1A).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The LocL model approximated
the posterior distribution accurately for small tolerance rates (≤20%), but
the performances of the LocL method deteriorated as the tolerance rate in-
creased (Figure 1, curves with diamonds).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The performances of the NCH
model were signiﬁcantly less sensitive to the tolerance rate, staying at values
15


close to the optimum achieved by the LocL model (Figure 1B, curve with
triangles point-up).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The adaptive NCH algorithm achieved even superior
performances for values of the tolerance rate ranging between 0 and 90%
(Figure 1B, curve with triangles point-down).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The black dot in Figure 1B
represents the performance of the ANCH algorithm without weighting and
allowing total acceptance.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Having eliminated the concept of rejection in the
approximate Bayesian algorithm, i.e.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
setting Pδ = 1, the accuracy of the
algorithm remained close to the optimum achieved by all algorithms.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
This
ﬁrst example illustrates the beneﬁt of the NCH model over the LocL model
and the other rejection methods.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The additional gain of the adaptive step
stems from the use of a vague prior, which, in this case, gave low weight
to the region of posterior values.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We note, however, that for the smallest
tolerance rate, the RMAE is smaller in the LocL model than in the NCH
models.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Because of the additional level of complexity introduced in FFNNs,
FFNNs require more data points to be trained than local linear regression,
but this not an issue for higher tolerance rates.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Turning to a more complex problem in which the posterior
distribution could not be estimated easily, we considered an exponentially
growing population model with 3 parameters.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Similarly to Weiss and von
Haeseler (1998), a population of size NA started to grow exponentially t0
years ago to reach a present size of N individuals where N = NA/α for a
value α ∈(0, 1).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We performed inference on the two parameters NA, t0 and α
was considered as a nuisance parameter.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In this example the data consisted
16


of a sample of n individuals genotyped at a multilocus subset of independent
microsatellite markers (see e.g.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Microsatellite
loci are characterized by a motif of two to four nucleotides that may repeat
itself several times, and the data are recorded as number of repeats for each
individual.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The generating mechanism for the implicit model can be described as
follows.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Simulate candidate coalescent genealogies with n tips in a growing pop-
ulation for each marker,
2.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Superimpose mutations on the tree branches according to a speciﬁc
mutation model.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Step 1 requires simulating coalescence times in a coalescent model with vary-
ing population size (see Tavar´e 2004).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In step 2, we used the single-step
mutation model, that can be viewed as a simple random walk for which the
+1 and -1 steps are equally likely (Ohta and Kimura 1973).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
To capture the pattern of genetic variation, we computed six summary
statistics previously reported to be sensitive to the genetic diversity in the
sample and to the intensity of the demographic expansion.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The amount of
genetic diversity was measured by the mean (over the loci) of the variance in
the number of repeats and by the mean of their heterozygosities (Pritchard
and Feldmann 1996).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
For the demographic pattern, we used two imbalance
indices studied by King et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
(2000), the interlocus statistic introduced
by Reich and Goldstein (1998), and the expansion index of Zhivotovsky et
17


al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We also computed a seventh summary statistic based on an
observation of Shriver et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
(1997) who studied the distribution, SK, of
pairwise comparisons that diﬀer by K repeat units.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
This distribution has its
peak at the value 0 for a recent expansion, and the peak shifts to the value
1 for older expansions.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
To compute the seventh statistic, we averaged the
quantity S1 −S0 over all the loci.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We took a uniform prior distribution ranging from 0 to 100,000 years
for the onset of the expansion, a uniform distribution over the interval (0,
10,000) for the ancestral population size, and a uniform distribution over the
interval (1, 6) for −log10(α).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
One hundred test data sets were generated using t0 = 18, 000 years for
the date of onset of the expansion, NA = 1, 500 for the ancestral population
size, and α = 0.0012 (log10(α) = −2.92) for the ratio of the ancestral size
to the present population size.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
These values were very similar to those used
in Pritchard et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text: (1999) in a study of the Y chromosome in humans.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
For
each algorithm, we computed the posterior distribution of the 3 parameters
given the observation of the 7 summary statistics in a sample of n = 100
individuals surveyed at 50 microsatellite loci.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
For the three algorithms, we generated samples from the posterior dis-
tribution using 2,000 replicates from the implicit model.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We recorded the
quartiles and the 0.025 and 0.975 quantiles of the output distributions for
the three ABC algorithms, and we compared these 5 values for the condi-
tional distributions of each parameter t0, NA, and α.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The median value of
each quantile was then computed over 100 runs.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
18


For each of the three parameters, the median estimates of the quantiles
of the marginal posterior distribution were very similar in the NCH model
and in the ANCH implementation (Figure 2, black and red curves).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
For large
tolerance rates (Pδ ≥50%), we observed a strong agreement with the values
estimated by the LocL model (Figure 2, green curves) used with small toler-
ance rates (Pδ = 5%), indicating that the NCH model can eﬃciently exploit
simulation results that fall far apart from the observed values of the summary
statistics.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The performances of the LocL model decreased as the tolerance
rate increased above 20%, and the estimation of the conditional distribution
of the ancestral size provided evidence that the bias was substantial (Figure
2, bottom right panel).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The three algorithms gave similar results regarding
the estimation of α (results not shown).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
To further compare the performances of the NCH model and its ANCH
variant, we studied a particular simulated data set corresponding to the same
ground truth as before.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
After running the three algorithms 100 times for each
tolerance rate, the variance of each quantile in the posterior distribution was
of order three times higher in the NCH model than in the ANCH algorithm
(2,000 simulations for each algorithm, Table 1).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Clear evidence of the stabi-
lization phenomenon was also obtained under the inﬁnitely-many-sites model.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Given s = 10 segregating sites, we ran the ANCH algorithm using 200 sim-
ulations of the implicit model at each step (tolerance rate Pδ = 85%).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
To
compare estimations obtained after the initial step with those obtained after
adapting the support, we replicated the estimation procedure 100 times.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The
reduction in variance ranged from a factor 2.7 to a factor 34.7.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The highest
19


reduction in variance was obtained for the estimation of the upper quantile.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Our third example arose from a totally diﬀerent context, and
was formerly studied by Heggland and Frigessi (2004) using indirect infer-
ence.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text: The connection of indirect inference to ABC is the following.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
1993) is a non-Bayesian method that proceeds
with 3 steps.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
1) an auxiliary model is introduced, usually as a simpliﬁed
version of the true model.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
2) Estimates of the parameters in the auxiliary
model are obtained and play the role of summary statistics.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
These estimates
can be obtained, for example, by maximizing the likelihood in the auxiliary
model.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
3) An estimate of the parameter φ is built by minimizing a weighted
Euclidean distance between simulated summary statistics and the observed
summary statistics.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Note that the introduction of an auxiliary model can
also be a useful means of ﬁnding informative summary statistics for ABC
methods.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The model considered in (Heggland and Frigessi 2004) was a queueing
system with a ﬁrst-come-ﬁrst-serve single-server queue (G/G/1).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The service
times were uniformly distributed in the interval [θ1, θ2], and the inter-arrival
times had exponential distribution with rate θ3.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Let Wn be the inter-arrival
time of the nth customer and Un be the corresponding service time.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The
process of inter-departure times {Yn, n = 1, 2, .
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
.} can be described by the
following generative algorithm

title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
20


Bayesian inference on (θ1, θ2, θ3) was done by assuming that only the inter-
departure times were observed.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Because the inter-arrival times were unob-
served, likelihood-based inference would involve high-dimensional integra-
tion.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We generated a test data set with n = 50 successive inter-departure time
observation using θ1 = 1, θ2 = 5, and θ3 = 0.2.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We set a uniform prior over
[0, 10] for θ1, θ2 −θ1, and for θ3.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
To investigate the sensitivity of the NCH
model to the number of summary statistics, we ran the ABC-NCH algorithm
using 5, 10 and 20 summary statistics.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Here, the set of summary statistics
included the minimum and the maximum of the inter-departure times and the
3, 8 and 18 equidistant quantiles of the inter-departure times.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We used 10,000
replicates and the tolerance rate was set to the value Pδ = 50% resulting in
a posterior sample of size 5,000.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Figure 3 shows that posterior distributions of the 3 parameters had their
mode and median values close to the ground truth values whatever the num-
ber of summary statistics.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
This provided evidence that the NCH ABC algo-
rithm was robust to an increase in the dimensionality of the set of summary
statistics.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In addition, we found that the posterior distributions were more
concentrated around the true values when 20 summary statistics were used.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
To investigate the variability of the ABC algorithms from one run to
the other, we ran the LocL, NCH and ANCH algorithms 100 times on the
same data set.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We used 2,000 replicates (a rather small number) in order to
observed an exaggerated variability, and we varied the tolerance rate from 0
to 1.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
21


Figure 4 displays estimated posterior quantiles for θ3.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The LocL ABC
algorithm was the less variable algorithm, but the posterior credibility inter-
vals produced by this method were wider than those produced by the NCH
and ANCH algorithms.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The latter were less sensitive to the variation of the
tolerance rates, and the medians of the posterior distributions were closer to
the true value in the non-linear models than in the LocL model.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Compared
to the NCH algorithm, the ANCH algorithm reduced the variance of the
quantile estimates.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
We suspect that the variance of the posterior quantile es-
timates came from the use of local optimization during the learning phase of
the feed-forward neural networks.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
For θ1 and θ2, the LocL ABC and the NCH
ABC algorithms led to similar approximate posterior distributions when the
tolerance rate was set at values close to zero in the LocL ABC algorithm.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
4
Discussion
Approximate Bayesian computation encompasses a wide range of useful meth-
ods for making inference in implicit statistical models.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In this context re-
jection algorithms have greatly beneﬁted from ideas coming from regression-
based conditional density estimation.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
So far conditional density estimation
in ABC approaches has relied on linear adjustment exclusively (Beaumont et
al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
While the linear regression-based ABC method can approximate
posterior distribution accurately, this is usually achieved at the expense of
a heavy computational load.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
For example, using the LocL ABC method for
estimating parameter in complex models of modern human expansion, Fa-
gundes et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
(2007) required an amount of computational time equivalent
22


to 10 CPU-months.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
To increase the tolerance of the algorithm, we have pro-
posed to use non-linear regression-based ABC.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In three examples, non-linear
neural networks proved to be able to reduce computational generation costs
signiﬁcantly.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
A heuristic reason why neural networks worked well when the number
of summary statistics was large is that their ﬁrst layer allows a nonlinear
projection onto a subspace of much lower dimensionality, and nonlinear re-
gression can then be performed using the reduced number of projection vari-
ables.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Increasing the number of summary statistics has a dramatic eﬀect
on the variability of the estimators of the conditional mean ˆm(si) and vari-
ance ˆσ2(si) and consequently inﬂates the variances of the estimated posterior
distributions.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The variance can be reduced with the Bayesian predictive ap-
proach of Ripley (1996) that consists of training a large number of FFNNs
for each conditional regression and averaging the results over the replicate
networks.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
In addition Bayesian neural network theory includes general rules
for choosing appropriate regularization parameters which makes the method
rather automatic.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Compared to other regression models, neural networks
share many properties of projection pursuit regression (Friedman and Stuelze
1981), which may then lead to equivalent performances.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
As well SVM have
gained increased popularity in machine learning approaches during the recent
years (Vapnik 1998), and the algorithms described here could be modiﬁed to
include SVM regression without change in spirit.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
A second justiﬁcation for using feed-forward neural networks is their abil-
ity to implement probabilistic outputs, hence allowing a uniﬁed Bayesian
23


treatment of model choice.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Indeed model choice may be performed by consid-
ering the model itself as an additional parameter to infer.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Beaumont (2007)
proposed to estimate the posterior probability of each candidate model by
an approach based on a weighted multinomial logistic regression procedure.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
This approach is an extension of logistic regression to more than two cate-
gories, and it is equivalent to the use of a multinomial log-linear model.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
As
they pertain to a more ﬂexible class of models, neural networks may achieve
equal or better predictive values than multinomial logistic regression (Ripley
1996).
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
The ABC approach has been recently used in connected domains like
human population genetics (Pritchard et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
2009, Blum and Tran 2008)
or for the evolution of protein networks (Ratmann et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
It has also
recently been suggested in the context of compositional data (Butler and
Glasbey 2008), and applied in extreme value theory (Bortot et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
2007) and
Gibbs random ﬁelds (Grelaud et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Although inference from synthetic
data that mimic observations has a long lasting record in frequentist statistics
(Diggle and Gratton 1984, Gourieroux et al.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Because the ABC method combines the power of simulating from stochastic
individual-based models with sound methodological grounds from Bayesian
theory, it has the potential to open doors to inference in many complex
models in ecology, evolution, and epidemiology, or other domains like the
social science.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
Improved statistical ABC models, like those presented in this
study, will then be useful to deal with increased model complexity, and with
24


the need to raise the dimension of the vector of summary statistics.
title: arXiv:0809.4178v2  [stat.CO]  23 Feb 2009

text:
An R
code for performing ABC with the NCH model is available at the author’s
website.

Abstract
We propose an efﬁcient framework for enabling secure
multi-party numerical computations in a Peer-to-Peer net-
work.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
This problem arises in a range of applications such as
collaborative ﬁltering, distributed computation of trust and
reputation, monitoring and numerous other tasks, where the
computing nodes would like to preserve the privacy of their
inputs while performing a joint computation of a certain
function.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Although there is a rich literature in the ﬁeld of dis-
tributed systems security concerning secure multi-party
computation, in practice it is hard to deploy those meth-
ods in very large scale Peer-to-Peer networks.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In this work,
we examine several possible approaches and discuss their
feasibility.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Among the possible approaches, we identify a
single approach which is both scalable and theoretically se-
cure.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
An additional novel contribution is that we show how to
compute the neighborhood based collaborative ﬁltering, a
state-of-the-art collaborative ﬁltering algorithm, winner of
the Netﬂix progress prize of the year 2007.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Our solution
computes this algorithm in a Peer-to-Peer network, using a
privacy preserving computation, without loss of accuracy.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Using extensive large scale simulations on top of real
Internet topologies, we demonstrate the applicability of our
approach.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
As far as we know, we are the ﬁrst to implement
such a large scale secure multi-party simulation of networks
of millions of nodes and hundreds of millions of edges.

text:
1
Introduction
We consider the problem of performing a joint numeri-
cal computation of some function over a Peer-to-Peer net-
work.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Such problems arise in many applications, for ex-
ample, when computing distributively trust [18], ranking
of nodes and data items [10], clustering [5], collaborative
ﬁltering [6, 27], factor analysis [12] etc.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
The aim of se-
cure multi-party computation is to enable parties to carry
out such distributed computing tasks in a secure manner.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Whereas distributed computing classically deals with ques-
tions of computing under the threat of machine crashes and
other inadvertent faults, secure multi-party computation is
concerned with the possibility of deliberate malicious be-
havior by some adversarial entity.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
That is, it is assumed that
a protocol execution may come under attack by an exter-
nal entity, or even by a subset of the participating parties.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
The aim of this attack may be to learn private information
or cause the result of the computation to be incorrect.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Thus,
two central requirements on any secure computation proto-
col are privacy and correctness.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
The privacy requirement
states that nothing should be learned beyond what is ab-
solutely necessary; more exactly, parties should learn their
designated output and nothing else.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
The correctness re-
quirement states that each party should receive its correct
output.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Therefore, the adversary must not be able to cause
the result of the computation to deviate from the function
that the parties had set out to compute.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In this paper, we consider only functions which are built
using the algebraic primitives of addition, substraction and
multiplication.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In particular, we focus on numerical meth-
ods which are computed distributively in a Peer-to-Peer net-
work, where in each iteration, every node interacts with
a subset of its neighbors by sending scalar messages, and


computing a weighted sum of the messages that it receives.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Examples of such functions are belief propagation [22], EM
(expectation maximization) [12], Power method [18], sepa-
rable functions [20], gradient descent methods [25] and lin-
ear iterative algorithms for solving systems of linear equa-
tions [9].
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
As a speciﬁc example, we describe the Jacobi
algorithm in detail in Section 5.1.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
There is a rich body of research on secure computation,
starting with the seminal work of Yao [26].
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Part of this re-
search is concerned with the design of generic secure pro-
tocols that can be used for computing any function (for ex-
ample, Yao’s work [26] for the case of two participants, and
e.g.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
[8, 16] for solutions for the case of multiple partici-
pants).
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
There are several works concerning the implemen-
tation of generic protocols for secure computation.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
For ex-
ample, FairPlay [19] is a system for secure two-party com-
putation, and FairPlayMP [7] is a different system for secure
computation by more than two parties.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
These two systems
are based (like Yao’s protocol) on reducing any function
to a representation as a Boolean circuit and computing the
resulting Boolean circuit securely.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Our approach is much
more efﬁcient, at the cost of supporting only a subset of the
functions the FairPlay system can compute.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
A different line of work studies secure protocols for com-
puting speciﬁc functions (rather than generic protocols for
computing any function).
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Of particular interest for us are
works that add a privacy preserving layer to the computa-
tion of functions such as the factor analysis learning prob-
lem (for which [12] describes a secure multi-party protocol
using homomorphic encryption), computing trust in a Peer-
to-Peer network (for which [18] suggests a solution using
a trusted third party), or the work of [25], which is closely
related to our work, but is limited to two parties.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Most previous solutions for secure multi-party compu-
tation suffer from one of the following drawbacks: (1)
they provide a centralized solution where all information
is shipped to a single computing node, and/or (2) require
communication between all participants in the protocol,
and/or (3) require the use of asymmetric encryption, which
is costly.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In this work, we investigate secure computation in
a Peer-to-Peer setting, where each node is only connected to
some of the other nodes (its neighbors).
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
We examine differ-
ent possible approaches, and out of the different approaches
we identify a single approach, which is theoretically secure,
efﬁcient, and scalable.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Security is often based on the assumption that there is
an upper bound on the global number of malicious partici-
pants.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In our setting, we consider the number of malicious
nodes in each local vicinity.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Furthermore, most of the ex-
isting algorithms scale to tens or hundreds of nodes at the
most.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In this work, we address the problem in a setting of a
large Peer-to-Peer network, with millions of nodes and hun-
dreds of millions of communication links.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Unlike most of
the previous work, we have performed a very large scale
simulation, using real Internet topologies, to show our ap-
proach is applicable to real network settings.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
As an example for applications of our framework, we
take the neighborhood based collaborative ﬁltering [6].
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
This
algorithm is a recent state-of-the-art algorithm.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
There are
two challenges in adapting this algorithm to a Peer-to-Peer
network.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
First, the algorithm is centralized and we propose
a method to distribute it.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Second, we add a privacy pre-
serving layer, so no information about personal ranking is
revealed during the process of computation.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In Section 2 we for-
mulate our problem model.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In Section 3 we give a brief
background of cryptographic primitives that are used in our
schemes.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text: Section 4 outlines our novel construction.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
We
give a detailed case study of collaborative ﬁltering as an ex-
ample application in Section 5.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Large scale simulations are
presented in Section 6.

We use the semi-honest adversaries model: in this model

title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

However, the adversary obtains the
internal states of all the corrupted parties (including the

this information to learn information that should remain pri-

We deﬁne a conﬁgurable local system parameter di,
which deﬁnes the maximum number of nodes in the local
vicinity of node i (direct neighbors of node i) which are cor-
rupt.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

Whenever this assertion is violated, the security of our

title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

This is a stronger requirement

the number of adversarial nodes.

3
Cryptographic primitives
We compare several existing approaches from the liter-
ature of secure multi-party computation and discuss their
relevance to Peer-to-Peer networks.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
3.1
Random perturbations
The random additive perturbation method attempts to
preserve the privacy of the data by modifying values of the
sensitive attributes using a randomized process (see [4, 13,
14]).
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In this approach, the node sends a value ui + v, where
ui is the original scalar message, and v is a random value
drawn from a certain distribution V .
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In order to perturb
the data, n independent samples v1, v2, · · · , vn, are drawn
from a distribution V .
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
The owners of the data provide the
perturbed values u1 + v1, u2 + v2, · · · , un + vn and the cu-
mulative distribution function FV (r) of V .
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
The goal is to
use these values, instead of the original ones, in the com-
putation.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
(It is easy to see, for example, that if the expected
value of V is 0, then the expectation of the sum of the ui+vi
values is equal to the expectation of the ui values.) The

3.2
Shamir’s Secret Sharing (SSS)
Secret sharing is a fundamental primitive of crypto-
graphic protocols.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
We will describe the secret sharing
scheme of Shamir [23].
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
The scheme works over a ﬁeld F,
and we assume the secret s to be an element in that ﬁeld.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In a k-out-of-n secret sharing the owner of secret wishes to
distribute it between n players such that any subset of k of
them is able to recover the secret, while no subset of k −1
players is able to learn any information about the secret.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In order to distribute the secret, its owner chooses a
random polynomial P() of degree k −1, subject to the
constraint that P(0) = s.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
This is done by choosing ran-
dom coefﬁcients a1, .
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
, ak−1 and deﬁning the polynomial
as P(x) = s + Pk−1
i=1 aixi.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Each player is associated
with an identity in the ﬁeld (denoted x1, .
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
The share that player i receives
is the value P(xi), namely the value of the polynomial eval-
uated at the point xi.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
It is easy to see that any k players can
recover the secret, since they have k values of the polyno-
mial and can therefore interpolate it and compute its free
coefﬁcient s.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
It is also not hard to see that any set of k −1
players does not learn any information about s, since any
value of s has a probability of 1/|F| of resulting in a poly-
nomial which agrees with the values that the players have.

3.3
Homomorphic encryption
A homomorphic encryption scheme is an encryption
scheme which allows certain algebraic operations to be car-
ried out on the encrypted plaintext, by applying an efﬁcient
operation to the corresponding ciphertext (without knowing
the decryption key!).
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In particular, we will be interested
in additively homomorphic encryption schemes: Here, the
message space is a ring (or a ﬁeld).
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:

cient algorithm +pk whose input is the public key of the
encryption scheme and two ciphertexts, and whose output
is Epk(m1) +pk Epk(m2) = Epk(m1 + m2).

this algorithm computes, given the public key and two ci-

ciphertexts.) There is also an efﬁcient algorithm ·pk, whose
input consists of the public key of the encryption scheme, a
ciphertext, and a constant c in the ring, and whose output is
c ·pk Epk(m) = Epk(c ·pk m).

4.1
Random perturbations
In each iteration of the algorithm, whenever a node needs
to send a value mji to a neighboring node, the node gener-
ates a random number rj,i using the GMP library [1], from
a probability distribution with zero mean.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

4.2
Homomorphic Encryption
We chose to utilize the Paillier encryption scheme,
which is an efﬁcient realization of an additive homomor-
phic encryption scheme with semantic security.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Key generation:
We use the threshold version of
the Paillier encryption scheme described in [15].
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In this
scheme, a trusted third party generates for each node i pri-
vate and public key pairs.3 The public key is disseminated
to all of node i neighbors.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
The private key λi = prvk(i)
is kept secret from all nodes (including node i).
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

Instead,
it is split, using secret sharing, to the neighbors of node
i.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
There is a threshold di, which is at most equal to |Ni|,
the number of neighbors of node i.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
The scheme ensures
that any subset of di of the neighbors of node i can help
it decrypt messages (without the neighbors learning the
decrypted message, or node i learning the private key).

neighbor j a random value sji subject to the constraint

We propose a construction based on Shamir’s secret
sharing, which avoids the computation cost of asymmet-

text:
In a nutshell, we use the neighborhood of
a node for adding a privacy preserving mechanism, where
only a coalition of di or more nodes can reveal the content
of messages sent to that node.

4.5
Working in diﬀerent ﬁelds
The operations that can be applied to secrets in the
Shamir secret sharing scheme, or to encrypted values in
a homomorphic encryption scheme, are deﬁned in a ﬁnite
ﬁeld or ring over which the schemes are deﬁned (for exam-
ple, in the secret sharing case, over a ﬁeld Zp where p is a
prime number).
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
The operations that we want to compute,
however, might be deﬁned over the Real numbers.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
Working
in a ﬁeld is sufﬁcient for computing additions or multipli-
cations of integers, if we know that the size of the ﬁeld is
larger than the maximum result of the operation.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
If the ba-
sic elements we work with are Real numbers, we can round
them ﬁrst to the next integer, or, alternatively, ﬁrst multi-
ply them by some constant c (say, c = 106) and then round
the result to the closest integer.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
(This essentially means that
we work with accuracy of 1/c if the computation involves
only additions, or an accuracy of 1/cd if the computation
involves summands composed of up to d multiplications.)
Handling division is much harder, since we are essen-
tially limited to working with integer numbers.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
One pos-
sible workaround is possible if we know in advance that a
number x might have to be divided by a different number
from a set D (say, the numbers in the range [1, 100]).
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
In
that case we ﬁrst multiply x by the least common multiple
(lcm) of the numbers in D.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

text:
This initial step ensures that di-
viding the result by a number from D results in an integer
number.

Experimental Results
We have implemented our proposed framework using a
large scale simulation.

Our simulation is written in C, con-
sists of about 1500 lines of code, and uses MPI, for running
the simulation in parallel.

We run the simulation on a cluster

memory.

We use the open source Paillier implementation
of [3].

We use several large topologies for demonstrating the
applicability of our approach.
title: arXiv:0810.1624v1  [cs.CR]  9 Oct 2008

The DIMES dataset [24] is
an Internet router topology of around 300,000 routers and
2.2 million communication links connecting them, captured
in January 2007.

The Blog network, is a social network,
web crawl of Internet blogs of half a million blog sites
and eleven million links connecting them.

Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared 
1,2,3Ian Foster, 4Yong Zhao, 1Ioan Raicu, 5Shiyong Lu 
foster@mcs.anl.gov, yozha@microsoft.com, iraicu@cs.uchicago.edu, shiyong@wayne.edu 
1 Department of Computer Science, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA  
2Computation Institute, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA 
3Math & Computer Science Division, Argonne National Laboratory, Argonne, IL, USA 
4Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA 
5 Department of Computer Science, Wayne State University, Detroit, MI, USA 
 
Abstract– Cloud Computing has become another buzzword after Web 
2.0.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
However, there are dozens of different definitions for Cloud 
Computing and there seems to be no consensus on what a Cloud is.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
On the other hand, Cloud Computing is not a completely new concept; 
it has intricate connection to the relatively new but thirteen-year 
established 
Grid 
Computing 
paradigm, 
and 
other 
relevant 
technologies such as utility computing, cluster computing, and 
distributed systems in general.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
This paper strives to compare and 
contrast Cloud Computing with Grid Computing from various angles 
and give insights into the essential characteristics of both.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
1 
100-Mile Overview  
Cloud Computing is hinting at a future in which we won’t 
compute on local computers, but on centralized facilities 
operated by third-party compute and storage utilities.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We sure 
won’t miss the shrink-wrapped software to unwrap and install.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In fact, back in 1961, 
computing 
pioneer 
John 
McCarthy 
predicted 
that 
“computation may someday be organized as a public utility”—
and went on to speculate how this might occur.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In the mid 1990s, the term Grid was coined to describe 
technologies that would allow consumers to obtain computing 
power on demand.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Ian Foster and others posited that by 
standardizing the protocols used to request computing power, 
we could spur the creation of a Computing Grid, analogous in 
form and utility to the electric power grid.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Researchers 
subsequently developed these ideas in many exciting ways, 
producing for example large-scale federated systems (TeraGrid, 
Open Science Grid, caBIG, EGEE, Earth System Grid) that 
provide not just computing power, but also data and software, 
on demand.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Standards organizations (e.g., OGF, OASIS) 
defined relevant standards.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
More prosaically, the term was also 
co-opted by industry as a marketing term for clusters.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
But no 
viable commercial Grid Computing providers emerged, at least 
not until recently.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text: So is “Cloud Computing” just a new name for Grid?
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In 
information technology, where technology scales by an order 
of magnitude, and in the process reinvents itself, every five 
years, there is no straightforward answer to such questions.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Yes: the vision is the same—to reduce the cost of computing, 
increase reliability, and increase flexibility by transforming 
computers from something that we buy and operate ourselves 
to something that is operated by a third party.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text: But no: things are different now than they were 10 years ago.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We have a new need to analyze massive data, thus motivating 
greatly increased demand for computing.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Having realized the 
benefits of moving from mainframes to commodity clusters, 
we find that those clusters are quite expensive to operate.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
And, above all, we have multiple 
billions of dollars being spent by the likes of Amazon, Google, 
and Microsoft to create real commercial large-scale systems 
containing hundreds of thousands of computers.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The prospect 
of needing only a credit card to get on-demand access to 
100,000+ computers in tens of data centers distributed 
throughout the world—resources that be applied to problems 
with massive, potentially distributed data, is exciting!
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
So we 
are operating at a different scale, and operating at these new, 
more massive scales can demand fundamentally different 
approaches to tackling problems.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
It also enables—indeed is 
often only applicable to—entirely new problems.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Nevertheless, yes: the problems are mostly the same in Clouds 
and Grids.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
There is a common need to be able to manage large 
facilities; to define methods by which consumers discover, 
request, and use resources provided by the central facilities; 
and to implement the often highly parallel computations that 
execute on those resources.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Details differ, but the two 
communities are struggling with many of the same issues.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
1.1 
Defining Cloud Computing 
There is little consensus on how to define the Cloud [49].
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We 
add yet another definition to the already saturated list of 
definitions for Cloud Computing: 
A large-scale distributed computing paradigm that is 
driven by economies of scale, in which a pool of 
abstracted, virtualized, dynamically-scalable, managed 
computing power, storage, platforms, and services are 
delivered on demand to external customers over the 
Internet.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text: There are a few key points in this definition.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
First, Cloud 
Computing is a specialized distributed computing paradigm; it 
differs from traditional ones in that 1) it is massively scalable, 
2) can be encapsulated as an abstract entity that delivers 
different levels of services to customers outside the Cloud, 3) it 
is driven by economies of scale [44], and 4) the services can be 
dynamically configured (via virtualization or other approaches) 
and delivered on demand.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Governments, research institutes, and industry leaders are 
rushing to adopt Cloud Computing to solve their ever-
increasing computing and storage problems arising in the 
Internet Age.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
There are three main factors contributing to the 
surge and interests in Cloud Computing: 1) rapid decrease in 
hardware cost and increase in computing power and storage 
capacity, and the advent of multi-core architecture and modern 
supercomputers consisting of hundreds of thousands of cores; 


2) the exponentially growing data size in scientific 
instrumentation/simulation 
and 
Internet 
publishing 
and 
archiving; and 3) the wide-spread adoption of Services 
Computing and Web 2.0 applications.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
1.2 
Clouds, Grids, and Distributed Systems 
Many discerning readers will immediately notice that our 
definition of Cloud Computing overlaps with many existing 
technologies, such as Grid Computing, Utility Computing, 
Services Computing, and distributed computing in general.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We 
argue that Cloud Computing not only overlaps with Grid 
Computing, it is indeed evolved out of Grid Computing and 
relies on Grid Computing as its backbone and infrastructure 
support.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The evolution has been a result of a shift in focus 
from an infrastructure that delivers storage and compute 
resources (such is the case in Grids) to one that is economy 
based aiming to deliver more abstract resources and services 
(such is the case in Clouds).
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
As for Utility Computing, it is not 
a new paradigm of computing infrastructure; rather, it is a 
business model in which computing resources, such as 
computation and storage, are packaged as metered services 
similar to a physical public utility, such as electricity and 
public switched telephone network.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Utility computing is 
typically implemented using other computing infrastructure 
(e.g.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text: Grids) with additional accounting and monitoring services.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
A Cloud infrastructure can be utilized internally by a company 
or exposed to the public as utility computing.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
See Figure 1 for an overview of the relationship between 
Clouds and other domains that it overlaps with.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Web 2.0 
covers almost the whole spectrum of service-oriented 
applications, where Cloud Computing lies at the large-scale 
side.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Supercomputing and Cluster Computing have been more 
focused 
on 
traditional 
non-service 
applications.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Grid 
Computing overlaps with all these fields where it is generally 
considered of lesser scale than supercomputers and Clouds.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Figure 1: Grids and Clouds Overview 
Grid Computing aims to “enable resource sharing and 
coordinated problem solving in dynamic, multi-institutional 
virtual organizations” [18][20].
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
There are also a few key 
features to this definition: First of all, Grids provide a 
distributed computing paradigm or infrastructure that spans 
across multiple virtual organizations (VO) where each VO can 
consist of either physically distributed institutions or logically 
related projects/groups.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The goal of such a paradigm is to 
enable federated resource sharing in dynamic, distributed 
environments.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The approach taken by the de facto standard 
implementation – The Globus Toolkit [16][23], is to build a 
uniform computing environment from diverse resources by 
defining standard network protocols and providing middleware 
to mediate access to a wide range of heterogeneous resources.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Globus addresses various issues such as security, resource 
discovery, resource provisioning and management, job 
scheduling, monitoring, and data management.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Half a decade ago, Ian Foster gave a three point checklist [19] 
to help define what is, and what is not a Grid: 1) coordinates 
resources that are not subject to centralized control, 2) uses 
standard, open, general-purpose protocols and interfaces, and 3) 
delivers non-trivial qualities of service.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Although point 3 holds 
true for Cloud Computing, neither point 1 nor point 2 is clear 
that it is the case for today’s Clouds.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The vision for Clouds and 
Grids are similar, details and technologies used may differ, but 
the two communities are struggling with many of the same 
issues.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
This paper strives to compare and contrast Cloud 
Computing with Grid Computing from various angles and give 
insights into the essential characteristics of both, with the hope 
to paint a less cloudy picture of what Clouds are, what kind of 
applications can Clouds expect to support, and what challenges 
Clouds are likely to face in the coming years as they gain 
momentum and adoption.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We hope this will help both 
communities gain deeper understanding of the goals, 
assumptions, status, and directions, and provide a more 
detailed view of both technologies to the general audience.

This section aims to compare Grids and Clouds across a wide

2.2 
Architecture 
Grids started off in the mid-90s to address large-scale 
computation problems using a network of resource-sharing 
commodity machines that deliver the computation power 
affordable only by supercomputers and large dedicated clusters 
at that time.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The major motivation was that these high 
performance computing resources were expensive and hard to 
get access to, so the starting point was to use federated 
resources that could comprise compute, storage and network 
resources from multiple geographically distributed institutions, 
and such resources are generally heterogeneous and dynamic.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Grids focused on integrating existing resources with their 
hardware, operating systems, local resource management, and 
security infrastructure.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In order to support the creation of the so called “Virtual 
Organizations”—a logical entity within which distributed 
resources can be discovered and shared as if they were from 
the same organization, Grids define and provide a set of 
standard protocols, middleware, toolkits, and services built on 
top of these protocols.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Interoperability and security are the 
primary concerns for the Grid infrastructure as resources may 
come from different administrative domains, which have both 
global and local resource usage policies, different hardware 
and software configurations and platforms, and vary in 
availability and capacity.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Grids provide protocols and services at five different layers as 
identified in the Grid protocol architecture (see Figure 2).
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
At 
the fabric layer, Grids provide access to different resource 
types such as compute, storage and network resource, code 
repository, etc.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Grids usually rely on existing fabric 
components, for instance, local resource managers (i.e.

General-purpose components such as

and specialized resource management services such as Falkon 
[40] (although strictly speaking, Falkon also provides services 
beyond the fabric layer).

authentication protocols for easy and secure network

title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

The resource layer defines protocols for the publication, 
discovery, negotiation, monitoring, accounting and payment of

The GRAM (Grid

The collective layer captures interactions across collections of 
resources, directory services such as MDS (Monitoring and

The application layer comprises whatever user applications 
built on top of the above protocols and APIs and operate in VO

TeraGrid Science gateway (http://www.teragrid.org)).

text:
Clouds are developed to address Internet-scale computing 
problems where some assumptions are different from those of 
the Grids.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Clouds are usually referred to as a large pool of 
computing and/or storage resources, which can be accessed via 
standard protocols via an abstract interface.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Clouds can be 
built on top of many existing protocols such as Web Services 
(WSDL, SOAP), and some advanced Web 2.0 technologies 
such as REST, RSS, AJAX, etc.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In fact, behind the cover, it is 
possible for Clouds to be implemented over existing Grid 
technologies leveraging more than a decade of community 


efforts in standardization, security, resource management, and 
virtualization support.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
There are also multiple versions of definition for Cloud 
architecture, we define a four-layer architecture for Cloud 
Computing in comparison to the Grid architecture, composed 
of 1) fabric, 2) unified resource, 3) platform, and 4) application 
Layers.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Figure 3: Cloud Architecture 
The fabric layer contains the raw hardware level resources, 
such as compute resources, storage resources, and network 
resources.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The unified resource layer contains resources that 
have been abstracted/encapsulated (usually by virtualization) 
so that they can be exposed to upper layer and end users as 
integrated resources, for instance, a virtual computer/cluster, a 
logical file system, a database system, etc.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The platform layer 
adds on a collection of specialized tools, middleware and 
services on top of the unified resources to provide a 
development and/or deployment platform.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
For instance, a Web 
hosting environment, a scheduling service, etc.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Finally, the 
application layer contains the applications that would run in 
the Clouds.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Clouds in general provide services at three different levels 
(IaaS, PaaS, and Saas [50]) as follows, although some 
providers can choose to expose services at more than one level.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) [50] provisions hardware, 
software, and equipments (mostly at the unified resource layer, 
but can also include part of the fabric layer) to deliver software 
application environments with a resource usage-based pricing 
model.

text:
Infrastructure can scale up and down dynamically 
based on application resource needs.

Typical examples are 
Amazon EC2 (Elastic Cloud Computing) Service [3] and S3

Platform as a Service (PaaS) [50] offers a high-level 
integrated environment to build, test, and deploy custom 
applications.

Generally, developers will need to accept some 
restrictions on the type of software they can write in exchange 
for built-in application scalability.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

An example is Google’s 
App Engine [28], which enables users to build Web

Software as a Service (SaaS) [50] delivers special-purpose

This leads to

As Clouds mature, and more sophisticated

text:
2.3 
Resource Management 
This section describes the resource management found in 
Grids and Clouds, covering topics such as the compute model, 
data model, virtualization, monitoring, and provenance.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
These 
topics are extremely important to understand the main 
challenges that both Grids and Clouds face today, and will 
have to overcome in the future.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Compute Model: Most Grids use a batch-scheduled compute 
model, in which a local resource manager (LRM), such as PBS, 
Condor, SGE manages the compute resources for a Grid site, 
and users submit batch jobs (via GRAM) to request some 
resources for some time.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Many Grids have policies in place 
that enforce these batch jobs to identify the user and 
credentials under which the job will run for accounting and 
security purposes, the number of processors needed, and the 
duration of the allocation.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
For example, a job could say, stage 
in the input data from a URL to the local storage, run the 
application for 60 minutes on 100 processors, and stage out the 
results to some FTP server.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The job would wait in the LRM’s 
wait queue until the 100 processors were available for 60 
minutes, at which point the 100 processors would be allocated 
and dedicated to the application for the duration of the job.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Due to the expensive scheduling decisions, data staging in and 
out, and potentially long queue times, many Grids don’t 
natively support interactive applications; although there are 
efforts in the Grid community to enable lower latencies to 
resources via multi-level scheduling, to allow applications with 
many short-running tasks to execute efficiently on Grids [40].
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Cloud Computing compute model will likely look very 
different, with resources in the Cloud being shared by all users 
at the same time (in contrast to dedicated resources governed 
by a queuing system).
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
This should allow latency sensitive 
applications to operate natively on Clouds, although ensuring a 
good enough level of QoS is being delivered to the end users 
will not be trivial, and will likely be one of the major 
challenges for Cloud Computing as the Clouds grow in scale, 
and number of users.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
