Data Model: While some people boldly predicate that future 
Internet Computing will be towards Cloud Computing 
centralized, in which storage, computing, and all kind of other 
resources will mainly be provisioned by the Cloud, we 
envision that the next-generation Internet Computing will take 
the triangle model shown in Figure 4: Internet Computing will 
be centralized around Data, Clouding Computing, as well as 
Client Computing.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Cloud Computing and Client Computing 
will coexist and evolve hand in hand, while data management 
(mapping, 
partitioning, 
querying, 
movement, 
caching, 
replication, etc) will become more and more important for both 
Cloud Computing and Client Computing with the increase of 
data-intensive applications.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The critical role of Cloud Computing goes without saying, but 
the importance of Client Computing cannot be overlooked 
either for several reasons: 1) For security reasons, people 
might not be willing to run mission-critical applications on the 
Cloud and send sensitive data to the Cloud for processing and 
storage; 2) Users want to get their things done even when the 
Internet and Cloud are down or the network communication is 
slow; 3) With the advances of multi-core technology, the 
coming decade will bring the possibilities of having a desktop 
supercomputer with 100s to 1000s of hardware threads/cores.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Furthermore, many end-users will have various hardware-
driven 
end-functionalities, 
such 
as 
visualization 
and 
multimedia playback, which will typically run locally.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text: Figure 4 The triangle model of next-generation Internet Computing.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The importance of data has caught the attention of the Grid 
community for the past decade; Data Grids [10] have been 
specifically designed to tackle data intensive applications in 
Grid environments, with the concept of virtual data [22] 
playing a crucial role.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Virtual data captures the relationship 
between data, programs and computations and prescribes 
various abstractions that a data grid can provide: location 
transparency where data can be requested without regard to 
data location, a distributed metadata catalog is engaged to keep 
track of the locations of each piece of data (along with its 
replicas) across grid sites, and privacy and access control are 
enforced; materialization transparency: data can be either re-
computed on the fly or transferred upon request, depending on 
the availability of the data and the cost to re-compute.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
There is 
also representation transparency where data can be consumed 
and produced no matter what their actual physical formats and 
storage are, data are mapped into some abstract structural 
representation and manipulated in that way.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Data Locality: As CPU cycles become cheaper and data sets 
double in size every year, the main challenge for efficient 
scaling of applications is the location of the data relative to the 
available computational resources – moving the data 
repeatedly to distant CPUs is becoming the bottleneck.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
[46] 
There are large differences in IO speeds from local disk 
storage to wide area networks, which can drastically affect 
application performance.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
To achieve good scalability at 
Internet scales for Clouds, Grids, and their applications, data 
must be distributed over many computers, and computations 
must be steered towards the best place to execute in order to 
minimize the communication costs [46].
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Google’s MapReduce 
[13] system runs on top of the Google File System, within 
which data is loaded, partitioned into chunks, and each chunk 
replicated.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Thus data processing is collocated with data storage: 
when a file needs to be processed, the job scheduler consults a 
storage metadata service to get the host node for each chunk, 
and then schedules a “map” process on that node, so that data 
locality is exploited efficiently.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In Grids, data storage usually 
relies on a shared file systems (e.g.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
NFS, GPFS, PVFS, Luster), 
where data locality cannot be easily applied.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
One approach is 
to improve schedulers to be data-aware, and to be able to 
leverage 
data 
locality 
information 
when 
scheduling 
computational tasks; this approach has shown to improve job 
turn-around time significantly [41].
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Combining compute and data management: Even more 
critical is the combination of the compute and data resource 
management, which leverages data locality in access patterns 
to minimize the amount of data movement and improve end-
application performance and scalability.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Attempting to address 
the storage and computational problems separately forces 
much data movement between computational and storage 
resources, which will not scale to tomorrow’s peta-scale 
datasets and millions of processors, and will yield significant 
underutilization of the raw resources.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
It is important to 
schedule computational tasks close to the data, and to 
understand the costs of moving the work as opposed to moving 
the data.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Data-aware schedulers and dispersing data close to 
processors is critical in achieving good scalability and 
performance.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Finally, as the number of processor-cores is 
increasing (the largest supercomputers today have over 200K 
processors and Grids surpassing 100K processors), there is an 
ever-growing emphasis for support of high throughput 
computing with high sustainable dispatch and execution rates.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We believe that data management architectures are important 
to ensure that the data management implementations scale to 
the required dataset sizes in the number of files, objects, and 
dataset disk space usage while at the same time, ensuring that 
data element information can be retrieved fast and efficiently.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Grids have been making progress in combining compute and 
data management with data-aware schedulers [41], but we 
believe that Clouds will face significant challenges in handling 
data-intensive applications without serious efforts invested in 
harnessing the data locality of application access patterns.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Although data-intensive applications may not be typical 
applications that Clouds deal with today, as the scales of 
Clouds grow, it may just be a matter of time for many Clouds.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Virtualization: Virtualization has become an indispensable 
ingredient for almost every Cloud, the most obvious reasons 
are for abstraction and encapsulation.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Just like threads were 
introduced to provide users the “illusion” as if the computer 
were running all the threads simultaneously, and each thread 


were using all the available resources, Clouds need to run 
multiple (or even up to thousands or millions of) user 
applications, and all the applications appear to the users as if 
they were running simultaneously and could use all the 
available resources in the Cloud.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Virtualization provides the 
necessary abstraction such that the underlying fabric (raw 
compute, storage, network resources) can be unified as a pool 
of resources and resource overlays (e.g.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
data storage services, 
Web hosting environments) can be built on top of them.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Virtualization also enables each application to be encapsulated 
such that they can be configured, deployed, started, migrated, 
suspended, resumed, stopped, etc., and thus provides better 
security, manageability, and isolation.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
There are also many other reasons that Clouds tend to adopt 
virtualization: 1) server and application consolidation, as 
multiple applications can be run on the same server, resources 
can be utilized more efficiently; 2) configurability, as the 
resource requirements for various applications could differ 
significantly, some require large storage, some compute, in 
order to dynamically configure and bundle (aggregate) 
resources for various needs, virtualization is necessary as this 
is not achievable at the hardware level; 3) increased 
application availability, virtualization allows quick recovery 
from unplanned outages, as virtual environments can be 
backed up and migrated with no interruption in service; 4) 
improved responsiveness: resource provisioning, monitoring 
and maintenance can be automated, and common resources can 
be cached and reused.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
All these features of virtualization 
provide the basis for Clouds to meet stringent SLA (Service 
Level Agreement) requirements in a business setting, which 
cannot be easily achieved with a non-virtualized environment 
in a cost-effective manner as systems would have to be over-
provisioned to handle peak load and waste resources in idle 
periods.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
After all, a virtualization infrastructure can be just 
thought as a mapping from IT resources to business needs.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Grids do not rely on virtualization as much as Clouds do, but 
that might be more due to policy and having each individual 
organization maintain full control of their resources (i.e.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
However, there are efforts in Grids to use 
virtualization as well, such as Nimbus [56] (previously known 
as the Virtual Workspace Service [26]), which provide the 
same abstraction and dynamic deployment capabilities.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
A 
virtual workspace is an execution environment that can be 
deployed dynamically and securely in the Grid.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Nimbus 
provides two levels of guarantees: 1) quality of life: users get 
exactly the (software) environment they need, and 2) quality of 
service: provision and guarantee all the resources the 
workspace needs to function correctly (CPU, memory, disk, 
bandwidth, availability), allowing for dynamic renegotiation to 
reflect changing requirements and conditions.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In addition, 
Nimbus can also provision a virtual cluster for Grid 
applications (e.g.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
a batch scheduler, or a workflow system), 
which is also dynamically configurable, a growing trend in 
Grid Computing.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
It is also worth noting that virtualization – in the past – had 
significant performance losses for some applications, which 
has been one of the primary disadvantage of using 
virtualization.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
However, over the past few years, processor 
manufacturers such as AMD and Intel have been introducing 
hardware support for virtualization, which is helping narrow 
the performance gap between applications performance on 
virtualized resources as it compares with that on traditional 
operating systems without virtualization.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Monitoring: Another challenge that virtualization brings to 
Clouds is the potential difficulty in fine-control over the 
monitoring of resources.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Although many Grids (such as 
TeraGrid) also enforce restrictions on what kind of sensors or 
long-running services a user can launch, Cloud monitoring is 
not as straightforward as in Grids, because Grids in general 
have a different trust model in which users via their identity 
delegation can access and browse resources at different Grid 
sites, and Grid resources are not highly abstracted and 
virtualized as in Clouds; for example, the Ganglia [25] 
distributed (and hierarchical) monitoring system can monitor a 
federation of clusters and Grids and has seen wide adoption in 
the Grid community.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In a Cloud, different levels of services 
can be offered to an end user, the user is only exposed to a pre-
defined API, and the lower level resources are opaque to the 
user (especially at the PaaS and SaaS level, although some 
providers may choose to expose monitoring information at 
these levels).
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The user does not have the liberty to deploy her 
own monitoring infrastructure, and the limited information 
returned to the user may not provide the necessary level of 
details for her to figure out what the resource status is.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The 
same problems potentially exist for Cloud developers and 
administrators, as the abstract/unified resources usually go 
through virtualization and some other level of encapsulation, 
and tracking the issues down the software/hardware stack 
might be more difficult.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Essentially monitoring in Clouds 
requires a fine balance of business application monitoring, 
enterprise server management, virtual machine monitoring, and 
hardware maintenance, and will be a significant challenge for 
Cloud Computing as it sees wider adoption and deployments.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
On the other hand, monitoring can be argued to be less 
important in Clouds, as users are interacting with a more 
abstract layer that is potentially more sophisticated; this 
abstract layer could respond to failures and quality of service 
(QoS) requirements automatically in a general-purpose way 
irrespective of application logic.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In the near future, user-end 
monitoring might be a significant challenge for Clouds, but it 
will become less important as Clouds become more 
sophisticated and more self-maintained and self-healing.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Provenance: Provenance refers to the derivation history of a 
data product, including all the data sources, intermediate data 
products, and the procedures that were applied to produce the 
data product.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Provenance information is vital in understanding, 
discovering, validating, and sharing a certain data product as 
well as the applications and programs used to derive it.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In 
some disciplines such as finance and medicine, it is also 
mandatory to provide what is called an “audit trail” for 
audition purpose.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In Grids, provenance management has been 
in general built into a workflow system, from early pioneers 
such as Chimera [22], to modern scientific workflow systems, 
such as Swift [53], Kepler [35], and VIEW [34] to support the 
discovery and reproducibility of scientific results.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
It has also 
been built as a standalone service, such as PreServ [29], to 
facilitate the integration of provenance component in more 
general computing models, and deal with trust issues in 
provenance assertion.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Using provenance information, scientists 


can debug workflow execution, validate or invalidate scientific 
results, and guide future workflow design and data exploration.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
While provenance has first shown its promise in scientific 
workflow systems [22] and database systems [47], a long-term 
vision is that provenance will be useful in other systems as 
well, necessitating the development of a standard, open, and 
universal representation and query model.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Currently, the 
provenance challenge series [39] and the open provenance 
model initiative [38] provide the active forums for these 
standardization effort and interaction.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
On the other hand, 
Clouds are becoming the future playground for e-science 
research, and provenance management is extremely important 
in order to track the processes and support the reproducibility 
of scientific results [45].
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Provenance is still an unexplored area 
in Cloud environments, in which we need to deal with even 
more challenging issues such as tracking data production 
across different service providers (with different platform 
visibility and access policies) and across different software and 
hardware abstraction layers within one provider.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In other 
words, capturing and managing provenance in Cloud 
environments may prove to be more difficult than in Grids, 
since in the latter there are already a few provenance systems 
and initiatives, however scalable provenance querying [55] and 
secure access of provenance information are still open 
problems for both Grids and Clouds environments.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
2.4 
Programming Model  
Although programming model in Grid environments does not 
differ fundamentally from traditional parallel and distributed 
environments, it is obviously complicated by issues such as 
multiple administrative domains; large variations in resource 
heterogeneity, stability and performance; exception handling in 
highly dynamic (in that resources can join and leave pretty 
much at any time) environments, etc.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Grids primarily target 
large-scale scientific computations, so it must scale to leverage 
large number/amount of resources, and we would also 
naturally want to make programs run fast and efficient in Grid 
environments, and programs also need to finish correctly, so 
reliability and fault tolerance must be considered.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We briefly discuss here some general programming models in 
Grids.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
MPI (Message Passing Interface) [36] is the most 
commonly used programming model in parallel computing, in 
which a set of tasks use their own local memory during 
computation and communicate by sending and receiving 
messages.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
MPICH-G2 [32] is a Grid enabled implementation 
of MPI.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
It gives the familiar interface of MPI while providing 
integration with the Globus Toolkit.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Coordination languages 
also allow a number of possibly heterogeneous components to 
communicate and interact, offering 
facilities 
for the 
specification, interaction, and dynamic composition of 
distributed (concurrent) components.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
For instance, Linda [1] 
defines a set of coordination primitives to put and retrieve 
tuples from a shared dataspace called the tuple space.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
It has 
been shown to be straightforward to use such primitives to 
implement a master-worker parallel scheduler.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The Ninf-G 
GridRPC [37] system integrates a Grid RPC (Remote 
Procedure Call) layer on top of the Globus toolkit.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
It publishes 
interfaces and function libraries in MDS, and utilizes GRAM 
to invoke remote executables.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In Grids, however, many 
applications are loosely coupled in that the output of one may 
be passed as input to one or more others—for example, as a 
file, or via a Web Services invocation.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
While such “loosely 
coupled” computations can involve large amounts of 
computation and communication, the concerns of the 
programmer tend to be different from those in traditional high 
performance computing, being focused on management issues 
relating to the large numbers of datasets and tasks rather than 
the optimization of interprocessor communication.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In such 
cases, workflow systems [54] suit better in the specification 
and execution of such applications.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
More specifically, a 
workflow system allows the composition of individual (single 
step) components into a complex dependency graph, and it 
governs the flow of data and/or control through these 
components.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
An example is the Swift system [53], which 
bridges scientific workflows with parallel computing.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
It is a 
parallel programming tool for rapid and reliable specification, 
execution, and management of large-scale science and 
engineering workflows.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The Swift runtime system relies on the 
CoG Karajan [33] workflow engine for efficient scheduling 
and load balancing, and it integrates the Falkon light-weight 
task execution service for optimized task throughput and 
resource efficiency [40].
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
WSRF (Web Services Resource 
Framework) has emerged from OGSA (Open Grid Service 
Architecture) [11] as more and more Grid applications are 
developed as services.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
WSRF allows Web Services to become 
stateful, and it provides a set of operations to set and retrieve 
the states (resources).
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The Globus Toolkit version 4 contains 
Java and C implementations of WSRF, most of the Globus 
core services have been re-engineered to build around WSRF, 
these altogether will enable service oriented Grid programming 
model.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
MapReduce [13] is only yet another parallel programming 
model, providing a programming model and runtime system 
for the processing of large datasets, and it is based on a simple 
model with just two key functions: “map” and “reduce,” 
borrowed from functional languages.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The map function applies 
a specific operation to each of a set of items, producing a new 
set of items; a reduce function performs aggregation on a set of 
items.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The 
MapReduce runtime 
system 
automatically 
partitions input data and schedules the execution of programs 
in a large cluster of commodity machines.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The system is made 
fault tolerant by checking worker nodes periodically and 
reassigning failed jobs to other worker nodes.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Sawzall is an 
interpreted language that builds on MapReduce and separates 
the filtering and aggregation phases for more concise program 
specification and better parallelization.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Hadoop [30] is the 
open source implementation of the MapReduce model, and Pig 
is a declarative programming language offered on top of 
Hadoop.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Microsoft has developed the Cosmos distributed 
storage system and Dryad processing framework, and offers 
DryadLINQ [31] and Scope as declarative programming model 
on top of the storage and computing infrastructure.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
DryadLINQ uses the object oriented LINQ query syntax where 
Scope provides basic operators similar to those of SQL such as 
Select, Join, Aggregation etc, both translate the abstract 
specification into detailed execution plan.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Mesh-up’s and scripting (Java Script, PHP, Python etc) have 
been taking the place of a workflow system in the Cloud world, 
since there is no easy way to integrate services and 
applications from various providers.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
They are essentially data 


integration approaches, because they take outputs from one 
service/application, transform them and feed into another.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Google App Engine uses a modified Python runtime and 
chooses Python scripting language for Web application 
development, the interface to its underlying BigTable storage 
system is some proprietary query language (named, as you 
would think, GQL) that is reminiscent of SQL, although all 
these will probably change.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Clouds (such as Amazon Web 
Services, Microsoft’s Azure Services Platform) have generally 
adopted Web Services APIs where users access, configure and 
program Cloud services using pre-defined APIs exposed as 
Web services, and HTTP and SOAP are the common protocols 
chosen for such services.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Although Clouds adopted some 
common communication protocols such as HTTP and SOAP, 
the integration and interoperability of all the services and 
applications remain the biggest challenge, as users need to tap 
into a federation of Clouds instead of a single Cloud provider.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
2.5 
Application Model 
Grids generally support many different kinds of applications, 
ranging from high performance computing (HPC) to high 
throughput computing (HTC).
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
HPC applications are efficient 
at executing tightly coupled parallel jobs within a particular 
machine with low-latency interconnects and are generally not 
executed across a wide area network Grid; these applications 
typically use message passing interface (MPI) to achieve the 
needed inter-process communication.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
On the other hand, Grids 
have also seen great success in the execution of more loosely 
coupled applications that tend to be managed and executed 
through workflow systems or other sophisticated and complex 
applications.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Related to HTC applications loosely coupled 
nature, there are other application classes, such Multiple 
Program Multiple Data (MPMD), MTC, capacity computing, 
utility computing, and embarrassingly parallel, each with their 
own niches [42].
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
These loosely coupled applications can be 
composed of many tasks (both independent and dependent 
tasks) that can be individually scheduled on many different 
computing resources across multiple administrative boundaries 
to achieve some larger application goal.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Tasks may be small or 
large, uniprocessor or multiprocessor, compute-intensive or 
data-intensive.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The set of tasks may be static or dynamic, 
homogeneous or heterogeneous, loosely or tightly coupled.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The aggregate number of tasks, quantity of computing, and 
volumes of data could be small but also extremely large.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
On the other hand, Cloud Computing could in principle cater 
to a similar set of applications.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The one exception that will 
likely be hard to achieve in Cloud Computing (but has had 
much success in Grids) are HPC applications that require fast 
and low latency network interconnects for efficient scaling to 
many processors.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
As Cloud Computing is still in its infancy, 
the applications that will run on Clouds are not well defined, 
but we can certainly characterize them to be loosely coupled, 
transaction oriented (small tasks in the order of milliseconds to 
seconds), and likely to be interactive (as opposed to batch-
scheduled as they are currently in Grids).
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Another emerging class of applications in Grids is scientific 
gateways [51], which are front-ends to a variety of applications 
that can be anything from loosely-coupled to tightly-coupled.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
A Science Gateway is a community-developed set of tools, 
applications, and data collections that are integrated via a 
portal or a suite of applications.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Gateways provide access to a 
variety of capabilities including workflows, visualization, 
resource discovery and job execution services through a 
browser-based user interface (which can arguably hide much 
of the complexities).
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Scientific gateways are beginning to 
adopt a wide variety of Web 2.0 technologies, but to date, 
much of the developments in Grids and Web 2.0 have been 
made in parallel with little interaction between them.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
These 
new technologies are important enhancements to the ways 
gateways interact with services and provide rich user 
interactivity.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Although scientific gateways have only emerged 
in Grids recently, Clouds seem to have adopted the use of 
gateways to Cloud resources almost exclusively for end-user 
interaction.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The browser and Web 2.0 technologies will 
undoubtedly play a central role on how users will interact with 
Grids and Clouds in the future.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
2.6 
Security Model 
Clouds mostly comprise dedicated data centers belonging to 
the same organization, and within each data center, hardware 
and software configurations, and supporting platforms are in 
general more homogeneous as compared with those in Grid 
environments.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Interoperability can become a serious issue for 
cross-data center, cross-administration domain interactions, 
imagine running your accounting service in Amazon EC2 
while your other business operations on Google infrastructure.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Grids however build on the assumption that resources are 
heterogeneous and dynamic, and each Grid site may have its 
own administration domain and operation autonomy.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Thus, 
security has been engineered in the fundamental Grid 
infrastructure.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The key issues considered are: single sign-on, 
so that users can log on only once and have access to multiple 
Grid sites, this will also facilitate accounting and auditing; 
delegation, so that a program can be authorized to access 
resources on a user’s behalf and it can further delegate to other 
programs; privacy, integrity and segregation, resources 
belonging to one user cannot be accessed by unauthorized 
users, and cannot be tampered during transfer; coordinated 
resource allocation, reservation, and sharing, taking into 
consideration of both global and local resource usage policies.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The public-key based GSI (Grid Security Infrastructure) 
protocols 
are 
used 
for 
authentication, 
communication 
protection, and authorization.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Furthermore, CAS (Community 
Authorization Service) is designed for advanced resource 
authorization within and across communities.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Gruber (A Grid 
Resource Usage SLA Broker) [14] is an example that has 
distributed policy enforcement points to enforce both local 
usage policies and global SLAs (Service Level Agreement), 
which allows resources at individual sites to be efficiently 
shared in multi-site, multi-VO environments.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Currently, the security model for Clouds seems to be relatively 
simpler and less secure than the security model adopted by 
Grids.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Cloud infrastructure typically rely on Web forms (over 
SSL) to create and manage account information for end-users, 
and allows users to reset their passwords and receive new 
passwords via Emails in an unsafe and unencrypted 
communication.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Note that new users could use Clouds 
relatively easily and almost instantly, with a credit card and/or 
email address.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
To contrast this, Grids are stricter about its 
security.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
For example, although web forms are used to manage 


user accounts, sensitive information about new accounts and 
passwords requires also a person to person conversation to 
verify the person, perhaps verification from a sponsoring 
person who already has an account, and passwords will only be 
faxed or mailed, but under no circumstance will they be 
emailed.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The Grid approach to security might be more time 
consuming, but it adds an extra level of security to help 
prevent unauthorized access.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Security is one of the largest concerns for the adoption of 
Cloud Computing.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We outline seven risks a Cloud user should 
raise with vendors before committing [6]: 1) Privileged user 
access: sensitive data processed outside the enterprise needs 
the assurance that they are only accessible and propagated to 
privileged users; 2) Regulatory compliance: a customer needs 
to verify if a Cloud provider has external audits and security 
certifications and if their infrastructure complies with some 
regulatory security requirements; 3) Data location: since a 
customer will not know where her data will be stored, it is 
important that the Cloud provider commit to storing and 
processing data in specific jurisdictions and to obey local 
privacy requirements on behalf of the customer; 4) Data 
segregation: one needs to ensure that one customer’s data is 
fully segregated from another customer’s data; 5) Recovery: it 
is important that the Cloud provider has an efficient replication 
and recovery mechanism to restore data if a disaster occurs; 6) 
Investigative support: Cloud services are especially difficult to 
investigate, if this is important for a customer, then such 
support needs to be ensured with a contractual commitment; 
and 7) Long-term viability: your data should be viable even the 
Cloud provider is acquired by another company.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
3 
Conclusions and lights to the future 
In this paper, we show that Clouds and Grids share a lot 
commonality in their vision, architecture and technology, but 
they also differ in various aspects such as security, 
programming model, business model, compute model, data 
model, applications, and abstractions.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We also identify 
challenges and opportunities in both fields.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We believe a close 
comparison such as this can help the two communities 
understand, share and evolve infrastructure and technology 
within and across, and accelerate Cloud Computing from early 
prototypes to production systems.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We will hazard a few predictions, 
based on our beliefs that the economics of computing will look 
more and more like those of energy.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Neither the energy nor the 
computing grids of tomorrow will look like yesterday’s 
electric power grid.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Both will move towards a mix of micro-
production and large utilities, with increasing numbers of 
small-scale producers (wind, solar, biomass, etc., for energy; 
for computing, local clusters and embedded processors—in 
shoes and walls) co-existing with large-scale regional 
producers, and load being distributed among them dynamically.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Yes, computing isn’t really like electricity, but we do believe 
that we will nevertheless see parallel evolution, driven by 
similar forces.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
In building this distributed “Cloud” or “Grid”, we will need to 
support on-demand provisioning and configuration of 
integrated “virtual systems” providing the precise capabilities 
needed by an end-user.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We will need to define protocols that 
allow users and service providers to discover and hand off 
demands to other providers, to monitor and manage their 
reservations, and arrange payment.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We will need tools for 
managing both the underlying resources and the resulting 
distributed computations.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
We will need the centralized scale of 
today’s Cloud utilities, and the distribution and interoperability 
of today’s Grid facilities.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Unfortunately, at least to date, the methods used to achieve 
these goals in today’s commercial clouds have not been open 
and general purpose, but instead been mostly proprietary and 
specialized for the specific internal uses (e.g., large-scale data 
analysis) of the companies that developed them.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
The idea that 
we might want to enable interoperability between providers (as 
in the electric power grid) has not yet surfaced.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Grid 
technologies and protocols speak precisely to these issues, and 
should be considered.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Some of the required protocols and tools will come from the 
smart people from the industry at Amazon, Google, Yahoo, 
Microsoft, and IBM.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Others will come from the smart people 
from academia and government labs.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
Others will come from 
those creating whatever we call this stuff after Grid and Cloud.
title: Cloud Computing and Grid Computing 360-Degree Compared

text:
It will be interesting to see to what extent these different 
communities manage to find common cause, or instead 
proceed along parallel paths.

Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing
Loads on Shared Cluster System for Large
Organization
Jianfeng Zhan∗, Lei Wang∗, Bibo Tu∗, Yong Li∗, Peng Wang∗, Wei Zhou∗and Dan Meng∗
∗Institute of Computing Technology,Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing, China 100190
† Email: jfzhan@ncic.ac.cn
Abstract—Different departments of a large organization often
run dedicated cluster systems for different computing loads,
like HPC (high performance computing) jobs or Web service
applications.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
In this paper, we have designed and implemented a
cloud management system software Phoenix Cloud to consolidate
heterogeneous workloads from different departments afﬁliated
to the same organization on the shared cluster system.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
We have
also proposed cooperative resource provisioning and management
policies for a large organization and its afﬁliated departments,
running HPC jobs and Web service applications, to share
the consolidated cluster system.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
The experiments show that in
comparison with the case that each department operates its
dedicated cluster system, Phoenix Cloud signiﬁcantly decreases
the scale of the required cluster system for a large organization,
improves the beneﬁt of the scientiﬁc computing department,
and at the same time provisions enough resources to the other
department running Web services with varying loads.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
INTRODUCTION
Since 2007, a client from a large organization, which we
keep anonymous at its request, requires us to build the system
software for managing a shared infrastructure.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
This large
organization has two representative departments: one running
a batch queuing system for HPC jobs, and the other one
responsible of providing Web services, of which the ratios of
peak loads to normal loads are high.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
So two representative
departments from this big organization have operated two
cluster systems with independent administration staffs and
found many annoying problems: ﬁrst, resource utilization rates
of two cluster systems are varying.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
For peak loads, dedicated
cluster systems can not provision enough resources, while for
normal loads lots of resources are idle; second, the number
of administration staffs for two separated cluster systems is
high.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
The client inquired us whether it is possible to help
them consolidate two cluster systems on one shared system.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
At same time, we have noticed that many famous IT com-
panies are advocating and experiencing cloud computing.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
For
example, Amazon [1] has provided cloud computing services
like elastic computing cloud (EC2) and simple storage service

summary of experiences of this project, which also available from the
web site of the First Workshop of Cloud Computing and its Applica-
tion (http://www.cca08.org/papers/Poster-8-Jianfeng-Zhan.pdf).
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
The extended
version with the title of PhoenixCloud: Provisioning Resources for Het-
erogeneous Workloads in Cloud Computing can be downloaded from
http://arxiv.org/abs/1006.1401.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
What is the link between services provided
by Amazon and the requirement of our anonymous client?
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
In
our opinion, driven by the cost, cloud computing is a new wave
of reconstructing and consolidating data centers.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
Traditional
cluster system software is self-containing [2], inadequate for
adapting to this change.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
EC2 and S3 are big efforts to
provide virtualized hosting environments for end users, but
it can not provide the customized system stack software to
consolidate heterogeneous loads on shared cluster systems for
large organizations.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text: In fact, there lies no one-ﬁt-all solution.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
In this paper, we focus on developing cloud computing
management software that enables the consolidation of het-
erogeneous workloads on shared cluster systems for large
organizations, and we stress that we do not target the design
of capability-oriented system software stack [3].
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
To the best
of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst paper to propose the layered
architecture of cloud computing management software for
large organizations that intend to consolidate heterogeneous
workloads from different departments on shared cluster sys-
tems.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
[4] proposes the utility computing service framework to
facilitate code reuse in the context of traditional data centers,
but do not consider how to enable consolidating different types
of workloads.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
[5] [6] propose Cluster on Demand(COD) as a
new mechanism for dynamical cluster resource management
in the contexts of Internet hosting center [5] or scientiﬁc
computing [6], but their works mainly focus on dynamic
resource provisioning in respective computing contexts.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
The distinguished differences of our system and architecture
from others are that: ﬁrst, we develop a common service
framework as a foundation for cloud computing system soft-
ware; second, with the support of a common service frame-
work, we create cloud management services respectively for
scientiﬁc computing (HPC jobs) and web service applications;
third, we propose optimal resource management and provision
policies for heterogeneous workloads to cooperatively share
cluster resources.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
The contribution of this paper can be con-
cluded as:
• We have designed and implemented a cloud manage-
ment system software Phoenix Cloud with the layered
architecture to consolidated HPC jobs and Web service
applications on shared cluster systems.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
• We have proposed cooperative resource provisioning and
management policies for a large organization and its


2
afﬁliated departments to share the cluster system.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
• Our experiments show that in comparison with the case
that each department maintains its dedicated cluster sys-
tem, consolidating HPC jobs and Web service applica-
tions with cooperative resource provisioning and man-
agement policies can signiﬁcantly decrease the scale of
the required cluster system for a large organization, at the
same time improve the beneﬁt of the scientiﬁc comput-
ing department while provisioning enough resources to
the department who runs Web service applications with
varying loads.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
In Section II, we explain
the design and implementation issue of Phoenix Cloud.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION ISSUES
In Section II-A, we introduce the layered architecture of
Phoenix Cloud.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
In Section II-B, we propose cooperative re-
source provision and management policies for Phoenix Cloud.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
The Layered Architecture of Phoenix Cloud
We divide our cloud computing management software into
three independent layers: shared infrastructure for the resource
provider, cloud management services for service providers
who are different departments afﬁliated to the same large
organization, and client tools for end user.

text:
Cooperative Resource Provision and Management Policies
In this section, we propose cooperative resource provision-
ing and management policies for a large organization and its
afﬁliated departments.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
As shown in Fig.2, we could specify the
resource provisioning policy for Resource Provision Service,
and different resource management policies for ST Server and
WS Server.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
The resource provisioning policy is as follows:
• The resource demands from WS Server have higher
priority than that of ST Server.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
• If there are idle resources for Resource Provision Service,
it will provision all idle resources to ST Server.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
• If WS Server claims urgent resources, Resource Provision
Service will force ST Server to return resources with the
size claimed by WS Server and then reallocate to WS
Server.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
The resource management policy of ST server is as follows:
• ST Server passively receives resources provisioned by
Resource Provision Service.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
• If Resource Provision Service forces ST Server to return
resources, the latter will release resources immediately
with the size demanded by the former.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
• If there are no enough idle resources for ST Server, it
will kill jobs in turn from the beginning of job with
minimum size and shortest running time, and release
enough resources to Resource Provision Service.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
The resource management policy of WS Server is as follows:
• If WS Server owns idle resources, it will release them
to Resource Provision Service immediately.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
If WS Server
needs more resources, it will request enough resources
from Resource Provision Service.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
EVALUATION AND DISCUSSION
In this section, we will demonstrate that with the cooper-
ative resource provision and management policies proposed
in Section II-B, consolidating HPC jobs and Web services
on the shared cluster system, of which we call dynamic
conﬁguration, can decrease the cost of a large organization
in term of resource consumption in comparison with the
static conﬁguration, of which each department maintains its
dedicated cluster system.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
The beneﬁt and cost models
For a large organization, we use the size of nodes to measure
the cost of owning a cluster system.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
For HPC jobs, we use the
number of completed jobs to measure the beneﬁt of a service
provider; at the same time, we use the reciprocal of the average
turnaround time per job to measure the beneﬁt of end user.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
For Web service application, we use the throughput in term of
request/second to measure the beneﬁt of a service provider; at
the same time we use the average response time of requests
to measure the beneﬁt of an end user.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
CONCLUSIONS
Different departments of large organizations often maintain
dedicated cluster systems for different computing loads.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
In
this paper, we have designed and implemented a cloud man-
agement system software Phoenix Cloud to consolidate HPC
jobs and Web service application on the shared cluster system.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
We have also proposed cooperative resource provisioning and
management policies of large organizations and their afﬁliated
departments to share the consolidated cluster systems.
title: Phoenix Cloud: Consolidating Different Computing Loads Shared Cluster System Large Organization

text:
Our
experiments show that in comparison with the case that each
department of the same large organization runs its dedicated
cluster system, consolidating HPC jobs and Web service appli-
cations from different departments with cooperative resource
provisioning and management policies not only signiﬁcantly
decreases the scale of the required cluster system for a large
organization, but also improves the beneﬁt of the scientiﬁc
computing departments while provisioning enough resources
to the other department running Web service applications with
varying loads.

ZHONGXIAO JIA∗AND DATIAN NIU†
Abstract.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
The harmonic Lanczos bidiagonalization method can be used to compute the small-
est singular triplets of a large matrix A.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We prove that for good enough projection subspaces
harmonic Ritz values converge if the columns of A are strongly linearly independent.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
On the other
hand, harmonic Ritz values may miss some desired singular values when the columns of A almost
linearly dependent.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Furthermore, harmonic Ritz vectors may converge irregularly and even may
fail to converge.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Based on the reﬁned projection principle for large matrix eigenproblems due to
the ﬁrst author, we propose a reﬁned harmonic Lanczos bidiagonalization method that takes the
Rayleigh quotients of the harmonic Ritz vectors as approximate singular values and extracts the
best approximate singular vectors, called the reﬁned harmonic Ritz approximations, from the given
subspaces in the sense of residual minimizations.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
The reﬁned approximations are shown to converge
to the desired singular vectors once the subspaces are suﬃciently good and the Rayleigh quotients
converge.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
An implicitly restarted reﬁned harmonic Lanczos bidiagonalization algorithm (IRRHLB)
is developed.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We study how to select the best possible shifts, and suggest reﬁned harmonic shifts that
are theoretically better than the harmonic shifts used within the implicitly restarted Lanczos bidi-
agonalization algorithm (IRHLB).
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We propose a novel procedure that can numerically compute the
reﬁned harmonic shifts eﬃciently and accurately.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Numerical experiments are reported that compare
IRRHLB with ﬁve other algorithms based on the Lanczos bidiagonalization process.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
It appears that
IRRHLB is at least competitive with them and can be considerably more eﬃcient when computing
the smallest singular triplets.

Therefore, we obtain the following formulation of

title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Compute numerically the k smallest positive eigenvalues and the
associated eigenvectors of ˜A.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
For the k smallest eigenpairs of ˜A, Problem 2 is a symmetric interior eigenvalue
problem.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Since M and N are assumed to be large, we can only resort to projection
methods.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text: A typical method is the symmetric Lanczos method [28].
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
It and other
standard projection methods usually favor the extreme eigenvalues and the associated
eigenvectors but are generally very ineﬃcient for computing interior eigenpairs [28].
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Another drawback is that in ﬁnite precision the computed eigenvalues do not come
in plus-and-minus pairs and the computed eigenvectors do not respect the special
structures that the true eigenvectors have.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Because of the mentioned drawbacks, we should not work on ˜A explicitly for
computing the smallest singular triplets of A.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Instead we attempt to solve Problem
1 directly by working on ˜A implicitly.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
It appears that Lanczos bidiagonalization type
methods [3, 11, 12, 20, 22, 24, 29] and Jacobi-Davidson SVD type methods [11, 12] can
solve the mentioned problems elegantly.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
The Lanczos bidiagonalization type methods
available have in common that they are all based on the Lanczos bidiagonalization
process to build up orthonormal bases of certain Krylov subspaces.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
However, their
mathematical backgrounds can be fundamentally diﬀerent.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Basically, there are three
kinds of projection principles that extract diﬀerent approximate singular triplets with
respect to the subspaces.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Some methods use the standard projection principle [2, 28,
32] to extract Ritz approximations [3, 4, 10, 11, 12, 20, 24, 29, 33], some methods use
the harmonic projection principle [2, 32, 34] to extract harmonic Ritz approximations
[3, 4, 11, 12, 22] and some methods use the reﬁned projection principle [2, 13, 32, 34] to
extract reﬁned singular vector approximations [12, 20, 22].
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Jacobi-Davidson type SVD
methods for Problem 1 have several versions that are based on the three projection
principles as well as their generalizations, respectively.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
As observed and claimed in
[3, 12], the reﬁned extraction version appears to give the best accuracy in general.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
For Problem 1, due to the storage requirement and computational cost, all the
Lanczos bidiagonalization type methods as well as Jacobi-Davidson type methods
have to be restarted generally in order to make them converge.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
That is, for given
projection subspaces, if the methods do not converge, then one repeatedly chooses
new better starting vectors, constructs better subspaces and computes new approx-
imate singular triplets until they converge.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
The implicit restarting technique due to
Sorensen [30] is a powerful tool for restarting Krylov subspace algorithms in various
contexts including large SVD problems [3, 4, 11, 12, 20, 22, 24, 29].
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
The success of an


A REFINED HARMONIC LANCZOS BIDIAGONALIZATION METHOD
3
implicitly restarted algorithm heavily depends on both the underlying method itself
and a proper selection of the shifts involved; see, e.g., [15, 30].
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Based on the Lanc-
zos bidiagonalization method and one of its harmonic versions, Jia and Niu [20] and
Larsen [24] have developed an implicitly restarted Lanczos bidiagonalization algorithm
(IRLB), and Kokiopoulou et al.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
[22] have proposed an implicitly restarted harmonic
Lanczos bidiagonalization algorithm (IRLANB) for computing the smallest singular
triplets.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
IRLB uses the unwanted Ritz values and IRLANB uses the unwanted Ritz
or harmonic Ritz values as shifts, respectively.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
These shifts are called exact shifts
and harmonic shifts.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Baglama and Reichel [3, 4] propose a thick restarting technique
that explicitly augments small subspaces with certain Ritz or harmonic Ritz vectors,
leading to augmented restarted Lanczos bidiagonalization algorithms (IRLBA).
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text: [10] analyze a parallel implementation of this algorithm.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Based on
Stewart’s work for large eigenproblems [31], Stoll [33] presents a Krylov-Schur type
algorithm that is restarted explicitly and is easily implemented.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
It is shown in [20] that the Lanczos bidiagonalization method may fail to com-
pute singular vectors though it converges for computing singular values for suﬃciently
good subspaces.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
To correct this deﬁciency, applying the reﬁned projection principle
proposed by the ﬁrst author [13] (see also [2, 32, 34]), we have proposed a reﬁned
Lanczos bidiagonalization method, analyzed its convergence and developed an implic-
itly restarted reﬁned Lanczos bidiagonalization algorithm (IRRLB) [20].
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Based on the
reﬁned approximations to singular vectors, we have proposed reﬁned shifts that are
theoretically better than the exact shifts used within IRLB.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Numerical experiments
have demonstrated that IRRLB often outperforms IRLB [20, 24] considerably and is
more eﬃcient than several other available schemes: PROPACK [24], LANSO [23, 24],
the MATLAB internal function svds and some others when computing the largest and
smallest singular triplets.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Hochstenbach [11, 12] shows that for nested subspaces Ritz values approach the
largest singular values monotonically but approach the smallest ones irregularly.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
So
the Lanczos bidiagonalization method is more suitable for computing the largest sin-
gular triplets and may exhibit irregular convergence behavior when computing the
smallest singular triplets.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
In contrast, the smallest harmonic Ritz values converge to
the smallest singular values monotonically from above and may be better approxi-
mations.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We continue to study how to compute the smallest singular triplets more
eﬃciently in this paper.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Based on the Lanczos bidiagonalization process, we propose
a harmonic Lanczos bidiagonalization method by combining it with the harmonic
projection principle.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text: Our derivation is diﬀerent from that in [3, 22].
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
The method is
the same as that in [3] but diﬀerent from the one in [22].
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We prove that for good
enough projection subspaces harmonic Ritz values converge if the columns of A are
strongly linearly independent.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
On the other hand, harmonic Ritz values may miss
some desired singular values when the columns of A are almost linearly dependent.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text: So harmonic Ritz values may not be reliable.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Furthermore, harmonic Ritz vectors
may converge irregularly and even may fail to converge.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
These results imply that
either implicitly or explicitly restarted algorithms may converge very slowly, con-
verge irregularly or fail to converge.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
To circumvent these drawbacks, combining the
harmonic projection principle with the harmonic projection principle, we propose a
reﬁned harmonic Lanczos bidiagonalization method that takes the Rayleigh quotients
of harmonic Ritz vectors as more accurate and reliable approximate singular values
and extracts the best approximations to the desired singular vectors from the given
subspaces that minimize the residuals formed with the Rayleigh quotients.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We prove


4
ZHONGXIAO JIA AND DATIAN NIU
that reﬁned harmonic Ritz approximations converge once the Krylov subspaces are
good enough and the Rayleigh quotients converge.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We then develop an implicitly
restarted reﬁned harmonic Lanczos bidiagonalization algorithm (IRRHLB).
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Based on
the reﬁned harmonic Ritz approximations to the desired singular vectors, in the spirit
of Jia’s work [15, 17], we propose a new shifts scheme, called the reﬁned harmonic
shifts, that we show to be theoretically better than the harmonic shifts used within
the implicitly restarted harmonic Lanczos bidiagonalization algorithm (IRHLB) and
IRLANB.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Motivated by [15, 17], we propose an eﬃcient procedure to compute the
reﬁned harmonic shifts accurately.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text: It is worth noting that Kokiopoulou et al.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
[22] also use the reﬁned projection prin-
ciple to compute the reﬁned harmonic Ritz approximations.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
They exploit the lower
Lanczos bidiagonalization process, use the Ritz or harmonic Ritz values as shifts in
the algorithm and compute the smallest singular triplets one by one by exploiting de-
ﬂation.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
They only use the reﬁned projection principle as reﬁnement postprocessing at
the end of each restart.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
The authors demonstrate that computing reﬁned (harmonic)
Ritz vectors and thus reﬁned Ritz values beneﬁts the overall convergence process.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
In
particular, they show that while convergence is not apparent in terms of harmonic
residual norms, monitoring reﬁned residuals predicts convergence more accurately
and safely.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
In contrast, based on the upper Lanczos bidiagonalization process and
the reﬁned projection principle, we propose a truly new method–the reﬁned harmonic
Lanczos bidiagonalization method that computes reﬁned harmonic Ritz vectors as new
approximations.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We then develop IRRHLB with use of the new better shifts, called
reﬁned harmonic shifts, based on reﬁned harmonic Ritz approximations.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
IRRHLB
computes all the desired smallest singular triplets simultaneously.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
In §2, based on the Lanczos bidiagonalization
process, we derive the harmonic Lanczos bidiagonalization method and then present
some basic and important properties of approximate singular vectors to be used later.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text: Exploiting Jia’s results in [19], we then make a convergence analysis.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
In §3 we propose
the reﬁned harmonic Lanczos bidiagonalization method.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We prove that the reﬁned
harmonic Ritz approximations converge for good enough subspaces once the Rayleigh
quotients converge.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text: In §4, we consider selection of the shifts involved.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
For IRHLB,
similar to what is done in [3, 22], we use the harmonic Ritz values.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
For IRRHLB,
by exploiting the available reﬁned harmonic Ritz approximations, we propose the
reﬁned harmonic shifts that are proved to be theoretically better than the harmonic
shifts.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text: We then present an eﬃcient procedure to compute them.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We show that in
ﬁnite precision the reﬁned harmonic shifts can be computed accurately.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Meanwhile,
we extend the adaptive shifting strategy proposed by Larsen [24] and modiﬁed by
Jia and Niu [20] to IRHLB and IRRHLB.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
In §5, we report numerical results and
compare IRRHLB with the ﬁve other state of art algorithms: IRHLB, IRRLB, IRLB,
IRLANB and IRLBA, indicating that IRRHLB is at least competitive with the ﬁve
other algorithms and can be considerably more eﬃcient when computing the smallest
singular triplets.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text: Finally, we conclude the paper with some remarks in §6.

until 10−14, the accuracy of the computed singular values was not improved further
as residual norms decreased from opts.tol = 1e −12 to opts.tol = 1e −14.

text:
This was
reﬂected by the ﬁgures, where we saw that relative errors did not decrease further and
stabilized, starting from some restart for each s except s = 9.

All these are in accordance with the predicted relative errors, which should
not be bigger than a very modest multiple of κ(As) × opts.tol.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Another important
observation is that IRRHLB used more restarts as s increases.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Since the ratio σN −σ1
σ2−σ1 ,

IRRHLB to solve the SVD problem as s increases.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We also saw that the curves of
relative errors oscillated quite often in the middle of convergence processes.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
A careful
observation revealed that IRRHLB started to be on its way to compute the desired
singular value at some stage but lost it soon.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Then it adaptively adjusted convergence
repeatedly and eventually was on the correct way to converge.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
These phenomena may
be explained by Theorem 2.3 and the comments followed.

less eﬃcient than IRRHLB if they worked.

was, the more restarts IRRHLB and IRRLB used for the same m.

surprising as the problem for a bigger k is generally more diﬃcult to solve than that
for a smaller k.

with relative errors no more than a modest multiple of κ(A) × 10−6.

text:
The ﬁgures clearly demonstrate that IRRHLB is the fastest, IRRLB is the second
best, IRHLB is faster than IRLB while IRHLB, IRLB, IRLBA and IRLANB are com-
parable and competitive though IRLANB may be slightly slower.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
The tables tell us
that IRHLB was faster than IRLB.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
We see from the ﬁgures that after some stages
the algorithms started converging quite smoothly and they used more but not too
more restarts for the smaller opts.tol = 1e −9.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Besides, for IRLANB, we see that
they computed the smallest singular triplet after many restarts then found the second
and third smallest singular triplets very quickly.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
This is because after the previous
singular triplet(s) was (were) computed the available subspaces had contained rich
information on the later desired singular vectors.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text: We have done more experiments and have similar ﬁndings.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Based on them, we
may conclude that IRRHLB is the best and the most robust for general purpose
and IRRLB is the second best.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
As far as overall eﬃciency is concerned, in terms
of restarts and matrix-vector products, IRRHLB is the fastest and IRRLB is the
second best while IRHLB, IRLB, IRLBA and IRLANB are all comparable each other
and no one is considerably superior to the others.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
That IRRHLB is superior to IRRLB and IRHLB is better
than IRLB sheds light on the fact argued in the introduction: The reﬁned harmonic
projection and the harmonic projection are more suitable for computing the smallest
singular triplets than the reﬁned standard projection and the standard projection,
respectively.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

text:
Meanwhile, we ﬁnd that, as far as CPU timings are concerned, IRRHLB
can be inferior to IRLBA.
title: arXiv:0906.2242v1  [math.NA]  12 Jun 2009

sparse, so that the savings of the ﬁrst k + 3 steps of the Lanczos bidiagonalization
process cannot compensate implicit restarting with m −(k + 3) shifts, and partly

ABSTRACT 
Cloud computing represents a shift away from computing as a 
product that is purchased, to computing as a service that is 
delivered to consumers over the internet from large-scale data 
centers – or ‘clouds’.
title: Proceedings Template - WORD

text:
This paper discusses some of the research 
challenges for cloud computing from an enterprise or 
organizational perspective, and puts them in context by reviewing 
the existing body of literature in cloud computing.
title: Proceedings Template - WORD

text:
Various 
research challenges relating to the following topics are discussed: 
the organizational changes brought about by cloud computing; the 
economic and organizational implications of its utility billing 
model; the security, legal and privacy issues that cloud computing 
raises.
title: Proceedings Template - WORD

text:
It is important to highlight these research challenges 
because cloud computing is not simply about a technological 
improvement of data centers but a fundamental change in how IT 
is provisioned and used.
title: Proceedings Template - WORD

text:
This type of research has the potential to 
influence wider adoption of cloud computing in enterprise, and in 
the consumer market too.
title: Proceedings Template - WORD
