High-Performance Physics Simulations Using Multi-Core CPUs 
and GPGPUs in a Volunteer Computing Context 
 
 
Kamran Karimi 
Neil G.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Dickson Firas Hamze 
 
D-Wave Systems Inc.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
100-4401 Still Creek Drive 
Burnaby, British Columbia 
Canada, V5C 6G9 
{kkarimi, ndickson, fhamze}@dwavesys.com 
 
 
Abstract  
This paper presents two conceptually simple methods for parallelizing a Parallel 
Tempering Monte Carlo simulation in a distributed volunteer computing context, where 
computers belonging to the general public are used.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The first method uses conventional 
multi-threading.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: The second method uses CUDA, a graphics card computing system.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Parallel Tempering is described, and challenges such as parallel random number 
generation and mapping of Monte Carlo chains to different threads are explained.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
While 
conventional multi-threading on CPUs is well-established, GPGPU programming 
techniques and technologies are still developing and present several challenges, such as 
the effective use of a relatively large number of threads.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Having multiple chains in 
Parallel Tempering allows parallelization in a manner that is similar to the serial 
algorithm.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Volunteer computing introduces important constraints to high performance 
computing, and we show that both versions of the application are able to adapt 
themselves to the varying and unpredictable computing resources of volunteers’ 
computers, while leaving the machines responsive enough to use.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We present 
experiments to show the scalable performance of these two approaches, and indicate that 
the efficiency of the methods increases with bigger problem sizes.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Introduction 
Many fields of science and technology require vast computational resources.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Simulation 
of physical systems is one notable example.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Insufficient computing power can result in 
unfeasibly long running times or poor accuracy of results.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Parallelizing such applications 
enables use of more processing power.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
However, parallelization of different applications 
may need different approaches in order to effectively use the processing units.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In this 
paper, we parallelize a common Monte Carlo simulation technique known as Parallel 
Tempering Monte Carlo (PTMC) [8].
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We focus on two technologies that enable parallelism: 1) multi-core Central Processing 
Units (CPU), and 2) streaming processors on Graphics Processing Units (GPU) [15].
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In 
particular, we use NVIDIA’s CUDA for GPU processing [15], though similar design 
principles may be applied to other GPU brands.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Our primary design goals have been 
suitability for a volunteer computing environment, simplicity of the parallelization 


method, and low synchronization overhead.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
All of these goals have been achieved by 
leveraging the characteristics of our original (serial) algorithm.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The nature of Parallel Tempering Monte Carlo allows us to partition a large simulation 
into smaller, independent simulations, groups of which can be solved by threads on a 
CPU.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The number of threads is chosen to be the same as the number of cores present in 
the system to avoid cache contention among the threads.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
GPGPUs allow for the execution 
of threads on a larger number of processing elements.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Although these processing 
elements are typically much slower than those of a CPU, having a large number of 
threads may make it possible to surpass the performance of current multi-core CPUs.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In GPU programming, the creation of small, short-lived threads has been emphasized as a 
means towards achieving good speedup.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
An example would be multiplying two matrices, 
which can be done by dividing the task into threads, each of which computes one element 
of the target matrix.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
This low-level parallelism can be used in many algorithms and has 
been a significant source of GPU parallelization success.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We show that, similar to CPU 
multi-threading, one can design a suitable GPU parallel algorithm that uses a coarser 
level of parallelization, running longer sequences of code on each GPU processor.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
One matter that differs between multi-threaded CPU and GPU programming is memory 
structure.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In a multi-threaded CPU application, all threads have access to a common 
memory space, so the primary challenge is synchronizing access to shared data structures.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
GPU programming, on the other hand, involves threads that run in a separate memory 
space from the main application, (which runs on the CPU).
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The implication is that the 
code and the data on which the GPU threads operate must be transferred to the GPU 
memory before any processing can be started, and the results of the computation must be 
copied back to the main memory of a host computer.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
This data transfer can result in poor 
performance and must be kept to a minimum.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
It is thus important to make sure that the 
time spent processing data on the GPU is long compared to data transfer times.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Another characteristic of parallel programming with GPUs is the ability to start a large 
number of threads with little overhead [15].
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
This is unlike traditional CPU threads, where 
each individual thread is treated as an entity independent of others, requiring separate 
resources such as stack memory, and whose creation and management (scheduling, 
keeping statistics of resource usage, etc.) are not cheap [15].
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
To absorb these costs, one 
option is to create as few CPU threads as possible and to make them run as long as 
possible.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
GPU threads, on the other hand, are cheaper to create and manage, since batches 
of GPU threads (blocks) are treated the same, so it is possible to create a large number of 
them and run them for shorter durations.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The specific application examined in this paper, called Adiabatic QUantum Algorithms 
(AQUA) [16], uses a Quantum Monte Carlo [3] algorithm to compute the minimum 
energy gap between two quantum states undergoing an adiabatic evolution.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
These 
simulations require substantial computational resources, and we need to solve many 
problem instances.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We have employed the Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network 


Computing (BOINC) [2], to create the AQUA@home project and run the AQUA 
application on volunteers’ computers in a massively distributed manner.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: Resorting to volunteer computing entails serious considerations.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
An application that runs 
on a volunteer’s computer cannot drain the computing resources, as that would make it 
hard for the volunteer to use his or her machine.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
It also cannot dynamically communicate 
with other computers.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The problem of varying system resources and processing power on 
different computers must also be considered.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Our algorithm has been designed with these 
constraints in mind, and the first constraint has had a large effect on the design of the 
GPU version.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The problem is that using a GPU at full throttle makes the computer’s user 
interface very slow or even non-responding, so caution must be used.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: The rest of the paper is organized as follows.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Section 2 briefly presents the PTMC 
algorithm and how its design naturally leads to parallel execution.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Section 3 describes the 
method we used to parallelize random number generation similarly in both the CPU and 
GPU environments.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Section 4 shows how our application was parallelized to use multiple 
CPU cores, while Section 5 explains the corresponding design for the GPU.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We dedicate 
more space to the description of GPU parallelization because it is a less developed topic.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: Section 6 presents the results of performance and scalability tests.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Parallel Tempering Monte Carlo 
GPUs have been used to speed up QMC simulations before [1].
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In those 
implementations, the parallelized components are primarily low-level matrix operations.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Here, we present PTMC as an algorithm that is particularly well-suited for parallel 
execution.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
This variant allows a natural mapping of the algorithm to parallel execution 
units such as a CPU’s cores or a GPU’s streaming processors, enabling a high-level break 
down of the algorithm.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
PTMC is based on the idea of running multiple Markov chains (sometimes referred to as 
replica) at the same time, each of which has as its stationary distribution that of the 
system at a different temperature.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
After a certain number of sweeps through all of the 
chains, i.e.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
flipping bits with the Metropolis algorithm according to the relevant 
temperatures [11], adjacent chains are probabilistically swapped.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The probability of a 
chain swap is determined by the relative probability of the chains’ states occurring at 
each other’s temperature.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In a non-parallel implementation of PTMC, the program would 
sequentially iterate through the set of chains to perform a sweep.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
After all the chains have 
been swept the required number of times, the program attempts to swap the chains.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
This 
cycle continues until the application’s criteria for termination, such as a specified number 
of sweeps or satisfaction of a convergence test are met.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
More information about our 
implementation of Parallel Tempering comes in [7].
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Each Monte Carlo chain can be swept independently of the others, so sweeping can be 
done in parallel.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In our implementation, swapping chains can also be parallelized, 
because we consider only every two neighboring chains as possible swapping candidates, 


and then move to the next two chains.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
With N chains, up to N/2 swap operations could be 
done concurrently.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Selecting logical temperature values to achieve a desired minimum swap rate, even in the 
presence of first-order phase transitions, is described in [7].
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
After the process of chain 
generation, the number of chains and their temperature values are held constant during 
the PTMC simulation.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In this paper we consider the chains to have been already 
generated.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Parallel Random Number Generation 
PTMC simulations, like other stochastic methods, depend on a vast supply of 
(pseudo)random numbers, because both sweeping a chain and swapping chains require 
random numbers.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
It is very important to make sure that in a parallel environment, random 
numbers are generated in a fast and valid manner.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The original (serial) version of our application uses the well-known Mersenne-Twister 
algorithm [9].
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The code for this algorithm is compact and contains simple integer 
operations.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
It relies on a global state vector and an index into that vector to generate 
random integers.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
This global set of variables makes it difficult to run the algorithm in 
parallel.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Enforcing mutually exclusive access to this data structure through locks would 
cause poor performance, as a significant portion of time would be spent generating 
random numbers in serial.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
A simple and effective solution to this problem is to create multiple state vectors, one for 
each CPU thread.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Even though the code remains almost identical, each thread uses its 
own state to generate the next random number.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Each chain’s state has a different initial 
seed to prevent the problem of generating the same random numbers for different chains 
at every step.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
This simple solution allows us to maintain the same per-thread random 
number generation speed as in the single-thread case, with no compromise on the quality 
of the results.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
On a CPU, each chain is swept by a single core, but as explained later, on a GPU, each 
chain is swept by a number of streaming processors.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In both cases, a state vector is 
created for every execution thread that could be running in parallel with other execution 
threads to avoid the need for synchronization.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
As a result, on the CPU, a chain has a 
single random state, while on the GPU, each divisible part of a chain has its own random 
state.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Figures 1, 2, and 3 show how the original (serial), multi-threaded, and GPU versions 
initialize 
their 
Mersenne-Twister 
states, 
respectively.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The 
Mersenne-Twister 
implementation itself is effectively identical between the three.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv
MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: Original (serial) Mersenne-Twister initialization.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
#define MT_STATE_LENGTH 624 
static void initializeRandom(unsigned long seed, 
                         unsigned long* randomState, 
                         int& randomIndex); 
...
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv
MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: Multi-threaded Mersenne-Twister initialization.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv
MT-CUDA-arxiv
MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Multi-Threading on Multi-Core CPUs 
We parallelized the sweep and swap parts of the Parallel Tempering code using OpenMP 
[5].
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
By default, OpenMP creates the same number of threads as the number of available 
cores in the computer.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Since this number is currently less than the number of chains 
(typically 4 or 8 cores vs.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
25 to 200 chains), each thread is responsible for sweeping 
multiple chains.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: An alternative to one thread per core is to have one thread per chain.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
For a small number 
of chains, this scheme can have advantages in terms of less time spent in waiting on 
barriers.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
However, miscellaneous timing tests suggested that even for a relatively small 


number of chains, the performance was worse.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We suspect this to be because of increased 
CPU cache misses and thread management overhead.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
When parallelizing a loop with I iterations, where each iteration of the loop can be done 
independently, OpenMP assigns I/N iterations (or one of the nearest integers thereof) to 
each of the N threads.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Its default behavior is to start the worker threads when the loop is 
encountered, and wait for all threads to finish their iterations before continuing.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Figure 4 
shows the outline of our first attempt at parallelizing the Parallel Tempering algorithm.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv
MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Outline of Parallel Tempering with OpenMP 
 
In Figure 4, chains contains a pointer to the Parallel Tempering chain data.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Each thread is thus responsible for running the inner loop for one 
or more chain values.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
To indicate that OpenMP should parallelize the for-loop, one adds 
the #pragma statement.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
No data that are modified within the for-loop are shared between 
the threads, so they can run with no need for synchronization.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In this code the threads join 
before the doSwap() method.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: In our simulation, different chains are at different effective temperatures.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Chains at higher 
temperatures have more bit flips and therefore require more work to update the state after 
a flip.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
OpenMP’s default assignment of chains to threads does not result in a balanced 
load distribution, because it assigns successive chains to each thread, resulting in some 
threads with many easy (cold) chains and some threads with many hard (hot) chains.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Therefore, we form a work pool of chains, and start by assigning harder chains to each 
available thread in a first-come, first-served manner.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We 
observe the number of active cores to determine the efficiency of our work-assignment 
method, and the described method results in all the cores being occupied most of the 
time.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Further improvement in CPU utilization was achieved by keeping the threads active 
throughout the simulation.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
However, barriers must then be specified explicitly to 
synchronize the threads between phases.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Swapping was also parallelized, so it required 
the current thread index and the total number of threads.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: Figure 5 shows the relevant code that implements the above improvements.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv
MT-CUDA-arxiv
MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: Keeping threads active; sweeping loop with workpool.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: AQUA@home is the first BOINC project to support CPU multi-threading.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
With BOINC, 
the user can determine how many cores are to be used, so BOINC provides the 
application with the number of threads that should be created.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
BOINC usually runs an 
application at a below-normal priority to make sure the computer remains responsive.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: However, this priority level is not respected for newly created OpenMP threads.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
AQUA 
explicitly sets the priority of all the newly created OpenMP threads to the same value as 
determined by BOINC.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
As a result, even though AQUA has a high CPU utilization rate 
(about 94% on 8-core computers), we have observed that the above method of 
parallelizing the PTMC algorithm allows volunteers to continue to use and interact with 
their machines.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Parallelization on GPGPUs 
GPU programming involves more overhead than CPU programming because of the need 
to transfer data to and from the graphics card.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Once the data are in place on the card, 
many threads can be started with little overhead.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The code that is invoked on the GPU 
and runs in many threads is called the kernel.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
At the end of the computation, the results 
should be copied back to the main memory of the computer.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: A GPU contains a number of Multi-Processors (MP).
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Each of these in turn has a certain 
number of processing elements, so parallelism on a GPU is both at the MP and at the 
processing element level.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
These two levels of parallelism are reflected in adapting the 
PTMC method to run on a GPU.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: The first level involves mapping the chains to the MPs.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: This is similar to the multi-threading case, where each chain is swept by a thread.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Each 
MP thus plays a role similar to a CPU core.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The second level of parallelism is using the 
streaming processors in each MP to parallelize the sweep of individual chains.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Significant factors in obtaining good speedup with a GPU include reducing the data 
transfer overhead, reducing the required GPU resources per thread so that more threads 
can be started, and keeping all of the MPs busy.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
A Monte Carlo sweep usually involves changing the state of the chain, and the implied 
write operations need synchronization if performed in parallel.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
However, chains in our 
simulations have regions that can be updated independently, since they are laid out such 
that a change in one region does not directly affect another.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In our case, one group of 
many independent regions (64 in results below) covers half of the chain, and a second 
group covers the other half.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The first group can be swept in parallel without 
synchronization.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
After that the threads are synchronized before continuing with the 
second group of regions.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Each thread block sweeps different parts of the same chain, and some data common to the 
chain are placed in the shared memory in order to be accessed faster than if they were in 
the device’s global memory.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
An added benefit to this scheme is that more registers are 
freed to be used for other purposes.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
However, in our case managing the shared memory 
block was difficult, because each chain has more data than could fit into the shared 
memory.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
To keep all the streaming processors busy, we assign multiple chains to each MP, a 
method we call chain packing.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
This is similar to the CPU case where multiple chains 
were assigned to the same core by OpenMP.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The main limiting factors in the GPU case 
are the number of registers available per MP and the maximum number of threads per 
MP.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Each MP in current NVIDIA GPUs can take up to 512 threads, giving us a 
maximum of 8 chains per MP (assuming 64 threads per chain).
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
All threads in an MP 
share a pool of registers, so the maximum number of used registers must not exceed this 
maximum.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
On older cards with 8,192 registers, our code can run 4 chains per MP, while 
with cards with 16,384, we can run the maximum possible 8 chains per block (these 
numbers may change for future GPUs).
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
For example, with 30 MPs we can run 120 or 240 
chains in parallel, or more if fewer threads per chain are used.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
This high number explains 
the attractiveness of GPU parallelization, because in spite of streaming processors being 
slower than a typical CPU, their sheer number can result in an overall speedup.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
On the other hand, with a small number of chains, packing the MPs to the maximum may 
result in some idle MPs.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
For this reason, we stop packing chains in the MPs as soon as we 
see that some MPs are not being utilized.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Under BOINC, it became apparent that volunteers expect as little CPU activity as 
possible from a GPU application.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
One reason is that many volunteers use their computers 
to run CPU-heavy BOINC applications at the same time as running GPU applications.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
However, loading the GPU with long-running kernels makes the system sluggish and 
eventually freezes the computer’s user interface, making it unusable for the volunteer.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The responsiveness of the computer can be adjusted by changing the ratio of the time 
spent executing code on the GPU vs.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We chose for swapping to be done on 
the CPU, which allows us to change the GPU vs.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
CPU running time ratio by changing the 


number of sweeps between each swap operation.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The application thus alternates between 
using the GPU to sweep the chains and then using the CPU to swap them.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Data need to be transferred to the GPU before sweeping, and must be moved back to the 
host computer before swapping.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
As we mentioned before, copying data to and from the 
GPU is a concern.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We increase the number of sweeps in between swap phases to absorb 
the cost of the data copying, but not so much as to make the computer unresponsive.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The issue of the required floating point precision of the application must also be 
addressed.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Recent graphics cards support double-precision floating point operations, but 
they may run slower than single-precision operations [15].
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In our application, the 
sweeping phase performs a mix of integer and floating-point operations.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Real-valued 
data that are processed on the GPU are represented as single-precision floating-point 
numbers.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: The corresponding code in the CPU-only version also uses single-precision.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In 
both versions, the results are accumulated on the CPU in double-precision numbers in 
order to minimize building up round-off error.

text:
Performance and Scaling Experiments 
In this section, we investigate the performance and scaling of our CPU-only and CUDA 
applications.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
It is difficult to make a fair comparison between an application that runs 
only on a CPU and the same app that uses a GPU, because the comparison results will 
change if the employed CPU or GPU are changed.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
For this reason we will not perform 
any direct comparisons between the two implementations.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We used 6 different problems for our experiments, ranging from 8 to 96 qubits, as listed 
in Table 1.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In order to approximate the quantum equilibrium properties of a quantum 
system, we connect together many copies (128 in this case) of the corresponding classical 
system [14].
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text: This larger classical system is then simulated in each chain.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The total 
number of variables in the simulation is the product of the number of qubits, the number 
of copies in each chain, and the number of chains.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
For example, to simulate an 128 copies 
of an 8-qubit quantum system with 27 chains we have 128 × 8 × 27 = 27,648 classical 
variables to manage.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The rapid increase in the number of variables required to simulate a 
quantum system necessitates good simulation performance.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The size of problems used in the experiments 
 
To measure the effectiveness of our multi-threaded CPU code, we ran the AQUA 
application on 32-qubit and 96-qubit Ising model [6] problems with 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8 
threads, on a Mac Pro computer with two 2.8 GHz Intel Quad Core Xeon processors 
(total of 8 cores) and 2 GB of 800 MHz DDR2 memory, running Mac OS 10.5.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Each run was repeated 10 times to obtain reliable 
average running times.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The amount of time needed to perform the parallel tempering, 
which involves no I/O, is noted in Table 2.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
For completeness, we also note the total 
running time of the application, which involves some I/O operations.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

We see a good scaling of the running time with the 
number of threads, which improves with larger problem sizes, since larger problems have 
more chains, with each chain needing the sweeping of more variables.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

There are thus 
more independent tasks that can be run in parallel between barriers.

Our GPU experiments were performed on a mid-range NVIDIA GeForce GTX 260 
graphics card in a dual-core PC running Windows XP.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

In this case we packed the card to 
the maximum possible, and solved problems that differed in size, to observe performance 
of the GPU as a function of the problem size.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

The 32- and 96-qubit problems are the 
same as in the multi-threaded case.

Running time for problems of different size for the GPU application in seconds 
 
Here again, we see an improvement in performance as the problem size increases.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
One 
reason is that with bigger problems, proportionally more time is spent sweeping the 
chains than copying data over to the host computer for swapping.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Figure 9 shows this 
relative performance increase in terms of the number of variables per unit time spent in 
the parallel tempering part of the code.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
In this log-linear plot, the number of variables in 


the problem is displayed next to the corresponding data point.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The data points are 
obtained by dividing the total number of variables by the parallel tempering time.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The 
observed gain in performance saturates by 654,336 variables (72 qubits), which is where 
the maximum number of the GPU streaming processors are utilized.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
GPU performance in relation to problem size  
 
The main reason for the relatively low performance of the GPU version compared to the 
CPU version is that high GPU utilization has a dramatic effect on the responsiveness of 
the computer.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We consciously refrained from putting maximum load on the GPU, to 
allow the volunteers to be able to use their computers while our application is running.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
There are also algorithmic issues that rob performance: sweeping each chain involves 
randomly deciding whether or not to flip each bit.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
On a GPU MP, even if only one 
streaming processor decides to flip a bit, all threads on that MP must wait an amount of 
time equal to executing that flip, since they share an instruction pointer.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The resulting 
performance is as if most chains always flip all bits.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The main cost of data transfer to the GPU is the latency time required to start a transfer, 
while the data transfer itself is relatively fast.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We observed improvements in execution 
speed by coalescing data structures into array forms, so the data can be transferred in 
fewer operations.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
Concluding Remarks 
We introduced two methods to parallelize a Parallel Tempering Monte Carlo algorithm 
on multi-core CPUs and on GPGPUs.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The methods are conceptually simple, because they 


assign independent data processing to CPU threads (PTMC chains) or GPU threads (parts 
of PTMC chains).
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The resulting software is meant to run on volunteer computers 
belonging to members of the general public.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
It adapts itself to the available hardware, and 
employs the computing resources in a manner that leaves the computer on which it runs 
usable.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
We presented experimental data showing that the parallel algorithms are scalable within 
the ranges of the currently available computational resources.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The constraint of leaving 
the computer with an appropriate level of usability makes our code slower than if it could 
use all of the available computing resources, particularly for the GPU application.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
However, it has the advantage of being able to run on thousands of volunteer computers, 
making up for lowered efficiency.
title: MT-CUDA-arxiv

text:
The resulting application, AQUA, successfully solves 
problems that require vast computing resources.

A Generalized Streaming Model For Concurrent Computing∗
Yibing Wang†
Abstract- Multicore parallel programming has some
very diﬃcult problems such as deadlocks during synchro-
nizations and race conditions brought by concurrency.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Added to the diﬃculty is the lack of a simple, well-
accepted computing model for multicore architectures—
because of that it is hard to develop powerful program-
ming environments and debugging tools.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
To tackle the
challenges, we promote a generalized stream comput-
ing model, inspired by previous researches on stream
computing, that uniﬁes parallelization strategies for pro-
gramming language design, compiler design and operat-
ing system design.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Our model provides a high-level ab-
straction in designing language constructs to convey con-
cepts of concurrent operations, in organizing a program’s
runtime layout for parallel execution, and in scheduling
concurrent instruction blocks through runtime and/or
operating systems.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
In this paper, we give a high-level
description of the proposed model: we deﬁne the founda-
tion of the model, show its simplicity through algebraic/-
computational operation analysis, illustrate a program-
ming framework enabled by the model, and demonstrate
its potential through powerful design options for pro-
gramming languages, compilers and operating systems.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
1
Introduction
1.1
Motivation
When searching for a general approach to the chal-
lenges [2] faced by multicore programming, partic-
ularly deadlocks during synchronizations and race
conditions [47] introduced by concurrency, which
render solutions built on conventional multithread-
ing models [13, 52, 68] unappealing to programmers,
we found that there was a need for a uniﬁed com-
puting model on which computer professionals at
programming language design level, compiler design
level, and operating system design level could bene-
ﬁt from each others’ works; and a generalization of
the stream computing model [12] seemed to have the
potential to serve as such a design model for future
generation computing.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Information processing on modern computers has
never followed a monotonous path, but the main-
stream has come along a relatively uniﬁed way due
to the Turing machine abstraction in theory [26] and
von Neumann model [3] in design.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
The adoption
of multicore architectures, however, brings the in-
dustry into a new chaos at various computing levels
ranging from programming language designs to op-
erating system designs.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Not only are programmers
often frustrated with primitive solutions or the lack
of ideal software tools (e.g.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
programming languages
and debuggers), but also are chip makers facing chal-
lenges in delivering new designs [34, 48]; whereas
tools’ builders are constrained by the multithread-
ing model, such as in the cases of OpenMP [52] and
C++-0x thread library extension [68], or by impera-
tive languages, such as in the cases of CUDA [49, 51]
and OpenCL [31].
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
To change the impasse situa-
tion where researchers and developers at diﬀerent
computing levels have uncertain expectations from
each other, ﬁrst a well-accepted computing model is
needed, i.e.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
we need a model that can guide designs
at diﬀerent computing levels.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
PRAM [19] has often been used as a conceptual
parallel computing model in demonstrating synchro-
nized executions such as concurrent read concurrent
write and concurrent read exclusive write.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
We ar-
gue that PRAM captures certain essences such as
parallelism in concurrent computing1 but not other
substances such as precedence constraints in opera-
tion; and the very nature of its dependence on shared
memory limits PRAM’s power in design.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Therefore,
if PRAM is only a generalization (or parallelization)
of the RAM [26] model (Turing machine equivalent)
for abstract analysis, what is the parallel-formed gen-
eralization of the von Neumann model and its al-
ternatives for design?
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Conventional threads and
transactional memory [11, 24, 35] are not the an-
swer; they are implementation details with little ex-
tension to the von Neumann model.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Many people
1In this paper, concurrent and parallel are interchange-
able in most cases, though we tend to regard concurrent
as having broader meaning in computing than parallel does.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
The authors of [16] think parallel systems are mostly syn-
chronous, whereas concurrent systems also include distributed
cases that are mostly asynchronous.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
1


agree that threads are low-level programming util-
ities and should remain so; transactional memory
may not be computationally productive nor energy-
eﬃcient when transactions are large in size or long
in time [24].
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Stream computing [12, 17, 33, 44] has been around
for more than a decade.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Perhaps due to their hum-
ble origin (i.e.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
graphics processors; not their noble
originators) in the computer industry, technologies
based on stream computing were often used only as
performance accelerators.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
While surveying the land-
scape of multicore parallel computing, we realized
that, maybe, the application of stream computing
model should go beyond even GPGPU computing,
and a generalization of the model could be applied to
general purpose software designs and programming
as well.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Note our pursuit of a general design model
was not to ﬁnd a killer solution (i.e.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
the implementa-
tion of a certain method) for all applications, but to
ﬁnd a design principle in handling some of the most
diﬃcult yet fundamental problems, such as paral-
lelization and nondeterminism.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
To serve our purpose, we recommends the separa-
tion of computing models for abstract analysis from
computing models for generalized design.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
In [57],
Snyder expressed similar idea but from a diﬀerent
angle; he emphasized that a useful parallel machine
model should be able to capture key features that
have impact on performance, which to us is a de-
sign (model) issue.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Based on such understanding,
plus other people’s publications [10, 11, 20, 25, 35,
36, 37, 40] and our own experiences2, we propose
a generalized stream computing (hereinafter known
as GeneSC, pronounced “g-e-n-e-s-i-s”) model as a
guideline for multicore computing.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Our expectations
of the model can be summarized as follows.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
• It will help with deﬁning language constructs for
expressing concurrency structures in programs
and algorithms, but leaving parallelization and
synchronization controls to compilers, runtimes
and/or operating systems.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
• It will bring parallelizing compilers out of the
conﬁnement of sequential execution constructs
such as loop nests.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
• It will bring in operating system designs for
tractable, reliable and concurrent instruction
sets executions.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
• It will support backward compatible program-
ming schemes, be it structured, object-oriented,
2For example, the author wrote his ﬁrst multithreaded
server in 1997.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Part of that early experience was published
in [64].
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
or functional; and the re-use of existing (modi-
ﬁed when necessary) library routines.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
• It can be reduced to sequential case for debug-
ging purpose or when used for single core archi-
tectures.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Furthermore, we regard algorithm design as an in-
separable part of achieving high-performance in mul-
ticore parallel computing.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
We believe that, due to
diﬀerent algorithmic thinking, solutions to an ap-
plication problem may show diﬀerent concurrency
structures, which have diﬀerent levels of diﬃculty
when mapped to the underlying runtime environ-
ment and hardware.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
By supplying an expressive
computing model, we give programmers the needed
power in deﬁning the lest convoluted concurrency
structures in their solutions.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
We use the following
example to further justify our motivation.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
1.2
Example
A naive solution to the N-body problem [5, 66] has
the computation complexity of O(N 2).
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Figure 1
shows such an algorithm, where gforce() is a function
for calculating gravitational forces from the other
N −1 objects to the jth object, following the New-
tonian laws of physics.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
To parallelize this algorithm,
we often rely on loop nest parallelization by hand or
through compilers [1, 18].
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010
arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Instead of doing O(N 2) direct force integrations,
an improved design [5] recursively divides the space
into smaller cubic cells until each cubic cell contains
no or only one of the N objects, then builds a tree
with cubic cells that have more than one objects as
the intermediate nodes and cells with only one object
as the leaves.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Gravitational forces among the N ob-
jects are calculated in a way where far away objects
2


are approximated by their conglomeration masses at
their geometry centers.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Figure 2 shows the stream-
like skeleton of such an algorithm with complexity
O(NlogN), where each inner-loop function consists
data parallelism.

Third, it has the potential to show how
languages (i.e.

Further improved algorithms such as [4, 65] aim

Multicore pro-

1.3
Organization
The rest of the paper explains what is this gener-
alized stream computing and what are the enabling
technologies.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Section 2 ﬁrst highlights a few impor-
tant concepts in the problem domain of interests and
then gives a deﬁnition of the GeneSC model, fol-
lowed by Section 3 on algebraic/computational op-
eration analyses, Section 4 on a programming frame-
work enabled by our model, and Section 5 on design
considerations including three crucial additions that
depart from traditional practices.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Section 6 intro-
duces one potential application.

text:
Section 8 gives the concluding re-
marks.

text:
2
Deﬁnition
We use synchronism and asynchronism for discussing
operations’ timing or ordering characteristics.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
We
use determinism and non-determinism for discussing
bounded program behaviors, with non-determinism
refers to program behaviors that are diﬀerent (but
well-deﬁned) from run to run even for the same
given inputs; and indeterminacy for unbounded,
i.e.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Synchronous
operations without randomized functions normally
yield deterministic results; asynchronous operations
may yield either deterministic (when no ordering
is needed) or non-deterministic (when ordering is
required but, by mistake, not enforced) results.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text: Shared memory could add more complexities, e.g.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
when supposedly deterministic operations show non-
deterministic or even indeterminacy behaviors, or
when non-deterministic operations show indetermi-
nacy behaviors, due to race conditions.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Deadlocks and race conditions are notorious be-
cause they bring indeterminacy.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
General races [47]
can be deﬁned as concurrent accesses to shared data
with at least one access is a write operation.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Gen-
eral races may be acceptable if they just cause non-
determinism, but are unacceptable if they cause in-
determinacy.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Data races are special cases of general
races; data races are program bugs, e.g.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
missing
shared locks in concurrent accesses to shared data.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Applications
show
parallelism
in
two
ways:
data parallelism and task parallelism (we consider
pipelined concurrency as a subtype of task paral-
lelism).
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Performance in data parallelism cases relies
on data processing speed, whereas performance in
task parallelism cases relies on overall throughput.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
To make a parallel program work correctly, we
prevent indeterminacy; to make the behavior of
a parallel program tractable, we deal with non-
determinism.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
In our GeneSC model, programming, compilation
and runtime designs adopt a concept that views com-
puting as applying well-deﬁned functions to ﬂows of
data sets, which we call stream data.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
At the core of
the model is an entity, E = (k, d, r), that encapsu-
lates an execution unit consisting of three elements:
• k: a close-form function
• d: well-deﬁned input/output data
• r: relations with other entities
The close-form function is in fact a non-trivial pri-
vate algorithm and is often called a (mathematical)
kernel.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
The input/output data deﬁnes a function’s
interactions with the outside, without exposing in-
termediate computation results.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Inter-stream-entity
relations oﬀer timing/ordering dependence.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
This model is diﬀerent from conventional multi-
threading models in at least two ways: First, stream
3


entities are functional units, whereas threads are ex-
ecution units.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Second, explicit concurrency struc-
tures deﬁned by stream entity’s syntax and seman-
tics allow optimization in compilation and schedul-
ing at runtime, whereas threads prescribe execution
structures without rich timing/ordering knowledge.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Some people might suggest that a stream entity
resembles a neuron in artiﬁcial neuron networks, ex-
cept that the former normally has a linear function
whereas the latter a non-linear function.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
We will not
diverge too far along that direction.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
3
Operations
According to its deﬁnition, a stream entity contains
a miniature Turing machine whose input symbols are
from a subset or a segment of all input symbols to
a larger Turing machine, and whose ﬁnite control is
deﬁned by the stream entity’s kernel function.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
But
the overall program deﬁned by stream entities oper-
ates as a ﬁnite automata (FA), where each state in
the FA has a miniature Turing machine inside.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Inter-
stream-entity relations deﬁne precedence constraints
among the FA states but do not deﬁne connection
(i.e.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
transition) policies, thus the program operates
as a FA with ǫ-moves, shown in Figure 3, where the
ǫ-moves simply mean undeﬁned transition functions,
not important to stream entities3.

text:
The GeneSC model has all the advantages such as
concise foundations and simple semantics of simple
operational models without being weak in program
clarity, which is guaranteed by detailed designs and
implementations of individual stream entities.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
For

the GeneSC model, the author could instantly recognize the
similarity between his ideal of an operational stream comput-

architecture (CTA) abstraction for MIMD parallel machines.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
As another note, from our point of view, one major dif-
ference between multicore and manycore resembles the diﬀer-
ence between shared-memory systems and distributed mem-
ory (i.e.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
networking) systems, where inter-process commu-
nication mechanisms set them apart.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
examples, addition operations in the form of paral-
lel executions of stream entities are supported; con-
catenation operations are allowed as long as inter-
stream-entity relations, if any, are preserved; also
allowed are composition operations.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
With these op-
erations, building large-scale software systems and
reusing library components are safe and tractable.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
The composition capability is even more crucial for
hierarchical and scalable computing, which will be
discussed in Sections 5.2 and 5.3.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
The proposed streaming model preserves asyn-
chronism inherited from the problem domain, but
reduces non-determinism to the minimum through
explicit concurrency structures in a program4.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
By
encapsulating internal computation states, isolating
external states, and separating computation from
communication, stream entities help reducing data
races.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Meanwhile, inter-stream-entity relations help
reducing general races.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
4
Programming
Figure 4 shows a programming framework based on
the GeneSC model.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
At the top level, programmers
focus on coding concurrency structures deﬁned by
stream entities, which relate to each other accord-
ing to precedence constraints, if any, that exist in
high-level control ﬂows and data ﬂows.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Each stream
entity has a kernel function, which may consist of
none, one or more than one lower-level stream enti-
ties.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
The lowest level kernel functions will call rou-
tines in conventional (e.g.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
non-threaded but thread-
safe) programming libraries.

In the above ﬁgure, hierarchical structures among
stream entities embody compositional operations.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Dependence constraints among stream entities de-
cide their runtime execution orders; if there is no
dependence constraint between two stream enti-
ties, there is no mandatory execution order between
them.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
For example, because stream entity No.4 is in-
dependent of others, it may be executed in parallel
with stream entity No.1, No.2 or No.3.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Program-
mers see no thread or any low-level parallel execu-
tion controls, which are left to compilers, runtime
and operating systems to handle.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Programmers do
have the responsibility to write kernel functions and
conventional library routines, if there are no existing
ones for reuse.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
5
Designs
The GeneSC model provides a highly abstracted,
mostly tractable view of concurrent operations.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Here are some examples as design considerations
that support the programming framework discussed
in Section 4.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
5.1
Language
Stream entity is the foundation of conveying con-
currency structures in a program.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Though similar
concept may already exist in some programming lan-
guages, we decide to make it explicit.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
A stream en-
tity’s API may have the following contents in a new
programming-language construct:
{
r e l a t i o n s :
{
bef ore : { ( function_k , [ hard/ s o f t ] ) ,
.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
}
a f t e r :
{( function_i , [ hard/ s o f t ] ) ,
.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010
arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Elements in the rela-
tion sets are kernel function and relation constraint
pairs.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
A “hard” relation constraint means “this” en-
tity must ﬁnish before related entities begin, or must
begin after related entities ﬁnish; a “soft” constraint
means “this” entity should ﬁnish before related enti-
ties begin, or “this” entity should begin after related
entities ﬁnish.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Compositional relations are gener-
ated automatically by compilers and are kept in an
internal data structure for stream entities.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
One major diﬀerence between a stream entity and
a conventional task in the form of a thread is that
the former makes composition operations easier and
safe, whereas the latter harder and unsafe.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
One ma-
jor diﬀerence between a stream entity and a class
object is that the former performs an overall well-
deﬁned, close-form function independent of context,
whereas the latter does not perform such a function
without context, except in the case of a function
object or functor [56].
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Diﬀerent from a functor, a
stream entity’s internal states are not important.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Stream entity does not imply how its kernel func-
tion is implemented, thus does not enforce an im-
perative language implementation targeting CPU or
GPU, or a functional language implementation, or
something else.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Building stream entities on exist-
ing, low-level library routines is possible provided
that the library routines do not create POSIX-like
threads.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
In the proposed streaming model, user pro-
grams are not encouraged to create threads; library
routines should not create threads at all.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
The introduction of the stream-entity construct
in a programming language is the ﬁrst crucial addi-
tion required by our steaming model.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
In this model,
kernel functions deﬁne computations while inter-
stream-entity relations deﬁne precedence constraints
in concurrent executions.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Inter-stream-entity com-
munications are purposely left out because they
are considered as implementation details; both dis-
tributed memory methods (e.g.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
message passing)
and shared memory methods are allowed.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
At program control level, two more constructs
may be desirable: one for data parallelism and one
for task parallelism.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
In the data parallelism case,
on the one hand, concurrent executions have a ﬂat
structure in term of precedence constraint; some
stream entities may have multiple instances at run-
time, when each instance takes a portion of a large
stream data set.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
On the other hand, data partition
algorithms are often non-trivial.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Therefore, a lan-
guage construct, such as map in pMatlab [60], will
be useful for conveying the data partition informa-
tion.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Loops had often been used to do the job, but
expressing parallel concept in sequential executions
reduces program clarity.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
In the task parallelism case, sometimes concurrent
tasks are divided into groups for completely diﬀer-
ent functionalities, and have limited synchronization
points; sometimes increased security requirements,
such as those of a modern web browser [6], demand
greater isolation among the tasks.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Thus, a task par-
allelism construct may be needed to deﬁne such par-
allel structures to allow special runtime scheduling
and layout treatments.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
The research community has been trying to in-
vent new language constructs for the needs of
5


multithreaded parallel computing, such as in the
cases of Cilk/Cilk++ [9, 15] and Galois [32].
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
The
former emphasized the idea of separating designs
for computation from concerns for runtime load-
balancing and scheduling; the latter emphasized
auto-parallelization of sequential programs with new
language abstractions.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Our language designs align
well with those interests, but are not handicapped
by the reliance on POSIX-like multithreading model.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
5.2
Compiler
The introduction of new language constructs such
as that for stream entity has two major impacts on
compiler designs.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
First, increased power in program analysis and
parallelization.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Stream entity deﬁnes a scope that
can be bigger than loop nests, and the scope is ﬁ-
nite so is superior than intractable number of pro-
cedures that hinder previous practices in interpro-
cedural analyses [1, 21].
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
In the GeneSC model, a
control construct for task parallelism as mentioned
in Section 5.1 can guide code generation; a control
construct for data parallelism can specify the num-
ber of concurrent streams, if programmers provide
that information.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Second, added to compiler generated code thus
a program’s virtual address space layout, see Fig-
ure 5, is a new segment for storing hypergraphs of
inter-stream-entity relations, where the hypergraph
vertices are stream entities, and the edges are sets of
data-ﬂow- or control-ﬂow-connected stream entities;
the size of an edge can be one.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
The hypergraph in-
formation is the second crucial addition enabled by
the proposed stream computing model.

text:
a stream entity, is de-
signed as a non-distributive execution unit, thus
compilers (and later runtime schedulers) are al-
lowed to optimize computations through restructur-
ing (e.g.

title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Architectural designs [63, 67] have been proposed
to provide much homogeneous programming en-
vironment on asymmetric or heterogeneous multi-
core.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Such works make mapping stream entities to
asymmetric multicore through compilers practically
achievable.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Depending on what the underlying pro-
cessor architecture is, just-in-time (JIT) compilation
may be employed to further optimize a program at
runtime.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
5.3
Operating System
Program speedup technologies that take advantage
of parallelism, such as instruction-level pipelines,
data-level SIMD, and task-level hyperthreading [22,
28], all have hardware assistants.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
However, in the
multicore case, the up-scaled, parallel processing re-
source is exposed directly to programmers.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Speciﬁ-
cally, parallel task creation, mapping and scheduling
to multiple cores become programmers’ responsibil-
ity, with or without operating system involvement.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Such arguable architectural defect or design trade-oﬀ
may be regarded as the chief culprit for current diﬃ-
culties in parallel programming on multicore proces-
sors.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Architectural support for multi-thread (-block,
-ﬁber, -shred, -strand, etc.) programming, like those
in [23, 63], would be helpful.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Unfortunately, to our
best knowledge, no such CPU production exists.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
To
solve that problem, we propose software emulated,
e.g.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
operating-system initiated, task pipelines where
a task is a stream entity plus stream data.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Such
superscalar pipelines are the third crucial addition
enabled by the proposed streaming model.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
To illus-
trate the idea, we use the following shared memory
model for more detailed discussions.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
First, change how kernel creates and destroys
a program’s runtime image.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
For example, when
the exec system calls are invoked, a kernel thread,
named micro scheduler to be distinguished from
the process level scheduler, parses a program’s hy-
pergraphs information, and decides the number of
worker threads that form the superscalar pipelines.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Work-load information and power management in-
structions may be available to the micro scheduler.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Ideally, it will take those information into consider-
ation when creating worker threads.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
To reduce con-
text switching5 overhead introduced by process level
5Context switching is a multiprogramming strategy on sin-
gle core.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
In multicore systems, the strategy may need en-
hancement or extension.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
6


scheduling, the micro scheduler dynamically changes
the number of worker threads.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Second, schedule a process’ concurrent instruc-
tion blocks through work-stealing [9].
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Although the
micro scheduler speculates inter-stream-entity rela-
tions and dynamically control the number of super-
scalar pipelines (i.e.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
worker threads), stream entities
are scheduled through work-stealing.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Parsed and
maybe further optimized hypergraphs information
is saved as process context for reuse.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Since diﬀerent
operating systems have very diﬀerent thread mod-
els [42, 45], we do not enforce how worker threads
are implemented.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Figure 6 shows a hypothetical
case where the application process has three worker
threads, assisted at runtime by a micro scheduler.

title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Third, monitor virtual memory accesses and man-
age worker threads synchronizations based on an ap-
plication’s hypergraphs.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Virtual memory access con-
trol is enforced through shadowing, e.g.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
locking a
memory address so that only one worker thread can
write to the address at a speciﬁc time; or coloring,
i.e.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
making certain addresses accessible by only one
of the worker threads at any time.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
When race condi-
tions happen, block the contender thread(s) or issue
a signal.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
One immediate question is: how can such
ﬁne-grained memory coloring be possible, if mod-
ern virtual memory systems are page based?
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
We
are considering a dynamic version of memory over-
lays [39] on top of virtual memory.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Memory overlays
provide task-level program isolation.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Finally, let operating system kernel cleanup the
worker threads at process exit, and output tractable
runtime states in case of errors.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
For example, when
system signals make a process abort, hypergraphs
information is dumped to a core ﬁle.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
A snapshot
of current running stream entities is useful but may
not be possible in practice.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
We’ve noticed a recent publication [59] on archi-
tecture design built on a concept called chunk execu-
tion, which was deﬁned as a set of sequential instruc-
tions executed as one operation unit with processor
hardware assistance.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Although it is still early for us
to assess the hardware design itself, the chunk exe-
cution idea reaﬃrmed us the value of our task-level
pipelines for multicore.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
6
Application
The modern web browser as a computing platform
and a familiar but non-trivial application is used to
show the advantages of stream computing.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Besides plain text HTML contents, current and
future web browsers are expected to present to end
users dynamic and rich media such as video, 3D im-
ages, virtual worlds, computer games, semantic web
information, etc.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Those complex contents require
part, if not all, of the computations be done on user
computers or smart hand held devices.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
For each dif-
ferent content format, the browser may run a virtual
machine, e.g.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
a language interpreter, to process the
content.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
There is also the need to isolate content
handling tasks inside the browser for privacy and
security reasons [6, 54].
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Figure 7 shows a simpliﬁed pipeline of the render-
ing engine in a browser.
title: arXiv:1012.1641v1  [cs.PL]  7 Dec 2010

text:
Each of the three functional
units, namely parsing, synthesis, and rendering has
multiple sub-units of diﬀerent capabilities, and the
sub-units may be composed of diﬀerent algorithms
in implementation.
