The required number of resources is 
passed to the Dynamic Provisioning service, which 
acquires these resources from external sources such as 
public Clouds.
title: untitled

text:
Figures 6 and 7 illustrate the iteration of diverse Aneka 
services in order to meet application’s QoS and the diverse 
states a job can experience during their lifetime.
title: untitled

text:
When a 
QoS-enabled job is received by Aneka, it goes to the QoS 
state, which means that tasks that compose the job will 
have higher scheduling priority than non QoS-enabled 
tasks.
title: untitled

text:
Both QoS and regular tasks can go to Queued state if 
no resources are promptly available to them.
title: untitled

text:
However, for 
the case of QoS-enabled tasks extra resources will be 
provisioned.
title: untitled

text:
When the Scheduler service detects that extra 
resources are required for a job, either because the QoS-
enabled job is queued or because the estimation is such that 
deadline 
cannot 
be 
met, 
the 
job 
goes 
to 
the 
underprovisioned state.
title: untitled

text:
If deadline is achievable with 
available resources, the job goes to the provisioned state.
title: untitled

text:
Finally, if deadline cannot be met (for example, because 
deadline is smaller than the boot time of provisioned 
resources), the job goes to unfeasible state.
title: untitled

text:
When the job goes to the underprovisioned state, a 
message is sent from the Scheduler service to the Dynamic 
Provisioner service.
title: untitled

text:
This message contains the number of 
resources required by the job.
title: untitled

text:
The scheduler is not aware of 
possible sources from resources for the tasks; decision on 
the suitable resource pool is done by the Resource Pool 
Manager.
title: untitled

text:
The Resource Pool Manager returns to the 
Scheduler references for the new resources.
title: untitled

text:
However, these 
resources will only be able to receive tasks for execution 
when the corresponding Aneka worker starts running and 
announces its availability to the Scheduler.
title: untitled

text:
When extra resources become available, feasibility of 
the corresponding underprovisioned job is recalculated.
title: untitled

text:
From that, it can go to the state provisioned, if enough 
resources are available, it can stay in the underprovisioned 
state, in which case it can receive more dynamically 
provisioned resources, or it can go to the unfeasible state.
title: untitled

text:
Jobs in the latter stage continue to receive dynamic 
provisioned resources, but no extra allocations are made for 
them.
title: untitled

text:
If for some reason an unfeasible job returns to 
underprovisioned state (for example, because some tasks 
completed before the expected time), it may be candidate to 
receive extra dynamically provisioned resources.
title: untitled

text:
Also, 
changes in state may happen every time a task completes 
execution and the estimation of finish time for the job is 
recalculated.
title: untitled

text:
For both regular and QoS-enabled jobs, finished state is 
reached in three different situations: (i) execution of all the 
tasks finished; (ii) execution of the job failed; and (iii) the 
user cancelled the job.

In the case of resources acquired from public Cloud 
providers, there is typically a time window for which the 
utilization of the resource is paid.
title: untitled

text:
In this case, resources are 
not decommissioned before the end of such time window, 
in order to maximize utilization of such resources.
title: untitled

text:
Therefore, when a QoS-enabled job achieves the finished 
state, the corresponding resources are evaluated for the 
available time before their next billing period.
title: untitled

text:
Those 
resources that can be used are made available for other 
QoS-enabled jobs.
title: untitled

text:
If there is no other QoS-enabled jobs, 
resources are made available for regular tasks until the end 
of the billing period.
title: untitled

text:
When the end of billing period of a 
resource is achieved, a check is made to verify if removing 
such resource will cause a QoS-enable task to go to 
underprovisioned state.
title: untitled

text:
If this situation is detected, 
resource is not decommissioned.
title: untitled

text:
Notice that the Scheduler is not the Aneka service that 
is responsible for decommissioning resources; when it 
detects the resource can be decommissioned, a message is 
sent to the Resource Pool to proceed with the 
decommission process.
title: untitled

text:
This is because procedure for 
decommission varies depending on the specific source of 
resources, and these different sources are associated to 
different Resource Pools.
title: untitled

text:
The Resource Pool Manager is 
the service that keeps track of available resource pools and 
that is able to interact with them for executing resource 
management tasks.
title: untitled

text:
This mechanism enables execution of 
jobs inside a user-defined deadline.
title: untitled

An evaluation of such a 
mechanism is presented in the next section.

CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS 
In the next twenty years, service-oriented computing will 
play an important role in sharing the industry and the way 
business is conducted and services are delivered and 
managed.
title: untitled

text:
This paradigm is expected to have major impact 
on service economy; the service sector includes health 
services (e-health), financial services, government services, 
etc.
title: untitled

text:
This involves significant interaction between clients 
and service providers.
title: untitled

text:
With increased dependencies on ICT 
technologies in their realization, major advances are 
required in user QoS-based allocation of resources to 
competing 
applications 
in 
a 
shared 
environment 
provisioning though a secure virtual machines.
title: untitled

text:
In this paper, we pointed out many challenges in 
addressing the problem of enabling SLA-oriented resource 
allocation in data centers to satisfy competing applications 
demand for computing services.
title: untitled

text:
In particular, the user 
applications are becoming more complex and need multiple 
services to execute instead of a single service.
title: untitled

text:
These 
complex user applications often require collaboration 
among multiple organizations or businesses and thus 
require their specific services to function successfully.
title: untitled

text:
Moreover, fast turnaround time is needed for running user 
applications in today’s increasingly competitive business 
environment.
title: untitled

text:
Hence, by addressing SLA-oriented resource 
allocation in data centers, we provide a critical link to the 
success of the next ICT era of Cloud computing.
title: untitled

text:
We also 
showed how the proposed framework can be effectively 
implemented using the Aneka platform.
title: untitled

text:
We envision the need for a deeper investigation in SLA-
oriented resource allocation strategies that encompass 
customer-driven service management, computational risk 
management, and autonomic management of Clouds in 
order to improve the system efficiency, minimize violation 
of SLAs, and improve profitability of service providers.

individuals that are allowed to crossover with each other, analogous to gene sharing through

reproduction in biological organisms.

Abstract
In this work, we extend the topology-based approach for characterizing computability in
asynchronous crash-failure distributed systems to asynchronous Byzantine systems.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
We give the
ﬁrst theorem with necessary and suﬃcient conditions to solve arbitrary tasks in asynchronous
Byzantine systems where an adversary chooses faulty processes.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
In our adversary formulation,
outputs of non-faulty processes are constrained in terms of inputs of non-faulty processes only.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
For colorless tasks, an important subclass of distributed problems, the general result reduces
to an elegant model that eﬀectively captures the relation between the number of processes, the
number of failures, as well as the topological structure of the task’s simplicial complexes.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
1
Introduction
A task is a distributed coordination problem involving multiple computing processes.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Each pro-
cess starts with a private input, taken from a ﬁnite set, communicates with other processes, and
eventually decides on a private output, also taken from a ﬁnite set.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
One of the central questions in
distributed computing is characterizing which tasks can be solved in which models of computation.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text: Those models specify synchrony, communication, and failure characteristics/guarantees.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
A protocol
is a distributed algorithm that solves a task given a model of computation.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
In this work, we consider asynchronous systems, where processes have diﬀerent relative speeds,
and communication is subject to unbound, yet ﬁnite delays.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
We are interested in situations where a
subset of faulty processes can exist.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text: Two failure models are often discussed in the literature.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
In well-
studied crash-failure models [19], faulty processes simply halt without warning, at possibly diﬀerent
times.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
In the more severe Byzantine-failure models [18], faulty processes can behave arbitrarily,
even maliciously.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Here, we address the problem of characterizing which tasks are solvable in asyn-
chronous Byzantine systems.

Our Contributions
Tools adapted from combinatorial topology have been successful in characterizing task solvability in
synchronous and asynchronous crash-failure systems, as in [15].
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
This paper extends the approach
to tasks in asynchronous Byzantine systems [18, 19].
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
The results presented here suggest that the
language of combinatorial topology (a generalization of the language of graphs) is a convenient
and eﬀective way to formalize a range of distinct distributed computing models.

1.2
Related Work
The Byzantine failure model was initially introduced by Lamport, Shostak, and Pease in [18].
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Most of the literature in this area has focused on the synchronous model (survey in [10]), not
on the (more demanding) asynchronous model considered here.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
The reliable broadcast protocol
is adapted from Bracha [4] and from Srikanth and Toueg [24].
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
[20] propose several
computational models in which processes communicate via shared objects (instead of messages),
and display Byzantine failures.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
[7] consider the k-set agreement problem in a
variety of asynchronous settings.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Their notion of the validity condition for the k-set agreement
problem, however, is weaker than ours.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Neiger [23] discusses a stronger validity condition similar
to the constraints used here.

text:
2


2
Operational Model
We have n + 1 processes1 P0, .
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text: , Pn, that exchange messages via pairwise distinct channels.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
These
channels form a complete graph, and are reliable and FIFO: all transmitted messages are eventually
delivered, in the order they were sent.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Communication is asynchronous: the delivery of any message
happens after a ﬁnite, yet unbounded delay.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Given that the channels are pairwise distinct, the
sender of any message is reliably identiﬁed (authenticated channels in the literature [5]).
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
The
processes are asynchronous as well, with unbound relative speed.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text: We discuss two classical models for process failures.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
In
the crash-failure model [19], processes execute the protocol as prescribed, yet the faulty processes
become permanently silent at any point in the execution (i.e., halt and never send additional
messages).
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
In the Byzantine-failure model [18], faulty processes display arbitrary, even malicious
behavior, which includes collusion to prevent the protocol to terminate correctly.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
In a crash-failure
system, the faulty processes are precisely the ones that halt during the execution.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
In our Byzantine-
failure system, however, the faulty processes are a set of no more than t processes chosen by an
adversary.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Byzantine processes may execute the protocol correctly or incorrectly, at the discretion
of the adversary.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Regarding notation, the set of all processes is denoted by P, partitioned in
non-faulty processes G ⊆P and faulty processes ¯G = P \ G.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Each process Pi has an internal state, or view, written
view(Pi).
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text: Initially, view(Pi) is the process’ starting input.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
In this work, we are interested in task
solvability, but not in communication complexity (i.e., number and size of messages).
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Hence, we
assume that processes follow a full-information protocol [14].
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Each process repeatedly: (1) receives
the state information from other processes; (2) concatenates that information to its own internal
state; (3) sends its internal state to all other processes.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
After completing some number of iterations,
each process applies a decision function δ to its current state in order to decide.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
As a ﬁrst measure in this work, we use higher-level communication abstractions on top of the
bare message-passing model.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text: These new abstractions are described below.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
2.1
Reliable Broadcast
Reliable broadcast is a well-known technique that forces Byzantine processes to communicate con-
sistently with other processes [4, 24, 2, 5].
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
The communication is organized in asynchronous rounds,
where a round may involve several message exchanges.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Messages have the form (P, r, c), where P is
the sending process, r is the current round, and c is the actual content.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Messages not conforming to
this structure can safely be discarded.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
The technique, which works as long as n+1 > 3t, guarantees
the following:
Non-Faulty Integrity: If a non-faulty P never reliably broadcasts (P, r, c), then no non-faulty
process ever reliably receives (P, r, c).
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Non-Faulty Liveness: If a non-faulty P reliably broadcasts (P, r, c), then all non-faulty processes
will reliably receive (P, r, c) eventually.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Global Uniqueness: If two non-faulty processes Q and R reliably receive, respectively, (P, r, c)
and (P, r, c′), then the messages are equal (c = c′), even if the sender P is Byzantine.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

A simplicial complex K consists of a ﬁnite set V along with a collection of subsets of V closed
under containment.

usually denoted by lower-case Greek letters: σ, τ, etc.

dimension dim(σ) of a simplex σ is |σ| −1.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

simplex”, also in “k-face”.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
The dimension dim(K) of a complex is the maximal dimension of its
simplices.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text: The set of vertices of K is denoted by V (K).
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
The set of simplices of K having dimension
at most ℓis a subcomplex of K, which is called ℓ-skeleton of K, denoted by skelℓ(K).
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text: A vertex map f carries vertices of K to vertices of L.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

to L takes each simplex σ ∈K to a subcomplex Φ(σ) ⊆L, such that for all σ, τ ∈K, we have
Φ(σ ∩τ) ⊆Φ(σ) ∩Φ(τ).

3.3
Tasks in the Byzantine Failure Model
In Byzantine-failure tasks, we only care about the relation between inputs and outputs of the non-
faulty processes.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
The task’s outputs should be consistent, despite the participation (sometimes
even correct) of the Byzantine processes, a property sometimes called strong validity, as in [23].
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
We
consider an adversarial model in which any set of up to t processes may be chosen as faulty, with
those processes displaying arbitrary behavior.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Regardless of which processes are faulty, any ﬁnal
conﬁguration of the non-faulty processes must be permitted in respect to the initial conﬁguration of
the non-faulty processes.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
For that goal, our task speciﬁcation T = (I, O, ∆) constrains the behavior
of non-faulty processes only.

4
The Equivalence Theorem
In this section, we will present our main theorem.

We show that, in asynchronous t-resilient
systems, a task Tb = (I, O, ∆) is solvable in the Byzantine failure model if and only if its dual task

deﬁned in terms of I, O, and ∆.

6
Conclusion
In this work, we give novel necessary and suﬃcient conditions for task solvability in asynchronous
Byzantine systems.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
While analogous results have long existed for crash-failure systems [15], we
provide solvability conditions for arbitrary Byzantine tasks for the ﬁrst time.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Here, we presume an
adversarial model to specify which processes are Byzantine.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Independently of which processes are
deemed faulty, any ﬁnal conﬁguration of the non-faulty processes must be permitted in respect to
the initial conﬁguration of the non-faulty processes, according to a formal task speciﬁcation.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
For Byzantine colorless tasks, a specialized, more ﬁtting model permits us to express slightly
more speciﬁc conditions for solvability.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
In particular, we show that the strict k-set agreement
requires a certain number of processes, except in trivial cases.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Furthermore, we show that a
colorless Byzantine protocol under asynchronous systems implies the existence of a continuous map
f : | skelt I∗| →|O∗| carried by the carrier map ∆∗, and that n + 1 > t(dim(I∗) + 2) is enough to
solve an arbitrary colorless task when such map indeed exists.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
In this work, we demonstrate how the language and techniques of combinatorial topology can
produce novel results in distributed computing, facilitating existential arguments while avoiding
complicated, model-speciﬁc argumentation.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
As future work, we intend to explore other require-
ments for solvability in colorless tasks, speciﬁcally in regard to the number of processes, perhaps
unifying Theorems 5.6 and 5.8.

B
Barycentric Agreement via Approximate Agreement
In this section, we show how to transform a protocol for the multidimensional ϵ-approximate agree-
ment problem, deﬁned in [21], into barycentric agreement.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text: The multidimensional ϵ-approximate agreement task is deﬁned as follows.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Consider a set of
n + 1 processes, including no more than t Byzantine processes.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Every process Pi ∈G has an input
Ii ∈Rm and an output Oi ∈Rm.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
After we run the protocol, we require:
Agreement: for any non-faulty processes Pi and Pj, the Euclidean distance between their outputs
Oi and Oj is ≤ϵ, an error tolerance ﬁxed a priori.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Convexity: for any non-faulty process Pi, its output Oi is in the convex hull of the inputs of the
non-faulty processes.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
The point-set occupied by I is compact, and the open stars of the vertices of Bary I form an
open cover of I.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Any such cover has a Lebesgue number λ > 0 [22], such that every set of diameter
less than λ is contained in some member of the cover.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text: We now describe a Byzantine barycentric agreement protocol.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Suppose the non-faulty processes
start at the vertices of an input simplex σ.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Using (λ/2)-approximate agreement, each non-faulty
process pi chooses a point inside σ, the convex hull of the inputs, such that the distance between
any pair of points is less than λ/2.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Equivalently, each open ball of radius λ/2 around vi contains
all values chosen by the approximate agreement protocol.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Because the diameter of this set is less
than the Lebesgue number λ, there is at least one vertex ui in Bary I such that B(vi, λ/2) lies in
the open star around ui.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
We must still show that the vertices ui that were chosen by the processes Pi lie on a single
simplex of Bary σ.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
Note that ui, uj are vertices of a common simplex if and only if the open star
around ui intersects the open star around uj.
title: arXiv:1302.6224v5  [cs.DC]  10 Jun 2014

text:
By construction, vj ∈B(vi, λ/2), which is in the open
star around ui, and vj is in the open star around uj, hence ui, uj are vertices of a single simplex.

Abstract—Although Cloud computing emerged for business
applications in industry, public Cloud services have been widely
accepted and encouraged for scientiﬁc computing in academia.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The recently available Google Compute Engine (GCE) is claimed
to support high-performance and computationally intensive tasks,
while little evaluation studies can be found to reveal GCE’s
scientiﬁc capabilities.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Considering that fundamental performance
benchmarking is the strategy of early-stage evaluation of new
Cloud services, we followed the Cloud Evaluation Experiment
Methodology (CEEM) to benchmark GCE and also compare it
with Amazon EC2, to help understand the elementary capability
of GCE for dealing with scientiﬁc problems.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The experimental
results and analyses show both potential advantages of, and
possible threats to applying GCE to scientiﬁc computing.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
For
example, compared to Amazon’s EC2 service, GCE may better
suit applications that require frequent disk operations, while it
may not be ready yet for single VM-based parallel computing.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Following the same evaluation methodology, different evaluators
can replicate and/or supplement this fundamental evaluation of
GCE.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Based on the fundamental evaluation results, suitable GCE
environments can be further established for case studies of solving
real science problems.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Keywords—Cloud Services Evaluation; Google Compute En-
gine; Public Cloud Service; Scientiﬁc Computing
I.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
INTRODUCTION
Cloud computing has emerged originally as a business
model [29]; therefore, public Cloud services are provided
mainly to meet the technological and economic requirements
from business enterprises.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
However, a previous study shows
that Cloud computing is also widely accepted as a potential
and encouraging paradigm to solve scientiﬁc problems [17],
for the same beneﬁts of on-demand resource provisioning and
cost effectiveness.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In fact, the existing public Cloud services
can be improved for scientiﬁc computing through appropriate
optimizations [6], [22].
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
On the other hand, once commercial
Cloud vendors pay more attention to academic requirements,
they can make the current Cloud more scientiﬁc-oriented by
slightly changing their infrastructures [10].
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Driven by the diversity of requirements [17], Google
launched its infrastructure service, namely Google Compute
Engine (GCE), and recently made it available to the public
[7].
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Being “designed to run high-performance, computationally
intensive virtual compute clusters” [8], GCE seems to be a
promising public Cloud service that can satisfy the requirement
of scientiﬁc computing.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Unfortunately, to the best of our
knowledge, no formal GCE evaluation work has been done
to date.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Although a set of relevant evaluation studies can be
found in technical websites, most of them lack comprehensive
experiments to reveal GCE’s performance, not to mention
summarizing GCE’s characteristics for scientiﬁc computing.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
To help understand GCE for dealing with scientiﬁc issues, we
decided to systematically evaluate GCE following the Cloud
Evaluation Experiment Methodology (CEEM) [16].
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
When it comes to evaluating public Cloud services for
scientiﬁc computing, the efforts can be distinguished between
two types according to their evaluation strategies.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The ﬁrst type
is to reveal fundamental performance of Cloud services by
using traditional and/or scientiﬁc benchmarks, which happens
usually during the early stage of investigating new Cloud
services.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
For example, data durability, availability and access
performance of Amazon S3 were particularly analyzed for
supporting science grids [23]; and the NAS Parallel Bench-
marks (NPB) was used to verify Amazon EC2 for high
performance computing [1], [26].
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The second type is to
investigate sophisticated Cloud applications as real scientiﬁc
cases, which is normally based on the aforementioned early-
stage evaluation.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
For example, satellite image processing was
studied on Windows Azure [11]; and a metabolic ﬂux analysis
was implemented by employing multiple types of Amazon
services [3].
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Given the recently available GCE, this paper reports an
early-stage performance evaluation.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
By employing four pop-
ular benchmarks, our study exhibits the fundamental perfor-
mance of four GCE types, and also compares them with
nine Amazon EC2 types.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Based on the experimental results
and analyses, we further show the potential advantages of,
and possible threats to applying GCE to scientiﬁc comput-
ing.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
For example, GCE would be particularly suitable for
applications that require frequent disk operations, while it
may not well support single VM-based parallel computing.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Following the same evaluation methodology, even different
evaluators would be able to replicate and/or supplement this
fundamental evaluation of GCE.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Moreover, according to the
outcome of this study, researchers and engineers can establish
suitable GCE environments to carry out sophisticated and
scientiﬁc case studies.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Overall, the contribution of this work is
twofold.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Firstly, to our best knowledge, this is the ﬁrst study
that systematically reveals GCE’s performance for scientiﬁc
computing.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Secondly, this evaluation practice can be viewed
as a case study for validating the methodology CEEM.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

RELATED WORK
As revealed in [17], the requirements in the Cloud market
are diverse; Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS, e.g., Amazon
EC2) and Platform as a Service (PaaS, e.g., Google Ap-
pEngine) would then serve different types of requirements,
and they cannot be replaced with each other.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
This could
be the motive for Google to ﬁnally launch its infrastructure
service GCE [7].
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Although GCE has been widely viewed as
a strong competitor against the other IaaS services, especially
against Amazon EC2, not much evaluation work can be found
for understanding GCE’s performance.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The very early GCE
evaluation studies tended to be qualitative discussions around
service level agreement (SLA) [4], [27].
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
More quantitative
evaluations appeared in the latter GCE studies.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
For example,
Zencoder compared GCE’s n1-standard-8-d with two Amazon
cluster instance types for video transcoding [28].
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
As argued
in [5], however, this work did not reveal suitable EC2 types
for “apple-to-apple” comparison to GCE.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
On the contrary, it is
able to identify comparable EC2 types for GCE n1-standard-4
in a serial of evaluation experiments [19], [20].
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Nevertheless,
as suggested by the author himself, those ad hoc and short-
time experiments could result in biases and misleading con-
clusions.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
A various-type virtual machine (VM) evaluation of
GCE and EC2 was given in [25].
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
However, the non-standard
benchmarks and unclear evaluation procedure make this study
hard for experimental replication and comparison.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Given the
lack of a systematic GCE evaluation, we use this paper to
report our empirical study to help understand the fundamental
performance of GCE, particularly for scientiﬁc computing.

CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
Cloud computing with public Cloud services has been
widely regarded as a potential and encouraging paradigm
for scientiﬁc computing.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Since the recently available GCE is
supposed to meet high-performance and computationally in-
tensive workloads [8], we performed an early-stage evaluation
of GCE to verify its fundamentally scientiﬁc capabilities.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
By
contrasting with a set of Amazon EC2 types, the experimental
results and analyses exhibit both possible advantages of, and
threats to employing GCE, as listed below.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The potential advantages of using GCE:
•
Relatively high memory data throughput.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Different
GCE types seem to have consistent type of virtual
memory.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
•
Relatively fast storage transaction speed.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
•
Relatively fast computation transaction speed with
single process.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
•
Relatively computationally economic, given generally
high computation performance/price ratio.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The possible threats to using GCE:
•
Relatively low communication data throughput be-
tween US and European data centers.
title: Early Observations Performance Google Compute Engine Scientiﬁc Computing

Distributed
computing crossing both data centers may need to be

•
Considerable variability of storage performance.

GCE

Considerable variability of computation transaction

Relatively poor (original) scalability when switching

GCE’s hyper-

text:
Based on the outcomes of this study, our future work will
be unfolded along two directions.

supplement the fundamental evaluation of GCE.

The second

title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
DOI: 10.1109/HPCSim.2016.7568421
Abstract—Lattice Quantum ChromoDynamics (QCD), and by
extension its parent ﬁeld, Lattice Gauge Theory (LGT), make
up a signiﬁcant fraction of supercomputing cycles worldwide.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
As such, it would be irresponsible not to evaluate machines’
suitability for such applications.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
To this end, a benchmark has
been developed to assess the performance of LGT applications
on modern HPC platforms.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Distinct from previous QCD-based
benchmarks, this allows probing the behaviour of a variety of
theories, which allows varying the ratio of demands between on-
node computations and inter-node communications.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The results
of testing this benchmark on various recent HPC platforms are
presented, and directions for future development are discussed.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Keywords—benchmarking; quantum chromodynamics; beyond
the standard model; Xeon Phi
I.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Introduction
Quantum ChromoDynamics (QCD), the theory of the strong
interaction of quarks and gluons, is a highly successful theory
with high-precision predictive power.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
However, calculations
of physical interest are rarely analytically tractable, instead
requiring Monte Carlo simulation of a discretised treatment
referred to as Lattice QCD (LQCD).
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Lattice QCD codes are
developed by a number of theoretical particle physics re-
search groups internationally, and these codes use a signiﬁcant
fraction of available supercomputing capacity worldwide—for
example, NVIDIA quote that up to 20% of North American
supercomputing cycles are used for QCD research [1].
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
QCD lies in a family of models known as gauge theories,
and the numerical techniques developed to study QCD can also
be applied to other gauge theories, forming a broader area of
research known as Lattice Gauge Theory (LGT).
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Such theories
may diﬀer from QCD in a number of ways; computationally,
the diﬀerence is typically the dimensionality and structure of
the sub-matrices related to each point in the discretised space.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
These diﬀerences can have an impact on the demands that LGT
code makes of the computer on which it runs—for example,
altering the ratio of computations to communications demands.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Non-QCD LGT has become of interest recently as a tool for
theoretical physicists to probe physics Beyond the Standard
Model (BSM), for example relating to recent discoveries at
the Large Hadron Collider at CERN.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Recent reviews of such
techniques include [2], [3].
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Benchmarks have previously been developed out of QCD
codes, and many of these benchmarks have been adopted in
common benchmark suites used for machine evaluation (for
example, the NERSC MILC benchmark developed from the
MILC research code [4]).
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
However, the QCD codes used
for these benchmarks do not have suﬃcient ﬂexibility to
probe BSM theories of physical interest.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Thus in order to
characterise the diverse performance demands of BSM LGTs,
a novel benchmark is necessary, derived from (or at least
approximating) a ﬂexible LGT code.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
arXiv:1401.3733v2  [cs.DC]  22 Sep 2016


In this work, we present BSMBench, a benchmark satisfying
this criterion, derived from the HiRep research LGT code
[5], [6].
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
In the remainder of this paper, in section II we will
outline the relevant details of LGT (in particular highlighting
diﬀerences from QCD), then in section III, we will describe
the methodology of the benchmark.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
In section IV we will
then present some selected results, characterising some recent
machines’ performance in the tests set up by the benchmark,
before concluding and suggesting future directions our work
will take.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Field content
The “lattice” in Lattice Gauge Theory is a hypercubic array
of points (“sites”), forming a discretised space (or spacetime).
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
This space is most frequently four-dimensional, and the length
in the three spatial directions is generally made to be the same,
giving a total number of sites L3 × T.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Each lattice site has
eight nearest neighbours (up and down in each of the four
dimensions); the lines joining a point to a nearest neighbour
is referred to as a “link”.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The lattice typically has periodic
boundary conditions, so the number of links is four times
the number of sites (avoiding double counting positive and
negative links), with no edge corrections.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
A gauge theory will typically have one gauge ﬁeld (the
gluon ﬁeld of QCD), and Nf ≥1 “ﬂavours” of fermion (the
quark ﬁelds).
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
On the lattice, the gauge ﬁeld is an N × N
complex-valued matrix on every link, while the fermion ﬁelds
are M-dimensional complex-valued vectors at every site.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
N
and M are integer-valued tunable parameters of the theory;
N ≥2 may be freely chosen, while M ≥N is constrained to
certain values allowed by group theory (speciﬁcally, the M-
vector must transform under some non-trivial representation
of the group of which the N × N matrix is an element).
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Counting up, at each site the gauge ﬁeld contributes 4
links ×(N × N) elements × 2 real numbers; i.e.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The fermion ﬁelds, meanwhile, contributes
Nf × M × 2 = 2MNf real numbers per site.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The contributions
to the whole lattice are then multiplied by L3T; i.e.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
the gauge
ﬁeld comprises 8N2L3T real numbers, and the fermion ﬁelds
2MNfL3T.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
In the case of QCD, N = M = 3 (the three colors
of QCD—red, green and blue).
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Dirac operator
The physics of the fermions is encoded in the so-called
“Dirac operator”; on the lattice this is a matrix relating all
elements of the fermion ﬁeld to all elements of the fermion
ﬁeld—that is to say, it is a (2MNfL3T) × (2MNfL3T)-element
matrix.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The interactions in the fermion ﬁelds are taken to
be nearest-neighbour, resulting in the Dirac operator being
exceedingly sparse, and depend on the values of the gauge
ﬁeld elements.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The primary task of the Monte Carlo code is
to invert this matrix.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
This is typically done using a Conjugate
Gradient (CG) or related algorithm, and as such the dominant
(and to a reasonable approximation, only) contribution to the
runtime comes from the routine to multiply the fermion ﬁeld
by the Dirac operator; we will call this Dphi1.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
This overwhelming dominance of execution time by one
single subroutine has naturally led to it being the focus for
optimization; in QCD applications it is not uncommon for
Dphi to be hand-optimized with for example vector intrinsics
and manual prefetching, rather than written in a na¨ıve way
and relying solely on the compiler.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
For more general LGT
tools this kind of optimization is less practical; the need for
generality in N and M precludes us from hard-coding highly-
optimised code in the way that QCD codes can for a ﬁxed
N and M.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
For example, the HiRep research code uses a code
generator to produce sets of macros for the matrix-matrix and
matrix-vector operations required, which are then called from
Dphi.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Parallelisation
The hypercubic geometry and nearest-neighbour interac-
tions found in the problem means that it naturally lends itself to
spatial parallelisation, with the lattice being sliced up in each
dimension, and each resulting piece of lattice being handled by
a dedicated process (with processes generally communicating
via MPI, although hybrid OpenMP+MPI approaches exist).
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The need to store and communicate boundary terms places a
lower bound on the piece size that can be eﬃciently handled,
and thus an upper bound on the degree of parallelisation for
a particular problem size.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The Benchmark
The priorities when developing BSMBench were to reﬂect
the computational demands and portability of the HiRep
research code, to be able to probe more than one theory
(i.e.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
set of values of (N, M) above—since the performance
demands change as a function of these parameters), to run
in reasonable time, and to spend suﬃciently long that the
run time is not dominated by startup overheads.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Additionally,
the test suite should be easily run by non-LGT specialists,
so that it may, for example, be used by hardware vendors
to quote performance of development machines early on in
procurement cycles, without having to grant system access to
end-users.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The strategy chosen to meet these criteria was based on
that of L¨uscher [7].
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
It takes three tasks—two more elementary
vector and matrix-vector operations, followed by the full
Dphi—and in turn iterates them on randomly-generated ﬁelds
for a ﬁxed period of time2.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
(The CG inversion is currently
not benchmarked, but can be requested as a check on the
machine’s numerics.) The number of ﬂoating point operations
for each task has previously been calibrated, and thus the
1Some other works refer to this as Dslash.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
2To avoid spending excessive time on time checks, the numbers of iterations
between time checks doubles after each check.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
performance can be quantiﬁed by FLOPs/s = Number of
iterations × FLOPs per iteration / Time Taken.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The problem size is ﬁxed, thus the benchmark probes strong
scaling behaviour.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Since the problem size in production is
typically ﬁxed by physical demands, research use of the
benchmark is less interested in weak scaling; however, it is
possible that it will be added in a future version.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The benchmark is provided with case scenarios, correspond-
ing with three theories: (N, M) = (2, 4) (communications-
dominated), (3, 3) (balanced, and equivalent to QCD), and
(6, 6) (compute-dominated).
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Rather than including the full
code generator, output header ﬁles for these theories are
included with the benchmark.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Even for the communications-dominated theory, each itera-
tion has a ﬁxed number of FLOPs, and so the FLOP/s rate
for the benchmark gives a proxy to the performance.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The
advantage of using the same measure for all three theories is
that the benchmark statistics may then be directly compared
between theories.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
BSMBench was constructed by paring down the HiRep
research code to the essential elements, thus the benchmarked
code closely reﬂects the workloads in production runs.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Further,
optimisations can cross-pollinate between HiRep and BSM-
Bench.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Owing to the need to be able to adopt new HPC infrastruc-
ture as it becomes available, the HiRep research code is highly
portable—in general, it can be run on a new machine simply by
setting the correct compiler and running make.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
This property is
inherited by BSMBench; in the results shown below, no code
changes needed to be made to allow the benchmark to run,
and to be reﬂective of the de factor usage of the research
code the only optimisation performed was some tuning of
the compiler ﬂags.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
As mentioned, were system vendors to
adopt the benchmark and optimise it more aggressively, the
optimisations could be backported to the research code to
beneﬁt all users.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
The ﬂexibility of the benchmark thus manifests in three
ways: it is easily portable to many architectures, it can run in
reasonable time on a diverse range of machine sizes, and most
importantly, it can tune the relative demands on computation
and inter-process communication.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Results
BSMBench has been tested on a variety of HPC platforms,
including IBM Blue Gene/P and /Q machines, an SGI ICE
XA system with Haswell CPUs, Fujitsu x86 clusters (West-
mere and Sandy Bridge-based, at HPC Wales), a Xeon Phi-
based cluster (at the Hartree Centre), commodity clusters
(both Inﬁniband and gigabit Ethernet setups), and a Mac
Pro workstation.3 Details of MPI libraries, compilers, and
3The benchmark has also more recently been used on other recent prototype
architectures; however, the results of these analyses are currently subject to
non-disclosure agreements.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
compiler ﬂags are shown in Table I; in all cases, the default
MPI conﬁguration was used, with no hand-tuning of process
placement or run-time ﬂags.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Full results of each sub-test on every machine tested would
be cumbersome to present here, thus we have chosen an
interesting subset of results to highlight.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Since the Dphi test is
most representative of a typical production workload, it is this
test that we focus on in presenting results.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Results are plotted
on a logarithmic scale, to avoid one or two data dominating
the plots; plots are shown both of the total FLOP/s, and also

At smaller problem sizes, the maximum parallelisation
is reached more quickly, and so it would be preferable to
minimise the use of the communications links (by using
only one or a small number of nodes) rather than needing
to procure the fastest available links.

text:
Conclusion
We have developed a novel benchmark, BSMBench, based
on Beyond the Standard Model Lattice Gauge Theory.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Unlike
previous benchmarks based on QCD, it has the capacity to
adjust the theory under study, and consequently modify the
workload’s demands in terms of the ratio of computations to
communications.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Thanks to this, BSMBench could be applied
in a variety of user scenarios (e.g.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
as a monitoring and fault
diagnostic tool or as a general-purpose performance evaluation
utility) that transcend its original goals.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
We have tested this benchmark on a variety of recent
supercomputing platforms, including CPUs and Xeon Phi
coprocessors.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Our results show good strong scaling in the
presence of a suﬃciently fast interconnect, and exhibit the
expected splitting between theories under study.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
One limitation of the benchmark (and the underlying re-
search code) is an inability to make use of vector units wider
than two double precision ﬂoating-point numbers; work is
underway to lift this restriction, which would signiﬁcantly
boost the performance on more modern architectures featuring
AVX and QPX vector instructions.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Other future improvements
to BSMBench will be to reduce the reliance on parameter
sets, with the core code instead able to calculate the necessary
parameters, and potentially to introduce a weak scaling test.
title: BSMBench: Flexible Scalable Benchmark from Beyond Standard Model Physics

text:
Interesting potential tests of the benchmark currently under
investigation include assessing the relative performance of
diﬀerent MPI libraries on the same architecture, and observing
how the results compare with those of other benchmarks—for
example, those based on QCD (for example, [4]), and those
based on Conjugate Gradient solvers (for example, [8]).

ABSTRACT
Modern day continued demand for resource hungry services and applications in IT sector has led to
development of Cloud computing.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Cloud computing environment involves high cost infrastructure on one
hand and need high scale computational resources on the other hand.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
These resources need to be
provisioned (allocation and scheduling) to the end users in most efficient manner so that the tremendous
capabilities of cloud are utilized effectively and efficiently.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
In this paper we discuss a selective algorithm
for allocation of cloud resources to end-users on-demand basis.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
This algorithm is based on min-min and
max-min algorithms.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text: These are two conventional task scheduling algorithm.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The selective algorithm uses
certain heuristics to select between the two algorithms so that overall makespan of tasks on the machines is
minimized.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text: The tasks are  scheduled on machines in either space shared or time shared manner.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
We
evaluate our provisioning heuristics using a cloud simulator, called CloudSim.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
We also compared our
approach to the statistics obtained when provisioning of resources was done in First-Cum-First-
Serve(FCFS) manner.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The experimental results show that overall makespan of tasks on given set of VMs
minimizes significantly in different scenarios.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
KEYWORDS
Resource Provisioning, Cloud Computing, Makespan, Selective Algorithm, Min-Min, Max-Min
1.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Introduction
Today due to consistently changing requirements of users and increase in demand of services and
applications requiring huge processing power and heavy resources has led to the development of
cloud computing technology wherein all high cost infrastructure and computational resources are
installed in single datacenter.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Cloud Computing uses SOA (Service Oriented Architecture) to
provide IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) [1],[2],[3], SaaS (Software as a Service) [1],[2],[3],
PaaS (Platform as a Service) [1],[3], DaaS (Data Storage as a Service) [1][2], CaaS
(Communication as a Service) [2],[3], HaaS (Hardware as a Service) [1],[2] to cloud users.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The
end users can use these resources over a network on-demand basis in pay-as-you-say manner.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text: International Journal on Cloud Computing: Services and Architecture (IJCCSA) ,Vol.

2
Resource Provisioning is an aggregation of both Resource allocation and Task Scheduling.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
“Resources available on the cloud must be provisioned in such a manner that their tremendous
capabilities are efficiently utilized and effectively available to end users on-time without much
delay in completion of tasks given by the cloud users.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The Provisioning must qualify service level
requirements (Requirements specified in Service Level Agreement, SLA) based on availability,
capability, performance, and costs of resources.”
Resource provisioning must take into account the consideration of all kind of cloud users.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
It must
fulfill the requirements of all its users (i.e.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text: the provider and end user of cloud services).
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Therefore, while designing a resource provisioning technique the developer must emphasize on
the needs of Cloud Users on one hand and Cloud Provider on the other hand.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The pre-requisite of
cloud users is minimum response time.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
They expect their jobs to be completed in fastest possible
manner with high availability of resources.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
On the other hand the Cloud Provider invests such
huge capital with the aim to maximize the use of all the installed resources in efficient and
effective manner.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Both Cloud users and Cloud providers expect maximum throughput and
improved performance for the money they invest.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Cloud users pay to use the services of cloud
and cloud providers invest huge amount in installation and maintenance of Cloud.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
In this paper, we discuss allocation of resources to tasks using min-min or max-min algorithm and
then scheduling them on either space shared or time shared basis.

introduced.

text: In section 4, the experimental results are presented and discussed.

Related Work
Resource provisioning in cloud computing environment is done with the main aim of achieving
load balancing.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Based on various factors like spatial distribution of cloud nodes, algorithm
complexity, storage/replication, point of failure etc.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
different techniques have evolved to
provision the resources in balanced manner.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The provisioning is done taking into account whether
the environment is static or dynamic.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text: Many related works have been done to achieve efficient resource allocation scheme.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Statistical
based Resource allocation (SLB) introduced by Zhenzhong Zhang in paper [4] is based on prior
learning and performance statistics, SLB involves analysis of huge on-line historical data for
forecasting resource demands.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
In paper [5], an algorithm given for load balancing is an
inspiration from the honeybee.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
It is biologically inspired technique that uses behavior of
honeybees foraging and harvesting for food.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
It does not take into consideration the waiting time
of the tasks and overall turnaround time.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Similar techniques mentioned in paper [6], [7] are used
for load balancing but none reduce the overall waiting time of tasks.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Resource Allocation Using Selective Algorithm
To achieve our goal of minimizing the overall makespan of  tasks on machines and provide better
quality of service we design an algorithm that assigns tasks to best machines in such a way that it
provides satisfactory performance to both, cloud users and providers.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The algorithm is designed
to make a choice between Min-Min and Max-Min scheduling algorithm based on certain criteria.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

Min-Min algorithm follows the following procedure:
Phase1:  It first computes the completion time of cloudlets on each VM and then for each cloudlet
it chooses the VM which processes the cloudlet in minimum possible time.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Phase2: Then among all the cloudlets in MT the cloudlet with minimum overall completion time
is chosen and is allocated to VM on which minimum execution delay is expected.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The cloudlet is
removed from the list of MT and the process continues until MT list is empty.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text: Max-Min algorithm works similarly like Min-Min in phase 1.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Unlike Min-Min, Max-Min
allocates the cloudlet with maximum expected completion time to VM (i.e.
title: Application of Selective Algorithm for Effective Resource Provisioning In Cloud Computing Environment

Cloud v/s Cluster and Grid
Clusters [1] are parallel and distributed systems, governed 
under the supervision of single administrative domain.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The node (stand-alone computers) in the cluster integrates 
to form a single computing resource.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Grid [1] is aggregation of autonomous resources that 
are geographically distributed.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The nodes in grid permit 
sharing and selection dynamically at runtime.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Clouds [1], [2] are not the combination of clusters and 
grid but are next generation to clusters and grid.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Similar 
to Cluster and Grid, Cloud is also a collection of parallel 
and distributed systems.

Unlike cluster and grid, cloud has multiple domains and 
the nodes of cloud are “Virtualized” [9].

text:
Load Balancing in Cloud 
Computing Environment
Load balancing in cloud computing provides an efficient 
solution to various issues residing in cloud computing 
environment set-up and usage.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Load balancing must 
take into account two major tasks, one is the resource 
provisioning or resource allocation and other is task 
scheduling 
in 
distributed 
environment.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Efficient 
provisioning of resources and scheduling of resources as 
well as tasks will ensure:
	 a.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text: Resources are easily available on demand.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Resources are efficiently utilized under condition of 
high/low load.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text: Energy is saved in case of low load (i.e.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
when usage 
of cloud resources is below certain threshold).
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
For measuring the efficiency and effectiveness of Load 
Balancing algorithms simulation environment are 
required.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
CloudSim [12] is the most efficient tool that can 
be used for modeling of Cloud.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
During the lifecycle of a 
Cloud, CloudSim allows VMs to be managed by hosts 
which in turn are managed by datacenters.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text: Cloudsim provides architecture with four basic entities.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
These entities allow user to set-up a basic cloud 
computing environment and measure the effectiveness 
of Load Balancing algorithms.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
A typical Cloud modeled 
using CloudSim consists of following four entities 
Datacenters, Hosts, Virtual Machines and Application 
as well as System Software.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Datacenters entity has the 
responsibility of providing Infrastructure level Services 
to the Cloud Users.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
They act as a home to several Host 
Entities or several instances hosts’ entities aggregate 
to form a single Datacenter entity.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Hosts in Cloud are 
Physical Servers that have pre-configured processing 
capabilities.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Host is responsible for providing Software 
level service to the Cloud Users.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Hosts have their own 
storage and memory.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Processing capabilities of hosts 
is expressed in MIPS (million instructions per second).
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
They act as a home to Virtual Machines or several 
instances of Virtual machine entity aggregate to form a 
Host entity.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Virtual Machine allows development as well 
as deployment of custom application service models.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
They are mapped to a host that matches their critical 
characteristics like storage, processing, memory, software 
and availability requirements.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Thus, similar instances 
of Virtual Machine are mapped to same instance of a 
Host based upon its availability.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Application and System 
software are executed on Virtual Machine on-demand.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Class diagram of Cloud architecture illustrating 
relationship between the four basic entities is shown in fig 
1.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Thus, the object oriented approach of CloudSim can be 
used to simulate Cloud Computing environment.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Resource Allocation
Resource provisioning is the task of mapping of the 
resources to different entities of cloud on demand basis.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Resources must be allocated in such a manner that no node 
in the cloud is overloaded and all the available resources in 
the cloud do not undergo any kind of wastage (wastage of 
bandwidth or processing core or memory etc.).
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Mapping 
of resources to cloud entities is done at two levels:
2.1.1.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
VM Mapping onto the Host
Virtual machines reside on the host (physical servers).
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
More than one instance of VM can be mapped onto a 
single host subject to its availability and capabilities.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Host is responsible for assigning processing cores to 
VM.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Provisioning policy define the basis of allocating 
processing cores to VM on demand.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Allocation policy or 
algorithm must ensure that critical characteristics of Host 
and VM do not mismatch.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
2.1.2 Application or Task Mapping onto VM
Applications or tasks are actually executed on VM.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Each application requires certain amount of processing 
power for their completion.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
VM must provide required 
processing power to the tasks mapped onto it.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Tasks
