must be mapped onto appropriate VM based upon its 
configuration and availability.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Task Scheduling
Task scheduling is done after the resources are allocated to 
all cloud entities.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Scheduling defines the manner in which 
different entities are provisioned.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Resource provisioning 
defines which resource will be available to meet user 
requirements whereas task scheduling defines the manner 
in which the allocated resource is available to the end 
user (i.e.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
whether the resource is fully available until 
task completion or is available on sharing basis).
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Task 
scheduling provides “Multiprogramming Capabilities” in 
cloud computing environment.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Task scheduling can be done in two modes:
	 a.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Time shared
Both hosts and VM can be provisioned to users either in 
space shared mode or time shared mode.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
In space sharing mode resources are allocated until task 
does not undergo complete execution (i.e.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
resources are not 
preempted); whereas in time sharing mode resources are 
continuously preempted till task undergoes completion.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
gives the comparison of resource allocation and 
task scheduling and specifies the issues resolved by each 
technique of load balancing.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Based on resource provisioning and scheduling, four cases 
can be examined under different performance criteria so 
as to get efficient load balancing scheme.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Case 1: Hosts and VMs, both are provisioned in space 
sharing manner.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Case 2: Hosts and VMs, both are provisioned to VMs and 
tasks respectively in time sharing manner.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Case 3: Hosts are provisioned to VMs in space sharing 
manner and VMs are provisioned to tasks in time sharing 
manner.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Case 4: Hosts are provisioned to VMs in time sharing 
manner and VMs are provisioned to tasks in space sharing 
manner.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Related Work to Load 
Balancing Algorithms
Cloud is made up of massive resources.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Management of 
these resources requires efficient planning and proper 
layout.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
While designing an algorithm for resource 
provisioning on cloud the developer must take into 
consideration different cloud scenarios and must be 
aware of the issues that are to be resolved by the proposed 
algorithm.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Therefore, resource provisioning algorithm 
can be categorized into different classes based upon the 
environment, purpose and technique of proposed solution.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Load Balancing on the basis of Cloud 
Environment
Cloud computing can have either static or dynamic 
environment based upon how developer configures the 
cloud demanded by the cloud provider.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Static Environment
In static environment the cloud provider installs 
homogeneous resources.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Also the resources in the cloud 
are not flexible when environment is made static.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
In this 
scenario, the cloud requires prior knowledge of nodes 
capacity, processing power , memory, performance and

title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
These user requirements 
are not subjected to any change at run-time.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Algorithms 
proposed to achieve load balancing in static environment 
cannot adapt to the run time changes in load.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Although 
static environment is easier to simulate but is not well 
suited for heterogeneous cloud environment.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Round Robin algorithm [13] provides load balancing in 
static environment.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
In this the resources are provisioned 
to the task on first-cum-first-serve (FCFS- i.e.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
the task that 
entered first will be first allocated the resource) basis and 
scheduled in time sharing manner.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The resource which is 
least loaded (the node with least number of connections) 
is allocated to the task.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Eucalyptus uses greedy (first-fit) 
with round-robin for VM mapping.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Radojevic proposed an improved algorithm over round 
robin called CLBDM (Central Load Balancing Decision 
Model) [14].
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
It uses the basis of round robin but it also 
measures the duration of connection between client and 
server by calculating overall execution time of task on 
given cloud resource.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Dynamic Environment
In dynamic environment the cloud provider installs 
heterogeneous resources.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The resources are flexible in 
dynamic environment.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
In this scenario cloud cannot rely 
on the prior knowledge whereas it takes into account 
run-time statistics.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
The requirements of the users are 
granted flexibility (i.e.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Algorithm proposed to achieve load balancing in dynamic 
environment can easily adapt to run time changes in load.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Dynamic environment is difficult to be simulated but is 
highly adaptable with cloud computing environment.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Based on WLC [15] (weighted least connection) 
algorithm, Ren proposed a load balancing technique in 
dynamic environment called ESWLC.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
It allocates the 
resource with least weight to a task and takes into account 
node capabilities.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Based on the weight and capabilities 
of the node, task is assigned to a node.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
LBMM (Load 
Balancing Min-Min) algorithm proposed in paper [16] 
uses three level frameworks for resource allocation in 
dynamic environment.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
It uses OLB (opportunistic load 
balancing) algorithm as its basis.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Since cloud is massively 
scalable and autonomous, dynamic scheduling is better 
choice over static scheduling.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Load Balancing based on Spatial 
Distribution of Nodes
Nodes in the cloud are highly distributed.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Hence the node 
that makes the provisioning decision also governs the 
category of algorithm to be used.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
There can be three types 
of algorithms that specify which node is responsible for 
balancing of load in cloud computing environment.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Centralized Load Balancing
In centralized load balancing technique all the allocation 
and scheduling decision are made by a single node.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
This 
node is  responsible for storing knowledge base of entire 
cloud network and can apply static or dynamic approach 
for load balancing.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
This technique reduces the time 
required to analyze different cloud resources but creates a 
great overhead on the centralized node.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Also the network 
is no longer fault tolerant in this scenario as failure 
intensity of the overloaded centralized node is high and 
recovery might not be easy in case of node failure.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Distributed Load Balancing
In distributed load balancing technique, no single node 
is responsible for making resource provisioning or task 
scheduling decision.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
There is no single domain responsible 
for monitoring the cloud network instead multiple 
domains monitor the network to make accurate load 
balancing decision.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Every node in the network maintains 
local knowledge base to ensure efficient distribution of 
tasks in static environment and re-distribution in dynamic 
environment.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
In distributed scenario, failure intensity of a node is 
not neglected.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Hence, the system is fault tolerant and 
balanced as well as no single node is overloaded to make 
load balancing decision.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:

algorithms is given in Table 3.

Biased random sampling [18] is another

title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Hierarchical Load Balancing
Hierarchical load balancing involves different levels of 
the cloud in load balancing decision.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Such load balancing 
techniques mostly operate in master slave mode.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
These 
can be modeled using tree data structure wherein every 
node in the tree is balanced under the supervision of its 
parent node.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Master or manager can use light weight 
agent process to get statistics of slave nodes or child 
nodes.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Based upon the information gathered by the parent 
node provisioning or scheduling decision is made.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Three-phase hierarchical scheduling proposed in paper 
[19] has multiple phases of scheduling.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Request monitor 
acts as a head of the network and is responsible for 
monitoring service manager which in turn monitor service 
nodes.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
First phase uses BTO (Best Task Order) scheduling, 
second phase uses EOLB (Enhanced Opportunistic 
Load Balancing) scheduling and third phase uses EMM 
(Enhanced Min-Min) scheduling.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Load Balancing Based on Task 
Dependencies
Dependent tasks are those whose execution is dependent 
on one or more sub-tasks.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
They can be executed only after 
completion of the sub-tasks on which it is dependent.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Therefore, scheduling of such task prior to execution of 
sub-tasks is in-efficient.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Task dependency is modeled 
using workflow based algorithms.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Workflow basically uses DAG [25] as knowledge base 
to represent task dependency.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Different workflow based 
solution consider different parameters.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Algorithm are 
designed keeping in mind whether single or multiple 
workflows are to be modeled or single or multiple QoS 
parameters are to be maintained in the system.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Different 
workflows with or without completely different structure 
are termed as multiple workflows.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Workflows can also 
be classified as Transaction Incentive (multiple instances 
of one workflow that have same structure) and Data 
Incentive workflows (size and quantity of data is large).
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Cost based scheduling algorithm in [26] is designed for 
single workflows.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
It partitions the workflows and assigns 
each partition a deadline.
title: A Comparative Study of Load Balancing Algorithms in Cloud Computing Environment

text:
Zhifeng Yu and Weisong Shi 
designed an algorithm for multiple workflows which 
focus only on execution time.

arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014
Academic Cloud Computing Research: Five Pitfalls and Five Opportunities
Adam Barker, Blesson Varghese, Jonathan Stuart Ward and Ian Sommerville
School of Computer Science, University of St Andrews, UK
Abstract
This discussion paper argues that there are ﬁve funda-
mental pitfalls, which can restrict academics from con-
ducting cloud computing research at the infrastructure
level, which is currently where the vast majority of aca-
demic research lies.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Instead academics should be con-
ducting higher risk research, in order to gain understand-
ing and open up entirely new areas.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
We call for a renewed mindset and argue that academic
research should focus less upon physical infrastructure
and embrace the abstractions provided by clouds through
ﬁve opportunities: user driven research, new program-
ming models, PaaS environments, and improved tools to
support elasticity and large-scale debugging.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The objec-
tive of this paper is to foster discussion, and to deﬁne
a roadmap forward, which will allow academia to make
longer-term impacts to the cloud computing community.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
1
Introduction
Imagine a world where there was no academic cloud
computing research.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Would the ﬁeld of cloud comput-
ing really be any different from what it is today?
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
This paper argues that
academics are addressing the wrong class of problems to
have any lasting impact, and that cloud computing has
evolved without substantial inﬂuence from academia.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The core of this problem comes down to scale: aca-
demics generally do not have low-level infrastructure
(e.g., compute, storage, network) access to data centre
sized resources, in order to design, deploy and test al-
gorithms.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
To circumvent this access problem academics
simulate the behaviour of data centres, and run exper-
iments on small (toy) private clouds deployments.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
If
this research is then deployed at scale, there is the ever
present risk it is non representative of real world data
centres, and is therefore of limited value to the commu-
nity.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
In addition, a large proportion of academic research
focuses on incremental improvements to existing frame-
works created by industry, e.g., Hadoop optimisation for
a small set of edge cases.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Typically these contributions
are short-lived and have no lasting impact on the cloud
computing community; not because these contributions
are irrelevant, but because these kinds of problems are
already being solved by industry, who do have access to
low-level infrastructure at scale [26].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Instead academics should be conducting higher risk
research, which sheds light on more complex problems,
in order to gain understanding and open up entirely new
areas.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
We expect to see genuine cloud research focus
less upon physical infrastructure and continue to em-
brace abstraction through user driven research, program-
ming models, and Platform as a Service (PaaS) clouds.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
In addition, research needs to focus on providing soft-
ware engineers with better tools to program truly elastic
applications, and debug large-scale applications, which
utilise existing cloud infrastructure.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The objective of this
paper is to foster discussion, and to deﬁne a roadmap
forward, which will allow academia to make longer-term
impacts.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Many of these observations have been derived
from an eight year UK research programme focused on
Large Scale Complex IT Systems (LSCITS) [25].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
2
Five Pitfalls of Academic Research
Pitfall 1: Infrastructure at Scale
The presence of unused capacity within large-scale data
centres led to the development of what became known as
cloud computing.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Therefore, since its inception, cloud
computing and scale are inseparably linked.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Today, rapid
scalability and on demand resource provisioning are af-
forded to users through the ever increasing scale of cloud
providers.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Current estimates of the scale of Amazon
EC2, the dominant public cloud provider, vary between
156,225 and 454,400 servers [27].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Amazon Web Ser-
vices (AWS) are now the largest web host on the planet,
1


which hosts numerous high proﬁle customers including
Netﬂix, Instagram, DuckDuckGo and Reddit.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The scale of AWS and equivalent cloud providers (in
terms of servers, users, data, etc.) cannot be easily repli-
cated.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
To produce a similar environment requires signif-
icant capital expenditure, which is extremely prohibitive
for academic researchers.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
At best, academic researchers
can hope to reproduce a tiny subsection of the resources
available through AWS.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Typically this is achieved though
the use of a small testbed built from commodity hard-
ware running, for example OpenStack [30].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Such de-
ployments typically number between the tens and hun-
dreds of servers, supported by gigabit Ethernet and com-
modity network attached storage.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
As such they cannot
come close to replicating the scale of the compute, net-
work or storage capacity that is expected from even the
smallest public clouds.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
In order to perform an evaluation which indicates per-
formance on a public cloud, there is no substitute for a
real world public cloud deployment.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Researchers who
wish to investigate applications or phenomena running
on top of Virtual Machines (VMs) and storage from a
public cloud provider can feasibly do so.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Any research
which must be evaluated at scale can incur signiﬁcant
costs but remains a feasible means of evaluation.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
If however research is focused upon low-level com-
pute, storage, network, energy or other systems there is
the ever present risk of producing an evaluation which
is non representative of real world cloud deployments.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Without access, academics cannot modify and evaluate
low-level cloud mechanics, making useful research in
this area all but infeasible.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Work which is targeted at
the cloud infrastructure level and evaluated on a non rep-
resentative private testbed can at best deliver interim re-
sults, which suggest how it may behave when deployed
in a real world context.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
This has caused a dichotomy within academic cloud
research: between those researchers with access and
partnership with cloud providers and those without.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Two
recent examples to illustrate the point include: the latest
best paper award at IEEE Cloud 2013 [31] was awarded
for collaborative research between Princeton and NEC,
the best paper at SIGCHI (non-cloud research but re-
quires access to data) was awarded for research between
Facebook and Carnegie Mellon University [12].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
This ac-
cess problem prevents academics from having any last-
ing impact, and has signiﬁcant implications for systems
research investigating the lower levels of the cloud stack.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
For academics that are used to low-level access this bar-
rier to research is unprecedented.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
There are efforts underway with the European Union
BONFIRE [9] project, and Open Cirrus [29] to provide
academics with access to large-scale resources.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Indi-
vidual academics are predominantly concerned with re-
search and not maintaining testbeds and research sys-
tems.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
A high turnover of researchers and a emphasis on
research (and not maintenance) often leads to the neglect
and eventually the premature abandonment of testbeds.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
To ensure the longevity of a research system, with appro-
priate documentation and maintenance, dedicated staff
are necessary.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
This cannot be easily afforded be indi-
vidual institutions.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Academics need to collaborate, self
organise and build their own data centres at the national
level (through government funding etc.) in order to pro-
vide the facilities and maintenance necessary for aca-
demics to conduct meaningful cloud computing research.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Pitfall 2: Abstraction
Abstraction is one of the key features of the cloud com-
puting model.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The main principle of public cloud com-
puting models is that a user can make use of VMs as if
they were offered as a service, and the complexities of
managing and maintaining hardware are abstracted from
an end user.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
This translates into the fact that such an ab-
straction results in an ‘observation-only’ or a ‘black box’
model.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Unlike the grid, the low-level machine details
are concealed on the cloud.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
This has a number of com-
pelling advantages over grid computing architectures in-
cluding elastic on-demand architecture and high service
availability [6].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
However, in academic cloud computing research, such
an abstraction in which the cloud is merely used as a ser-
vice or tool for computing has been of minimal interest,
e.g., deployment of a Physic’s application on the cloud
to compare performance with a cluster environment.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
In
addition, a lot of academic cloud computing research has
a reverse engineering focus, where low-level infrastruc-
ture components are often (poorly) reimplemented for
the purposes of research prototypes.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
This not only con-
tradicts the underlying principle of public cloud comput-
ing models (to be used as a service), but such research
meets with little support from the cloud providers them-
selves.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
However, research which has built on top of exist-
ing cloud platforms in order to provide new functionality
has been enormously successful.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
RightScale [32] is an
exemplar of how academic cloud computing research has
added innovative new features and been commercialised.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Pitfall 3: Non-reproducible Results
As academics do not have low-level access to data cen-
tre resources, why not simulate a data centre instead?
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
This is a reasonable response from academia to the prob-
lem of access to such large-scale resources, and has
worked well in the networking community, e.g., NS3
[28].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
There are multiple simulators, which attempt to
model and simulate a cloud computing environment, in-
2


cluding CloudSim [13] and GreenCloud [24].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Simula-
tions can be effectively used as a prototyping mechanism
to provide a rough idea of how a particular algorithm
may perform.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The problem with each of these simula-
tion tools is that it is very difﬁcult to verify if the simu-
lation environment is an accurate representation of a real
world data centre environment.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
To date there have been
no attempts by the community to align simulations with
real world data from industry – refer to pitfall 5 for a
further discussion of industrial relations.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Furthermore,
real world data centres are constantly evolving, and are
subject to both planned and unplanned changes.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
There-
fore even if a simulation model is veriﬁed at a particular
point in time, this will no longer hold if the simulation
is rerun at a later point in time.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Research which is built
on top of these simulation environments (e.g., simulation
of VM migration) has next to no real world application,
other than to demonstrate a prototype algorithm or appli-
cation.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
An alternative approach for academics without direct
access to large-scale infrastructure is to build simulations
with real world trace data.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
While there are a few exam-
ples [8, 36] of companies releasing trace data for aca-
demics, we consider this to be the exception rather than
the rule, and traces are only available for a very limited
set of applications.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
In order to get a paper accepted to one of the top-tier
cloud computing conferences a thorough evaluation must
be presented for peer-review.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Usually this evaluation has
a very speciﬁc environment in terms of hardware and
software, which may very well be a bespoke setup up
for the purposes of getting a paper accepted for publi-
cation.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Reproducing these results is next to impossible
unless a replica of the evaluation environment can be de-
ployed, or access is granted to the original environment.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Furthermore, results of an evaluation are usually not gen-
eral purpose; just because an expected behaviour was ob-
served on a 10 node private cloud, does not mean that the
same results will be observed on a 10,000 node data cen-
tre.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
There are currently no reliable mathematical models
of how clouds scale over time, this is something that we
highlight as an immediate research opportunity, and can
only be solved through improved relationships between
academia and industry, discussed further in pitfall 5.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Pitfall 4: Rebranding
Academia is notoriously trend driven, and in order to
gain competitive funding, government PhD programmes
and collaboration academics must be working in certain
current areas of research.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Much of academic cloud com-
puting research is simply grid computing, or cluster com-
puting, or e-Science rebranded as cloud computing re-
search.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The novelty of the cloud over preceding infrastruc-
tures such as clusters and grids include features such as
elasticity, scalability, on-demand availability and mini-
mal user maintenance of the resources [18].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The majority
of academic cloud computing research does not require
any of these core properties, which differentiate clouds
from other forms of infrastructure.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Researchers within the cloud domain must embrace
the avenues of research which the paradigm allows for.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Research which places its focus at the bottom of the
cloud stack at the level of virtualisation, OS and systems
research may have signiﬁcant fundamental implications
for cloud computing, but many of these results cannot
be tested by the wider academic community due to lack
of access to infrastructure at scale listed in pitfall 1.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
We
believe that academic research which operates higher up
the stack is likely to have a longer-term impact.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Pitfall 5: Industrial Relations
As discussed throughout this short paper, the only effec-
tive way to develop and test new cloud services is to de-
ploy them at a scale.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Unfortunately there are virtually
no mechanisms which allow academics to gain access
to data centres in order to conduct low-level systems re-
search.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
This is a completely understandable stance by
industry, why would a company like Google, or Amazon
allow academics access to production, or even test data
centres in order to evaluate new academic research?
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Vis-
iting programmes at Google such as the Visiting Faculty
Programme [20] do exist, but are not available to the vast
majority of the academics working on cloud computing
research.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
There are examples of University research labs
working in tandem with cloud infrastructure providers;
a recent success story is the Algorithms Machines and
People Lab (AMPLab) [1], at UC Berkeley.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
However,
these relationships are difﬁcult to establish, and are only
available to the very top-tier institutions with access to
reliable industry contacts.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
There are multiple programmes which allow aca-
demics to use the cloud as a service, for example the
AWS Education programme [7], Windows Azure for Re-
search programme [39], and Google App Engine Re-
search Awards [19].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
These programmes are ideal for
building and testing applications which sit within an IaaS
or PaaS cloud.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
However these programmes do not solve
the problem with low-level infrastructure access, which
is where the majority of current academic research lies.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
3


3
Five Opportunities for Academic Re-
search
Opportunity 1: User Driven Research
We believe the enthusiasm in the academic community
for cloud research needs to be directed towards problems
that genuinely require the exploitation of elasticity, scal-
ability and abstractions offered by the cloud.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
A num-
ber of such problems exist in science, but a large pro-
portion can be addressed on clusters and simply do not
require the core properties of clouds.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The requirements
of such domain experts need to be understood and then
cloud-based environments developed in order to facili-
tate scientiﬁc discovery.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Here we make the differenti-
ation between building clouds for science applications,
which is not what we are suggesting, but using existing
cloud services effectively, which make use of elasticity,
scalability and suitable abstractions.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
One potential area
that can be explored in this context are virtual private
research environments using simple cloud tools but tai-
lored to suit speciﬁc domain requirements.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Such an ap-
proach is adopted in the ELVIRA [37] and CARMEN
[38] projects.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Another area that needs to be investigated is the de-
velopment of environments that support budget-limited
computation based on a set of user driven requirements.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Let us assume that a job needs to be executed for a pro-
longed period but is constrained in the total available
budget for computation.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
How can the job be most effec-
tively executed across clouds, and what models of pre-
dicting computational workloads and calculating costs
need to be developed.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Here again we make a differenti-
ation between developing cost models for the cloud, and
cost computation and prediction models on top of exist-
ing clouds, and the latter is our suggestion for pursuing
in an academic environment.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
User driven research on the
cloud overlaps with research that needs to focus on PaaS
environments which is considered in opportunity 4.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Opportunity 2: Programming Models
Engineers need more efﬁcient, scalable and usable pro-
gramming models, which will allow them to take full
advantage of the core properties of cloud computing.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Through the use of programming models built on top
of cloud resources, developers should be able to write
scalable, elastic code without having to mange low-level
cloud primitives.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
At present, MapReduce is the default programming
model for applications which deal with large data sets,
and has been a highly usable approach to dealing with
data.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
However, MapReduce is not always the appro-
priate model and there are seldom alternatives.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
There
is some variation available from tools which are built
upon MapReduce including Apache Hive [4], Cloud-
era Impala [17] and Apache Pig [5].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
These tools of-
fer programming abstractions which are not available in
vanilla Hadoop, however they still rely upon the under-
ling MapReduce functionality.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
There are several alternative programming models
which are beginning to emerge which deviate from con-
ventional MapReduce semantics.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The Apache Spark [41]
project is a successful example of a project which has
made the transition from academic research into produc-
tion cluster environments in major companies.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Spark
is an engine for large-scale data processing which of-
fers higher levels of performance for certain application
classes when compared to MapReduce.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Another emerg-
ing programming model is Apache Drill [3], an open
source reimplementation of Google BigQuery which
is designed for high throughput queries on very large
datasets.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Drill is currently an incubator project at Apache
and like many other programming models hinges on fur-
ther development and mass adoption to ensure its suc-
cess.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Opportunity 3: Bugs in Large-Scale Appli-
cations
Large-scale systems are inherently difﬁcult to manage.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The level of complexity and rate of change in such sys-
tems presents a constantly moving target, which requires
substantial talent and manpower to mange.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Debugging
large-scale cloud applications is exceptionally difﬁcult,
due to the scale of a deployment, the abstraction from
the underlying hardware, and the nature of a remote de-
ployment.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Research should focus on a tool chain which
allows engineers to collect, visualise and inspect the state
of jobs running across many thousands of cores.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Tools
should focus on the emergent properties of large-scale
applications; properties which can only be observed
when applications are deployed at the scale offered by
cloud resources.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Research into this area can be built on
top of existing cloud platforms and wouldn’t necessarily
require low-level access to large-scale testbeds.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
In academia, however, this area has received insuf-
ﬁcient attention hitherto the means to develop and de-
bug large-scale applications are under researched.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
There
remains only a small body of research in this crucial
area [42, 15], which limits the ability of academics to
translate prototypes into real world software.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
A lack of
knowledge forces current research to be discarded or sig-
niﬁcantly rewritten in order to be applicable to large-
scale systems.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Through further investigation into the
software engineering of large-scale systems, academics
can produce superior cloud research which supports the
scale of systems that are now becoming commonplace.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
4


Opportunity 4: PaaS Environments
Platform as a Service (PaaS) clouds aim to offer a higher
level of abstraction, away from bare-bones infrastructure
services.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
At this level of the cloud stack the focus is
on automating certain tasks, which if done by manually
writing programs can be a time consuming task.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
In other
words an abstract environment, which incorporates elas-
ticity and on-demand service features offered through an
easy to use interface [11, 40].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Generic frameworks such as StarCluster [35] and
Cloud Foundry [16] exist to address some of the au-
tomation described above.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
PaaS environments for sci-
ence are gaining momentum (for example, Helix Neb-
ula: The Science Cloud [21]).
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
We believe this is one
avenue of research that can beneﬁt from being pursued.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Here the focus needs to be placed on building environ-
ments, which make use of cloud infrastructure provided
by multiple vendors, and at the same time providing a
high-level interface that will allow scientists to quickly
and easily access the resources.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Such research can reap
maximum beneﬁt if based on user driven requirements
and directed towards developing stand-alone and inde-
pendent environments, which make use of the variety of
PaaS features offered by the providers.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Opportunity 5: Elasticity
The most signiﬁcant beneﬁts of cloud computing are ob-
tained by applications that scale over a large number of
resources.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Traditionally, in grid and cluster environments
the resources requested for an application had to be pro-
visioned before its execution.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Cloud computing, how-
ever, facilitates dynamic resource provisioning and pro-
vides a high level abstract interface for doing this.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
While
elasticity is often confused with scalability and work-
load management, there are overlaps which should not be
avoided [22].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Within this area, we believe that there are
numerous challenges, which can be addressed for driving
academic cloud research forward.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The ﬁrst challenge within elasticity is related to re-
source provisioning, an area which overlaps with scala-
bility [23, 33].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Through the Infrastructure as a Service
layer large pools of abstracted resources can be quickly
provisioned.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
This facilitates a wide range of research op-
portunities.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Notably the issues of efﬁcient provisioning
are not yet fully addressed.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
There is a need for research
which investigates how to avoid under and over provi-
sioning, how to provision for performance and cost, and
how to efﬁciently compute requirements.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The second challenge is related to workload manage-
ment, which again overlaps with the issue of scalabil-
ity [2].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
How can frameworks use workload information
for provisioning resources, or is it possible to anticipate
the workload which can be used to provision resources
thereby reducing the effects of variable times in provi-
sioning resources.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
The third challenge is related to modelling elasticity
[14, 10].
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
An attractive feature of the cloud is its abstract
view of elasticity and how easily resources can be provi-
sioned.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
One important question that arises is can the ab-
stract view also present different views of the system.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
For
example, what level of performance can be obtained by
provisioning n resources when the workload increases by
m%, what cost models can best capture these scenarios,
what additional costs will be incurred when n resources
are added.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
There are ongoing efforts to address these
issues (e.g., the SPEC RG Cloud Working Group [34]),
but we believe this needs to be a direction for refocusing
academic cloud computing research.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Addressing these
challenges can elicit collaborations with industry.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
4
Conclusion
Contemplating whether academics are addressing the
wrong class of problems to have any lasting impact on
the cloud computing community motivated this discus-
sion paper.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
Its objective is to foster a useful discussion
about how academia can focus its efforts to solve mean-
ingful problems.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
We have argued that there are ﬁve fundamentalpitfalls,
which restrict academics from conducting research at the
infrastructure level, which is where the vast majority of
current academic research focuses.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
These pitfalls are re-
lated to restricted access to data centre sized resources,
the abstraction provided by the cloud, reproducing re-
sults in a real cloud environment, rebranding previous
research, and a lack of industrial relations that prohibit
meaningful cloud research in academia.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
We expect to see genuine cloud research focus less
upon physical infrastructure and continue to embrace
abstraction through user driven research, programming
models, and PaaS clouds.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

text:
In addition research needs to
focus on providing software engineers with better tools
to program truly elastic applications, and debug large-
scale applications, which utilise existing cloud infras-
tructure.
title: arXiv:1406.4974v1  [cs.DC]  19 Jun 2014

Cluster is a connected group of loosely coupled

Scheduling Fundamentals and Terminology 
1) What is Scheduling?
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
Scheduling is a decision process of assignment of 
the relatively large number of jobs to the relatively 
small number of workers in either space or time or 
both 
dimensions 
in 
order 
to 
achieve 
desired 
objective(s).
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
This decision may depend on duration of 
tasks/activities, predecessor tasks/activities, resource 
availability, and target completion time depending 
upon target environment made of workers, types of 
jobs, and desired requirements pertaining to the 
completion of jobs.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
For example, scheduling in 
Operating System allocates CPU, a worker, to the live 
processes, jobs, running in the system.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
Scheduling is 
also used in multi-processor systems, automated 
manufacturing 
systems, 
flight 
scheduling, 
train 
scheduling, etc.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
2) Scheduling Terminology 
• 
Release-time (date): The earliest time at which 
a job can start its processing.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
• 
Processing-time: The time-duration needed by 
a job to ﬁnish its processing.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
• 
Start-time: The actual time at which a job starts 
its processing.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
• 
Finish-time: The actual time at which a job 
ﬁnishes its processing.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
• 
Expected execution time: It is a time expected 
to be taken up by a job to ﬁnish its execution.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

Scheduling in Systems 
1) Scheduling in Operating System v/s Scheduling in 
Grid 
If scheduling decision is taken by OS, then why one 
needs to learn one more scheduling, i.e., Grid 
Scheduling.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
In Operating System, most applications are 
user interactive.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
OS does instruction level (CPU) 
scheduling.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
It exploits interleaving of I/O operations 
and CPU operations.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
The main objective of scheduling 
in 
OS 
is 
fairness 
among 
processes.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
In 
Grid 
environment, 
most 
applications 
are 
not 
user 
interactive.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
Grid scheduling works at task level in 
which parallelism of independent tasks is exploited.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
The main objective in Grid scheduling is finish job or 
application at earliest.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
The scheduling of OS is of type 
local scheduling as it determines how the processes 
resident on a single CPU are allocated and executed.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
The scheduling in Grid is of type global scheduling as 
it allocates processes to multiple resources to optimize 
system wide performance objective or application 
specific objective.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

3) Relating Machine Scheduling with Grid Scheduling 
The machine scheduling problem is mentioned here 
to make reader familiar with how Grid scheduling and 
machine scheduling [2] are related.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
The novel 
approaches used for machine scheduling problem can 
be explored for their applicability in Grid scheduling.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
In machine scheduling problem, there are m machines, 
n jobs, and m tasks (operation in each job) per job.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
Three 
shop 
scheduling 
problems 
are 
concisely 
presented below.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
• 
Open-shop scheduling: Different tasks of the 
same job may be scheduled in any order.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
If 
preemption of tasks is allowed, the tasks can be 
interleaved.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
• 
Flow-shop scheduling: If the order of tasks is 
ﬁxed and it is same for all jobs, then scheduling 
is called ﬂow-shop scheduling.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
• 
Job-shop scheduling: In this scheduling, tasks 
of a job are totally ordered, But the order of 
tasks is possibly different for each job.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
Based on above definition of different machine 
scheduling problems, the problem of scheduling of 
independent tasks in Grid can be related to the Open-
shop scheduling and the problem of scheduling of 
dependent tasks in Grid can be related to the Job-shop 
scheduling.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
Scheduling of looping part of the control 
flow graph can be related to Flow-shop scheduling.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
Characteristic of the problem of scheduling in Grid 
In Grid computing, the problem of scheduling 
involves a number of tasks and a number of resources.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
General objective of scheduling in Grid is to generate 
optimal mapping of the tasks onto the resources.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
This 
mapping of tasks in distributed environment is NP-
Complete [17] problem.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
Therefore, we need to use 
heuristic to solve such problems in polynomial time.
title: Scheduling in Grid Computing Environment

text:
A 
workflow scheduling is a specialized version of 
scheduling of jobs in distributed environment, in 
which there exists dependencies among jobs.

SYSTEMS FOR GRID COMPUTING AND SCHEDULING 
This section presents understandings of various 
sub-systems/systems 
that 
could 
be
