ashraf_shahen@ccis.imamu.edu.sa 
 
 
Abstract— In the past few years, computer worms are seen as one of significant challenges of cloud 
computing.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Worms are rapidly changing and getting more sophisticated to evade detection.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
One major issue 
to defend against computer worms is collecting worms’ payloads to generate their signature and study their 
behavior.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
To collect worms’ payloads, we identified challenges for detecting and collecting worms’ payloads 
and proposed high-interactive honeypot to collect payloads of zero-day polymorphic worms in homogeneous 
and heterogeneous cloud computing platforms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Virtual machine (VM) memory and VM disk image are 
inspected from outside using open-source forensics tools and VMWare Virtual Disk Development Kit.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Our 
experiments show that the proposed approach overcomes the identified challenges.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Keywords— Computer Worms, Virtual Machine Monitoring (VMM), Cloud Computing, Virtual Machine 
Introspection (VMI), Polymorphic Worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
INTRODUCTION 
Rapid growth of the demand for computational outsourcing has led to the creation of large-scale cloud 
computing data centers.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Organizations outsource their computational needs to cloud data centers instead of 
incurring high upfront costs in purchasing IT infrastructure, and dealing with maintenance and upgrades of both 
software and hardware [2].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Cloud computing data centers leverage virtualization technology to allow creation of 
multiple Virtual Machine (VM) instances on a single physical server and allow creation of multiple virtual 
networks (VN) on a single physical network [1].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Cloud computing networks contain thousands of VMs.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Such networks are susceptible to attack from attackers 
and malware programs, so that the cloud providers have to take pre-emptive steps to ensure security in their 
cloud networks.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Computer worms are the most danger malware computer programs that harm cloud networks [4, 
15].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Worms can be used to perform many malicious activities (e.g., steal information, launch-flooding attacks 
against servers, etc.) [14].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Worms’ writers try to make their worms undetectable as long as possible to infect 
many more hosts.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
In another side, cloud providers try to minimize worms’ life and spreading in their cloud 
networks.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Using virtualization software (e.g., VMWare, Xen, and KVM), all components in the real physical networks 
can be virtualized, and spreading of worms can be minimized by isolating the traffic of each virtual network 
from the traffic of other networks.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The traffic is isolated even if their VMs are on the same physical server and 
their virtual interfaces transmit traffic across the same underlying NIC [6].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Any VM outside of the virtual 
network cannot sniff or inject traffic into the virtual network [6].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
However, VMs are still susceptible to attack 
from worms running in VMs in the same virtual network.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Detecting and collecting worms’ payloads are very significant processes in defending against unknown 
worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Collected payloads can be used to generate worms’ signatures and to study their malicious activities.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
In 
this paper, we identified a set of challenges for detecting and collecting worms’ payloads.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Additionally, we 
proposed an approach to detect and collect payloads of unknown and self-replicated polymorphic worms in 
homogeneous and heterogeneous cloud computing platforms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The proposed approach attaches honeypots with 
the inspected virtual networks to get the payload of the running worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Different polymorphic worm instances 
are collected using double honeypot.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Honeypots’ VMs are inspected in hypervisor layer using open-source 
forensic tools together with virtual disk image management tools.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Finally, we evaluated the proposed approach 
based on the previously defined challenges.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Section 2 gives some background of computer worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Section 3 gives a 
short overview of related works.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Section 4 presents our approach and illustrates the design and implementation 
of the proposed approach.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: The proposed approach is evaluated in section 5.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
COMPUTER WORMS  
A worm is a self-replicated malware computer program, which propagated over the network with or without 
human intervention.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Worms send copies of their code to victim machines and gain control of the execution of 
remote programs to execute their code in remote machines.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Worms gain control of a program’s execution by 


2
injecting new code into the program, injecting new control-flow edges into the program, or corrupting data used 
by the program [14].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The most popular techniques to detect computer worms can be categorized into two major categories [15], [7]: 
anomaly-based detection and signature-based detection.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Anomaly-based detection techniques use the knowledge 
of what is considered as a normal behavior to identify computer worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Although, anomaly-based detection is 
able to detect new and unknown computer worms, it reduces the network speed by checking every packet and 
reduces the computer performance by monitoring all activities.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Signature-based detection techniques detect known computer worms from other programs by comparing them 
against signatures of known computer worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
A signature is a pattern generated using instances of known 
computer worm to identify it.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
However, signature-based detection cannot detect new computer worms and 
maintaining signature database is not easy task [15].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Detection of computer worms can be improved by combining techniques from both categories.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
For example, 
a signature-based detection technique can be used to filter know computer worms and an anomaly-based 
detection technique can be used to detect unknown computer worms and collect their payloads.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Collected 
payloads are forwarded to a signature generator, which generates signatures.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Based on the generated signatures, 
signature-based detector will detect these worms in the future.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
By inspecting the behavior of the collected 
payloads, we can gain sufficient knowledge about their malicious activities, which will help in decontaminating 
infected VMs.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Worms use different techniques to be hidden and undetectable.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
For Example, to avoid detection by analyzing 
network traffic patterns, Worms blend their attack traffic within normal traffic.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
To avoid detection by 
monitoring the running processes and the loaded modules, worms attach themselves with trusted processes and 
modules.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
To avoid detection by monitoring the scanned IP addresses, worms collect addresses in infected 
computers to find new victims instead of scanning complete IP address space.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
To circumvent detection by 
monitoring changes in file system, worms may remain in memory for a period of time and perform some 
malicious activities, such as opening a back door on the host or sending the confidential information on the host 
to the worms’ writers before modifying the file system [19].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
To evade detection by memory scanners that scan 
the inspected memory linearly, worms move their memory structures to a region that has already been scanned 
[19].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
To evade detection by detectors, worms try to identify if the remote system is a detector before sending their 
code and try to infer if they are running inside detection environment before starting their malicious actions.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Worms can identify detectors remotely by analyzing its responses to network messages and identify detectors 
locally by monitoring their behavior.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
To avoid detection by anomaly-based detectors, worms can try to be smooth and silent by performing small 
amounts of malicious activities and avoid loud activities (e.g., consuming the computer resources, sending a 
large number of Emails, establishing a large number of network connections, etc.).
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: To avoid detection by signature-based detectors, worms use polymorphism.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Polymorphic worms change their 
payloads in every infection using encryption and code obfuscation.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
This change makes it difficult to generate 
signatures for these worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Generating signature for a polymorphic worm requires collecting a large number of 
payload’s instances and identifying the common byte strings in these payloads to be used as a worm signature.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
However, polymorphic worms can change their payload completely, which make it impossible to generate 
signatures [14].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Furthermore, polymorphic worms can avoid payloads’ collectors (e.g., double-honeynet systems) 
by checking if the worm is already running on the remote system before sending their code.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Another technique to evade detection by signature-based detectors is designing worms as a set of components.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Each standalone component is not harmful by itself and can stay in your computer without any malicious actions.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Different combinations of these components perform Worm’s activities.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Worms are designed with a large 
number of combinations to make it difficult to collect their pattern [8].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Finally, we can identify the following challenges for detecting and collecting worms’ payloads in cloud 
computing: 
• Polymorphic worms: the proposed approaches have to be able to collect a large number of payload 
instances for the same worm even if the worm uses polymorphism technique or checks its existence in the 
target machine before sending its code [15].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
•  Customer privacy: the proposed approaches have to avoid violating the customers’ privacy, which can be 
violated by accessing the VM memory, VM disk image, or running VM processes.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
• Computational resources: the proposed approaches have to provide effective technique to detect and 
collect worms with minimal computational resources [16].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
• Worms spreading: the proposed approaches have to avoid usage of tools that can be attacked by worms 
and accelerate worms spreading.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
• Out-box inspection: the proposed approaches have to use out-box inspection tools (e.g., virtual machine 
introspection (VMI), Virtual machine monitor (VMM), etc.) instead of using in-box inspection tools that 
inspect VM from inside to avoid detecting or attacking them by worms [4].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
3
• Homogeneous and heterogeneous platforms: cloud providers provide different platforms to gain a large 
number of customers.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Customers customize the provided virtual servers by installing specific software to 
achieve their businesses requirements.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The proposed approaches have to be able to detect and collect 
worms in a wide range of platforms, which is existed due to the big variation between customers’ 
requirements.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Different platforms means different types of worms because worms’ writers usually write 
their worms based on specific vulnerabilities.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
• Cloud computing management techniques: The proposed approaches have to be able to work with 
different cloud computing management techniques such as VM migration.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
In cloud computing, VM 
migration is used to consolidate VMs to the minimal number of physical servers according to their current 
resource requirements [2].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The proposed approach has to inspect VMs even if their locations are 
dynamically changed.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Scalability: Cloud computing datacenters are large-scale datacenters.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The proposed approaches have to be 
scalable to work with such centers.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
RELATED WORK 
In recent years, we have observed a rapid growth of using VMI in intrusion detection instead of using the 
legacy tools.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
In traditional approaches [10], [14], [15], [17], inspection tools are installed and running inside 
VMs, which are vulnerable to attack from attackers and malware programs.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Over the last years, many 
approaches have been proposed to inspect VM from outside to improve inspection and avoid attaching [3], [5], 
[11], [18].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: In this section, we are going to overview some of previous approaches.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The authors in [4] proposed an anomaly-based intrusion detection mechanism, which exploited virtual 
machine introspection (VMI) to collect a list of the running processes or modules of the running virtual 
machines.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
All collected information are gathered and analyzed by a centralized anomaly detector on a single 
virtual machine.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Any unknown process or module that occurs on an increasing number of virtual machines is 
considered as a computer worm.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The authors proposed a technique to collect information about unknown 
harmless processes.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Although, using single point to gather information provides an abstract centralized view on 
entire cloud network, it congests network links because cloud network maybe contains hundreds of thousands of 
VMs.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Furthermore, the proposed approach cannot detect computer worm that attached itself to trusted process.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The authors in [21] proposed a distributed network of detection agents to coordinate detection across whole 
cloud network.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Each agent is deployed in virtual machine monitor (VMM) of a physical cloud server.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Using 
VMI, agents collect information of the running VMs on servers they are associated with.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Agents monitor VM 
disk image, network activity, and state of VM memory.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Agents share information to determine threats that 
crosscut physical servers.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The proposed approach reduces the load on the network links by distributing the 
detection.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
However, monitoring all running VMs in the cloud data centers is a resources consuming process and 
increases the cost of cooling and operating these data centers, which will decrease the income profit.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: The authors in [8] identified a set of symptoms to indicate the possibility of malicious activities.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
For each 
symptom, a Forensic virtual machine (FVM) is defined to look for this symptom in running VMs.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
FVMs use 
VMI to inspect running VMs from outside.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
If a symptom is discovered in any VM, other FVMS are directed to 
inspect this VM for other symptoms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Collected information is sent to a centralized module to analyze them and 
take further actions.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
In [19], the authors proposed high-interaction honeypot monitor, which inspects memory of the running 
virtual machine on Xen by using the open source forensics tool Volatility.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Volatility accesses the VM’s memory 
by using interface functions provided by LibVMI API.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
LibVMI provides interfaces for low-level functionalities 
provided by Xen hypervisor.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Changed binaries in the inspected VM have been extracted by using Libguestfs, 
which is an open source library to analyze and manipulate file system.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Although the proposed approach 
succeeded in capturing a wide range of malware including normal worms, it did not provide a technique to 
collect polymorphic worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
In [14], the authors proposed a high-interaction double honeynet to collect polymorphic worms and proposed 
algorithms to generate signatures for the collected worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
However, the authors used in-box introspection tools 
(tools installed in inspected VMs) such as Honeywall, Sebek, and Snort-inline, which are susceptible to be 
detected or attacked by worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Furthermore, the proposed approach cannot collect polymorphic worms that 
check their existence in the target host before sending their code because the proposed double honeynet works 
by forming a loop to collect all polymorphic worm instances.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
In [16], the authors started by using VMI to detect incoming files and objects, and trigger file clustering 
module, which classifies incoming files and monitors their execution.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Two algorithms have been proposed to 
detect malicious activities for incoming files and objects.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Using VMI, data and information flow of malicious 
processes have been recorded instead of recording all data or information flow of all processes to simplify the 
analysis task.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
However, the proposed approach inspects all incoming files and object, and monitors their 
execution to detect malicious activities, which consumes many computer resources.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
4
As was shown previously, most of current approaches either inspect VMs from inside, inspect all running 
VMs, inspect all running processes and modules, or cannot collect polymorphic worm instances.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
In the next 
section, we will introduce our approach to collect polymorphic worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
THE PROPOSED APPROACH DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION 
The aim of the proposed approach is detecting and collecting payloads of zero-day active polymorphic worms 
in homogeneous and heterogeneous cloud computing platforms without violating the customer privacy.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
In the proposed approach, worms’ spreading is limited by isolating traffic of each virtual network from the 
traffic of other networks by using virtual switches in XenServer [6] or in VMware vCenter Server [20].
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
1 shows the isolation between two virtual networks using virtual distributed switches in 
VMware vCenter Server.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Each virtual network contains two virtual servers, which belong to the same distributed 
port group.

EVALUATION 
Now, we return to the previously listed challenges in section 2 to show that the proposed approach overcome 
these challenges.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
• Polymorphic worms: the proposed approach collects polymorphic worms payload using double honeynet , 
and periodically restores honeypots to the original state (before contamination) to collect worms that 
check if they are running in the target machine before sending their code.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
•  Customer privacy: to avoid violating the customers’ privacy, the proposed approach does not inspect the 
customers’ VMs directly.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The proposed approach uses honeypots to allow existing worms (if any) to 
infect them and inspect the infected honeypots instead of inspecting the customers’ VMs.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
• Worms spreading: honeypots are created from clean VMs’ templates and each honeypot is connected with 
only one virtual network to avoid transferring worms between virtual networks.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
All inspection tools are 
running outside the inspected honeypots (in hypervisor layer).
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Therefore, worms cannot detect or 
contaminate them.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
• Out-box inspection: in the proposed approach, VMs inspectors inspect honeypots from the outside by 
inspecting snapshots.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Therefore, worms cannot manipulate or detect them.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
• Homogeneous and heterogeneous platforms: the proposed approach uses different VMs’ template for 
honeypots to achieve variations between virtual networks.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Each VM template is designed to capture a 
category of worms that are designed to use vulnerabilities in its software.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
• Cloud computing management techniques: in the proposed approach, VMs inspectors connect honeypots 
with virtual networks by adding them to the port groups in virtual distributed switches, which allows 
honeypots to keep on connected with virtual networks even if they are migrated between hosts.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
• Scalability: introspection controller creates and destroys VM inspectors based on the number of the 
running virtual networks to follow the growing and the shrinking of the cloud computing datacenters.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: • Computational resources: the proposed approach does not inspect all running virtual machines.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Each VM 
inspector uses one honeypot for each virtual network and inspects virtual networks sequentially to 
minimize computer resources used during inspection process.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
To accelerate the introspection, all created 
VM inspectors running concurrently.

CONCLUSION 
In this paper, we have identified challenges facing current approaches during collecting polymorphic 
computer worms in cloud computing.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
A high-interactive double honeypot has been proposed to address the 
identified challenges.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
The proposed approach inspects VMs from outside to detect hidden processes and to 
avoid detection by worms.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: Customers’ privacy has been conserved by avoiding directly inspecting their VMs.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Used computer resources have been reduced by inspecting cloud datacenters by virtual network instead of by 
VM.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text: The proposed approach keeps tracking VMs even if there locations are changed over time.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
In our future work, we plan to investigate how to reduce the time of inspecting VM memory and how to 
reduce the number of honeypots required to inspect virtual networks.
title: Polymorphic Worms Collection in Cloud Computing

text:
Furthermore, we plan to extend our 
approach to inspect network traffic beside memory and file system.

title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Performance-per-watt is a critical metric for the evaluation of computer architectures for cost-
eﬃcient computing.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Additionally, future performance growth will come from heterogeneous,
many-core, and high computing density platforms with specialized processors.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
In this paper,
we examine the Intel Xeon Phi Many Integrated Cores (MIC) co-processor and Applied
Micro X-Gene ARMv8 64-bit low-power server system-on-a-chip (SoC) solutions for scientiﬁc
computing applications.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We report our experience on software porting, performance and energy
eﬃciency and evaluate the potential for use of such technologies in the context of distributed
computing systems such as the Worldwide LHC Computing Grid (WLCG).
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Introduction and Motivation
Processing the data produced by High Energy Physics (HEP) experiments like those at the
Large Hadron Collider (LHC) [1] at the European Laboratory for Particle Physics (CERN)
requires signiﬁcant computing resources.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The scale is beyond those available in a typical single
computer center.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The Worldwide LHC Computing Grid (WLCG) was established to provide the
computing resources needed for the LHC experiments, and used, for example, by the CMS and
ATLAS experiments for the discovery of the Higgs boson [2, 3].
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
It is a distributed computing
resource across 170 computing centers in 40 countries.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The CMS experiment, for example, used
between 80,000 and 100,000 x86 64 cores from the WLCG for its processing needs in 2012.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Planned luminosity upgrades of the LHC [4] will result in a 2-3 order of magnitude increase in
dataset sizes over the next 15 years, requiring commensurate increases in processing capacity.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: Intel is the leading company in general purpose server processors market.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Alternative
solutions, like ARMv8 64-bit, aim to provide high-density and energy eﬃcient platforms for
computing centers.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
These platforms delivered by multiple vendors are optimized for speciﬁc
market segments while ensuring compatibility by running a common instruction set, i.e.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
General purpose solutions provide beneﬁts to a full software stack
arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014


unlike graphics processing units (GPU), which require software redesign and only applicable for
portions of the application.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
In this paper we focus on two general purpose central processors: Applied Micro (APM)
X-Gene 1 ARMv8 64-bit Server-on-Chip and Intel’s Xeon Phi coprocessor.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We investigate these
two platforms as alternatives to the x86 64 family of processors used in the WLCG today.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We
base our results on performance (events per second) scalability over power (watts) usage.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The
power measurements we provide in this paper are for the silicon chip and not for a full computing
node.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Market
According to Gartner, Intel sold 92 percent of all server processors in 2013 [5].
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Distributed High
Throughput Computing (DHTC) is also dominated by x86 64.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
In contrast, ARM Holdings is a
leader in low power and high energy eﬃciency processors market.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Their business model diﬀers
from Intel as they provide license agreements for their intellectual property (IP) to partners.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Instruction set (ISA) licenses allow partners to create custom silicon chips for wide variety of
applications: mobile phones, notebook, servers and many others.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
In addition to providing ISA
licenses ARM Holdings oﬀers already designed and veriﬁed building blocks (CPU and GPU cores,
on-chip interconnect and similar) for manufacturing of silicon chips solutions.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Each solution is
designed to meet speciﬁc market requirements, while keeping the compatibility by running a
common ISA, like ARMv8 64-bit.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
ARM Holdings and partners introduced a new high energy
eﬃcient general purpose server products in 2014.

Integrated Cores (MIC) computer architecture.

combining beneﬁts of CPU and GPU into a single product.

a host system Intel Xeon processors.

It provides high computational power and high energy-
eﬃciency solution for HPC market.

CMS Software (CMSSW) port (still incomplete due to issues with the Intel C++ Compiler).

were provided with XC-1 development boards with a single X-Gene 1 APM883208 silicon chip

We have been working with APM for more
than a year to deliver CMS Software (CMSSW) and Open Science Grid (OSG) [7] software stack
for ARMv8 64-bit.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Software Porting Issues
We have previously reported work to port the CMS Software (CMSSW) to ARMv7 32-bit
System-on-Chip silicon chips [8, 6].
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
It allowed us to understand many issues arising when
porting to non-x86 64 architectures and to prepare for ARMv8 64-bit platforms.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Indeed issues
resolved for ARMv7 32-bit were often also relevant for ARMv8 64-bit, however some issues
speciﬁc to ARMv8 64-bit were encountered:
• Update of autoconf package was required for successful detection of ARMV8 64-bit
platform, aarch64.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
• In cases where ARMv8 64-bit support was already present, software packages were updated
to the newer version.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: • We added ARMv8 64-bit support to the ROOT [9] software package.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The ROOT (version
5) was extended with linuxarm64 target.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
One important feature, Reﬂex dictionary
generation, is not supported for ARMv8 64-bit.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
ROOT uses GCCXML as the underlying
implementation for data reﬂection, and GCCXML (based on GCC 4.2.1) is far too old for
ARMv8 64-bit support.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
However, because the data model – LP64 – is the same between
x86 64 and ARMv8 64-bit, we were able (as a workaround) to pre-generate dictionaries
on x86 64 and then compile them on ARMv8 64-bit.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We found that such dictionaries
work successfully.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
More recent releases of ROOT (version 6) use LLVM/Clang in place of
GCCXML for dictionary generation, but this still does not support ARMv8 64-bit due to
the use of the old Just-in-Time (JIT) interface.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
This JIT interface will be removed from
LLVM/Clang after the version 3.5 release and ROOT is scheduled to migrated to MCJIT
interface in 2015 [10].
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Until this migration happens rootcling will not work on ARMv8
64-bit systems.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
• Oracle Instant Client is only provided as proprietary binary blobs and not as source code,
and is not available for the ARMv7 32-bit and ARMv8 64-bit architectures.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
However, none
of the standard CMS workﬂows run on the WLCG depend on Oracle.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Only a few specialized
applications used at CERN alone need Oracle, for example, loading detector calibrations.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: • Toolchain (GCC and binutils) issues were found and reported upstream to the projects.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: The ﬁnal GCC 4.9.1 and binutils (bfd linker) 2.24 is now capable of compiling CMSSW.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
However, one issue remains open with CERN Virtual File System (CVMFS) package used
for CMSSW distribution across Grid sites.

We had to modify the way CVMFS components
(libcvmfs only.a, libz.a, libsqlite3.a, libcurl.a and libcares.a) are merged into
the ﬁnal libcvmfs.a library.

text:
ARMv8 64-bit Validation
To conﬁrm that CMSSW provides comparable results on ARMv8 64-bit and x86 64, an initial
validation was done using the reconstruction software workﬂow.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The validation necessarily
compared not only the two diﬀerent architectures (ARMv8 64-bit to x86 64), but also two
diﬀerent Linux distributions (Fedora 19 to Scientiﬁc Linux CERN 6.5).
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Any discrepancies due to
the latter, such as diﬀerent math libraries, should be resolved in future validations.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
In addition,


given that only a single board was available for ARMv8 64-bit, the validation was statistics
limited to see any very subtle eﬀects.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
With these minor caveats the observed diﬀerences are
minimal (ﬁgure 1 shows two examples) and within physics validation limits.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Grid Software
A new architecture such as ARMv8 64-bit would likely be initially deployed as a batch worker
node.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Thus we have also built the minimal set of required OSG software packages to support
that: voms-clients, HTCondor and CVMFS.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
CVMFS is used by CMS to distribute software and
small data packages around Grid sites.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: Thus no local installation of these packages is required.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: CMSSW for ARMv8 64-bit is available alongside with CMSSW for x86 64 in CVMFS.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We have
successfully used CMSSW release validation test suite on a local ARMv8 64-bit machine.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
It
runs a number of predeﬁned CMSSW (cmsRun) workﬂows with small number of events (10 or
100).
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The input for workﬂows was generated locally as the ﬁrst step or fetched from a remote
location.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The CMSSW workﬂows successfully fetched their input data from a remote xrootd
server [12, 13], which demonstrates a functioning voms-clients package on ARMv8 64-bit.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We installed and conﬁgured HTCondor on XC-1 development board to be a 8 slots (1-core
and 2GB memory) worker node at Princeton University.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
An additional x86 64 machine was
conﬁgured with HTCondor as a master node for our ARMv8 64-bit worker node.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The master
node was able to communicate with the worker node and successfully execute the tasks.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Test Environments for Power and Performance Measurements
We now describe the test environments we have used to do power and performance measurements
for an Intel Xeon processor, an APM ARMv8 64-bit X-Gene 1 Server-on-Chip and an Intel Xeon
Phi coprocessor.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
As described above, we have demonstrated standard CMSSW applications
running on the APM ARMv8 64-bit XC-1 board, however no three-way comparison of the
platforms with CMSSW was possible due to the lack of a full CMSSW port on the Xeon Phi.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We have thus used the Geant4 [14] benchmark, ParFullCMS, as a simple cross-platform test
capable of running in multi-threaded mode.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
This benchmark uses a complex geometry (from
CMS), but it is a standalone application distributed with Geant4.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Table 1 shows the selected
general purpose platforms used for the performance and energy eﬃciency benchmark.

text:
Intel Xeon
Our reference platform is a dual-socket Intel Xeon CPU E5-2650 @ 2.00GHz launched in Q1 2012.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: It is an 8 physical core Sandy Bridge CPU with hyper-threading (HT) enabled.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The particular
system was equipped with 256GB DDR3 memory.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
For silicon-to-silicon comparison we only
measured power consumption of a single socket.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
For the test, the ParFullCMS benchmark was
compiled with GCC 4.9.1.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Intel’s Running Average Power Limit (RAPL) [15, 11] technology was used for measuring
power usage of diﬀerent parts of the silicon chip.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
It is available in modern Intel micro-
architectures starting from Sandy Bridge.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
It is intended for controlling and limiting power
usage in silicon chip.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
In addition, RAPL provides capabilities to measure energy and power
usage.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: We used this capability to acquire readings from the silicon chip.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The following RAPL
domains are supported by server-grade silicon chips:
• PP0 (Power Plane 0) – processors cores subsystem.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: • DRAM (Memory) – directly-attached DRAM.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: The processors core subsystem consists of execution units, ALU, FPU, L1 and L2 caches.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The uncore subsystem (energy(PKG) - energy(PPO)) consists of Intel QuickPath Interconnect
(QPI), Last Level Cache (LLc), on-chip memory and I/O.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
RAPL provides ∼1ms [15] resolution
measurements.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: For the test we only measured PKG power domain for a single socket.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Reading
RAPL sensor data was done via model-speciﬁc registers (MSR) exposed to Linux user-land via
devfs.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Intel Xeon Phi
The Xeon Phi card is a highly parallel machine with 61 physical cores and 4-way multi-threading
running at 1.24GHz.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
It includes GPU-class 16GB GDDR5 memory, which provide ultra-high
bandwidth compared to standard DRAM solutions.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: The card we used had only passive cooling.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: The card supports two execution modes: native and oﬄoading.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
For simplicity our tests were
done using native execution on the card itself.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The Intel C++ Compiler (Intel Composer XE
2013 SP1 Update 2, 14.0.2 20140120) was used to compile the test as GCC does not provide Xeon
Phi support.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The Xeon Phi card includes a number of sensors to acquire power usage from diﬀerent domains
on the card.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We used libmicmgmt from Manycore Platform Software Stack (MPSS) 3.2 to read
the sensor data for diﬀerent domains (PCIe, 2x3, 2x4, VCCP, VDDG, VDDQ, instant power
and more).
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: There is drawback of non-direct sensor reading.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
libmicmgmt sends an interrupt over
PCIe bus to uOS (Linux) forcing Xeon Phi to switch to higher power state.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
This method cannot
be used for measuring idle power consumption.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We measured idle power consumption of the card
by physically removing it from the server enclosure.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We found that idle power consumption was
17W.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Two distinct datasets were used for Xeon Phi: one for
the whole card and another for VCCP + VDDG power domains.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
According to Performance API
(PAPI) [16] source code, VCCP power rail is processors core subsystem and VDDG – uncore
subsystem.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
APM X-Gene
APM X-Gene 1 is 8 physical core processor running at 2.4GHz.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The particular system, XC-1
development board, contains 16GB DDR3 memory.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The board provides 2 memory channels, but
APM883408 is capable of addressing 512GB of memory using 4 memory channels.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Investigation
done by APM showed that ParFullCMS test does not require high memory bandwidth.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We
would like to emphasize that the ﬁrmware for managing processor ACPI power states was not
available in time for the test.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We expect X-Gene 1 eﬃciency to increase once the ﬁrmware is
available.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: XC-1 is running a custom build of Fedora 19 provided by Red Hat.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
APM is working on X-Gene 1 optimizations for GCC, but changes were
not integrated upstream in time for the benchmark.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The XC-1 development board includes sensors for reading the power usage of diﬀerent
domains of the silicon chip.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We estimated power usage for the silicon chip by combining readings


for PMD (core subsystem) and SOC (uncore subsystem) power domains.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The XC-1 is an IPMI-
enabled device, thus readings from the sensors can be acquired by ipmitool tool.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We used IPMI
before in previous research, but we found that executing ipmitool is expensive and restricts the
measurements resolution.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
For XC-1 we read sensor data via I2C bus and avoided unnecessary
overheads caused by execution of ipmitool tool.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Results of Power and Performance Measurements
4.1.

text:
Platform Eﬃciency
Our energy eﬃciency benchmark provided three-way silicon level comparison between APM
X-Gene 1 – the ﬁrst on the market ARMv8 64-bit Server-on-Chip solution, Intel Xeon – the
dominating processor family in server market and Intel Xeon Phi – a highly parallel long-vector
processor family product intended for HPC workloads.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We sampled power usage readings from
sensors with one second resolution on all platforms.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
First we compared absolute performance provided by diﬀerent solutions by running on
all available hardware threads (ﬁgure
2).
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We found that Intel Xeon Phi provided the best
performance, 1.07 times higher performance to Intel Xeon.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
In the absence of the anticipated
compiler optimizations, APM X-Gene 1 provided 2.48 times lower performance than Intel Xeon,
but it was also operating at signiﬁcantly lower power usage.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text: Then we measured how performance scales over power (ﬁgure 3, ﬁgure 4).
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We found that
APM X-Gene 1 running at full capacity (8 threads) was drawing less power than Intel Xeon
running a single thread and delivered 2.73 times higher performance.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
The Hyper-Threading (HT)
on Intel Xeon did not deliver higher energy eﬃciency.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Additional few percent of performance
were gained at similar cost in power consumption (ﬁgure
3).
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
We also over committed APM
X-Gene 1 with 2 threads per physical core, but we did not observe signiﬁcant change in energy
eﬃciency.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Intel Xeon Phi as expected required at least 2 threads to achieve high utilization of
card.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:

performance

text:
Conclusions
We have built the software used by the CMS experiment at CERN, as well as portions of
the OSG software stack, for ARMv8 64-bit.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
It has been made available in the oﬃcial CMS
software package repository and via the CVMFS distributed ﬁle system used by Grid sites.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
Performance scalability over power usage
Our initial validation has demonstrated that APM X-Gene 1 Server-on-Chip ARMv8 64-
bit solution is a relevant and potentially interesting platform for heterogeneous high-density
computing.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
In the absence of platform speciﬁc optimizations in the ARMv8 64-bit GCC compiler
used, APM X-Gene 1 shows excellent promise that the APM X-Gene hardware will be a valid
competitor to Intel Xeon in term of power eﬃciency as the software evolves.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
However, Intel
Xeon Phi is a completely diﬀerent category of product.
title: arXiv:1410.3441v1  [cs.DC]  10 Oct 2014

text:
As APM X-Gene 2 is being sampled right now, built on the TMSC 28nm process, we look
forward to extending our work to include it into our comparison.

text:
Eﬃcient Straggler Replication in Large-scale Parallel Computing∗
Da Wang †
dawang@alum.mit.edu
Gauri Joshi ‡
gaurij@andrew.cmu.edu
Gregory Wornell†
gww@mit.edu
Abstract
In a cloud computing job with many parallel tasks, the tasks on the slowest machines (strag-
gling tasks) become the bottleneck in the job completion.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Computing frameworks such as
MapReduce and Spark tackle this by replicating the straggling tasks and waiting for any one
copy to ﬁnish.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Despite being adopted in practice, there is little analysis of how replication aﬀects
the latency and the cost of additional computing resources.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In this paper we provide a frame-
work to analyze this latency-cost trade-oﬀand ﬁnd the best replication strategy by answering
design questions such as: 1) when to replicate straggling tasks, 2) how many replicas to launch,
and 3) whether to kill the original copy or not.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Our analysis reveals that for certain execution
time distributions, a small amount of task replication can drastically reduce both latency as well
as the cost of computing resources.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
We also propose an algorithm to estimate the latency and
cost based on the empirical distribution of task execution time.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Evaluations using samples in
the Google Cluster Trace suggest further latency and cost reduction compared to the existing
replication strategy used in MapReduce.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
1
Introduction
In cloud computing, large-scale sharing of computing resources provides users with great ﬂexiblity
and scalability.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Computing frameworks such as MapReduce [6] and Apache Spark [27] are developed
to harness these beneﬁts.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
These frameworks employ massive parallelization by dividing a large job
into many tasks that can be executed parallely on diﬀerent machines.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
These frameworks can be used
to run optimization and machine learning algorithms that can be easily divided into independent
parallel tasks, for example alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) [2] and Markov
Chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC) [15].
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
The execution time of a task on a machine is subject to stochastic variations due to co-hosting,
virtualization and other hardware and network variations [5].
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Thus, a key challenge in executing a
job that consists of a large number of parallel tasks is the latency in waiting for the slowest tasks,
or the “stragglers” to ﬁnish.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
As pointed out in [5, Table 1], the latency of executing many parallel
tasks could be signiﬁcantly larger (140 ms) than the median latency of a single task (1 ms).
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In this work we provide a mathematical framework to analyze how replication of straggling
tasks aﬀects the latency and the cost of computing resources, and propose better scheduling policy
designs.

1.1
Related prior work
The idea of replicating tasks in parallel computing has been recognized by system designers [10],
and ﬁrst adopted at a large scale via the “backup tasks” in MapReduce [6].
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
A line of systems
work [1, 16, 26] and references therein further developed this idea.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
For example, Apache Spark
implements “speculative execution” to allow relaunching slow running tasks.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
While task replication has been studied in systems literature and also adopted in practice,
there is not much work on mathematical analysis of replication strategies.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Replication strategies
are analyzed in [25], mainly for the single task case.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In this paper we consider task replication for
a job consisting of a large number of tasks, which corresponds more closely to today’s large-scale
cloud computing frameworks.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
The use of redundancy to reduce latency has also attracted attention in other contexts such
as cloud storage and networking [8, 12, 13, 20, 21, 23].
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Most of these works that consider queueing
focus on the case of one task.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Waiting for many tasks is harder to analyze as indicated by fork-join
queue analysis.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
1.2
Our contributions
In this work we propose a framework to analyze strategies for replicating straggling tasks of a large
computing job.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In particular we consider three parameters of a straggler replication strategy: 1)
the fraction of tasks declared as stragglers, 2) number of replicas for each straggling tasks, and 3)
whether the original copy should be killed or kept running.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
We characterize how these parameters
impact the trade-oﬀbetween latency and computing cost.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Our characterizations allow us to identify
regimes with the surprising property that replicating a small fraction of tasks drastically reduces
latency while saving computing cost.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
These insights allow one to apply optimization to search for
scheduling policies based on one’s sensitivity to computing latency and computing cost.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text: The rest of the paper is organized as follows.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In Section 2 we introduce notation, formulate the
problem, and deﬁne performance metrics used in the paper.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In Section 3 we provide an analysis
of single-fork task replication policies and defer all proofs to Appendix A.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Then in Section 4 we
describe an algorithm that ﬁnds a good scheduling policy for execution time distributions that are
not analytically tractable (e.g., empirical distributions from real-world traces).
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In Section 5 we
conclude with a discussion of the implications and future perspectives.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

2.2
System Model
We consider a job consisting of n parallel tasks, where n is large1 and each task is assigned to
a diﬀerent machine.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
We use the probability distribution FX to model the random variation in
machine response time due to factors such as congestion, queueing, virtualization, and competing
jobs being run on the same machines, and assume this execution time distribution is independent
and identically distributed (i.i.d.) across machines.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
The identical assumption of FX implies that
tasks in this job are assigned to machines with processing power proportional to task size, with
the simplest case being a group of homogeneous tasks are assigned to a group of homogeneous
machines.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
The independent assumption of FX could be satisﬁed when machine response times
ﬂuctuate independently over time, or when each new task (or new replica) is assigned to a new
machine that is not previously used to run tasks of the current job.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Note that we treat the
variability that FX captures as an exogenous factor from a user’s perspective—in general a user
renting machines from a cloud computing service has little or no control over other jobs that share
the resources.2
2.3
Scheduling Policy
A scheduling policy or scheduler assigns one or more replicas of each task to diﬀerent machines,
possibly at diﬀerent time instants.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In this work, we assume the scheduler receives instantaneous
feedback notifying it when a machine ﬁnishes its assigned task, and there is no intermediate feedback
indicating the status of processing of a task.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
We focus our attention on a set of policies called single-
fork policies, deﬁned as follows.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text: Deﬁnition 1 (Single-fork scheduling policy).
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
A single-fork scheduling policy π (p, r) launches
all n tasks at time 0.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
For each of the remaining pn straggling
tasks, it chooses one of the following two actions:
• replicate and keep the original copy (πkeep (p, r)): launch r new replicas;
• replicate and kill the original copy (πkill (p, r)): kill the original copy and launch r + 1
new replicas.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
When the earliest replica of a task ﬁnishes, all the other remaining replicas of the same task are
terminated.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text: Note that in both scenarios there are a total of r +1 replicas running after the forking point.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
1
illustrates these two cases of keeping or killing the original copy of a task.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
For simplicity of notation
we assume that p is such that pn is an integer.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
We note that p = 0 corresponds to running n tasks
in parallel and waiting for all to ﬁnish, which is the baseline case without any replication or killing
any original tasks.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text: Remark 1 (Backup tasks in MapReduce and Spark).
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
The idea of “backup tasks” in Google’s
MapReduce [6], and “speculative execution” in Apache Spark [27] corresponds to a single-fork pol-
icy with r = 1 and πkeep.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text: The value of p is tuned dynamically and hence not speciﬁed in [6].
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
The
spark.speculation.quantile conﬁguration in Apache Spark corresponds to p in the single-fork
policy.

Although we focus on single-fork policies in this paper, the analysis can be generalized to multi-
fork policies, where new replicas of straggling tasks are launched at multiple times during the
execution of the job [24, Section 6.4].

text:
Forking multiple times can achieve a better latency-cost
trade-oﬀ, but could be undesirable in practice due to additional delay and complexity in obtaining
new and killing existing replicas.

text:
In this section we propose an algorithm to estimate the latency and cost from
the empirical distribution of task execution time.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
This enables users to evaluate the latency-cost
trade-oﬀof various replication strategy using execution trace directly, instead of a ﬁtted execution
time distribution.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Applying our algorithm to the Google Cluster Trace data [19], we show that it
is possible to improve upon the performance of the default replication policy in MapReduce-style
frameworks.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
4.1
Latency and Cost Estimation
To estimate the latency and cost from empirical execution time samples, we apply the bootstrapping
method [7] that uses the empirical distribution as an approximation of the true distribution.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Since the performance metrics E [T] and E [C] are functions of both X and Y , we need samples
for both X and Y .
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Drawing samples of Y is more involved, especially for the case of killing the
original task.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text: To handle this, we compute ˆFY (·) using (7), thus avoiding excessive sampling.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
We
present the algorithm for performance characterization in Algorithm 1.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
By Theorem 4, the standard deviation of the error in estimating E [C] and ˜T1, ﬁrst term in
E [T], converges to zero as O(1/√mn), where m is the number of times the sampling procedure
is repeated.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
And generally ˜T2, the maximum order statistic term in E [T], converges to zero as
O (1/√m).
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text: Thus, the estimation of ˜C is more robust than that of ˜T.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Nonetheless, with large
enough m, we can make the estimation errors of both metrics small enough.

4.2
Demonstration using Google Cluster Trace
The Google Cluster Trace data [19] gives timestamps of events such as SCHEDULE, EVICT,
FINISH, FAIL, KILL etc.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
for each of the tasks of computing jobs that are run on Google’s cluster
machines.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In this section we apply Algorithm 1 to two jobs in the Google Cluster Trace, and study
the latency-cost trade-oﬀs for these real-world task service distributions.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In our demonstration we only consider tasks with SCHEDULE and FINISH times, as we would
like to obtain samples that represent a normal execution (not killed or evicted).
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In a few rare cases,
a task is associated with multiple SCHEDULE and FINISH events due to duplicate execution.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
For
these we choose to keep the ﬁrst occurrences in each event category.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text: We choose two jobs (Job ID 6252284914 and 6252315810) with diﬀerent numbers of tasks.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
For
each task in a job, we obtain the task execution time by calculating the time diﬀerence between
SCHEDULE and FINISH.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
The normalized histograms of the task execution times of the two jobs
are shown in Fig.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Both the distributions have straggling tasks whose
execution time is signiﬁcantly longer than average.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
To emphasize the importance of such stragglers,
we modify the trace for Job 6252315810 by removing the 3 samples with execution time longer than
1400 seconds, leading to the execution time distribution shown in Fig.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
We then apply these
execution time samples as inputs to Algorithm 1 with m = 1000.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
By varying the value of r
(r ∈{1, 2, 3}) and p (0 ≤p ≤0.5), we plot the E [T]-E [C] trade-oﬀs for all three jobs in Figures 8
to 10.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
For the two Google cluster jobs (Job 1 and 2), we observe that a small amount of replication
(small p) reduces both E [T] and E [C] signiﬁcantly, demonstrating the eﬀectiveness of replication
for real-world execution time distributions.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In both cases, it is better to replicate while keeping
the original task, because at the “fork” point, the additional time needed for the original copy to
ﬁnish is more likely to be shorter than the execution time of a new copy.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
We also observe that for
the Job 2 (Job ID 6252315810), too much redundancy may hurt, because at some point increasing
p actually leads to increases in both E [T] and E [C].
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
However, this phenomenon does not exist for
Job 1 (Job ID 6252284914) when r = 2 or r = 3.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text: We conjecture this is due to the tail in Fig.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
We recall that the back-up tasks option in MapReduce uses r = 1 and keeps the original task,
and show that for certain jobs it may be more desirable to improve the performance trade-oﬀby
using more replicas, such as in Job 1, where a higher r could lead to lower latency E [T] with a
slightly higher cost E [C].
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:

πkeep (p, r = 2) achieves (E [C] , E [T]) = (815, 1798).

5
Concluding remarks
5.1
Main Implications
Replication of the slowest tasks of a computing job (straggling tasks) has been observed to be
highly eﬀective in practice to speed-up job completion.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
In this paper we provide a theoretical
framework to understand the eﬀect of straggler replication on the job completion latency, and
the additional computing time spent on running the replicas.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Our latency-cost analysis gives the
insight that the scaling of job completion latency with the number of tasks depends on the tail of
the per-task execution time.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
We identify regimes where replicating a small fraction of stragglers
can drastically reduce latency and computing cost simultaneously.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
With the guidance from this
asymptotic analysis, we propose a bootstrapping-based algorithm to estimate the latency and cost

text:
5.2
Future Directions
Generalizations of this straggler replication model include considering heterogeneous servers, de-
pendencies between tasks (some tasks need to complete in order to begin others), and taking into
account queueing delay of tasks as considered in [8, 9, 11, 13] for the single task case.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
Another
direction is to analyze approximate computing, where we need only a subset of the tasks of a job
to complete, a relevant model for information retrieval and machine learning jobs.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
This idea is de-
veloped in the context of coded distributed storage in [12,20].
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
We also aim to develop an algorithm
that learns the task execution time distribution FX online, and use it to decide when and how
many replicas to launch.
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
This has an exploration-exploitation trade-oﬀ, similar to the multi-arm
bandit problems studied in reinforcement learning [22].
title: arXiv:1503.03128v3  [cs.DC]  13 Sep 2017

text:
More broadly, our analysis framework can be applied to other systems with stochastically vary-
ing components, for example, in crowdsourcing, each worker may take a variable amount of time
to complete a task [24].

Abstract - The paper concerns the hype idea of “Citizen 
Science” and the related paradigm shift: to go from the 
passive “volunteer computing” to other volunteer actions 
like “volunteer measurements” under guidance of scientists.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
They can be carried out by ordinary people with standard 
computing gadgets (smartphone, tablet, etc.) and the various 
standard sensors in them.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
Here the special attention is paid 
to the system of volunteer scientific measurements to study 
air showers caused by cosmic rays.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
The technical 
implementation is based on integration of data about 
registered night flashes (by radiometric software) in 
shielded camera chip, synchronized time and GPS-data in 
ordinary gadgets: to identify night “air showers” of 
elementary particles; to analyze the frequency and to map 
the distribution of “air showers” in the densely populated 
cities.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
The project currently includes the students of the 
National Technical University of Ukraine “KPI”, which are 
compactly located in Kyiv city and contribute their 
volunteer measurements.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
The technology would be very 
effective for other applications also, especially if it will be 
automated (e.g., on the basis of XtremWeb or/and BOINC 
technologies for distributed computing) and used in some 
small area with many volunteers, e.g.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
in local communities 
(Corporative/Community Crowd Computing).
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
INTRODUCTION 
The proposed topic concerns the new hype idea of 
―Citizen Science‖ and volunteer involvement in science 
[1].
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
The main principle here is the paradigm shift: to go 
from the passive ―volunteer computing‖ (widely used now 
in many fields of sciences [2-5]) to other volunteer actions 
under guidance of scientists as ―volunteer measurements‖, 
―volunteer data processing and visualization‖, ―volunteer 
data mining‖, etc.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
They can be carried out by ordinary 
people with modern standard computing units (e.g.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
wearable PC, smartphone, tablet, smart watch, etc.) with 
various operational systems (Android, iOS, Windows, 
Tizen, etc.) and the standard sensors in them or easily 
accessible external measuring units.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
The main components of the idea or conditions for 
effective implementation of volunteer measurements are 
as follows: (a) they should be used by ordinary people – 
not scientists only, (b) they should be performed by easily 
accessible measuring units – like modern smartphones 
with numerous sensors, and (c) in unobtrusive way.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
The most important expectations (and potential criteria 
of success) are possibilities to:  
• 
leverage the available ―crowdsource‖ resources: 
machine (personal CPUs + sensors) and human 
(brains, manual operations of sensors) ones,  
• 
get huge number of volunteers (up to millions),  
• 
obtain the new scientific ―quality‖ from these 
huge ―quantities‖,  
• 
involve ordinary citizens in scientific process,  
• 
report to society about the current scientific 
activities and priorities.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
PREVIOUS WORK AND STATE OF THE ART 
The feasibility of the proposed idea was already tested 
in several awarded volunteer projects with the several 
types of activities in different fields of science, which is 
illustrated by some use cases below in this section.

text:
Scientific Problem 
Cosmic rays originate mainly outside the Solar 
System.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
They may produce showers of secondary particles 
(―air showers‖) that penetrate and impact the Earth's 
atmosphere and sometimes even reach the surface.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
―Air 
showers‖ of secondary elementary particles affect 
electronics, health, environment.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
Their study is expensive 
(>$50 mln.) and limited in scale.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
The most energetic 
cosmic rays (>5×1019 eV) are most important, but very 
rare were observed, for example, 1 high-energy event is 
registered per month by Pierre Auger observatory.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
Pierre 
Auger Observatory — is an international cosmic ray 
observatory designed to detect ultra-high-energy cosmic 
rays [10,11].
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
It detects cosmic rays in the range of 
1017-1021 eV, costs >$50 mln., and has a detection area 
>12 km2 and huge installation area >3000 km2 (like 
Luxemburg).
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
Cosmic rays affect electronics, because they 
have sufficient energy to alter the states of circuit 
components 
in electronic integrated 
circuits, 
causing 
transient errors like corrupted data in electronic memory 
devices, and incorrect performance of CPUs, often 
referred to as "soft errors" (not to be confused with 
software errors caused by programming mistakes/bugs!).
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
They affect health, especially the health threat from 
cosmic rays is the danger posed by galactic cosmic rays 
and 
solar 
energetic 
particles 
to 
astronauts 
on 
interplanetary missions.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
They are one of the most 
important barriers standing in the way of plans for 
interplanetary travel by crewed spacecraft [12,13].
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
Cosmic 
rays affect environment directly or via solar-induced 
modulations in climate change, because solar variations 
modulate the cosmic ray flux on Earth, they would 
consequently affect the rate of cloud formation and hence 
the climate [14].
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:

As far as ―air showers‖ of elementary particles created 
by cosmic rays affect electronics, they can be monitored 
by some available devices (like CMOS-camera chips).

massive involvement of volunteers with creation 
of virtual online map of ―air showers‖.

 
camera chips as embedded sensors in GPS-
enabled smartphones;  
 
volunteer communities in densely populated 
locations for real time monitoring the ―air 
showers‖ and analysis of their effects (on 
environment, electronics, health).

in shielded camera chip, synchronized time and GPS-data 
in ordinary smartphones/tablets/other gadgets.

Moreover, its crowd measuring/computing infrastructure

text:
CONCLUSIONS 
Some lessons were learned during these three different 
volunteer measuring/computing projects.
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
First of all, the 
positive aspects consist in feasibility: 
 
to leverage the available ―crowdsource‖ resources 
(hardware and ―brain-ware‖) even at this level – it 
is feasible, if sensors are embedded already 
(integration with external sensors is hardly can be 
attractive for potential volunteers), 
 
to get huge number of volunteers (millions) – it is 
feasible for project without sensitive data, but it 
could be hardly feasible for projects related with 
personal location and health data due to privacy 
issues, 
 
to obtain the new scientific ―quality‖ from these 
huge ―quantity‖ of data – it is feasible, and porting 
to the standard platforms for volunteer computing 
should help, because the limited automation is 
used at the moment, 
 
to involve ordinary citizens in scientific process – 
it is feasible, if task, results, and volunteer 
management will be fully automated, for example, 
by porting to BOINC [15] and XtremWeb 
environments [16], 
 
to report to society about the current scientific 
activities and priorities – it is feasible, again after 
porting 
to 
BOINC 
[15] 
and 
XtremWeb 
environments [16].
title: Paper Title (use style: paper title)

text:
Taking into account these considerations and 
comparative analysis (Table 1) the immediate ways for 
improvement are seem to be based on porting this crowd 
measuring/computing infrastructure to the standard 
platforms for volunteer computing.

text:
Some of them (like 
BOINC and XtremWeb) are proved to be effective for
