text:
Ad hoc Cloud Computing: From Concept to Realization
Gary A.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
McGilvary∗, Adam Barker†, Malcolm Atkinson∗
∗Edinburgh Data-Intensive Research Group, School of Informatics, The University of Edinburgh
Email: gary.mcgilvary@ed.ac.uk, mpa@staffmail.ed.ac.uk
†School of Computer Science, University of St Andrews
Email: adam.barker@st-andrews.ac.uk
Abstract—This paper presents the ﬁrst complete, integrated
and end-to-end solution for ad hoc cloud computing en-
vironments.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Ad hoc clouds harvest resources from existing
sporadically available, non-exclusive (i.e.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
primarily used for
some other purpose) and unreliable infrastructures.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In this
paper we discuss the problems ad hoc cloud computing solves
and outline our architecture which is based on BOINC.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Keywords-cloud computing; ad hoc; virtualization; volunteer
computing; reliability
I.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
INTRODUCTION
This paper introduces and develops a prototype of an
ad hoc cloud computing framework.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Ad hoc clouds harvest
resources from existing sporadically available, non-exclusive
(i.e.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
primarily used for some other purpose) and unreliable
infrastructures.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Examples of such infrastructures range from
personal infrastructure users with a number of underutilized
computers, to startup companies through to large-scale or-
ganizational infrastructures.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The nature of providing a cloud service by harvesting
resources from a set of unreliable hosts does have similar
elements to Grid and volunteer computing.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Despite being
similar to volunteer and Grid computing as well as clouds
(e.g.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Amazon EC2 [1]) and clusters (e.g HTCondor [2]), the
ad hoc cloud computing paradigm has many key differences.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The ad hoc cloud model:
• Volunteer resources: Operates over a set of non-
exclusive and sporadically available hosts, which may
be unpredictable in nature.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
This is in contrast to offering
a service from a dedicated cloud, cluster or Grid
infrastructure where each host’s resources are fully
committed to the service.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
• Lack of trust: Does not assume a level of trust exists
between an end-user and the infrastructure provider;
a relationship that currently exists between end-users,
clouds, clusters and Grids.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
• Ensures continuity: Maintains service availability in
the presence of host membership churn or failure to
ensure job continuity when running over a set of
unreliable hosts.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
• Low interference: Does not interfere with executing
host processes, especially in cases where these impor-
tant processes consume a varying amount of resources
at any given time.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
• Diverse workloads: Targets a set of more diverse
applications such as memory, I/O and disk-intensive
tasks as opposed to typical CPU-intensive applications
commonly executed by volunteer computing systems.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Our research has developed solutions to each of the chal-
lenges above, and to our knowledge no other research in this
ﬁeld has presented such a complete, integrated and end-to-
end solution for ad hoc cloud computing environments.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In
this paper we detail the research challenges and solutions of
developing an ad hoc cloud computing prototype.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Primarily
we focus on our cloud continuity solution, however we
explore possible solutions for the remaining problems.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
For simplicity and brevity in this paper, we assume
that our implementation will be predominately deployed
on Local Area Networks to ensure reasonable security and
performance guarantees; we aim to extend it to Wide Area
Networks after evaluating and optimizing the architecture.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Subsequently, applications that require extremely high levels
of security, may not be suited to the ad hoc cloud, or
perhaps any cloud implementation.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Furthermore, interactive
applications or those that write to external dependencies
may not function as expected due to data inconsistencies
when a host fails abruptly.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Such applications may need
further reliability mechanisms, however there are approaches
to solve such problems [3].
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section
2 provides an overview of the concepts and foundations of
ad hoc cloud computing followed by an in-depth feature
and implementation overview of our platform in Section 3.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Section 4 brieﬂy reports our initial evaluation while Section
5 outlines related research.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Section 6 concludes with a
summary and plans for future work.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
CONCEPTS AND FOUNDATIONS
We now discuss the architecture, components and pro-
cesses of the ad hoc cloud computing platform.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
System Overview
An ad hoc cloud harvests resources from existing non-
exclusive and sporadically available hosts used by host
users (e.g.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
company employees) and exposes these resources
to cloud jobs submitted by cloud users.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Cloud jobs are
submitted to the ad hoc server which then schedules jobs
arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015


to ad hoc guests, or virtual machines, running on each of
the hosts within the cloud.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Each host has an ad hoc client
installed to control the guest, monitor resources and provide
state information to the server.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In particular, within an ad
hoc cloud, we create a set of cloudlets; a set of connected
ad hoc guests that offer a particular service or environment.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text: Figure 1 gives a high-level overview of these concepts.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:

Figure 1: The Ad hoc Cloud Architecture
We see many cloudlets may exist which are deployed over
multiple hosts to provide a unique service to the current
infrastructure users.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
For instance, cloudlet ‘1’ and ‘2’ may
hold the necessary environments for Matlab and BLAST
applications to execute respectively.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
A guest may either be
dedicated to a single cloudlet, or part of many if multiple
jobs are scheduled onto the same guest and require different
operating environments.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Grouping guests into cloudlets makes it easier to sched-
ule jobs and monitor and manage the infrastructure.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
For
example, only hosts within a speciﬁc cloudlet need to be
taken into account when scheduling a job destined for that
cloudlet.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Cloudlets can also be managed to determine if
a cloudlet’s resources should be adjusted based on cur-
rent computational requirements.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Note that for simplicity,
cloudlet members are co-located in Figure 1, however in
reality these will be physically distributed across an infras-
tructure.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Cloudlets, hosts and guests are all centrally managed via
the ad hoc server, for example, the server accepts jobs,
schedules jobs to hosts, maintains system state and ensures
cloud jobs successfully complete.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
From the perspective of a
cloud user, the processes and resources that underpin the ad
hoc cloud are hidden, therefore our cloud implementation
conforms to a Platform as a Service (PaaS) infrastructure.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
With minor adjustments, such as passing the virtual ma-
chine’s IP address back to the cloud user, the ad hoc cloud
can be converted into an Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
cloud, giving cloud users the ability to login and control
their assigned virtual machines.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
We now give an outline of the events that occur from
cloud user job submission to result retrieval; these processes
are explained further in subsequent sections.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
• A cloud user submits a job (application and/or data) to
a job submission service on the ad hoc cloud server via
a web interface.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
• A host which is instructed or wishes to donate their
machine to the ad hoc platform ﬁrst connects to the ad
hoc server.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
A virtual machine is sent to their machine
and the host then awaits further instructions.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
• The ad hoc server schedules a job to a host for
execution based on host reliability.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Upon a job arriving,
the host starts the virtual machine and job execution
begins.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
• The ad hoc client dynamically controls the virtual
machine resources to minimize cloud job interference
with executing host processes.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Furthermore the client
monitors the resource loads of both host and guest and
passes this information to the server on a regular basis.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
• Periodically the ad hoc client informs the ad hoc server
of host and virtual machine availability to indicate that
they have not failed.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
• Periodically the ad hoc client captures virtual machine
snapshots and distributes these in a Peer-to-Peer (P2P)
fashion to other reliable and available hosts within the
platform; only the most recent snapshot is stored to
minimize disk consumption.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
• Upon a host or residing guest failing, the ad hoc
server detects this and restores the guest’s most current
snapshot upon another host to allow the job to continue.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Integrating Volunteer Computing and Virtualization
The foundation of our ad hoc platform relies on BOINC;
an open source client-server volunteer computing middle-
ware system [4].
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
As the ad hoc cloud computing paradigm
also involves harvesting resources from unreliable hosts,
BOINC is well suited to our purposes.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
However, in order
to protect cloud jobs running upon unreliable and perhaps
unsecure hosts, as well as the need to protect the pro-
cesses running on the hosts themselves, we have created
a virtualized version of BOINC, named V-BOINC [5].
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
V-
BOINC takes advantage of virtualization to run BOINC
computations within virtual machines as opposed to directly
on volunteer machines.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
V-BOINC sends these lightweight VirtualBox virtual ma-
chines from a V-BOINC Server to volunteer BOINC hosts
when instructed by the host’s installed modiﬁed BOINC
client, called the V-BOINC Client.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
A regular BOINC client
within the virtual machine is used to download a BOINC
project’s task.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The process of obtaining a virtual machine
and a BOINC task is shown in Figure 2.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Upon a volunteer user submitting the details of both the
regular BOINC scientiﬁc project and the V-BOINC project
they wish to attach to via the V-BOINC Client, the host

This

however for the context of this paper, we omit these details.

The V-BOINC Server sends the virtual machine image
and a script that conﬁgures it (e.g.

text:
sets CPUs, memory and

The virtual
machine is then conﬁgured (3) and started (4) to allow it to

title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text: More information about V-BOINC can be found in [5].
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
FROM VOLUNTEER TO CLOUD COMPUTING
We now describe how the ad hoc cloud was developed
and the major components that underpins the concept.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The
basis of this work involves transforming V-BOINC into a
platform that not only takes into account the requirements
of a cloud computing system but also one that can operate
over an unreliable infrastructure.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
As such, all subsequent modiﬁcations and features men-
tioned have been made either to the V-BOINC Server or
V-BOINC Client, which are now named the ad hoc server
and ad hoc client respectively.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
To ensure the ad hoc server
does not become a single point of failure, the server can be
replicated and load balanced in the same way regular BOINC
servers currently are.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
We also assume that an ad hoc client
and virtual machine both reside on each host within the ad
hoc infrastructure, i.e.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
processes (1) and (2) of Figure 2 have
been completed.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
BOINC Job Submission
To utilize the resources available in the ad hoc cloud, a
user must submit a job to the service; we currently assume a
job is an application executable with an option to upload data
to be analysed.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In the case of V-BOINC, a virtual machine
obtains an application by connecting to a speciﬁc BOINC
project; BOINC project jobs are however statically created
before the BOINC service begins.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In contrast, we would
like cloud users to submit any job at any moment in time,
hence the ad hoc cloud must allow user-deﬁned jobs to be
submitted on-the-ﬂy to BOINC while the service is running.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
This is not a trivial task and other research has taken place to
enable job submission to BOINC (e.g.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
[6], [7], [8]) however
these methods either split single tasks into independent jobs
to be executed or would generate too much overhead for this
type of platform.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
To enable on-the-ﬂy and independent job submission to
BOINC, we created a BOINC project named Job Service
upon the ad hoc server to accept and distribute jobs.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
This is
in addition to the V-BOINC project, which is modiﬁed and
renamed to VM Service, that allows hosts within the ad hoc
platform to obtain virtual machines.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Figure 3 shows how
both the job and virtual machine BOINC projects interact.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:

First a cloud user uploads an application and optional data
via a web interface.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
All uploaded ﬁles to the service are
placed in a jobs/ folder within the Job Service project which
are then processed by our developed work creator (WC)
daemon; BOINC allows project developers to create and add
daemons to the BOINC default daemon set to perform user-
deﬁned actions.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The work creator daemon distinguishes
application from data, creates XML descriptions of these
ﬁles and calls BOINC API functions to ultimately create a
BOINC workunit.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The Job Service then informs the VM Service that a
cloud job exists and that the VM Service’s vm controller
(VC) daemon can begin instantiating a virtual machine
upon a volunteer host to execute this job.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Currently failed
volunteer hosts are determined by the availability checker
(AC) daemon which deems a host failed if they do not poll
within two minutes; a host is set to periodically poll the
server every minute.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Reliability Scheduling
Upon being notiﬁed a job awaits for execution, the VM
Service begins scheduling a job to the most reliable host
with a virtual machine ready to be used.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The scheduler does
this based on the following characteristics for each host:


1) The total number of cloud jobs previously assigned,
2) The total number of cloud jobs previously completed,
3) The number of host failures, e.g.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
host termination,
hardware or OS failures,
4) The number of guest failures, e.g.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
virtual machine
conﬁguration, instantiation, execution, and shutdown
errors,
5) The current resource load.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The reliability factors (1)-(3) are monitored by the ad hoc
server and are recorded in the Job Service database.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The
number of ad hoc host failures are monitored by the VM
Service’s availability checker daemon which sets an ad hoc
host to terminated or failed after two minutes of inactivity.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The reliability factors (4)-(5) are monitored by the ad hoc
client when a cloud job is assigned to execute.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
To determine
whether an ad hoc guest is still executing, it is periodically
polled every ten seconds using VirtualBox’s VBoxManage
API ensuring those that have failed are detected quickly with
minimal resource overheads.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Any unexpected behaviour is
reported to the server.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The current resource loads of an ad
hoc host can be monitored either by Ganglia or via BOINC’s
basic monitoring mechanisms.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
For brevity, we omit the in-
corporation of resource load within our reliability scheduling
due the signiﬁcant size of the topic.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
More information about
our reliability scheduling can be found at [9].
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Based on the data sent from the ad hoc client and the
data collected on the ad hoc server, the server is then able
to calculate the reliability of each ad hoc host using the
following formula:
host reliability =



0
if NF = CA
100
if NF = 0
(CC/CA) ∗100
otherwise
where,
NF = the total number of ad hoc host and guest failures,
CA = the total number of cloud jobs assigned to the host,
CC = the total number of cloud jobs completed by the
host.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
An ad hoc host’s reliability is calculated after a cloud job
has completed, when the ad hoc guest has become non-
operational or when the ad hoc host has not polled within
the last two minutes.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The calculated reliabilities are then
stored in the VM Service project database alongside the
information of each candidate ad hoc host.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
This reliability
calculation gives an estimate of the ad hoc host’s behaviour
for the entire time the host is part of the ad hoc cloud.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Transferring Control
As a volunteer platform, BOINC and its virtual coun-
terpart V-BOINC, are inherently controlled by the volunteer
users.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
If a host user wishes to donate resources to a scientiﬁc
project, receive jobs, change the amount of resources used or
detach from a project, a host user is free to do so.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
However
within an ad hoc cloud platform, the server has to instruct
the ad hoc client to perform tasks, in turn transforming
a client controlled infrastructure into a sever controlled
infrastructure; we have modiﬁed our V-BOINC platform
to allow this.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The ad hoc client receives and issues these
commands via the ad hoc BOINC client component to other
middleware components shown in Figure 4.

text:

After the scheduler decides which virtual machine is to
execute the cloud job, the server’s VM Service instructs the
ad hoc client to start the virtual machine on the host.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
It does
so by passing the command from the vm controller to the
client’s Command Listener via a BOINC XML message.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The
server also passes a description of the job such as whether
any dependencies exist and the URL to download the correct
job.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
If the former applies, the ad hoc client downloads the
dependencies and attaches it to the virtual machine before
it begins, otherwise the virtual machine simply begins and
it is then instructed to attach to the Job Service to obtain a
job.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Commands relating to the operation of virtual machines
are passed to the VirtualBox API for execution.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Cloud users are able to execute such commands via the
Interface, which in turn informs the server to instruct the
ad hoc client to perform virtual machine commands via the
VirtualBox API.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Similarly, host users also have access to
this and the regular commands of BOINC via our modiﬁed
BOINC API.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Figure 4 also shows the Resource Monitor and Failure De-
tection components.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The Resource Monitor uses BOINC’s
default monitoring daemon and sends information back to
the server for use in scheduling decisions.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The component
also monitors the current resource usage of the BOINC task
to ensure the resource limits speciﬁed by the host user are
not exceeded for prolonged periods of time, in which case
the ad hoc client will suspend the virtual machine until
resource utilization has dropped to an acceptable level.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
This
ensures that there is minimal interference with operating host
processes.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In order to ensure the system state is up-to-date at any
given time, each host periodically polls the ad hoc server
to signify the host’s and virtual machine’s availability.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The
latter is tested via the Failure Detection component; an
independent process to test virtual machine availability.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In
response to a host poll, the ad hoc server returns a list of
all other available hosts in the BOINC XML message along
with their IP addresses and reliability values.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Making the Unreliable Reliable
These reliability values (discussed in the previous Section)
are used by our P2P Snapshot component, shown in Figure
4, which has the task of periodically taking virtual machine
snapshots and transferring these to other clients in parallel
using pssh [10] to ensure cloud job continuity.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
After a suc-
cessful transfer, the ad hoc server is informed of receiving
hosts which now store the snapshot the location(s).
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
When
a host or virtual machine fails, the server is then able to
instruct one of the receiving hosts to restore the snapshot.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Take Figure 5 as an example, where each host’s percentage
failure probability is displayed.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:

Figure 5: Snapshot Scheduling and Failure Probabilities (%).
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
At time t=0 node A check-
points the virtual machine and the snapshot is sent to nodes
B, D and E at t=1.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The virtual machine A terminates
due to a host failure (t=2), the ad hoc server detects this
(t=3) and instructs node D to restore virtual machine A’s
snapshot (t=4).
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
This process is repeated for each node where
periodic snapshots are taken and sent to others.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Snapshots
are however not blindly pushed to a random subset of hosts.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The P2P Snapshot component schedules snapshots to be
stored on the most reliable hosts.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
It does this by ﬁltering
potential snapshot receivers based on whether they are in
use, the sender’s cloudlet membership and the descending
reliability of potential receivers, all of which are taken from
the list of available hosts within the BOINC XML message
sent from the server.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The algorithm will then select the ﬁrst
n hosts that have less than a 5% chance of all n failing.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
To maintain a reliable service, we want to ensure that
95% of the time a cloud job will complete successfully.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
To
satisfy this requirement, we must always have at least one
current snapshot present on another host as its presence is
directly related to the future success of an application if
it is interrupted in any way.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
As such, we require that the
combined probability of a group of hosts failing that store
a particular virtual machine’s snapshot is less than or equal
to 5%; this can be calculated by multiplying the respective
failure probabilities of each host.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
For example, Figure 5
shows that the probability of a cloud job never completing
while running on virtual machine A is 0.03%.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
This scheduling method does however mean that reliable
destinations may end up storing many snapshots.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
However,
the maximum host storage that can be used by the ad
hoc cloud (e.g.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
the ad hoc client, snapshots, etc) can be
speciﬁed by the ad hoc host user via regular BOINC.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In the
event this limit is reached, the ad hoc server does not send
the details of that host to polling ad hoc clients, ensuring
further snapshots are not sent to the host.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
We note there are
many improvements that could be made to our P2P Snapshot
Scheduler, however we leave these for future work.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In the event a virtual machine or host running a cloud
job is deemed unreachable, the server begins the process
of restoring the virtual machine’s snapshot on another host.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
It does this based on the host reliability formula when
selecting the best host for initially deploying a job onto
a virtual machine.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Finally, all hosts that store the restored
snapshot are instructed to delete it.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
EVALUATION
The prototype of our ad hoc cloud computing concept was
evaluated in terms of reliability and performance.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Our relia-
bility experiment tested our prototype running on 30 nodes
the EDIM1 cluster [11].
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In order to accurately simulate
an unreliable infrastructure, we obtained Nagios monitoring
data over a period of 36 months from 650 hosts in The
School of Informatics at The University of Edinburgh.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
We
parsed this monitoring data, calculated the host activity for
every hour and selected the hour where 30 hosts had the
most activity.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
We replayed these events on EDIM1 with our ad hoc
cloud installed and measured the completion rates of a
variety of workloads; our prototype achieved up to 93.3% re-
liability.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
This is a signiﬁcant improvement to BOINC, which
simply restarts a failed task, unless application checkpoint-
ing is enabled, in turn requiring application modiﬁcation and
the checkpoint to be present in memory.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In order to evaluate performance, we compared the times
of executing a cloud job on our ad hoc cloud and Amazon
EC2 [1]) instance with similar resources.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
We showed that our
ad hoc cloud can offer similar performance for a variety of
workloads, even in the event of one or multiple ad hoc guest
failures, when taking into account the various overheads of


both models.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
More information about our evaluation of the
ad hoc cloud can be found in [9].
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
RELATED WORK
Authors of [12] propose the concept of the ad hoc cloud
within enterprise settings to harness unused resources to
improve overall utilization, reduce net energy consumption
and allow organizations to take advantage of operating their
own in-house cloud.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Their focus of the paper is to outline the
major implementation challenges and describe one approach
to creating an ad hoc cloud computing infrastructure.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The
main challenges outlined relate to coping with the sporad-
ically available hosts and how to minimize the impact on
non-cloud processes to an acceptable level.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
propose a similar idea using Nebulas
(synonymous to an ad hoc cloud) where volunteer resources
are used to create a cloud platform [13].
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
They note that
Nebulas are particularly useful for applications that do not
have strong performance guarantees and hence the authors
focus on the performance and reliability of such platforms.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
describe their early experience with
a prototype of their Nebula cloud system [14]; this was
tested using a data-intensive blog analysis use case on
PlanetLab [15].
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Their architecture consists of the same core
components found in our system, namely a master server to
coordinate all activities backed by a database and clients to
execute cloud jobs.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The authors do not use virtual machines
to execute cloud jobs but instead use the NativeClient plugin
for web browsers to execute code as web applications.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Their
method shows that at times, little overhead can be seen when
executing code in this way.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
CONCLUSIONS
We have outlined our developed ad hoc cloud computing
platform that deploys a cloud service upon an end-user’s
existing infrastructure where member hosts are sporadically
available and used for some other primary purpose.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
The
ad hoc cloud concept is useful for those who wish to
improve their infrastructure efﬁciency and utilization as well
as reduce costs by improving their return on IT investments.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Furthermore, those who are not able to or do not wish to
to migrate to the commercial or private cloud models can
experiment and explore the potential of ad hoc clouds before
adopting either of the commercial or private models.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
In order to successfully develop an ad hoc cloud comput-
ing platform, a large number of technological and research
ﬁelds must be visited such as virtualization, volunteer com-
puting and scheduling.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
Despite this, we showed by outlining
our architecture that the concept of ad hoc cloud computing
is feasible and based on our initial evaluation, can be reliable
and offer comparable performance to Amazon EC2.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
We are
conﬁdent that the reliability and performance of our ad hoc
cloud development can increase in a range of other scenarios,
however these extrapolations are based on assumptions that
need to be tested by deploying the ad hoc cloud on a
live operational infrastructure with real workloads in the
near future.
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

text:
A more detailed insight into our ad hoc cloud
computing prototype, the challenges solved and performance
can be found at [9].
title: arXiv:1505.08097v2  [cs.DC]  19 Jul 2015

Abstract.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
This paper describes a programme to study the computing model in CMS after
the next long shutdown near the end of the decade.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Introduction
One of the recurring challenges for HEP computing in recent years has been data management,
access and organisation when using distributed computing resources.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The computing model
chosen by CMS for the LHC startup used a distributed data management architecture [1] which
placed datasets statically at sites.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Dataset replicas in multiple sites were made manually as
required, and jobs were sent to sites where their input data could be read from site-local storage.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The wide area network (WAN) was underutilised as a resource, despite being signiﬁcantly more
robust than originally imagined.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The reliability of all WLCG computer centres has greatly improved through the experience
gained during LHC Run 1.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
More sophisticated data management and access models are thus
possible.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The use of “opportunistic” compute resources also becomes much easier, as they can
be used without requiring local data storage.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
For LHC Run 2 CMS is deploying additional
technologies to monitor dataset popularity and use PhEDEx [3] to remove unnecessary dataset
replications.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
These evolutionary changes will allow eﬀective data management and access
through Run 2.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Data Management at the HL-LHC
Planning is currently underway for a High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) [2] with
an objective of accumulating 3000fb−1 by 2030.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Taking into account the upcoming increase in
energy for Run 2, and expectations for evolving pile-up and trigger rate through Run 3 and
HL-LHC, the data volume increase over the next 15 years will be O(103).
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
This may imply that HL-LHC (and perhaps Run 3) will require larger, potentially non-
evolutionary, changes to the experiment’s computing model, data management, access and
organisation.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:

community: Can the architectures and algorithms used for caching and to reduce latencies

text:
Computing Model Simulation
To aid in deciding which type of model could produce the most eﬃcient use of resources a
simulation has been developed.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The ﬁrst results from that simulation under three diﬀerent
scenarios are described in this paper.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Description
The simulation is a event driven discrete simulation.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
In the
results reported in this paper the time slices are every 100 seconds.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
A site also contains a batch system, a disk storage
system, and a set of network links to other sites.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The relationship between the software deﬁned
components is shown in Figure 1.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: The batch system has a set of cores for running jobs.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
It also contains, but doesn’t currently
use, a internal site bandwidth which could further constrain the speed of jobs running at that
site.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: It maintains a list of jobs for each state, queued, running or done.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: The disk storage system is conﬁgured as an available resource.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Files can be stored locally
and use up this space.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: There is no tertiary data storage system deﬁned.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The network links to other sites are deﬁned with information on the bandwidth of the link,
the latency implicit in that link and the quality of the link.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
This information is used to determine
how fast data will ﬂow over the links.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
In addition there is also an Event Store that is used to deﬁne information about ﬁles used
in the system.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: It contains the Logical File Name (LFN) and the size of each ﬁle.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
It also has
knowledge of which sites have the ﬁles stored.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The information deﬁned for a job is the CPU time required to carry it out, the site it will
run at, which LFNs it will read and what fraction of that data it will read (currently deﬁned to
be 100%).
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: It also remembers the original wall clock time required to run the job.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Information Sources
The simulation uses current system information to setup a complex and realistic experiment
wide computing system.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: Site information can be extracted from the CMS SiteDB service.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
This
provides information on the resources pledged to the experiment for disk space and CPU power
(deﬁned in HEPSpec06).
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
There is an automated tool to extract this information (which was
the most recent 2014 pledges) and format it as input for the simulation.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
In addition, when only
considering the CMS infrastructure in the US these numbers were extracted from REBUS.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Once the sites are setup the links between them get setup then using information extracted
by a script from PhEDEx.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: This provides a list of links between the sites.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Each of those links
can have a quality associated with it.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
This provides information on how often ﬁle transfers need
to be retried.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: In addition information on the actual transfer rate is available.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
However, this
information is only available as an aggregated number.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
It used as an indication of the bandwidth
available on the link.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: This number is constrained to be between 1GB/s and 10GB/s.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The other
information associated with a link is the latency of the link.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Currently this number is estimated
based on the distance between sites (see Table 1 for the values used).
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
In a future update to the
simulation this should be an relatively easy number to measure.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Once sites and the links between them are setup the ﬁle size and location information are
loaded.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: These have also been extracted from PhEDEx.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The list of ﬁles required is found from
the list of jobs to be run.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
When considering only US locations, ﬁles that are needed but not
present in the US are artiﬁcially given a location at Fermilab, the US Tier-1 site.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Simulation Parameters
There are a few distributions used as parameters of the simulation.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
These are also read from
ﬂat ﬁles but the information is from diﬀerent sources.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The ﬁrst of these is the drop in CPU eﬃciency seen when running jobs that access data from
a remote storage element.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
For example a job reading data at Fermilab while running at UCSD
could drop from a 95% eﬃciency to 75% CPU eﬃciency.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The numbers used currently are merely
an estimate till more accurate information can be gathered.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: Another parameter is the maximum single ﬁle transfer rate of a given link.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: The last set of parameters used is to Monte-Carlo the CPU eﬃciency of jobs.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
A set of jobs
run in September of last year is used as the sample set.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
A distribution is derived from them,
which is also binned by CPU time as it is observed that shorter jobs can have a much worse
CPU eﬃciency than longer jobs.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
There are 100 CPU eﬃciency bins and 10 CPU time bins in
the distribution.

text:
Scenarios
In each case the CMS computing system in the US is used.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
This consists of one Tier-1 site
(FNAL) and eight Tier-2 sites.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Figure 2 shows the location of these sites together with the
resources available there today according to REBUS.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Data preplaced at sites
In this scenario data is already mostly preplaced at the site where the job will execute.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
This is
the situation today where bulk data transfers are done using PhEDEx and in the vast majority
of cases data is already at a site before the job starts running.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
In the simulation there are some
jobs which do access remote data.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
In addition there were some jobs where the data read wasn’t
present anywhere in the US.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
In this latter case a copy of the data was placed at FNAL to allow
them to run.

text:
Data Replication
With this scenario data is replicated to sites as the job starts.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
This introduces a small ineﬃciency,
depending on how long the job would run.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
In this case all data is placed at FNAL and every
job run outside FNAL would copy the data it requires, except in the case where an earlier job
had already used the data in question.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: Copies are cached at sites in this scenario.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Remote Reading
In this scenario all data is located at FNAL and nowhere else.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Each job must read over the
network to access its data.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: In this scenario there is no disk space required at the Tier-2s.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Execution
When execution begins all jobs are read in.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
For the results presented 56949 jobs were extracted
from the dashboard, as run during a week in February 2015.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
To provide a more even distribution
of jobs across the infrastructure each job was duplicated and for the Tier-2 based jobs, ran at
another site.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
For the ﬁrst scenario described in Section 4.1 the data was also duplicated with
the job.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: The jobs are added to the queue at the sites they are to be run at.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: Each site is then polled to start any jobs it has capacity to start.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Then data transfers are
constrained for those jobs, this is needed to determine the run time of the job.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Jobs are also
checked to see if they’ve ﬁnished since the last poll.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
This may allow some transfers to complete
sooner, and hence the jobs that depend on them.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Each job has the CPU eﬃciency Monte-Carlo run for it to determine a ﬁrst order wall clock
time.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: This can be further extended if data movement is required for the job.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
A site to site
transfer would add a ﬁxed amount of time.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
A remote read will add a CPU Eﬃciency penalty
while that ﬁle is being read.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The CPU time of the job is shared between the ﬁles based on the
size of the ﬁle.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The simulation takes account of bad quality links while transferring ﬁles and
has a mechanism to generate retries, and will eventually give up if too many retries occur.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
It
would then locate another copy of the ﬁle to use.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Once the job does complete there is a total
wall clock time recorded for the job.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Total Wall Clock Time
We can use the total wall clock time required to run all the jobs in each of the scenarios to make
a comparison.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: Table 4 shows these total wall clock time for the three scenarios.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
It also shows
the results if we vary the simulation parameters by a factor of two in each direction.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
There is a very small diﬀerence in the Transfer File time with the change in maximum single
ﬁle transfer speed.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
This isn’t evident as it is only apparent beyond the ﬁrst three signiﬁcant
ﬁgures.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
You can see that in each set of parameters that not preplacing the data costs almost 20%
more wall clock time to be used.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The penalty for doing remote reads varies from 36% up to 53%,
depending on the actual set of remote read parameters used.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The simulation is more sensitive
to this parameter.

text:
CPU Eﬃciency
The latencies and penalties that jobs are exposed to cause their CPU eﬃciency to drop.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
In the
diﬀerent scenarios we can see a slightly diﬀerent behaviour.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
We can see various CPU Eﬃciency
distributions in Figure 3.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: The distribution in Figure 3a shows the case where data is preplaced at sites.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
There is very
little change if the remote read penalty or the maximum ﬁle transfer speed is varied.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The average
CPU eﬃciency in this case is 84.5%.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
In Figures 3b-3d you can see the eﬀect on the CPU eﬃciency when the maximum ﬁle transfer
rate is ﬁrst halved, normal and then doubled.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The eﬀect is small, and the average number varies
from 76.1% up to 76.4%.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: In the case of reading the data remotely there is a much larger variation.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: Here the average varies from 68.3% down to 61.6%.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
You can also see the artiﬁcial
nature of the imposed penalty producing a two peak structure.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
As the penalty increases it
moves the set of jobs with a lower penalty out of those jobs run at FNAL, which have no
penalty, producing three peaks.

Job Queues During Simulation
While the simulation is running the state of each of the job lists at the sites is monitored.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
We
can graph these to see the progression of jobs through the system.

Figure 4 shows these queues
for each of the nine sets of input parameters.

text:
Network Usage
Another observation from the simulation is the network bandwidth used in each case.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Each of
the scenarios has been studied with varying the input parameters.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The variation is in line with
expectations and only the “normal” parameter set will be shown for each of the scenarios.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: In Figure 5 you are able to see the network out of FNAL to each of the Tier-2 sites.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
As
expected when data is preplaced (Figure 5a) at the Tier-2 sites the network used is very minimal.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
If data is copied (Figure 5b) the network usage is more uneven as the transfers happen as quickly
as possible.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
Whereas when data is read remotely (Figure 5c) data is only consumed at the speed
of the job on the Tier-2 site.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text: The network load between the Tier-2 sites was also examined.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
The total Tier-2 to Tier-2
bandwidth used is show in ﬁgure 6, again only the “normal” parameter set is shown.
title: arXiv:1507.07430v1  [cs.DC]  20 Jul 2015

text:
For the
case when the majority of the data is preplaced (Figure 6a) at the job execution site there is
very little Tier-2 to Tier-2 activity.

Conclusions

arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015
The Computational Power of Beeps
Seth Gilbert∗
National University of Singapore
seth.gilbert@comp.nus.edu.sg
Calvin Newport†
Georgetown University
cnewport@cs.georgetown.edu
Abstract
In this paper, we study the quantity of computational resources (state machine states and/or prob-
abilistic transition precision) needed to solve speciﬁc problems in a single hop network where nodes
communicate using only beeps.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: We begin by focusing on randomized leader election.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We prove a lower
bound on the states required to solve this problem with a given error bound, probability precision, and
(when relevant) network size lower bound.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: We then show the bound tight with a matching upper bound.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Noting that our optimal upper bound is slow, we describe two faster algorithms that trade some state
optimality to gain efﬁciency.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We then turn our attention to more general classes of problems by proving
that once you have enough states to solve leader election with a given error bound, you have (within
constant factors) enough states to simulate correctly, with this same error bound, a logspace TM with
a constant number of unary input tapes: allowing you to solve a large and expressive set of problems.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
These results identify a key simplicity threshold beyond which useful distributed computation is possible
in the beeping model.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
