†Supported in part by NSF grant CCF 1320279


1
Introduction
The beeping model of network communication [1–3,10,14,19] assumes a collection of computational nodes,
connected in a network, that interact by beeping in synchronous rounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If a node decides to beep in a given
round, it receives no feedback from the channel.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
On the other hand, if a node decides to listen, it is able to
differentiate between the following two cases: (1) no neighbor in the network topology beeped in this round,
and (2) one or more neighbors beeped.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Existing work on this model provide two motivations.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The ﬁrst concerns digital communication net-
works (e.g., [10, 12]).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Standard network communication (in which nodes interact using error-corrected
packets containing many bits of information) requires substantial time, energy, and computational overhead
(at multiple stack layers) to handle the necessary packet encoding, modulation, demodulation, and decoding.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Beeps, on the other hand, provide an abstraction capturing the simplest possible communication primitive:
a detectable burst of energy.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In theory, beep layers could be implemented using a fraction of the complexity
required by standard packet communication, establishing the possibility of micro-network stacks for set-
tings where high speed and low cost are crucial.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The second motivation for the beeping model concerns a
connection to biological systems (e.g., [3,18,19]).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Network communication in nature is often quite simple;
e.g., noticing a ﬂash of light from nearby ﬁreﬂies or detecting a chemical marker diffused by nearby cells.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Therefore, understanding how to achieve distributed coordination using such basic primitives can provide
insight into how such coordination arises in nature (see [18] for a recent survey of this approach).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
As detailed below, existing work on the beeping model seeks to solve useful problems as
efﬁciently as possible in this primitive network setting.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In this paper, by contrast, we focus on solving useful
problems as simply as possible (e.g., as measured by factors such as the size of the algorithm’s state machine
representation), asking the key question: is it possible to solve problems with both simple communication
and simple algorithms?
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Notice, the answer is not a priori obvious.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It might be the case, for example, that
complexity is conserved, so that simplifying the communication model requires more complex algorithms.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Or it might be the case that simple algorithms coordinating with beeps are sufﬁcient for even complex tasks.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Given the above motivations for studying beeps, answering this question is crucial, as it will help us probe
the feasibility of useful networked systems—be them constructed by engineers or evolution—that are truly
simple in both their communication methods and control logic.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We study a collection of n nodes connected in a single hop topology (i.e., the network
graph is a clique).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We model the randomized algorithmic process executing on each node as a probabilistic
state machine.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The two parameters describing the complexity of these algorithms are: (1) an upper bound
on the number of states (indicated by integer s ≥1); and (2) an upper bound on the precision of the
probabilistic transitions (indicated by integer q ≥2, where we allow probabilistic transitions to be labeled
with probability 0, 1, or any value in the interval [1
q, 1 −1
q]).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We ask how large these values must grow to
solve speciﬁc problems.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Our motivating premise is that smaller values imply simpler algorithms.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
(Notice,
by considering both s and q, we can capture the trade-off between memory and probabilistic precision; a
question of standalone interest; c.f., [15]).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: We begin by considering leader election, a fundamental primitive in distributed systems.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We prove that
for a given error bound ǫ ∈[0, 1/2] and probabilistic precision q, any algorithm that guarantees to solve
leader election with probability 1 −ǫ requires s = Ω(logq (1/ǫ)) states.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Provided a lower bound e
N on the
size of the network, this lower bound reduces to s = Ω(logq (1/ǫ)/ e
N) states.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
That is, the more nodes in the
network, the fewer states each node needs to solve the problem.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: This lower bound leverages a reduction argument.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We begin by deﬁning and lower bounding a helper
problem called (1, k)-loneliness detection, which requires an algorithm to differentiate between n = 1 and
1


n ≥k (but has no requirements for intermediate network sizes).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
This bound uses an indistinguishability
argument regarding how nodes move through a speciﬁed state sequence.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We then show how to transform
a solution to leader election for size lower bound e
N, to solve (1, e
N)-loneliness detection—allowing our
loneliness bound to carry over to leader election.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: We then turn our attention to leader election upper bounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We begin by proving our lower bound
tight by showing, for every network size lower bound e
N ≥1, how to solve leader election with s =
O(logq (1/ǫ)/ e
N) states.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The key idea behind this algorithm is to have nodes work together to implement a
distributed timer.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The more nodes in the network, the longer the distributed timer runs, and the longer the
distributed timer runs, the higher the probability that we succeed at leader election.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In this way, increasing
the network size reduces the states required to hit a speciﬁc error bound.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
A shortcoming of this new algo-
rithm, however, is that its expected running time is exponential in the network size.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
With this mind, we then
describe two faster algorithms (their time is polylogarithmic in the relevant parameters) that require only the
minimum precision of q = 2.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The cost for their efﬁciency, however, is a loss of state optimality in some
circumstances.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The ﬁrst algorithm requires s = O(log (1/ǫ)) states and solves leader election with probability at least
1 −ǫ, for any network size n.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It terminates in O(log (n + 1/ǫ) log (1/ǫ)) rounds, with probability at least
1 −ǫ.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The key idea behind this algorithm is to test a potentially successful election by having the poten-
tial leader(s) broadcast with probability 1/2 for log (1/ǫ) rounds, looking for evidence of company.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It is
straightforward to see that a single such test fails with probability no more than (1/2)log (1/ǫ) = ǫ.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The
problem, however, is that as the network size grows, the number of such tests performed also increases,
making it more likely that one fails.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We neutralize this problem in our analysis by showing that the test
failure probabilities fall away as a geometric series in the test count—bounding the cumulative error sum as
the network grows.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The second algorithm requires only s = O(1) states, and yet, for every network size n, it solves leader
election with high probability in n when run in a network of that size.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It requires only O(log2 n) rounds,
with high probability.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The key idea driving this algorithm is to harness the large amount of total states in
the network to implement a distributed timer that requires Θ(log n) time to countdown to 0, when executed
among n nodes.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: This duration is sufﬁcient for the nodes to safely reduce contention down to a single leader.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
After studying leader election, we turn our attention to more general classes of distributed decision
problems.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Leveraging our leader election algorithms as a key primitive, we show how to simulate a logspace
decider Turing Machine (TM) with a constant number of unary inputs (all deﬁned with respect to the network
size n).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Perhaps surprisingly, this algorithm requires only O(log (1/ǫ)) states to complete the simulation
with probability 1 −ǫ, and only O(1) states to achieve high probability in n.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
(Notice that this is not enough
states for an individual node to store even a single pointer to the tape of the simulated machine.) Our
simulation uses the same general strategy ﬁrst highlighted in the study of population protocols [4]: simulate
a counter machine with a constant number of counters that hold values from 0 to O(n), and then apply a
transformation due to Minsky [16] to simulate a logspace TM with this machine.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Due to the differences
between the beeping and population protocol models, however, our counter machine simulation strategies
are distinct from [4].
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The results summarized above establish that the log (1/ǫ) state threshold for leader election
with bounded error is (in some sense) a fundamental simplicity threshold for solving useful problems with
beeps.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It is striking that if you have slightly less than this much memory, even the basic symmetry breaking
task of leader election is impossible, but if you instead have slightly more, then suddenly you can solve
large classes of complicated problems (i.e., everything solvable by a logspace TM).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If you are satisﬁed
with high probability solutions (which is often the case), then this treshhold reduces even more all the way
down to O(1).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Given these results, we tentatively claim a positive answer to the key question posed above:
2


complexity is not destiny; you can solve hard problems simply in simple network models.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Before proceeding into the technical details of our paper, we will ﬁrst take the time to place both our model
and our results in the context of the several different areas of relevant related work.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Among other questions,
we want to understand the relationship of our bounds to existing beep results, and how the beeping model
compares and contrasts to similar settings.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The algorithmic study of beeping networks began with Degesys
et al.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
[12], who introduced a continuous variant of the beeping model, inspired by the pulse-coupled os-
cillator framework.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: They studied biologically inspired strategies for solving a desynchronization problem.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Follow-up work generalized the results to multihop networks [11, 17].
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Cornejo and Kuhn [10] introduced
the discrete (i.e., round-based) beeping model studied in this paper.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
They motivated this model by noting
the continuous model in [11,12,17] was unrealistic and yielded trivial solutions to desynchronization, they
then demonstrated how to solve desynchronization without these assumptions.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
[3] described a maximal independent set (MIS) algorithm in a strong version of the discrete beeping
model.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
They argued that something like this algorithm might play a role in the proper distribution of sen-
sory organ precursor cells in fruit ﬂy nervous system development.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Follow-up work [1,2,19] removed some
of the stronger assumptions of [3] and improved the time complexity.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
[14]
considered deterministic leader election in a multihop beeping network.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To place this paper in this context of the existing work on the beeping model, it is important to note
that the above-cited papers focus primarily on two goals: minimizing time complexity and minimizing
information provided to nodes (e.g., network size, max degree, global round counter).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
They do not, however,
place restrictions on the amount of states used by their algorithms.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Accordingly, these existing results require
either: the ability to store values as large as Θ(n) [1–3,10,19], or uniques ids [14] (which in our framework
would require a machine with n different initial states, or equivalently, n different machines).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In this paper,
we prove that the algorithmic complexity threshold for solving many useful problems is actually much
lower: O(1) states are sufﬁcient for high probability results and O(log (1/ǫ)) states are sufﬁcient for ﬁxed
error bound results.1 We argue the direction pursued in this paper (how complex must algorithms become
to solve useful problems with beeps) complements the direction pursued in existing papers (how fast can
algorithms solve useful problems with beeps).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Answers to both types of queries is necessary to continue to
understand the important topic of coordination in constrained network environments.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The standard radio network model allows nodes to send large
messages, but assumes concurrent transmissions lead to message loss (that may or may not be detectable).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The key difference between the radio network model and the beeping model is that in the former you can
recognize the case where exactly one node broadcast (e.g., because you receive a message).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
This capability,
which the beeping model does not offer (a single beeper looks like multiple beepers), is powerful.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It allows,
for example, algorithms that can solve leader election with deterministic safety using only a constant amount
of state, when run in network of size at least 2.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If you assume receiver collision detection, these solutions
require only polylogarithmic expected time.2 These results violate our lower bounds for leader election with
1Notice, direct comparisons between many of these results is complicated by the variety of possible assumptions;
e.g., synchronous versus asynchronous starts, multihop versus single hop, small versus large probability precision.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: 2For example: divide rounds into pairs of even and odd rounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In even rounds, nodes broadcast a simple message
with constant probability.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: If a node ever succeeds in broadcasting alone, all other nodes become heralds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
They stop
competing in even rounds and begin competing in odd rounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
When the winner (who is now the only non-herald in
the network) eventually hears a message in an odd round, it elects itself leader.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If we assume collision detection, we
can reduce contention fast in the even rounds with basic knockout protocols; e.g., if you choose to listen and detect a
collision you are knocked out and just wait to become a herald.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
3


beeps (where the state size grows toward inﬁnity as you drive the error bound toward 0)—indicating that the
communication limitations in the beeping model matter from a computability perspective.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Comparison to the Stone Age Computing Model.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It is also important to place our results in the context
of other simpliﬁed communication/computation models.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Consider, for example, the stone age distributed
computing model introduced by Emek and Wattenhofer [13].
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
This model assumes state machines of constant
size connected in a network and executing asynchronously.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The machines communicate with a constant-size
message alphabet and when transitioning can distinguish between having received 0, 1, or ≥b messages
of each type, for some constant parameter b ≥1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For b = 1, this model is essentially an asynchronous
version of the beeping model.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To this end, nodes in our model can simulate nodes in the stone age model
with b = 1 indeﬁnitely using a constant amount of states.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For b > 1, however, any such simulation likely
becomes impossible in the beeping model with a constant amount of states.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
As noted in our discussion of
the radio network model, the ability to safely recognize the case of exactly one message being sent provides
extra power beyond what is achievable (without error) using only beeps.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Comparison to the Population Protocol Model.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Another relevant simpliﬁed communication/computation
setting is the well-studied population protocol model [4–9] .
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
This model describes nodes as state machines
of constant size that interact in a pairwise manner—transforming both states asymmetrically.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In the basic
version of the model, a fair scheduler chooses pairs to interact.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
A version in which the scheduler is random-
ized adds more power.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
There are similarities in the goals pursued by the beeping and population protocol
models: both seek (among other things) to understand the limits of limited state in distributed computation.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: The core difference between the two settings is the role of the algorithm in communication scheduling.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In
the beeping model, algorithms must reduce contention and schedule communication on their own.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In the
population protocol model the scheduler ensures fair and reliable interactions.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Imagine, for example, a con-
tinuous leader election problem where every node has a leader bit, and the problem requires in an inﬁnite
execution that: (1) every node sets leader to 1 an inﬁnite number of times; and (2) there is never a time
at which two nodes both have leader set to 1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
This problem is trivial in the population protocol: simply
pass a leader token around the network.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In the beeping model, by contrast, it is impossible as it essentially
requires nodes to solve leader election correctly an inﬁnite number of times—a feat which would require an
unachievable error bound of 0.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It follows that in some respects these two models are studying the impact of
limited state on different aspects of distributed computation.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
2
Model
We model a collection of n probabilistic computational agents (i.e., “nodes”) that are connected in a single
hop network and communicate using a unary primitive; i.e., beeps.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In
each round, each node can either beep or receive.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Receiving nodes can distinguish between the following two
cases: (1) no node beeped; (2) one or more nodes beeped.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We characterize these agents by s (a bound on the
number of states in their state machine deﬁnition), and q (a bound on the precision allowed in probabilistic
transitions, with larger values enabling more accurate transition probabilities).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We now formalize these
model deﬁnitions and assumptions.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We formalize the algorithm executing on each node as a probabilistic state machine
M = (Qr, Qb, qs, δ⊥, δ⊤), where: Qr and Qb are two disjoint sets of states corresponding to receiving and
beeping, respectively; qs is the start state; and δ⊥and δ⊤are the probabilistic transition functions3 applied
3These transition functions map the current state to a distribution over the states to enter next.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
4


in the case where the node detects silence and where the node beeps/detects a beep, respectively.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Some problems have all nodes execute the same state machine, while others include multiple machine
types in the system, each corresponding to a different initial value.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Executions proceed in synchronous rounds with all nodes in the network starting in their ma-
chine’s start state.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
At the beginning of each round r, for each node u running a machine (Qr, Qb, qs, δ⊥, δ⊤),
if its current state qu is in Qb, then u emits a beep, otherwise it receives.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If at least one node beeps in r,
then it follows that all nodes either beep or detect a beep in this round.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Therefore, each node u applies the
transition function δ⊤to its current state qu and selects its next state according to the resulting distribution,
δ⊤(qu).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If no node beeps in r, then each node u applies the transition function δ⊥, selecting its next state
from the distribution, δ⊥(qu).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: We parameterize the state machines in our model with two values.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The ﬁrst, indicated by
s ≥1, is an upper bound on the number of states allowed (i.e., |Qr| + |Qb| ≤s).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The second, indicated
by q ≥2, bounds the precision of the probabilistic transitions allowed by the δ functions.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In more detail,
for a given q, the probabilities assigned to states by distributions in the range of δ must either be 0, 1, or in
the interval, [1
q, 1 −1
q].
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For the minimum value of q = 2, for example, probabilistic transitions can only
occur with probability 1/2.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
As q increases, smaller probabilities, as well as probabilities closer to 1, become
possible.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Finally, we parameterize a given execution with n—the number of nodes executing in the network.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
3
Leader Election
The ﬁrst computational task we consider is leader election: eventually, one node designates itself leader.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
An algorithm state machine that solves leader election must include a ﬁnal leader state qℓthat is terminal
(once a node enters the state, it never leaves).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If a node enters this state it indicates the node has elected
itself leader.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For a given error bound ǫ ∈[0, 1/2], we say an algorithm solves leader election with respect
to ǫ if when executed in a network of any size, it satisﬁes the following two properties: (1) liveness: with
probability 1, at least one node eventually enters the leader state; and (2) safety: with probability at least
1 −ǫ, there is never more than 1 node in the leader state.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We also consider algorithms for leader election
that are designed for networks of some minimal size e
N.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In this case, the algorithm must guarantee liveness
in every execution, but it needs to guarantee safety only if the network size n is at least e
N.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Our goal is to
develop algorithms that use a minimum number of states to solve leader election for a given error bound ǫ,
probability precision q, and, when relevant, network size minimum e
N.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: In Section 3.1, we present a lower bound for leader election.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In Section 3.2, we present a
universal algorithm template, followed by three speciﬁc instantiations in Sections 3.3, 3.4, and 3.5.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
3.1
Leader Election Lower Bound
Here we analyze the number of states required to solve leader election given a ﬁxed ǫ, q, and network size
lower bound e
N.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Our main result establishes that the number of states, s, must be in Ω(⌈
logq (1/ǫ)
e
N
⌉).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To prove this result, we begin by deﬁning and bounding a helper problem called (1, k)-loneliness de-
tection, which requires an algorithm to safely distinguish between n = 1 and n ≥k.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The bound leverages
a probabilistic indistinguishability argument concerning a short execution of the state machine in both the
n = 1 and n = k cases.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We then show that loneliness detection captures a core challenge of leader election
by demonstrating how to transform a leader election algorithm that works for n ≥e
N into a solution to
(1, e
N)-loneliness detection.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: The bound for the latter then carries over to leader election by reduction.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The (1, k)-loneliness detection problem is deﬁned for some integer k > 1
and error bound ǫ.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It assumes all nodes run the same state machine with two special terminal ﬁnal states
that we label qa (indicating “I am alone”) and qc (indicating “I am in a crowd”).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The liveness property of
this problem requires that with probability 1, every node eventually enters a ﬁnal state.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The safety property
requires that with probability at least 1 −ǫ, the following holds: if n = 1, then the single node in the system
eventually enters qa; and if n ≥k then all nodes eventually enter qc.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Crucial to this problem deﬁnition is
that we do not place any restrictions on the ﬁnal states nodes enter for the case where 1 < n < k.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The following bound formalizes the intuition that it becomes easier to break symmetry, and therefore
easier to solve loneliness detection, as the threshold for detecting a crowd grows.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Put another way: the
presence of a big crowd is easier to detect than a small crowd.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Let L be an algorithm that solves (1, k)-loneliness detection with error
bound ǫ and probability precision q using s states.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Fix some integer k > 1, error bound ǫ, and probability precision q.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Fix some algorithm L that solves
(1, k)-loneliness detection with error probability ǫ, using precision q.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Let (Qr, Qb, qs, δ⊥, δ⊤) be L’s state
machine description.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Let qa and qc be the two terminal ﬁnal states required by the problem deﬁnition.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We
note that when q ≥(1/ǫ), the lower bound claim on the state size reduces to a constant (or smaller), which
is trivially true.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: The remainder of this proof therefore addresses the more interesting case where q < (1/ǫ).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Our goal is prove the required lower bound on the number of states, s, needed for L to solve loneliness
detection given these ﬁxed values of k, ǫ, and q.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Our ﬁrst step toward this goal is to introduce the notion of a solo reachable path, deﬁned with respect to
L.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In more detail, we say a sequence P = q1, q2, ..., qx of x states from Qr ∪Qb is a solo reachable path for
L’s state machine if and only if q1 = qs, and for each consecutive pair of states qi, qi+1 in P, the following
hold:
1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
if qi ∈Qr, then the probability assigned to qi+1 in δ⊥(qi) is greater than 0;
2.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: if qi ∈Qb, then the probability assigned to qi+1 in δ⊤(qi) is greater than 0.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Put another way, a solo reachable path is a sequence of states that a node running this machine might feasibly
follow (i.e., it occurs with a non-zero probability) in a network with n = 1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Fix any such solo reachable path P = q1, q2, ..., qx.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We will now consider the probability that a network
consisting of exactly k nodes follows this path.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In more detail, we claim that for every r ∈{1, 2, ..., x}, the
probability that all k nodes are in state qr (from P) after r rounds is at least ((1/q)k)r.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We can prove this
claim by induction on the state index r.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: By deﬁnition, all nodes start in state qs, so this occurs with probability 1 > (1/q)k.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To show it holds for r+1, we note that the probability that
any single node transitions from qr to qr+1 is greater than 0 (by our deﬁnition of reachable).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The smallest
probability greater than 0 in our system is 1/q.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Therefore, we can reﬁne our statement to say this occurs
with probability at least (1/q).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It follows that the probability that all k nodes make the same transition is
at least (1/q)k.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Multiply this probability by the probability ((1/q)k)r that all nodes followed P up to qr
(provided by the inductive hypothesis), and we get the desired ﬁnal probability of ((1/q)k)r+1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We next argue that there exists a useful solo reachable path that is not too long:
(*) There exists a solo reachable path P = q1, q2, ..., qx, deﬁned with respect to L, such that
q1 = qs, qx = qa, and x ≤s.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The fact that there exists a solo reachable path that begins in the start state qs and ends in the ﬁnal state
qa, follows from the safety property of loneliness detection, which says that when n = 1, with probability
6


at least 1 −ǫ > 0, the single node, starting in state qs, ends up in ﬁnal state qa.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The fact that x ≤s follows
from the observation that if there is any such solo reachable path leading qa, then we can excise the loops to
get a path that remains reachable, but that never visits the same state more than once.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Let P be the solo reachable path identiﬁed above by claim (*).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If we apply our inductive argument to P,
and leverage the fact that the length of P is no more than s (i.e., x ≤s), we get that the probability that all
k nodes in a network of k nodes follow path P is at least (1/q)k·s.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Notice, if this occurs, we have violated
safety.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We can set up this requirement as a simple constraint that
will provide the minimum allowable value for s:
(1/q)k·s ≤ǫ ⇒qk·s ≥(1/ǫ) ⇒s · k log q ≥log (1/ǫ) ⇒s ≥log (1/ǫ)
k log q
= logq (1/ǫ)
k
.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Combining these pieces, we have shown that if L solves (1, k)-loneliness detection, than it must be the case
that s ≥
logq (1/ǫ)
k
, as required by the lemma statement.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Reducing Loneliness Detection to Leader Election.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We now leverage the above result on (1, k)-loneliness
detection to prove a lower bound for leader election under the guarantee that the network size n ≥e
N.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The
proof proceeds by reduction: we show how to transform such a leader election solution into a loneliness
detection algorithm of similar state size.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Fix some network size lower bound e
N ≥1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Let A be an algorithm that solves leader election
with error bound ǫ and probability precision q using s states in any network where n ≥e
N.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Fix some algorithm A that solves leader election with error bound ǫ and probability precision q using
s states in a network where n ≥e
N, for some integer e
N ≥1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Our ﬁrst step is to use A to create an algorithm
LA that solve (1, e
N)-loneliness detection for the same ǫ and q, using O(s) states.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Our new algorithm LA
works as follows:
The algorithm partitions rounds into pairs.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: During the ﬁrst round of each pair, it executes A.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: The second round is used to announce the election of a leader.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
That is, if a node becomes
leader according to A, it beeps in the second round.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If any node beeps in a second round, the
algorithm stops its execution of A and moves onto the next phase.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
This next phase consists of
single round.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: During this round, any node not elected leader beeps.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If this round is silent, then
the algorithm enters ﬁnal state qa, otherwise it enters state qc.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To analyze LA, we ﬁrst note that liveness follows directly from the liveness guarantee of A: once the
simulation of A elects the leader, LA will lead all nodes to the second phase where they will then enter a ﬁnal
state after an single additional round.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
There are three relevant cases, depending on
the value of n.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In the case, the liveness guarantee of A (which holds regardless of the network size)
implies that the single node in the system will eventually become leader.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Because there are no other
nodes in the system, the second phase round will be silent.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It follows that the single node will enter
state qa, as required.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: It follows that safety is satisﬁed with probability 1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In this case, by assumption, A correctly solves leader election with probability
at least 1 −ǫ.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Assume this occurs and u is the single leader elected.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If n = 1 (which is possible
when e
N = 1), the argument for Case #1 applies, and u will enter qa, as required.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: In this case, the second phase round will not be silent.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It follows that all nodes will enter state
qc, as required.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: It follows that safety is satisﬁed with probability at least 1 −ǫ.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: In this case, there are no safety requirements.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Therefore, safety is vacuously
satisﬁed with probability 1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We have just shown that given a solution to leader election that satisﬁes safety for n ≥e
N, we can
solve (1, e
N)-loneliness detection while growing the state size by at most a constant factor.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
By Lemma 1, any solution to (1, e
N)-loneliness detection for a given ǫ and q, requires
a state size s′ = Ω(
logq (1/ǫ)
e
N
).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It follows that the states used by A to solve leader election for e
N can be
no more than a constant factor larger than s′, proving the same asymptotic bound on s, which matches the
theorem statement.

We now turn our attention to leader election up-
per bounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The three results that follow adopt
a template/subroutine approach.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In more detail,
Figure 3.1 describes what we call the universal
leader election algorithm.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
This algorithm, in turn,
makes calls to a “termination subroutine.” Differ-
ent versions of this subroutine can be plugged into
the universal algorithm, yielding different guar-
antees.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Notice, this universal algorithm is pa-
rameterized with probability precision q and error
bound ǫ, which it uses to deﬁne the useful param-
eter ˆq = min{q, (1/ǫ)}.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
This algorithm (as well
as one of our termination subroutines) uses 1/ˆq,
not 1/q, as its smallest transition probability (in-
tuitively, there is little advantage in using a prob-
ability too much smaller than our error bound ǫ).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The basic operation of the algorithm is sim-
ple.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Until the
termination subroutine determines that it is time
to stop, nodes repeatedly execute the knockout
loop (lines 7–25).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In each iteration of the loop,
each active node beeps with probability 1 −1/ˆq
and listens otherwise.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If a node ever hears a
beep, it is knocked out, setting ko = true and
active = false.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In any silent iteration where no
node beeps, they execute the termination subrou-
tine to decide whether to stop.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Once termination
is reached, any node that remains active becomes the leader.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The goal of the termination subroutine is to decide whether leader election has
been solved: it returns true if there is a leader and false otherwise.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The termination subroutine is called simultaneously by all the nodes in the system, and it is passed
two parameters: the value of active, which indicates whether or not the calling node is still contending to
8


become leader, and ko, which indicates whether or not it has been knocked out in the main loop since the
last call to the subroutine.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We ﬁx R = 4 logˆq(max(n, 1/ǫ)): a parameter, which as we will later elaborate,
captures a bound on the calls to the subroutine needed before likely termination.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We consider the following
properties of a termination detection routine, deﬁned with respect to error parameter ǫ and R:
1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Agreement: Every node always returns the same value.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Safety: Over the ﬁrst R invocations, the probability that it returns true in any invocation with more
than 1 active node is at most ǫ/2.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Eventual Termination: If it is called inﬁnitely often with only one active node, then eventually (with
probability 1), it returns true.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Fast Termination: If it is called with only one active node, and with at least one node where ko = true,
then it returns true.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We now observe that the universal leader election algorithm is
correct when combined with a termination subroutine that satisﬁes the relevant properties from above.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To
do so, we ﬁrst determine how many rounds it takes until there is only one active node, and hence one possible
leader.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: We say that an iteration of the knockout loop (lines 7–25) is silent if no node beeps during it.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
(Notice
that the termination routine is only executed in silent iterations of the knockout loop.) We ﬁrst bound how
long it takes to reduce the number of active nodes:
Lemma 3.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Given probability ǫ ≤1/2 and parameter R = 4 logˆq(max(n, 1/ǫ)): after R silent iterations of
the knockout loop (lines 7–25), there remains exactly one active node, with probability at least 1 −ǫ/2.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Notice that there is always at least one active node, because a node becomes inactive only upon
detecting a beep from another active node.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For p to remain active, node q has
to remain silent whenever p listens.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Thus, if in some preﬁx of the execution, node p listens r times, the
probability that both p and q remain active is at most 1/ˆqr.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Taking a union bound over all pairs of nodes, we can upper bound by n2/ˆqR the probability that there
exist any pair of nodes p and q where one of the nodes listens R times and both nodes remain active.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Equivalently, we have shown that the probability of R silent iterations of the knockout loop, while at least 2
nodes are active, is bounded by n2/ˆqR.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Now recall that R = 4 logˆq(max(n, 1/ǫ)).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Consider the two cases:
• If ǫ ≥1/n, then R = 4 logˆq n, and therefore: n2/ˆqR ≤n2/n4 ≤ǫ/2.

text: • If ǫ < 1/n, then R = 4 logˆq(1/ǫ)), and therefore: n2/ˆqR ≤n2/(1/ǫ)4 ≤ǫ2 ≤ǫ/2.

text: In both cases, within R silent iterations, there is exactly one leader with probability at least 1 −ǫ/2.

text: Let T be a termination subroutine that satisﬁes Agreement and Eventual Termination.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In addition,
assume that T satisﬁes safety in networks of size at least e
N.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We can now show that the universal leader
election algorithm is correct with termination subroutine T:
Theorem 4.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If termination subroutine T uses s states and precision q, then the universal algorithm solves
leader election with error ǫ, s + O(1) states, and q precision (guaranteeing safety only in networks of size
n ≥e
N).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: We consider the two properties of leader election in turn.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Liveness: First, there is always at least one active node, because a node becomes inactive only upon
receiving a beep from another active node.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In every iteration of the knockout loop that starts with more than
one active node, there is a non-zero probability that at least one active node is knocked out, and therefore with
probability one there is eventually only one active node remaining.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
From that point on, in every iteration,
there is a constant probability that the remaining active node is silent and hence the termination subroutine
is executed by all nodes.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: By the Termination property, eventually it will return true and all nodes terminate.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Thus with probability one, eventually there is at least one leader.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Safety: Assume the network is of size at least e
N (the only case for which safety must hold).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The
probability that the algorithm makes it through R silent iterations of the knockout loop with more than
one leader is at most ǫ/2, via Lemma 3.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Notice that the termination routine is only executed in silent
iterations of the knockout loop, and over these R (potentially bad) iterations, there is a probability of at most
ǫ/2 of improperly terminating and entering the leader state with multiple active nodes (as provided by the
termination detection safety property).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
A union bound combines these errors for a total error probability
less than ǫ.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
While the preceding theorem can be used to show the feasibility of solving leader election, it does not
bound the performance.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For that, we rely on termination subroutines that ensure fast termination:
Theorem 5.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If termination subroutine T satisﬁes Fast Termination instead of Eventual Termination, and if
it uses s states and q precision, and if it runs in time t, then the universal algorithm solves leader election
with error ǫ with s + O(1) states and q precision (guaranteeing safety only in networks of size ≥e
N).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Furthermore, it terminates in O(t logˆq(n + 1/ǫ)) rounds, with probability at least 1 −ǫ.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Notice that Fast Termination implies Eventual Termination: eventually, there will be only one active
node, since if there is more than one active node, then in every iteration of the knockout loop there is
a positive probability that one node is knocked out; in the iteration immediately after the last knockout
occurs, the conditions for Fast Termination are satisﬁed.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We can, therefore, apply Theorem 4 to establish
the algorithm as a correct leader election algorithm.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: It remains only to consider the running time.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In this case, in Lines 1–3, the lone node calls the termination subroutine with ko and
active both equal true.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

By the fast termination property, the lone node terminates before it even enters the
knockout loop.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

By Lemma 3, we know that with probability at least 1 −ǫ, there is only one active node
within O(tR) time.

text: Consider the last round that begins with at least two active nodes.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In that round, at least
one node is knocked out, and hence the termination routine is called with only one active node and at least
one node with ko equal to true.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
By the fast termination property (and the agreement property), all nodes
terminate after this call.

satisfying the claimed time complexity upper bound.

The leader election algorithm from Section 3.3 can solve the problem with the optimal amount of states

text: The Fixed Error Termination Detection Subroutine.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
This termination subroutine consists of a ﬁxed
schedule of ⌈log (2/ǫ)⌉+2 rounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
During the ﬁrst round, any node that calls the subroutine with parameter
ko equal to 1 beeps while all other nodes receive.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If no node beeps, then the subroutine is aborted and all
nodes return false.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Moving forward, assume this event does not occur (i.e., at least one node beeps in the ﬁrst round).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For
each of the ⌈log (2/ǫ)⌉rounds that follow, every node with parameter active = 1, will ﬂip a fair two-sided
coin.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: If it comes up heads, it will beep, otherwise it will receive.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Each node with active = 1 will start these
rounds with a ﬂag solo initialized to 1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If such a node ever detects a beep during a round that it receives, it
will reset solo to 0 (as it just gained evidence that it is not alone).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The ﬁnal round of the subroutine is used to determine if anyone detected a non-solo execution of the
subroutine.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: To do so, every node with active = 1 and solo = 0 beeps.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If no node beeps in this ﬁnal round,
then all nodes return true.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We proceed as before, observing that all nodes return the same value from this subroutine since
all observe the same channel activity in the ﬁrst and last rounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It is also straightforward to verify that im-
plementing this subroutine requires O(log (1/ǫ)) states to count the rounds and record solo.

follows directly from a case analysis of the algorithm.

least one node where ko = true, then it returns true.

solo = 1.

text: Thus, no node beeps in the ﬁnal round and everyone returns true.

3.5
Fast Leader Election with O(1) States and High Probability
The ﬁnal termination detection subroutine we consider requires only a constant number of states, and when
executed in a network of size n, for any n > 1, it solves leader election with high probability in n.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
At
ﬁrst glance, this result may seem to violate the lower bound from Section 3.1, which notes that the state
requirement grows with a log (1/ǫ) factor as ǫ decreases.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The question is why a constant number of states
is sufﬁcient for our algorithm here even though this term grows with n.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The answer relies on the fact that ǫ
is always a function of n, such that for any ﬁxed n, it is true that e
N ≥n, and therefore the e
N factor in the
denominator of our lower bound swamps the growth of the log n factor in the numerator.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: The Constant State Termination Detection Subroutine.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The subroutine here is identical to the Fixed
Error subroutine, except the length of subroutine is not ﬁxed in advance (no node has enough states to count
beyond a constant number of rounds—which is not enough for our purposes).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Instead, we dynamically adapt
the length of the subroutine to a sufﬁciently large function of n using a distributed counting strategy.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In more detail, during the ﬁrst round, any node that called the subroutine with parameter ko equal to 1
beeps while all other nodes receive.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If no node beeps, then subroutine is aborted and all nodes will return
value false (as is true for Fixed Error).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Assuming the subroutine has not aborted, the nodes then proceed to
the main body.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: During the main body, we partition rounds into even and odd pairs.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
During the odd numbered
rounds, we proceed as in Fixed Error: every node with parameter active = 1, ﬂips a fair coin; if it comes
up heads, it will beep, otherwise it will receive; each node with active = 1 will start these rounds with a
ﬂag solo initialized to 1; if such a node ever detects a beep during a round that it receives, it will reset solo
to 0 (as it just gained evidence that it is not alone).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
During the even rounds, the nodes run a repeated knockout protocol for O(1) iterations, for some ﬁxed
constant bounded in our below analysis.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In more detail, each node (regardless of whether or not it has active
equal to true) begins the subroutine with a ﬂag attack = 1 and a counter count = 0.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In each even round,
each node with attack = 1 ﬂips a fair coin and beeps if it comes up heads; otherwise it listens.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Any node
that listens in an even round and hears a beep sets attack = 0.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If there is an even round in which no node
beeps, then all nodes increment count and reset attack = 1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
This continues until count grows larger than
the ﬁxed constant mentioned above, When this occurs, all nodes move the ﬁnal round, which is deﬁned the
same as the ﬁnal round in Fixed Error.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: That is: every node with active = 1 and solo = 0 beeps.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If no node
beeps in this ﬁnal round, then all nodes return true.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The Liveness and Fast Termination properties follow from the same arguments used in our
analysis of Fixed Error.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: The main difﬁculty in analyzing this subroutine is proving Safety.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To do so, we ﬁrst
bound how long the subroutine is likely to run on any given invocation:
Lemma 11.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For any constant c, there exists a c′ > c and a constant bound for count, such that the
main body of the subroutine runs for at least c log(n) rounds but no more than c′ log n rounds, with high
probability.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We will show that with high probability, each iteration of the knockout protocol runs for Θ(log n)
rounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
By choosing an appropriate constant bound for count (i.e., the number of iterations of the knockout
protocol), we can increase this length by any constant factor.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We begin by noting that as long as there are Θ(log n) nodes with attack = 1, then, with high proba-
bility, the iteration does not end in that round, as it is likely that at least one node will beep (this follows
because the probability of silence in this case is upper bounded by 1/2Θ(log n)).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Also note that whenever
a node ﬂips a tails, it is eliminated.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Thus, we show that with high probability, at least Θ(log n) nodes ﬂip
Θ(log(n/ log log n) = Θ(log n) heads in a row.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: One easy way to to see why this is so is as follows.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Divide the nodes in Θ(log n) different groups of
n/Θ(log n) nodes each.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For each group, the probability that no node ﬂips sufﬁciently many heads in a row
is at most:

Thus each group, independently, has a constant probability of having one node survive.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Since each group
is independent and there are Θ(log n) groups, by a Chernoff bound there are Θ(log n) survivors with high
probability.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Thus we conclude that with high probability, the subroutine does not terminate for Θ(log(n/ log n)) =
Θ(log n) rounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To show that the subroutine does eventually terminate for some larger term in Θ(log n) is more straight-
forward.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For every even round such that u has attack = 1, there is a probability of
at least 1/2 that it receives a beep (and resets attack) or there is a silence.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It follows that with high prob-
ability one of these two things has happened after Θ(log n) rounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
A union bound over all nodes shows
that with high probability this is true for all nodes, indicating either a silence has occurred or every node has
attack = 0 so a silence is about to occur.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Over the ﬁrst R invocations of the subroutine, the probability that it returns true in any
invocation with more than one active node is at most 1/nc, for a constant c we can grow with our constant
bound on count.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: The proof here proceeds much as in Lemma 9.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
As before, we can conclude that the probability of
returning true when there is more than one active node is bounded by 1/2s, where s is the number of round
of the main body of the subroutine.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We have shown in Lemma 11 that s = Ω(log n) with high probability,
and so overall we conclude that the lemma holds with high probability.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: We can then show that the subroutine guarantees safety.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Combined with the Theorem 5, these properties
yields the following conclusion:
Theorem 13.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For any network size n, the universal leader election algorithm combined with the Constant
State termination detection subroutine, solves leader election with high probability in n using s = O(1)
states and q = 2.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Also with high probability in n, it terminates in O(log2 n) rounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
14


4
Solving General Distributed Decision Problems
In the previous section, we studied upper and lower bounds for solving leader election in the beeping model.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Here we establish these leader election bounds to be (in some sense) fundamental for useful distributed
computation in this setting.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In more detail, we use a combination of our leader election algorithms as a key
primitive in constructing an algorithm that can simulate a logspace (in n) decider Turing Machine (TM)
with a constant number of unary input tapes (of size O(n) each).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The simulation has error probability at
most ǫ, requires only the minimum probabilistic precision (q = 2), and uses s = O(log (1/ǫ)) states.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If high
probability in n is sufﬁcient, then the state size can be reduced to s = O(1).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For any problem solvable by a logspace TM with a constant number of unary input tapes,
there exist constants c, d ≥1, such that for any error probability ǫ ∈[0, 1/2] and network size n ≥1,
we can solve the problem in the beeping model in a network of size n with probability at least 1 −ǫ using
s = c log (1/ǫ) states, precision q = 2, and an expected running time of O(nd log2 (n + 1/ǫ)) rounds.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For
high probability correctness, s = O(1) states are sufﬁcient.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: We now highlight some important observations about the above result.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
First, we should not expect to sim-
ulate a more powerful class of TM.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: This follows from a conﬁguration counting argument.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For s = O(1),
for example, the n nodes in our model can collectively encode at most O(ns) unique conﬁgurations (there
is no explicit ordering of nodes, so a given conﬁguration of our system is described by the number of nodes
out of n in each of the s possible states).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
A TM with more than log space, by contrast, might have many
more possible conﬁgurations that need to be simulated.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
What is perhaps more surprising is that we can
successfully simulate a logspace machine even though nodes do not have enough states for unique ids or
even to store a single pointer to the simulated TM’s tape.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In some sense, our algorithm is making full use
(asymptotically) of the available memory in our distributed system.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Second, notice that the size of this algorithm is independent of the network size.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The same number of
states successfully simulates the TM even as n, and therefore the potential length of the simulated TM com-
putation, grows to arbitrarily large values.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Third, this results establishes log (1/ǫ) as a key state complexity
threshold in the beeping model.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If you have fewer than this many states, you cannot even safely solve basic
symmetry breaking tasks (e.g., leader election).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Once you reach this threshold, however, suddenly you can
solve a rich set of expressive problems (e.g., anything solvable by a logspace TM).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Finally, we emphasize that we do not present this simulation as a practical algorithm for solving prob-
lems in limited communication scenarios (simulating a TM typically adds many more layers of indirection
than is necessary).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We instead use this result to identify the threshold beyond which beeping nodes can start
to solve interesting problems.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Finding elegant solutions to individual problems in this class is a separate and
useful endeavor.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Before proceeding to the proof details, we ﬁrst summarize the main ideas.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Our result depends on a
TM simulation strategy that follows the outline originally identiﬁed in [4], where it was used to simulate
a TM using a population protocol in the randomized interaction model.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In more detail, we ﬁrst simulate
a simple counter machine with a constant number of counters that can take values of size O(n).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We then
apply a classical computability result due to Minsky [16] which shows how to simulate a logspace TM (with
unary input tapes) using a counter machine of this type.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The counter machine simulation in the beeping
model, combined with Minsky’s TM simulation in the counter model, yields a TM simulation in the beeping
model.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Though we follow the same outline as in [4], the details of our counter simulation of course differ as
we are implementing this simulation in the beeping model whereas [4] implements their simulation in the
population protocol model.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
What our two approaches do share (along with many network simulations of
TMs) is the use of leaders to coordinate the simulation.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The core concept in our counter machine simulation is to elect a leader to play the role of the simulation
coordinator.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: This coordinator can announce the counter operations that need to be simulated by the network.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
15


We show for every operation required of a counter machine, there is a way to simulate its operation with
at most a constant number of leader election instances.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To elect leaders, we use our universal algorithm
combined with the conjunction of both our fast termination detection subroutines (i.e., termination requires
both to return true).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We show that the error probability of this combination is bounded by ǫ/nc—allowing us
to safely solve leader election for the needed polynomial number of instances before the simulated logspace
TM reaches its ﬁnal decision.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: We now tackle these elements in more detail.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The counter machine we simulate has access to a constant number of
counters that can hold values from 0 to O(n).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Control is captured by a ﬁnite state machine.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Each state
transition can increment, decrement, or reset to 0 any of the counter values.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The transition function can also
integrate the outcome of a comparison operator that compares the value stored in a given counter to 0.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Our simulation leverages leader election as a key subroutine.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
In particular, we use the primitive that
results when we combine the universal leader election algorithm with the the conjunctive combination of
both the Fixed Error and Constant State termination detection subroutines.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
That is, every time the universal
algorithm calls a termination subroutine, it will now call both of these subroutines, one after the other, and
then return the value out1 ∧out2, where out1 and out2 are the outcomes of the ﬁrst and second subroutine
called, respectively.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
For the remainder of this discussion, we call this instantiation of the universal algorithm
the double-safe fast leader election algorithm.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Because the back-to-back executions of these subroutines are
independent, and they offer error bounds of ǫ and n−c (for some constant c > 1 that grows with the available
state), respectively, we get the following claim about this algorithm:
Claim 15.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The probability that a given call to the termination subroutine fails in the double-safe leader
election algorithm is no more than ǫ/nc.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Returning to our simulation description, the ﬁrst step is to run the double-safe protocol to elect a leader
to play the role of coordinator.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
This node is responsible for simulating the state transitions of the ﬁnite-state
control of the counter machine.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It is also responsible for announcing to the other nodes (using predetermined,
constant length beep patterns) which operation will be simulated next.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We make use of the states distributed among all n nodes in the network to store the counter values in
a distributed fashion.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To so so, we assume for each counter ci, each node has a local bit labelled c[i] in its
state.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Our simulation will store counter values in unary using these bits.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
That is, we represent ci = x at a
given point in our simulation by having exactly x nodes in our beep model with their c[i] bit set to 1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
(To
handle counter values larger than n, but still in O(n), we can expand the size of these c[i] local counters to
larger constant sizes as needed).
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Two of these counters (let us call them c1 and c2) are needed to run the TM simulation, and we assume
are initialized to zero.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Accordingly, we assume all nodes begin with c[1] = c[2] = 0.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The simulation
also assumes the values stored in unary on the input tape(s) of the simulated TM are also initially stored in
counters.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We can capture this in a similar manner; e.g., if c3 corresponds to an input tape storing value x in
unary, we assume exactly x nodes begin with c[3] = 1.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We now describe each of the operations that may need to be simulated, and show how the nodes can
successfully simulate each of these operations using only O(1) correct calls to double-safe leader election.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: The coordinator, true to its name, coordinates these operation simulations.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
That is, it announces the next
operation to be simulated with a ﬁxed beep pattern.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
It then uses the results of operation simulation to advance
its local copy of the counter machine control, which determines which operation to simulate next.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: To increment a counter ci, the set of nodes (if any) with c[i] = 0 run leader election.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
(If all nodes have c[i] = 1 then no election is necessary as the counter does
not grow beyond its maximum value.)
16


• Decrement.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To decrement a counter ci, we follow the same strategy as the increment operation, except
now nodes with c[i] = 1 compete, and the leader resets c[i] to 0.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
(If all nodes have c[i] = 0, then no
election is necessary as the counter cannot reduce below 0.)
• Zero.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: To zero a counter ci, all nodes with c[i] = 1 reset c[i] to 0.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To compare a counter to ci to 0, it is sufﬁcient to assign a round for all nodes with
c[i] = 1 to beep.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If the coordinator detects silent then it knows the stored counter value is 0, otherwise
it is greater than 0.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The TM Simulation
Though the counter machine described above is quite simple, Minsky [16] shows it
is sufﬁciently powerful to simulate a logspace TM with a constant number of unary input tapes.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Minsky’s
simulation requires up to a polynomial number of steps of the counter machine for each simulated step of
the TM.4 Therefore, our TM simulation will require up to a polynomial number of successful leader election
calls per simulated TM step.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The total number of simulated TM steps can also be bounded by a polynomial,
as the machine has only logarithmic space and it is a deterministic decider.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Therefore, our simulation must
correctly implement leader election a (larger) polynomial number of times to correctly simulate the TM until
its decision.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We note that a sufﬁciently large constant number of states is enough for the coordinator to
simulate the ﬁnite control of the counter machine.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
We also note that an additional constant number of states
is enough for the nodes to store their constant-sized pieces of the constant number of counter values used in
the simulation.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
More interesting is the question of how many states are needed to ensure that the leader elections calls in
the simulation are all correct.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
To answer this question, let na, for some constant a ≥1 dependent on the TM
deﬁnition and Minsky simulation details, be the maximum number of leader election calls our simulation
might make.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: We note that our double-safe algorithm uses two termination detection subroutines.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The ﬁrst
requires s = O(log (1/ǫ)) states to reduce the error probability to no more than ǫ.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
The second requires
s = O(1) states to reduce the error probability to n−c, for some c we can grow by increasing the constant in
the state size.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
If we ﬁx c ≥a, we see the probability that a particular call to leader election fails is no more
than ǫ/na.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
A union bound over the no more than na leader elections needed by the simulation tells us that
the probability at least one fails is less than ǫ.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text: Finally, we turn our attention to time complexity.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
Because each of the fast termination detection subrou-
tines terminate in time O(log2 (n + 1/ǫ)), we get O(na log2 (n + 1/ǫ)) as an expected time bound.
title: arXiv:1508.03859v1  [cs.DC]  16 Aug 2015

text:
These
results combine to establish Theorem 14.
