title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Abstract: We give a new theoretical solution to a leading-edge experimental challenge,
namely to the veriﬁcation of quantum computations in the regime of high computational
complexity.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: Our results are given in the language of quantum interactive proof systems.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Speciﬁcally, we show that any language in BQP has a quantum interactive proof system with
a polynomial-time classical veriﬁer (who can also prepare random single-qubit pure states),
and a quantum polynomial-time prover.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
e., it holds
even for computationally unbounded provers.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Compared to prior work achieving similar
results, our technique does not require the encoding of the input or of the computation;
instead, we rely on encryption of the input (together with a method to perform computations
on encrypted inputs), and show that the random choice between three types of input (deﬁning
a computational run, versus two types of test runs) sufﬁces.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Because the overhead is very
low for each run (it is linear in the size of the circuit), this shows that veriﬁcation could be
achieved at minimal cost compared to performing the computation.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
As a proof technique, we
use a reduction to an entanglement-based protocol; to the best of our knowledge, this is the
ﬁrst time this technique has been used in the context of veriﬁcation of quantum computations,
and it enables a relatively straightforward analysis.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

Introduction
Feynman [24] was the ﬁrst to point out that quantum computers, if built, would be able to perform
quantum simulations (i.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
e., to compute the predictions of quantum mechanics; which is widely believed to
be classically intractable).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
But this immediately begs the question: if the output of a quantum computation
cannot be predicted, how do we know that it is correct?
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Conventional wisdom would tell us that we
can rely on testing parts (or scaled-down versions) of a quantum computer—conclusive results would
then extrapolate to the larger system.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
But this is somewhat unsatisfactory, since we may not rule out
the hypothesis that, at a large scale, quantum computers behave unexpectedly.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
A different approach
to the veriﬁcation of a quantum computation would be to construct a number of quantum computers
based on different technologies (e.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
g., with ionic, photonic, superconducting and/or solid state systems),
and to accept the computed predictions if the experimental results agree.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Again, this is still somewhat
unsatisfactory, as a positive outcome does not conﬁrm the correctness of the output, but instead conﬁrms
that the various large-scale devices behave similarly on the given instances.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: This problem, though theoretical in nature [6], is already appearing as a major experimental challenge.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
One of the outstanding applications for the veriﬁcation of quantum systems is in quantum chemistry,
where the current state-of-the-art is that the inability to verify quantum simulations is much more the
norm than the exception [29].
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Any theoretical advance in this area could have dramatic consequences on
applications of quantum chemistry simulations, including the potential to revolutionize drug discovery.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Another case where experimental techniques are reaching the limits of classical veriﬁability is in the
Boson Sampling problem [1], where the process of veriﬁcation has been raised as a fundamental objection
to the viability of experiments [30] (fortunately, these claims are refuted [2], and progress was made in
the experimental veriﬁcation [45]).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
As mere classical probabilistic polynomial-time1 individuals, we appear to be in an impasse: how
can we validate the output of a quantum computation?2 For some problems of interest in quantum
computing (such as factoring and search), a claimed solution can be efﬁciently veriﬁed by a classical
computer.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
However, current techniques do not give us such an efﬁcient veriﬁcation procedure for the
hardest problems that can be solved by quantum computers (such problems are known as BQP-complete,
and include the problem of approximating the Jones polynomial [5]).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Here, we propose a solution
based on interaction, viewing an experiment not in the traditional, static, predict-and-verify framework,
but as an interaction between an experimentalist and a quantum device.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In the context of theoretical
computer science, it has been established for quite some time that interaction between a probabilistic
polynomial-time veriﬁer and a computationally unbounded prover allows the veriﬁcation of a class of
problems much wider than what static proofs allow.3
Interactive proof systems traditionally model the prover as being all-powerful (i.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
e., computationally
unbounded).4 For our purposes, we restrict the prover to being a “realistic” quantum device, i.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
e., we
model the prover as a quantum polynomial-time machine.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Our approach equates the veriﬁer with a
1I.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
e., assuming humans can ﬂip coins and execute classical computations that take time polynomial in n to solve on inputs of
size n.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: 2Assuming the widely-held belief that BQP ̸= BPP, i.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
e., that quantum computers are indeed more powerful than classical
computers.

of being able to prepare random single pure-state qubits (chosen among a speciﬁc set, see Section 3).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Our
veriﬁer does not require any quantum memory or quantum processing power.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Without loss of generality,
the random quantum bits can be sent in the ﬁrst round, the balance of the interaction and veriﬁer’s
computation being classical.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Formally, we present our results in terms of an interactive proof system,
showing that in our model, it is possible to devise a quantum-prover interactive proof system for all
problems solvable (with bounded error) in quantum polynomial time.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
1.1
Related work
The complexity class QPIP, corresponding to quantum-prover interactive proof systems, was originally
deﬁned by Aharonov, Ben-Or and Eban [3], who, using techniques from [11], showed that BQP = QPIP
for a veriﬁer with the capacity to perform quantum computations on a constant-sized quantum register
(together with polynomial-time classical computation).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
The main idea of [3] is to encode the input
into a quantum authentication code [9], and to use interactive techniques for quantum computing on
authenticated data in order to enable veriﬁcation of a quantum computation.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
This result was revisited
in light of foundations of physics in [6], and the protocol was also shown secure in a scenario of
composition [16].
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In a different line of research, Kasheﬁand Fitzsimons [27] consider a measurement-based approach to
the problem, giving a scheme that requires the veriﬁer to prepare only random single qubits: the main idea
is to encode the computation into a larger one which includes a veriﬁcation mechanism, and to execute the
resulting computation using blind quantum computing [15].
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Thus, success of the encoded computation
can be used to deduce the correctness of actual computation.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
A small-scale version of this protocol was
implemented in quantum optics [10].
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Further work by Kapourniotis, Dunjko and Kasheﬁ[37] shows how
to combine the [3] and [27] protocols in order to reduce the quantum communication overhead; Kasheﬁ
and Wallden [38] also show how to reduce the overhead of [27].
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
To the best of our knowledge, the proof techniques in these prior works appear as sketches only,
or are cumbersome.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In particular, the approach that uses quantum authentication codes [3] is based
on [11].
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: However, the full proof of security for [11] never appeared.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Although [3] makes signiﬁcant
progress towards closing this gap, it provides only a sketch of how the soundness is established in the
interactive case (see, however, the very recent [4]).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
A full proof of soundness for [3] follows from [16],
however the proof is very elaborate and phrased in terms of a rather different cryptographic task (called
“quantum one-time programs”).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In terms of the measurement-based approach, note that a proposed
protocol for veriﬁcation in [15] was deemed incomplete [27], but any gaps were addressed in [27].
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In
this case, however, the protocol (and proof) are very elaborate, and to the best of our knowledge, remain
unpublished.5 Note, however that follow-up work has appeared in peer-reviewed form [37,38], and that
these works consider the more general problem of veriﬁcation for quantum inputs and outputs.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
A related line of research also studies the problem of veriﬁcation with a client that can perform only
single-qubit measurements [35]; the case of untrusted devices is also considered in [34].
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In sharp contrast
to these approaches, Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani [42] show that it is possible to make the veriﬁer
completely classical, as long as we postulate two non-communicating entangled provers.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
(This could be
5This work has been published as [28] during the review period of the current paper.

be forbidden by the limit on the speed of light.) The main technique used is a rigidity theorem which,
provided that the provers pass a certain number of tests, gives the veriﬁer a tight classical control on the
quantum provers.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Very recently, Coladangelo, Grilo, Jeffery, and Vidick [19] have used the techniques
described here to achieve efﬁcient schemes for verifying quantum computations in the model of a classical
veriﬁer and two entangled provers.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
1.2
Contributions
Our main contributions are a new, simple quantum-prover interactive proof system for BQP, with a
veriﬁer whose quantum power is limited to the random preparation of single-qubit pure states, together
with a new proof technique.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
All prior approaches to the veriﬁcation of quantum computations required some type
of encoding (either of the input or of the computation), or otherwise had the veriﬁer perform part of the
computation.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In contrast, our protocol achieves soundness via the veriﬁer’s random choice of different
types of runs.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
This is a typical construction in interactive proofs, and in some sense it is surprising that it
is used here for the ﬁrst time in the context of verifying quantum computations.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
According to the new
protocol, the overhead required for veriﬁcation can be reduced to repetition of a very simple protocol
(with overhead at most linear compared to performing the original computation), and thus may lead
to implementations sooner than expected (in general, it is much easier to repeat an experiment using
different initial settings, than to run a single, more complex experiment!).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In order to prove soundness, we use the proof technique of a reduction to an
“entanglement-based” protocol.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
This proof technique originates from Shor and Preskill [44] and has been
used in a number of quantum cryptographic scenarios, e.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
To the best of our knowledge, this
is the ﬁrst time that this technique is used in the context of the veriﬁcation of quantum computations; we
show how the technique provides a much-needed succinct and convincing method to prove soundness.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In
particular, it allows us to reduce the analysis of an interactive protocol to the analysis of a non-interactive
one, and to formally delay the veriﬁer’s choice of run until after the interaction with the prover.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Furthermore, this work uniﬁes the two distinct approaches given above, (one based on quantum
authentication codes and the other on measurement-based quantum computing).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Indeed, one can view
our protocol as performing a very basic type of quantum computing on authenticated data [16]; with
hidden gates being executed via a computation-by-teleportation process [33] that is reminiscent of
measurement-based quantum computation, and thus of blind quantum computation [15].
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
On the conceptual front, this work focuses on the simplest possible way to achieve a quantum-prover
interactive proof system.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: Via this process, we have further emphasized links between various concepts.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: A link between input privacy and veriﬁcation.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Prior results [3, 15, 16, 27] all happened to
provide both privacy of a quantum computation and its veriﬁcation (one notable exception being
the recent [26]).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Here, we make this link explicit, essentially starting from input privacy and
constructing a veriﬁable scheme (this was also done, to a certain extent in [15,27]).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

2.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: A link between fault-tolerant quantum computation and cryptography.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Prior results [3,11,16]
used constructions inspired by fault-tolerant quantum computation.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Here, we make the link even
more explicit by using single-qubit gate gadgets that are adaptations of the gate gadgets used in
fault-tolerant quantum computation.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Furthermore, our results also emphasize how the ubiquitous
technique of “tracking the Pauli frame” from fault-tolerant quantum computation can be re-phrased
in terms of keeping track of an encryption key.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: A link between entanglement and parallelization.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
It is known that entanglement can reduce the
number of rounds in quantum interactive proof systems [39]; a consequence of our entanglement-
based protocol is that we can parallelize our interactive proof system to a single round, as long as
we are willing to allow the prover to share entanglement with the veriﬁer, and to perform adaptive
measurements.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
1.3
Overview of techniques
The main idea for our quantum-prover interactive proof system is that the veriﬁer chooses randomly to
interact with the prover in one of three runs.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Among these runs, one is the computation run, while the
two others are test runs.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In an honest interaction, the output of the computation run is the result (a single
bit) of evaluating the given quantum circuit.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
The test runs are used to detect a deviating prover; there are
two types of test runs: an X-test and a Z-test.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Intuitively (and formally proved in Section 7.1), we see
that the prover cannot distinguish between all three runs.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Thus, his strategy must be invariant over the
different runs.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
It should be clear now how this work links input privacy with veriﬁcation: by varying the
input to the computation, the veriﬁer differentiates between test and computation runs; by input privacy,
however, the prover cannot identify the type of run and thus any deviation from the prescribed protocol
has a chance of being detected.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In more details, the runs have the following properties (from the point of view of the veriﬁer)
• Computation run.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: In a computation run, the prover executes the target circuit on input |0⟩⊗n.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: In an X-test run, the prover executes the identity circuit on input |0⟩⊗n.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
At the end of
the computation, the veriﬁer veriﬁes that the result is 0.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
This test also contains internal checks for
cheating within the protocol.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: In a Z-test run, the prover executes the identity circuit on input |+⟩⊗n.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
This test run is
used only as an internal check for cheating within the protocol.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In order for the prover to execute the above computations without being able to distinguish between
the runs, we use a technique inspired by quantum computing on encrypted data (QCED) [14,25]: the input
qubits are encrypted with a random Pauli, as are auxiliary qubits that are used to drive the computation.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation
How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Furthermore, the X- and Z-test runs should (up to an encryption key), leave
the quantum wires in the |0⟩⊗n or |+⟩⊗n state, respectively.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Performing Pauli gates in this fashion is
straightforward, as this can be done by adjusting the encryption key (in the computation run only).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
As
we show in Section 4.2, the CNOT gate can be executed directly (since it does not have any effect on
the wires for the test runs).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
The T-gate (Section 4.3) is performed using a construction (“gate gadget”)
inspired both by QCED and fault-tolerant quantum computation [12] (see also [17]); the T-gate gadget

involves the use of an auxiliary qubit and classical interaction.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
The H is performed thanks to an identity
involving the H and P (Section 4.4).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In order to prove soundness, we consider any general deviation of the prover, and show that such
deviation can be mapped to an attack on the measured wires only, corresponding to an honest run of the
protocol (without loss of generality, we can also delay all measurements until the end of the protocol).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Furthermore, because the computation is performed on encrypted data, by the Pauli twirl [22], this attack
can be described as a convex combination of Pauli attacks on the measured qubits.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Since all measurements
are performed in the computational basis, Z attacks are obliterated, and thus the only family of attacks
of concern consists in X- and Y-gates applied to various measured qubits; these act as bit ﬂips on the
corresponding classical output.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
We show that the combined effect of test runs is to detect all such attacks;
this allows us to bound the probability that the veriﬁer accepts a no-instance.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Since only X and Y attacks
require detection, one may wonder why we use also a Z-test run.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
The answer to this question lies in
the implementation of the H-gate: while its net effect is to apply the identity in the test runs, its internal
workings temporarily swap the roles of the X- and Z-test runs; thus the Z-test runs are also used to detect
X and Y errors.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: Finally, some words on showing indistinguishability between the test and computation runs.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
This
is done by showing that the veriﬁer can delay her choice of run (computation, X- or Z-test) until after
the interaction with the prover is complete.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
This is accomplished via an entanglement-based protocol,
where the veriﬁer’s messages to the prover consist in only half-EPR pairs, as well as classical random bits.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
These messages are identical in both the test and computation runs; as the veriﬁer decides on the type
of run only after having the interacted with the prover.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Depending on this choice, the veriﬁer performs
measurements on the system returned by the prover, resulting in the desired effect.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
1.4
Open problems
The main outstanding open problem is the veriﬁability of a quantum computation with a classical veriﬁer,
interacting with a single quantum polynomial-time prover.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: In this context, we make a few observations.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
• If the prover is unbounded, there exists a quantum interactive proof system for BQP, since
QIP(= PSPACE) = IP.6
• If P = BQP, there is a trivial quantum interactive proof system.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
• One possible approach would be to relax the deﬁnition to require only computational soundness
(following the lines of Brassard, Chaum and Crépeau [13], this would lead to a quantum interactive
argument).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
This approach seems promising, especially if we consider a computational assumption
that is post-quantum secure.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
If, via its interaction with the prover, a classical veriﬁer accepts, then
we can conclude that either the veriﬁer performed the correct computation or the prover has broken
the computational assumption.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
1.5
Organization
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Section 2 presents some preliminary notation and
background.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: Section 3 deﬁnes quantum-prover interactive proofs and states our main theorem.

Deﬁnitions and statement of results
Interactive proof systems were introduced by Babai [8] and Goldwasser, Micali, and Rackoff [32].
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
An
interactive proof system consists of an interaction between a computationally unbounded prover and a
computationally bounded probabilistic veriﬁer.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
For a language L and a string x, the prover attempts to
convince the veriﬁer that x ∈L, while the veriﬁer tries to determine the validity of this “proof.” Thus, a
language L is said to have an interactive proof system if there exists a polynomial-time veriﬁer V with the
following properties.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

The class of languages having interactive proof systems is denoted IP.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: Watrous [46] deﬁned QIP as the quantum analogue of IP, i.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
e., as the class of languages having
a quantum interactive proof system, which consists in a quantum interaction between a computation-
ally unbounded quantum prover and a computationally bounded quantum veriﬁer, with the analogous
completeness and soundness conditions as given above.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
For our results, we are interested in the scenario of a polynomial-time prover (in the honest case), as
well as an almost-classical veriﬁer; that is, a veriﬁer with the power to generate random qubits as speciﬁed
by a parameter S (Deﬁnition 3.1).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Furthermore, as a technicality, instead of considering languages,
we consider promise problems.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
A promise problem Π = (ΠY,ΠN) is a pair of disjoint sets of strings,
corresponding to YES and NO instances, respectively.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
For a formal treatment of the model (which we
specialize here to our scenario), see [46].
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: Let S = {S1,...,Sℓ} where Si = {ρ1,...,ρℓi} (i = 1,...,ℓ) is a set of density operators.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
A S-quantum-prover Interactive Proof System for a promise problem Π = (ΠY,ΠN) is an interactive proof
system with a veriﬁer V that runs in classical probabilistic polynomial time, augmented with the capacity
to randomly generate states in each of S1,...,Sℓ(upon generation, these states are immediately sent to the
prover, with the index i ∈{1,...,ℓ} known to the veriﬁer and prover, and the index j ∈{1,...,ℓi} known
to the veriﬁer only).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: The interaction of the veriﬁer V and the prover P satisﬁes the following conditions.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
• (Completeness) if x ∈ΠY, there exists a quantum polynomial-time prover (called an honest prover)
such that the veriﬁer accepts with probability p ≥2/3;
• (Soundness) if x ∈ΠN, no prover (even unbounded) can convince V to accept with probability
p ≥1/3.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: The class of promise problems having an S-quantum interactive proof systems is denoted QPIPS.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Note
that by standard ampliﬁcation, the class QPIPS is unchanged if we replace the completeness parameter c
and soundness parameter s by any values, as long as c−s > 1/poly(n).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Comparing our deﬁnition of QPIPS to the class of quantum-prover interactive proof systems (QPIP)
as given in [3], we note that we have made some modiﬁcations and clariﬁcations, namely that the veriﬁer
in QPIPS does not have any quantum memory and does not perform any gates (QPIP allows a veriﬁer
that stores and operates on a quantum register of a constant number of qubits), and that soundness holds
against unbounded provers.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: Finally, we use the canonical BQP-complete problem [3], deﬁned as follows.

4
Quantum-prover interactive proof system
In order to prove Theorem 3.3, we give an interactive proof system (see Interactive Proof System 1).

text: This protocol uses the various gate gadgets as described in Sections 4.1–4.4.

Completeness is studied in
Section 6 and soundness is proved in Section 7.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
4.1
X- and Z-gate gadget
In order to apply an X on a qubit register i encrypted with key (ai,bi), the veriﬁer updates the key
according to ai ←ai ⊕1 (bi is unchanged).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In order to apply an Z on a qubit register i encrypted with
key (ai,bi), the veriﬁer updates the key according to bi ←bi ⊕1 (ai is unchanged).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
This operation is
performed only in the computation run.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
4.2
CNOT-gate gadget
In order to apply a CNOT gate on the encrypted registers (say with register i being the control and
register j the target), the prover simply applies the CNOT gate on the respective registers.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
The veriﬁer
updates the encryption keys according to ai ←ai;bi ←bi ⊕bj;a j ←ai ⊕aj; and bj ←bj.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
We mention
that CNOT(|0⟩|0⟩) = |0⟩|0⟩and CNOT(|+⟩|+⟩) = |+⟩|+⟩; thus in the X- and Z-test runs, the underlying
data is unchanged.

T-gate gadget
Here, we show how the T is performed on encrypted data.

text:
This is accomplished using an auxiliary qubit,
as well as classical interaction.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
For the computation run, we use a combination of a protocol inspired
from [14,25], as well as fault-tolerant quantum computation [12] (see also [17]).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: In the case of an X and Z test runs, as usual, we want the identity map to be applied.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
This is done as in
Figures 2 and 3, respectively.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: Correctness of Figures 1–3 is proven in Section 5.

text:
Note that we show in
Section 6.1 that the set of auxiliary quantum states required by the veriﬁer can be reduced via a simple
re-labeling, in order to match the resources required in Theorem 3.3.

in the EPR-based version and show how to simplify an attack (Section 7.2).

of a test run (Section 7.4) and of a computation run (Sections 7.5).

completes the proof of our main theorem (Theorem 3.3).

7.3
Conventions and deﬁnitions
In addition to the convention of representing an attack as in Equation (7.9), in the following Sections 7.4–
7.5, we use the following conventions.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
The circuit C that we consider is already “compiled” in terms of the H gates as in Section 4.4 (the
identity H = HPHPHPH is already applied).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
The number of T-gate gadgets is t (each such gadget uses two auxiliary qubits—one representing
an auxiliary quantum bit, and one representing a classical bit x), and the number of qubits in the
computation is n.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
In the T-gate gadget, the auxiliary wire is swapped with the measured wire immediately before
the measurement.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
This way, we may picture that only auxiliary qubits are measured as part of the
computation, and that the data registers for the input represent the computation wires throughout.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
Given the system as in Equation (7.9), we suppose that the ﬁrst T-gate gadget uses the ﬁrst EPR
pair as auxiliary quantum bit, and the second EPR pair as a qubit representing the classical bit (and
so on for the following T-gadgets).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
The last n EPR pairs are the data qubits, and we suppose that at
the end of the protocol, the last data qubit is the one that is measured, representing the output.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text: Finally, we deﬁne benign and non-benign Pauli attacks, based on their effect on the protocol.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
As
we will see, benign attacks have no effect on the acceptance probability (because all qubits are either
traced-out or measured in the computational basis).
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
However, non-benign attacks may inﬂuence the
acceptance probability.
title: How to Verify a Quantum Computation

text:
For a ﬁxed Pauli P ∈Pm, we call it benign if P ∈Bt,n, where Bt,n is the set of Paulis
acting on m = 2t +n qubits, such that the measured qubits in the protocol are acted on only by a gate in
{I,Z}.

Abstract.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Power consumption will be a key constraint on the future growth of Distributed
High Throughput Computing (DHTC) as used by High Energy Physics (HEP).
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
This makes
performance-per-watt a crucial metric for selecting cost-eﬃcient computing solutions.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
For this
paper, we have done a wide survey of current and emerging architectures becoming available
on the market including x86-64 variants, ARMv7 32-bit, ARMv8 64-bit, Many-Core and GPU
solutions, as well as newer System-on-Chip (SoC) solutions.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
We compare performance and
energy eﬃciency using an evolving set of standardized HEP-related benchmarks and power
measurement techniques we have been developing.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
We evaluate the potential for use of such
computing solutions in the context of DHTC systems, such as the Worldwide LHC Computing
Grid (WLCG).
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Introduction and Motivation
The data produced by the four experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) [1] or similar
High Energy Physics (HEP) experiments requires a signiﬁcant amount of human and computing
resources which cannot be provided by research institute or even country.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
For this reasons the
various parties involved created the Worldwide LHC Computing Grid (WLCG) in order to tackle
the data processing challenges posed by such a large amount of data.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
The WLGC consists of a
highly federated union of computing centers sparse in 40 countries and it represents an admirable
example of international organization.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment [2] at
the LHC alone uses the order of 100,000 x86 64 cores for its data analysis and similar happens for
the other general purpose LHC experiment, ATLAS.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Moreover, as the LHC and the experiments
will undergo planned luminosity upgrades over the next 15 years [3], its dataset size will increase
of 2-3 order of magnitude, which will require additional eﬀorts to increase its processing capacity.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
In this paper we continue our ongoing eﬀort to explore the performance and viability of various
computing platforms which we consider some of the most likely components of tomorrow data
centers.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
We asses their performance based on both synthetic benchmarks and realistic workﬂows
used in production at CMS.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Considered platforms
For this study we have selected ﬁve major product lines:
arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015


• Intel Xeon: Intel is the leading CPU manufacturer in the world.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Its Xeon product line
is its ﬂagship brand and provides solutions for all ranges of computing centers.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
While the
Xeon brand is usually associated to highly performant, architecturally advanced CPUs,
over the years Intel made sure to take into account power eﬃciency needs.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
This is reﬂected
by the inclusion of features, like SpeedStep and TurboBoost, speciﬁcally aimed at a more
power eﬃcient usage or RAPL which is used to monitor CPU power usage itself.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
• APM XGene: ARM architecture based products are, when considered as a single entity,
market leader for low power CPUs, in particular due to their wide spread adoption in a
wide range of consumer electronics product like cellular phones and tablets.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Thanks to
the economy of scale of cell phones aims to become a serious player in the server market,
in particular Applied Micro (APM) X-Gene product line is one of the ﬁrst attempts at
providing a 64-bit ARMv8 chip which is suitable for the low power, high density server
market.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
We have already detailed the main diﬃculties sustained to port to such an
architecture in a preceding work [4].
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text: • Intel Atom: Intel Atom architecture is Intel solution for the power eﬃcient market.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
It
consists of a standard x86 64 core, where particular trade-oﬀs have been made to reduce
complexity, sacriﬁcing performance for power eﬃcient.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Atom processors has a simpler,
in order, architecture without HyperThreading, limited vector units and cache subsystem
when compared to a standard Xeon.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Atom has however the advantage that code compiled
with standard optimizations (i.e.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
• IBM POWER8: The POWER8 is the latest incarnation of the POWER product line
which is the evolution of the old PowerPC.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
While the latter was the result of a strategic
alliance between Apple, Motorola and IBM, the former, initially an IBM only brand, is now
managed by an industry consortium, Open POWER Foundation [5], which includes big
players like Google, NVidia, Tyan.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Compared to the past, the POWER8 includes eﬀorts to
simplify platform ports from x86 64 and has the usual focus on highly threaded workloads,
by providing an high number of cores.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
• Intel Xeon Phi: the Xeon Phi is Intel answer to the GPGPU market, which in recent
years has dominated the scene of High Performance Computing when the problem to solve
maps well on a many-core architecture like the one of GPUs.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
The Phi consist of a very high
number of simpliﬁed x86 64 cores, running at a relatively low frequency, which however
have a large vector unit.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
The advantage touted by Intel for such an architecture is that
being real x86 64 cores, the porting eﬀort is lower when compared to writing software for a
GPU.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Test Environments for Power and Performance Measurements
We now describe the test environments we have used to do power and performance measurements
for two Intel Xeon processors, belonging respectively to the Sandy Bridge generation and to the
Haswell one, an APM ARMv8 64-bit X-Gene1 Server-on-Chip, an Intel Xeon Phi coprocessor,
an Intel Atom processor of Avoton class, an IBM POWER8 processor.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:

text:
Benchmarks setup
We selected three benchmarks for our study, which are commonly used in HEP and in particular
in CMS to determine the performance of a machine.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
• ParFullCMS: a standalone Geant4 [6] simulation using a geometry similar to the one used
in production by CMS, with simpliﬁed physics.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
This benchmark has been recently adopted
across LHC experiments for multithreading studies, since on traditional architectures it
already scales to a large number of threads.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
For our benchmark we used ParFullCMS which
ships with Geant4.10.3.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
• CMSSW RECO: the reconstruction of 100 tt events with pileup 35 at 25ns, using
CMS Oﬄine Software (CMSSW).
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
This is considered a standard candle to measure the
performance of CMS reconstruction as it guarantees good coverage of the code associated
to all of reconstructed objects.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
For our benchmark we used the development branch of
CMSSW, 7.5.x, as of April 1st 2015.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
• HEPSPEC06: a HEP driven benchmark suite, widely used as it should scale as HEP
speciﬁc workloads [7].
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text: In particular it is used for LCG site pledges and therefore purchases.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
All the benchmarks were compiled using the latest version of GCC 4.9.x available on a given
platform.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
The only notable exception to this was the Phi benchmarks, which used the Intel


Compiler (ICC 15.0.2) given the lack of support for vector units of GCC.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Since we wanted to
be as close as possible to the production setup used by CMS when running on the grid, we
switched on conservative optimization ﬂags (i.e.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
-O2) and we compiled code targeting vector
units, we did not use any platform speciﬁc optimization or aggressive optimization option (e.g.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
In particular we used the same exact binaries for Xeon and Atom as platform
compatibility is considered by Intel one of Atom advantages over other low power architectures in
an heterogeneous environment, like the Grid.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Of course, this limits the capabilities of the Xeon,
which for example supports much advanced vector instructions (AVX and AVX2) compared to
Atom (which only supports SSE4) or the other processors, however we deemed that this setup is
closer to what is actually done today in the Grid where usually there is no selection of optimized
binaries for more recent CPU architecture.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Enabling this and benchmarking results is of course
interesting, but outside the scope of this paper.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Given Xeon SandyBridge is right now one of the most popular CPUs on the Grid, and in
order to simplify comparisons between diﬀerent benchmarks, we normalized all the results to
those of the same benchmark running on in single core mode on our SandyBridge test system.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Methodology
In the ParFullCMS case we ran a total of 1220 events, subdividing the workload between an
increasing number of threads, up to the number of hardware threads the CPU had (in case
HyperThreading like mechanism was available) or double the number of hardware cores (in case
the CPU did not support hardware).
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
The throughput of the CPU was measured by dividing the
number of events by the number of seconds spent in the event processing loop, as reported by
ParFullCMS.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
This number is an underestimation of the performance of a CPU, but it’s deemed
to be a good enough approximation, especially for a low number of threads.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
In the CMSSW case we started an increasing number of processes, using the same logic
as before to determine the maximum number of processes.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Each process is running the same
amount of events and in the end we calculate the total throughput by summing the throughput
of each job.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
This ends up overestimating the actual throughput of short running jobs, but it’s
a closer match to the actual production case.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
For the HEPSPEC06 case we started the benchmark specifying the relevant option to run it
multithreaded and used the number reported at the end as indication of the performance of the
system.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text: We have previously detailed our methodology on how to measure CPU power utilization [8, 4].
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
On-chip sensors (Running Average Power Limit – RAPL) were used to measure silicon level
power consumption for Xeon CPUs.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Similar on-board sensors were available for X-Gene1 and
Xeon Phi products.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
HP Moonshot chassis was equipped with power consumption reporting, but
external power distribution unit (PDU) was used instead as it provided data logging capability.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Only a single power supply unit (PSU) was used in HP Moonshot systems while conducting
experiments.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Unfortunately we were not able to get power consumption measurements for the
POWER8 CPU or the box.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Atom systems did not provide RAPL reporting thus we used a full
node power consumption measurements.

text:
Box to box comparison
For our tests we had the privilege to try out an HP Moonshot chassis, which has the peculiarity
of supporting cartridges with Atom (the m300 model) and X-Gene1 (the m400 one).
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
This


allowed us to make a box to box comparison where the contribution to the power consumption
for the empty chassis is similar and the volume occupied in a rack is exactly the same.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
In
particular in our test setup we had 5 Atom cartridges and 15 X-Gene1 ones.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
We measured
the throughput of ParFullCMS by running it on an increasing number of cartridges, while at
the same time measuring the power consumption of the whole box.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
In ﬁgure 7 you have the
results for our measurements in form of blue dots and red crosses.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
Since the two boxes are ﬁlled
with a diﬀerent number of cartridges, we cannot compare the two dataset directly, as the power
cost due to idle cartridges is diﬀerent.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
What we did instead is to used the data we acquired
to evaluate the power consumption of a cartridge in running and idle mode and then use those
values to project the results for fully populated boxes.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
The results are extremely unsatisfactory
for the X-Gene1 based m400 cartridge which seems to be extremely underperforming in terms
of power consumption.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
We attribute this to actual maturity issues of the cartridge itself, which
suspiciously has the same power consumption of the development board, rather than actual
power consumption of the CPU.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
This well illustrates the fact that while promising, a lot needs
to be done in term of production readiness for ARMv8 based solution.

text:
Conclusions
We continued our investigation eﬀort in evaluating alternative platforms for HEP workloads.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text: In particular we have extended our analysis to include more benchmarks and novel platforms.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
While not ﬁnal, our conclusion shows that depending on the various operating constrains in
terms of power usage and performance, either Atom based systems or latest generation Intel
Xeon system provide the best power eﬃciency levels.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
While APM X-Gene platform is still
relevant, it’s clear that in order to compete with Intel, ARM based solutions need not only
to develop a performing CPU and match Intel pace in evolving their products, but they need
to address the maturity issues of their ecosystems, both in terms of software and of auxiliary
electronics.
title: arXiv:1510.03676v1  [cs.DC]  28 Jul 2015

text:
From the mere performance point of view, both the POWER8 and even more so
Xeon Phi results show how diﬃcult it is to take advantage of extremely parallel architecture
without speciﬁcally design software around them.

FRAMEWORK FOR CLOUD COMPUTING ADOPTION: 
A ROADMAP FOR SMES TO CLOUD MIGRATION 
 
Nabeel Khan and Adil Al-Yasiri 
 
School of Computing Science and Engineering, University of Salford, Manchester, 
United Kingdom 
 
ABSTRACT 
 
Small and Medium size Enterprises (SME) are considered as a backbone of many developing and 
developed economies of the world; they are the driving force to any major economy across the globe.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Through Cloud Computing firms outsource their entire information technology (IT) process while 
concentrating more on their core business.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
It allows businesses to cut down heavy cost incurred over IT 
infrastructure without losing focus on customer needs.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
However, Cloud industry to an extent has struggled 
to grow among SMEs due to the reluctance and concerns expressed by them.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Throughout the course of this 
study several interviews were conducted and the literature was reviewed to understand how cloud 
providers offer services and what challenges SMEs are facing.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The study identified issues like cloud 
knowledge, interoperability, security and contractual concerns to be hindering SMEs adoption of cloud 
services.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
From the interviews common practices followed by cloud vendors and what concerns SMEs have 
were identified as a basis for a cloud framework which will bridge gaps between cloud vendors and SMEs.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
A stepwise framework for cloud adoption is formulated which identifies and provides recommendation to 
four most predominant challenges which are hurting cloud industry and taking SMEs away from cloud 
computing, as well as guide SMEs aiding in successful cloud adoption.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Moreover, this framework 
streamlines the cloud adoption process for SMEs by removing ambiguity in regards to fundamentals 
associated with their organisation and cloud adoption process.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
KEYWORDS 
 
Cloud Computing, Cloud migration, cloud adoption, SMEs, framework & guidelines.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
INTRODUCTION 
 
The scalability and extensibility of distributed software architectures have led to the concept 
called Cloud Computing.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Cloud computing is a technology used to deliver the hosted services 
over the Internet.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Through this technology, users don’t have to manage their own IT resources; 
instead they purchase their IT needs as services over the internet [1, 2].
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
For SMEs cloud computing technology is an attempt which has allowed them to reduce the rates 
spent on computing infrastructure.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
With more and more explorations of cloud technology, it has 
faced new challenges that need to be resolved to improve the pace of cloud adoption among 
SMEs.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
With so much power of computation and data handling, there are numerous challenges that must 
be addressed promptly.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Some of these challenges are technical (Interoperability and data security) 
and some are non-technical (Cloud knowledge and Cloud contracts); some of them are related to 
computer science whilst others are beyond computing realm.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
One of the issues which is hurting 
cloud adoption among SMEs are data security, privacy law and legal jurisdiction bound to certain 
boundary of the globe [3].
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text: International Journal on Cloud Computing: Services and Architecture (IJCCSA) ,Vol.

2 
A major obstacle for SMEs in adopting cloud is how the software and hardware match and 
interact with each other while running the business applications.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
From a customer point of view it 
is an important factor to efficiently use the applications of cloud and mitigate any risks associated 
with it.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
This issue is often named as interoperability among clouds and addressing this issue is 
timely and necessary, and it’s the only way to avoid vendor lock-in situation.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
So for SMEs to 
switch to cloud it is more important to know how to handle this issue as the market is dominated 
by big cloud providers.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The knowledge of this potential issue is necessary as in case of multi 
provider scenario- SMEs can have plenty options to avail all the offered cloud services and at the 
same time takes the full advantage of cloud computing concepts like elasticity and pay per use 
model [4].
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text: In order to start thinking of migrating organization to cloud adequate knowledge is a prime.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
SMEs usually have limited knowledge about what cloud can do for their organization in a long 
run and how it can enhance the productivity of its employees.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Most SMEs IT professionals are 
not fully trained in guiding their organizations to cloud [5].
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Although, cloud computing has been really successful in attracting customers, it is still considered 
as an emerging technology among the SMEs due to some challenges [6].
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
In order to find out these 
challenges and propose a guideline to SMEs, this paper aims to showcase the challenges related 
to cloud adoption by SMEs and propose a guideline to assist cloud transition from conventional 
IT rooms.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
SMEs are not aware of cloud contract terms which are negotiated quite often by the cloud 
vendors.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
This issue is holding SMEs back to their conventional ways of doing business in the 
market, as they have fear of losing business by getting trapped into inconclusive terms of cloud 
contracts [7].
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text: This paper explores possible solutions and elaborates on these issues.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
All these issues have 
emerged as a viable threat to cloud industry.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Moreover, a stepwise guide in the form a framework 
has been proposed to aid cloud adoption process among SMEs.

RELATED WORK WITH CONTRIBUTION 
 
Several studies have been conducted on cloud issues and what is really affecting cloud industry.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
There are around more than 11 cloud frameworks in the market at present to deal with IT services 
or architecture but none of them is designed for cloud adoption for any size of an organization 
(this proposed cloud framework is only for SMEs in particular).
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Some of these frameworks are 
Cloud Business Model Framework (CBMF) by [8], IBM Framework for Cloud Adoption [9], 
Cloud Computing Business Framework [10] etc.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The cloud framework mentioned in this paper focuses on the readiness of the organization by 
making them aware of all the risks and preparedness associated with cloud computing and by 
proposing solutions to these.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The contribution of this paper and eventually a cloud framework is 
in cloud computing adoption among small organizations, as it not only raises issues inflicting 
cloud computing but also provides remedy to avoid these issues to an extent.

METHODOLOGY AND DATA ANALYSIS 
 
The research methodology in figure 1 has been adopted for this research program.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
This four-step 
guide (See Figure 5) is the vital part of the cloud preparation stage (CPS) of the proposed cloud 
framework.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The CPS focuses onto the preparation part of the enterprises, as it will help them to 
understand the current situation of their business processes and guide them to progress in cloud 
adoption.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The main stages of the methodology are outlined underneath: 
 
 
 
Figure 1.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Reviewing previous literature and relevant cloud computing issues: In this step, previous 
relevant literature, surveys and studies have been reviewed to identify issues with cloud 
adoption.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Identify and define the research problem: To do so, a qualitative research method has 
been adopted as a primary approach and following this; a number of semi-structured 
interviews were conducted with SMEs, cloud providers and developers to gather relevant 
information.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Analyzing data collected from interviews: The collected data from the interview is then 
analyzed by applying the content analysis approach.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Preparing a road map for SMEs: A structured guideline will then be designed in order to 
mitigate the cloud adoption barriers among SMEs.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The fifth step of the research methodology concentrates on verification and validation of 
the proposed framework and gathers a feedback from SMEs and Cloud Service Providers 
(CSPs).
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text: For this, reflexivity workshops will be held.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The feedback from the workshop will then be used to modify the framework to rectify 
and increase the efficiency of the framework.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Finally, the proposed framework will then be prepared for use by SMEs in cloud 
adoption.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The information required for the current research on finding cloud barriers among SMEs, has 
been collected by using primary research techniques and secondary research techniques.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Interviews were the main sources of finding the primary information; where the source of 
secondary information gathering is based on the literature review method.

text:
A similar approach was 
adopted by [11] in 2012 where she interviewed several IT experts to find out cloud computing

conducted by [12] in 2014 where he explored the factors influencing the adoption of cloud

CHALLENGES FOUND DURING INTERVIEWS 
 
Although, cloud computing has been successful in attracting customers, it is still considered as an 
emerging technology among the SMEs due to some challenges.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
There are a number of barriers 
hindering cloud computing adoption among SMEs.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
To identify and understand these, a pilot study 
was conducted in the form of interviews with the IT managers of eight leading cloud vendors and 
four cloud developers which have brought the following points into limelight: 
 
• 
Lack of internal staff expertise hindering cloud computing in transforming SMEs: 
Slow uptake of cloud computing was attributed to the fact that SMEs need to be educated 
on the benefits and potential of cloud computing and correlating these benefits with their 
current IT requirements.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
When asked about the services which cloud vendors often offer 
to SMEs, all cloud vendors answered that they have to deal with an issue of SMEs being 
perplex over services or solutions that cloud computing can offer them.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
This was also 
inferred during the first round of interviews, as most SMEs were blank regarding cloud 
computing concepts (See figure 2).
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
When asked about the in house cloud training to

FRAMEWORK FOR CLOUD COMPUTING ADOPTION 
 
The challenges identified above affect cloud adoption among SMEs which need to be addressed 
with adequate solutions and recommendations.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
All the above problems are directly related to a 
bigger problem; which is the lack of framework for SMEs that directs the process of migration to 
clouds.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Eventually, a framework for SMEs could offer an answer to such problems in a 
structured manner to expedite the cloud adoption among SMEs.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
This section provides the design 
and explanation of the components of cloud framework.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The framework in this research is the

stepwise guide for the SMEs to follow their journey on cloud adoption.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
This framework is 
divided in three stage migration process; cloud preparation stage, cloud requirement stage and 
cloud migration stage as shown below in figure 4.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The cloud computing process of migration requires a continuous process of improvement prior to 
migration to ensure the efficiency of the system (or solution) and for this framework works in a 
circular loop to provide firm and positive results.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
For this As-Is and To-Be business process is 
adopted where Cloud Requirement stage (CRS) of the framework is To-be, Cloud Preparation 
Stage (CPS) is As-is and Cloud Migration Stage (CMS) is transformation.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
As the CPS goes 
further, the goal should be set to prepare the enterprise for cloud computing adoption and regular 
modification needs to be made to refine the process of getting SME ready for cloud computing.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text: These refinements will be vital in deciding the efficiency and sustainability of the system.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
As the 
process enters in a CMS stage, it is ready to be transformed as per the proposed solution provided 
(or selected) to an enterprise.

5.1 CLOUD REQUIREMENT STAGE (CRS) 
 
This stage elaborates regarding cloud computing services and deployment models that may be 
required by SMEs depending upon their head count, turn over and nature of their businesses.

All

title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:

need in order to meet their requirements.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
SMEs with less than or equal to 10 employees and turnover of less than 2 million pounds (called 
micro enterprise), would only go for either software as a service or Infrastructure as a service over 
a public cloud model.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Whereas SMEs with less than or equal to 50 employees and with turnover 
of less than 10 million pounds, usually embraces IaaS as a standalone service deployed over 
public cloud environment and in some cases they go for amalgamated services over hybrid cloud.

This is the second stage of the cloud migration process and it is called the cloud preparation stage

5.2.1 Feasibility Study 
 
This usually comprises of the process of finding whether migration to cloud computing is suitable 
for an organisation, in both terms; financial and technical terms.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
This very first step in the 
transition to cloud involves the study of the existing data, the analysis of existing applications 
running in the organisation, the requirement analysis of the data for a desired output from the 
system, and study on any constraints that may be faced pre and post cloud migration.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
It also 
contains the detailed examination of the hardware available within the organisation in order to 
perceive the additional costs incurred in terms of hardware for embracing cloud.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
It’s highly 
recommended to use feasibility tools, like a maturity assessment tool, technical feasibility tool or 
business feasibility tool [18].
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
These tools give an insight about the technical and business 
feasibility of the organisation and helps in evaluating the effort and cost required in the process of 
migration to the cloud.

It’s important to know where an organisation stands in terms of preparedness to embrace the

FURTHER WORK 
 
The next stage of the research is to validate and verify the proposed framework and for this 
purpose all the previous participants will again be invited to attend the reflexivity workshop 
where they will be explained about this framework to know the validity and effectiveness of this 
framework.

SMEs and CSPs will be in a discussion regarding how helpful this framework can be 
in aiding cloud adoption among SMEs.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

Moreover, the purpose of this workshop is to know about 
the pre & post migration issues that SMEs face when they approach to CSPs, the collected data 
here will be useful in modifying a cloud framework for SMEs.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
CONCLUSION 
 
The usage of cloud computing is slow among SMEs, as SMEs require services more in the area of 
offering infrastructure and software as a service.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
A number of issues were discussed above, which 
have a great impact on cloud adoption among small and medium size enterprises.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
The study and 
analysis of these issues have led to proposition of framework for cloud computing adoption, 
which give the understanding and a roadmap to SMEs on how to approach cloud vendors or 
specifically how to adopt cloud computing and minimize potential barriers.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Such a framework 
will ease up cloud migration by assessing organization’s readiness for the cloud through 
parameters like governance, risks involved, standards, data classification and responsibilities.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
Also, it will enable organizations to identify stakeholder needs, select right CSP and sign a 
favourable cloud contract, which will help SMEs in a smooth transition to cloud.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:
We believe that this framework will encourage and accelerate the adoption of cloud computing 
among such enterprises.
title: Format guide for AIRCC

text:

We believe that research in the field of framework for cloud computing migration would benefit 
substantially if this framework is implemented in a real time environment where enterprises use 
this framework as an aid to their cloud migration process and provide feedback with case study.

effectiveness.

Abstract—Commodity 
video-gaming 
hardware 
(consoles, 
graphics cards, tablets, etc.) performance has been advancing at 
a rapid pace owing to strong consumer demand and stiff market 
competition.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
Gaming hardware devices are currently amongst 
the most powerful and cost-effective computational technologies 
available in quantity.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
In this article, we evaluate a sample of 
current generation video-gaming hardware devices for scientific 
computing and compare their performance with specialized 
supercomputing general purpose graphics processing units 
(GPGPUs).
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
We use the OpenCL SHOC benchmark suite, which 
is a measure of the performance of compute hardware on various 
different scientific application kernels, and also a popular public 
distributed computing application, Einstein@Home in the field of 
gravitational physics for the purposes of this evaluation.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
Index Terms—Scientific Computing, Accelerators, Parallel 
Computing, Supercomputing, GPU, GPGPU, OpenCL, SHOC, 
Physics 
 
I.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
INTRODUCTION 
HERE is considerable current interest in harnessing the 
advancements made in multi- and many-core technology 
for scientific high-performance computing (HPC).
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
An 
example of this trend is the rapid rise in the use of custom-
designed HPC general purpose graphics processing units 
(GPGPUs) as “accelerators” in workstations and even large 
supercomputers.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
In fact, the second-fastest supercomputer 
today, ORNL's Titan, makes use of Nvidia's custom-HPC 
Tesla (Kepler series) GPUs to achieve petascale performance 
[1] and there are over 100 such accelerated systems in the top 
500 supercomputers worldwide.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
One reason for this recent 
trend is that the large consumer video-gaming market 
significantly 
aids 
in 
“subsidizing” 
the 
research 
and 
development cost associated towards advancing these compute 
technologies, resulting in high performance at a low cost.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
In 
addition to their cost effectiveness, these GPU technologies

title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
Glenn Volkema, is a member of the Physics Department and the 
Center for Scientific Computing and Visualization Research at the University 
of Massachusetts Dartmouth, North Dartmouth, MA 02747 USA (e-mail: 
gvolkema@umassd.edu).
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
Gaurav Khanna is a Professor in the Physics Department and the 
Associate Director of the Center for Scientific Computing and Visualization 
Research at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, North Dartmouth, 
MA 02747 USA (e-mail: gkhanna@umassd.edu).
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
are substantially “greener” over CPUs, delivering higher 
computational performance per Watt of electrical-power 
consumed [2].
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
In a similar spirit, there is also the opportunity to utilize the 
commodity “off-the-shelf” video-gaming hardware itself for 
scientific computing.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
Here we are specifically referring to 
consumer-grade video-gaming cards and also game consoles 
themselves, as opposed to the custom-HPC variants.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
These 
often have similar high-performance characteristics and in 
addition, are sold at a significant discount (sometimes even 
below manufacturing cost) because the business model allows 
for making up the deficit through the sales of video games and 
other application software.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
Starting in 2007 the authors were 
pioneers in successfully utilizing a cluster of Sony PlayStation 
3 (PS3) [3] gaming consoles for scientific computation [4].
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
They were able to demonstrate order-of-magnitude gains in 
efficiency metrics such as performance-per-dollar and 
performance-per-Watt as compared with traditional compute 
clusters [5,6,7].
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
Since then many universities and research 
groups took a similar approach and evaluated the value of 
such PS3 hardware for their own computation needs.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
The 
largest such system has been built by the Air Force Research 
Laboratory (AFRL) in Rome, NY.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
This system, named 
“AFRL CONDOR” utilizes 1,716 PS3s alongside traditional 
servers and Nvidia Tesla (Fermi series) GPGPUs to achieve 
500 TFLOPS of computing power [8].
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
CONDOR has been 
demonstrated to be over 10× more cost-effective in similar 
metrics [9].
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
In this article we explore the capabilities of current 
generation consumer-grade, video-gaming hardware for 
scientific high-performance computing.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
Specific examples of 
the compute hardware that we consider interesting for this 
study are current gaming graphics cards like the AMD Radeon 
[10], Nvidia GeForce [11] series, and also the CPU-GPU 
“fused” or heterogeneous processor architectures like the 
AMD’s Accelerated Processing Unit (APU) [12] and the 
Nvidia’s Tegra System-on-a-Chip (SoC) [13].
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
The main 
advantage of considering such consumer-grade hardware for 
scientific HPC is low cost and high power-efficiency.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
Rapid 
advances and significant innovation is being enabled through 
major investments made by the gaming industry.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
This is 
driven by strong consumer demand for immersive gaming 
experiences that require computational power.
title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
High volume 
and intense competition keep costs low, while improvements 
to power-efficiency are forced by the engineering challenges 
and costs associated with dissipating increasing amounts of

Gaming Hardware Devices

title: VolkemaKhanna2016v4

text:
