Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a go-to solution 
for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences; it 
passes through learning a reward model that subsequently optimizes the 
LLM’s policy.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
However, an inherent limitation of current reward models 
is their inability to fully represent the richness of human preferences 
and their dependency on the sampling distribution.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
In the first part 
we turn to an alternative pipeline for the fine-tuning of LLMs using 
pairwise human feedback.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Our approach entails the initial learning of a 
preference model, which is conditioned on two inputs given a prompt, 
followed by the pursuit of a policy that consistently generates responses 
preferred over those generated by any competing policy, thus defining 
the Nash equilibrium of this preference model.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
We term this approach 
Nash learning from human feedback (NLHF) and give a new algorithmic 
solution, Nash-MD, founded on the principles of mirror descent.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
NLHF 
is compelling for preference learning and policy optimization with the 
potential of advancing the field of aligning LLMs with human preferences.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
In the second part of the talk, we delve into a deeper theoretical 
understanding of fine-tuning approaches as RLHF with PPO and offline 
fine-tuning with DPO (direct preference optimization) based on the 
Bradley-Terry model and come up with a new class of LLM alignment 
algorithms with better both practical and theoretical properties.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
We 
finish with the newest work showing links between and building on top 
of them.

Fine-Grained Object Detection  
for Precision Beekeeping
Gabriela Vdoviak, Tomyslav Sledevič
Vilnius Gediminas Technical University
gabriela.vdoviak@vilniustech.lt
Real-time and non-invasive bee monitoring at the hive entrance is 
crucial for the advancement of precision beekeeping practices and 
the maintenance of colony health.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Conventional monitoring methods 
are characterized by their labour-intensiveness and disruptive nature, 
thus requiring the development of autonomous vision-based systems.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
However, robust detection models must effectively handle challenging 
real-world scenarios, including lighting variations, frequent object 
occlusion, motion blur, and the complexity of classifying multiple insect 
groups and distinguishing small objects like pollen grains.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
In this study, we investigated the performance of the YOLO model 
on a dataset consisting of honeybee and wasp classes.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The model was 
refined to enhance computational efficiency while preserving sensitivity 
to fine-grained details.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
A comparative analysis of two annotation 
approaches for pollen carrying-bees was also conducted.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The findings showed that the architecturally modified model achieved 
higher detection precision in comparison to the baseline model, while 
maintaining comparable inference speed.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
This demonstrates model’s 
suitability for efficient deployment on embedded platforms.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The analysis 
of annotation strategies provided valuable insights into labeling choices.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The separate pollen class posed significant challenges due to the size 
of the target, but targeted architectural modifications successfully 
improved its detection rate by a substantial margin.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
In contrast, the 
combined pollen-bee class demonstrated a higher overall detection 
stability, a critical factor for maintaining tracking continuity in subsequent 
behavioral analysis.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
This work demonstrates that fine-grained object detection, achieved 
through strategic architectural modifications and data labeling, is 
essential for robust, multi-class surveillance, indicating the potential for 
efficient, autonomous hive monitoring in diverse field environments.

A Methodological Review of Anomaly 
Detection Methods for Maritime Hybrid 
Warfare Analysis
Julius Venskus1,2, Robertas Jurkus1,2,  
Povilas Treigys2, Darius Drungilas1
1 Klaipeda University
2 Vilnius University
julius.venskus@ku.lt
The seabed is host to the critical arteries of the global economy and digital 
communication, including a vast network of gas pipes, electrical intercon-
nectors, and submarine fiber-optic cables.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
In the contemporary landscape 
of hybrid warfare, these vital assets have become a prime target for state-
sponsored actors seeking to exert pressure and disrupt Western nations.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Adversaries are increasingly leveraging commercially-flagged vessels – of-
ten part of a “shadow fleet” – to conduct covert operations, creating a sig-
nificant challenge for maritime security.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Recent incidents, where vessels 
have allegedly damaged subsea infrastructure by dropping anchor, high-
light a critical vulnerability: the difficulty of distinguishing between legiti-
mate maritime activity and preparations for sabotage.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
This paper conducts a methodological review of anomaly detection 
methods to assess their efficacy in identifying ship behaviors potentially 
indicative of threats to subsea infrastructure.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The central analytical 
challenge lies in the ambiguity of the raw data; actions such as slowing 
down, loitering, or anchoring can appear benign in isolation.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
This review 
therefore moves beyond simplistic kinematic analysis to synthesize and 
evaluate methods that achieve contextual awareness by fusing data 
from multiple scientific domains.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The reviewed approaches include: 
(1) Geospatial and Oceanographic models, which provide context on 
seabed topography and the precise location of critical infrastructure; 
(2) Behavioral and Economic baselines, which define normative vessel 
activity (e.g., designated anchorage zones, typical fishing patterns) for 
specific areas; and (3) Advanced Kinematic analysis, for detecting subtle 
deviations in a vessel’s dynamic signature.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS FOR SOFTWARE SYSTEMS
146
The principal finding of this review is that standard anomaly 
detection algorithms are insufficient and generate an unacceptably 
high rate of false positives when applied in isolation.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The most effective 
methodologies are those that fuse a vessel’s dynamic behavior with its 
geospatial context relative to known infrastructure.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The review concludes 
that the ability to detect threats of this nature is critically dependent on 
an analytical paradigm that can answer not just “what is the ship doing?” 
but “is what the ship doing normal for this specific location?” 
This paper provides a structured overview of the methods capable of 
meeting this complex challenge, offering a roadmap for developing the 
next generation of surveillance tools required to protect our most critical 
undersea assets.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

Enhancing Financial Insight  
Through Machine Learning-Driven  
KPI Correlation Analysis
Ilona Veitaitė1, Audrius Lopata2, Saulius Gudas3

The research explores how financial auditing is being reshaped by the 
rapid expansion of digital data and the integration of artificial intelligence 
(AI) and machine learning (ML).
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Traditional methods that rely on manual 
checks and limited data samples are no longer sufficient to ensure 
reliability in today’s complex financial environment.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
By leveraging KPI 
ratio correlation analysis, predictive algorithms, and process mining, 
auditing can move beyond retrospective reviews and provide continuous, 
data-driven assurance.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
This shift, sometimes referred to as “Auditing 
2.0,” enhances the detection of anomalies and strengthens financial 
oversight.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
A central theme is the role of KPI correlation analysis in 
uncovering subtle links between financial indicators.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
These relationships 
are valuable for identifying anomalies, assessing financial health, and 
predicting potential risks before they escalate.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The study emphasizes that while simple ML models such as decision 
trees offer transparency, they often fail to capture the complexity of 
financial data.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
More advanced techniques, including neural networks and 
Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based systems, excel in predictive tasks 
but present challenges in terms of interpretability.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Hybrid approaches 
that combine both simplicity and sophistication appear to be the most 
effective, offering a balance between accuracy and explainability.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The research also highlights the importance of continuous auditing, 
where monitoring and testing occur in real-time rather than at periodic 


16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS FOR SOFTWARE SYSTEMS
148
intervals.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
This proactive approach allows errors and fraudulent activities 
to be detected and addressed immediately, reducing the possibility of 
them becoming embedded in financial statements.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The integration of 
AI-driven process mining adds further depth, enabling auditors to model 
and analyze business processes more effectively, compare expected 
workflows with actual performance, and provide near-instant assurance 
after critical business events.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Finally, an experimental analysis of KPI datasets revealed that most 
indicators are not strongly correlated, suggesting that a broad range 
of them can provide unique insights for ML applications.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
However, 
correlation analysis alone is insufficient for identifying the most valuable 
features; additional statistical and feature-selection methods are needed 
to refine the inputs and improve model reliability.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The findings point to a future where AI-enhanced auditing combines 
advanced analytics, transparency, and regulatory alignment to improve 
trust and effectiveness, while also raising important questions about 
fairness, security, and ethical use of AI in financial decision-making.

Utilizing Latent Diffusion Models
Eimantas Zaranka1,2, Monika Katilienė1,2,

1 Vytautas Magnus University

The recent rapid advancements in generative image models have intro-
duced a possibility for the personalisation and customisation of images 
while preserving subject-specific features across various generated sce-
narios.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Traditional fine-tuning approaches often require large datasets 
or manual artistic interventions, therefore limiting the accessibility and 
needing a constant model retraining for new subject integration.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
This research investigates the application of latent diffusion-based 
generative models for personalised dog avatar generation, which en-
ables innovative interactions in digital environments such as social media 
platforms, pet owner communities, and other related services.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Person-
alised avatars hold a significant emotional value for owners, strengthen 
client-provider relationships, and boost engagement with products or 
services.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The experiments conducted in this research consisted of three 
fine-tuning/inference techniques: DreamBooth with Low-Rank Adapta-
tion (LoRA), Textual Inversion, and Image Prompt (IP) Adapters, which 
were applied to different base models, including Stable Diffusion 1.5 
(SD1.5), Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL), and Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3), along 
with their fine-tuned variants for specific realistic or pet focused gen-
erations.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
By fine-tuning DreamBooth LoRA and Textual Inversions on a 
limited set of user-provided images, or running an inference with a pre-
trained IP adapter, the models generate avatars that accurately replicate 
the pet’s distinctive traits while supporting stylistic modifications from 
text and/or image prompts.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Furthermore, experiments were conducted 
using commercial solutions, including DALL-E 3, Grok Image Banana 
Nano, SeeDream, Adobe Firefly and others.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
After the experiments, the 


16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS FOR SOFTWARE SYSTEMS
150
pivotal role of model variation selection is noticed, which drastically im-
pacts personalisation efficacy, as it remarkably influences output quality.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Among variants, SDXL-based models such as Juggernaut and Ratatoskr 
demonstrated superior performance.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Notably, default base Stable Diffu-
sion models proved inadequate, often producing artefacts during infer-
ence; thus, additionally fine-tuned variants were essential for artefact 
mitigation.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Evaluating different fine-tuning strategies, DreamBooth LoRA 
personalisation method showed the most promise in visual feature pres-
ervation, while generating dog avatars that closely resembled original 
images and allowing for a wide range of stylistic variations.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Meanwhile, 
Textual Inversion unsatisfactorily retained specific subject features, fre-
quently reverting to generic representations.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
IP Adapters were not fine-
tuned, and during the experiments, only generalised open-source ver-
sions were used in order to validate the feasibility of usage.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
While IP 
Adapters showed promising results, the results were suboptimal, where 
newly generated images showed feature preservation capabilities but 
fell short in image customisation.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
The main limitation of DreamBooth 
LoRA usage in production is the requirement for per-subject adapter 
training, which increases computational demand and processing time, 
complicating deployment in scalable pipelines.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
Future research will focus on developing a novel, first of its kind, IP 
Adapter specialized for dog feature extraction, enabling a robust zero-
shot personalization pipeline that will be efficient and preserves subject 
identity without a need of fine-tuning the adapter.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

text:
This study will advance 
the theoretical framework of generative models for personalisation 
and will support practical applications, allowing pet owners to digitally 
commemorate and share their companions’ achievements and unique 
features with the world.

Modern commerce platforms are frequent targets for cybercriminals.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

cases is an essential resource in organisational data stores.
title: 16th Conference on DATA ANALYSIS METHODS for Software Systems

Most breaches 
lead to monetisation through the resale of data on various platforms.

Songze Li, Mohammad Ali Maddah-Ali, and A.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
ABSTRACT
Redundancy is abundant in Fog networks (i.e., many com-
puting and storage points) and grows linearly with network
size.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
We demonstrate the transformational role of coding in
Fog computing for leveraging such redundancy to substantially
reduce the bandwidth consumption and latency of comput-
ing.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
In particular, we discuss two recently proposed coding
concepts, namely Minimum Bandwidth Codes and Minimum
Latency Codes, and illustrate their impacts in Fog computing.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
We also review a uniﬁed coding framework that includes the
above two coding techniques as special cases, and enables a
tradeoff between computation latency and communication load
to optimize system performance.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
At the end, we will discuss
several open problems and future research directions.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
INTRODUCTION
The Fog architecture (see Fig.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
1) has been recently proposed
to better satisfy the service requirements of the emerging
Internet-of-Things (IoT) (see, e.g., [1]).
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Unlike the Cloud com-
puting that stores and processes end-users’ data in remote and
centralized datacenters, Fog computing brings the provision
of services closer to the end-users by pooling the available
resources at the edge of the network (e.g., smartphones, tablets,
smart cars, base stations and routers) (see, e.g., [2], [3]).
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
As a
result, the main driving vision for Fog computing is to leverage
the signiﬁcant amount of dispersed computing resources at
the edge of the network to provide much more user-aware,
resource-efﬁcient, scalable and low-latency services for IoT.

The main goal of this paper is to demonstrate how cod-
ing can be effectively utilized to trade abundant computing
resources at network edge for communication bandwidth and

In particular, we illustrate two recently proposed novel
coding concepts that leverage the available or under-utilized
computing resources at various parts of the network to enable
coding opportunities that signiﬁcantly reduce the bandwidth
consumption and latency of computing, which are of particular
importance in Fog computing applications.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The ﬁrst coding concept introduced in [4], [5], which we
refer to as Minimum Bandwidth Codes, enables a surprising
inverse-linear tradeoff between computation load and commu-
nication load in distributed computing.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Minimum Bandwidth
Codes demonstrate that increasing the computation load by a
factor of r (i.e., evaluating each computation at r carefully cho-
sen nodes) can create novel coding opportunities that reduce
the required communication load for computing by the same
factor.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Hence, Minimum Bandwidth Codes can be utilized to
pool the underutilized computing resources at network edge
to slash the communication load of Fog computing.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The second coding concept introduced in [6], which we
refer to as Minimum Latency Codes, enables an inverse-
linear tradeoff between computation load and computation
latency (i.e., the overall job response time).
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
More speciﬁcally,
Minimum Latency Codes utilize coding to effectively inject
redundant computations to alleviate the effects of stragglers
and speed up the computations by a multiplicative factor that
is proportional to the amount of injected redundancy.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Hence,
by utilizing more computation resources at network edge,
Minimum Latency Codes can signiﬁcantly speed up distributed
Fog computing applications.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
In this paper, we give an overview of these two coding con-
cepts, illustrate their key ideas via motivating examples, and
demonstrate their impacts on Fog networks.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
More generally,
noting that redundancy is abundant in Fog networks (i.e., many
computing/storage points) and grows linearly with network
size, we demonstrate the transformational role of coding in
Fog computing for leveraging such redundancy to substantially
reduce the bandwidth consumption and latency of computing.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
We also point out that while these two coding techniques
are also applicable to Cloud computing applications, they are
expected to play a much more substantial role in improving
the system performance of Fog applications, due to the fact
that communication bottleneck and straggling nodes are far
more severe issues in Fog computing compared with its Cloud
counterpart.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
We also discuss a recently proposed uniﬁed coding frame-
work, in which the above two coding concepts are system-
atically combined by introducing a tradeoff between “com-
putation latency” and “communication load”.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
This framework
allows a Fog computing system to operate at any point on
the tradeoff, on which the Minimum Bandwidth Codes and
the Minimum Latency Codes can be viewed as two extreme
points that respectively minimizes the communication load and

the computation latency.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
We ﬁnally conclude the paper and highlight some exciting
open problems and research directions for utilizing coding in
Fog computing architectures.

MINIMUM BANDWIDTH CODES
We illustrate Minimum Bandwidth Codes in a typical Fog
computing scenario, in which a Fog client aims to utilize the
network edge for its computation task.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
For instance, a driver
wants to ﬁnd the best route through a navigation application
offered by the Fog, in which the map information and trafﬁc
condition are distributedly stored in edge nodes (ENs) like
roadside monitors, smart trafﬁc lights, or other smart cars that
collaborate to ﬁnd the best route.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Another example is object
recognition that is the key enabler of many augmented reality
applications.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
To provide an object recognition service over
Fog, edge nodes like routers and base stations, each stores
parts of the dataset repository, and collaboratively process the
images or videos provided by the Fog client.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
For the above Fog computing applications, the computa-
tion task is over a large dataset that is distributedly stored
on the edge nodes (e.g., map/trafﬁc information or dataset
repository), and the computations are often decomposed us-
ing MapReduce-type frameworks (e.g., [7], [8]), in which a
collection of edge nodes distributedly Map a set of input ﬁles,
generating some intermediate values, from which they Reduce
a set of output functions.

MINIMUM LATENCY CODES
We now move to the second coding concept, named Min-
imum Latency Codes, and demonstrate it for a class of Fog
computing applications, in which a client’s input is processed
over a large dataset (possibly over multiple iterations).
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The
application is supported by a group of edge nodes, which have
distributedly stored the entire dataset.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Each node processes the
client’s input using the parts of the dataset it locally has, and
returns the computed results to the client.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The client reduces
the ﬁnal results after collecting intermediate results from all
edge nodes.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Many distributed machine learning algorithms fall
into this category.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
For example, a gradient decent algorithm
for linear regression requires multiplying the weight vector
with the data matrix in each iteration.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
To do that at network
edge, each edge node stores locally a sub-matrix of the data
matrix.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
During computation, each edge node multiplies the
weight vector with the stored sub-matrix and returns the results
to the client.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text: 4: Matrix multiplication using a Minimum Latency Code.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The
code generates 3 coded tasks each executed by an EN.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The client
recovers the ﬁnal result after receiving the results from EN 1 and 3.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text: The runtime is not affected by the straggling EN 2.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
To be more speciﬁc, let us consider a simple distributed
matrix multiplication problem, in which as shown in Fig.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
4, a
client wants to multiply a data matrix A with the input matrix
X to compute AX.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The data matrix A is stored distributedly
across 3 nearby ENs, i.e., EN 1, EN 2, and EN 3, on which
the matrix multiplication will be executed distributedly.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
One natural approach to tackle this problem is to vertically
and evenly divide the data matrix A into 3 sub-matrices,
each of which is stored on one EN.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Then when each EN
receives the input X, it simply multiplies its locally stored sub-
matrix with X and returns the results, and the client vertically
concatenates the returned matrices to obtain the ﬁnal result.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
However, we note that since this uncoded approach relies
on successfully retrieving the task results from all 3 ENs, it
has a major drawback that once one of the ENs runs slow
or gets disconnected, the computation may take very long
or even fail to ﬁnish.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Minimum Latency Codes deal with
slow or unreliable edge nodes by optimally creating redundant
computations tasks.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
4, a Minimum Latency
Code vertically partitions the data matrix A into 2 sub-matrices
A1 and A2, and creates one redundant task by summing A1
and A2.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Then A1, A2 and A1 + A2 are stored on EN 1, EN 2,
and EN 3 respectively.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
4, the computation
is completed when the client has received the task results only
from EN 1 and 3, from which A2X can be decoded.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
In fact, it
is obvious that the client can recover the ﬁnal result once she
receives the task results from any 2 out of the 3 ENs, without
needing to wait for the slow/unreachable EN (EN 2 in this
case).
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
In summary, Minimum Latency Codes create redundant
computation tasks across Fog networks, such that having any
set of certain number of task results is sufﬁcient to accomplish
the overall computation.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Hence, applying Minimum Latency
Codes on the abundant edge nodes can effectively alleviate the
effect of stragglers and signiﬁcantly speed up Fog computing.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
As illustrated in the above example, the basic idea of Mini-
mum Latency Codes is to apply erasure codes on computation
tasks, creating redundant coded tasks that provide robustness
to straggling edge nodes.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Erasure codes have been widely
exploited to combat symbol losses in communication systems
and disk failures in distributed storage systems.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The simplest
form of erasure codes, i.e., the repetition code, repeats each
information symbol multiple times, such that a information
symbol can be successfully recovered as long as at least
one of the repeats survives.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
For example, modern distributed
ﬁles systems like Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS)
replicates each data block three times across different storage
nodes.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Another type of erasure code, known as the Maximum-
Distance-Separable (MDS) code, provides better robustness to
erasures.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
An (n, k) MDS code takes k information symbols and
encodes them into n ≥k coded symbols, such that obtaining
any k out of the n coded symbols is sufﬁcient to decode all k
information symbols.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
This “any k of n” property is highly
desirable due to the randomness of erasures.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
A successful
application of the MDS code is the Reed-Solomon Code used
to protect CDs and DVDs.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
5
As introduced in [6], Minimum Latency Codes are exactly
MDS codes that are used to encode computation tasks.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
For a
Fog computing job executed on n edge nodes, a (n, k) Mini-
mum Latency Code ﬁrst decomposes the overall computation
into k smaller tasks, for some k ≤n.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Then it encodes them
into n coded tasks using an (n, k) MDS code, and assigns each
of them to a node to compute.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
By the aforementioned “any
k of n” property of the MDS code, we can accomplish the
overall computation once we have collected the results from
the fastest k out of n coded tasks, without worrying the tasks
still running on the slow nodes (or stragglers).
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Minimum Latency Codes can help to signiﬁcantly improve
the response time of Fog applications.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Let’s consider a com-
putation task performed distributedly across n edge nodes.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The response time of the uncoded approach is limited by the
slowest node.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
An (n, k) repetition code breaks the computation
into k tasks, and repeats each task
n
k times across the n
nodes, and the computation continues until each task has
been computed at least once.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
On the other hand, for an (n, k)
Minimum Latency Code, the response time is limited by the
fastest k out of n nodes that have ﬁnished their coded tasks.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
As shown in [6], for a shifted-exponential distribution, the
average response times of the uncoded execution and the
repetition code are both Θ( log n
n ).
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The Minimum Latency Codes
can reduce the response time by a factor of Θ(log n).
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
For
example, in a typical Fog computing scenario with 10 ∼100
nodes, Minimum Latency Codes can theoretically offer a
2.3× ∼4.6× speedup.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Moreover, experiments on Amazon
EC2 clusters were performed in [6], in which for a gradient
descent computation for linear regression, Minimum Latency
Codes reduce the response time by 35.7% on average.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
We
further envision that in a Fog computing environment where
computing nodes are much more heterogeneous and likely
to be irresponsive, the performance gain by using Minimum
Latency Codes will be much larger.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Other than speeding up the Fog computing applications,
Minimum Latency Codes also maximize the survivability of
the computation when faced with nodes failure/disconnection,
i.e., when the task results may never come back.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
We note that
an (n, k) Minimum Latency Code requires any k out of n tasks
to be returned to guarantee a successful computation, and this
level of robustness can not be provided by either the uncoded
computation or the the repetition code.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
A UNIFIED CODING FRAMEWORK
We have so far discussed two different coding techniques
that aim at minimizing the bandwidth consumption and the
computation latency of Fog computing.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
However, under a
MapReduce-type computing model, a uniﬁed coded frame-
work has been recently developed in [15] by introducing a
tradeoff between “computation latency” in the Map phase and
“communication load” in the Shufﬂe phase.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
5 we have illustrated the tradeoff
between “computation latency” and “communication load”
that is achieved by the uniﬁed framework for running a
distributed matrix multiplication over 18 edge nodes (see [15]
Section III for details).

approximately exhibits an inverse-linearly proportional rela-

title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
In particular, we
can see that the Minimum Bandwidth Codes and the Minimum
Latency Codes can be viewed as special instances of the
proposed coding framework, by considering two extremes of
this tradeoff: minimizing either the communication load or the
computation latency individually.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Next, we further illustrate
how to utilize this tradeoff to minimize the total response
time that is the sum of the communication time in the Shufﬂe
phase and the computation latency in the Map phase.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
For
the matrix multiplication problem in Fig.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
5, we consider real
entries each represented using 2 bytes, a shift-exponential
distribution for the Map task execution time, and a wireless
network with speed 10 Mbps.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Then, the Minimum Bandwidth
Codes that wait for all 18 nodes to ﬁnish their Map tasks
achieve a total response time of 302s,1 and the Minimum
Latency Codes that terminate the Map phase when the fastest
3 nodes (minimum required number) ﬁnish their Map tasks
achieve a total response time of 263s.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Using the uniﬁed
coding framework, we can wait for the optimal number of
the fastest 12 nodes to ﬁnish, and achieve the minimum total
response time of 186s.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Hence, this uniﬁed coding approach
provides a performance gain of 38.4% and 29.3 % over the
Minimum Bandwidth Codes and the Minimum Latency Codes
respectively.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
This uniﬁed coding framework, which is essentially a sys-
tematic concatenation of the Minimum Bandwidth Codes and
the Minimum Latency Codes, takes advantage of both coding
techniques in difference stages of the computation.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
In the Map
phase, MDS codes are employed to create coded tasks, which
are then assigned to edge nodes in a speciﬁc repetitive pattern
for local execution.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
According to the interested computation
latency of the Map phase, all running Map tasks are terminated
as soon as a certain number of nodes have ﬁnished their
local computations.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Then in the Shufﬂe phase, coded multicast
opportunities speciﬁed by Minimum Bandwidth Codes are
greedily utilized, until the data demands of all nodes are

For example, we can consider executing a linear

To be able to end the Map phase when only the

For more detailed illustrative
examples, we refer the interested readers to Section IV of [15].
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The uniﬁed coding framework allows us to ﬂexibly select
the operation point to minimize the overall job execution time.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
For example, when the network is slow, we can wait for
more nodes to ﬁnish their Map computations, creating better
multicast opportunities to further slash the amount of data
movement.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
On the other hand, when we have detected that
some nodes are running slow or becoming irresponsive, we
can shift the load to the network by ending the Map phase as
soon as enough coded tasks are executed.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS
We demonstrated how coding can be effectively utilized
to leverage abundant computing resources at the network
edge to signiﬁcantly reduce the bandwidth consumption and
computation latency in Fog computing applications.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
In par-
ticular, we illustrated two recently proposed coding concepts,
namely Minimum Bandwidth Codes and Minimum Latency
Codes, and discussed their impacts on Fog computing.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
We
also discussed a uniﬁed coding framework that includes the
above two coding techniques as special cases, and enables a
tradeoff between computation latency and communication load
to optimize the system performance.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
We envision codes to play a fundamental role in Fog
computing by enabling an efﬁcient utilization of computation,
communication, and storage resources at network edge.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
This
area opens up many important and exciting future research
directions.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Here we list a few:
Heterogeneous computing nodes: In distributed Fog net-
works, different nodes have different processing and storage
capacities.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
The ideas outlined in this paper can be used to
develop heuristic solutions for heterogeneous networks.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
For
example, one simple approach is to break the more powerful
nodes into multiple smaller virtual nodes that have homoge-
neous capability, and then apply the proposed coding tech-
niques for the homogeneous setting.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
However, systematically
developing practical task assignment and coding techniques for
these systems, that are provably optimum (approximately), is
a challenging open problem.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Networks with multi-layer and structured topology: The
current code designs for distributed computing [4], [5], [15]
are developed for a basic topology, in which the processing
nodes are connected through a shared link.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
While these results
demonstrate the signiﬁcant gain of coding in distributed Fog
computing, we need to extend these ideas to more general
network topologies.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
In such networks, nodes can be connected
through multiple switches and links in different layers with
different capacities.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Multi-stage computation tasks: Another important di-
rection is to consider more general computing frameworks,
in which the computation job is represented by a Directed
Acyclic Task Graph (DAG).
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
While we can apply the aforemen-
tioned code designs for each stage of computation locally, we
expect to achieve a higher reduction in bandwidth consumption
and response time by globally designing codes for the entire
task graph and accounting for interactions between consecutive
stages.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Coded computing overhead: The current Fog computing
system under consideration lacks appropriate modeling of the
coding overhead, which includes the cost for the encoding
and decoding processes, the cost for performing multicast
communications, and the cost for maintaining desired data
redundancy across Fog nodes.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
To make the study of coding in
practical Fog systems more relevant, it is important to carefully
formulate a comprehensive model that systematically accounts
for these overhead.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Veriﬁable distributed computing: Fog architecture facil-
itates ofﬂoading of computational tasks from relatively weak
computational devices (clients) to more powerful nodes in
the edge network.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
As a result, there is a critical need for
“Veriﬁable Computing” methods, in which clients can make
sure they receive the correct calculations.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
This is typically
achieved by injecting redundancy in computations by the
clients.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
We expect codes to provide much more efﬁcient
methods for leveraging computation redundancy in order to
provide veriﬁed computing in Fog applications.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Exploiting the algebraic structures of computation tasks:
Recall that the Minimum Bandwidth Codes can be applied to
any general computation task that can be cast in a MapRe-
duce framework.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
However, we expect to improve the overall
performance, if we exploit the speciﬁc algebraic properties
of the underlying tasks.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
For example, if the task has some
linearity, we may be able to incorporate it in communication
and coding design in order to further reduce the bandwidth
consumption and latency.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
On the contrary, Minimum Latency
Codes work only for some particular linear functions (e.g.,
matrix multiplication).
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
It is of great interest to extend these
codes to a broader class of computation tasks.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Communication-heavy applications: Recall that by ex-
ploiting Minimum Bandwidth Codes we can envision a Fog
system that can handle many distributed Fog nodes with a
bounded communication load.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Such a surprising feature would
enormously expand the list of applications that can be offered
over Fog networks.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
One research direction is to re-examine
some communication-heavy tasks to see if Minimum Band-
width Codes allow them to be implemented over distributed
Fog networks.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Plug-and-Play Fog nodes: We can ﬁnally envision a soft-
ware package (or App) that can be installed and maintained
distributedly on each Fog node.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
This package should allow
a Fog computing node to join the system anytime to work
with the rest of the nodes or leave the system asynchronously,
still the entire network operates near optimum.
title: Coding Distributed Computing

text:
Designing
codes that guarantee integrity of computations despite such
network dynamics is a very interesting and important research
direction.

Cloudroid: A Cloud Framework for Transparent and
QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing
Ben Hu, Huaimin Wang, Pengfei Zhang, Bo Ding, and Huimin Che
National Key Laboratory for Parallel and Distributed Processing,
National University of Defense Technology, 410073, China
Email: {huben11, hmwang, pfzhang, dingbo, chehuimin15}@nudt.edu.cn
Abstract—Many robotic tasks require heavy computation,
which can easily exceed the robot’s onboard computer capability.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
A promising solution to address this challenge is outsourcing the
computation to the cloud.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
However, exploiting the potential of
cloud resources in robotic software is difﬁcult, because it in-
volves complex code modiﬁcation and extensive (re)conﬁguration
procedures.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Moreover, quality of service (QoS) such as timeliness,
which is critical to robot’s behavior, have to be considered.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In
this paper, we propose a transparent and QoS-aware software
framework called Cloudroid for cloud robotic applications.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
This
framework supports direct deployment of existing robotic soft-
ware packages to the cloud, transparently transforming them
into Internet-accessible cloud services.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
And with the automati-
cally generated service stubs, robotic applications can outsource
their computation to the cloud without any code modiﬁcation.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Furthermore, the robot and the cloud can cooperate to maintain
the speciﬁc QoS property such as request response time, even
in a highly dynamic and resource-competitive environment.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
We
evaluated Cloudroid based on a group of typical robotic scenarios
and a set of software packages widely adopted in real-world
robot practices.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Results show that robots capability can be
enhanced signiﬁcantly without code modiﬁcation and speciﬁc QoS
objectives can be guaranteed.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In certain tasks, the ”cloud + robot”
setup shows improved performance in orders of magnitude
compared with the robot native setup.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Keywords-Cloud robotics; Platform as a service; Computation
outsourcing; Quality of service
I.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
INTRODUCTION
To support precise environmental perception and appropriate
decision making, many algorithms in the robotic ﬁeld must
consume massive computing resources at runtime.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
For ex-
ample, a classic robotic problem, Simultaneous Localization
and Mapping (SLAM), which aims to simultaneously draw
the map of the surroundings and locate the robot itself, has
been widely investigated in the past 20 years [1].
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Although the
precisions of mapping and localization have been improved
signiﬁcantly, the huge memory and CPU footprint are still
barriers for the real application of these algorithms [2].
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
An-
other example is object recognition in dynamically captured
images, which is essential to robotic vision.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In the state-of-art
deep neural network-based algorithm [3], using only a CPU is
an order of magnitude slower than using a graphic processing
unit (GPU) accelerator, which exhibits very poor performance
(≪1Hz).
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
It is far from meeting the requirement of the real-
time control of mobile robots (at least 5-10Hz).
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Because of
constraints such as cost, size, and energy, many robots cannot
be equipped with a high-performance GPU accelerator.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The lack of computing resources severely restrains the
capability of autonomous robots, especially in tasks that
emphasize timeliness.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
These issues can be observed in the
above-mentioned SLAM and object detection problems: robots
require localization/mapping results from the SLAM algorithm
to determine their movements in the next moment, and the
result from the object detection algorithm can prevent robots
from bumping into obstacles.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Without accurate and timely
results, the consequences may be catastrophic.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In traditional
practice, people have to compromise the autonomy of robots
or tremendously increase the hardware cost to avoid this kind
of accidents.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Recently, along with the growth in cloud and Internet-
based computing, a novel paradigm called ”cloud robotics” [4]
has been proposed, which is a promising solution to address
challenges in the ﬁeld.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In this paradigm, a bridge between the
robots and the cloud is set up, so that rich resources on the
cloud can be utilized to enhance the capabilities of the robots.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Although this idea seems attractive and much effort has been
devoted (c.f., Section II-B), exploiting the potential of cloud
computing for robot software remains difﬁcult in practice.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The
two major reasons are the following:
• The established software development method in the
robotic community has to be changed.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In particular,
drastic modiﬁcation and (re)conﬁguration are necessary
to enable existing robotic software to outsource their
computation to the cloud.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The situation worsens because
of the lack of a mature ecosystem of cloud services
designed particularly for robotic tasks (e.g., the service
that encapsulates compute-intensive SLAM algorithms on
the Internet).
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
• Given that robots directly interact with the physical
world, robotic applications have an inherent requirement
for quality of service (QoS) assurance.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
When combined
with the cloud, the QoS in cloud service invocation must
be considered.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
However, the initial attempt in general-
purpose cloud robotic frameworks, such as those intro-
duced in [5] and [6] still cannot provide the corresponding
solution.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In this paper, we propose a software framework called
Cloudroid for cloud robotics.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
This framework is basically
a Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) cloud infrastructure with the
following prominent features:
1)Transparent service wrapping.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
It adopts the robot operat-
ing system (ROS) [7] package model, a de facto standard for
robotic software, as its application model.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
It supports the direct
deployment of compiled native robot software packages, and
transparently transforms them into Internet-accessible cloud

text:
Therefore, numerous existing software packages
which are accumulated by the robotic community, especially
those that encapsulate the computation-intensive algorithms
independently, can be quickly converted into cloud services.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Furthermore, Cloudroid can automatically generate a stub of
the deployed cloud service whose interface is identical to
the deployed ROS package.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
With this function, existing robot
applications can transparently outsource their computation to
the cloud without any code modiﬁcation.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
2)Cooperated QoS awareness The QoS-assurance mecha-
nisms built in the robot-side stub and the resource schedul-
ing/isolation mechanisms on the cloud can effectively maintain
certain QoS properties e.g., desirable Request Response Time
(RRT).
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In extreme cases e.g., when the network is down, the
service stub can even substitute for the cloud service with a
local instance of the original software package for failover to
avoid a complete task crash down.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The implementation of Cloudroid is opensourced and can
be accessed at https://github.com/cyberdb/Cloudroid.

of this paper is organized as follows.

background of ROS and the highly related work.

BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
This section introduces the background of our work, that is,
ROS and its application model.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Then, related works in cloud
robotics are discussed in detail, focusing on our innovation in
comparison with them.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
ROS and ROS package model
The most impressive work in robotic software infrastructure
in recent years is ROS [7], which includes an open-source
middleware framework and a comprehensive tool chain for
robotic development and management.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
As a de facto standard
is widely accepted by the robotic community, thousands of
reusable, independently encapsulated packages have been ac-
cumulated in the ROS software ecosystem.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Most well-known
compute-intensive algorithms for autonomous robots can be
found in this ecosystem.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
For example, searching in the ROS
ofﬁcial software list1 using the keyword ”SLAM”, results in
more than 20 packages, including the realization of various
well-known SLAM algorithms.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
From the viewpoint of distributed computing, ROS can be
regarded as message-oriented middleware.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
A ROS application
is made up of a group of self-described software entities called
”packages”, which can run on different physical locations
and interact with each other through well-deﬁned message
channels called ”topics”.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
To advertise and subscribe to a
topic, ROS packages must interact with a special and pre-
deployed software entity called ”ROS Master”, which acts as
a directory service in the current robotic system.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
ROS also
supports synchronous interaction through Remote Procedure
1ROS packages, http://www.ros.org/browse/list.php
Figure 1.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
ROS Packages and Theirs Interactions
Call (RPC).
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
It is simulated by a ﬁxed pair of speciﬁc messages
at the bottom layer of ROS.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Although the message-oriented interaction is inherently
distributed, ROS is originally designed for small-scale robotic
systems with a local network.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
It assumes a ”white box” deploy-
ment model, where each package is assumed to be deployed
manually and conﬁgured appropriately by the operators, for
example, with the address of the ROS Master.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In addition, most
existing ROS packages are designed to serve only a single
robot, and the ROS communication protocol is unsuitable
for the Internet environment as well.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Therefore, providing a
general solution to deploy ROS packages as cloud services,
which can be accessed in a black-box and on-demand style,
is a challenge.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Outsourcing Robotic Computation to Cloud
The term of ”cloud robotics” was coined in 2010 to describe
the combination of robotics and cloud computing.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
A major
purpose of this computing paradigm is to outsource compu-
tation to the cloud [4].
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The related work can be divided into
two categories: task-speciﬁc solutions and general solutions.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Task-speciﬁc solutions are concerned with how to utilize
the cloud to support the computation outsourcing in spe-
ciﬁc robotic tasks such as SLAM, robotic vision, and robot
grasping.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Most existing related works in cloud robotics can
be classiﬁed into this category.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
For example, to ofﬂoad the
heavy computation in robotic SLAM processes, cloud-assisted
systems are proposed in [8], which validated the beneﬁt of
introducing cloud as the back-end of robots.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The Monte Carlo
sampling process in robot grasp planning is parallelized by the
computing clusters in the cloud to cope with uncertainty in [9].
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
A cloud-based object recognition engine, CORE, is proposed
in [10].
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The practice in cloud-based semantic mapping [11]
shows that outsourcing computation to the cloud improves the
request response time.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In addition to boosting performance,
some initial discussions on QoS are provided in this ﬁeld,
such as the real-time assurance in [12] and [13].
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
All of these existing works in this branch are highly related
to speciﬁc tasks and the solutions cannot be easily generalized
to other tasks.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
On the contrary, our study aims to provide
a general solution for robotic software on the infrastructure
level.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Speciﬁcally, if a package only interacts with the outside
world through standard ROS messages and RPC-based APIs,
Cloudroid can transparently convert it into a cloud service
which can be accessed through the mainstream Internet service
accessing protocol in an on-demand manner.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
3
General solutions aims to provide infrastructure-level sup-
ports for cloud robotics, so that diverse robotic applications
can beneﬁt from the introduction of the cloud.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
A seminal work in this ﬁeld is DAvinCi
[5], a framework that magniﬁes the ROS architecture to the
large-scale Internet environment.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
DAvinCi inherits the ”white-
box” deployment model (cf.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Section II-A) of ROS, thus, the
cloud-side software entities are not real ”service” yet.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
These
software entities only run on the cloud but must be deployed
and conﬁgured manually.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Another closely related work is
Rapyuta [6], a platform enabling robot to ofﬂoad their com-
plex computation to the cloud.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
It provides virtual computing
environments based on the Linux Container for robots.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
This
environment can be controlled by the robot, thereby allowing
the execution of ROS packages in this environment remotely
instead of locally.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Compared with these two works, Cloudroid
is much more aggressive in its goal: It transparently wraps
a ROS package into an Internet-accessible cloud service and
automatically generates the service stub operating on the robot
side.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Therefore, the ROS applications can exploit the potential
of the cloud without any code modiﬁcation.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In addition,
Cloudroid provides QoS guarantees during service invocation,
which are critical to many robotic applications and are not
considered in existing general solutions yet.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Another research branch in cloud robotics, which is highly
related to our work, is the bridging between mainstream
Internet service accessing protocols (e.g., REST, SOAP, and
WebSocket) and the ROS message protocol [14].
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Cloudroid
utilizes one of these works, ROSBridge [15], as an underlying
component.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
However, we provide a complete PaaS infrastruc-
ture instead of only the protocol conversion function.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Cloud PaaS Infrastructure
From the cloud computing perspective, Cloudroid is a PaaS
infrastructure.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
After years of development, a large number of
mature commercial and open-source PaaS infrastructures exist,
such as Google App Engine, CloudFoundry, and OpenShift.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
However, they are designed to support general cloud services
and not optimized for cloud robotics.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
By contrast, Cloudroid
adopts the widely accepted and de facto standard of robotic
software, the ROS package model, as its application model,
and provides QoS-assurance function which is essential to
many robotic applications.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Therefore, we can quickly get a
lot of cloud services which can be used in robotic tasks, and
the cloud robotic software ecosystem can be constructed efﬁ-
ciently based on the accumulation in the robotic community.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
CLOUDROID METHODOLOGY
Cloudroid aims to explore a convenient, practicable, and
general-purpose solution to outsource robotic computation to
the cloud.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In this section, we focus on the methodology used
to achieve two most prominent features of Cloudroid, that is,
transparency and QoS-awareness.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Transparent Service Wrapping
In Cloudroid, the service wrapping is responsible for encap-
sulating a robotic software package as an Internet-accessible
cloud service.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
We emphasize transparency in this process,
(a) Original robotic application
(b) Outsourcing part of computation to cloud
Figure 2.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Example of Service Wrapping
which means: (1) native robotics software packages can be
wrapped as cloud services without any modiﬁcation, and (2)
the robotic applications invoking these packages can invoke
the wrapped service without any modiﬁcation.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
1) Feasibility and Gap
Much of the autonomous behavior of the robot is achieved
in a similar paradigm that consists of three main stages, as
shown in Fig.2.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The perception stage acquires data from robot
sensors.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The decision making stage aggregates the environ-
mental data, obtains high-level information of the world and
makes appropriate decisions accordingly.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The execution stage
drives robot actuators to perform the decision.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Among these
three stages, decision making is compute-intensive and need
not interact with the robotic hardware directly.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Therefore,
this stage can be partly or fully outsourced to the cloud and
can likely gain a signiﬁcant performance promotion.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
At the
same time, in virtue of the well-deﬁned package model of
ROS, many algorithms related to robot decision making have
been encapsulated as independent, self-described, and reusable
packages.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
They are the foundation of the feasibility of our
work in transparently wrapping a ROS package as a cloud
service.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
However, a wide gap still exists between the ROS package
model and the cloud service model.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
A cloud service is a ”black
box” that can be accessed in an on-demand style through
its interface, which is a logical abstraction of its function.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The client should not be concerned about the deployment,
conﬁguration, and other realization details of this service.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In
addition, such a service should be able to support ubiquitous
access and rapid elasticity with multiple clients.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
These re-
quirements directly contradict the characteristics of the ROS
package model described in Section II-A.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
2) Mechanisms to Bridge the Gap
To bridge the gap between the ROS package model and the
cloud service model, Cloudroid introduces the following four
mechanisms:
Self-contained VM encapsulation.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The operation of the ROS
package strongly relies on the ROS runtime, especially the
ROS Master.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
When we migrate a ROS package to the cloud,


4
this package cannot interact with the ROS Master on the robot
side, because our goal is to convert it into a ”black box”.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Therefore, all ROS packages being uploaded to Cloudroid are
automatically encapsulated into a Docker [16] VM image that
contains all software entities which is necessary to operate this
package.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The ROS communication protocol is not
a standard cloud service accessing protocol.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
To address this
issue, Cloudroid adopts ROSBridges [15], an open-source
protocol bridge that can convert the ROS protocol to JSON
and WebSocket-based protocol.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
On-demand
Servant
Instantiation
and
Multiplex.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In
Cloudroid, a service is composed of two parts: the interface
and the servant, that is, the Docker instance containing the
ROS package.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
While a ROS package is uploaded to Cloudroid,
its interface is automatically generated and published.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
How-
ever, the servant is not instantiated until a client requests this
service.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
For the ROS packages that are originally designed to
serve a single robot (e.g., most SLAM packages), Cloudroid
instantiates different servant (i.e., the Docker instance) for
different clients, and the request for this service is multiplexed
to the corresponding servant.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Then, we can wrap a ROS
package that can only maintain the states of a single robot into
a service which can be accessed simultaneously by multiple
robots.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Moreover, we can gain the rapid elasticity of service
capacity in this scenario, which is discussed further in the next
subsection.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
The cloud services
operating on Cloudroid can be accessed by manually written
WebSocket clients.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In addition, Cloudroid can automatically
generate the service stub, which can be regarded as a special
kind of service SDK in the form of a ROS package.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Its local
interface is identical to the original ROS package and the
original ROS package can be directly substituted by the service
stub with alias as shown in Fig.2(b).
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
As a result, the ROS
application on the client side can outsource computation to the
cloud by just replacing the ROS package.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
It can be realized by
modifying the ROS application meta ﬁles, without any code-
level modiﬁcation.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Cooperated QoS Awareness
Another challenge in outsourcing computation to the cloud
is that it may introduce uncertainties that can inﬂuence the
speciﬁc QoS properties of a robotic application.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
For example,
the network may not always meet the demand of data transfer
between the robot and the cloud, or the resource competition
on the cloud may cause performance degradation, especially
when multiple robots simultaneously access a service that
encapsulates heavy computation.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
To minimize the impact of
these uncertainties, Cloudroid was built into a set of QoS
awareness mechanisms both on the robot and the cloud side.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
These mechanisms cooperate to meet the QoS requirement
speciﬁed by the robot applications.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
1) Client-side QoS Mechanism
The client-side QoS mechanism resides in the automatically
generated service stub.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
Its basic idea is that when the cloud
service cannot be accessed or a certain QoS threshold cannot
be fulﬁlled, a local copy of the ROS package acts as a
substitute for the cloud service which wraps this package.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
In
this situation, at least a bottomline of the concerned QoS can
be guaranteed.
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:
When the service is ﬁrst requested through the
stub, the client can specify two values for the Service Level
Agreement (SLA).
title: Cloudroid: Cloud Framework Transparent QoS-aware Robotic Computation Outsourcing

text:

Output:

2:

3: else if Tcurrent ⩽Tmax then
4:

5: else
6:

7: end if

9:

10: else if Qcurrent > Qt then
11:
