6.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
Literature Review  
Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing 
In literature, several architectures have been proposed to enable mobile devices to share 
resources either with pre-existing network infrastructure-based computing systems                  
[30-33, 41-48] such as cloud or with other mobile devices using short range wireless 
communication technologies [22-23, 29, 34-39].
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
One such architecture is proposed in [20] in which mobile devices are connected to a locally 
available powerful computer named cloudlet through short range wireless communication 
technologies such as Wi-Fi.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
Cloudlet is then connected to a cloud computing system through a 
satellite.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text: The aim is to reduce satellite communication latency.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
Cloudlet system architecture is 
presented in Figure 18.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text: Object recognition application has been implemented to evaluate the performance.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The solider 
captures and sends image of an individual to cloudlet which preprocesses the image and sends it 
to cloud computing system through a satellite for further processing.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
In [50] authors have proposed a system that allows students to offload image and video 
processing tasks on internet cloud.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
In [51] a single hop ad hoc cloud has been suggested to 
compute a climate model.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
In proposed scenario, train commuters form an ad hoc cloud 
comprised of smart phones which is used to forecast local weather and ozone concentrations at 
the destination using data collected and transmitted by passengers in another train coming from 
the destination.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
A hybrid cluster comprised of stationary and mobile nodes interconnected by 
wireless and wired networks has been proposed in [52].
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The proposed system could be used by 
an architect equipped with wearable computing devices to execute a computationally intensive 
3D rendering application.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
Six online and batch scheduling heuristics are proposed in [53] to 
offload computationally intensive independent tasks on mobile ad hoc cloud.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
MinHop allocates 
task to a node accessible through minimum number of hops.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
Minimum Execution Time with 
Communication algorithm selects a node which takes least amount of time to execute a task 
whereas Minimum Completion Time with Communication algorithm assigns task to a node with 
minimum expected completion time.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
Both online scheduling algorithms take into account 
Figure 18: Cloudlet System Architecture 


 
 
computation and communication cost but former focuses on execution time while later one on 
completion time.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
For batch scheduling, MinMinComm and MaxMinComm algorithms are 
proposed.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
MinMinComm estimates completion time of each task on each node and selects the 
node with minimum earliest completion time while MaxMinComm focuses on maximum earliest 
completion time.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The proposed scheduling heuristics are based on traditional MET, MCT, 
MinMin, and MaxMin heuristics and are extended to consider communication cost when 
estimating task completion time.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The problem of deciding whether to execute tasks locally or on 
a remote system has been investigated in [54].
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The evaluations suggest that tasks with high 
computation-to-communication ratio should be executed on a powerful remote system.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The 
scheme proposed in [55] performs task allocations under varying assumptions about the 
connectivity environment.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
For example, in the ideal network environment where the future 
contact can be accurately predicted, the authors proposed a greedy task allocation algorithm that 
iteratively chooses the destination node for every task with the minimum task completion time.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The scheme is based on a decentralized architecture and it does not provide any mechanism to 
address node mobility.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
In [56], various job stealing techniques such as random stealing, best rank 
aware stealing and worst rank aware stealing based on a centralized architecture were developed 
to reduce the processing energy consumption.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The rank is calculated based on a benchmark 
factor for each device, the estimated uptime of a device and the number of jobs assigned to that 
device.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
In [57] three offloading architecture for mobile clouds are described: (i) offloading to a 
cloud server accessible through a wide area network, (ii) offloading to a nearby server accessible 
through a local area network, and (iii) offloading to nearby mobile devices.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The problem of 
unpredictable network connectivity, node mobility, energy consumption, and device failure has been 
addressed in [58].
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
Sensor Cloud 
Several approaches have been proposed to integrate sensing nodes with grid and cloud 
computing systems.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
For example, a hybrid static and mobile grid computing system is proposed 
in [16] in which mobile and static computing devices and bio-sensing nodes are integrated and 
presented as a one unified system.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The bio-sensors collect vital signs such as blood pressure, 
temperature, electrocardiogram, and oxygen saturation of an individual.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The collected data is 
processed and analyzed on mobile grid computing infrastructure in order to determine the health 
of an individual.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
To deal with uncertainty, an idea of application waypoints has been introduced 
in which service provider executing application task reports to the broker with an estimate of 
residual task completion time.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
If the broker does not receive feedback about the estimated 
residual task completion time from the service provides at the specified waypoint, it marks 
service provider as failed and assigns additional resources to take over the incomplete tasks.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
A 
resource allocation algorithm to efficiently process telemedicine data in the grid is proposed in 
[21].
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
In proposed algorithm sensors attached to patient’s body collect and send health related 


 
 
data to grid through a mobile device.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
A patient management application deployed on the grid 
processes and analysis the patient’s data.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text: A sensor-cloud infrastructure proposed in [15] integrates sensors with cloud computing system.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
In sensor-cloud infrastructure physical sensors integrated with cloud computing system are 
virtualized as virtual sensors and are provided as a service.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
A pull-based resource allocation 
algorithm is proposed in [17] in which a service provider node pulls tasks from the service 
broker nodes, executes them and submits results once task completes its execution.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
In [18] 
authors have proposed a sensor grid platform to combine real-time data about the environment 
with vast computational resources.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The proposed sensor grid platform can be deployed using 
centralized architecture or decentralized architecture.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
In centralized architecture, a sensor 
network connected to grid collects data while processing of data is carried out on the grid.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
In 
distributed architecture, a sensor network collects data and performs simple data processing tasks 
while computationally intensive data processing and analysis tasks are executed on the grid.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
A sensor data collection network to integrate sensor data into grid applications is discussed in 
[19].
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The sensor data collection network includes three key components: the data collection 
network, sensor entry points, and application entry points.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The data collection network discovers, 
filters, and queries multiple sensor networks.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
Each sensor network has one or more sensor entry 
points that map application data requirements onto low-level sensor network operations.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The 
application entry points provide application connectivity to data collection network.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The 
proposed system is based on publish-subscribe paradigm.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
A sensor network publishes sensor 
data and metadata through service entry points while application subscribes to sensor network 
and receives a data in real time.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
In [20] authors have proposed a scalable proxy-based 
architecture for sensor grid in which nodes in wireless sensor network are provided as a service 
on the grid.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
The use of proxy-based architecture where proxy acts as an interface between grid 
and sensor network supports a wide range of sensor network implementations.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
All these systems 
and schemes including [4-14] assume pre-existing network infrastructure and therefore are not 
suitable for ad hoc network environments.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
Conclusion 
Due to recent advances in mobile computing and communication technologies it has become 
feasible to develop next generation of distributed computing systems where mobile nodes such 
as robots and aerial vehicles should be able to share resources either with pre-existing network 
infrastructure-based computing systems such as cloud or with other mobile nodes using short 
range wireless communication technologies such as Wi-Fi Direct.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
Compared to traditional parallel and distributed computing systems, mobile grid and cloud 
computing systems pose numerous challenges due to node mobility, shared and unreliable 
communication medium, low bandwidth, high latency, limited battery power, and infrastructure-


 
 
less network environment.
title: Recent Advances in Mobile Grid and Cloud Computing

text:
This paper discussed applications of mobile grid and cloud computing 
systems, research challenges, future research directions, and recent advances in the field.

Using Machine Learning to reduce the energy
wasted in Volunteer Computing Environments
A.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Stephen McGough and Matthew Forshaw
School of Computing
Newcastle University
Newcastle, UK
Email: {stephen.mcgough,matthew.forshaw}
@newcastle.ac.uk
John Brennan, Noura Al Moubayed, Stephen Bonner
Department of Computer Science
Durham University
Durham, UK
Email: {john.brennan, noura.al-moubayed, s.a.r.bonner}
@durham.ac.uk
Abstract—High Throughput Computing (HTC) provides a
convenient mechanism for running thousands of tasks.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Many
HTC systems exploit computers which are provisioned for other
purposes by utilising their idle time – volunteer computing.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
This has great advantages as it gives access to vast quantities
of computational power for little or no cost.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The downside is
that running tasks are sacriﬁced if the computer is needed for
its primary use.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Normally terminating the task which must be
restarted on a different computer – leading to wasted energy and
an increase in task completion time.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We demonstrate, through
the use of simulation, how we can reduce this wasted energy
by targeting tasks at computers less likely to be needed for
primary use, predicting this idle time through machine learning.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
By combining two machine learning approaches, namely Random
Forest and MultiLayer Perceptron, we save 51.4% of the energy
without signiﬁcantly affecting the time to complete tasks.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Index Terms—volunteer computing; machine learning; energy;
I.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
INTRODUCTION
Many research problems that we face today require the ex-
ecution of large computational workloads which can seriously
hinder progress.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
To mitigate the impact of these computa-
tional workloads two main approaches have become prevalent
– those of High Performance Computing (HPC) and High
Throughput Computing (HTC).
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Both of these approaches take
advantage of running the workload across many computational
units1.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
HPC is used in cases where the workload requires
inter-communication between computers, whilst HTC allows
the workload to be decomposed into separate, non interacting,
tasks2 which run independently.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Although HTC can be seen as a ‘simpler’ problem than
HPC – removing the need to simultaneously provision large
numbers of computers, handle inter-computer communication
issues, and issues over communication versus computation –
the efﬁcient deployment and execution of HTC tasks have
their own problems.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
These include: the timely deployment of
tasks; ensuring the, potentially thousands or more, tasks run
to completion; and the deployment / collection of the required
data and code.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
These problems are compounded when the
1Here we shall refer to these as computers, without loss of generality.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text: 2In the literature these may be referred to as task or jobs.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We will use the
term tasks in this work without loss of generality.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
tasks are run on computers which are not owned or provisioned
for HTC tasks – often referred to as volunteer computing –
as HTC tasks are sacriﬁced when the computer is required
for its primary role.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Despite this, volunteer computing is often
desired due to the signiﬁcant computational power it provides
– often at little or no cost to the user.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Two common platforms
for volunteer HTC are HTCondor [1] and BOINC [2].
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
In volunteer computing HTC tasks are normally run when
the computer is ‘idle’ and not performing their primary role.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
However, if the computer is needed again for its primary
role then the HTC system needs to relinquish the computer.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
This may be through the termination of the HTC task, task
suspension or migrating the task to a different computer.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Task
termination can be performed in any environment and for
any task, however, suspension and migration require support
from both the underlying infrastructure and the task being
performed.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Thus, in many cases HTC users will default to
task termination in which case the HTC system will attempt
to re-run the task on a different computer.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Re-running the task on a different computer leads to two
detrimental impacts: an increase in the time, in excess of
the task execution time, the user must wait to obtain results
– referred to as task overhead, and an increase in energy
consumed due to the, potentially multiple, aborted task exe-
cutions.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Thus we seek to reduce the energy consumed, whilst
at the same time maintaining or reducing overhead.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Ideally
we wish to identify those computers which are less likely to
be required for their primary use during the execution time
of the task.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
This will lead to a reduction in wasted energy as
the task will not have aborted executions.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
However, this may
increase the overhead due to delay in ﬁnding an appropriate
computer.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Alternatively it may reduce overhead as time will
not be wasted on partial executions.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
In order to identify those computers less likely to be needed
for their primary use we use machine learning to predict the
time, for each computer, between primary usage – referred to
as idle time.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We can then select the computer with the largest
predicted idle time to run a task.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We evaluate two machine
learning approaches for predicting the lengths of idle periods.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
These are Random Forest [3] and MultiLayer Perceptron [4]
a form of feedforward artiﬁcial neural network [5].
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We also
arXiv:1810.08675v1  [cs.DC]  19 Oct 2018


combine these using various Ensemble techniques [6] in order
to identify the ‘best’ prediction.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
In an ideal scenario we would
also seek to predict the execution time of the tasks submitted
to the HTC system, however, prior research has shown that
this is not easy for the user [7].
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Nor is this easy for machine
learning as although there is signiﬁcant correlation between
tasks submitted at the same time there is little correlation to
future tasks.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
In Section II we discuss the HTC-Sim which we used in
order to evaluate our different machine learning approaches.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
This is followed by a discussion of the dataset made available
with the HTC-Sim system in Section III.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We present our machine learning
approaches to predicting computer idle time in Section V
before discussing the experimental setup in Section VI.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We
present the results and analysis in Section VII before providing
conclusions and future directions in Section VIII.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
HTC-SIM SYSTEM
The HTC-Sim System [8] is a trace-driven simulation
framework for a generic High Throughput Computing system.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
It is capable of simulating both dedicated computer resources
and computers which are provided on a voluntary basis.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Each
run of HTC-Sim consumes a number of trace log ﬁles – a trace
ﬁle for the primary users (referred to as interactive users) of
the volunteer computers and a trace ﬁle for the tasks submitted
to the HTC system (referred to as tasks from High-Throughput
users).
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Different scheduling algorithms can be developed and
deployed within the simulation system and evaluated using the
provided metrics.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text: Figure 1 illustrates the model view of HTC-Sim.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Computers
within the system may be in one of three states: i) servicing the
primary user of the computer, ii) executing a HTC task, or, iii)
in an idle state.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The idle state can be sub-divided into: a) idle
and powered up, or, b) idle and in sleep state.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Computers will
transition from idle powered up to idle sleep after a pre-deﬁned
period of inactivity – thus minimising wasted energy.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
This is
one example of the Cluster Policy which covers such issues
as when the computers should reboot (for software updates),
whether HTC tasks can be performed on the computer and
the minimum time between a primary user logging out and
a HTC task being deployed.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The current state of the HTC
system is maintained by the High-Throughput Management
which handles task deployment along with the transferring of
ﬁles.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
If a computer is in idle sleep, but is required for a task
the High-Throughput Management can wake up the computer,
provided that this is currently allowed by policy.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We have augmented Figure 1 with a machine learning
scheduler and a service which constructs models of individual
computer idle times – highlighted in blue.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

RELATED WORK
Previous work by McGough et al.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
[9], using HTC-Sim,
has used Reinforcement Learning to identify computers less
likely to be needed for primary use.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Achieving an energy
reduction of up to 53%.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
However, this was only possible
by signiﬁcantly increasing the overhead.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Instead we apply
an alternative machine learning approach which allows us to
predict the idle time for each computer – using these for task
execution.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
This allows us to reduce the energy consumed by
up to 51% without signiﬁcantly increasing the overheads.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Machine learning is seeing increased use in optimising
the operation of High Throughput and High Performance
Computing environments.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We do not seek to provide an
exhaustive survey here, rather to highlight prominent works
and the various areas of opportunity for machine learning to
improve the performance of HTC systems.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Scheduling Decisions:
The scheduling decisions made within HTC and HPC
environments are typically governed by heuristics, taking as
input characteristics of the workload and available computa-
tional resources.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The use of machine learning opens up the
opportunity to move from ﬁxed heuristic to dynamic policies
for scheduling workloads.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Carastan-Santos et al [10] provide
one such work, demonstrating notable improvements in task
slowdown against existing scheduling approaches.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Resource Allocation:
A substantial body of work has focused on the resource
selection and allocation using machine learning.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
In particular,
Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been shown to provide
signiﬁcant improvements over naive approaches.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
[11] apply RL for a datacenter workload subject to QoS
constraints.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
[12] applied Q-learning with an
ε-greedy selection rule for resource selection in a grid envi-
ronment.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
[13] proposed the Sarsa(0) approach
for resource allocation in multiple server hosting environments
for web applications.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Several works speciﬁcally target energy
conservation using RL, e.g.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Runtime prediction:
Accurate estimates of task execution times can be used
to improve scheduler decision making.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
However, users of
clusters have been shown to provide poor estimates of task
runtimes [7].
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Empirical studies from production environments
have shown tasks typically to consume only 30% of the

text:
This sometimes arises due
to premature termination due to misconﬁguration [18], due
to performance variability within often-heterogeneous clus-

preemption of tasks which exceed their estimated runtime.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Machine learning approaches have shown promise in tackling
some of these challenges.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
For example, Gaussier et al [20]
adopt online regression to predict task running times, and
in turn optimise backﬁlling strategies with respect to a task
slowdown metric.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
User assistance:
Machine learning approaches have also been shown to be
useful in assisting the users of HPC systems.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Rodrigues et
al [21] demonstrate a tool which uses multiple model types
(including Multilayer Perceptron and Random Forest, as we
use in this work) to assist users to predict the memory
requirements for their workloads.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The authors found no single
model provided the best predictions, so adopt an ensemble of
several models.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The accurate prediction of memory utilisation
opens up the potential for more efﬁcient resource allocation
and workload consolidation.

PREDICTION OF COMPUTER IDLE TIME THROUGH
MACHINE LEARNING
We describe here the process of converting the interactive
user trace-log into a format which can be used for the purposes
of machine learning along with the two machine learning
algorithms used.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We train a model for each computer individ-
ually as this gave slightly lower Mean Squared Error (MSE)
than working at the cluster or whole system level – more
signiﬁcantly the training time was much shorter.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Numerous
machine learning algorithms were evaluated, however, as the
data was highly non-linear, Random Forest and MultiLayer
Perceptron produced the best results (lowest MSE).
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We predict
a months worth of interactive user data based on a number of
previous months worth of data.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
It should be noted that we do not consider predicting the
duration of tasks – although it is possible to train a machine
learning algorithm accurately on a set of tasks [22], it is
not easy to predict future tasks durations.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
As although there
is signiﬁcant local correlation between tasks, this correlation
dissipates quickly – e.g.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
a user may submit thousands of tasks
of similar duration at the same time, however, once these are
complete their future work differs markedly.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Figure 3 presents an autocorrelation plot (correlogram) for
task durations within the trace.

The plot presents levels of
autocorrelation for data values at varying time lags.

We see a very strong positive correlation for lags up to
20000, demonstrating that successive tasks are likely to exhibit
similar durations.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

For lag values greater than 20000 we see
negative correlation, arising from the interplay between dom-
inant groups of tasks exhibiting relatively large and relatively
small durations.

Data
Each interactive user interaction is a tuple:
(Li, c, Lo)
where Li, Lo are the login and logout times, and c is the
computer used.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We extend this with a predicted idle time:
(Li, c, Lo, i)
where i is the actual or predicted time between two consecutive
interactions on the same computer.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
1) Dealing with Reboots: There are two types of event
which cause a task to terminate: logging in of an interactive
user, or, an automated computer reboot – for software updates
and system clearing.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
If an interactive user is logged in at reboot
time then the reboot is postponed until the user logs out.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
This
effectively extends the interactive user’s login time and can be
ignored here.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
However, if the reboot happens during an idle
period then the idle period is split into multiple shorter idle
periods.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text: Figure 4 illustrates the different scenarios.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
In case
A there is no reboot between a logout and the next login,
therefore the idle period is equivalent to the time difference
between the logout and login events.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Case B contains a reboot
between the logout and the next login event.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We place a
‘synthetic’ interactive user at the time of the reboot – splitting
the idle interval.

consume zero time and once we have predicted the idle periods

Case C is the extension of
Case B where there are no interactive user login events over
several days.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Thus multiple ‘synthetic’ interactive users are
entered for each reboot time.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
As these computers have very
little interactive user activity these are potentially the best
computers to run HTC tasks on and hence we wish to capture
this information.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
2) Dealing with sparse data: Sparsity of the interactive
user log when used for training can reduce the ability for the
machine learning approaches to accurately predict – especially
for points far from the training data – e.g.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
a computer in a
locked cluster room will only have synthetic reboots in the
log and will lack training data for what may happen far from
the reboots.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The same applies if there are long periods between
interactive users.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
To overcome this we create a further set of
‘synthetic’ interactive users at regular intervals between each
logout and subsequent login (including reboot synthetic users).
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
For a logout at time Lo and subsequent login at time Li we
create the set of ‘synthetic’ (overlapping) users:
{(Li, c, Lo, i), (Li + δ, c, Lo, i −δ), ...,
{(Li + nδ, c, Lo, i −nδ)},
such that n = ⌊i/δ⌋, and δ is the time between these synthetic
interactive user records.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
This signiﬁcantly improves the ability
of the machine learning approaches to predict.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
3) Preparation of data for Machine Learning: Machine
learning algorithms require numeric data ideally in the range
of -1 to 1.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
As our trace-log contains timestamps and computer
names these need converting:
Timestamps: Can be converted into a Unix epoch.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
How-
ever, this does not make such concepts as day of the week,
month or term available as features.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Thus we add to the tuple
the following features extracted from the logout time:
• activeDuration: duration for the last interactive user,
• minute: number of minutes past the hour,
• hourOfDay: hour of the day,
• dayOfWeek: day of the week,
• dayOfMonth: day of the month,
• month: month of the year,
• year: the year,
• termWeeks: week of the current term – in the range 1 –
10, with -1 representing outside of the term,
• term: term [1–3] with -1 indicating outside of a term.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Computer: One hot encoding could be used where each
computer becomes a separate feature.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
However, as we have
1386 computers this would lead to an equivalent number of
features, slowing down training and prediction.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Instead we use
an integer encoder based on the cluster name, and the computer
within that cluster – only adding two features.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
In order to scale our features to be in the range 0 – 1 we
divide each feature by the maximum value that the feature can
take – e.g.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text: the dayOfMonth value can be divided by 31.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We now train the machine learning algorithms on several
months’ worth of training data (including actual idle times).

A simple Random Forest
Once trained we can predict the idle times for the following
month (which lacks the idle times).
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
As the data we are
predicting on only contains information that would be known
at the time the interactive user logs out we do not break the
temporal rule for our simulation.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Random Forest
Random Forest [3] (RF) is a machine learning method
which combines multiple decision trees into a single model
and can be used for classiﬁcation or regression.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
With regres-
sion being used in the work presented here.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
A RF creates
a collection of decision trees each trained on a subset of the
features.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
A decision tree is a construct where at each branching
point a question is answered which moves one closer to the
leaf containing the ‘correct’ result.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
When predicting, each
decision tree produces a predicted value with the modal value
returned for the whole RF.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
An advantage of RF is that it is
tolerant to overﬁtting to the data.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Figure 5 depicts a simple RF of three trees derived from
three features (c - cluster number, m - machine number, d -
day of week) to predict the idle time.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments
Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
MultiLayer Perceptron
A MultiLayer Perceptron [4] (MLP) is a feed-forward
artiﬁcial neural network [5] with a minimum of three fully
connected layers – an input layer, one or more hidden layers
and an output layer.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Each hidden and output layer contains
a non-liner activation function, examples of which include
ReLU, sigmoid or tanh.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The MLP is trained through back-
propagation, most commonly via some form of the Gradient
Decent algorithm.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The MLP works by taking a set of features in on the input
layer.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
These values are fed forward to the next layer where
they are scaled via a learnt weighting value at each node in
the hidden layer, before being summed together.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
This summed
value is then passed through the activation function before
being fed forwards to the next layer.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The network is trained by
repeatedly feeding the network with input data and an output
target label, where the prediction of the network is compared
with the target label using a loss function – mean squared error
for regression tasks.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The weights of the network are then tuned
via backpropagation to minimise the error given by the loss
function.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Ensemble Approaches
A machine learning ensemble approach combines the pre-
dictions from multiple independently trained machine learning
models to produce a ‘better’ overall result.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We present a
number of ensemble techniques used to improve the accuracy
of our predictions:
• Max: of the RF and MLP predictions.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The expectation
is that this will lead to a more speculative scheduler.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The expectation is
that this will lead to a more conservative scheduler.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text: • Average: of the RF and MLP predictions.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The expecta-
tion is that this will reduce extreme values.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
• Last Month: At the end of a month evaluate the MSE
between the real and predicted values for both RF and
MLP and use the lower for the following month.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The
expectation is that a good approach for one month is
likely to be good for the next month.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
• Best on average: Extending the ‘Last Month’ to take into
account the best from all previous months.

text:
Scheduler for HTC-Sim
Here we describe Machine Learning scheduler developed
to work within HTC-Sim – Algorithm 1.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The algorithm ﬁrst
determines if the task has been attempted before and uses the
longest attempt as a lower bound on the execution length.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
It
then ﬁnds the idle computer with the longest predicted idle
time and returns it (unless the predicted idle duration is less
than the previous run attempt).
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
If no suitable idle computer
is free it attempts to ﬁnd a sleeping computer which has
at least the previous runtime free.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
If no sleeping computer
is found then no computer is returned.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Where runBefore is
a boolean indicating if the task has been run previously,
maxPreviousRunDuration returns the maximum duration of
the previous run attempts, idle is the set of all currently idle
computers, sleep is the set of all currently sleeping computers,
ﬁndLongestIdle returns the computer from the set with the
longest predicted idle time and predictedIdle computes the
remaining idle time at time t as the computer holds the idle
time since the last logout.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Hence:
predictedIdle = lastLogout + idle −t.

EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
As HTC-Sim consumes a trace-log of interactive user and
HTC tasks we have augmented the interactive user trace-log
with the predicted idle values.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We used Scikit-Learn (version
0.19.1) to generate the predicted RF and MLP values.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Data
We run our experiments against the 2010 exemplar datasets
used with HTC-Sim.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We train the interactive user time in
intervals of one month and train on all data from the start
of 2009 until immediately before the start of the month to be
predicted.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
to predict February 2010 we train on January
2009 through to January 2010 inclusive.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Parameters and Features
1) Maximising prediction accuracy through ‘synthetic’
tasks: We performed a search-space analysis on δ – the time
interval between ‘synthetic’ users when reducing data sparsity.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Evaluating δ between 5 and 60minutes, achieved maximal
accuracy at δ = 10minutes.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
2) Identiﬁcation of optimal feature set: Although we could
use all of our features as deﬁned in Section V it is often the
case that training on a subset will give better accuracy.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
RF
allows for the identiﬁcation of the most important features.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
This identiﬁed the best feature set as: {epochLogin, epochL-
ogout, activeDuration, hourOfDay, dayOfWeek, dayOfMonth,
month}.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
3) MLP hidden layers: The number of hidden layers and
number of nodes per layer can signiﬁcantly affect the accuracy
of a MLP.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We performed a search space analysis of all possible
networks with up to four hidden layers and forty nodes per
layer.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
This identiﬁed a four hidden layer MLP with 18, 14, 9,
and 10 nodes per layer minimised the MSE for the majority
of computers.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
The best activation function was RELU along
with the Adam solver.

The lowest overhead is observed for the MAX
ensemble approach – which matches in with our assumption

It would appear that this approach paid off with

Likewise
MIN leads to the largest overhead for the machine learning

puters which may not have enough time to complete the task.

This would suggest that the time waiting to ﬁnd a computer to

All other machine
learning approaches have overheads lower than the Random

As the Crystal approach is fully aware of the future

The lowest energy consumption was observed

text:
CONCLUSION
In this paper we have utilised two machine learning al-
gorithms – Random Forest (RF) and MultiLayer Perceptron
(MLP) – to predict the amount of idle time between consec-
utive primary user activity on a computer within a volunteer
computing environment.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Allowing us to develop a scheduler
which targets work to those computers with the longest ex-
pected idle time.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Reducing the amount of energy consumed
by reducing the number of aborted task executions due to
the primary user wishing to make use of their computer.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
To
improve the results we use ensemble approaches to combine
the different machine learning algorithms.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We demonstrate, through the use of simulation that we
can save between 45.6% and 51.4% of the energy consumed
through the High Throughput Computing (HTC) system with
minimal impact on the overhead observed by the HTC user –
in the worst case increasing the overhead by 4.9%.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
If energy
saving is the primary goal then taking the minimum of the
RF and MLP predictions is best – saving 51.4%.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
However,
this increases the overhead by 4.9%.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
If reducing the overhead
is most important then taking the maximum of RF and MLP
will reduce the overhead by 19.3% whilst still decreasing the
energy consumption by 47.7% – only 3.6MWh more per year.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
We re-train the machine learning algorithms on a monthly
basis.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
However, it may be possible to improve energy savings
by performing re-training more frequently.
title: Using Machine Learning reduce energy wasted Volunteer Computing Environments

text:
Currently we take
no account of the execution time of the tasks – save for using
prior (aborted) runs to provide a minimum – although this has
proven to be a hard value to predict a priori it may be possible
to provide course intervals and classify tasks into these.

Abstract— The emerging trend of edge computing has led
several cloud providers to release their own platforms for per-
forming computation at the ‘edge’ of the network.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We compare
two such platforms, Amazon AWS Greengrass and Microsoft
Azure IoT Edge, using a new benchmark comprising a suite
of performance metrics.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We also compare the performance of
the edge frameworks to cloud-only implementations available
in their respective cloud ecosystems.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Amazon AWS Greengrass
and Azure IoT Edge use different underlying technologies, edge
Lambda functions vs.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
containers, and so we also elaborate on
platform features available to developers.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Our study shows that
both of these edge platforms provide comparable performance,
which nevertheless differs in important ways for key types
of workloads used in edge applications.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Finally, we discuss
several current issues and challenges we faced in deploying
these platforms.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
INTRODUCTION
As the Internet of Things (IoT) is becoming mainstream,
the number of connected devices is growing at an exponential
rate [1].
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In this paradigm, IoT devices, which are often
geographically distributed at the edge of the network, will
generate a massive quantity of data.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Transmitting, storing,
and processing this huge amount of data in the cloud is
expected to lead to high bandwidth usage and prohibitive
costs [2].
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Further, many applications that run at the edge of
the network, such as autonomous vehicles and augmented
reality, have real-time requirements that are difﬁcult to meet
with relatively distant cloud datacenters [3].
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Edge computing has the potential to mitigate these cost
and performance bottlenecks.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
This computing paradigm en-
ables applications to leverage compute nodes in close prox-
imity to data sources to perform data processing, such as
aggregation, ﬁltering, and classiﬁcation, before forwarding
the results to other nodes and cloud servers [2], [4].
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
For
example, instead of sending an image to the cloud to
perform facial recognition, and edge device may simply
report whether the image contains the particular signature.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
This approach reduces bandwidth usage and can speed up
application response.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
To make application development in the edge computing
model easier, several cloud providers, have put forward their
own edge computing platforms.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
These platforms provide
the ability to deploy and orchestrate applications, such as
machine learning models, on edge devices in the form of

The resource provisioning and runtime is provided by the
edge platforms.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Such serverless functions or user scripts
in containers then act on raw data, and depending on the
conﬁguration, send results to the cloud and additionally also
make them available in other cloud services.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Since these platforms use different paradigms and tech-
nologies, it is important to compare them to understand their
tradeoffs and to select the best platform for a given use
case.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Criteria of interest include the platform architecture,
programmability, performance, and cost.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
To quantify these
differences consistently requires benchmarks of common
uses cases.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Further, it requires standardized collection of
metrics, such as end-to-end latency, device compute time,
device resource utilization, bandwidth usage, and cost.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
To
make an informed choice between edge and cloud platforms,
the benchmarks and metrics must also allow fair comparison
across different types of deployments.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We present EdgeBench 1 – an open-source benchmark
suite for serverless edge computing platforms.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
EdgeBench
features three key applications: a speech/audio-to-text de-
coder, an image recognition machine learning model, and a
scalar value generator emulating a sensor.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Each application
processes a bank of input data on an edge device and
sends results to cloud storage.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We target EdgeBench for
two of the most popular edge computing platforms currently
available, AWS Greengrass [5] and Microsoft Azure IoT
Edge [6].
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
EdgeBench also provides cloud-based workload
implementations.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Our aim is to quantify the differences be-
tween the different edge platforms, as well as the providers’
respective cloud-only alternatives.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In future work, we plan
to extend EdgeBench to other emerging edge platforms,
such as Google’s Cloud IoT Edge [7] and IBM Watson IoT
Platform Edge [8], as these offerings mature.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We report on
initial experiments with EdgeBench using a Raspberry Pi
3B, a relatively resource-constrained device, to emulate the
IoT device that sends trafﬁc to the AWS and Azure cloud
platforms.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We provide a performance comparison across the
different workloads and platforms.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
EdgeBench complements previous work on benchmarking
serverless cloud computing platforms.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
SYSTEM ARCHITECTURES
On an abstract level, both platforms, AWS Greengrass
(henceforth, Greengrass) and Azure IoT Edge (henceforth,
Azure Edge) share a common general architecture.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
There
is an edge device that runs user code in the platform’s
runtime system.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
This user code can access local volumes
or local devices, such as sensors and cameras, performs
computations, and sends messages to the cloud.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In both
platforms, the cloud has a high throughput message ingestion
service, the IoT Hub.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The cloud ingests the messages from
the edge devices and sends them to conﬁgurable destinations,
such as AWS S3 or Azure blob for storage using ‘Rule’ (for
AWS) or a ‘Route’ (for Azure).
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Below, we highlight some of the details of each platform:
A.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
AWS Greengrass
The Greengrass pipeline is shown in Fig.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Greengrass
edge devices run the Greengrass core software.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The core
software allows users to run Lambda functions locally on the
edge devices and manage, modify or update them through the
AWS console website or deployment API.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Developers can
constrain the maximum memory usage of the local Lambda
functions.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The Greengrass core software also takes care of
the authentication, authorization, and secure message routing,
through the MQTT protocol [13], between the devices,
Lambda functions, and the cloud.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Greengrass core Lambda runtime currently supports code
deployment in Python 2.7, Node.JS 6.10, Java 8, C, C++,
and any language that supports importing C libraries.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Code
running inside Lambda functions can also access all other
AWS services, such as Amazon S3 or DynamoDB, using
the standard AWS SDKs.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Once the AWS IoT Hub receives
a message in the cloud, a ‘Rule’ can be deﬁned to trigger
one of 15 actions (as of now), including invoking Lambda
functions that run in the cloud or saving data in S3 or

Microsoft Azure IoT Edge
Azure Edge uses lightweight virtualization, speciﬁcally,
Docker compatible containers, to deploy computation on
edge devices.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The Docker containers run as ‘edge modules’
in the Azure Edge platform, as shown in Fig.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The modules
can contain Azure Functions, user code, and libraries.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
As of
now, the platform supports ﬁve languages: C#, C, Node.JS
ver > 0.4.x.x, Python (both 2.7 and 3.6), and Java 7+.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
It is
also possible to deploy Streaming Analytics and Azure ML
models directly in the containers.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The former is a managed
service from Azure for doing analytics on streaming data
and the latter are the models developed in Azure’s machine
learning service.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Modules can be deployed, updated, and
modiﬁed via the Azure IoT Edge Cloud web interface or
the Azure command line interface.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The runtime system on a single edge device consists of
an edgeAgent module and an edgeHub module.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The
edgeAgent takes care of provisioning and monitoring user
deployed modules.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The edgeHub takes care of the connec-
tion between the modules and the cloud and also maintains
security and authentication.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The edgeHub supports edge-
to-cloud connections using the MQTT and AMQP protocols
The edgeAgent sends messages to the cloud-hosted Azure
IoT Hub, as shown in Fig.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Messages are then routed from
the IoT Hub to a user-speciﬁed IoT Hub Endpoint, such
as Azure Blob Storage.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
For the Blob Storage Endpoint, the
IoT Hub batches the incoming messages and writes multiple
results in a single blob ﬁle.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
If user selects Blob Storage
endpoint, batching is the only option.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The batching window
can be conﬁgured by either time window, the smallest being
60 s, or by chunk size, the smallest being 10 MB.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
EDGEBENCH
In this section, we describe EdgeBench benchmark suite
and the performance metrics.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We also summarize the cloud-
based implementations of the benchmark applications.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Benchmark Applications and Workloads
We selected three canonical applications: a speech/audio-
to-text application; an image recognition application; and
a scalar value generator that emulates a sensor, e.g.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
With the popularity hike in use of a
myriad of smart speakers, such as Amazon Echo and Google
Home, has made audio and speech decoding and translation


very relevant.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Similarly, with the proliferation of smart
cameras and autonomous vehicles, image processing and
image classiﬁcation has become very common.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Currently,
these applications are often executed in the cloud.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Hence, it is
interesting to investigate performance of such applications in
an edge computing setting.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The scalar benchmark, however,
is an example of an extremely lightweight workload; it allows
us to measure the performance of each framework when the
computation and data volume at the edge are negligible.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text: All benchmark codes are written in Python.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In all three
pipelines, the edge devices send data in messages to the
IoT Hub We use a either a ‘Rule’ or ‘Route’ to push each
message payload in the cloud to an AWS S3 bucket or an
Azure Blob, respectively.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
• Audio/Speech to Text Translation (Audio Pipeline)
Here, the edge application reads audio ﬁles from a local
directory, decodes them to get the translated text, and then
sends the text to the cloud.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Each audio ﬁle is processed
one at a time.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
For our experiments, we use a mobile
version of Carnegie Mellon University’s Sphinx speech
recognition system, called PocketShpinx [14].
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We use the
default acoustic model provided with the package.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
For the
audio workload, we use 104 samples contributed by user
‘rhys mcg’ in Tatoeba Corpus [15], a free collaborative
online database of example sentences.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We have converted
the audio ﬁles into 16khz, 16 bit, mono ‘wav’ ﬁle format
to comply with the requirements of PocketSphinx.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The
average realtime length of ﬁles in the dataset is about 2.4 s.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
• Image Recognition (Image Pipeline): The serverless
function performs an image recognition task; speciﬁcally,
given an image as input, the function recognize the objects
present in the image and generates class labels for these
objects.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In both platforms, the edge application reads an
image from a directory.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
It then uses OpenCV [16] to resize
the image to standard (224 × 224 × 3) size.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Finally, the
application uses the open-source, deep learning framework
MXNet [17] to recognize and classify the objects in that
image.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
This is repeated
for all images in the directory.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
For the classiﬁer archi-
tecture, we chose a pretrained classiﬁer, Squeezenet [18]
because its small model size (≈5 MB) and low com-
pute footprint are suitable for resource-constrained edge
devices.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
For the input workload, we select 500 images
from the ILSVRC2012 image dataset [19].
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The input is
stored on a local directory on the device.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
• Scalar Sensor (Scalar Pipeline): The application is a
simple sensor emulator.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The serverless function generates
random scalar values at a user-speciﬁed frequency.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
At a
user-speciﬁed interval, e.g., 1s, the set of values generated
in that interval is sent to the cloud in a single message.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The cloud side of the pipeline then simply stores these
values in the speciﬁed storage location.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Metrics
In all pipelines of both platforms, each message receives
three UTC timestamps during the pipeline execution, as
shown in Fig.

text:
3: Schematic of a cloud only pipeline using AWS/Azure

title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Here, for valid calculations on these metrics, we
need the time of both the edge device and cloud to be
independently synced with accurate clocks.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The user code
in the edge device adds the T1 timestamp before sending
the result message from the edge device.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Timestamp T2 is
added automatically by the platform when the message is
en-queued in the IoT Hub, and ﬁnally, T3 is the creation
timestamp of the blob ﬁle in which the message is stored
after it is routed out of the IoT Hub.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We capture the following metrics to study performance:
• Compute time: This is the total time required for process-
ing one image or audio or to generate the scalar values in
the Raspberry Pi and is denoted by Cedge.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
• Time-in-ﬂight: This is the time taken for a message to
reach the IoT Hub after it is sent from the edge device.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
• End-to-end latency: This is the difference between the
time when the input is ingested at the edge device and
the time when the ﬁnal results are available in the storage.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
• Payload size: This is the size of the message sent from
the edge device without the framework overhead.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
• CPU and memory utilization: As the platforms use
different architectures, i.e., Lambda vs Docker, it is in-
teresting to look at the memory and CPU usage patterns.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We measure the average CPU and memory utilization on
the edge device over the execution of a given benchmark.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
For AWS, we use the top command in Linux and for
Azure we use the docker stats command to obtain
the resource utilization while the applications are running.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Our applications log compute time, the payload size, and
resource utilization locally on the edge device, while T1 is
added to the header.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Therefore, T1, T2 and T3 are retrieved
from the message meta-data in the cloud.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Cloud-Only Pipelines
We implement cloud-only versions of the three benchmark
workloads described in Sec.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
III-A for both the Amazon
and Microsoft Azure cloud platforms.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The pipelines use the
serverless architecture, as shown in Fig.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
For the image classiﬁcation and speech-to-text bench-
marks, we upload either image or audio ﬁle from the edge
device to a S3 bucket using boto3 library.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
For the scalar
pipeline in Amazon AWS, we generate and upload the sensor
values as JSON blob ﬁles in S3.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Lambda functions are
triggered by the creation of the new blob ﬁle in the bucket.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The Lambda function reads the value from the blob ﬁle and


simply stores it in another S3 bucket.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The upload of a ﬁle
triggers the Lambda function which, in turn, either performs
the image recognition or the audio-to-text conversion.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
After
the computation, the results are stored as blobs in another
S3 bucket.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In the Azure implementations, we use Azure
Functions, which are similar to Lambda functions.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The Azure
functions are triggered by the upload of an audio or image
ﬁle or a scalar value JSON ﬁle in Azure blob storage.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
After
the computation, the results are stored in a different blob.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The
majority of the code in cloud and edge pipelines are the same,
excepting changes for handling input/output and receiving
and handling the events due to different API speciﬁcations.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Note that in our benchmarks, Azure functions run on
Windows while Lambda functions run on Amazon Linux.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Linux is available on a preview basis for Azure Functions,
but it supports only JavaScript and .Net runtime as of now.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Moreover, even in Windows in Azure Functions, the support
of Python is in the experimental phase.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We manually installed
MXNet, OpenCV, PocketSphinx and other necessary libraries
from the KUDU console in Azure Python runtime to use the
libraries in Azure Functions.In AWS, the dependencies are
packaged along with the Lambda function.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Experimental Setup
We run the set of benchmarks using a standard Raspberry
Pi 3B model as the edge device.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The edge device is connected
to the internet via a wireless router using 2.4 Ghz spectrum.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We have used a dedicated Stratum 1 NTP time server,
TM2000A [20] with accuracy ≈50 µs to synchronize the
time of the Raspberry Pi.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Also, AWS and Azure are known
to use highly precise clocks to accurately sync their services.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We use AWS and Azure cloud services in the US East
region, both in Virginia.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We used ping to ﬁnd the round
trip latency from our institution’s server to virtual machines
in both Azure and AWS.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We are unable to measure this
from the edge device, due to security restrictions on ping.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The average delay for AWS is 9.5 ms and for Azure is
11.36 ms.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Assuming the extra delay within the institution
network is same for both Greengrass and Azure Edge, we
observe latencies to both the cloud platforms are close.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We use Greengrass core version 1.5.0 and Azure IoT Hub
Device client 1.4.0.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In the experiments with Greengrass,
each Lambda function is provisioned with 256 MB RAM
and made ‘long lived’, i.e., it will run indeﬁnitely.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
However,
this option is absent in Azure Edge.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In Greengrass, the
image, audio and local statistics directories for storing metric
values are mounted into the execution environment as ‘Local
Resources’.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In Azure Edge, the same directories are directly
mounted as volumes in the Docker container.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In Azure Edge,
we use the geo-redundant storage option RA-GRS for blob
storage in the cloud.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
AWS S3 replicates data automatically
across at least 3 availability zones.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We also measure performance of the cloud-only pipelines
in AWS and Azure.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
For AWS, the memory of the Lambda
functions is set to 3008 MB.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In AWS, CPU allocation is
proportional to the memory, hence, this conﬁguration has the

As Lambda CPU is
not conﬁgurable, to keep the setups comparable, we select the
Consumption Host Plan for Azure functions that auto-scales
Azure functions based on system load.
