text:
In all cloud pipelines,
we wait for a period of 10 to 15 s between uploading
subsequent image/audio ﬁles to avoid congesting the system.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Uploading too many image/audio ﬁles very quickly resulted
in many functions being triggered concurrently and out of
order.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
This results in reordering of results and some missed
images, making it difﬁcult to ﬁnd the end-to-end latency.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The
input data sizes are shown in Table I.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Results
1) End to End Latency: We give the average end-to-end
latency for each of the various benchmark conﬁgurations in
Fig.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We observe that in all three applications, across both
the cloud and edge pipelines, Azure Edge has the largest end-
to-end latency.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
This is because the Azure IoT service batches
the messages from the edge device in the IoT Hub in the
cloud, and it writes the results from the multiple messages
in a batch in a single blob ﬁle.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We also found that when the
batching interval is 60 s, the average time spend in hub is ≈
90 s, while for a 90 s batching interval, the average time in
the hub is ≈93-94 s.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
It appears that messages are held back
in the IoT hub in Azure for some time interval before being
written to the blob ﬁle, and this time does not coincide with
the batching interval.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
If this were not the case, given that
the messages are received by the IoT Hub approximately
uniformly across a batching interval, the average time a
message spends in hub should have been roughly equal to
half the batching interval.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
This extra delay, adding to latency,
exists irrespective of the blob storage type used.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We observe that the end-to-end latency for Azure cloud
pipelines is larger than both AWS edge and cloud pipelines
across all applications.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The majority of the latency is caused
by the total time of execution of Azure function in the cloud.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Though, the average time for audio to speech and image
recognition in Azure cloud is 5.57 s and 1.19 s respectively,
for each message, added to this is the time for loading
libraries and trigger the function, which is very high for
Azure python runtime.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
This may have been be caused by the
fact that the Python runtime in Azure is still experimental
and hence, not optimized.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
It may also be that importing
the libraries takes a lot of time.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We obtain the smallest
end-to-end latency results using the AWS Cloud (1.79 s for

The ﬂight times of AWS
and Azure edge are very close, which suggests that as long as

title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
5b shows that Azure, in general, has a higher
compute time for all pipelines compared to Greengrass.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

The
highest is the audio pipeline, with Azure Edge taking 6 s,
on average, and Greengrass taking 4.77 s, on average.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
This
difference may indicate a place where the different architec-
tures (Lambda vs.

If
this time is large, then it has a signiﬁcant impact on end-
to-end latency.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We also observe that, for the audio pipeline
in the edge, considering the average length of each clip is
approximately 2.4 s, it may not be possible to analyze the
audio in real time using a Raspberry Pi without optimizing
the code.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
However, using a more powerful edge device would
help to reduce compute time.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
2) Bandwidth Utilization: The average payload size in
both platforms for audio pipeline is 162 bytes, for image
pipeline it is 752 bytes and for scalar it is 234 bytes.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
On
comparing ﬂight times for each edge pipeline in Fig.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
5a we
observe that the transmission delay (ﬂight time) of messages
between the edge and cloud is roughly proportional to the
message size.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
A cloud-only approach requires the upload
of the raw image or audio ﬁle to the cloud service.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In the
edge pipelines, we only the send results of the applications
as text to the cloud.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Hence, we observe that there is drastic
reduction in the per message size in edge pipelines compared
to cloud.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We also used vnstat [21] to obtain the total
bandwidth usage of the applications in the edge and cloud
pipelines, shown in Table I.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
The results are measured with
respect to 200 scalar values, 500 images, and 104 audio ﬁles,
respectively.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
To avoid measuring the TLS handshakes and
other module startup network overhead, we explicitly add a
conﬁgurable delay (60 s, in this case) before the application
begins processing data.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We see that framework data overhead
itself is negligible and comparable in both platforms.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Com-
paring the total data transmitted during pipeline executions,
we see a massive reduction of data transmission while using
the edge pipelines compared to cloud.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
AWS sends 36 times
and 81 times more data when using the cloud pipelines
compared to the edge, for the audio and image applications,
respectively.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Azure sends 36 times and 77 times more data
using the cloud pipelines compared to the edge in audio and
image applications, respectively.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
3) Local Resource Utilization: We study the average
resource usage of the edge device (Raspberry Pi) across the
edge pipelines over three separate runs of the experiments.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In
Azure Edge, we look at the average total CPU and memory
percentage used by all of the containers running speciﬁc to
Azure Edge.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In Greengrass, we look at the total average CPU
and memory percentage usage by all processes under the
greengrass user, ggc user.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
5c, 5d that the image recognition
application is predominantly a CPU intensive job, with CPU
utilization as high as 88-90% in both Azure and AWS.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We
also observe that audio-to-text is not very CPU-heavy, but
it consumes more memory than the other applications.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We
further observe that within each application, the CPU % of
Greengrass and Azure Edge are very similar, though the
RAM consumed in Azure Edge is always higher.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Azure
Edge consumes on average about 29.5 MB to 54.5 MB more
memory on the Raspberry Pi.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

We believe this difference
would be less discernible if a more powerful edge device
were used.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Overall, we observe that the edge pipelines,
on average, consume less than 200 MB RAM and do not
saturate the CPU usage.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
This strengthens the case for the
feasibility of running some carefully chosen computations
on resource-constrained devices.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
4) Infrastructure Cost: We do a rough infrastructure cost
estimate of running the applications in the edge pipelines
versus the cloud-only pipelines.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Cost of running pipelines
in both vendors are comparable and so, for simplicity, here,
we look only at the image pipeline in AWS.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

Assume there
is one trafﬁc camera, generating one image every 10 s.

Let
us further assume the average image size is similar those
used in our image benchmarks, i.e., 143.12 KB (In general,
image size and rate would be larger in real world scenarios.)
This amounts to 6 × 60 × 24 × 30 = 259, 200 images
per month.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

Also, on average, the duration for which AWS
charges for Lambda function execution is 300ms in the image
recognition cloud only pipeline in our study for image of that
size.

In the Greengrass image pipeline, the average size of a
message to the cloud is 752 bytes.

We assume, with headers,
it would be approximately 1 KB per message.

calculated in region US-East, Virginia.

title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
This rough
cost estimate indicates that executing image recognition on
the cloud setting is ≈5.2 x more expensive than edge, with
only an extra 230 ms in average end-to-end latency.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
It is pos-
sible to reduce the cost of the cloud-only pipeline by using
less powerful Lambda functions, however, the storage cost
alone is larger than the entire edge pipeline cost.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Bandwidth
usage-wise, the edge pipeline sends around 253.125 MB data
over the network per month, whereas uploading images to
cloud requires sending 35.38 GB data/month.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Discussion
We observed that both platforms do not handle very
high throughput messaging well yet.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In this case either the
messages are delayed or fail to reach the cloud from the edge
device.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text: In future we want to benchmark this throughput.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Another important consideration is the relative ease of
deploying dependencies and libraries.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We can package all
necessary libraries in the Docker container with a single
Dockerﬁle in Azure Edge.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
On the contrary, in Greengrass
Lambda functions, we need to compile external dependencies
in required environment and add them in a zip ﬁle for
deploying.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
We feel that the former is a cleaner choice for
adding and managing a lot of external libraries.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In the end, from our experience, we feel both these
approaches are suitable for carrying out edge computation.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
However, the higher end-to-end latency of Azure may be a
problem for latency sensitive applications.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Although Azure
has richer customization options, we found development and
integration to be easier in the AWS Greengrass platform.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
CONCLUSION
We have presented EdgeBench, a benchmark suite for
serverless edge computing plaforms.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
With this suite, we have
studied two managed edge computing platforms, Greengrass
and Azure Edge.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Further, we have compared the performance
of these platforms with that of cloud-only implementations
of the same benchmarks.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Our results show that the perfor-
mance of Greengrass and Azure Edge are comparable, with
the exception that Azure Edge exhibits higher end-to-end
latency due to its batch-based processing approach.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
Further,
our results show that for the image and scalar pipelines,
the performance of Greengrass is comparable to that of
the AWS cloud-only pipelines, while reducing the network
bandwidth usage.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
These results indicate that edge computing
is a promising alternative to cloud computing for CPU light
workloads.
title: arXiv:1811.05948v1  [cs.NI]  14 Nov 2018

text:
In future work, we plan to extend EdgeBench to
include additional applications and edge platforms.

Abstract
We present an algorithm to compute the minimum orbital intersection distance (MOID), or global minimum
of the distance between the points lying on two Keplerian ellipses.
title: urange.eps

text:
This is achieved by ﬁnding all stationary
points of the distance function, based on solving an algebraic polynomial equation of 16th degree.
title: urange.eps

text:
The al-
gorithm tracks numerical errors appearing on the way, and treats carefully nearly degenerate cases, including
practical cases with almost circular and almost coplanar orbits.
title: urange.eps

text:
Benchmarks conﬁrm its high numeric relia-
bility and accuracy, and that regardless of its error–controlling overheads, this algorithm pretends to be one
of the fastest MOID computation methods available to date, so it may be useful in processing large catalogs.
title: urange.eps

text:
Keywords: close encounters, near-Earth asteroids, NEOs, catalogs, computational methods

text:
Introduction
The MOID parameter, or the minimum distance
between points on two Keplerian orbits, has an im-
portant value in various Solar System studies.
title: urange.eps

text:
It
measures the closeness of two trajectories in the R3
space, and hence ascertains whether two bodies have
a risk to collide.
title: urange.eps

text:
For example, if MOID appeared be-
low the sum of radii of two bodies than such bodies
may avoid a collision only if they orbit in a mean-
motion resonance, or via a perturbating eﬀect that
may increase the MOID to a safe level before the
bodies could actually collide.
title: urange.eps

text:
Otherwise, the bodies
will necessarily collide in some future.
title: urange.eps

text:
Therefore, computing the MOID is very old task
with an application to Potentially Hazardous Objects
(PHOs) and Near-Earth Asteroids (NEAs).
title: urange.eps

text: Email address: r.baluev@spbu.ru (Roman V.
title: urange.eps

text:
Baluev)
This problem is investigated over decades al-
ready, see e.g.
title: urange.eps

text:
(Sitarski, 1968; Dybczy´nski et al.,
1986) and more recent works by Armellin et al.
title: urange.eps

text:
The MOID is a minimum of some distance or
distance-like function ρ(u, u′) that depends on two
arguments, determining positions on two orbits.
title: urange.eps

text:
The
methods of ﬁnding the minima of ρ(u, u′) can be split
in several general cathegories, depending on the di-
mensionality of the optimization task to be solved.
title: urange.eps

text:
This depends on how much work is pre-computed
analytically.
title: urange.eps

text:
As an ultimately
simple example this includes e.g.
title: urange.eps

text:
the 2D brute-
force (exhaustive) search of ρ(u, u′) on a 2D
grid.
title: urange.eps

text:
Thanks to the existence of rigorous and
ﬁnite upper limits on the gradient of ρ(u, u′),
which appears to be a trigonometric polyno-
mial, we can always limit the ﬁnite diﬀerence

u| and ∆u′ max |ρ′
u′|.
title: urange.eps

text:
Thanks to
such error predictability, algorithms of the 2D
class appear the most reliable ones, because we
can always determine the MOID, along with
the orbital positions u and u′, to any desired ac-
curacy.
title: urange.eps

text:
An advanced method based on the 2D
global optimization of ρ, which includes high-
order Taylor models and interval arithmetics,
was presented by Armellin et al.
title: urange.eps

text:
Nev-
ertheless, even advanced methods of this type
cannot be fast due to the need of considering
2D domains.
title: urange.eps

text:
Here we eliminate u′ from
the numeric search by solving it from an ana-
lytic equation.
title: urange.eps

text:
The remaining orbital position
u is determined by numeric optimization of the
1D function ˜ρ(u) = ρ(u, u′(u)).
title: urange.eps

text:
In general, this
is faster than 2D minimization, but the deriva-
tive of ˜ρ(u) is no longer bounded, because
du′/du may turn inﬁnite sometimes.
title: urange.eps

text:
Such
cases may appear even for very simple circu-
lar orbits.
title: urange.eps

text:
Therefore, in general this method
cannot provide a strict mathematical guaran-
tee of the desired numerical accuracy.
title: urange.eps

text:
How-
ever, it appears more reliable than the methods
of the next class.
title: urange.eps

text:
Methods of the 0D class, in which both u and
u′ are solved for rather than found by numeric
optimization.
title: urange.eps

text:
This includes the method by
Kholshevnikov and Vassiliev (1999b) and by
Gronchi (2002, 2005), because they do not ex-
plicitly deal with any numeric optimization at
all.
title: urange.eps

text:
The task is analytically reduced to solving
a nonlinear equation with respect to u and then
express u′ also analytically.
title: urange.eps

text:
Methods of this
class are ultimately fast but relatively vulner-
able to loosing roots due to numerical errors
(in nearly degenerate cases).
title: urange.eps

text:
This eﬀect be-
comes important because the equation for u is
quite complicated and subject to round-oﬀer-
rors.
title: urange.eps

text:
Also, this equation often have close (al-
most multiple) roots that are always diﬃcult
for numeric processing.
title: urange.eps

text:
Here we present an eﬃcient numeric imple-
mentation of the algebraic approach presented by
Kholshevnikov and Vassiliev (1999b), similar to the
one presented by Gronchi (2002, 2005).
title: urange.eps

text:
This method
belongs to the fast 0D class.
title: urange.eps

text:
It is based on analytic
determination of all the critical points of the distance
function, |r −r′|2, augmented with an algebraic elim-
ination of one of the two positional variables.
title: urange.eps

text:
Math-
ematically, the problem is reduced to a single poly-
nomial equation of 16th degree with respect to one
of the eccentric anomalies.
title: urange.eps

text:
(2018) suggested a method
that does not rely on necessary determination of all
the stationary points for the distance.
title: urange.eps

text:
It basically
splits the problem in two tasks of 1D optimization,
so this method belongs to the 1D class.
title: urange.eps

text:
Neverthe-
less, it proved ∼20 per cent faster than the 0D
Gronchi algorithm, according to the benchmarks.
title: urange.eps

text:
Though the performance diﬀerences appeared rel-
atively moderate, there were revealed occurences
when the Gronchi’s code suﬀered from numeric er-
rors, reporting a wrong value for the MOID.
title: urange.eps

text:
There-
fore, in this task the numeric reliability of the method
is no less important than just the computing speed.
title: urange.eps

text:
Direct
implementation
of
the
methods
by
Kholshevnikov and Vassiliev (1999b) and Gronchi
(2002) might be vulnerable, because ﬁnding roots
of a high-degree polynomial might be a numerical
challenge sometimes.
title: urange.eps

text:
When dealing with large as-
teroid catalogs, various almost-degenerate cases ap-
pear sometimes, if the equations to be solved contain
almost-double or almost-multiple roots.
title: urange.eps

text:
Such roots
are diﬃcult to be estimated accurately, because they
are sensitive to numeric errors (even if there were
no errors in the input orbital elements).
title: urange.eps

text:
Moreover,
we have a risk of ambiguity: if the polynomial has
two or more very close real roots then numeric er-
rors may result in moving them to the complex plane
entirely, so that we may wrongly conclude that there
are no such real roots at all.
title: urange.eps

text:
Such eﬀect of lost of
real roots may potentially result in overestimating the
MOID, i.e.
title: urange.eps

text:
it may appear that we lost exactly the so-
lution corresponding to the global minimum of the
distance.
title: urange.eps

text:
This issue can be solved by paying atten-
tion not only to the roots formally identiﬁed as real,
but also to all complex-valued roots that appear sus-
piciously close to the real axis.
title: urange.eps

text:
To deﬁne formally
what means ‘suspiciously close’ we need to estimate
2


numeric error attached to a given root, not just its
formal value.
title: urange.eps

text:
In other words, our task assignes an increased
role to the numeric stability of the computation,
because errors are known to dramatically increase
when propagating through mathematical degenera-
cies.
title: urange.eps

text:
This motivated us to pay major attention to
error control when implementing the method by
Kholshevnikov and Vassiliev (1999b) in a numerical
algorithm.

Since the number of real roots of g(u) is highly
variable and a priori unknown, certain diﬃculties ap-

text:
In
practice g(u) often becomes close to being degen-

title: urange.eps

text:
in the case of almost circular or almost
coplanar orbits, which is frequent for asteroids and
typical for major planets in the Solar System.
title: urange.eps

text:
In such
cases, real roots of g(u) combine in close pairs or
even close quadruples.
title: urange.eps

text:
The graph of g(u) passes then
close to the abscissa near such roots.
title: urange.eps

text:
This means
that numeric computing errors aﬀect such nearly-
multiple roots considerably, implying increased un-
certainties.
title: urange.eps

text:
Moreover, we might be even uncertain
about the very existence of some roots: does the
graph of g(u) really intersects the abscissa or it passes
slightly away, just nearly touching it?
title: urange.eps

text:
In practice
this question may become non-trivial due to numeri-
cal errors, that might appear important because g(u)
is mathematically complicated.
title: urange.eps

text:
Therefore, treating
g(u) only in the real space might result in loosing its
roots due to numeric errors.
title: urange.eps

mean to vulnerably overestimate the MOID, because
there is a risk that the minimum distance |r−r′| occa-
sionally corresponds to a lost root.

more safe to overestimate the number of real roots of
g(u), i.e.

text:
we should also test “almost-real” complex
roots that correspond to a near-touching behaviour of
g(u), even if it does not apparently intersect the ab-
scissa.

This would imply some computational over-
heads and additional CPU time sacriﬁced for the al-
gorithmic reliability and numeric stability.

would mean to treat g(u) in the complex plane and
ﬁnd all its complex roots, rather than just the real

This

|z| = 1 (such roots do not combine into inverse
pairs), or if zk−1 turns out to be that second root

text:
Then such a starting approximation
would be equal to either zk−1 or zk−2, so the next
extracted root zk will likely appear close to one
of these.
title: urange.eps

text:
Each root is reﬁned by Newtonian iterations (i)
until some least required relative accuracy δmax
is achieved, and then (ii) until we reach the de-
sired target relative accuracy δmin or, at least,
the maximum possible machine accuracy, if
δmin is unreachable.
title: urange.eps

text:
On the ﬁrst phase, we it-
erate until the last Newtonian step |dn| falls be-
low δmax|z|.
title: urange.eps

text:
The iterations are restarted from
a diﬀerent starting point, if they are trapped
in an inﬁnite loop at this phase (this is the
known curse of the Newton method).
title: urange.eps

text:
On the
second phase, the stopping criterion relies on
the last and pre-last Newtonian steps, |dn| and
|dn−1|.
title: urange.eps

text:
The iterations are continued either until
|dn| < δmin|z|, or until the relative step change,
γn = (|dn−1|2 −|dn|2)/|dn|2, drops below the ma-
chine epsilon ǫ.
title: urange.eps

text:
The latter criterion is moti-
vated as follows.
title: urange.eps

text:
In the middle of iterations,
whenever numeric round-oﬀerrors are not sig-
niﬁcant yet, the parameter γn should remain
large positive, since each |dn| is much smaller
than |dn−1|.
title: urange.eps

text:
But in the end either γn →0, if
iterations get ﬁnally stuck at almost the same
numeric value near the root, or γn occasionally
attains negative values, if the iterations start to
randomly jump about the root due to numeric
errors.
title: urange.eps

text:
A good practical assumption for the ac-
curacy parameters might be δmax ∼√ǫ and
δmin = 0 or about ǫ.

text:
Self-testing numerical reliability
Finally, our algorithm includes a self-diagnostic
test that veriﬁes the following post-conditions:
1.
title: urange.eps

text:
All roots that passed (17) must comply with
the requested least accuracy: νεz < δmax.
title: urange.eps

text:
The minimum of ∆z among all the roots that
failed (17) must exceed 10, meaning that there
is no other suspicious root candidates.
title: urange.eps

text:
That
is, the families |z| = 1 and |z| , 1 must be
separated by a clear gap.
title: urange.eps

text:
The number of roots that passed (17) must be
even and greater than four (necessary algebraic
conditions following from the theory).
title: urange.eps

text:
After the 2D reﬁning, the Hessian Hrsd is
strictly positive-deﬁnite, so we indeed are at a
local minimum (rather than maximum or sad-
dle point).
title: urange.eps

text:
On the 2D reﬁning stage, the total cumulative
change in u satisﬁes the condition |∆u| < δmax.
title: urange.eps

text:
In some part this condition duplicates (i), en-
suring the initial approximation of the corre-
sponding root did not appear to have inaccept-
able accuracy.
title: urange.eps

text:
But it also ensures that the 2D
reﬁning did not switch us to a completely dif-
ferent root of g(u) (another stationary point of
ρ).
title: urange.eps

text:
We pay no attention to u′ here, because it is
always derived from u using (4), so its numeric
error, even if large, is not indicative regarding
the selection of a correct root of g(u).
title: urange.eps

text:
If some of these conditions are broken, the algorithm
sets a warning ﬂag.
title: urange.eps

text:
Receiving such a signal, the re-
sults should be considered unreliable.
title: urange.eps

text:
In practice this
is a very seldom case (see next section), but still pos-
sible.
title: urange.eps

text:
Then the following sequence can be done to
verify the results: (i) run the same algorithm on the
same orbits E and E′, but swap them with each other;
(ii) if failed again, run the same algorithm using the
long double precision instead of double; (iii) run the
long double computation on swapped orbits; (iv) if
everything failed, invoke an alternative MOID algo-
rithm, e.g.
title: urange.eps

text:
We notice that since the task is solved asym-
metrically, the algorithm may yield slightly dif-
ferent results when computing MOID(E, E′) and
MOID(E′, E).
title: urange.eps

text:
If the orbital conﬁguration does not
imply degeneracies, both computations should oﬀer
the same MOID value, within the reported uncertain-
ties.
title: urange.eps

text:
If they diﬀer unacceptably, this can serve as an
additional indicator that something went wrong.
title: urange.eps

text:
However, this notice does not apply to the es-
timated MOID uncertainty.
title: urange.eps

text:
This uncertainty can
appear diﬀerent when computing MOID(E, E′) and
MOID(E′, E), because the polynomials g(u) and
g(u′) may have (and usually do have) diﬀerent alge-
braic properties.
title: urange.eps

text:
In fact, if the goal is accuracy rather
than speed, one may always compute the MOID in
the both directions, E →E′ and E′ →E, selecting
the value oﬀering better accuracy.
title: urange.eps

text:
On the choice of error tolerances
The algorithm involves three main parameters re-
lated to the error control: δmin, δmax, and ν.
title: urange.eps

text:
It controls the
resulting accuracy of the roots zk, and of the eccen-
tric anomalies u, u′, but not of the MOID itself and
not even of the adimensional function ρ.
title: urange.eps

text:
By setting
δmin to a larger or smaller value we may obtain less
or more accurate result (in terms of u, u′).
title: urange.eps

text:
We can set
δmin = 0, meaning to seek maximum precision possi-
ble with the hardware (though this probably requires
to use the long double arithmetic, see below).
title: urange.eps

text:
The auxiliary error tolerance δmax does not ac-
tually control the accuracy of the results.
title: urange.eps

text:
Setting a
smaller δmax won’t result in a more numerically ac-
curate MOID estimate.
title: urange.eps

text:
This parameter has two as-
pects: (i) it is used in the root-ﬁnding part to control
the initial ‘burn-in’ stage of the Newton scheme and
(ii) it is used as an indicative threshold to separate
numerically ‘reliable’ cases from ‘unreliable’ ones.
title: urange.eps

text:
Therefore, the common sense requires that δmax
must be greater (preferably, signiﬁcantly greater)
than δmin.
title: urange.eps

text:
Forcing δmax too small may result in the
following undesired eﬀects.
title: urange.eps

text:
First, the Newton root-
ﬁnding scheme may drastically slow down, because
its ‘burn-in’ stage does not expect that it may reach
the machine precision and may otherwise iterate the
roots until the internal iteration limit.
title: urange.eps

text:
The output pre-
cision would then be worse than δmax anyway.
title: urange.eps

text:
Sec-
ondly, too small δmax may trigger an unnecessary in-
crease of the number of the unreliability warnings.
title: urange.eps

text:
Concerning the unreliability warnings, the prac-
tical value of δmax can be selected based on the obser-
vational uncertainty of orbital elements (relative un-
certainty in terms of a, a′ or absolute one in terms of
the angular elements).
title: urange.eps

text:
This input uncertainty is typi-
cally considerably larger than the machine precision.
title: urange.eps

text:
With so-selected δmax, the warning ﬂag would indi-
11


cate that the numeric accuracy of zk might be worse
than the errors inferred by input observational uncer-
tainties.
title: urange.eps

text:
Then the intermediate (inferred by zk) nu-
meric uncertainty of u and u′ may appear larger than
what we can trigger by varying the orbital elements
within their error boxes.
title: urange.eps

text:
In this case the warning is
physically reasonable.
title: urange.eps

text:
But if the numeric uncertainty
always remains below the observational one then sig-
naling any warning does not make sense.
title: urange.eps

text:
In any case, it does not make sense to set δmax
too much below the physical sizes of the objects (rel-
ative to ∼max(a, a′)).
title: urange.eps

text:
For the Main Belt, this is
∼10−11 AU corresponding to the smallest known as-
teroids of ∼1 m in size.
title: urange.eps

text:
If the uncertainty of orbital elements is unknown
or irrelevant than the good choice of δmax is √δmin,
which follows from the properties of the Newton-
Raphson method.
title: urange.eps

text:
In such a case, for each root zk
we need to make just one or two iterations after the
‘burn-in’ part of the Newton scheme.
title: urange.eps

text:
This is because
the number of accurate digits is roughly doubled af-
ter each Newtonian iteration.
title: urange.eps

text:
For example, if the ac-
curacy of √ǫ has been reached, on the next iteration
we will likely have ǫ.
title: urange.eps

text:
As to the last control parameter, ν, it may be
used to manually scale up all the error assessments.
title: urange.eps

text:
So far in our tests we did not ﬁnd practical reasons
to set it to something diﬀerent from ν = 1.
title: urange.eps

text:
But
whenever necessary, it can be used to disentangle
the value δmax used by the Newtonian root-ﬁnding
scheme from the threshold used in the error control
part.
title: urange.eps

text:
Since ν scales all the error estimates up, its ef-
fect is equivalent to reducing the error threshold from
δmax to δmax/ν, but the Newton scheme is always us-
ing δmax and ignores the scale factor ν.
title: urange.eps

text:
Summarizing, it appears that in the general case
it is reasonable to set δmin about the machine epsilon,
δmax ∼√δmin, and to select such ν that δmax/ν is about
the physically justiﬁed MOID uncertainty (relative to
∼max(a, a′)).
title: urange.eps

text:
Practical validation and performance bench-
marks
We tested our algorithm on the ﬁrst 10000 num-
bered asteroids from the Main Belt, implying ∼108
orbit pairs.
title: urange.eps

text:
The orbital elements were taken from the
catalog astorb.dat of the Lowell observatory.4
Our algorithm succeeded nearly always.
title: urange.eps

text:
When
using the standard double ﬂoating-point arithmetic,
the self-test conditions listed above were failed only
once per 25000 orbit pairs.
title: urange.eps

text:
In case of such a warn-
ing the ﬁrst attempt was to rerun the same algo-
rithm interchanging the orbits E and E′.
title: urange.eps

text:
Since
the method treats orbits asymmetrically, this usually
helps.
title: urange.eps

text:
Double-warnings occured in our test once per
2.5 × 106 orbit pairs.
title: urange.eps

text:
We note that if the algorithms returns a bad self-
diagnostic ﬂag, this does not yet mean that it failed
to compute the MOID and the result is necessarily
wrong or just absent.
title: urange.eps

text:
One of the reasons for a warn-
ing is that some root zk (not even necessarily related
to the global minimum) is worse than the required
least accuracy δmax.
title: urange.eps

text:
But worse does not mean neces-
sarily useless.
title: urange.eps

text:
This just means that the result needs
an attention and probably needs a more detailed in-
vestigation using diﬀerent other methods to conﬁrm
or reﬁne the results.
title: urange.eps

Occurences when the resulting
MOID appears entirely wrong and has inacceptable
accuracy, represent only a small fraction of all those
cases when the warning was reported.

the same setting.

We found only two orbit pairs for
which it failed with a error and no-result, and swap-

the ﬁrst attempt to compute MOID failed, but swap-

To accurately measure the time spent purely in-
side just the MOID computation, and not on the ﬁle
IO or other algorithmic decorations around it, we al-
ways performed three independent runs on the test
catalog: (i) an ‘empty’ run without any calls to any
MOID algorithm, only iteration over the catalog; (ii)
computation of all MOIDs using the algorithm of this
paper, without writing results to a ﬁle; (iii) same for
the Gronchi algorithm.

The time diﬀerences (ii)-(i)
or (iii)-(i) gave us the CPU time spent only inside
the MOID computation.

We never included the CPU
time spent in the kernel mode.

nipulation or other similar CPU activity that appears
when the program iteratively accesses data from a
big catalog.

In any case, this system time would be
just a minor addition to the result (∼1 −2 per cent at

The reader may notice that the hardware can gen-

Moreover, even
the performance on the same AMD machine dif-

tests.

diﬀerent number of Newtonian itera-

rather than long double one.

Therefore, our algorithm possibly pretends to be
the fastest one available to date, or at least it belongs
to the family of the fastest ones.

In the majority of
cases it yields considerably more accurate and reli-
able results, usually close to the machine precision,
and its accuracy may seriously degrade only in ex-
traordinary rare nearly degenerate cases, which are
objectively hard to process.

Additional tools
Our main algorithm based on determining the
roots of g(u) is fast but might become vulnerable in
the rare cases of lost roots.
title: urange.eps

text:
Whenever it signals a
warning, alternative algorithms should be used, trad-
ing computing speed for better numeric resistance
with respect to degeneracies.
title: urange.eps

text:
In addition to the basic 0D method based on g(u)
root-ﬁnding, our library implements a “fallback” al-
gorithm of the 1D type, based on the brute force-like
minimization of ˜ρ(u).
title: urange.eps

text:
This method is numerically
reliable thanks to its simplicity, and its slow speed
is not a big disadvantage, because it needs to be run
only if the basic fast method failed.
title: urange.eps

text:
In our bench-
marking test it appeared ∼6 times or ∼4 times
slower than our fast algorithm or the Gronchi code,
respectively.
title: urange.eps

text:
But this is likely sensitive to its input
parameters.

text:
First of all, the algorithm scans only a restricted
range in the u variable, discarding the values where
the MOID cannot be attained.

The requied u range
is determined as follows.

(Kholshevnikov and Vassiliev, 1999a), compute the
minimum internodal distance dΩ.

Since MOID is
usually attained near the orbital nodes, this quantity
and its corresponding orbital positions already pro-
vide rather good approximation to the MOID.

Then
consider two planes parallel to the orbit E′, and sep-

This

The detailed formulae for the re-

Moreover, this algorithm automatically selects
the optimal orbits order (E, E′) or (E′, E) to have a
smaller angular range to scan.

In the case if the cu-
mulative ranges appear equal (e.g.

if we occasion-

the user-supplied order is preserved.

text:
The fraction of
the cases in which this range could not be reduced at
all (remained at [0, 2π]) is only ∼2%, and in the ma-
jority of occurences it could be reduced to something
well below 1 rad.
title: urange.eps

text:
The eﬃciency of the reduction in-
creases if MOID is small.
title: urange.eps

text:
Then the total scan range
may be reduced to just a few degrees.
title: urange.eps

text:
The minimization of ˜ρ(u) is based on subsequent
sectioning of the initial angular range for u.
title: urange.eps

text:
The
user can set an arbitrary sequence of integer num-
bers n1, n2, n3, .
title: urange.eps

text:
, np that deﬁne how many segments
are considered at diﬀerent stages.
title: urange.eps

text:
The initial angular
range is partitioned into n1 equal segments separated
by the equidistant nodes uk, and the node with a min-
imum ˜ρ(uk) is determined.
title: urange.eps

text:
We note that the input pa-
rameter n1 is always interpreted as if it corresponded
to the entire [0, 2π] range, even if the actual scan
range is reduced as described above.
title: urange.eps

text:
The segment
length on the ﬁrst step is normally set to h1 = 2π/n1
regardless of the scan range, unless this scan range
is itself smaller than h1.
title: urange.eps

text:
On the second stage, the
segment [uk−1, uk+1] surrounding the minimum uk is
considered.
title: urange.eps

text:
It is sectioned into n2 equal segments,
and the node corresponding to the minimum ˜ρ(uk)
is determined again.
title: urange.eps

text:
On the third stage, the segment
[uk−1, uk+1] is sectioned into n3 smaller segments, and
so on.
title: urange.eps

text:
On the kth stage, the length of the segment
between subsequent nodes is reduced by the factor
2/nk, so only nk ≥3 are meaningful.
title: urange.eps

text:
Starting from
the stage number p, the segments are always parti-
tioned into np subsegments, until the global mini-
mum of ˜ρ(u) is located with a desired accuracy in
u and ρ.
title: urange.eps

text:
It is recommended to set n1 large enough,
e.g.
title: urange.eps

text:
∼1000, in order to sample the objective func-
tion with its potentially intricate variations densely
enough, whereas the last np can be set to 4, meaning
the bisection.
title: urange.eps

text:
We notice that this method was not designed for
a standalone use.
title: urange.eps

text:
It was not even supposed to be ei-
ther more reliable or more accurate in general than
our primary fast method.
title: urange.eps

text:
It was supposed to pro-
vide just yet another alternative in rare special cases
when the primary method did not appear convinc-
ingly reliable.
title: urange.eps

text:
Its practical reliability depends on the
input parameters very much: too small n1 may lead
to frequent loosing of local minima in ˜ρ(u), if they
are narrow.
title: urange.eps

text:
Hence we may miss the correct global
minimum sometimes.
title: urange.eps

text:
But this eﬀect can be always
suppressed by selecting a larger n1.
title: urange.eps

text:
In our tests,
with n1 = 1000 this algorithm generated one wrong
MOID per ∼3000 trials, so it is not recommended
for a general sole use.
title: urange.eps

text:
This could be improved by
implementing an adaptive sampling in the u variable,
e.g.
title: urange.eps

text:
depending on the derivative |˜ρ′|, but we did not
plan to go that far with this method.
title: urange.eps

text:
We note that
narrow local minima of ρ are, informally speaking,
in some sense antagonistic to almost-multiple crit-
ical points, so this fallback algorithm is vulnerable
to rather diﬀerent conditions than our primary fast
16


method.
title: urange.eps

text:
Therefore it can serve as a good comple-
ment to the latter.
title: urange.eps

text:
Also, we include in the library several fast tools
that may appear useful whenever we need to actu-
ally compute the MOID only for those object that are
close to an orbital intersection.
title: urange.eps

text:
These tools may help
to eliminate most of the orbit pairs from the process-
ing.
title: urange.eps

text:
The ﬁrst one represents an obvious pericenter–
apocenter test: MOID ≥a(1 −e) −a′(1 + e′), and
MOID ≥a′(1 −e′) −a(1 + e).
title: urange.eps

text:
If any of these quanti-
ties appeared positive and above some upper thresh-
old MOIDmax then surely MOID > MOIDmax, and
one may immediately discard such orbital pair from
the detailed analysis.
title: urange.eps

text:
Our library also includes functions for comput-
ing the so-called linking coeﬃcients introduced by
Kholshevnikov and Vassiliev (1999a).
title: urange.eps

text:
The linking
coeﬃcients are functions of two orbits that have the
dimension of squared distance, like |r −r′|2 = 2aa′ρ,
and they are invariable with respect to rotations in
R3.
title: urange.eps

text:
Kholshevnikov and Vassiliev (1999a) introduced
three linking coeﬃcients that should be selected de-
pending on whether the orbits are (nearly) coplanar
or not.
title: urange.eps

text:
See all the necessary formulae and discussion
in that work.
title: urange.eps

text:
For our goals it might be important that at least
one of these linking coeﬃcients, l1 = d1d2, can
be used as an upper limit on the MOID.
title: urange.eps

text:
It repre-
sents a signed product of two internodal distances
from (A.6), so the squared MOID can never be larger
than |l1|.
title: urange.eps

text:
This allows us to limit the MOID from an-
other side, contrary to the pericenter-apocenter test.
title: urange.eps

text:
Moreover, based on l1 we introduce yet another link-
ing coeﬃcient deﬁned as
l′
1 = min (|d1|, |d2|)2 sign l1.
title: urange.eps

text:
(45)
This modiﬁed l1 provides even tighter upper limit on
the squared MOID, but still preserves the sign that
indicates the orbital linkage in the same way as l1
did.
title: urange.eps

text:
It is important for us that all linking coeﬃcients
are computed very quickly in comparison to any
MOID algorithm, because they are expressed by sim-
ple elementary formulae.
title: urange.eps

text:
The linking coeﬃcients were named so because
their original purpose was to indicate whether two or-
bits are topologically linked like two rings in a chain,
or not.
title: urange.eps

text:
The intermediate case between these two is
an intersection, when the linking coeﬃcient vanishes
together with the MOID.
title: urange.eps

text:
Therefore, these indicators
can be potentially used as computationally cheap sur-
rogates of the MOID.
title: urange.eps

text:
But in addition to measuring
the closeness of two orbits to an intersection, linking
coeﬃcients carry information about their topologi-
cal conﬁguration.
title: urange.eps

text:
Also, these quantities can be used
to track the time evolution of the mutual topology of
perturbed non-Keplerian orbits, for example to locate
the moment of their intersection without computing
the MOID.

Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based on

Burak Bartan and Mert Pilanci
Department of Electrical Engineering

Email: {bbartan, pilanci}@stanford.edu
Abstract—We propose a serverless computing mechanism
for distributed computation based on polar codes.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Serverless
computing is an emerging cloud based computation model
that lets users run their functions on the cloud without pro-
visioning or managing servers.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Our proposed approach is a
hybrid computing framework that carries out computationally
expensive tasks such as linear algebraic operations involving
large-scale data using serverless computing and does the rest
of the processing locally.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
We address the limitations and relia-
bility issues of serverless platforms such as straggling workers
using coding theory, drawing ideas from recent literature on
coded computation.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The proposed mechanism uses polar codes
to ensure straggler-resilience in a computationally effective
manner.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
We provide extensive evidence showing polar codes
outperform other coding methods.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
We have designed a sequen-
tial decoder speciﬁcally for polar codes in erasure channels
with full-precision input and outputs.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In addition, we have
extended the proposed method to the matrix multiplication case
where both matrices being multiplied are coded.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The proposed
coded computation scheme is implemented for AWS Lambda.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Experiment results are presented where the performance of the
proposed coded computation technique is tested in optimization
via gradient descent.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Finally, we introduce the idea of partial
polarization which reduces the computational burden of encod-
ing and decoding at the expense of straggler-resilience.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
INTRODUCTION
Computations for large-scale problems on the cloud might
require a certain level of expertise for managing servers, and
certainly requires conﬁguration of resources ahead of time.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
It might be challenging to estimate beforehand exactly how
much RAM, storage, and time a certain problem requires.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
For server-based computing on the cloud, users have to
manage these conﬁgurations which if not done right, costs
more money for users.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Serverless computing, on the other
hand, emerges as a platform simpler to use with much less
overhead.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Serverless functions offer an alternative to large-
scale computing with a lot to offer in terms of cost and speed.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In this work, we work with a mechanism based on server-
less computing that enables users to run their computations
in their computers except whenever there is a large-scale
matrix multiplication, the computation is done in parallel
in a serverless computing platform.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The key advantages of
this mechanism that may not be available in server-based
approaches are:
• When serverless functions are not being used (during
some local computations in an algorithm), since there
are no servers running, users do not pay for the resources
they do not use.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
• The serverless approach has the ease of running the
overall algorithm in your own machine with only
computationally-heavy parts running on the cloud and
returning their outputs to your local machine for further
manipulation.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
• It is possible to request different numbers of serverless
functions in different stages of the algorithm.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
This might
be cost-effective when running algorithms with varying
computational loads.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Along with these advantages, serverless computing comes
with certain limitations for resources such as RAM and
lifetime.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
For instance, for AWS Lambda, each function can
have a maximum of 3 GB of RAM and has a lifetime up
to 15 minutes.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
A mechanism based on serverless computing
must take these limitations into account.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
One problem that serverless computing platforms and
server-based platforms have in common is that a portion
of the functions (or workers) might ﬁnish their task later
than the others (these slower workers are often referred to
as stragglers), and this may cause the overall output to be
delayed if no precaution is taken.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Furthermore, it is not
uncommon in serverless computing for a function to return
nothing because functions can crash due to the lifetime
constraint or for other reasons.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The straggler issue could be
more problematic in the case of serverless computing than in
server-based computing.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
For instance, if we assume that each
function will straggle with a given probability independent
of other functions, the probability that there will be at least
one straggling function increases as the number of functions
increases.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Since each function can have a limited amount
of memory, large-scale computations usually require many
functions to run in parallel.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
To overcome the issue of straggling functions, we use the
idea of inserting redundancy to computations using codes.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
This idea has been explored in the literature by many works
such as [9], [2], [14] for dealing with stragglers encountered
in distributed computation.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Codes not only help speed up
computations by making it possible to compute the desired
output without waiting for the outputs of the straggling
workers, but also provide resilience against crashes and
timeouts, leading to a more reliable mechanism.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
arXiv:1901.06811v2  [cs.IT]  13 Jul 2019


A straggler-resilient scheme designed for a serverless
computing platform needs to be scalable as we wish to allow
the number of functions to vary greatly.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Two things become
particularly important if the number of workers is as high
as hundreds or thousands.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The ﬁrst one is that encoding and
decoding must be low complexity.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The second one is that
one must be careful with the numerical round-off errors if the
inputs are not from a ﬁnite ﬁeld, but instead are full-precision
real numbers.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
To clarify this point, when the inputs are real-
valued, encoding and decoding operations introduce round-
off errors.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Polar codes show superiority over many codes
in terms of both of these aspects.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
They have low encoding
and decoding complexity and both encoding and decoding
involve a small number of subtraction and addition operations
(no multiplications involved in encoding or decoding).
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In
addition, they achieve capacity, and the importance of that
fact in coded computation is that the number of worker
outputs needed for decoding is asymptotically optimal.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
An Important Difference Between Server-Based and
Serverless Computing
We should note one important difference between using
serverless and server-based computing that helps highlight
the usefulness of polar codes.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In server-based computing,
one needs to use much fewer machines than the number of
functions one would need in serverless computing to achieve
the same amount of computing.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The reason for this is the
limited resources each function can have in serverless com-
puting.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Hence, the number of functions is usually expected
to be high, depending on the scale of the computation.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
This
is an important design criterion that needs to be addressed
as it necessitates efﬁcient encoding and decoding algorithms
for the code we are using.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
For instance, for a distributed
server-based system with N = 8 machines, using maximum
distance separable (MDS) codes with decoding complexity
as high as O(N 3) could still be acceptable.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
This becomes
unacceptable when we switch to a serverless system as
the number of functions that achieve the same amount of
computations could go up as high as a few hundreds.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In this
case, it becomes necessary to use codes with fast decoders
such as polar codes.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Even though polar codes do not have the MDS code
properties, as the block-length of the code increases (i.e.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
more
functions are used), the performance gap between polar codes
and MDS codes closes.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
We further discuss this point in the
Numerical Results section.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Related Work
Coded matrix multiplication has been introduced in [9]
for speeding up distributed matrix-vector multiplication in
server-based computing platforms.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
[9] has shown that it is
possible to speed up distributed matrix multiplication by us-
ing codes (MDS codes in particular) to avoid waiting for the
slowest nodes.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
MDS codes however have the disadvantage
of having high encoding and decoding complexity, which
could be restricting in setups with large number of workers.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
[2] attacks at this problem presenting a coded computation
scheme based on d-dimensional product codes.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
[14] presents
a scheme referred to as polynomial codes for coded matrix
multiplication with input matrices from a large ﬁnite ﬁeld.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
This approach might require quantization for real-valued
inputs which could introduce additional numerical issues.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
[4] and [15] are other works investigating coded matrix
multiplication and provide analysis on the optimal number
of worker outputs required.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In addition to the coding theo-
retic approaches, [6] offers an approximate straggler-resilient
matrix multiplication scheme where the ideas of sketching
and straggler-resilient distributed matrix multiplication are
brought together.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Using Luby Transform (LT) codes, a type of rateless
fountain codes, in coded computation has been recently
proposed in [11] and [10].
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The proposed scheme in [10]
divides the overall task into smaller tasks (each task is a
multiplication of a row of A with x) for better load-balancing.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The work [11] proposes the use of inactivation decoding and
the work [10] uses peeling decoder.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Peeling decoder has a
computational complexity of O(N log N) (same complexity
as the decoder we propose), however its performance is not
satisfactory if the number of inputs symbols is not very large.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Inactivation decoder performs better than the peeling decoder,
however, it is not as fast as the peeling decoder.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
There has been some recent work on serverless computing
for machine learning training.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In [7], serverless machine
learning training is discussed in detail, and challenges and
possible solutions for designing serverless machine training
are provided.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Authors in [5] consider an architecture with
multiple master nodes and state that for small neural network
models, serverless computing helps speed up hyperparameter
tuning.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Similarly, the work in [13] shows via experiments that
their prototype on AWS Lambda can reduce model training
time greatly.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Main Contributions
This work investigates the use of serverless computing
for large-scale computations with a solution to the issue of
stragglers based on polar codes.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
We identify that polar codes
are a natural choice for coded computation with serverless
computing due to their low complexity encoding and decod-
ing.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Furthermore, we propose a sequential decoder for polar
codes designed to work with full-precision data for erasure
channels.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The proposed decoder is different from successive
cancellation (SC) decoder given in [1], which is for discrete
data and is based on estimation using likelihoods.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
We also
analytically justify the use of the polar code kernel that we
used in this work when the inputs and outputs are not from
a ﬁnite ﬁeld but are full-precision real-valued data.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Next, we
discuss the polarization of distributions of worker run times
and provide some numerical results to that end.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
This provides
some important insights towards understanding polarization
phenomenon in a setting other than communication.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Given the work of [9], it is not very surprising that any
linear code like polar codes could also be used in coded
computation.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The main novelty of this work lies in the design
of a mechanism based on serverless computing that is easy


to use and can handle large-scale data.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
We adopt coded
computation as the tool to make the mechanism more resilient
and reliable, and polar codes are our choice of code to ensure
scalability.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Differently from other erasure codes, polar codes offer
a very interesting interpretation in terms of run times of
machines due to the polarization phenomenon.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
By bringing
together a number of machines in polar code construction,
we achieve virtually transformed machines with polarized run
times.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
To clarify, the polar coding transformation polarizes
the run times of the workers, that is, as a result of the
transformation, we will obtain faster and slower transformed
machines.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
This interpretation is equivalent to channels po-
larizing when polar codes are used for channel coding in
communications [1].
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
If we set the rate to 1 −ϵ, then we
choose the best N(1 −ϵ) machines out of the N machines
as the data machines whereas the remaining machines are
frozen (i.e.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
DISCUSSION ON FAST DECODERS FOR MDS CODES
Most works in coded computation literature employ MDS
codes as their way of inserting redundancy into computa-
tions.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Decoding in the case of Reed-Solomon codes and
full-precision data requires solving a linear system.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In the
case where one wishes to work with full-precision data, the


decoding becomes expensive (using Gaussian elimination it
takes O(n3) operations) and in addition gets unstable for
systems with high number of workers since the linear system
to be solved is a Vandermonde based linear system.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
There are many works that restrict their schemes to work-
ing with values from a ﬁnite ﬁeld of some size q.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In that
case, it is possible to use fast decoding algorithms which are
based on fast algorithms for polynomial interpolation.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
One
such decoding algorithm is given in [12], which provides
O(n log n) encoding and decoding algorithms for Reed-
Solomon erasure codes based on Fermat Number Transform
(FNT).
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
The complexity for the encoder is the same as taking
a single FNT transform and for the decoder, it is equal
to taking 8 FNT transforms.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
To compare with polar codes,
polar codes require n log n operations for both encoding and
decoding.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Another work where a fast erasure decoder for
Reed-Solomon codes is presented is [3] which presents a
decoder that works in time O(n log2 n).
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
There exist many other fast decoding algorithms for RS
codes with complexities as low as O(n log n).
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
However,
the decoding process in these algorithms usually requires
taking a fast transform (e.g.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
FNT) many times and are
limited to ﬁnite ﬁelds.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Often these fast decoding algorithms
have big hidden constants in their complexity and hence
quadratic time decoding algorithms are sometimes preferred
over them.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Polar codes, on the other hand, provide very
straightforward and computationally inexpensive encoding
and decoding algorithms.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
One of our contributions is the
design of an efﬁcient decoder for polar codes tailored for
the erasure channel that can decode full-precision data.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
PARTIAL CONSTRUCTION
In this section, we introduce a new idea that we refer to
as partial construction.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Let us assume we are interested in
computing Ax where we only encode A and not x.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
If the
data matrix A is very large, it might be challenging to encode
it.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
A way around having to encode a large A is to consider
partial code constructions, that is, for A = [AT
1 , ..., AT
p ]T , we
encode each submatrix Ai separately.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
It follows that decoding
the outputs of the construction for the submatrix Ai will
give us Aix.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
This results in a weaker straggler resilience,
however, we get a trade-off between the computational load
of encoding and straggler resilience.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Partial construction
also decreases the computations required for decoding since
instead of decoding a code with N outputs (of complexity
O(N log N)), now we need to decode p codes with
N
p
outputs, which is of total complexity O(N log( N
p )).
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In addition, partial construction makes it possible to
parallel compute both encoding and decoding.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Each code
construction can be encoded and decoded independently from
the rest of the constructions.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Partial construction idea can also be applied to coded
computation schemes based on other codes.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
For instance, one
scenario where this idea is useful is when one is interested in
using RS codes with full-precision data.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Given that for large
N values, using RS codes with full-precision data becomes
impossible, one can construct many smaller size codes.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
When
the code size is small enough, solving a Vandermonde-based
linear system can be painlessly done.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In-Memory Encoding
Another beneﬁt of the partial construction idea is that
for constructions of sizes small enough, encoding can be
performed in the memory of the workers after reading the
necessary data.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
This results in a straggler-resilient scheme
without doing any pre-computing to encode the entire dataset.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In-memory encoding could be useful for problems where the
data matrix A also is also changing over time because it
might be too expensive to encode the entire dataset A every
time it changes.

Then, in each
iteration of the gradient descent, the master node decodes
the downloaded outputs, updates xt, sends the updated xt to
AWS S3 and initializes the computation AT Axt.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
In the case
of uncoded computation, we simply divide the multiplication
task among N(1−ϵ) serverless functions, and whenever all of
the N(1 −ϵ) functions ﬁnish their computations, the outputs
are downloaded to the master node, and there is no decoding.

Then, master node computes and sends the updated xt, and
initializes the next iteration.

Note that in a given iteration, while computation with polar

text:
Note that
in coded computation we pay for N serverless functions,
and in uncoded computation we pay for N(1 −ϵ) serverless
functions.
title: Straggler Resilient Serverless Computing Based Polar Codes

text:
Using ϵ as a tuning parameter for redundancy, we
achieve different convergence times.

Abstract
In this study, a cluster-computing environment is employed
as a computational platform.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
In order to increase the efﬁ-
ciency of the system, a dynamic task scheduling algorithm is
proposed, which balances the load among the nodes of the
cluster.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The technique is dynamic, nonpreemptive, adaptive,
and it uses a mixed centralised and decentralised policies.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
Based on the divide and conquer principle, the algorithm
models the cluster as hyper-grids and then balances the
load among them.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
Recursively, the hyper-grids of dimen-
sion k are divided into grids of dimensions k −1, until the
dimension is 1.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
Then, all the nodes of the cluster are almost
equally loaded.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The optimum dimension of the hyper-grid is
chosen in order to achieve the best performance.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The sim-
ulation results show the effective use of the algorithm.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
In
addition, we determined the critical points (lower bounds)
in which the algorithm can to be triggered.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
1
Introduction
A computational cluster (CC) can be deﬁned as a set of in-
dependent computers (workstations, PCs, etc.) intercon-
nected by a high-speed communication network such as
Fast or Giga Ethernet [9].
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The number of the participat-
ing processing elements or nodes can range from tens to
hundreds [1, 3, 14, 17].
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
However, to fully exploit and ef-
fectively use any CC platform, resource management soft-
ware must be provided to manage the complexity of dif-
ferent physical architectures for the user.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
This complex-
ity arises in managing communication, synchronisation and
scheduling a large number of tasks, in dealing with porta-
bility of libraries facilities used to parallelise/distribute user
applications, and in many other related issues [13].
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The
scheduling of the submitted tasks to processing-nodes is a
major concern with regard to performance and effective use
of any CC.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The problem of ﬁnding an optimal solution to
the scheduling problem is NP-complete [16], where heuris-
tic methods appear to be a suitable approach to solve this
class of problems [15].
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
Scheduling tasks on computational clusters can be divided
into two main classes:
static and dynamic.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
In static
scheduling, information regarding tasks’ execution times
and nodes’ resources is assumed to be known beforehand.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The assignment of tasks to processing nodes is done in such
a way that the communication and the execution time of the
whole application is minimised.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
While, dynamic schedul-
ing techniques are based on the tasks assignment during
their execution, taking into account over-loaded and under-
loaded nodes, with the assumption that if the load among
all nodes is balanced, then the overall execution time of the
application is minimised.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
Here, the system has to decide,
according to some centralised or distributed information,
whether a task has to be transferred or not and to which
node should be transferred [2, 6, 7, 8, 12].
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
In this paper, we propose a dynamic task scheduling tech-
nique based on ”divide and conquer” principle.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
During the ﬁrst phase the
network is mapped onto a hyper-grid.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The second phase
deals with the redistribution of tasks among the nodes by
dividing the hyper-grid into hyper-grids of smaller dimen-
sion.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
Recursively, the load balanced hyper-grids of dimen-
sion k are divided again into hyper-grids of k−1 dimension,
until their dimensionality is equal to 1.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The proposed tech-
nique is dynamic, mixed, nonpreemptive, and adaptive [5],
and fully distributed.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The transfer and placement decisions
constitute the output of the technique.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The paper is organised as follows: In the next two sections
the mathematical models of both network and tasks are pre-
sented.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
In section 4, we present our dynamic load schedul-
ing technique.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The section 5 discusses the performance is-
sues of the technique and gives an example.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The simulation
results are given in section 6 and ﬁnally, concluding remarks
and the future work are given in section 7.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
2
System Model & Hyper-Grids
A Computational Cluster (CC) is a collection of indepen-
dent processing-nodes interconnected by a network.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
We as-

• Each node vi is autonomous, has a full information on

• There are two parameters associated with each task ti:
1) the number of work units (in terms of computations)
within the task (βi), and 2) the number of packets re-

2.1
Hyper-Grids
Usually, a computational cluster has an irregular topol-
ogy.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
This topology can be described by non-oriented graph
G(V, E), where V represents the cluster nodes and E the set
of links between nodes.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The ﬁrst phase of this technique is
to embed (map) the graph G(V, E) into a multi-dimensional
grid, called hyper-grid.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The resulting grid is usually incom-

and/or nodes are missing.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The missing links and nodes are
called virtual links and virtual nodes respectively.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The sec-

the original hyper-grid into hyper-grids of smaller dimen-
sions.

of the same dimensions starting from 1-dimension.

formance, introduces additional overhead in both computa-
tions and communications, due to its execution.

nique is considered to be worth implementing if its over-
head is smaller than gained performance.

Conclusion
We proposed a new task scheduling mechanism for comput-
ing clusters, called PSTS.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
The PSTS algorithm is based on
the PSLB algorithm, a pure dynamic load-balancing tech-
nique.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
We studied its cost and performance in both theoret-
ically and experimentally.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
Is is shown that PSTS is highly
parallel and efﬁcient.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
It was shown from the crossover-
points that PSTS can be used for very low imbalance sys-
tems.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
In addition, PSTS can be used as a scheduler for new
tasks arriving to the system.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
Further extension of this study will be at system level; for
instance, include irregular networks where the routing prob-
lem will be the main issue.
title: Dynamic task scheduling in computing cluster environments

text:
We would like also to extend
this work to tasks which are node oriented and having de-
pendencies between them.
