Anomaly Detection in High Performance Computers:
A Vicinity Perspective
Siavash Ghiasvand† and Florina M.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Ciorba∗
†Technische Universit¨at Dresden, Germany
∗University of Basel, Switzerland
Abstract—In response to the demand for higher computational
power, the number of computing nodes in high performance
computers (HPC) increases rapidly.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Exascale HPC systems are
expected to arrive by 2020.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
With drastic increase in the number
of HPC system components, it is expected to observe a sudden
increase in the number of failures which, consequently, poses a
threat to the continuous operation of the HPC systems.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Detecting
failures as early as possible and, ideally, predicting them, is a
necessary step to avoid interruptions in HPC systems operation.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Anomaly detection is a well-known general purpose approach
for failure detection, in computing systems.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The majority of
existing methods are designed for speciﬁc architectures, require
adjustments on the computing systems hardware and software,
need excessive information, or pose a threat to users’ and systems’
privacy.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
This work proposes a node failure detection mechanism
based on a vicinity-based statistical anomaly detection approach
using passively collected and anonymized system log entries.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Application of the proposed approach on system logs collected
over 8 months indicates an anomaly detection precision between
62% to 81%.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
INTRODUCTION
In response to the demand for higher computational power,
the number of components in high performance computers
(HPC) rapidly increases [1].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
It is expected that Exascale HPC
systems become available by 2020 [2].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Besides increasing the
quantity of computing resources, achieving high performance
is also dependent on the optimized utilization of available
resources, as well as on the continuous operation of the HPC
system as a whole.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Over the past decades, scientists proposed
various methods and algorithms to adjust the workload on HPC
systems to achieve the highest possible performance.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
With the
drastic increase in the number of HPC system components, it is
expected to observe a sudden increase in the number of failures
which consequently poses a threat to the continuous operation
of the HPC systems [3].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, detecting failures as early
as possible and, ideally, predicting them, is a necessary step
to avoid interruptions in continuous HPC systems operation.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
A failure in general is an (observed) incorrect behavior with
respect to the expected behavior.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Failures can be observed and
analyzed at different granularities, from a single transistor to
an entire HPC system.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Nodes are the smallest units in HPC
systems that have a fully functional computational software
stack and can be added or removed from HPC systems with
minimum side-effects on the other computing units.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore,
the granularity of failure detection in this work is set at the
node level.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Heterogeneity of computing nodes, as well as
the topology of HPC systems, are other effective factors that
inﬂuence the overall system performance.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In accordance with
node-related effective factors such as physical location, role
in the cluster, computational workload, hardware properties,
and so forth, various categorizations of computing nodes are
possible.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Hereafter, the term vicinity is used to refer to nodes
that exhibit similar properties such as the ones mentioned
above.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The concept of vicinity deﬁnes new dimensions of
node correlation, beyond the natural temporal and spatial
correlations.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Subsection II-A provides examples and describes
the vicinity of the nodes in more detail.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
An anomaly is an (observed) unexpected behavior with
respect to the expected behavior.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In contrast to failures, un-
expected behaviors are not necessarily incorrect behaviors.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Anomaly detection is a well-known general purpose approach
for detecting failures in computing systems [4].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In HPC
systems, system log analysis can be used for anomaly detection
for the purpose of preventing failures [5]–[8].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
All HPC systems
on the current TOP500 [9] list are Linux-based.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore,
they all generate system log (Syslog) [10] messages by default.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The goal of this work is to detect node failures via analyzing
fully anonymized system logs using a vicinity-based statistical
anomaly detection approach.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The use-case of this study is a
production Petascale HPC system, called Taurus1.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In addition to technical data, system log entries contain sen-
sitive data about the system and its users.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, addressing
the data privacy [11] concerns is a fundamental requirement
of any mechanism that detects anomalies on production HPC
systems via system log analysis.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The anonymization of system
log entries, prior to performing Syslog analysis while retaining
useful data, addresses the data privacy concerns [12].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In this work, the Taurus nodes are ﬁrst categorized into
four different vicinities based on similarities they exhibit in
terms of (1) hardware architecture, (2) resource allocation,
(3) physical location, and (4) time of failures.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Then, the
anomalies are detected within each vicinity.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Subsequently, the
effectiveness of performing anomaly detection in each vicinity
for the purpose of failure detection is compared and discussed.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
To assess the usefulness of the proposed method of anomaly
detection on anonymized data, a copy of 8 months of Taurus
system logs was anonymized via the PaRS [13] anonymization
mechanism and the anonymized system logs were used as the
input data.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The main contributions of this work are: (1) proposing a
node failure detection mechanism via a vicinity-based statis-
tical anomaly detection approach that employs a passive data
collection approach, as well as (2) analyzing the effectiveness
of anomaly detection method in various vicinities using the
8 months of Taurus HPC cluster system logs.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In addition,
1https://doc.zih.tu-dresden.de/hpc-wiki/bin/view/Compendium/SystemTaurus
arXiv:1906.04550v1  [cs.DC]  11 Jun 2019


(3) to the best of our knowledge this is the ﬁrst work on
anomaly detection that is capable of utilizing both original and
anonymized Syslog entries with a high degree of equivalence
between the analysis results.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text: The remainder of this work is organized as follows.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The
node vicinities, data sources, and anonymization method are
introduced in Subsections II-A, II-B, and II-C respectively.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The method to identify node failures employed in this work is
described in Subsection II-D.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The proposed anomaly detection
method is described in detail in Subsection II-E.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The impact
of anomaly detection in different node vicinities is analyzed
in Section III.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The background and current related works are
introduced in Section IV.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Finally, the work is concluded and
future work directions are discussed in Section V.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
PROPOSED ANOMALY DETECTION METHODOLOGY
Taurus is an HPC cluster composed of 2,046 computing
nodes.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The computing nodes are organized in 6 islands based
on their hardware properties2.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Figure 1 provides a schematic
illustration of the Taurus node topology.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Each letter represents
a single computing node.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Nodes with identical colors are of
identical hardware (processing unit) architecture.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Vicinities
Computing nodes with similar characteristics are consid-
ered to be in the vicinity of each other.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Node characteristics
include any physical, spatial, temporal, or logical properties
of the computing nodes.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
A group of computing nodes located
in the same rack, performing different tasks of the same job,
or sharing a common resource (e.g., ﬁle system, power supply
unit), are all examples of nodes in the vicinity of each other.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The concept of vicinity deﬁnes new dimensions of node
correlation, beyond the natural temporal and spatial correla-
tions.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Each vicinity can be imagined as a new dimension in
which two separated entities (nodes) become correlated.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
For
example, points A : (1, 10) and B : (4, 6) in a 2D Cartesian
representation are separated by a distance of 4 −1 = 3 on the
X axis and 10−6 = 4 on the Y axis, respectively.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Deﬁning the
new dimension Z, according to a common (but so far unseen)
feature of A and B would result in a 3D representation of
A : (1, 10, 5) and B : (4, 6, 5).
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In the new 3D representation, even though A and B
are still separated on X and Y , their distance on the dimension
Z will be 5 −5 = 0.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In another word, A and B will be in the
vicinity of each other from the Z axis perspective.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In this work, node vicinities are observed from four dif-
ferent perspectives: (1) hardware architecture, (2) resource
allocation, (3) physical location, and (4) time of failure.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The
ﬁrst perspective denotes a node vicinity according to the node’s
physical properties, the second perspective emphasizes the
node’s logical properties, while the third and fourth perspec-
tives denote spatial and temporal properties, respectively.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
All
other correlations among nodes can be mapped onto these
four proposed vicinities, e.g., nodes connected to a single
switch can be mapped onto the physical location vicinity.

title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Node colors represent
the dominant processing unit type of a node.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Thick border lines indicate the
6 islands of Taurus.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Subsections II-A1, II-A2, II-A3, and II-A4 these four vicinities
are explained in more detail, based on the Taurus architecture.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The node vicinities are intended to mitigate the major char-
acteristic differences between nodes.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, in cases that
several parameters inﬂuence a certain node’s characteristic, the
most dominant parameter is considered to identify the node’s
vicinity.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
All nodes in island 2 beside their Sandy bridge or
Haswell CPUs are equipped with graphical processing units
(GPU).
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Since the majority of jobs submitted to island 2
mainly utilize GPUs rather than CPUs, GPUs are considered
as dominant processing units of these nodes.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, in this
work, island 2 is considered as a homogeneous GPU island,
despite the heterogeneity of its nodes’ CPUs.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
It is important to emphasize that in the context of this
work, two nodes in the vicinity of each other are not neces-
sarily physically co-located.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In fact, they may even belong to
physically separated partitions of the HPC system.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
1) Hardware Architecture Vicinity: Computing nodes on
Taurus may be of 4 different processors architectures: Intel
Haswell, Broadwell, Sandy Bridge, and Westmere.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
108 nodes
with Sandy Bridge and Haswell processors are also equipped
with GPUs (NVIDIA Tesla K20X and K80).
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
According to their
hardware architectures, the 2,046 computing nodes on Taurus
can be divided into 5 categories.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The node’s dominant proces-
sor architecture and the number of nodes in each architecture
category are shown in Table I.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
A schematic illustration of the
Taurus topology, including the type of each node’s hardware
architecture is provided in Figure 1.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Nodes with identical
colors in Figure 1 are in the vicinity of each other from
the hardware architecture perspective.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
2) Resource
Allocation
Vicinity:
Taurus
employs
Slurm [14] for job scheduling.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The submitted jobs are
allocated resources based on direct requests of the users,
system policies, and the status of available resources.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
All
nodes that execute tasks of the same job are in the vicinity
of each other from the resource allocation perspective.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In contrast to the static nature of the hardware architecture
vicinity perspective, the resource allocation vicinity is fully
dynamic and may change frequently as the running jobs are
completed and new jobs are submitted to the cluster.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
3) Physical Location Vicinity: Various granularities can be
used to express the physical location of a node in Taurus,
e.g., chassis, rack, or island.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Since the power, temperature, and
connectivity of all nodes located in a single rack are controlled
together, this work considers racks as the physical location
granularity.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Each row of an island shown in Figure 1 represents
one rack of nodes.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
All nodes located in the same rack are
in the vicinity of each other from the physical location
perspective.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
4) Time of Failure Vicinity: Often failure is a consequence
of various node-level events on and of properties of several
nodes.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
However, a failure in itself is observable on a particular
node at a speciﬁc moment.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, the time of failure
is considered as a temporal property of that particular node
even though, several nodes may fail due to the same reason.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
From this perspective, all nodes that experience a failure
within the same predeﬁned time interval, fall into the
same vicinity category.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In this work, the time of failure
interval considered is 10 minutes.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The 10-minute time interval
is chosen according to the results of the previous study on
Taurus failure correlations [8].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
That study revealed that the
majority of failures correlated on Taurus occurred within 10
minutes of each other.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, failures that occur across the
entire system within 10 minutes of each other are assumed to
be in the same temporal vicinity.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Thus, the nodes on which
such failures occur are in the vicinity of each other from the
time of failure perspective.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Data Sources
System logs represent the main data source in this work.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Syslogs of Taurus were collected for a period of one year
from January to December 2017.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Syslog daemons on each
node collected the system log entries and forwarded them
to a central log collector.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
To maintain the neutrality of the
results and to provide a general approach, the pre-conﬁgured
Syslog daemons were used without any changes, except for
being conﬁgured to forward Syslog entries to the central log
collector.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In addition to Syslog entries, three other data sources were
considered to improve the accuracy of the failure identiﬁcation
method: outage database, service notiﬁcations, and job status
reports.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The outage database reports all system outages from
the users’ perspective, the service notiﬁcations notify users
regarding future scheduled maintenances and system-wide
outages, and the job status reports indicate the ﬁnal status of
a job after its execution.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Table II provides an overview of the
four data sources used in this work.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
There are certain data gaps in the four data sources used in
this work.

Anonymization of System Logs
System log entries contain sensitive data about the system
and its users.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, addressing data privacy concerns is
a fundamental requirement of any mechanism that performs
system log analysis.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The anonymization of system log entries,
prior to performing Syslog analysis, addresses the data privacy
concerns.

text:
Taurus Node Failures
To assess the proposed method’s functionality, all Taurus
node failures must be known.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Due to various technical reasons,
the complete list of all node failures on Taurus for the period
of this work is not available.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
This step is aimed to provide a
complete list of Taurus node failures as the ground truth for
further analysis and comparisons in Section III.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Node failures in computing systems can be divided into
two main categories according to their root causes: (1) Failures
that occur during the normal operation of the HPC system
caused by internal factors, such as software and hardware
errors or race conditions (i.e., regular failures).
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
(2) Failures
that occur due to external factors, such as power outages and
human errors.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Analyzing the impact of the external causes of
node failures requires additional information regarding external
factors that are not available, e.g., detailed information about
the behavior of the HPC system power supply.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, the
focus in this work is on the ﬁrst group of node failures namely
regular failures, typically caused by internal factors.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The next
step to identify such failures is to detect node outages and to
distinguish regular failures from those which may occur as a
result of external factors, such as maintenance, human errors,
and others.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The failure detection workﬂow in Taurus is shown
in Figure 4.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Computing nodes of Taurus generate and send Syslog
entries to a central log collector which stores them for future
analysis.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
This is a passive log collection mechanism chosen
due to imposing no additional overhead, and to be applicable to
other HPC systems.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
However, the failure identiﬁcation process
becomes more challenging in comparison to the use of active
log collection mechanisms.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Due to using the passive log col-
lection mechanism, a node outage can be conﬁdently detected
only when a direct indication in the form of a log entry is
generated by the failing node and correctly received and stored
by the central log collector, e.g.,” Kernel panic - not syncing:
Fatal Exception.” However, in many cases, a node outage
leaves no direct indication in system logs.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
A workaround is to
assume the absence of log entries for more than a certain period
of time as an indication of a potential outage.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Nonetheless, this
assumption is not accurate.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
For various reasons such as CPU
overloading or network congestion, the ﬂow of system log
entries from the computing nodes to the central log collector
may be interrupted or delayed, which could be assumed as an
outage, even though the computing nodes are functional.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Also,
in many cases immediately after the occurrence of an outage,
the protection mechanisms recover the node.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In both latter
scenarios (temporary interruption in data ﬂow and automatic
node recovery), an active node probing approach may also fail
to correctly detect all node outages.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Analyzing Taurus system logs revealed that during a
healthy boot all nodes leave similar footprints in Syslog entries.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
When a node fails to generate the expected footprint at boot
time, it is an indication of a faulty boot process and thus the
node will be either automatically rebooted or it will fail shortly
thereafter.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The higher frequency of log generation at boot time
in comparison with the normal operation is another indicator of
a boot event, which can be used to identify even a problematic
boot process.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The proposed node outage detection method in this work
ﬁrst detects the node boot events.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Afterward, Syslog entries are
backtracked until the last Syslog entry before the boot event
is found.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The timestamp of the last Syslog entry prior to the
boot event is considered as the point of the outage.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
All node
outages will be identiﬁed using the proposed method.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The only
exception is when a node fails and has no further successful
boot process.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In such cases, comparing the timestamp of the
last available Syslog entry with the current time (i.e., 31-10-
2017 23:59:59) reveals the missing node outages.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Figure 3
illustrates all detected node outages on Taurus over the course
of 2017.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The detected outages are compared against the information
from other available data sources (mentioned in Table II).
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
When a node outage occurs outside of the scheduled main-
tenance period and no job could be accomplished on that
particular node at the time of the detected outage, the detected
outage represents a regular failure.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
As Figure 2 illustrates, it is
common that certain jobs on a speciﬁc node fail, although other
jobs on the same node are accomplished simultaneously.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Also,
when a node outage is recorded in the outages database that
monitors the availability of the HPC system from the users’
perspective, it is considered as a regular failure.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Anomaly Detection
The common behavior of most nodes within a node vicinity
is considered as normal behavior in that vicinity.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
A node’s
behavior is deﬁned as the Syslog Generation frequency of
the node (hereafter SG).
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The SG parameter is dynamically
calculated based on the number of Syslog entries received from
a computing node during a ﬁxed time window (e.g.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
30 minutes)
prior to the current (observation) moment.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The SG parameter
of each node is compared against the SG of other nodes in the
same vicinity.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Based on these comparisons, the normal value of
the SG parameter of certain nodes at a given moment in time is
calculated.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Impact of Hardware Architecture Vicinity
Taurus nodes are located in 6 islands.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
As shown in Figure 1,
island 4 hosts nodes with different processor types, while
islands 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 are homogeneous.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Although the
nodes’ hardware architecture inﬂuences the job allocation, as
Figure 2 illustrates there is no noticeable difference among
job allocation patterns on various Taurus islands.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
However, as
shown in Figure 3, with the exception of islands 5 and 6 -
which comprise of identical processor types- the node outages
have different distribution patterns on each island.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Figure 7 illustrates a one-to-one comparison of Syslog
generation patterns in all 6 islands of Taurus.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
This ﬁgure
visualizes the temporal and spatial patterns among more than
46K, 82K, 45K, 968K, 940K, and 1M Syslog entries generated
by islands 1 to 6, respectively.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Islands 5 and 6 present an
almost identical pattern, which is also very similar to island 4.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In contrast, the system log generation pattern on each of the
islands 1, 2, and 3 has a completely different pattern.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The comparison shown in Figure 7 indicates that the
processor architecture has a direct impact on node behavior.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, the behavior of nodes in island 1 (Sandy Bridge)
should not be predicted based on the behavior of nodes in
island 3 (Westmere), while a similar behavior is expected from
nodes in island 5 (Haswell) and island 6 (Haswell).
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
No additional patterns were detected when conducting
a similar analysis based on the amount of node’s physical
memory.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The use of the proposed anomaly detection method
on nodes with different hardware architecture proved to be
virtually impossible.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Detecting anomalies within the hardware
architecture vicinity on Taurus also revealed several false
positives.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
It is intended to improve the accuracy of the proposed
statistical anomaly detection method by identifying the most
relevant vicinity perspective among the four vicinities consid-
ered in this work.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The proposed method detects anomalies
by analyzing fully anonymized system logs.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
To the best of
our knowledge, there is no similar approach for detecting
anomalies using fully anonymized system logs.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore,
a quantitative comparison cannot be conducted.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
However,
Table IV shows a qualitative comparison of the proposed
method’s accuracy inside and outside of each vicinity.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Impact of Resource Allocation Vicinity
Figure 2 illustrates jobs that failed due to node failures,
as reported by Slurm.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Several jobs which were allocated on
multiple nodes were terminated due to node failures during
the 8-month period considered in this work.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
However, except
for one incident in which a misbehaving job was causing the
node failures, no direct correlation between the node failures
and resource allocation was found.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, among a group
of computing nodes executing various tasks of the same job, as
long as the running job is not causing a node failure itself, the
probability of a second node failure occurrence is not higher
than on the rest of the cluster.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
It is important to emphasize that the globally shared
resources are not included in this analysis and conclusion.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The
abnormal behavior of globally shared resources such as the
distributed ﬁle system may cause node failures itself.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Globally
shared resources are, however, unique entities in the cluster.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Thus, directly including them in anomaly detection will not
bring any additional beneﬁt.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Globally shared resources are, in
fact, indirectly considered in anomaly detection as correlations
between nodes.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The use of the proposed anomaly detection method on
resource allocation vicinity did not improve the accuracy
of anomaly detection.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
However, the low number of failed
jobs allocated on multiple nodes prevents drawing a robust
conclusion.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Impact of Physical Location Vicinity
Computing nodes are located inside HPC systems accord-
ing to their function and architecture.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, the physical
location of the nodes is not an independent factor.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The physical
location of each computing node on Taurus can uniquely be
addressed by its island, rack and chassis number.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Analyzing
the distribution of failures on Taurus as shown in Figures 2
and 3, reveals a strong correlation among failures in each
rack.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, in comparison with the rest of the cluster,
it is more likely to observe the second failure in a rack that
already experienced a node failure.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Out of the 2,046 computing nodes on Taurus, about 20%
of nodes never reported a node failure, and 60% of computing
nodes experienced 10 or fewer node failures during the time
period considered in this work.

Results and Discussions
Table IV summarizes the outcome of Subsections III-A,
III-B, III-C, and III-D in which the efﬁciency of anomaly
detection was studied in various vicinities.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
According to these
preliminary results, the impact of failure detection via the
proposed method inside resource allocation and time of failure
vicinities of Taurus is negligible and thus, should be avoided.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Failure detection inside the Physical location vicinity, on the
other hand, has a high impact on the accuracy of the ﬁnal
results.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
It also became evident that the application of the
proposed method outside the hardware architecture vicinity
of nodes can signiﬁcantly degrade the accuracy of the failure
detection mechanism.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, based on the preliminary results shown in
Table IV the proposed method was applied to the physical
location vicinities within each hardware architecture vicinity.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
With the exception of one rack in island 4 as shown in
Figure 1, on Taurus this vicinity is practically a single rack
with homogeneous computing nodes.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Table V summarizes the ﬁnal results of applying the
proposed failure detection mechanism on Taurus system logs.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Using the original Syslog entries as the input data, with
a precision of 62% the majority of failures were detected.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Since the proposed method only considers the frequency of
log entries rather than the content of each log entry, the
similar output could be achieved by using the anonymized
Syslog entries without endangering the users’ privacy.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The
PaRS anonymization method, used in this work, preserves the
similarity of Syslog entries such that the frequency of each type
of entries can be precisely calculated.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Filtering out frequent
log entries from the input data further improves the precision,
with a 6% penalty on recall.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Filtering frequent entries from
anonymized system logs also improves the precision of the
failure detection mechanism, although the recall factor is


reduced to 75%.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The difference between the results of ﬁltered
Syslog entries and ﬁltered anonymized Syslog entries lies in
the ﬁltering approach.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Since the content of anonymized system
logs cannot be read, frequent log entries are detected based
on their hash key and time-stamp.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Therefore, some log entries
have been mistakenly ﬁltered out.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Filtering frequent log entries
before data anonymization requires further analysis of original
system logs and may endanger user privacy.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The majority of the undetected anomalies (false negatives)
are related to sudden failures that do not leave large footprints
in system logs (e.g., power outage).
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Several false negatives
were also caused by calculating the wrong threshold for
the SG parameter (e.g.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Fine tuning the threshold calculator -via comparing similar
vicinities- improves the recall rate by about 4%.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
RELATED WORK
Failures in traditional high performance computing systems
were either completely ignored, avoided or at most addressed
in the middleware layer [16].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The advances in the size and
complexity of the HPC systems, demanded more ﬂexible
approaches against failures since they are a norm rather than an
exception [17].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The checkpoint/restart and redundancy became
the de-facto methods to protect HPC systems against node
failures.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
However, both methods impose performance and
energy consumption penalties.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Knowing the point of failure
and adapting the checkpointing period or the redundancy
level accordingly will increase performance and reduce energy
consumption signiﬁcantly [18].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Despite the existence of failure
protection mechanisms, the ever decreasing mean time be-
tween failures remains a key challenge for Exascale computing
systems [19].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Considering the high number of components in modern
HPC systems and the strong correlations between node failures
[8], [15], several studies investigate behavioral analysis to
predict failures via anomaly detection.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Both supervised [20]
and unsupervised [21] approaches were proposed.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Addition-
ally, several tools were designed to assist in the detection
of node failure correlations [22], [23].
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Many of the proposed
approaches, such as proactive failure detection [24] are limited
to certain components of the system.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
More general approaches,
such as a framework for detecting anomalous messages [25]
requires access to the full text of the original Syslog entries.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
All the above-mentioned works are based on system log
analysis.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The huge volume of system logs generated by HPC
systems demands more automated approaches that take advan-
tage of big data analysis [26] and machine learning algorithms.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Algorithms, models and tools such as those proposed by
Anwesha [27], Zhang [28], Gupta [29], and Du [30] are few
examples of using deep learning for predicting failures in HPC
systems via Syslog analysis.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The drawback of all application-dependent approaches is
the overhead incurred to the HPC system.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Using high levels of
redundancy and special purpose designed architectures are also
not general solutions for existing and operational HPC systems.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In addition, the available failure prediction methods are either
using models conﬁgured for a speciﬁc HPC system or require
detailed information about all events occurring on the HPC
system which endangers users’ privacy.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
A working solution
should be applicable to existing operational HPC systems and
should not incur extensive overhead to the underlying system.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Furthermore, to the best of our knowledge, none of the existing
approaches consider users’ privacy protection as a fundamental
principle in their analysis.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The proposed approach in this work employs a statistical
Syslog analysis to detect anomalies in existing and operational
HPC systems.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In contrast to other approaches, the proposed
approach protects users’ privacy by design.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Since the input data
(system logs) are passively collected, always anonymized, and
no modiﬁcation of the original HPC system is required, the
proposed approach is applicable to virtually all existing and
operational HPC systems.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Furthermore, system logs can be
replaced by any other persistent source of information which
reﬂects the HPC system status.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
Given that failures are becoming an integral part of HPC
systems, employing mechanisms that detect failures as early as
possible signiﬁcantly reduces the recovery costs and reduces
the interruptions in the normal operation of HPC systems.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
In
this work, a node failure detection mechanism via anomaly
detection on system logs was proposed, which calculates the
nodes system log generation frequency (the SG parameter)
during a ﬁxed time interval and compares this parameter
against other nodes in the vicinity.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The concept of vicinity
deﬁnes new dimensions of node correlation, beyond the natural
temporal and spatial correlations.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Abnormal behavior and thus
a node failure is detected by reaching a deviation threshold
from the SG parameter of the majority of the nodes.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Eight
months of system logs collected from the Taurus HPC cluster
were used as the main data source.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
The proposed failure
detection mechanism was applied to Taurus system logs in
four different vicinities.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
According to the results, the most
effective vicinities were identiﬁed as physical location and
hardware architecture.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Finally, the proposed mechanism was
applied to each rack of computing nodes with similar hardware
architecture within the Taurus HPC cluster.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Using each of
the original or fully anonymized system log entries a node
failure detection precision of 62% could be reached.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Filtering
out frequent common Syslog entries improved the precision of
node failure detection to 87%.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
It has been also shown that the
proposed mechanism could detect 75% of node failures with
more than 80% precision via analyzing ﬁltered anonymized
Syslog entries.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
For future work, it is planned to dynamically adjust the
interval of the sliding time window which calculates the SG
parameter of each node, according to the feedback received
from the time of failure vicinity.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Also, at the moment, the
detection occurs rather close to the time of failure, which could
be improved by better ﬁltering of the input data.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Furthermore,
the resource allocation vicinity will be further studied via
analyzing jobs’ information that are executed across multi-
ple nodes.
title: Anomaly Detection High Performance Computers: Vicinity Perspective

text:
Performing similar analyses on publicly available
system logs, such as those from the Failure Trace Archive
(FTA)5 or the Computer Failure Data Repository (CFDR)6, as
well as other types of monitoring data, such as node power
consumption, are also planned as future work.

ABSTRACT
Fog computing envisions that deploying services of an application
across resources in the cloud and those located at the edge of the
network may improve the overall performance of the application
when compared to running the application on the cloud.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
How-
ever, there are currently no benchmarks that can directly compare
the performance of the application across the cloud-only, edge-
only and cloud-edge deployment platform to obtain any insight
on performance improvement.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This paper proposes DeFog, a first
Fog benchmarking suite to: (i) alleviate the burden of Fog bench-
marking by using a standard methodology, and (ii) facilitate the
understanding of the target platform by collecting a catalogue of
relevant metrics for a set of benchmarks.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The current portfolio of
DeFog benchmarks comprises six relevant applications conducive
to using the edge.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Experimental studies are carried out on multiple
target platforms to demonstrate the use of DeFog for collecting
metrics related to application latencies (communication and compu-
tation), for understanding the impact of stress and concurrent users
on application latencies, and for understanding the performance
of deploying different combination of services of an application
across the cloud and edge.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
DeFog is available for public download
(https://github.com/qub-blesson/DeFog).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

INTRODUCTION
The premise of the emerging Fog computing model is to bring
appropriate services of an application from the cloud to the edge
of the network [3, 27].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Since the edge is closer to end user-devices,
running services on edge resources will reduce the communication
latencies of applications by enabling more data to be processed
near the end user-device before it is sent to (or processed on) the
cloud [22, 24, 30].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Consequently, the overall Quality-of-Service
(QoS) and Quality-of-Experience (QoE) of an application can be
improved [4].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Given that Fog computing is in its nascent stages of develop-
ment, there are a number of challenges that need to be addressed.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
One such challenge is understanding the relative performance of
Fog applications by comparing target hardware platforms from
different vendors due to diversity of hardware architectures and
the impact on performance when system software level changes
or new networking protocols are introduced.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Fog benchmarking
solutions are required to address this.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Benchmarking is a commonly used technique for evaluating the
relative performance benefits of different target computing mod-
els (or platforms) and the applications that run on them [15, 26].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Benchmarks capture a variety of workloads that are likely to be
executed using a computing model.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
These workloads are system-
atically and repeatedly executed so as to obtain a large catalogue
of relevant metrics related to performance, which is subsequently
analysed for obtaining concrete answers to questions posed by hard-
ware vendors or system software developers.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
There are dedicated
benchmarks that have been developed for supercomputers, namely
LINPACK [7] and NAS Parallel Benchmarks [1], or for the cloud,
namely CloudRank-D [17] and DCBench [12].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
However, we note
that there are no such benchmarking solutions available for Fog
computing.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Therefore, the focus of the research presented in this
paper is to report the development of a first Fog benchmarking suite,
referred to as DeFog (the rationale for the name is to ‘demystify
cloud-edge interactions of a Fog system’).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The DeFog suite is underpinned by a six step benchmarking
methodology that operates in three deployment modes, namely
a cloud-only mode, edge-only mode, and cloud-edge (Fog) mode.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
We anticipate that DeFog can be used to understand at least the
following three fundamental questions:
Q1: How can the relative performance of using a Fog platform
over the cloud-only platform be understood and quantified?
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Q2: If there are multiple services of an application that can be
moved to the edge, then how can performance of using the Fog be
understood?
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
1
arXiv:1907.10890v1  [cs.DC]  25 Jul 2019


SEC ’19, November 07–09, 2019, Washington, DC
McChesney, et al.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Q3: If there are multiple competing resources available at the
edge suited for a specific service, then which resource should be
selected for maximising the overall performance gain?
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Benchmarking across different deployment modes will address
Q1.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
DeFog is as hardware agnostic as possible (to the extend current
container technology supports) in building and deploying the cloud
and edge services of the Fog application.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The methodology captures
a catalogue of performance metrics that are related to the target
platform (cloud and edge resources) and applications running on
the platform.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
It would also be possible to obtain insight into the
best distribution of services for a given class of application across
the cloud and the edge, thereby addressing Q2.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Six applications that are Fog relevant workloads, namely a deep
learning-based object recognition, a text-to-speech converter, a
text-to-audio forced alignment, an online mobile game, an Internet-
of-Things (IoT) application, and real-time face detection from video
streams, are considered.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The applications are latency critical, stream-
based and/or bandwidth intensive, thereby making them ideal candi-
dates for use in DeFog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The experimental results presented highlight
the relative performance of the benchmarks across the deployment
modes on different target platforms.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This demonstrates the fea-
sibility of DeFog for addressing Q3 considered above.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The DeFog
software is publicly available1.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The contributions of this paper are as follows: (i) The devel-
opment of a platform agnostic Fog benchmarking methodology,
DeFog, that operates in three deployment modes.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
(ii) The evaluation
of six application benchmarks that are relevant to Fog computing
and making them available in a repository.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
(iii) The identification
and collection of a catalogue of metrics that capture the proper-
ties of the target platform and the application running on it.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
(iv)
An experimental evaluation of DeFog across cloud resources and
multiple single board computers that are used as edge resources.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text: The remainder of this paper is organised as follows.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Section 2
provides an overview of the benchmarking methodology and the
deployment modes of DeFog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Section 3 presents DeFog’s current
portfolio of six benchmarks that are candidate Fog applications
and the catalogue of metrics that are collected by DeFog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Section 4
presents the results obtained from an experimental study.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Section 6 concludes this paper by pre-
senting future work.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
2
DEFOG BENCHMARKING
This section firstly presents a few observations that have led to the
design and development of DeFog, followed by the benchmarking
methodology that is incorporated in DeFog, and finally the deploy-
ment modes of DeFog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The first version of DeFog is available for
download from (https://github.com/qub-blesson/DeFog).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
2.1
Motivation
Fog benchmarking as a research area is still in its early stages of
development.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The dependencies between cloud-edge services of
an application are not fully known given that there are only a few
open source Fog applications available.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The following five general
observations regarding Fog benchmarking have been considered
while developing DeFog:
1https://github.com/qub-blesson/DeFog
(i) Fog benchmarking is complex as dependencies between cloud
and edge services of a Fog application need to be considered: In cloud
benchmarking, the dependencies of the application are mostly in
the cloud.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
However, the dependencies between cloud and edge
services of a Fog application will need to be considered for Fog
benchmarking.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In other words, the bespoke requirements and de-
pendencies of an application will need to be considered ideally for
benchmarking the interactions in a Fog system, which is considered
in DeFog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This makes Fog benchmarking more complex than cloud
benchmarking.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
(ii) Fog benchmarks are not readily available: There is a limited
understanding of the real workloads that can benefit the most from
using Fog computing.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Consequently, there are no open source Fog
benchmarks readily available.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
While the portfolio of benchmarks for
traditional computing platforms, such as high-performance clusters
or even the cloud are diverse and comprehensive, Fog benchmarks
are not yet developed.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
DeFog attempts to create an early repository
of six benchmark applications that can be expanded upon by the
community as our understanding of Fog applications evolves and
as applications become available.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
(iii) Fog benchmarking should generate rapid results: Ideal bench-
marking should generate results quickly and in the context of the
Fog it is essential given that the edge is a transient environment.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Resources located on the edge (routers or gateways made accessible
for general purpose computing) are anticipated to have intermit-
tent profiles when compared to dedicated resources in a data center.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
DeFog is therefore designed to execute in a lightweight manner and
under one minute.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
(iv) Metrics captured during Fog benchmarking must be generalised
to a wide variety of workloads: Many benchmarking solutions are
workload specific and therefore generate workload specific metrics
on a target platform.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Hence, they cannot provide insight into the
suitability of the target platform for a different class of workloads.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The aim of DeFog is to evolve over time by adding more workloads
so that a wide range of metrics can be captured for diverse Fog
platforms and application benchmarks.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
(v) Benchmarking needs to be consistent: To ensure that bench-
marking is consistent each execution of the benchmark must be on
the same application build version and package dependencies.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This
is ensured in DeFog so that cloud-edge services are consistently
benchmarked.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In addition, to minimise the impact of any noise
within the Fog platform (due to temporary network congestion or
spikes in workloads), the benchmark needs to be executed multiple
times for a range of input data using identical containers to obtain
an averaged values of metrics.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
2.2
Benchmarking Methodology
The aim of DeFog is to automate the deployment of benchmark ap-
plications on the target platform, the transfer of assets required for
these applications to run on the target platform, the generation of
metrics relevant to the target platform and benchmark, and finally
gather results.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The proposed benchmarking methodology used by
DeFog accounts for these and is a sequence of six steps, which is
as follows: (1) Build and run the benchmark application container
image for the target platforms, (2) transfer the required asset to
the cloud resource on the target platform, (3) transfer the required
2


DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks
SEC ’19, November 07–09, 2019, Washington, DC
asset to the edge resource on the target platforms, (4) execute the
benchmark application, (5) gather the values for the catalogue of
metrics, and (6) return the metrics to the user.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The third step is
required for the edge-only or cloud-edge (Fog) deployment modes.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The second to fifth step is repeated multiple times for each appli-
cation for consistency.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The metrics are measured by an observing
system.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The methodology in detail is as follows:
Step 1 - Build and run a container: In this first step, a container
image is built and tagged for a target platform (cloud and/or edge)
to ensure that a consistent execution environment is available for
all future runs of the benchmark.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This research employs Docker
containers and it is run in the detached mode to allow for concurrent
benchmarking tasks to be executed on other application containers.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Step 2 - Transfer assets to the cloud: An asset that is transferred to
the cloud is the input data required by the application’s service that
runs on the cloud.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Each benchmark application has its correspond-
ing asset and a single benchmark application may have multiple
assets.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For example, there are currently six benchmark applications
in DeFog and each application has its own assets.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In addition, each
application may have multiple assets corresponding to similar or
different sizes or types of input.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This ensures that DeFog can be
used for varying inputs of the application to identify performance
gain under different operating conditions for the application.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Some
of the communication related metrics discussed in a subsequent
section are also measured during this step.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Step 3 - Transfer assets to the edge: The asset transferred in this
case is the input data required by the application’s service that will
be hosted on the edge resource.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Currently, the data required by the
application benchmark has to be manually partitioned and provided
as assets.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Automation within this step is desirable, but is not within
the scope of this article.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Some of the communication related metrics
discussed in a subsequent section are measured during this step.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Step 4 - Execute the benchmark application: Given the running
container (from Step 1) and the assets (Step 2 and Step 3) for each ap-
plication the number of times the benchmark needs to be executed is
determined.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
If there are N assets for an application, then the bench-
mark is executed N times.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The benchmark applications are further
considered in Section 3.1.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Additional benchmarking tools, namely
UnixBench2 and Sysbench3 are included within DeFog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
They pro-
vide a large number of target platform related metrics, including
CPU performance, concurrency and I/O read write.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Step 5 - Gather the values for a catalogue of identified metrics: A
combination of communication and computation related metrics
obtained from DeFog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
They can be categorised as: (i) target platform
metrics, which are attributes that capture the characteristics of the
specific target platform under consideration, (ii) Fog application
performance metrics, which are attributes that provide insight into
the performance of the application on the target platform, and (iii)
metrics obtained from external tools, which are attributes obtained
by using third party tools.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The metrics will be discussed further in
Section 3.2.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Step 6 - Provide the metrics to the user: The target audience that
can benefit from DeFog, include (i) vendors of new edge hardware
2https://github.com/kdlucas/byte-unixbench/tree/master/UnixBench
3https://github.com/akopytov/sysbench
Figure 1: DeFog deployment modes, namely cloud-only, edge-
only and cloud-edge (Fog).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
who want to demonstrate the benefit of using the Fog via bench-
marks, (ii) Internet Service Providers (ISPs) who want to deploy
micro data centres at the edge of the network and want to tabulate
performance of Fog applications for their customers, (iii) system
software administrators who want to investigate the impact on
Fog applications when a system level change, such as update to
operating system or libraries, is required on the edge resource, and
(iv) network administrators who want to quantify the performance
of Fog applications when a new networking protocol is introduced.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
When the benchmarks have completed execution the metrics are
provided to the observing system in the form of both comma sepa-
rated and verbose text files.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
2.3
Deployment Modes
The DeFog benchmarking suite works across three distinct deploy-
ment modes, namely a cloud-only, edge-only, and cloud-edge (Fog),
as shown in Figure 1 and considered below.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The underlying princi-
ple is that the relative performance of the benchmark applications
should be compared on different target platforms to quantify any
benefit of leveraging the edge for a cloud application.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The resources available for the target platform as shown in Fig-
ure 1 are from: (i) the cloud resource layer in which a large amount
of computational and storage resources are available, (ii) the edge
resource layer, which comprises either dedicated micro clouds or
traffic routing nodes, such as gateways, routers and base stations,
that are augmented with computing and/or storage capabilities,
and (iii) the user devices layer, which comprises devices, such as
smartphones, wearables, and sensors.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
A computer system is utilised
to observe the benchmarking process and collect the metrics.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:

text:
(i) Cloud-only deployment: The cloud-only deployment is typ-
ical of conventional cloud applications in which all requests origi-
nating from an end user-device are serviced by a cloud resource.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Figure 2 shows the two tier cloud-only deployment mode compris-
ing the cloud resources and user devices.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In DeFog, the application
is built and deployed on the cloud resource using Docker containers.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The application is then executed in the container and the benchmark
metrics are generated.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The method adopted is based on a container-
based cloud benchmarking approach previously reported [28].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The
user device uses the secure shell to interact with the cloud container
during the benchmarking process.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text: Figure 2: The DeFog cloud-only deployment mode.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
A DeFog user specifies which applications in the repository need
to be benchmarked and the accompanying asset is transferred to the
cloud (in this research we used Amazon Web Services (AWS) Elastic
Compute Cloud (EC2)4).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The output data from the application is
uploaded to an AWS Simple Secure Storage (S3)5 bucket.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The output
is also transferred to the observing system along with the metrics
generated during the benchmarking process.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
(ii) Edge-only deployment: The edge-only deployment mode
assumes that all services of an application can be entirely run on
an edge resource as shown in Figure 3.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This is practical if it is
assumed that dedicated micro clouds or modular data centres are
located at the edge of the network and the application provider
replicates the application on multiple geographic locations closer
to the end user.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Similar to the cloud-only deployment mode, the
application is deployed on the the edge resource using Docker
containers.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The application is then run within the container and
metrics are generated.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In this research resource constrained single
board computers, such as Odroid XU46 and Raspberry Pi 37 are
used as edge resources.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The outputs and the metrics are stored in
an S3 bucket as well as sent to the observing system.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
(iii) Cloud-edge (Fog) deployment: In the Fog deployment mode,
services of an application may be distributed across the cloud and
edge as shown in Figure 4.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Communication latency or bandwidth
sensitive services of the application are offloaded to the edge so
that the overall QoS of the application can be maximised.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Consider for example a deep learning application for object
detection.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This application will require the training of a model,
which is a computationally intensive task, and cannot be easily
carried out on the edge.

Benchmark Applications
The original version of the applications had to be modified to suit the
deployment modes reported in the previous section.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The modified
version of the applications used in DeFog is available in the project
repository14.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Additional workloads can be added to this portfolio
to enhance DeFog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Application 1 - Deep learning based object classification us-
ing YOLOv3: The You Only Look Once (YOLO)15 is a real-time deep
learning based object detection system that uses a single neural
network for the entire image [20].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The image is decomposed into
different regions and the bounding boxes and probabilities for each
region are estimated.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
These bounding boxes are weighted by the pre-
dicted probabilities.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The YOLOv3 [21] is a faster system compared
to competing systems that implement Region-based Convolutional
Neural Networks (R-CNN).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The original application resizes a pro-
vided image asset and detects objects within the image using a
pre-trained model.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
A labelled image is generated with percentage
weights providing the accuracy of estimation.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text: This system is an ideal candidate for the Fog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Fog applications
that rely on this system may use the edge node to resize the original
image (pre-process) so that the amount of data eventually trans-
ferred to the cloud beyond the edge is reduced.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In addition, the
objects can be detected at the edge to minimise communication
latencies.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The cloud server will need to send the pretrained model
to the edge to allow the detection service to be hosted on the edge.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Application 2 - Speech-to-text conversion (PocketSphinx):
PocketSphinx is an open-source large vocabulary, speaker-independent
continuous speech recognition engine [11].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
A supplied audio file
(.wav) is converted to a defined language in text form using a pre-
trained acoustic model to determine the source and destination
language for speech-to-text conversion.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The integrated assets are
sourced from a large scale speech repository16.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In the Fog applica-
tion, the end user-device provides a .wav asset to the edge container.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
A pre-trained acoustic model is offloaded from the cloud to the edge
to facilitate text-to-speech conversion.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Application 3 - Text-audio synchronisation or forced align-
ment (Aeneas): The Aeneas tool automatically synchronises text
and audio segments17.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Generating synchronisation maps for a list
of text fragments and an audio file containing the relevant text is

15https://pjreddie.com/darknet/yolo/
