referred to as forced alignment.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Aeneas determines the mapping
between corresponding audio segment for each text asset supplied.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In the Fog application, the end user-device transfers an audio
file (.wav) to the edge node.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Text segmentation occurs on the cloud
and the text segment (.xhtml) is offloaded from the cloud to the
edge where the forced alignment occurs.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Application 4 - Geo-location based online mobile game (iPoke-
Mon): The original version of iPokeMon is a cloud-based online
game that is similar to the popular virtual reality game, Pokémon
Go18.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The user device interacts with the cloud server from the be-
ginning to the completion of the game.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The Fog version employed
in DeFog is the use-case that is employed for validating research
on resource management at the edge of the network [31].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In the Fog version, the user creation and verification requests
from the user device are made to the cloud server, after which the
cloud server manager makes a request for computing services on
the edge node.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
If this request is accepted by the edge node, then
the edge manager initialises a container for the iPokeMon edge
server.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The cloud manager deploys the iPokeMon edge server and
clones (to the edge database) location specific data and user-specific
data (of those who will be connected to the edge).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
User data rapidly
changes when the game is played.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For example, the GPS coordinates
of the player and the Pokémons.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The local view on the edge server
is updated by frequent requests sent to the server.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For experimentation, JMeter and Taurus are used to simulate
players behaviour by generating synthetic workloads [31].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The
user device supplies the .jmx file to JMeter.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This allows for the
automated generation of workloads for a range of concurrent users.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Application 5 - Internet-of-Things (IoT) edge gateway ap-
plication (FogLAMP): This is an open source IoT application that
integrates cloud storage and sensors19.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
FogLAMP interacts with
endpoint sensors to collect and aggregate data.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
A text payload con-
taining a curl command is transferred to the edge from endpoints.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The service running on the edge executes the curl command by
invoking a simulated API call that gathers the localised data.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Application 6 - Real-time face detection from video streams
(RealFD): The original application uses an end device with an
embedded video camera to capture a continuous video stream.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The
stream is transmitted to a cloud server where faces are detected on
individual video frames using Pillow20 and OpenCV21.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:

text:
The server comprises the following three services for detecting
faces from a frame of the video: (i) Grey-scale converter (GSC) re-
duces the amount of computation done on an image that would
otherwise be required if it was a colour image.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The size of the
stream is reduced by nearly a third, (ii) Motion Detector (MD) is a
data filtering service that performs a condition check on successive
video frames to reduce computations on similar frames (for example
a security feed in a static environment, such as a home or museum).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
(iii) Face Detector (FD) is a computationally expensive service that
identifies frontal faces in a video frame using machine learning.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The application can be distributed in the following four ways:
(i) Cloud-only services – all the services are deployed in the cloud;
(ii) Fog-based pre-processing – GSC is deployed at the edge and
other services on the cloud; (iii) Fog-based data filtering – GSC and
MD are offloaded to the edge and FD is deployed on the cloud; (iv)
Edge-only services – all services are offloaded to the edge.

3.2
Metrics Collected by Benchmarking
Existing benchmarking methods that contain Fog conducive bench-
marks either are workload specific benchmarking techniques, such
as the speech-to-text benchmark22 and TailBench [13], or are provider
specific services benchmarking (AWS Greengrass and Microsoft
Azure IoT Edge), such as EdgeBench23 [6].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The motivation of DeFog
is a general purpose Fog benchmarking method that can be used
for a diverse range of workloads and at the same time provide both
the target platform and application related benchmarks.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Three types of metrics, namely platform, application specific
and from external tools are considered.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
These provide a bird’s eye
view of the target platform, including network characteristics and
applications running on the platform.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
(i) Target Platform Metrics: DeFog gathers platform metrics
for the three deployment modes (cloud-only, edge-only, cloud-edge).

4.1
Implementation and Setup
The cloud resource used is an AWS EC2 instance that is set up in
the Dublin eu-west-1 region.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The AWS command line interface
(CLI) is used to set up Information Access Management (IAM)
credentials.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
When an IAM user is instantiated, public and private
keys are configured to allow for secure remote access and control
of the EC2 instance.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Secure Shell (SSH) is used to ensure a secure
connection is maintained with the cloud.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
A data volume is allocated
to the instance on S3 for adequate space to build several distinct
applications simultaneously.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The latest Docker dependencies are
installed to allow for seamless deployment and execution.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Given that edge resources are hardware limited when compared
to the cloud, this research employs embedded single board comput-
ers, namely Odroid XU4 and a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B as shown in
Figure 5.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
These single board computers have resources comparable
to the compute that is available on a base station [31].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The Odroid
board has 2 GB of DRAM memory, and one ARM Big.LITTLE archi-
tecture Exynos 5 Octa processor running Ubuntu 14.04 LTS.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The
Raspberry Pi has 1 GB of RAM memory, and a Quad Core 1.2GHz
Broadcom BCM2837 64 bit CPU running Raspbian.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The applications are deployed using the container technology,
specifically Docker26.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Docker 17.12.1-ce is used to automate build-
ing and deploying the application.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Application specific Dockerfiles
install the relevant dependencies and packages when the containers
are build.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Container instances are then run using the same appli-
cation image.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
A combination of Python and bash scripting is used
along with Dockerfiles to execute the benchmarks.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For each benchmark a data payload is transferred from the ob-
serving system to the edge or cloud.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Fog deployment requires assets
to be offloaded from the cloud to edge.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Data generated on the cloud
and/or edge is transferred to the S3 bucket and observing system.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
YOLO, PocketSphinx, iPokeMon, Aeneas and RealFD are bench-
marked across all three deployment modes.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Taurus and Apache
JMeter are used to simulate concurrent users.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
FogLAMP does not
require a cloud asset, and is not used in the Fog mode, but for the
cloud-only and edge-only deployment modes.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The aim of the experiments are to demonstrate the metrics that
can be obtained to compare the relative computational and commu-
nication performance when the edge is leveraged.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The experiments
are performed on the three deployment modes (cloud-only, edge-
only, and cloud-edge) for gaining insight to Q1 that was posed in
Section 1.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The results obtained from the RealFD application (mul-
tiple services that can be moved to the edge) highlight the use of
DeFog to answer Q2.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The experiments are carried out on two edge
resources (Odroid XU4 and Raspberry Pi 3), which enhances our
knowledge of the performance of the benchmark in relation to Q3.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

Results
The results obtained are presented as: (i) application latencies for
different deployments, (ii) impact of stressing the edge on latencies,

text:
4.2.1
Application latencies for different deployment modes.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Figure 6
show the communication and computation round trip times for
the three deployment modes, namely the cloud-only, edge-only,
and cloud-edge (Fog) deployments.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The standard deviation of the
executions is highlighted in the observed results.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In these execu-
tions, the edge resources are exclusively used by the benchmark
application.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The communication latency (Figure 6a) is consistently
lower for all applications running on the edge when compared
to the cloud.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The computation latency (Figure 6b) is significantly
larger for applications, such as YOLO and PocketSphinx, on the
edge compared to the cloud.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This is because the edge resources
employed in this research are hardware limited compared to a cloud
resource.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The computational cost of these applications exceeds the
gains in communication latencies on the edge.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
There is a slight
increase in the latency times for the cloud-edge deployment modes
when compared to the edge only deployment, which is due to the
time needed to transfer assets from the cloud to the edge.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Aeneas
and FogLAMP show comparable and sometimes lower computa-
tional latency on the edge when compared to the cloud.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The lack
of performance gain for the former two applications may be due to
the specific manner in which the application is partitioned.

results obtained using the Odroid XU4 are presented.

Communica-

gle video frame.

There are two potential deployment options across
the cloud and edge - FD on the cloud, and MD and GSC on the edge,
or alternatively FD and MD on the cloud, and GSC on the edge.

4.2.2
Impact of stressing edge resources on application latencies.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For this experiment Gaussian workloads are simulated on the
edge nodes in the cloud-edge deployment mode for YOLO, Pocket-
Sphinx, Aeneas, and RealFD and the edge-only deployment mode
for FogLAMP.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The motivation is to simulate a real world multi-
tenant distributed system where there are competing workloads
residing on the same edge under variable network conditions.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The
stress27 package is used to stress the edge resource by simulating
computations in the background.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The stress-ng28 package is used
to stress the network.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
These packages use stressors to subject the
computing cores and network to various levels of stress.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In this paper, we explicitly define minimal stress when one CPU
core of the edge resource is stressed.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The network is stressed by
transferring a file of size 256MB at roughly 21740 bytes per second.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
27https://people.seas.harvard.edu/~apw/stress/
28https://kernel.ubuntu.com/git/cking/stress-ng.git/
For low stress, two CPU cores are stressed.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For medium and high
stress, three CPU cores and four CPU cores are stressed respectively.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For very high stress all CPU cores are stressed and the RAM memory
is stressed using two stressor processes.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The communication latency of benchmark applications when
network bandwidth is stressed is shown in Figure 8 (for the RealFD
application on Odroid XU4 is shown in Figure 10a).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Applications
that transfer larger amounts of data, such as Aeneas, are affected.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Figure 9 shows the trend in the computation latencies of the ap-
plications when the computing cores are stressed (Figure 10b).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
As
expected there is a significant increase in the computation latencies.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Computationally less intensive applications, such as Aeneas and
FogLAMP have less effect with stressed CPU cores.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
It is immedi-
ately inferred that applications demonstrate different trends when
edge resources are stressed.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For RealFD it is noted that different
combination of services across the cloud and the edge have different
performance.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For the iPokeMon application as shown in Figure 11,
the edge node is subject to similar stress as above.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
There is an im-
provement in the response latency of the cloud-edge deployment by
over 7 times when compared to the cloud-only deployment when
the stress as defined in this paper is very high.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

4.2.3
Impact of concurrent users on application latencies.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For this
experiment, concurrent users (2, 5, 10, and 50) of the application
benchmark are considered as shown in Figure 12.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The individual
requests from the application are simulated for concurrent users
using JMeter.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
It is noted that the communication latency as shown
in Figure 12a and Figure 12b increases with the number of users.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This is because the time in flight and time to transfer the results
also increases because with the increasing number of users the
rate at which data movement occurs decreases (this is highlighted
in Figure 13).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text: Similar increases are noted for computation latency.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Although the rate at which the computation latency increases is
different.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For example, FogLAMP has a much lower rate of increase
in computation latency when compared to PocketSphinx.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This is
because of the nature of the computational intensity underpinning
the benchmarks.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The figures highlight the need for DeFog - to
differentiate workloads that may not have a significant increase
in computation or communication latencies even when there are
multiple users versus those that may have the computation or
communication latencies significantly affected.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Applications that have a larger execution time for a single user,
are impacted the most by concurrent users, which results in larger
computation latencies.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For example, consider PocketSphinx as shown
in Figure 14.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Given the current decomposition of services for the
PocketSphinx application it is evident that the cloud-edge deploy-
ment is not advantageous over the cloud-only deployment.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
However, consider the impact of concurrent users on iPokeMon
as shown in Figure 15.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The cloud-edge deployment clearly has
significant advantages over the cloud-only deployment.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Latency
spike observed for the edge nodes when there are 250 concurrent
users was due to a single communication request that increased
the average response time of the requests.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The experimental results have demonstrated that
the communication and computation latencies vary across the dif-
ferent deployments, namely cloud-only, edge-only and cloud-edge.

5
RELATED WORK
There are multiple techniques for understanding the performance of
a target platform and applications running on it.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Two dominant tech-
niques, include simulation-based and benchmarking approaches,
which are applicable in the context of edge computing [10].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The simulation-based approach uses computational models to
simulate the target platform.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The application is modelled on top
of the simulated platform.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The application and target environment
are usually abstract representations of the real application and the
underlying hardware platform on which it will run is defined by a
fine-grain or aggregate set of input parameters.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The accuracy of run-
ning a simulation to gather performance metrics is fully dependent
on the underpinning models, which may be simply abstract repre-
sentations or more fine-grain models.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
It is worthwhile to note that
it is harder to accurately model the variability seen on a real target
platform, and is more complex when modelling distributed systems,
such as the Fog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Popular Fog and Edge computing based simula-
tors include EdgeCloudSim [25], iFogSim [8], MyiFogSim [16] and
FogExplorer29.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Recently, emulation is also used to evaluate the
performance of Fog applications [9].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The advantages of using simulation-based approaches include
reproducibility of the experiments and is a cheaper solution to
understand the performance of a target platform since physical
hardware is not required.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
However, simulation approaches may not
be sufficiently accurate and running fine-grain simulation models
(such as discrete event simulators) can be time consuming.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
On the other hand benchmarking approaches run the application
on the target platform in more realistic conditions.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Nonetheless,
external factors that influence performance may be simulated; for
example, network conditions or noise on the target platform.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Since
benchmarking is usually performed in the real setting, reproducibil-
ity of results depends on how transient the platform is.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
For example,
reproducing results on the Fog, could be challenging.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Nonetheless,
29https://openfogstack.github.io/FogExplorer/
benchmark consistency can be achieved by using technologies, such
as containers.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text: Currently no Fog benchmarks are readily available.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Accuracy and reliability of results are advantages of benchmark-
ing since applications are executed on the target platform with
fewer abstractions.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
However, the platform needs to be set up, which
is more expensive than simulation.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The application source code
may also need to be modified if multiple target platforms have to
be benchmarked.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text: This paper adopts a benchmarking approach.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Existing benchmarks relevant to the discussion of this paper, in-
clude those for the cloud, end user-devices, and application specific
benchmarks.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Benchmarking on the cloud typically captures the per-
formance of an application across different categories of resources,
such as virtual machines (VMs) [28] and storage services [2].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Pop-
ular cloud benchmarks include Yahoo Cloud Serving Benchmark
(YCSB) [5], CloudRank-D [17], and DCBench [12].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The use of con-
tainers for benchmarking in the cloud environment has advantages,
such as consistency and making the benchmarking process faster
and automating it [29].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
However, as expected cloud benchmarking
methods do not need to include techniques to capture performance
of resources outside the cloud and consequently, does not need to
handle the more complex dependencies that are seen in Fog appli-
cation.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
In this paper, container-based benchmarking is extended
towards taking into account the dependencies between cloud-edge
services of an application as seen in the Fog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
There are benchmarking methods available for end user-devices,
such as mobile devices [18] and IoT devices [14].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
There is recent
research that focuses on understanding the interactions between
the mobile user and the edge system [19].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
IoT benchmarks focus on
power consumption30, Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
benchmarking [14], and low power wireless network applications
(such as the IoT Benchmarking Consortium’s31 D-Cube [23]).
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Server-
less application benchmarking for CPU intensive benchmarks on
edge platforms, such as Amazon Greengrass and Microsoft Azure
IoT Edge are considered in literature; multiple heterogeneous cloud
functions are benchmarked [6].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
More application specific bench-
marks have been developed.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
These include the TPC Express Bench-
mark IoT (TPCx-IoT)32 that is based on YCSB [5] and considers data
ingestion and query workloads.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
CAVBench is developed for bench-
marking connected and autonomous vehicle applications [32].
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The general observation is that there are no Fog benchmarking
suites.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
While there are those that specifically consider the cloud
or end user-devices, benchmarking the distribution of applications
across the cloud and edge has not been the focus.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This paper reports
a first Fog benchmarking suite.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

the following questions: (Q1) How can the relative performance
gain of using Fog platforms over the Cloud-only computing model

(Q2) If there are multiple services of an application
that can be moved to the edge, then how can the overall perfor-
mance of moving different services to the edge be quantified?
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

If there are multiple competing resources at the edge for a service,

DeFog comprises six benchmarks that can be deployed across the
cloud and the edge.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The current portfolio of application benchmarks
in DeFog includes, deep learning-based object detection, text-to-
speech conversion, text-audio forced alignment, geo-location based
online mobile game, IoT edge gateway application and real-time

face detection in video streams, that are deployed across a cloud-
only, edge-only, and cloud-edge deployment modes.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The approach
taken in this paper is benchmarking actual target platforms rather
than using simulation.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Experimental studies demonstrate the cata-
logue of target platform and application related metrics captured
by DeFog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The experiments also present the performance of bench-
marks due to concurrent users and stress on edge resources.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The approach taken by DeFog ensures that the build and deploy-
ment of the application are automated.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
DeFog ensures consistency
(same environment is available and dependencies are set up when
comparing two different edge nodes) when benchmarking.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Limitations and Future Work: The current approach in DeFog
assumes that all target platforms will be able to run Docker con-
tainers.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The container technology is limited in that processor archi-
tecture specific images are required.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Relying on containers as the
deployment technology for Fog computing will result in the need
to host a wide range of container images for application bench-
marks.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
More hardware agnostic deployment technologies will need
to be developed to alleviate this problem.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
It is also assumed in the
implementation and experimentation that dedicated single board
computer capabilities are available at the edge.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Edge resources, such
as routers and gateways that can be augmented with compute capa-
bilities have not been considered.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The partitioning of applications
is inherently across a single layer of cloud resources and a single
layer of edge resources.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The current research does not explore the
distribution of benchmarks across the entire cloud-edge continuum.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This is because applications that can leverage the entire cloud-edge
continuum are not fully understood.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The time taken for enacting
security measures in a cloud-edge application is not considered.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
This will be considered in the future to quantify performance more
accurately.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
Efforts will be made towards identifying appropriate
techniques to capture or estimate the overall energy consumption in
the Fog.
title: DeFog: Fog Computing Benchmarks

text:
The coverage of benchmarks will be widened in the future
to include applications that can ultimately test Fog computing by
simultaneously stressing all dimensions of latency, bandwidth and
availability of resources, such as augmented reality applications.

Abstract—Security is one of the most relevant concerns in
cloud computing.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
With the evolution of cyber-security threats,
developing innovative techniques to thwart attacks is of utmost
importance.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
One recent method to improve cloud computing
security is Moving Target Defense (MTD).
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
MTD makes use of
dynamic reconﬁguration in virtualized environments to ”confuse”
attackers or to nullify their knowledge about the system state.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
However, there is still no consolidated mechanism to evaluate the
trade-offs between availability and security when using MTD
on cloud computing.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
The evaluation through measurements is
complex as one needs to deal with unexpected events as failures
and attacks.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
To overcome this challenge, we intend to propose
a set of models to evaluate the availability and security of
MTD in cloud computing environments.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
The expected results
include the quantiﬁcation of availability and security levels under
different conditions (e.g., different software aging rates, varying
workloads, different attack intensities).
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Index Terms—Moving Target Defense, Security, Availability,
cloud computing
I.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
INTRODUCTION
Previous works show cloud computing security as a sig-
niﬁcant research challenge [1] [2].
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
One of the root problems
for cloud security is the intrinsic advantage of attackers over
defenders.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Attackers can perform a series of actions (e.g.,
repeated attacks, vulnerability analysis) until they achieve
their goal.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
So, the attackers can try to explore a speciﬁc
system vulnerability while the defenders have to protect all
the possible attack venues [3].
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Besides that, the generally static
nature of data centers facilitates the attacker to obtain enough
information to improve the chance of attack success.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
MTD is a ﬂexible technique for system security improve-
ment.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Previous papers showed the effectiveness of MTD
deployment in environments like the Internet of Things
(IoT) [4], Virtualized Containers [5], Software Deﬁned Net-
works (SDN) [6], and cloud computing [7].
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
In the cloud
computing context, MTD techniques can be used to thwart
or reduce the impact of security attacks as co-residency
attacks [8] and Distributed Denial of Service attacks [9].
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Matheus Torquato is also with Federal Institute of Alagoas (IFAL), Ara-
piraca, Brazil.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
The United States Department of Homeland Security deﬁnes
MTD as ”the concept of controlling change across multiple
system dimensions to increase uncertainty and apparent com-
plexity for attackers, reduce their window of opportunity and
increase the costs of their probing and attack efforts.” [10].
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Besides the security concern, cloud-hosted applications also
need high availability levels.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
There are several strategies to
achieve this goal as failover techniques, redundancy, and soft-
ware rejuvenation.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
But, the problem is to evaluate the possible
availability and security impacts of applying Moving Target
Defense along with availability improvement techniques.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Usually, there is a trade-off between security and availability
in cloud computing systems when applying Moving Target
Defense.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
For example, a common technique of MTD on cloud
computing is Virtual Machine Migration.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
VM migration moves
a VM from one physical machine to another.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
This remap-
ping can, for example, avoid co-residency attack.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
However,
each VM migration (even in Live Migration mode) has an
associated downtime [11].
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
So, if we decide to perform too
frequent VM migrations, we may achieve higher levels of
system security, but lower availability levels.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Otherwise, if the
system manager decides to deploy less frequent migrations, the
system may reach higher availability levels but jeopardizes the
system security.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Our research aims to propose a set of models to evaluate the
trade-offs between security and availability of cloud comput-
ing MTD based on different policies of VM placement.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
From
the models’ results, we will select speciﬁc policies to reach
the desired levels of security and availability.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Our models will be mainly based on Stochastic Reward
Nets (SRN) that are extensively used for cloud computing
availability evaluation [12].
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
SRNs are also suitable for security
evaluation [13].
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

the details of our research goals.

Finally, Section VI
contains ﬁnal remarks.

GOALS
The main research question (RQ) of this work is: What
are the trade-offs between cloud computing availability and
security when applying speciﬁc policies of MTD based on
VM placement techniques?
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
This work aims to propose a set
of models for availability and security evaluation of Moving
Target Defense on cloud computing, aiming to answer this
question.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
The following RQs will drive the design of the models to
be proposed:
1) What is the availability level of cloud computing archi-
tectures?
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
The ﬁrst step is to design a scalable model for
availability evaluation of different cloud architectures.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
2) What is the security level of a given cloud deployment
architecture?
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
The second step is to propose a model for
cloud security evaluation.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
In this step, we will also select
the considered threat models (i.e., security threats as
Denial of Service, Man-in-the-middle, and Side-channel
attacks).
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Our goal is to cover the Denial of Service (DoS)
and Man-in-the-Middle attacks.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
3) What are the side-effects of MTD based on Virtual
Machine (VM) placement on the system availability?
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Using the model from the ﬁrst step, our goal is to expand
the model including MTD based on VM placement.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
4) What are the cloud computing security levels achieved
by MTD techniques?
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Using the model from previous
steps, we aim to add the behavior related to MTD based
on VM placement techniques.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Finally, we aim to merge the models obtained from the
research questions mentioned above.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
The ﬁnal model will
allow evaluating the trade-offs between cloud availability and
security, considering MTD based on VM placement tech-
niques.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
In the future, we also intend to answer the following
research questions:
1) What are the actual levels of availability and security of
MTD based on VM placement when considering aspects
of software aging and rejuvenation?
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
2) What is the cloud computing performance overhead
caused by MTD based on VM placement?
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
3) Is there any cloud computing reliability improvement due
to MTD based on VM placement?
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

[15] provide a comprehensive security

return on attack, and availability.

account of the cost of MTD on cloud computing availability
and security, and including other relevant aspects on the
analysis (e.g., software aging and rejuvenation, and hardware
and software failure and repair).

[16] provides a theoretical point-of-view of
how to measure resiliency of a cloud which applies Software
Based Encryption (SBE) MTD.

text:
SBE uses software diversity
to improve system security, survivability, and resilience.

The
paper describes some of the essential concepts of security
evaluation as integrity, availability, survivability, and conﬁ-
dentiality.

Finally, the paper proposes a model for resiliency
quantiﬁcation in scenarios with SBE-based MTD.

We also

on Cloud Computing.

title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Ahmed and Bhargava [17] propose Mayﬂies MTD frame-
work for distributed systems.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Mayﬂies use a speciﬁc policy
of VM placement as MTD.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
The idea is to perform VM
substitution through creation and deletion cycles, obeying
certain time intervals.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
Every cycle of substitution changes
a VM characteristic.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
In Mayﬂies, VMs are created to use a
different operating system from the previous deleted VM.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
The
strategy avoids attack progress or the spread of an undetected
attack.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
The authors evaluate their proposed framework through
experiments in a real testbed.

text:
However, different from our
intended approach, the paper does not present a security
analysis of the proposed technique.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

[18] proposes SeReNe, a platform to deliver
Network-Security-as-a-Service (NSaaS) for multi-tenant data
center environments.

text:
SeReNe plans to apply MTD using
diversity techniques to mitigate software vulnerabilities as
Bohrbugs, Mandelbugs, and aging-related bugs.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

text:
However,
SeReNe is still in a conceptual phase, and the paper lacks

We also intend to
include the effects of MTD deployments on software aging
and rejuvenation.
title: Towards Models Availability Security Evaluation Cloud Computing with Moving Target Defense

But, different from SeReNe, our approach
is focused on shufﬂing VM placement techniques.

The majority of the papers in the area neglects the evalu-
ation of trade-offs between availability and security of MTD
deployments on cloud computing.

text:
Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler 
Frank Pallas*, Philip Raschke*, David Bermbach*° – *TU Berlin, °ECDF 
 
Despite broad discussions on privacy challenges arising from fog computing, the authors argue 
that privacy and security requirements might actually drive the adoption of fog computing.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
They 
present four patterns of fog computing fostering data privacy and the security of business 
secrets, complementing existing cryptographic approaches.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Their practical application is 
illuminated on the basis of three case studies.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Introduction 
Fog computing is an emerging computing paradigm in which applications and data are no 
longer deployed in the cloud alone.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Instead, the cloud is enhanced with machines running closer 
to end users, e.g., in mobile applications, or data producers, e.g., in Internet of Things (IoT) 
scenarios [1].
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
The typical drivers of this move towards fog computing are latency and bandwidth: Application 
domains such as autonomous driving or 5G mobile applications call for low latency responses.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text: Here, a local edge server is able to respond much faster than a remote cloud server.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
The IoT, in 
turn, is inherently limited by bandwidth constraints as the data output from large scale sensor 
deployments can quickly exceed the available bandwidth to the cloud.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In that case, 
preprocessing at the edge can significantly reduce the amount of data that needs to be sent 
over the wire.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
While these two drivers are intuitive and, thus, usually the first ones mentioned when motivating 
fog computing, there is another driver: privacy.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In light of recent legislation, i.e., the General 
Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), privacy will, in our opinion, be one of the most dominant 
drivers of fog computing.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Nevertheless, positive effects of fog computing for privacy have largely 
been neglected so far.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
To the contrary, this paper is actually inspired by an earlier article in this 
magazine which claimed that privacy might hamper broad fog adoption [2].
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
While we agree that 
there are indeed some privacy (and security) risks in fog computing, we believe that these are 
largely technical challenges that can be surmounted with existing technology.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
On the other 
hand, fog computing provides invaluable privacy opportunities that are primarily of structural 
nature and can valuably complement existing, especially cryptographic techniques such as 
homomorphic encryption [7], secure multi-party computation [9], or mechanisms for differential 
privacy [10].
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
These structure-based opportunities can be used to significantly heighten data 
privacy, as compared to well-established cloud-centric models of data processing.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In this paper, 
we give an overview of these privacy opportunities and demonstrate their potential through a 
number of case studies.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text: This paper has been accepted for publication in IEEE Internet Computing.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
This document is the authors’ 
own version before final copy-editing by IEEE.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
DOI: 10.1109/MIC.2020.2979161 


 
 
WHAT IS FOG 
Fog computing is the combination of cloud and edge computing enhanced with compute 
capacity in the network between edge and cloud.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
On an abstract level, this means that the 
centralized, homogeneous cloud is replaced with a geo-distributed, highly heterogeneous 
compute environment where compute infrastructure may be controlled by multiple entities.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
This implies that the fog can be seen as the natural evolution of hybrid clouds: public and 
private clouds are still used, but are augmented with large numbers of additional infrastructure 
elements in the network between public and private cloud as well as at locations even closer 
to the edge.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
These elements come in a variety of flavors ranging from single board computers 
to small clusters and are operated by a multitude of providers [1].
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Figure 1: Fog computing combines and integrates cloud and edge computing with additional 
compute capacity in the network in-between, leading to highly distributed and heterogeneous 
environments.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
PRIVACY and BUSINESS SECRETS 
Challenges with regard to privacy and business secrets often overlap.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In particular, this is the 
case for questions about who is able to access certain data in cloud computing settings.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
The 
computational overheads raised by approaches like fully homomorphic encryption – which are 
often proposed for such use cases [5, 7] – are still prohibitively high for most realistic 
scenarios [4].
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Even though data can be encrypted during transit and while at rest, cloud 
providers thus typically need access to unencrypted data as soon as reasonable functionality 
is desired.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Unable to actually exert control over the access to and usage of such data, a 
company employing cloud services for handling customer data therefore has to blindly trust 
the legal compliance of the cloud or SaaS provider.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
At the same time, it has to bear the 
ultimate risk of being held accountable in case of misbehavior resulting in high fines.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
A comparable challenge arises with regard to business secrets in case of using cloud-based 
services for processing sensitive internal data, such as production volume, material flow, or, in 
particular, large-volume monitoring and control data in the context of industry 4.0.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Again, any 
company employing cloud-based services for such purposes has to trust in the proper 
handling on the side of the provider.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Aside from such aspects of data secrecy, privacy regulations like the GDPR also raise 
additional requirements, ranging from data minimization obligations and purpose limitation to 
the provision of transparency and geographical limitation of storage and processing which go 
far beyond what cryptographic techniques can offer .
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Following the paradigm of privacy/data 
protection by design, all these and many more requirements need to be addressed using 
technical measures.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Opportunities 
In particular, we see four structural patterns of applied fog computing that provide significant 
benefits in matters of data privacy but also for the handling of business secrets.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
These patterns 
are not necessarily new and may already be known from, e.g., hybrid clouds.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In fog computing, 
however, they become inherent and fundamental principles of application architectures.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
1: Service Execution On-Premises 
A core functionality of fog computing is the movement (or: relocation) of data storage and 
processing away from centralized entities like cloud datacenters to on-premises edge servers.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Basically, fog computing allows to decouple the software part of a SaaS business from the 
execution environment this software runs on.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
While a software executable is still provided as a 
service, it is executed in an environment (including hardware as well as the underlying software 
stack) which remains under the control of the service customer.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In contrast to cloud-based 
models, customers therefore no longer need to completely hand-over control over their data to 
the service provider for being able to use said service.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
This, in turn, provides significant benefits 
for privacy as well as for the protection of business secrets.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
This pattern can already be found in 


practice.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Amazon, for instance, offers ready-to-use server racks which are installed as on-
premises edge servers under the physical control of the customer.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
These “Outpost” installations, 
however, run standard Amazon cloud services managed by the provider.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
2: Multi-Staged Filtering 
Data minimization is one of the core principles of privacy.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
This corresponds nicely to fog 
scenarios where data created near the edge is no longer streamed to the cloud for, e.g., 
bandwidth reasons.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Instead, it is processed across multiple stages, starting at the edge, with 
only aggregated values arriving in the cloud.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In a typical IoT scenario, for instance, sensor data 
is processed at the edge to either aggregate data or to filter out and discard irrelevant data 
items.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Depending on the use-case, its data requirements, and the computational constraints it 
raises, this filtering might also comprise mechanisms providing local differential privacy [5, 6].
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
The same happens at later filtering stages within the fog before eventually arriving in the cloud 
for final processing.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Every stage reduces the amount of data permanently stored in the cloud 
which will be accessible for the respective cloud providers.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
The pattern therefore allows to 
minimize the amount of data accessible for the different parties involved to the necessary 
minimum.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In the context of business secrets, this reduces the risk of disclosure while in the 
context of privacy, it allows for compliance with the principle of data minimization, which is 
mandatory in most respective regulations such as the GDPR.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
3: Decoupled Data Hubs 
One of the main privacy risks in cloud computing is the correlation of data which was collected 
for independent purposes.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Nowadays, such correlation of data – whether accidental or 
malicious – has become simple due to the wide availability of big data technology and the 
increasing accumulation of data in consolidated cloud data stores.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Even though these cloud 
data stores typically employ sophisticated access management systems, these do not solve the 
underlying structural risk emanating from large centralized data lakes.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
When data, however, is 
not stored in a centralized cloud but rather distributed geographically across a multitude of fog 
nodes operated by different providers, joins of data sets (even accidental) become incredibly 
expensive.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Fog-based decoupled data hubs cannot avert data correlation and inference 
completely (data correlation for single entities may still be possible), but it is no longer feasible 
to do that on a large scale.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Using federated learning approaches [11], decoupled data hubs, 
however, still support advanced machine learning use cases such as predictive maintenance 
across multiple machine users.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Overall, decoupled data hubs clearly counteract privacy 
intrusion as well as provider-side fiddling with internal business secrets.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
4: Fine-Granular Control of Data Placement 
Privacy legislation mandates that data may not move to certain countries.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Business secrets, in 
turn, shall not leave company premises, and users may feel more comfortable when they can 
actually know and control the place where their data is stored.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
This is in stark contrast to the 
cloud which through its virtualized nature here provides only limited transparency and control.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In 
fog computing, in contrast, the latency and bandwidth implications of geo-distribution call for 
explicitly exposing data placement to applications.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Furthermore, the sheer number of edge 
locations is an enabler for really fine-grained geo-placement [12].
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Respective strategies (see, 


e.g., [8]) can also be used to satisfy - going beyond performance- and QoS-related 
requirements - privacy-and security- related obligations and constraints.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Furthermore, users 
may also welcome the option to place their data with only a subset of fog providers.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
All these 
aspects together provide the means to let application developers better meet regulatory 
demands and to allow users to manage the physical location of their data.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Case Studies 
To illustrate how the four identified fog usage patterns help to improve privacy or handling of 
sensitive business secrets, consider the following example use cases: 
 
Figure 3: Fog Computing may provide data privacy and security benefits in such diverse 
scenarios as video-surveillance, predictive maintenance, or eHealth.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Privacy-Friendly, Fog-Based Video Surveillance 
Video surveillance is a widely used approach for improving safety in public places.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Typically, the 
resulting video feed is sent to the cloud where it is processed and stored indefinitely.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In [3], we 
presented an alternative approach where the video stream is analyzed at the edge.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Using facial 
recognition models pre-trained in the cloud, only the video snippets containing persons of 
interest are sent to the cloud.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
All other video data is buffered at the edge for a few days and 
may only be retrieved through a well-controlled process.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Both, the face search requests as well 
as extraordinary data retrieval require a court order (ensured, e.g., through a four eyes 
procedure) and a blockchain-inspired audit trail is created to avoid misuse.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
As the necessary 
edge infrastructure, we used standard off-the-shelf single-board computers (Raspberry Pi) 
which were already powerful enough to process high-definition video streams unless these 
contained large groups of people.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
This shows that such an approach is indeed feasible for 
deployments in practice which would significantly improve privacy of citizens over the state-of-
practice (cloud-based analytics).
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In this case, the patterns of multi-staged filtering (2) and of decoupled data hubs (3) are 
employed.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Here, filtering refers to the edge-side analysis of raw video footage and the reduction 
of transmitted data to those snippets actually containing persons of interest.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Intermediate nodes 
could also have been used to filter data based on further criteria (e.g., reporting only certain 
matches to federal agencies).
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
The temporary storage of full raw data at the edge for the 
carefully restricted case that further examination is necessary, in turn, resembles the pattern of 
decoupled data hubs – even though only temporary.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In established, cloud-based analytics, in contrast, the entire raw footage would be sent to a 
centralized cloud data store, structurally making it available for arbitrary analytics, especially 
across all covered locations.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In such deployments, it is hence possible to create movement 
profiles of arbitrary citizens.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Opposed to this, the above-sketched fog-based approach provides 
structural benefits from the perspective of data minimization as well as with regard to the risk of 
inappropriate or unintended correlation.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Business Secrets in Vendor-Provided Predictive Maintenance 
One of the core applications in Industry 4.0 scenarios is predictive maintenance – the prediction 
of necessary maintenance based on fine-grained, high-volume operational data of industrial 
facilities and respective machine learning algorithms.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
For manufacturers of industrial production 
machines, predictive maintenance is commonly seen as a natural extension of their existing 
service portfolio as, in particular, they are best-suited to interpret observed operational data.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
On 
the other hand, owners of the machines may fear the exposure of their internal operational data 
and therefore hesitate to participate in this – otherwise advantageous – model.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
With fog computing, in turn, manufacturer-provided services for maintenance prediction may be 
distributed across machine-attached devices and the company’s private cloud, both controlled 
by the machine owner, without sending detailed information on internal production processes to 
external parties.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
We implemented this model in collaboration with a manufacturer of digitally programmable high-
precision machines.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
This allows for predictive maintenance based on local analytics of high-
volume monitoring data being executed on the customers’ premises without revealing detailed 
production data to the machine-manufacturer.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Instead, only well-selected aggregates are sent to 
the manufacturer in specific cases.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Beyond maintenance-related analysis results, this can 
(depending on the agreement between customer and machine-manufacturer) also include, e.g., 
precalculated analysis results covering the last 24 hours to improve the prediction models.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Per 
machine, this required one node of the usual desktop class.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
An alternative approach, following 
the same principles, would have been to employ federated learning methods such as [11] which 
allow different entities to jointly train a (federated) model without exposing their individual 
training data possibly containing business secrets.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In this case, we employed the above-mentioned patterns of service execution on-premises (1), 
filtering (2), and decoupled data hubs (3).
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Compared to the alternative model of having all data 
sent to a centralized vendor-cloud, the customer is significantly less exposed to the risk of 
having their internal production data inappropriately analyzed or even exploited.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Also, the 
necessary bandwidth could be significantly reduced without noteworthy limitation of 
functionality.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
eHealth and Data Sharing and Reuse 
The use of health-related data for different purposes by different actors is one of the main 
principles driving eHealth adoption.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In particular, this provides benefits when multiple parties 
(e.g., multiple departments of a hospital or different hospitals or clinics of the same group, 
laboratories, etc.) are involved in the treatment of a single patient and can easily access existing 
examination data.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
However, regulations applicable to the health sector often raise strict 
constraints on where health-related data may be stored (within a given facility or a certain 
country).
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
As opposed to established models of cloud-based data sharing, compliance with such 
regulations can be significantly streamlined with fog computing’s inherent capabilities for data 
placement control (pattern 4 above).
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Another often-mentioned use case for health related data 
regards the reuse of examination data (e.g., blood tests) for medical research.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
In this case, 
regulations strictly require respective data to be pseudonymized or anonymized, depending on 
the party conducting the research.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
For the automated application of such data minimization 
measures, data might – following the above-sketched pattern of multi-staged filtering – be 
preaggregated per patient at the edge, pseudonymized in a hospital data center, and finally 
anonymized through aggregation across patients in a hospital group data center before 
releasing it to external entities.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
We are currently implementing this model together with a nation-wide hospital group in a 
European country through a novel data management and exchange platform.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Early results are 
promising and already confirm the expected benefits in matters of easing the collaboration 
between different parties in line with existing regulations.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Compared with an alternative model of 
a centralized cloud data store with traditional access restrictions, the sketched model allows us 
to clearly separate data of different levels of sensitivity and to clearly manage the storage 
locations of these data in line with regulations such as the GDPR or more specific national laws.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Roundup 
The case studies we presented highlight the privacy opportunities implied by fog computing.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
By 
relocating data storage and processing to the edge, applications can be executed on-premise, 
i.e., sensitive data of a natural person or business is never given away.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
If data transmission 
becomes indispensable, filters can be used to only disclose derived or aggregated data or to 
omit sensitive information.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text: Thus, data privacy as well as business secrets are better protected.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Furthermore, a distribution of data across multiple nodes makes it harder to aggregate it in order 
to reveal correlations.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text: Consequently, the privacy-affecting effects of big data can be mitigated.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text: In all our case studies, users’ data sovereignty is improved by the fog computing paradigm.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Data owners, natural persons or businesses, are able to decide which information – personal 
data or business secrets – they want to disclose to whom, where it should be stored, and who 
has access to it.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
This provides significant benefits over established cloud-based environments, 
where users effectively give away all these choices at the moment they upload their data to the 
cloud.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Given these achievable advantages in matters of legal compliance as well as the alignment with 
business interests, fog computing might become a serious competitor for the traditional cloud 
computing paradigm.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
However, cumbersome set ups and configurations currently hamper its 
adoption [1].
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text: The bar is raised high by cloud providers here, yet it is not out of reach.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text:
Fog 
computing can claim itself many advantages over the often problematic cloud computing 
paradigm.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler

text: Its respect for data privacy is definitely one of them.
title: Fog Computing as Privacy Enabler
