Abstract—Photonic reservoir computing is a promising can-
didate for low-energy computing at high bandwidths.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Despite
recent successes, there are bounds to what one can achieve simply
by making photonic reservoirs larger.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Therefore, a switch from
single-reservoir computing to multi-reservoir and even deep phys-
ical reservoir computing is desirable.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Given that backpropagation
can not be used directly to train multi-reservoir systems in our
targeted setting, we propose an alternative approach that still
uses its power to derive intermediate targets.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
In this work we
report our ﬁndings on a conducted experiment to evaluate the
general feasibility of our approach by training a network of 3
Echo State Networks to perform the well-known NARMA-10
task using targets derived through backpropagation.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Our results
indicate that our proposed method is well-suited to train multi-
reservoir systems in a efﬁcient way.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
INTRODUCTION
Reservoir computing was proposed in the early 2000s to
circumvent difﬁculties when training recurrent neural networks
[1], [2].
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
More recently, it has gained increased interest in
the unconventional computing community as it proves to be
an excellent framework to train physical nonlinear dynamic
systems to perform meaningful computations [3], [4], [5].
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
With
photonic reservoir computing, which uses light processing sub-
strates as reservoirs, competitive results have been achieved on
time series prediction, voice recognition, non-linear distortion
compensation and telecommunication tasks [6], [7], [8], [9].
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
In combination with currently researched technologies on non-
volatile optical weights [10], this technology is a promising
candidate to pave the way to efﬁcient low-energy computing
at large bandwidths (> 10 Gbps).
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Nevertheless it is well known in the reservoir computing
community that there are bounds to what one can achieve
simply by making a reservoir larger and using more observed
states in the readout.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
This is mostly due to the fact that the
states are usually highly correlated due to the interactions
inside the reservoir.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
This makes it difﬁcult to exploit the
residual information that is added by additional states as the
state space grows larger.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
For simulated reservoirs, such as
inﬁnite precision echo state networks, it would require an
increase of the amount of training data.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
In physical reservoirs,
noise and measurement inaccuracies effectively constrain the
exploitation of state information and performance tends to
saturate even faster as a function of reservoir size.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
In addition,
fabricating larger integrated (photonic) reservoirs increases the
technological challenge, e.g., due to routing problems and high
optical losses as well as cost and yield-related constraints on
the chip size.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
In summary, in order to move to more complex
tasks, simply making reservoirs larger is not enough.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Instead,
there is a need for approaches to design multi-reservoir or
even deep reservoir systems.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
[11] propose
to scale reservoir computing by building a large reservoir out
of a set of smaller reservoirs, where each reservoir injects
its output into the next reservoir without training intermediate
connections.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
The states of all reservoirs are then fed into the
readout.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
While it performs well, this approach is challenging to
implement with integrated photonic reservoirs due to its high
wiring effort, which subjects it to almost the same routing
issues and constraints as for large monolithic reservoirs.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
System Architecture of 3 connected Echo State Networks for which
intermediate desired signals have been derived using backpropagation.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
An alternative approach is to individually train many
smaller, interconnected reservoirs, which collaborate in a net-
work to solve the task at hand.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Two possible multi-reservoir
architectures, based on standard ensembling approaches from
machine learning, have been evaluated in [12].
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Yet, we expect
better performance can be achieved by a tailored network of
arXiv:1910.13332v1  [cs.LG]  25 Oct 2019


reservoir modules for each task.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Unfortunately, there is no
general way to derive desired signals necessary to train the
intermediate outputs of each reservoir in such an architecture.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Using backpropagation to train the readouts in a network of
physical reservoirs in simulation may appear as an obvious
solution.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
However, the differences between individual inte-
grated coherent photonic reservoirs due to process variations
are so large that readout weights trained in simulation are
not transferable.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
As a consequence, each reservoir or network
of reservoirs must be trained individually on the physical
hardware.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
A mass-market maturity of integrated reservoirs is
only achievable if large numbers of devices can be trained in
an acceptable time frame.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
To a degree, designing multi-reservoir systems poses a solu-
tion to this problem.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
A given class of tasks can be decomposed
by hand into a combination of smaller subtasks, which can be
mapped onto a corresponding network of reservoirs that are
trained on these subtasks.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Unfortunately, this approach has
two drawbacks: (i) it can not be guaranteed that a suitable
decomposition exists for each given task and (ii) there is
no general approach to ﬁnding an engineered decomposition.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Given that backpropagation can not be used directly to train
multi-reservoir systems in our targeted setting, we propose an
alternative approach that still uses its power to derive interme-
diate targets.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Our approach is to deﬁne a seemingly suitable
architecture of reservoirs and attempt to train this architecture
in simulation using backpropagation.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
The resulting trained
task decomposition works well for the speciﬁc reservoirs that
were simulated.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
We then assume that reservoirs from the same
class (i.e., with identical design parameters) can approximate
functions of the input history with similar accuracy.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Under this
assumption, the readout signals from the simulated reservoirs
can be used as training targets for physical reservoirs in the
same network conﬁguration.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
In general, there is no guarantee that an appropriate task
decomposition exists for a given network and task.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
To evaluate
the feasibility of our approach, we therefore provide a proof-
of-concept with a benchmark task for which we were able
to ﬁnd a good engineered task decomposition, i.e., one for
which the decomposed system has similar performance as a
monolithic reservoir.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
We decompose the input-output relation
analytically and map the resulting individual components to
the connected reservoirs shown in Figure 1.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
The resulting
trained system is then used as a baseline to evaluate our
approach, using simulated echo state networks (ESN) [2] as
reservoirs.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
We ﬁnd that backpropagation trains desired signals
that approximate our hand-designed signals where similarity
increases with the proximity to the output layer.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Finally, we
successfully use the intermediate signals found as targets for
a classic reservoir training approach.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Architectures As modules in the multi-reservoir architec-
ture of Figure 1, we used ESNs of 100 nodes.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Because the
aim was to use backpropagation on the architecture, we used
Exponential Linear Units (ELUs) [14] as nonlinearities to
ensure a smooth propagation of gradients.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
To verify whether our engineered solution is competitive,
we compared to a monolithic reservoir with similar resources,
i.e., an ESN with 300 nodes.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
While the main point of this
work is not to outperform previous training approaches and
networks on NARMA-10, but rather ﬁnding an efﬁcient way
to train multi-reservoir systems, we consider establishing a
simple baseline as a point of reference mandatory.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
We use
a hyperbolic tangent nonlinearity for the single-ESN system
since this nonlinearity exhibited the best performance for
single-reservoir systems in preliminary experiments.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text: We trained our multi-reservoir system in 3 different ways.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Firstly, we evaluated the engineered task decomposition by


training the three ESNs in the system to ﬁt the three desired
signals respectively.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
The ESNs were trained incrementally:
each ESN takes input from previously trained ESNs and/or
the input signal to solve its assigned subtask.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
This way, each
ESN is trained to be maximally robust to approximation
inaccuracies of its predecessor(s).
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Secondly, after having shown that the NARMA-10 task
can be solved by decomposing it by hand and mapping it
to a suitable reservoir architecture, we trained the multi-
reservoir architecture from the previous step (using different,
randomly initialized ESNs) as a whole using backpropagation
to automatically ﬁnd a good task decomposition.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Thirdly, we
evaluate the transferability of the learned decomposition.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Here,
the best performing network obtained in the previous step
was used to generate target signals for networks of different,
randomly initialised ESNs from the same class.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Training and parameter tuning To train our networks,
we generated train, validation and test set time series of
100000 samples each.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
The regularization strength of our ridge
regression reservoir readouts was determined by performing
grid search in combination with 5-fold cross-validation on the
train set.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
For both the monolithic ESN as well as mapping
the engineered task decomposition onto the multi-reservoir
architecture, the validation set was used to ﬁnd the hyper-
parameters that are intrinsic to the reservoir: spectral radius,
input scaling, and bias scaling, as well as the sparsity of the
reservoir input and connection matrices.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
The resulting hyperparameter values were
then transferred to initialise the architectures used to test the
automatic task decomposition.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
When backpropagating through multi-ESN architectures,
the necessary hyperparameters for that algorithm, i.e.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
learning
rate, batch size, weight decay and amount of gradient noise
were tuned on the validation set.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
The performance of all
approaches was compared on the test set.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
We have trained our network using backpropagation through
time with a batchsize of 60 samples for 120 epochs.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
We used
Adam [16], starting with a learning rate of 0.0005.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
After 60
epochs we divided the learning rate by 2.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
We have used standard deep learning
techniques to improve training convergence for our networks:
gradient clipping [17], batch normalisation [18], and gradient
noise [19].
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Mind that we only use techniques which can be
applied in simulated networks of integrated photonic reservoirs
as well.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
While we acknowledge that our method stands or falls
with the ability to successfully backpropagate through such
networks in simulation, this appears feasible since Hermans et
al.

text:
[20] have already demonstrated backpropagation through a
similar systems.

Analysis After achieving a satisfactory task performance on
our architecture, we compared the trained intermediate output
signals of the individual reservoirs in our architecture with the
desired signal we derived by hand.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
This was done as a ﬁrst
investigation into the task decomposition that was found with
backpropagation.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
RESULTS
We started out by training 10 monolithic ESNs as well as
10 engineered multi-ESN systems, each comprising three 100
node ESNs with different random weight initializations.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Our
monolithic ESN system achieves an average NMSE of 0.035
with a standard deviation of 0.016 on the test set, which is
close to the results reported in [21].
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
Note that, while the ESNs
in [21] are smaller, their reservoir state matrix is concatenated
with a squared version of itself prior to training/evaluation
in order to enhance state richness and utilize an additional
output nonlinearity.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
We omit these steps in favor of simplicity
and to ensure that our results allow us to judge the feasibility
of our approach for future hardware implementations, where
such operations would need to be omitted or implemented by
a circuit.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
As intended, the engineered multi-ESN system slightly out-
performs the single ESN baseline with an average test NMSE
of 0.027 at a standard deviation of 0.015.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
After establishing the
quality of our engineered task decomposition, we trained 10
new multi-reservoir systems using the same architecture and
ESN hyperparameters of our engineered system, but with new,
randomly initialized ESNs.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
The best of those models achieves
an NMSE of 0.039.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
However, we ﬁnd that the performance
of our models varies a lot, due to large variations in the
convergence of the backpropagation.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
These convergence issues
result in an average NMSE of 0.076 with a standard deviation
of 0.024.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
This indicates that there is still a lot of room for
improvement here, for example by identifying more suitable
learning rate adaption schemes and even more rigorous tuning
of all training hyperparameters in general.
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
What is commonly done when learning
convergence varies a lot across training runs is simply to select
the best solution across multiple runs (which is what we will
do here).
title: Towards Deep Physical Reservoir Computing Through Automatic Task Decomposition Mapping

text:
We found that the achieved performance of the best
solution found (referred to as Net 0 in all plots of this section)
is sufﬁcient to investigate the trained system and deliver a
proof of concept for our proposed training scheme.

In

Armstrong The University of Iowa marc-armstrong@uiowa.edu Abstract The pace of improvement in the performance of conventional computer hardware has slowed significantly during the past decade, largely as a consequence of reaching the physical limits of manufacturing processes.  To offset this slowdown, new approaches to HPC are now undergoing rapid development. This chapter describes current work on the development of cutting-edge exascale computing systems that are intended to be in place in 2021 and then turns to address several other important developments in HPC, some of which are only in the early stage of development. Domain- specific heterogeneous processing approaches use hardware that is tailored to specific problem types. Neuromorphic systems are designed to mimic brain function and are well suited to machine learning. And then there is quantum computing, which is the subject of some controversy despite the enormous funding initiatives that are in place to ensure that systems continue to scale-up from current small demonstration systems. 1.0 Introduction Rapid gains in computing performance were sustained for several decades by several interacting forces, that, taken together, became widely known as Moore’s Law (Moore, 1965).  The basic idea is simple: transistor density would double approximately every two years.  This increase in density yielded continual improvements in processor performance even though it was long-known that the model could not be sustained indefinitely (Stone and Cocke, 1991).  And this has come to pass. Part of the reason for this performance fall-off is related to Dennard Scaling, which correlates transistor density with power consumption per transistor: for many years as density increased, power consumption per unit area remained near-constant.  As described by Hennessy and Patterson (2019: 53) this relationship held up well until around 2007, when it began to fail, and fail big-time. This failure is a reason why clock frequencies have not continued to increase rapidly during the last decade. Instead, computer architects turned to the use of multiple cores to increase performance.  This multicore path, however, raised other issues such as inefficiencies that arise as a consequence of ineffective thread exploitation, as well as failures in speculative branch prediction, which, in turn, causes wasted processing effort, excessive power consumption.  Indeed, the use of increasing numbers of cores push chips past their thermal design limits and require selective power-gating approaches to prevent thermal failures (Perricone et al. 2018: 60). To offset this slowdown, new approaches to HPC are now undergoing rapid development. This chapter describes current work on the development of cutting-edge exascale computing systems that are intended to be in place in 2021 and then turns to address several other important developments in HPC, some of which are only in the early stage of development. Domain- specific heterogeneous processing approaches use hardware that is tailored to specific problem types. Neuromorphic systems are designed to mimic brain function and are well suited to machine learning. And then there is quantum computing, which is the subject of some controversy despite the enormous funding initiatives that are in place to ensure that systems continue to scale-up from current small demonstration systems. 1.0 Introduction Rapid gains in computing performance were sustained for several decades by several interacting forces, that, taken together, became widely known as Moore’s Law (Moore, 1965).  The basic idea is simple: transistor density would double approximately every two years.  This increase in density yielded continual improvements in processor performance even though it was long-known that the model could not be sustained indefinitely (Stone and Cocke, 1991).  And this has come to pass. Part of the reason for this performance fall-off is related to Dennard Scaling, which correlates transistor density with power consumption per transistor: for many years as density increased, power consumption per unit area remained near-constant.  As described by Hennessy and Patterson (2019: 53) this relationship held up well until around 2007, when it began to fail, and fail big-time. This failure is a reason why clock frequencies have not continued to increase rapidly during the last decade. Instead, computer architects turned to the use of multiple cores to increase performance.  This multicore path, however, raised other issues such as inefficiencies that arise as a consequence of ineffective thread exploitation, as well as failures in speculative branch prediction, which, in turn, causes wasted processing effort, excessive power consumption.  Indeed, the use of increasing numbers of cores push chips past their thermal design limits and require selective power-gating approaches to prevent thermal failures (Perricone et al. 2018: 60).  This has led to the problem of “dark silicon” in which cores only operate part-time.  These

Armstrong The University of Iowa marc-armstrong@uiowa.edu Abstract The pace of improvement in the performance of conventional computer hardware has slowed significantly during the past decade, largely as a consequence of reaching the physical limits of manufacturing processes.  To offset this slowdown, new approaches to HPC are now undergoing rapid development. This chapter describes current work on the development of cutting-edge exascale computing systems that are intended to be in place in 2021 and then turns to address several other important developments in HPC, some of which are only in the early stage of development. Domain- specific heterogeneous processing approaches use hardware that is tailored to specific problem types. Neuromorphic systems are designed to mimic brain function and are well suited to machine learning. And then there is quantum computing, which is the subject of some controversy despite the enormous funding initiatives that are in place to ensure that systems continue to scale-up from current small demonstration systems. 1.0 Introduction Rapid gains in computing performance were sustained for several decades by several interacting forces, that, taken together, became widely known as Moore’s Law (Moore, 1965).  The basic idea is simple: transistor density would double approximately every two years.  This increase in density yielded continual improvements in processor performance even though it was long-known that the model could not be sustained indefinitely (Stone and Cocke, 1991).  And this has come to pass. Part of the reason for this performance fall-off is related to Dennard Scaling, which correlates transistor density with power consumption per transistor: for many years as density increased, power consumption per unit area remained near-constant.  As described by Hennessy and Patterson (2019: 53) this relationship held up well until around 2007, when it began to fail, and fail big-time. This failure is a reason why clock frequencies have not continued to increase rapidly during the last decade. Instead, computer architects turned to the use of multiple cores to increase performance.  This multicore path, however, raised other issues such as inefficiencies that arise as a consequence of ineffective thread exploitation, as well as failures in speculative branch prediction, which, in turn, causes wasted processing effort, excessive power consumption.  Indeed, the use of increasing numbers of cores push chips past their thermal design limits and require selective power-gating approaches to prevent thermal failures (Perricone et al. 2018: 60). 6.0 Neuromorphic Computing 
Neuromorphic computer systems are designed to emulate brain functions using spiking neural networks 
and are said to be superior to traditional DNNs because they are somewhat immune to a problem called 
catastrophic interference; when novel inputs are presented to a neuromorphic system, they can flexibly 
adapt to them and do not require complete re-training, as do DNNs.

This multicore path, however, raised other issues such as inefficiencies that arise as a consequence of ineffective thread exploitation, as well as failures in speculative branch prediction, which, in turn, causes wasted processing effort, excessive power consumption. title: High Performance Computing for Geospatial Applications: A Retrospective View Marc P. Armstrong The University of Iowa marc-armstrong@uiowa.edu Abstract Many types of geospatial analyses are computationally complex, involving, for example, solution processes that require numerous iterations or combinatorial comparisons. This complexity has motivated the application of high performance computing (HPC) to a variety of geospatial problems. In many instances, HPC assumes even greater importance because complexity interacts with rapidly growing volumes of geospatial information to further impede analysis and display.  This chapter briefly reviews the underlying need for HPC in geospatial applications and describes different approaches to past implementations.  Many of these applications were developed using hardware systems that had a relatively short life-span and were implemented in software that was not easily portable. More promising recent approaches have turned to the use of distributed resources that includes cyberinfrastructure as well as cloud and fog computing. Introduction High performance computing (HPC) has been used to address geospatial problems for several decades (see, for example, Sandu and Marble 1988; Franklin et al . 1989; Mower 1992).  An original motivation for seeking performance improvements was the intrinsic computational complexity of geospatial analyses, particularly combinatorial optimization problems (Armstrong 2000).   Non-trivial examples of such problems require considerable amounts of memory and processing time, and even now, remain intractable.  Other spatial analysis methods also require substantial amounts of computation to generate solutions. This chapter briefly reviews the computational complexity of different kinds of geospatial analyses and traces the ways in which HPC has been used in the past and during the present era.  Several HPC approaches have been investigated, with developments shifting from an early focus on manufacturer-specific systems, which in most cases had idiosyncrasies (such as parallel language extensions) that limited portability.  This limitation was recognized and addressed by using software environments that were designed to free programmers from this type of system dependence (e.g., Message Passing Interface).  This is also acknowledged for example, by the work presented in Healey . (1998) with its focus on algorithms rather than implementations.  Later approaches used flexible configurations of commodity components linked using high-performance networks. In the final section of this chapter, still-emerging approaches such as cloud and edge computing are briefly described.

Armstrong The University of Iowa marc-armstrong@uiowa.edu Abstract Many types of geospatial analyses are computationally complex, involving, for example, solution processes that require numerous iterations or combinatorial comparisons. This complexity has motivated the application of high performance computing (HPC) to a variety of geospatial problems. In many instances, HPC assumes even greater importance because complexity interacts with rapidly growing volumes of geospatial information to further impede analysis and display.  This chapter briefly reviews the underlying need for HPC in geospatial applications and describes different approaches to past implementations.  Many of these applications were developed using hardware systems that had a relatively short life-span and were implemented in software that was not easily portable. More promising recent approaches have turned to the use of distributed resources that includes cyberinfrastructure as well as cloud and fog computing. Introduction High performance computing (HPC) has been used to address geospatial problems for several decades (see, for example, Sandu and Marble 1988; Franklin et al . 1989; Mower 1992).  An original motivation for seeking performance improvements was the intrinsic computational complexity of geospatial analyses, particularly combinatorial optimization problems (Armstrong 2000).   Non-trivial examples of such problems require considerable amounts of memory and processing time, and even now, remain intractable.  Other spatial analysis methods also require substantial amounts of computation to generate solutions. This chapter briefly reviews the computational complexity of different kinds of geospatial analyses and traces the ways in which HPC has been used in the past and during the present era.  Several HPC approaches have been investigated, with developments shifting from an early focus on manufacturer-specific systems, which in most cases had idiosyncrasies (such as parallel language extensions) that limited portability.  This limitation was recognized and addressed by using software environments that were designed to free programmers from this type of system dependence (e.g., Message Passing Interface).  This is also acknowledged for example, by the work presented in Healey . (1998) with its focus on algorithms rather than implementations.  Later approaches used flexible configurations of commodity components linked using high-performance networks. In the final section of this chapter, still-emerging approaches such as cloud and edge computing are briefly described.

Armstrong The University of Iowa marc-armstrong@uiowa.edu Abstract Many types of geospatial analyses are computationally complex, involving, for example, solution processes that require numerous iterations or combinatorial comparisons. This complexity has motivated the application of high performance computing (HPC) to a variety of geospatial problems. In many instances, HPC assumes even greater importance because complexity interacts with rapidly growing volumes of geospatial information to further impede analysis and display.  This chapter briefly reviews the underlying need for HPC in geospatial applications and describes different approaches to past implementations.  Many of these applications were developed using hardware systems that had a relatively short life-span and were implemented in software that was not easily portable. More promising recent approaches have turned to the use of distributed resources that includes cyberinfrastructure as well as cloud and fog computing. Introduction High performance computing (HPC) has been used to address geospatial problems for several decades (see, for example, Sandu and Marble 1988; Franklin et al . 1989; Mower 1992).  An original motivation for seeking performance improvements was the intrinsic computational complexity of geospatial analyses, particularly combinatorial optimization problems (Armstrong 2000).   Non-trivial examples of such problems require considerable amounts of memory and processing time, and even now, remain intractable.  Other spatial analysis methods also require substantial amounts of computation to generate solutions. This chapter briefly reviews the computational complexity of different kinds of geospatial analyses and traces the ways in which HPC has been used in the past and during the present era.  Several HPC approaches have been investigated, with developments shifting from an early focus on manufacturer-specific systems, which in most cases had idiosyncrasies (such as parallel language extensions) that limited portability.  This limitation was recognized and addressed by using software environments that were designed to free programmers from this type of system dependence (e.g., Message Passing Interface).  This is also acknowledged for example, by the work presented in Healey . (1998) with its focus on algorithms rather than implementations.  Later approaches used flexible configurations of commodity components linked using high-performance networks. In the final section of this chapter, still-emerging approaches such as cloud and edge computing are briefly described.

title: High Performance Computing for Geospatial Applications: A Retrospective View Marc P. Armstrong The University of Iowa marc-armstrong@uiowa.edu Abstract Many types of geospatial analyses are computationally complex, involving, for example, solution processes that require numerous iterations or combinatorial comparisons. This complexity has motivated the application of high performance computing (HPC) to a variety of geospatial problems. In many instances, HPC assumes even greater importance because complexity interacts with rapidly growing volumes of geospatial information to further impede analysis and display.  This chapter briefly reviews the underlying need for HPC in geospatial applications and describes different approaches to past implementations.  Many of these applications were developed using hardware systems that had a relatively short life-span and were implemented in software that was not easily portable. More promising recent approaches have turned to the use of distributed resources that includes cyberinfrastructure as well as cloud and fog computing. Introduction High performance computing (HPC) has been used to address geospatial problems for several decades (see, for example, Sandu and Marble 1988; Franklin et al . 1989; Mower 1992).  An original motivation for seeking performance improvements was the intrinsic computational complexity of geospatial analyses, particularly combinatorial optimization problems (Armstrong 2000).   Non-trivial examples of such problems require considerable amounts of memory and processing time, and even now, remain intractable.  Other spatial analysis methods also require substantial amounts of computation to generate solutions. This chapter briefly reviews the computational complexity of different kinds of geospatial analyses and traces the ways in which HPC has been used in the past and during the present era.  Several HPC approaches have been investigated, with developments shifting from an early focus on manufacturer-specific systems, which in most cases had idiosyncrasies (such as parallel language extensions) that limited portability.  This limitation was recognized and addressed by using software environments that were designed to free programmers from this type of system dependence (e.g., Message Passing Interface).  This is also acknowledged for example, by the work presented in Healey . (1998) with its focus on algorithms rather than implementations.  Later approaches used flexible configurations of commodity components linked using high-performance networks. In the final section of this chapter, still-emerging approaches such as cloud and edge computing are briefly described.

 p = proportion of the program that can be made parallel (1-p is the serial part) and,

Armstrong The University of Iowa marc-armstrong@uiowa.edu Abstract Many types of geospatial analyses are computationally complex, involving, for example, solution processes that require numerous iterations or combinatorial comparisons. This complexity has motivated the application of high performance computing (HPC) to a variety of geospatial problems. In many instances, HPC assumes even greater importance because complexity interacts with rapidly growing volumes of geospatial information to further impede analysis and display.  This chapter briefly reviews the underlying need for HPC in geospatial applications and describes different approaches to past implementations.  Many of these applications were developed using hardware systems that had a relatively short life-span and were implemented in software that was not easily portable. More promising recent approaches have turned to the use of distributed resources that includes cyberinfrastructure as well as cloud and fog computing. Introduction High performance computing (HPC) has been used to address geospatial problems for several decades (see, for example, Sandu and Marble 1988; Franklin et al . 1989; Mower 1992).  An original motivation for seeking performance improvements was the intrinsic computational complexity of geospatial analyses, particularly combinatorial optimization problems (Armstrong 2000).   Non-trivial examples of such problems require considerable amounts of memory and processing time, and even now, remain intractable.  Other spatial analysis methods also require substantial amounts of computation to generate solutions. This chapter briefly reviews the computational complexity of different kinds of geospatial analyses and traces the ways in which HPC has been used in the past and during the present era.  Several HPC approaches have been investigated, with developments shifting from an early focus on manufacturer-specific systems, which in most cases had idiosyncrasies (such as parallel language extensions) that limited portability.  This limitation was recognized and addressed by using software environments that were designed to free programmers from this type of system dependence (e.g., Message Passing Interface).  This is also acknowledged for example, by the work presented in Healey . (1998) with its focus on algorithms rather than implementations.  Later approaches used flexible configurations of commodity components linked using high-performance networks. In the final section of this chapter, still-emerging approaches such as cloud and edge computing are briefly described.

Armstrong The University of Iowa marc-armstrong@uiowa.edu Abstract Many types of geospatial analyses are computationally complex, involving, for example, solution processes that require numerous iterations or combinatorial comparisons. This complexity has motivated the application of high performance computing (HPC) to a variety of geospatial problems. In many instances, HPC assumes even greater importance because complexity interacts with rapidly growing volumes of geospatial information to further impede analysis and display.  This chapter briefly reviews the underlying need for HPC in geospatial applications and describes different approaches to past implementations.  Many of these applications were developed using hardware systems that had a relatively short life-span and were implemented in software that was not easily portable. More promising recent approaches have turned to the use of distributed resources that includes cyberinfrastructure as well as cloud and fog computing. Introduction High performance computing (HPC) has been used to address geospatial problems for several decades (see, for example, Sandu and Marble 1988; Franklin et al . 1989; Mower 1992).  An original motivation for seeking performance improvements was the intrinsic computational complexity of geospatial analyses, particularly combinatorial optimization problems (Armstrong 2000).   Non-trivial examples of such problems require considerable amounts of memory and processing time, and even now, remain intractable.  Other spatial analysis methods also require substantial amounts of computation to generate solutions. This chapter briefly reviews the computational complexity of different kinds of geospatial analyses and traces the ways in which HPC has been used in the past and during the present era.  Several HPC approaches have been investigated, with developments shifting from an early focus on manufacturer-specific systems, which in most cases had idiosyncrasies (such as parallel language extensions) that limited portability.  This limitation was recognized and addressed by using software environments that were designed to free programmers from this type of system dependence (e.g., Message Passing Interface).  This is also acknowledged for example, by the work presented in Healey . (1998) with its focus on algorithms rather than implementations.  Later approaches used flexible configurations of commodity components linked using high-performance networks. In the final section of this chapter, still-emerging approaches such as cloud and edge computing are briefly described.

title: High Performance Computing for Geospatial Applications: A Retrospective View Marc P. Armstrong The University of Iowa marc-armstrong@uiowa.edu Abstract Many types of geospatial analyses are computationally complex, involving, for example, solution processes that require numerous iterations or combinatorial comparisons. This complexity has motivated the application of high performance computing (HPC) to a variety of geospatial problems. In many instances, HPC assumes even greater importance because complexity interacts with rapidly growing volumes of geospatial information to further impede analysis and display.  This chapter briefly reviews the underlying need for HPC in geospatial applications and describes different approaches to past implementations.  Many of these applications were developed using hardware systems that had a relatively short life-span and were implemented in software that was not easily portable. More promising recent approaches have turned to the use of distributed resources that includes cyberinfrastructure as well as cloud and fog computing. Introduction High performance computing (HPC) has been used to address geospatial problems for several decades (see, for example, Sandu and Marble 1988; Franklin et al . 1989; Mower 1992).  An original motivation for seeking performance improvements was the intrinsic computational complexity of geospatial analyses, particularly combinatorial optimization problems (Armstrong 2000).   Non-trivial examples of such problems require considerable amounts of memory and processing time, and even now, remain intractable.  Other spatial analysis methods also require substantial amounts of computation to generate solutions. This chapter briefly reviews the computational complexity of different kinds of geospatial analyses and traces the ways in which HPC has been used in the past and during the present era.  Several HPC approaches have been investigated, with developments shifting from an early focus on manufacturer-specific systems, which in most cases had idiosyncrasies (such as parallel language extensions) that limited portability.  This limitation was recognized and addressed by using software environments that were designed to free programmers from this type of system dependence (e.g., Message Passing Interface).  This is also acknowledged for example, by the work presented in Healey . (1998) with its focus on algorithms rather than implementations.  Later approaches used flexible configurations of commodity components linked using high-performance networks. In the final section of this chapter, still-emerging approaches such as cloud and edge computing are briefly described.

The use of HPC in geospatial applications has had a checkered history with many implementations 
showing success only to see particular architectures or systems become obsolete.

Non-trivial examples of such problems require considerable amounts of memory and processing time, and even now, remain intractable.  Other spatial analysis methods also require substantial amounts of computation to generate solutions. This chapter briefly reviews the computational complexity of different kinds of geospatial analyses and traces the ways in which HPC has been used in the past and during the present era.  Several HPC approaches have been investigated, with developments shifting from an early focus on manufacturer-specific systems, which in most cases had idiosyncrasies (such as parallel language extensions) that limited portability.  This limitation was recognized and addressed by using software environments that were designed to free programmers from this type of system dependence (e.g., Message Passing Interface).  This is also acknowledged for example, by the work presented in Healey . (1998) with its focus on algorithms rather than implementations.  Later approaches used flexible configurations of commodity components linked using high-performance networks. In the final section of this chapter, still-emerging approaches such as cloud and edge computing are briefly described.

title: High Performance Computing for Geospatial Applications: A Retrospective View Marc P. Armstrong The University of Iowa marc-armstrong@uiowa.edu Abstract Many types of geospatial analyses are computationally complex, involving, for example, solution processes that require numerous iterations or combinatorial comparisons. This complexity has motivated the application of high performance computing (HPC) to a variety of geospatial problems. In many instances, HPC assumes even greater importance because complexity interacts with rapidly growing volumes of geospatial information to further impede analysis and display.  This chapter briefly reviews the underlying need for HPC in geospatial applications and describes different approaches to past implementations.  Many of these applications were developed using hardware systems that had a relatively short life-span and were implemented in software that was not easily portable. More promising recent approaches have turned to the use of distributed resources that includes cyberinfrastructure as well as cloud and fog computing. Introduction High performance computing (HPC) has been used to address geospatial problems for several decades (see, for example, Sandu and Marble 1988; Franklin et al . 1989; Mower 1992).  An original motivation for seeking performance improvements was the intrinsic computational complexity of geospatial analyses, particularly combinatorial optimization problems (Armstrong 2000).   Non-trivial examples of such problems require considerable amounts of memory and processing time, and even now, remain intractable.  Other spatial analysis methods also require substantial amounts of computation to generate solutions. This chapter briefly reviews the computational complexity of different kinds of geospatial analyses and traces the ways in which HPC has been used in the past and during the present era.  Several HPC approaches have been investigated, with developments shifting from an early focus on manufacturer-specific systems, which in most cases had idiosyncrasies (such as parallel language extensions) that limited portability.  This limitation was recognized and addressed by using software environments that were designed to free programmers from this type of system dependence (e.g., Message Passing Interface).  This is also acknowledged for example, by the work presented in Healey . (1998) with its focus on algorithms rather than implementations.  Later approaches used flexible configurations of commodity components linked using high-performance networks. In the final section of this chapter, still-emerging approaches such as cloud and edge computing are briefly described.

Several HPC approaches have been investigated, with developments shifting from an early focus on manufacturer-specific systems, which in most cases had idiosyncrasies (such as parallel language extensions) that limited portability.  This limitation was recognized and addressed by using software environments that were designed to free programmers from this type of system dependence (e.g., Message Passing Interface).  This is also acknowledged for example, by the work presented in Healey . (1998) with its focus on algorithms rather than implementations.  Later approaches used flexible configurations of commodity components linked using high-performance networks. In the final section of this chapter, still-emerging approaches such as cloud and edge computing are briefly described.

title: High Performance Computing for Geospatial Applications: A Retrospective View Marc P. Armstrong The University of Iowa marc-armstrong@uiowa.edu Abstract Many types of geospatial analyses are computationally complex, involving, for example, solution processes that require numerous iterations or combinatorial comparisons. This complexity has motivated the application of high performance computing (HPC) to a variety of geospatial problems. In many instances, HPC assumes even greater importance because complexity interacts with rapidly growing volumes of geospatial information to further impede analysis and display.  This chapter briefly reviews the underlying need for HPC in geospatial applications and describes different approaches to past implementations.  Many of these applications were developed using hardware systems that had a relatively short life-span and were implemented in software that was not easily portable. More promising recent approaches have turned to the use of distributed resources that includes cyberinfrastructure as well as cloud and fog computing. Introduction High performance computing (HPC) has been used to address geospatial problems for several decades (see, for example, Sandu and Marble 1988; Franklin et al . 1989; Mower 1992).  An original motivation for seeking performance improvements was the intrinsic computational complexity of geospatial analyses, particularly combinatorial optimization problems (Armstrong 2000).   Non-trivial examples of such problems require considerable amounts of memory and processing time, and even now, remain intractable.  Other spatial analysis methods also require substantial amounts of computation to generate solutions. This chapter briefly reviews the computational complexity of different kinds of geospatial analyses and traces the ways in which HPC has been used in the past and during the present era.  Several HPC approaches have been investigated, with developments shifting from an early focus on manufacturer-specific systems, which in most cases had idiosyncrasies (such as parallel language extensions) that limited portability.  This limitation was recognized and addressed by using software environments that were designed to free programmers from this type of system dependence (e.g., Message Passing Interface).  This is also acknowledged for example, by the work presented in Healey . (1998) with its focus on algorithms rather than implementations.  Later approaches used flexible configurations of commodity components linked using high-performance networks. In the final section of this chapter, still-emerging approaches such as cloud and edge computing are briefly described.

Material and Method
2.1
Image Acquisition
The proposed 2.5D thermometry relies on sampling the volume of interest (VOI)
using a common 2D GRE sequence and [1,...,n] diﬀerent orientations.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The GRE
sequence can directly reconstruct magnitude and phase images simultaneously.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
To ensure a proper sampling of the VOI in our setup the GRE sequence is ro-
tated by 22.5◦around the applicator’s main axis.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
This results in an evenly dis-
tributed sample of eight diﬀerent orientations.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
To increase the spatial resolution,
the angles between the acquired scans should be as high as possible, resulting
in the following acquisition order: 0◦, 90◦, 45◦, 135◦, 22.5◦, 112.5◦, 67.5◦, and
157.5◦.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
To reduce the delay between image acquisition and visualization of the
volumetric thermometry map, the SIEMENS Healthineers Access-I Framework
was integrated.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The framework allows for fetching the image data directly from
SIEMENS MR devices without an intermediate imaging archive system.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
2.2
2.5D Thermometry Reconstruction
Before treatment starts, reference phase images are acquired for each of the eight
orientations.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Each newly acquired phase image will start computing the up-to-

To
do so, the proton resonance frequency shift (PRFS) method is used as described
by Rieke et al.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

the following Equation

to the temperature since Equation 1 otherwise only computes the temperature
change, neglecting the tissue’s base temperature.

For each voxel

The 2D population map can be applied to every slice of the ﬁnal
3D output volume, reducing the computational power needed.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
During the inter-
vention, every acquired live image triggers the reconstruction of the up-to-date
2.5D thermometry map.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Here, the heat value for each voxel is reconstructed
using Equation 4,
Ti = Iw · (w1 · TIPleft + w2 · TIPright)
(4)
with Ti representing the temperature of the current voxel i and TIPleft, TIPright
representing the temperature of the adjacent interpolation partners.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Occurring
vessels or other structures, which cause a heat sink eﬀect are segmented during
the intervention planning.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Subsequently, the segmented structure is saved as an
additional Look-Up Volume.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Here, each voxel can be checked if it is part of a
heat sink structure.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Using this knowledge, the interpolation weight Iw, which
ranges between [0, 1], may be adjusted.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
To create a ﬁrst proof of concept, a pilot study was conducted
to evaluate the 2.5D thermometry reconstruction using 13 bio protein phantoms
as described by Bu Lin et al.[2].
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The coagulation zone’s visibility in the post-
treatment data sets increased by adding a contrast agent (0, 5µmol/L Dotarem)
to the phantoms.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
For six phantoms, additional polyvinyl chloride (PVC) tubes
with a diameter of 5mm and a wall thickness of 1mm were integrated into the
phantoms (three single-tubes, three double-tubes) to simulate a possible heat
sink (HS) eﬀect.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The applicator of the permittivity feedback control MWA
system (MedWaves Avecure, Medwaves, San Diego, CA, USA, 14G) was placed
inside the phantom by sight and secured in position.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Subsequently, the phan-
toms were placed inside a 1, 5T MR scanner (Siemens Avanto, Siemens Health-
ineers, Germany).
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The coaxial cables connected to the applicator and MW gen-
erator were led through a waveguide.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Chokes and electrical grounding mea-
sures were added as described by Gorny et al.[5] to reduce radio frequency

In the case of the perfusion phantoms, the PVC tubes were led
through the wave guide.

They were connected to a diaphragm pump and a
water reservoir outside the scanning room.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
A ﬂow meter (SM6000, ifm elec-
tronic, Essen, Germany) was interposed between the reservoir and the pump,
providing a ﬂow rate of 800mL/min.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Observations showed a moderate HS eﬀect
using this setup with a maximum antenna power of 36W.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Additionally, tem-
perature sensors were inserted in two phantoms to experimentally verify the
temperature accuracy of 1◦C.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Right before treatment, ten reference phase im-
ages were acquired and averaged for each orientation to compensate for static
noise.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The MWA duration was set to 15 minutes with a temperature limit of
90◦C.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The GRE sequence oﬀers a slice thickness of 5mm, a ﬁeld of view (FOV)
of 256mm ∗256mm, a matrix of 256 ∗256, and a bandwidth of 260Hz/Px.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Image acquisition took around 1.1s with a 5s break to simulate the temporal
resolution for a breathing patient.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The TE was 3.69ms, the TR 7.5ms, and the
ﬂip angle 7◦.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
For post-treatment observation a 3D turbo spin echo (TSE) se-
quence (TE = 156ms, TR = 11780ms, ﬂip angle = 180◦, matrix = 256 ∗256,
FOV = 256mm ∗256mm, bandwidth = 40Hz/Px, slice thickness = 1mm)
was used.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The 3D TSE allows for proper visualization of the real coagulation
zone due to a very high tissue contrast.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Extraction of the coagulation ground
truth was done manually by a clinical expert using MEVIS draw (Fraunhofer
MEVIS, Bremen, Germany).
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
All data sets used are available for download at
http://open-science.ub.ovgu.de/xmlui/handle/684882692/89.

4
Discussion and Conclusion
The aim of this work is to develop a volumetric thermometry map, which can
be applied to a wide variety of clinical setups.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Therefore, our work heavily re-
lies on the up-to-date standard 2D GRE sequence for image acquisition.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
This
allows for the standard accuracy of the thermometry up to 1.0◦C.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Nonetheless,
the sampling of the 3D volume also results in some disadvantages, which need
to be addressed in the future.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
First, the diﬀusion of the heat inside the tissue
is not linear over time.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Therefore, it would be necessary to include an adaptive
temporal and spatial resolution depending on the current intervention time.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
A
new study should be conducted to identify an optimal sequence protocol for this
2.5D thermometry approach.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Second, we found that the reconstruction some-
times shows stair-case artifacts.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Because only one image is acquired every few
seconds, the time diﬀerence between adjacent orientations may be very high.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The temperature diﬀerence for each voxel dependent on the applicator’s radius


2.5D Thermometry Maps for MRI-guided Tumor Ablation
9
may be computed and applied to the corresponding voxel on every other out-of-
date data to compensate for this error.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
This transfer of the heat gradient may
improve the reconstruction accuracy.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Another approach may be the use of a
model-based reconstruction to take diﬀerent tissue characteristics into account.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
To pseudo-increase the temporal resolution, bio heat transfer simulations may
also be included during reconstruction.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The acquired live data may be able to
adjust the simulation parameters to increase the simulation accuracy.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Finally,
our study only performs on bio protein phantoms.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Results show a proof of con-
cept for the proposed method, but it still has to be evaluated in real tissue and
a more realistic clinical environment.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Therefore, perfused ex vivo livers may be
a way to go in the future.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Additionally, we currently assume a breath-holding
state or at least a breath-triggered image acquisition.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Research shows that a
wide range of interventional registration methods is available, but further inves-
tigations in this area still need to be done to create an applicable method.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The
last issues arise because of the MR inhomogeneity during image acquisition.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The
slightest disturbances may result in heavy image artifacts.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Proper shielding of
the MW generator is needed to reduce the SNR loss over time thus increasing
the thermometry and reconstruction accuracy.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
In conclusion, we proposed a novel method for 2.5D thermometry map recon-
struction based on common GRE sequences rotated around the applicator’s main
axis.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
A pilot study was conducted using bio protein phantoms to simulate cases
with possible heat sink eﬀects and without.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
The evaluation shows promising
results regarding the DSC of the reconstructed 2.5D thermometry map and a
manually deﬁned ground truth.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Future work should address the reconstruction
method’s improvement by integrating further apriori knowledge like the esti-
mated shape of the heat distribution.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
Furthermore, a more realistic study should
be conducted with bigger sample size and real tissue.
title: arXiv:2108.05734v1  [eess.IV]  12 Aug 2021

text:
In sum, the method shows
a high potential to improve the clinical success rate of minimally invasive abla-
tion procedures without necessarily hampering the standard clinical workﬂow of
the individual clinician.
