assignment phase, different from the MBFD introduced in the
previous section, the VM manager sends an invitation to a
subset of all active hosts to obtain a list of hosts that accept the
incoming VM.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
After receiving the invitation, the host performs
a Bernoulli trial, which computes the value of an overall
assignment function to decide whether to accept a VM or not.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The assignment function considers the resource utilization and
utilization threshold, then calculates the probability to accept
the incoming VM.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
If the trial succeeds, the host sends back
a message to the manager.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The manager collects all messages
and selects one available host to allocate the incoming VM.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The second part of EcoCloud is VM migration, which utilizes
two Bernoulli trial based functions to handle the over-utilized
and under-utilized situations separately.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
If the trial of the
under-utilized situation is successful, a randomly selected VM
will be migrated.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
On the other hand, migrations with over-
utilized will migrate the VM that decreases resource utilization
to be lower than the over-utilized threshold.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The target host
to accept the VM is decided by another assignment function
with a slight modiﬁcation of a parameter.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
EcoCloud can be the representative algorithm aiming to
reduce energy while minimizing VM migrations.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The main
advantage of EcoCloud is that the approach can reduce down-
time duration and transmission bandwidth.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Furthermore, hosts
can make migration decisions by themselves, thus the pressure
of VM manager is relieved.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The limitation of this work is that
it investigates the effect of power consumption on SLAs while
the effects of VM migrations on SLAs are not evaluated.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
GRANITE
GRANITE [20] is a holistic virtual machine scheduling
algorithm capable of minimizing total data center energy
consumption, including computing energy and cooling energy.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
This work considers Computer Room Air Conditioner (CRAC)
as the only cooling devices and constructed their models.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Based on server models and cooling models, GRANITE uti-
lizes a greedy algorithm to conduct the VM initial placement
and dynamic migration.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
They assume that the users’ resource
demand can be predicted.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
In the initial placement stage, the
greedy algorithm is applied in GRANITE for all VMs to select
the host with the least increment of total energy after the
placement.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The CRAC will be adjusted if the CPU temperature
is above the threshold.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
In the dynamic VM consolidation
stage, the algorithm aims to balance the workloads and cool-
ing energy consumption.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The GRANITE deﬁnes a dynamic
temperature threshold and checks host status.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
If the host
temperature is above the temperature threshold, a set of VMs
will be migrated to other hosts.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The target host selection for
migration is the same as the greedy algorithm in the initial
placement stage.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
GRANITE can present the algorithms that consider the
holistic management of energy in cloud data centers.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The core
idea of the algorithm is similar to MBFD algorithm, while it
considers cooling power, which leads to more accurate and
holistic scheduling results.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The advantage of this work is that
it combines the server status and data center thermal control
to form the ﬁne-grained energy efﬁcient scheduling.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
However,
the model accuracy can be further improved by using a 3-
Dimensional computational ﬂuid dynamics model rather than
2-Dimensional one.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
LOAD
LOAD [21] is an algorithm based on learning automata
for energy and SLA efﬁcient consolidation of VMs in cloud
data centers.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The proposed algorithm considers the demanded
resource of users to predict overloaded hosts.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
By preventing
overloaded hosts and shutting down idle hosts, the proposed
algorithm aims to save energy consumption of data centers.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The learning automata-based overload detection enhances the
VM consolidation by predicting CPU usage of hosts upon re-
source usage history.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Each VM is equipped with one automata
including 3 actions, increasing CPU utilization, reducing CPU
utilization and no changing of CPU utilization.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
At the be-
ginning, the 3 actions are with equal probability.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
After the
beginning stage, the reward and penalty of learning automata
will be updated based on the environment.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The automata
selects one of the three actions in each iteration based on the
probability.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
And in the next iteration, if the automata’s decision
is right, the action will be rewarded, otherwise, the action will
be penalized.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The learning automata is applied to estimate
usage of VMs on the host.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
If the estimation shows that the
host may be overloaded, the VMs will be migrated and other
VMs will be prevented to be migrated to the current host.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The
migrated destination is based on the Best Fit Decreasing (BFD)
algorithm [23].
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The simulation results show that leveraging


learning-based prediction can reduce energy consumption of
data centers.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
LOAD is a typical algorithm applying learning techniques to
optimize VM consolidation.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
This work advances the existing
work by considering the dynamic prediction for resource us-
age.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
But the limitation is that this work predicts the overloaded
situations and does not handle the under-utilized situations.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
ACS
ACS [22] is an online optimization meta-heuristic algorithm
based on ant colony optimization and VM consolidation to
achieve the near-optimal solution.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Its objective is to balance
the energy consumption, the number of VM migrations and
QoS concerning performance.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
In this approach, the authors
formulate the energy efﬁcient VM consolidation as a multi-
objective optimization problem to optimize multiple metrics
simultaneously.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
To leverage ACO, the necessary entities, in-
cluding pheromone updating rules and probabilistic decision
rules are deﬁned.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
If one solution has more pheromone trails,
the VM has a larger probability to be placed on the host.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
ACS
also has updating rules for local and global pheromone, which
are applied in each iteration.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
In iterations, the local pheromone
is updated by ant when they perform a movement.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
After all ant
construct their solutions locally, the global pheromone update
is conducted as the migration process, and only the dominated
place will be kept.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The process is repeated until it reaches the
maximum iteration number.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
ACS represents a set of meta-heuristic algorithms proposed
to balance multiple objectives.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The results based on simu-
lations show that the proposed algorithm can reduce energy
consumption and VM migrations while guaranteeing QoS.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The performance can be further improved by investigating the
impact of VM migration on network.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
In summary, the investigated algorithms all follow the two-
phase energy efﬁcient scheduling process as shown in Fig.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The investigated algorithms apply different techniques to
optimize the placement of VMs.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Most of the investigated al-
gorithms focus on the optimization of VM consolidation phase
except EcoCloud spends more effort on the initial placement
based on probabilistic approach.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
In the algorithms focusing on
the VM consolidation optimization, MBFD applies heuristic
algorithms based on bin-packing modelling, while EcoCloud
utilizes a probabilistic approach to ﬁnd the host with the high-
est probability to accept migrated VM.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
GRANITE considers
energy and performance together by modelling cooling energy
consumption and VM performance degradation.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
ACS applies
a meta-heuristic algorithm to ﬁnd the optimized consolidation
solutions.

manager (which manages the virtual resources).
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Model: Equation (1) is used to calculate the energy con-
sumption for this research work, which represents the linear
model of power and CPU utilization.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
ACS
Architecture: In the architecture of ACS, two types of
agents are included: local and global agents.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The local agent
is deployed in a host to solve the host status detection sub-
problem by monitoring the host resource utilization.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The
global agent is responsible for supervising and optimizing
the VM placement by taking advantage of the ACO-based
algorithm.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Model: ACS utilizes the linear power model as MBFD in
Equation 2.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We note that the investigated algorithms have different
focuses on the phases of VM consolidation, and we show
the focuses in Fig.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
As introduced, the VM consolidation
process can be mainly divided into two phases: the initial
VM placement and dynamic VM migration.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
And for the
VM migration, the overloads and under-utilized detection,
VM selection and VM allocation are included.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
MBFD and
EcoCloud spend more effort on the VM placement phase,
including the initial VM placement and VM allocation in
Dynamic VM migration.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
On the other hand, LOAD focuses on
overloads detection by predicting the utilization via learning
automaton to optimize overload detection.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
GRANITE takes
the CPU temperature into consideration and optimizes the
overload detection policy.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
ACS improves all the phases in
dynamic VM consolidation.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
It utilizes LiRCUP [24] to forecast
overloads of servers, and adopts Ant Colony System to ﬁnd
the near-optimal solutions for VM selection and allocation.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
In summary, from the perspective of architecture, the inves-
tigated algorithms all adopt the layered architecture, and the
layers can be mainly divided into three parts.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The bottom layer
is the resource provisioner, which provides physical or virtual
resources.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The middle layer is responsible for the energy
efﬁcient scheduling, which handles the VM management and
provides the energy efﬁcient scheduling algorithms.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
At the top
layer, the users’ request and optimization goals are conﬁgured.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
From the modelling perspective, all algorithms adopt the
linear power model.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
As for power components, all algorithms
include the CPU energy consumption, MBFD, EcoCloud and
ACS consider the memory part, and GRANITE utilizes a more
comprehensive model including storage, network and cooling.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Algorithm complexity analysis: MBFD, GRANITE and
LOAD are based on heuristic algorithms, and the complexity
of them are all M ×N, where N is the number of hosts and M
is the number of VMs.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The complexity of EcoCloud equals
to the number of hosts to accept VMs, which is N.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Based
on meta-heuristic with iterations, the complexity of ACS is
M×N×A×I, where A is the number of ants that concurrently
build their migration plans, and I is the number of iterations.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
METRICS
For the objective of energy efﬁciency, energy consumption
is the major metric to be evaluated.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
However, the algorithms
are also making trade-offs between the energy consumption
and other metrics, such as SLA violations.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
In this section, we
discuss the adopted metrics in our investigated energy efﬁcient
algorithms.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Note that the investigated algorithms use some
similar metrics while having some other additional metrics.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Here we aim to cover the metrics applied in these algorithms
and identify the differences between these metrics.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Table II
summaries the algorithms with their corresponding adopted
metrics.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Metrics for energy efﬁciency
Total energy consumption: It is the total energy consump-
tion consumed by physical machines in the data centers.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
It is
derived from the power model in Equation (2).
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Number of active servers: It represents how many servers
are running as active during the observation time.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The value
should be minimized, and thus more idle serves can be
switched into low-power mode.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Metrics for SLA
SLA violation percentage (SLAV) [18]: It is the percentage
of SLA violations events relatively to the total number of the
processed time frame.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The SLA violation is identiﬁed when a
given VM cannot get the amount of MIPS as requested.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
VM migration times: The number of migrations triggered
by the algorithm during the VM scheduling process.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Average SLA violation: It is the average CPU performance
that has not been allocated to an application when requested,
resulting in performance degradation.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
In summary, we can notice that several metrics have been
adopted for evaluations by more than one algorithm, including
total energy, SLA violation percentage, VM migrations, aver-
age SLA violations and number of active hosts.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
PERFORMANCE EVALUATIONS
In this section, to compare the performance of investigated
algorithms, we conduct experiments for the ﬁve well-known
and investigated algorithms based on different performance
metrics and two traces.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We also include one provided algo-
rithm in CloudSim as baselines, the Interquartile Range (IQR)
[11] that manages a dynamic threshold for overload detection.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Experiments Settings
For host capacity, each host has two CPU cores with
millions of instructions per second (MIPS) of 1880 or 2660,
4 GB of RAM and 1 TB of storage.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We use the power model
derived from HP ProLiant ML110 G4 or HP ProLiant ML110
G5, which has been used in [18] and [22].
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
According to
the model, the energy consumption of the host with different
utilization is shown in Table III.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
For VM conﬁgurations, we
consider four types of VMs with MIPS of 500, 1000, 1500
and 2500, and the VMs number of each type is randomly
generated.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The detailed speciﬁcations of hosts and VMs are
shown in Table IV.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We ﬁrst carry out several experiments under synthetic
workloads, and then, to simulate the real cloud data center, we
utilize the real workload data of the CoMon project provided
by PlanetLab [25].
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The workload includes CPU utilization
data of thousands of VMs allocated to servers that are located
in more than 500 places around the world.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
And the data is
collected every ﬁve minutes for 10 days, which represents the
workload in the real cloud environment.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We select four metrics to evaluate the performance of these
algorithms, including Energy Consumption, SLA violation
percentage (SLAV), VM migration times and the number of
active hosts.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We choose these metrics as they have been
adopted widely and also used in more than one algorithms
as we discussed in Section V.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Due to the page limitation,
we evaluate SLAV to represent the SLA violations instead
of average SLA violations.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Implementation Details
The conﬁgurations in EcoCloud include a shape parameter
p, α and β in its probability function.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We set p = 3, α = β =
0.25 in our experiments, following the conﬁgurations of the
original paper.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
For LOAD, the reward and penalty parameters
for updating learning automaton, a and b, are both conﬁgured
to 0.1.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We utilize the parameters in the original paper of ACS,
however, we don’t have a training data set to estimate the
initial pheromone level.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Therefore, we set M to be the total
number of selected VMs, and P is conﬁgured as the number
of under-utilized servers.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The conﬁgured parameters of MBFD
and GRANITE are the same as the original paper.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Synthetic Workloads
To show the performance under synthetic workloads, the
ﬁrst part of the evaluations focuses on the experiments under
synthetic workloads, which has been used in MBFD and ACS.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We ﬁrstly generate the same number of hosts and VMs and
vary the lower utilization threshold that deﬁnes when the host
is under-utilized.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
And we varied the threshold from 0.1 to 0.5
with increment as 0.1.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The higher utilization threshold is set
as 0.4 more than the lower utilization threshold.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We follow
the conﬁguration of the utilization threshold interval in [18].
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Under each conﬁguration, we randomly generate workloads to
run the experiments and repeat 10 times.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Both the number of
hosts and VMs are set as 50.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
3 shows the average results of the experiments under
synthetic workloads.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Based on the results, the higher values
of lower utilization threshold can enable all the algorithms
to achieve better energy efﬁciency, fewer VM migrations and
more SLAV.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
To be more speciﬁc, ACS performs the best
on energy consumption by reducing 21.1% power compared
with MBFD.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
EcoCloud requires less than 600 migration times,
which are much fewer than other algorithms.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
The reason that
ACS achieves the best energy efﬁciency is that it has the lowest
number of active hosts.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
For SLA violation comparison, these
algorithms perform better when the lower threshold is set to
be 0.1.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
As setting the lower utilization threshold with 0.5 can
achieve the best performance for all the algorithms, we ﬁx
the lower utilization threshold as 0.5, and run the experiments
repeatedly with 10 times to show the variance of results, which
are shown in Fig.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We can notice that ACS can achieve the
best performance in energy consumption with 31.2 kWh, and
EcoCloud can reduce the VM migrations as 420.5 in average.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
To investigate the impacts of different numbers of hosts and
VMs, we also ﬁx the lower utilization threshold as 0.5, but
conﬁgure the ratio of the number of servers to the number of
VMs to be 1:1, 1:1.25, 1:1.5 and 1:1.75 respectively.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
With each
ratio, the experiments are repeated 10 times, and the results
as shown in Fig 5.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
We can observe that energy consumption
increases signiﬁcantly when there are more VMs.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
ACS is
the most energy efﬁcient algorithm and consumes 31.2 KWh
and 31.5 kWh when the ratio is 1:1 and 1:1.75 respectively,
which is about 21.2-34.4% less compared to MBFD.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
EcoCloud
achieves the best results in VM migrations.
title: Energy Efﬁcient Algorithms based Consolidation Cloud Computing: Comparisons Evaluations

text:
Although the
investigated algorithms can reduce more energy than IQR,
more SLAV happens in these algorithms.

CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
In this paper, we present an investigation of 5 state-of-the-
art energy efﬁcient algorithms based on VM consolidations
for cloud data centers.

synthetic and real traces, the results show that these algorithms
can efﬁciently reduce the energy consumption while balancing
the trade-offs between energy and some other metrics, such as
VM migrations and SLA violations.

units are physically separated and large amounts of data need to be shuttled back and forth 
between them during the execution of various computational tasks.

Deep learning is based on computational models that are, to a certain extent, bio-inspired, as they rely on networks of connected simple computing units operating in parallel. Deep learning has been successfully applied in areas such as object/pattern recognition, speech and natural language processing, self-driving vehicles, intelligent self-diagnostics tools, autonomous robots, knowledgeable personal assistants, and monitoring. These successes have been mostly supported by three factors: availability of vast amounts of data, continuous growth in computing power, and algorithmic innovations. The approaching demise of Moore's law, and the consequent expected modest improvements in computing power that can be achieved by scaling, raise the question of whether the described progress will be slowed or halted due to hardware limitations. These successes have been mostly supported by three factors: availability of vast amounts of data, continuous growth in computing power, and algorithmic innovations. Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in
the Cloud
PETER VAILLANCOURT, Cornell University, USA
BENNETT WINEHOLT, Cornell University, USA
BRANDON BARKER, Cornell University, USA
PLATO DELIYANNIS∗, Cornell University, USA
JACKIE ZHENG∗, Cornell University, USA
AKSHAY SURESH, Cornell University, USA
ADAM BRAZIER, Cornell University, USA
RICH KNEPPER, Cornell University, USA
RICH WOLSKI, University of California, Santa Barbara, USA
The increasing availability of cloud computing services for science has changed the way scientiﬁc code can be developed, deployed,
and run.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text: Many modern scientiﬁc workﬂows are capable of running on cloud computing resources.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Consequently, there is an increasing
interest in the scientiﬁc computing community in methods, tools, and implementations that enable moving an application to the cloud
and simplifying the process, and decreasing the time to meaningful scientiﬁc results.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In this paper, we have applied the concepts of
containerization for portability and multi-cloud automated deployment with industry-standard tools to three scientiﬁc workﬂows.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
We
show how our implementations provide reduced complexity to portability of both the applications themselves, and their deployment
across private and public clouds.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Each application has been packaged in a Docker container with its dependencies and necessary
environment setup for production runs.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Terraform and Ansible have been used to automate the provisioning of compute resources
and the deployment of each scientiﬁc application in a Multi-VM cluster.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Each application has been deployed on the AWS and Aristotle
Cloud Federation platforms.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Variation in data management constraints, Multi-VM MPI communication, and embarrassingly parallel
instance deployments were all explored and reported on.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
We thus present a sample of scientiﬁc workﬂows that can be simpliﬁed
using the tools and our proposed implementation to deploy and run in a variety of cloud environments.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

INTRODUCTION
Scientiﬁc computing applications often make use of large-scale, high-performance resources (computers, networking,
and storage, such as those provided by XSEDE) to achieve “capability” results – new scientiﬁc results that are made
possible by the capability of the resources.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Because these resources are expensive to provision and maintain, they
are often deployed in a bespoke conﬁguration that requires highly optimized coding, data management, and access
methodologies to ensure maximal utilization.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
However, there are a number of scientiﬁc workloads that innovate through other forms of computational scientiﬁc
exploration and discovery.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Speciﬁcally, researchers investigating new algorithms or developing new computationally
supported processes often require fast turn-around times (to support rapid prototyping), resource portability (to enable
collaboration), and maximal developer productivity.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text: Cloud computing has evolved as a commercial approach to meeting these goals for consumer-facing services.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Often,
cloud applications have life-cycles measured in days or weeks that are developed by a geographically distributed set
of collaborating developers whose labor cost has a considerable budgetary limitation.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Because cloud computing is
optimized for web services, however, it has proven diﬃcult to exploit for scientiﬁc workloads (even those driven by
developer productivity and not resource capability).
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In particular, the life-cycle of many scientiﬁc codes is long, creating
a valuable legacy that cannot easily be supplanted by new development.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In this paper, we explore the use of cloud computing, Linux containers [9, 14, 28], and an automated deployment
scheme as productivity enhancing technologies for scientiﬁc applications that include or are based on legacy software.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In particular, for many researchers, the ease of implementing and running software in multiple cloud environments
becomes a key element of leveraging the ﬂexibility and eﬃciency of the cloud computing paradigm.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
As a result, porta-
bility and reproducibility of application installation, deployment, and decommissioning (i.e.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
the reproducibility of the
software life-cycle) becomes critical 1.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Containerization software, which provides application software a lightweight virtualized environment to run in,
has recently become a popular strategy for deploying and running scientiﬁc software, portability across diﬀerent
types of systems, and ease of adoption for researchers[11].
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Further, software containers coupled with partially or fully
automated cloud deployment schemes oﬀer intriguing beneﬁts for a wide range of computational tasks in scientiﬁc
research, in the form of robust, scalable, and portable software deployments that can be used during development
through production[23].
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
This paper will describe work successfully performed to encapsulate, deploy, and run three diﬀerent existing scien-
tiﬁc workﬂows – which are broadly representative of common computational science applications – in multiple clouds
using automated containerized deployment.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Our system automatically
• manages the myriad of diﬀerent possible deployment options available from computing clouds,
• conﬁgures the cloud-hosted networking to support virtualized parallel application execution, and
• translates the legacy build and deployment mechanisms that accompany many application (e.g.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
from a cluster
or batch HPC environment) to the equivalent mechanisms in the cloud.

We make use of Docker containerization technology to provide portability and reproducibility, and Terraform[21] and
Ansible[22] to deploy, manage, and provision cloud resources automatically.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In the following sections we describe
each of the scientiﬁc workﬂows in detail, their data and computational requirements, the particular technical details
for containerized implementation, how the choice of deployment context aﬀected the implementation, an evaluation
of software runs performed, and discuss the practical outcomes of the experience, including the beneﬁts and disad-
vantages of this approach.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Each of these workﬂows was run on Amazon Web Services (AWS)[2], and Aristotle Cloud
Federation[27].
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The Aristotle Cloud Federation is an NSF-funded project between the Cornell University Center for Advanced
Computing, University at Buﬀalo Center for Computational Research, and the University of California Santa Barbara
Department of Computer Science, with the goal of joining cloud computing resources at each of these institutions
in order to develop a federated model for science users to easily access data, scale research problems using cloud
computing techniques, and lessen the time to science of research teams.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The federated model allows resources to be
shared between the Aristotle member clouds, including individual data sets, access to specialized software, and access
to site-speciﬁc resources.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
By leveraging the strengths of each of the member institutions, the overall cloud is able to
provide larger overall scale and more resources than each of those institutions separately.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Use cases described below
are largely the result of collaborations between the Aristotle Science Team members and the Infrastructure group
which drove the requirements for containerized applications.

Each case represents a user community that seeks the potential productivity gains oﬀered
by cloud computing.

2.2
WRF
The weather forecasting community has historically valued large data sets for predictive power, and utilized analyses
of past similar situations to both inﬁll data and make future projections.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The computational Weather Research and
Forecasting (WRF) Model[46] is popular for weather simulation with a long history of development and use by the
National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), contributors, and consumers.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The software is widely used by a
community of more than 48,000 researchers across 160 countries to produce a wide variety of results ranging from con-
tributions to real-time weather prediction, long term climate simulations, large-scale low resolution idealized physics
simulations, and small-scale high resolution detailed physics simulations leveraging large quantities of observational
grounding data as model inputs.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Numerical computation, data input, and data output can all grow large very quickly
when simulating detailed physics at high grid resolutions or long timescales.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The communication of intermediate
results at grid boundaries – necessary to advance simulation steps at suﬃcient accuracy – can also place a burden on
network capacity.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Therefore, to achieve desired modeling ﬁdelity, WRF is thus commonly run on resources with an
abundance of computational capacity, disk storage, and network throughput.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Common technologies used to meet these
needs include managed compute cluster resources with provided Fortran compilation guides and packages to facilitate
eﬃcient numerical simulation.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Network communication is facilitated by MPI libraries which may be optimized for
low latency use of specialized network hardware.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Disk storage may be fulﬁlled by high capacity Lustre distributed ﬁle
system hosting.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The speciﬁc WRF model we choose requires parallel execution across compute resources to allow for faster and
more detailed numerical grid simulation of weather properties, namely of interest to simulating wind speed near wind
turbine farms at high spatial and temporal resolution.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Useful simulation data for climate observations include wind
speed and temperature, as well as dependent measures such as estimated wind turbine power production.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In order to
obtain these measures in a reasonable timeframe, it is necessary to leverage large computational resources to quickly
and accurately simulate many numerical values over grids of varying density, with associated network communication
at tile boundaries and large demand for disk storage both for tile boundary grounding conditions derived from data
input as well as intermediate result storage.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Consequently, this scientiﬁc workﬂow represents an example of resource-
intensive HPC applications and the challenges they present to eﬀective cloud deployment.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
NCAR provides many public data sets, analysis tools, and regression suites suitable for conﬁrming the validity of the
numerical simulations produced by the model.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
We use these regression tests to validate the correctness of our cloud
WRF executions.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
A sample WRF version 4.0 run using an NCAR regression test Docker build was
run using 1.3GB of novel weather Global Forecast System data published by NCEP.

text:
Geographic reference data for grid
domain preprocessing and high resolution physics totaled 30GB.

This sample was run inside a Docker container on a
4 virtual CPU AWS instance.

The observed runtime was 9 minutes 20 seconds and should be scalable to moderately
larger data sets of similar nature.

Similar past simulation runs executing private builds and data have leveraged Docker
to execute for long time periods on Aristotle Cloud Federation and XSEDE Jetstream cloud resources.

2.3
FRB_pipeline
Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are astrophysical phenomena that occur as transient high energy pulses or bursts in radio
astronomy data.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
FRBs are expected to occur thousands of times per day, but conﬁrmed detections of unique sources are
below a hundred[13] since the ﬁrst recorded detection occurred in 2007[31].
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Since radio telescopes are on the earth’s
surface, radio astronomy data is plagued by large amounts of Radio Frequency Interference (RFI), which can block or
distort signals, making transient signals like FRBs even harder to detect, despite large quantities of data available to
search.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
A standard data presentation in time-domain radio observations is the dynamic spectrum, a plot
of intensity vs.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Typically, the time of arrival of an astrophysical radio transient is longer at lower
frequencies due to dispersion by plasma in the interstellar medium.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In particular, the time of arrival is proportional to
the inverse square of frequency and the dispersion measure (DM), a constant equal to the integral of electron density
in the interstellar medium along the line of sight.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Thus, in a dynamic spectrum, radio transients exhibit a characteristic
quadratic shape.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
A number of existing transient search techniques are based on de-dispersing dynamic spectra using
a bank of several plausible DMs, ﬂattening into a time series, and performing matched ﬁltering with the time series.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text: These methods are well-tested and have been reliable in discovering new FRBs in the past decade.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Exploring new detection techniques that have the potential to oﬀer advantages in accuracy or computation cost is
also of great interest to astronomers.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In the past three years, researchers have conducted successful transient searches
by applying multi-layer convolutional neural networks to dynamic spectra [12][1].
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The "Friends-Of-Friends" (FOF)
algorithm is a straightforward and eﬃcient way to locate radio transient candidates by identifying and characterizing
clusters of high signal pixels in the dynamic spectrum directly.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
For this scientiﬁc workﬂow, the software is called the FRB_pipeline[38] and was developed by the
Aristotle Cloud Federation Science Team in collaboration with Cornell researchers established within the radio astron-
omy community.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Thus, the software was designed with the computational needs of the science in mind, as well as the
ﬂexibility to expand as new methods of radio transient detection develop.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The FRB_pipelineis a customizable scien-
tiﬁc software package written in Python 3 designed to simplify the process of combing large datasets – from any of a
variety of radio telescopes – to detect FRBs.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The package enables ﬂexible use of established methods to ﬁlter RFI, detect
candidates, and determine viability of candidates as well as the availability of new methods, or even addition of cus-
tomized methods by the user.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
A commonly used package within radio astronomy, called PRESTO[42], is a dependency,
and newer methods such as our FOF algorithm are included as well.

(2) Compute the root mean square (RMS) background white noise, using an iterative method that discards outlier
pixels until a convergence threshold is reached
(3) Mark each pixel with signal greater than a constant parameter m1 times the RMS background noise
(4) Group the high-signal pixels marked in (2) in close proximity – deﬁned as being within a constant number of

text:
Smoothing and averaging reduce the variation in intensity between adjacent pixels,
which is essential for FOF to work properly.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Additionally, averaging reduces the size of the data by a signiﬁcant factor
(typically order 100), vastly reducing the computation time of FOF and other search algorithms.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
However, smoothing
does take signiﬁcant computational time.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The computational complexity of pure averaging is m × n × k, with n,m the
number of time and frequency bins respectively in the dynamic spectrum, andk the number of pixels averaged together.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
For example, if smoothing with a 2-D Gaussian ﬁlter followed by decimation is used, a computational complexity of
nm × log(n)log(m) is achieved using fast FFT based convolution.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
While smoothing has a signiﬁcant cost, savings made
running FOF on data whose size is multiple orders smaller than the raw data are essential.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The FOF algorithm itself has
a computational complexity ofm×n,withn the number of time bins andm the number of frequency bins in the dynamic
spectrum.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Both computing the RMS background noise and comparing each pixel’s signal to the ﬁrst threshold for the
bulk of computation time, while the two least squares regressions computed for each cluster are relatively insigniﬁcant.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In contrast to techniques using de-dispersion and matched ﬁltering, FOF is com-
pletely agnostic to signal shape.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
On one hand, this means that FOF will have no trouble identifying astrophysical signals
with any DMs, but also that FOF is vulnerable to a high rate of false positives due to RFI.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Additionally, because the DM
of a given signal is unknown a priori, de-dispersion and matched ﬁltering must be performed on a large set of trial
values, which entails a computational complexity equal to the number of trial DMs times the n log(n) time of matched
ﬁltering.

TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATION
Due to the aforementioned diﬀerences in the scientiﬁc workﬂows, not all of the details of implementation are the same.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text: However, the core steps of the process were the same, and we detail where they diﬀered in the coming sections.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In
general, for each workﬂow:
• A Docker container was built to enable portability and reproducibility
• Data was stored in locations easily accessible to cloud computing virtual machines (VMs)
• Compute VMs and communication networks were deployed with Terraform
• Secure shell (ssh) keys for communication between VMs were conﬁgured with Ansible
• Application containers and associated setup were deployed to multiple cloud VMs using Ansible
• Output data was staged on remote storage for user retrieval
• All compute resources were decommissioned using Terraform to curtail ongoing cost
All of these applications are non-interactive and batch-style, utilizing a single container image for each node (or
VM).
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text: Therefore, they do not require much or any orchestration of interacting services.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The utilized data storage was
commonly simple object storage such as Amazon S3[3] or a deployed NFS server on an additional cloud VM when a
ﬁle system mount was needed by the application.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
These compute runs were small-scale (relative to large jobs on an
HPC system) and intended as proof-of-concept for the applications.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Therefore, no more than 3 maximum size VMs
were provisioned per cluster in our testing runs performed for this work.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Other deployments have been made up
to 8 or more VMs, but a thorough study of maximum eﬀective cluster size or the point of decreasing gains at scale
due to communication overhead is deferred to future work.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Reproducibility was gauged by application completion on
basic testing scenarios, and was not thoroughly evaluated with an eye to numerical precision errors nor subtle kernel
diﬀerences that Docker cannot eliminate, being bound to run on the VM kernel as deployed.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
3.1
Containerization
Containers are OS-level virtualization: a single OS kernel can host multiple isolated environments.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Containers are
lighter weight than using hypervisor-based VMs wherein each VM runs a separate kernel, but comes with the obvious
restriction that all containers on the host must use the same OS kernel and the same version of the kernel.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
But in many
cases, this has been a more than acceptable trade-oﬀ.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
While container technology originated from Solaris Zones[40]
and FreeBSD Jails[39], the prevalence of Linux on commodity cloud hardware has synergistically aided in creating a
convergence of Linux containerization technology.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Docker has not only been responsible for both the popularity of Linux containers in the industry, it has seemingly
expanded the deﬁnition of a container.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The colloquial deﬁnition now includes the ability to distribute and deploy
applications with minimal conﬁguration: i.e., everything is self-contained within the container.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Singularity, another

text:
Linux container technology, targeted HPC users by trading security concerns: Singularity requires the user to grant
an application container access to all of the user’s ﬁles rather than running a container virtualization service as a
privileged user, as is the case with Docker.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In so doing, many of the traditional notions of a container were further
broken down, though Singularity has optional parameters to enable isolation [45].
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Other container technologies exist for Linux as well, including that which is provided by a core service of most
Linux distributions, systemd[18].
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
However, systemd-nspawn containers typically do not include the more modern
connotation of a container being a packaged application.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
But, it has been used by other technologies for this purpose,
such as nix-containers [17], a container technology for the NixOS [8, 15, 16] Linux distribution that allows packages to
be shared from the host’s package-store.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
While we have not yet used Nix containers in this work, we have containerized
Nix within Docker, which aﬀords its own advantages.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Nix provides a high degree of reproducibility due to package deﬁnitions being carefully check-summed for any
sources of diﬀerences, e.g.: URL change of binary or source blobs used for the package, checksum diﬀerences in the
binary or source blobs, version changes, conﬁguration changes, semantic changes in the package deﬁnition (i.e.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Nix
expression) — such as build or runtime conﬁguration, or any such changes in dependencies of the packages.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Once a nix
expression is written, it can then be shared for use within other Nix projects, without the need to worry about how to
integrate it into a container deﬁnition ﬁle.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Additionally, by using Nix, the environment could easily be run bare-metal
on NixOS or as a Nix container in the future.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
For this work, specializedDocker containers were developed for the Lake_Problem_DPS and
FRB_pipeline applications, but NCAR WRF has a publicly available Docker Container for WRF including a regres-
sion test[35].
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The Lake_Problem_DPS container makes full use of Nix within Docker to ensure reproducibility, even
using a Nix expression to simplify the process of including proprietary software within the container without publicly
sharing the software in a public GitHub repository[25].
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The FRB_pipeline container was based upon a container de-
veloped for North American Nanohertz Observatory for Gravitational Waves (NANOGrav)[33][34], but updated for
our work[37][36].
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
3.2
Automation
Terraform is an open source tool used for infrastructure management and provisioning developed by HashiCorp.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The
common use case for Terraform is managing resources on multiple cloud infrastructure providers – such as AWS and
Google Cloud – with minimal diﬀerences in scripts.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Terraform is under active development and supports a variety
of providers including AWS, Google Cloud Platform (GCP)[30], Microsoft Azure[32] , and OpenStack infrastructure
providers which includes XSEDE Jetstream, Aristotle Cloud Federation, and the Cornell CAC Red Cloud on-premise
hosting environments.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Terraform uses the HashiCorp Conﬁguration Language (HCL)[20] to automate the deployment
of various cloud resources among diﬀerent cloud vendors.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Terraform does this in a declarative manner, meaning that
cloud resource states are written in a Terraform ﬁle and Terraform attempts to create the declared resource or modify
the resource into the declared state.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
It manages the existing resource using metadata created from running a Terraform
conﬁguration ﬁle.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text: Ansible is an open source tool used for software provisioning, conﬁguration management, and automation.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Ansible
uses YAML to write conﬁgurations.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Similar to Terraform, Ansible is declarative, though it can also perform operations
procedurally.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
An Ansible YAML ﬁle declares states of various Ansible modules which are subsequently set up on the
8

PEARC ’20, July 26–30, 2020, Portland, OR, USA
remote machine.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Compared to using scripts for conﬁguration management, Ansible can achieve the same things scripts
can on multiple machines or VMs in parallel, which is advantageous to cluster management.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text: We used Terraform for provisioning and infrastructure management, and Ansible for conﬁguration management.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Concretely, Terraform was used to create the VMs and networks while Ansible was used to set up Docker application
containers including the associated environments for the science workﬂows to run on VMs and to issue commands
to initiate and control science runs.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
To create a cluster with communication, Terraform ﬁrst sets up a single base VM
with a custom network conﬁguration.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
From the network conﬁgurations, the VM can only receive ssh traﬃc from a
speciﬁed IP and TCP connection with another VM on the same network.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
There is no restriction on how the VM can
send traﬃc.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text: Next, Ansible imports the Docker containers.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Afterwards, Terraform creates copies of the VM to form a
cluster.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text: Finally, Ansible sets up the VMs in parallel for OpenMPI communication.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
It is important to note that while the Ansible script is portable across diﬀerent cloud infrastructure providers, the
Terraform script is not.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Ansible requires the IP addresses of the VMs while Terraform resources are dependent on the
cloud infrastructure providers.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Generally, to use Terraform on the various providers requires some form of credentials
and slight modiﬁcations to the Terraform script.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
By using simple VM hosting with standard OS images rather than
provider-speciﬁc services, our infrastructure level scripting is easily portable even though it requires some provisioning
code translation to adapt to diﬀerent underlying cloud providers based on commonly available templates, including
our own new public examples.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
3.3
Multi-VM MPI
After provisioning server and network resources, we conﬁgure them using both Ansible scripting and Docker container
deployment.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
A simple way to think of the process is that Terraform creates a server we can access, Ansible installs
libraries we need (much like user shell commands issued over ssh), and Docker will fetch a particular application
bundle to be run.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
For on-demand MPI clusters in particular, Ansible scripts perform some additional cluster level conﬁguration, such
as pushing a list of cluster hosts to each member upon setup.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The Docker images we created to run WRF, for example,
on the on-demand MPI cluster similarly have cluster level host conﬁguration injected by a scripted build process
to lower the burden of manual user setup on each cluster deployment.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Ansible can then perform scripted cluster
tests to verify success of all deployed components and successful networked science code execution.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Notably, the
entire process can be written as code or templates and run from Terraform commands on one researcher workstation.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
These concepts are similar to functions provided by another popular technology for cluster deployment – Kubernetes
– which specializes in deploying redundant web applications across multiple hosts and networks to provide high
availability and uptime for diverse workloads.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
However, due to MPI communication requiring long-lived guaranteed
hosting and our current focus on a small set of related applications per cluster deployment, neither the additional user
complexity of scripted Kubernetes setup nor the monetary and researcher familiarity costs associated with hosted
Kubernetes solutions sacriﬁcing portability are justiﬁed under the stated goals of this work.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
By using simple and
standard technologies summoned by a small set of scripts, users can easily create on-demand MPI clusters to achieve
science results.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Default usage of Terraform and Ansible examples will create network resources and servers and then conﬁgure
them to perform useful work, but in some cases advanced recurring communication between server instances pro-
vides for a new classes of applications to be hosted for eﬃcient computation.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Multiple VMs can be organized into
clusters running message passing interface (MPI) applications to deliver high-performance computations commonly

text:
Although we use cloud providers with commodity network and
storage services as well as hardware level hyperthreading or time sharing in this work, options exist to pay a premium
for specialized hardware appliances, dedicated hardware, and bare metal native execution with varying amounts of
increased conﬁguration complexity.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Here we defer detailed cost, complexity, and performance analyses to future work
and recount our experiences developing and deploying on-demand OpenMPI clusters with real scientiﬁc research ap-
plications on basic cloud provider oﬀerings.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
As noted above, the technologies used – namely Terraform, Ansible, and
Docker – are open source or publicly available, and were chosen to facilitate smooth researcher user experience, which
can be further facilitated by referencing our own published examples.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Our primary on-demand MPI application target for cluster deployment is the NCAR WRF Model widely used for
weather simulation.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
This application has intense compute, networking, and storage demands that lend well to scaling
diﬀerent grid tiles of simulation time steps to multiple VMs with periodic communication of intermediate results and
grounding grid tile boundary conditions against provided observational data.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
(1) User checks out deployment code and conﬁgures their desired cloud provider credentials and tools, and sets
cluster size
(2) User installs Terraform and Ansible with provided commands to perform deployment
(3) User executes deployment which creates a cluster of the desired size on the cloud provider and runs short tests
(4) User may use deployment script outputs to access the cluster for speciﬁc manual application runs
(5) User copies out result data and cleans up cluster using Terraform destroy command
Cluster deployment including resource provisioning and server instance conﬁguration is entirely automated, trig-
gered by the user calling a single Terraform command, reviewing the proposed changes, and choosing to execute.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
In more detail, the cluster provisioning automates the following processes:
(1) Terraform reads the resources desired from the appropriate cloud provider template folder
(2) Terraform reads the provided cloud provider credentials
(3) Terraform plans the resources it must create, namely networks, security groups, and VM instances
(4) Terraform requests approval to create the resources, which will incur potential costs
(5) Terraform uses an underlying provisioning API to create resources, starting with networks
(6) Terraform creates a VM where cluster software packages will be installed
(7) Ansible waits for the VM to come up, then installs software packages needed by all cluster nodes, including
Docker images with scientiﬁc application code
(8) Terraform tears down the VM to ensure a clean disk snapshot
(9) Terraform is notiﬁed of Ansible completion and takes a server image
3.3.3
Cluster Virtual Machines and Network.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
(1) Terraform creates more VM instances as above using the server image as a base copy
(2) Ansible gets IPs of created cluster VMs
(3) Ansible builds cluster speciﬁc Docker images with cluster info, and builds in ssh conﬁguration for later use with
MPI
(4) Terraform creates NFS server for the cluster (if needed by the application)
