(5) Ansible conﬁrms NFS mounts on each host (if needed by the application)
3.3.4
Application Runs and Cleanup.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
(1) Ansible is invoked upon completion of cluster node provisioning to start tests
(2) Tests are run over ssh inside of Docker on a designated head node and launch mpirun commands
(3) For speciﬁc user data processing jobs, the user uploads input data to the chosen cloud storage or cluster NFS
server
(4) Ansible or manual ssh performs a fetch of data needed, and then Ansible initiates scientiﬁc computation
(5) Upon completion of the application run, the user can fetch data using scp, aws s3 command-line, or other
convenient data movement tools
(6) The Terraform destroy command can be used to remove all compute resources and leave data and server image,
or all resources entirely
(7) Should a user desire to persist the cluster to restart, cloud provider speciﬁc commands can pause/restart the
compute resources
3.4
Deployment Contexts
The public cloud provider we deployed full scientiﬁc workﬂow runs on for this work is AWS, and we wrote and tested
Terraform and Ansible scripts for these applications (as well as other scientiﬁc workﬂows) on GCP.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Our choice of
basic network and VM infrastructure provisioning with Terraform also allows us to support extensions to other public
clouds including Microsoft Azure and many more.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Deployment to other platforms have been explored, but have not
been fully automated at this time.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
There are a dizzying array of available cloud provider services, with accompanying power and
convenience in equal measure to the volume of user documentation and choices presented to a user.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Towards the goal of
enabling users to quickly deploy scientiﬁc software to run massively parallel or on a communicating cluster to engage
many compute resources, we do not burden users immediately with undue choices nor present the full complexity of
cloud provider oﬀerings available.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Sensible defaults are chosen for the applications presented and these ﬁner details
are exposed in the Terraform infrastructure provisioning descriptions and can be modiﬁed as users see ﬁt, and as they
desire to learn more powerful controls of the performance and cost of the deployed systems.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The largest diﬀerences between the cloud infrastructure providers are the names of diﬀerent resources described in
the Terraform resource descriptions, written in a format similar to JSON dubbed HashiCorp Conﬁguration Language
(HCL).
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text: A GCP compute network is similar to an AWS virtual private cloud.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

Both are used to designate the network
the VMs are created on.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

To control the ingress and egress traﬃc of the VMs we used the AWS security group which
is equivalent to the GCP compute ﬁrewall.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

In order to facilitate MPI communication for on-demand cluster creation,
various security group port settings in combination with instance level Docker container settings and internal con-
tainer process launch commands were attempted to arrive at working conﬁgurations that have been captured in the
deployment, build, and run scripts we present.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Cluster access is secured by appropriate default network controls and
ssh access key conﬁguration.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

To make copies of the base VM in AWS, we used the Terraform resource "AMI from
instance" to create an image from the base VM and multiple VMs from the created image.

In GCP, we ﬁrst created a
Google compute snapshot of the VM, which was then converted to a Google compute disk, which was then used to
create a Google compute image.

4
PRACTICAL OUTCOMES
The primary beneﬁt of this work is the ability to quickly and easily move a scientiﬁc computing application – includ-
ing HPC applications which are communication-bound – with its dependencies and associated setup to any number
of cloud infrastructures.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
This has several resulting outcomes that are beneﬁcial, with a few disadvantages, and has re-
sulted in many lessons learned.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Our approach increases the accessibility of the cloud computing paradigm for scientiﬁc
computing, has the ability to leverage multi-cloud deployments, adds portability and reproducibility naturally to the
process of scientiﬁc software deployment in the cloud, and can simplify the process of iterative software development
due to rapid deployment options.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Our implementation drastically eases or removes the infrastructure implementation required of scientists and re-
searchers, both in understanding and in time to develop, freeing up precious time to target scientiﬁc results or perfor-
mance within an application.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
For researchers who do not otherwise have access to large-scale computational resources,
or who have access to the cloud but not the understanding of speciﬁc deployment contexts and tools to be able to lever-
age the cloud eﬀectively, our provided scripts can be employed to enable access more readily.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Furthermore, research
staﬀresponsible for supporting researchers in scientiﬁc computing can apply this work to on-premise clouds to auto-
mate deployments, or to public cloud deployments to expedite researcher progress.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Since Terraform and Ansible are already designed to handle deployments in a variety of clouds, there is no added
work to switch from one cloud to another other than the cloud-speciﬁc details that must change, but would need to
regardless of deployment method.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The same container can be used on any of the public cloud vendors and many private
clouds.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Furthermore, the same container can be utilized on a personal computer for development, then deployed in
multiple clouds, increasing the ability to push changes and rapidly deploy improvements or new scientiﬁc tests.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
A disadvantage is if you need to change the implementation, it may require understanding some cloud infrastructure
speciﬁc details (though it would anyway) and knowing enough Terraform or Ansible to be able to make the changes.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
It
is a smaller overall cost than complete manual deployment, but especially a downside if you are already familiar with
or targeting a single cloud vendor and already have understanding of other tools.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
A further disadvantage could be if a

container does not already exist for your application, or one of the cloud services you would like to leverage has not
already been scripted, then time would need to be spent in development.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The experience of containerizing, automating the deployment of, and running the computations for these scientiﬁc
applications has provided a wealth of lessons on both the diﬃculties and the simpliﬁcations available when moving
scientiﬁc research from a variety of disciplines to the cloud, which we shall summarize.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The simplest deployment,
especially if a Multi-VM setup is required, can be the best way to illustrate requirements that might otherwise have
been overlooked due to the diﬀerences between the cloud computing paradigm and other compute resources.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
As
with any new system, it pays to start with the simplest use case, and build up incrementally to the full scale of the
application.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
For deployment in the cloud, this means not only starting with a small-scale run, but also a small data
input and output, a single VM (as far as possible), a minimal-size container, as so on.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Starting with large data sizes can
cause undue complexity to the process of deployment and computation, whether in choosing the appropriate VM size
and type to handle the load, in large long-term storage costs while still developing, or in large egress charges on public
cloud (though this is not an issue for some private campus clouds such as Aristotle Cloud Federation).
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Thus, it is also
important to become familiar with the cost model of your chosen cloud provider(s) and determine cost requirements
concurrently with cloud infrastructure requirements.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
After a successful run of a small deployment of an application,
these requirements become clearer.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text: The importance of the choice of software tools one uses cannot be overstated.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
While there is a plethora of tools –
whether created by speciﬁc cloud vendors, industry partners, or otherwise – that can be used to facilitate conﬁguration,
deployment, automation, and computation in the cloud, it is vital to select the tools that are not only the best for the job,
but also enable the user to get scientiﬁc code running quickly.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Across a variety of clouds, we have found that Terraform
and Ansible provide rapid conﬁguration, deployment, and management of compute resources for scientiﬁc workﬂows
in a manner simpliﬁed for those familiar with scripting and similar tools.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Applications using Python, bash scripting,
or similar tools are convenient to run from Ansible, empowering the user to increase automation of the application
runtime in the deployed environment with low eﬀort.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
5
CONCLUSION
Initial adoption of cloud computing for deployment of scientiﬁc and HPC workﬂows can require a large lead time to
learn new technologies, develop containers that support software development and production work, comprehension
of how to translate requirements to cloud infrastructure options, and even learning the nuances of how particular
cloud vendors operate.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
The technologies we’ve presented in this paper can be very useful tools to reduce this lead time
and deploy scientiﬁc runs more rapidly, while increasing reproducibility and portability of the scientiﬁc workﬂows
in the process.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
We have provided open source code and examples in the hopes that others can leverage this work to
increase their own understanding of the cloud as an infrastructure to support scientiﬁc computing, and to deploy new
workﬂows to the beneﬁt of the scientiﬁc community at large.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
However, moving scientiﬁc research applications to the cloud has the potential to be an undertaking, and this is es-
pecially true for the aforementioned HPC applications which are communication-bound.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
For the researcher interested
in moving an MPI application to the cloud, this approach may decrease the deployment time and add other beneﬁts,
but several other factors are of concern as well in making the decision: cost, availability of compute resources, exis-
tence of a container template for the application (or time and knowledge to develop one), and familiarity with the
cloud and associated tools.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
A compelling case for cloud is when compute cycles are simply not available elsewhere, or
cloud resources (such as campus clouds) are more readily available than HPC-style resources.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Conversely, the public
13


PEARC ’20, July 26–30, 2020, Portland, OR, USA
Vaillancourt and Wineholt et al.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
cloud might be cost-prohibitive for very large-scale or large-output applications, but one is able to secure time on a
supercomputer.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
More work is needed to fully examine when is a good time to turn to cloud as a resource for scientiﬁc
computing and HPC applications.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Our plan for future work includes completing automation of these workﬂows on Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud,
cost analysis of deployments, and bare-metal performance comparisons on HPC resources.
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
There are also more appli-
cation areas to explore using this approach, including those that have need of specialized hardware (such as GPUs).
title: Reproducible and Portable Workflows for Scientific Computing and HPC in the Cloud

text:
Furthermore, while we have stated some reasons for selecting this approach in favor of others for the deployment of
these workﬂows, a broader analysis of other deployment methods (such as Kubernetes and vendor-speciﬁc strategies)
is another next step.

Abstract—This conceptual paper discusses how different as-
pects involving the autonomous operation of robots and vehicles
will change when they have access to next-generation mobile
networks.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
5G and beyond connectivity is bringing together a
myriad of technologies and industries under its umbrella.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
High-
bandwidth, low-latency edge computing services through network
slicing have the potential to support novel application scenarios
in different domains including robotics, autonomous vehicles, and
the Internet of Things.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In particular, multi-tenant applications at
the edge of the network will boost the development of autonomous
robots and vehicles offering computational resources and intel-
ligence through reliable ofﬂoading services.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The integration of
more distributed network architectures with distributed robotic
systems can increase the degree of intelligence and level of
autonomy of connected units.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We argue that the last piece to put
together a services framework with third-party integration will
be next-generation low-latency blockchain networks.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Blockchains
will enable a transparent and secure way of providing services
and managing resources at the Multi-Access Edge Computing
(MEC) layer.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We overview the state-of-the-art in MEC slicing,
distributed robotic systems and blockchain technology to deﬁne
a framework for services the MEC layer that will enhance the
autonomous operations of connected robots and vehicles.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020
arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
INTRODUCTION
5G and beyond connectivity has the potential for bringing
together the telecommunications, robotics [1], artiﬁcial intel-
ligence (AI) [2], Internet of Things (IoT) [3] and blockchain
domains [4], all of which share a recent trend in which com-
putation is shifting towards more distributed architectures [5],
[6], [7].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
This comes together with the concept of network
slicing and edge computing, key pillars behind the low-latency
and network load optimization in 5G and beyond networks [8].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Through multi-tenant slicing, new business opportunities are
being created at the edge of the network [9].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In this study,
we provide a vision for the future of 5G-connected robots and
vehicles, which will potentially beneﬁt from this connectivity
to increase their degree of autonomy and level of intelligence
through services offered by third parties at the MEC layer.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We explore the potential for combining the backbone of
today’s autonomous robotic navigation and localization, the
Robot Operating System [10], with the latest development
in 5G and slicing strategies at the MEC layer.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The MEC
layer is an inherently distributed computing platform that
enables high-performance computing (HPC) services with
minimal latency [11].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The most direct application is to extend
existing ofﬂoading schemes [12], and integrate them within
the 5G stack [13].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
This has clear potential in vehicular and
robotic navigation, especially when combined with predictive
schemes [14].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In addition, we envision that FPGA-based and
CGRA-based hardware accelerators at the base stations will
provide new levels of reconﬁgurability, energy efﬁciency, and
processing power within the ofﬂoading orchestrators.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
More-
over, we take into account integration between distributed
robotic systems [15], and distributed computation platforms
deﬁned within a blockchain [16].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We argue that permissioned
blockchains backed by a large public and trusted infrastruc-
ture will be a key element of MEC-based services.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
These
blockchains will be able to provide a transparent and secure
channel for connected vehicles to interact with third parties.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Slicing at the MEC layer in 5G and beyond can reduce the
computational load in connected robots and vehicles.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
This will
allow units with more constrained resources, such as delivery
drones, to enhance their situational awareness and increase
their autonomy.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In terms of safety and reliability in long-
term autonomous operation in both self-driving vehicles and
autonomous robots, challenges arise from the point of view
of (1) localization accuracy [17], (2) situational awareness
and level of understanding of the environment [18], and (3)
limitations of computational capabilities in smaller robots
or drones, with algorithms that might take longer to run
depending on the complexity of the environment [19].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Slicing
at the MEC layer has potential for providing services to
support the operation of connected autonomous vehicles and
robots by providing in respect to the above challenges (1)
streaming services of high deﬁnition (HD) maps for accurate
localization with online updates whenever the environment
changes; (2) semantic information of the environment, as
well as metadata from other connected vehicles; and (3) an
adaptive algorithm that autonomously provides in real-time
map models and environment data according to the operational
and computational capabilities of the vehicle requesting data.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Blockchain at the MEC Layer
The integration of Blockchain with slicing at the MEC layer
has recently been proposed by different researchers [20], [21],
[22].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Nevertheless, we focus on the use of Blockchain to
enable services at the MEC layer for autonomous robots and
vehicles.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Rather than focusing on data integrity and security,
arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020


we see that distributed consensus mechanisms in a blockchain
are ideal for managing the MEC hardware, services and
client-provider interaction.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
At the same time, the utilization
of blockchains in the robotics ﬁeld has recently shown its
potential [6].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We extend it as a framework for integrating ex-
ternal services into distributed robotic and vehicular systems.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
One of the key challenges in the utilization of a blockchain
for applications requiring real-time communication and data
processing is the scalability, as indicated by [23], [24].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
How-
ever, a more wider adoption of blockchain technology across
multiple ﬁelds, specially the robotics and automation ﬁeld, is
expected with the arrival of low-latency and high-throughput
next-generation blockchain networks [6].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Supporting Autonomy in Smart Cities
The concept of Smart City has been mostly tied to the IoT
since its inception [25].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Nonetheless, the IoT and the robotics
domain have since been integrated as connected robots become
the standard.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The new edge and fog computing paradigms have
only increased this synergy between the two domains [26].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
surveyed the early works on the topic and deﬁned
three fundamental dimensions of a Smart City: technological,
human and institutional [27].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Self-driving cars or autonomous
delivery robots extend the original concept of smart city from
passive technology (mainly sensors) to active participators
in an increasingly more complex cyber-physical dimension.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Nonetheless, little attention has been put on the role of the
institutional dimension towards a more widespread penetration
of autonomous robots and vehicles in Smart Cities.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In a recent
work, we argue that institutions and public infrastructure can
play a key role in enabling collaboration between autonomous
robots with a blockchain [6].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We extend this idea with the
introduction of MEC slicing.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The key areas of the system are
illustrated in Figure 1.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

Since the introduction of MEC, network slicing has been
seen as a key enabler of future autonomous vehicles [28].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
However, the deﬁnition of architectures and the speciﬁcations
of slices have been made mostly from the point of view of the
telecommunications domain, taking into account network re-
quirements [29].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

intelligent network slicing framework with differentiated slices
for (i) trafﬁc safety, (ii) autonomous driving, (iii) infotainment
and vehicular internet, and (iv) service slice that manages the

title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We believe
that efﬁcient slicing requires different granularity within the
autonomous driving concept, and therefore, we propose a
slicing architecture that takes into account both the network
requirements and the type of computing resources utilized for

entiation between ofﬂoading services and streaming services.

In addition, we replace the top managing slice in [30] with

work for interaction between clients and service providers.

channels and the actual services, which are hosted in their
corresponding slice, we argue that the robustness of the system

text:
Multi-Access Edge Computing and Network Slicing
The standardization of Multi-Access Edge Computing
(MEC) has been promoted by the European Telecommunica-
tions Standards Institute (ETSI) [31], with the MEC Industry
Speciﬁcation Group (ISG) launched at the end of 2014.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The
ETSI MEC ISG aims at deﬁning a multi-tenant distributed
cloud platform to be located at the edge of the radio access
network (RAN) [32].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Moving computation and data intensive
tasks towards the edge of the network enables the low-
latency and high-bandwidth requirements of 5G and beyond
connectivity.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Other fundamental technologies towards this end
include containerization and virtualization, software deﬁned
networking (SDN), and network function virtualization [28].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
One of the key pillars enabling multiple verticals within
MEC, and opening the RAN edge to a wide variety of indus-
tries and users, is network slicing [33].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Network slicing con-
sists of the co-existence of multiple logical software-deﬁned
networks (slices) on a common hardware infrastructure, i.e.,
a multi-tenant cloud infrastructure at the edge of the network,
with each of the slices being optimized to meet the require-
ments of a particular application [34].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We are particularly
interested in slicing for the automotive sector, where 5G will
be the key in vehicle-to-everything communication [35].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Since its early developments, MEC monetization has been
a central topic of discussion [28].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Blockchain can provide a
framework to democratize the monetization and utilization of
the MEC layer as a platform to offer automation services to
connected vehicles or robots.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
From the point of view of security, a recent report from
the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) on
the thread landscape for 5G networks has identiﬁed numerous
threats [36].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
A blockchain can directly provide a higher level
of resilience against multiple of these, such as authentication
trafﬁc spikes, manipulation of network trafﬁc, malicious di-
version of trafﬁc, among others.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Our focus is on utilizing
a blockchain as a transparent and distributed framework to
achieve consensus in terms of MEC resource provisioning.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
This has a direct impact on preventing threats such as abuse
of third party hosted network functions, manipulation of the
network resources orchestrator, or opportunistic and fraudulent
usages of shared resources, among others.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In summary, MEC offers the beneﬁts of cloud computing
at the edge of the network, with the potential to offer new
customer experiences.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
MEC allows for more scalable appli-
cations and network infrastructure by ensuring that raw data
is processed at the edge, and only the resulting metadata
is transmitted over to central cloud servers or other clients,
optimizing the network load and reducing unnecessary trafﬁc
with information that does not need to be stored.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Blockchain and Distributed Ledgers
Blockchain platforms can be classiﬁed into two main types,
permissionless and permissioned [37].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
These can also be de-
nominated public (permissionless), and consortium or private
blockchains (permissioned).
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In public blockchains, there is no
authority and all nodes are equivalent.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In consortium or private
blockchains, there are trusted authorities or nodes in charge of
validating transactions [38].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
One of the most famous and successful blockchains to date
is Hyperledger, a project initiated in 2016 within the Linux
Foundation [39].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Hyperledger is a permissioned blockchain
which has been successfully utilized in multiple industrial
domains [40].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The objective of Hyperledger is the deployment
of an open-source and cross-industry framework that can be
utilized as a standard platform to run smart contracts within a
decentralized ledger.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Consortium blockchains, and Hyperledger in particular,
have key advantages that have an impact over business net-
works such as a MEC-based blockchain [41]: (i) all partici-
pants have known identities, and therefore data protection laws
can be applied accordingly, with permission required in order
to join the network; (ii) data partitioning through channels,
ensuring that data is available on a need-to-know basis and is
only transmitted to the parties that need; (iii) scalability and
adaptable levels of trust, with endorsement policies deﬁning
the number and nature of validators required to verify a given
transaction, and subsequent network load optimization; (iv) a
modular architecture, where identities and other components
can be easily extended to meet the various requirements of
third parties or public authorities; and (v) ﬂexible and complex
queries over the ledger, simplifying the auditing process.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The data partitioning scheme seamlessly combines with
the multi-tenancy at the MEC layer, with different service
providers not being necessarily aware of other’s transactions
and data, even if this information is encrypted, as it would
happen in a public blockchain.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The endorsement policies can
be optimized to manage scalability in large networks, deﬁning
validators depending on the client’s location or the current
network load.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Then, alternating nodes across the network
could be validated in different locations at different times.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The smart contracts within Hyperledger can be leveraged to
manage the interaction between clients and service providers.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
First, by validating transactions and services before data is
actually exchanged.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Second, by provisioning and reconﬁgur-
ing the computing resources within the MEC layer that are
dedicated to that given service, optimizing the servers’ load to
improve users’ experience.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The data itself does not necessarily
go through the blockchain once the service has been approved.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We see the main opportunities as part of smart cities,
where the blockchain can be supported by either RAN or 5G-
connected public infrastructure, as well as industrial environ-
ments where there exists trust.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Figure 2 illustrates a generic
5G-MEC architecture with a blockchain to manage services
(tenant applications) and edge resources (reconﬁgurable and
on-demand hardware).
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In a smart city, a public blockchain for
data sharing could boost the deployment of autonomous robots
from both private and public entities.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Besides, the role of the
infrastructure should be considered not only as a platform
to manage the blockchain lifecycle but also as a static data
source and validating platform, where trafﬁc cameras and other
sensors that already exist can be integrated.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
BLOCKCHAIN-BASED SERVICES AT THE MEC LAYER
The integration of blockchain technology at the MEC
layer has been proposed by multiple authors [20], [21],
[22].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Nonetheless, these have been mostly focusing on the
blockchain as a secure way of sharing or data or an im-
mutable ledger to store transactions.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
However, one of the
key applications of blockchains is their utilization as a robust
decentralized computer that ensures the validity of execution
of pieces of code called smart contracts [16].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We exploit
these and the consensus protocols of blockchains to provide a
framework for managing edge resources and services.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
proposed the utilization of edge services to offer
resource-constrained devices opportunities to join a blockchain
by mining at the edge.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Then, the end-devices share the data
with third-party applications through a pricing scheme, model-
ing the interactions within the IoT as market activities.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
While
their focus is on utilizing blockchains as a cryptocurrency and
auditable platform, we focus on the distributed computation
that smart contracts enable instead.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
presented a similar approach, where the MEC
layer is used to ofﬂoad mining operations [42].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Nonetheless,
this was part of a wider ofﬂoading framework where the focus
was on deciding which ofﬂoaded operation would be cached.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
A similar scheme can be integrated within the ofﬂoading slice
proposed in this study.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text: Zhu et al.’s EdgeChain is the closest work to this work [43].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
EdgeChain is a blockchain-based architecture that is utilized to
place third-party applications across the MEC.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We extend this
idea for dynamic reconﬁguration with smart contracts based on
client-provider interactions, rather than considering the service
providers only.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

Managing MEC with Consortium Blockchains
A consortium blockchain such as Hyperledger deployed
across the MEC layer and connected public infrastructure,
which are the nodes acting as validators, can be utilized to
manage the interaction between connected clients and service
providers, and at the same time orchestrating the hardware
resources at the MEC layer.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:

We envision the existence of at least three separate network

title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
On
one side, efﬁcient ofﬂoading can be achieved with the on-
demand reconﬁguration of hardware accelerators, as well as
AI accelerators.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
This slice focuses on low-latency in terms of
fast data processing and optimization of computing resources
to support as large number of connected devices as possible.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Some key beneﬁts of this architecture are (i) identities
are managed directly by the consortium blockchain and all
transactions are signed and immutably recorded; (ii) the dis-
tribution of hardware resources or computing power is done
through smart contracts and agreed across the MEC layer, with
blockchain-enabled mobility; and (iii) a connected client, such
as an autonomous robot or a self-driving car, requests a service
from a third-party through the blockchain slice; if the smart
contract approves the service, then the corresponding resources
are conﬁgured and provisioned at the corresponding slice.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Distributed Robotic Systems for blockchain-based services
So far, the proposed architecture considers a distributed net-
work architecture with distributed consensus algorithms.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The
last part of the piece is a distributed framework for deploying
distributed robotic systems and algorithms to provide services
to connected vehicles and robots.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The Robot Operating System
(ROS) has been the de-facto standard in production-ready
robotic development for the past years [10].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
However, wider
adoption requires several challenges to be solved, including au-
tomated node discovery, real-time systems, non-ideal networks
and distributed multi-robot deployments.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
These and other use
cases are being developed within ROS2 [15].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We believe that
ROS2 will be an essential piece in connected vehicles and
robots by providing a common framework and standardization
to the MEC-based services.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
ROS2 can solve key challenges in
ﬂexible service deﬁnitions at the MEC layer.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
It will provide
standardization of data formats, channels and deployment of
algorithms, with a common underlying logic for all service
providers as will be discussed in the next section.

text:
Nonethe-
less, we focus on how this architecture can be integrated to
support the autonomous operation of autonomous robots and
vehicles, opening the door to new applications and business
opportunities in cities or areas which support such seamless
integration of third-party services within the telecommunica-
tions network stack.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We also outline the role of ROS2 and the
blockchain in the different application scenarios.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Provision of HD maps in real time
Autonomous navigation in dense urban areas requires self-
driving cars and more diverse autonomous robots to have the
ability to localize themselves with very high-accuracy.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
With
the current state-of-the-art, this is only possible utilizing high-
deﬁnition (HD) maps of the environment [44].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
However, HD
maps are expensive to generate, update and maintain [45].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In terms of generation and real-time updates, the proposed
architecture can smoothly integrate within the streaming slice
a data fusion module that gathers information from different
sources to obtain these maps, as described below.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Regarding
the maintenance, the main disadvantage of HD maps is that
they require large storage on-board the vehicles, and it is
impractical to keep maps of large areas within vehicles them-
selves.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
An evident solution is to provide streaming services
at the MEC layer.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
However, this requires tight mobility and
latency control.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We believe that this can be achieved with the
combination of ROS2 as a standardization framework, 5G and
beyond networks for low-latency and predictive mechanisms to
provide in advance data about the areas that robots or vehicles
will travel through.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
ROS messages serve as a standard for
data formats, which can be then processed by multiple third
parties without requiring extra communication to instruct on
the data structure.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Moreover, the nature of ROS topics enables
consistent integration within streaming services to provide HD
maps, with subtopics deﬁning various parameters, e.g.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Online Update of Local HD Maps
In Smart Cities, administrators can provide a framework to
support the online update of HD maps and utilize existing
infrastructure as a source of data.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Trafﬁc cameras and other
sensors utilized for monitoring can be repurposed and their
data forwarded to a data fusion scheme within a dedicated
MEC slice.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Moreover, connected infrastructure with enough
processing power can serve to increase the range or capacity
of the streaming network.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The role of ROS open source
algorithms is essential to deploy the state-of-the-art in multi-
source and multi-sensor data fusion in public infrastructure.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Moreover, the smart contracts within the blockchain can be
utilized to rank the available sources of data.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
By providing an open framework, city administrations open
the door to new local applications such as drone delivery or
various types of autonomous robots surveying, monitoring and


performing other tasks across the city.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
This has the potential
to boost both the city’s economy and technology innovation.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Distributed Reinforcement Learning
As the robotic ﬁeld has evolved over the past two decades,
deep learning has become an essential aspect in complex
robotics systems [46].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In particular, reinforcement learning
has allowed for traditional dynamics models to be replaced
for neural networks that have been able to outperform any
previous approaches.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
With the ﬁrst semi-autonomous cars roaming the roads of
large cities around the world, humongous amounts of data are
being collected to improve the performance of deep learning
algorithms.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
This is a process that requires ofﬂine training of
neural networks.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
However, various distributed reinforcement
learning algorithms enable robots and autonomous vehicles
to have online improvements of their models not only from
the real-time data and experiences but also from those of
cooperating vehicles.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Offering a distributed reinforcement learning service at the
MEC layer would enable connected vehicles to take advantage
of the data and experiences of other vehicles to learn faster and
better, with more and different experiences being analyzed in
shorter periods of time.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Nonetheless, such as a service would
require a tight control on identities and a mechanism to ensure
that model updates are valid and do provide an improvement.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
A permissioned blockchain provides a transparent and secure
identity management framework, while the robustness and vul-
nerabilities in distributed multi-agent reinforcement learning
is still an open problem [47].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
If raw data is provided to the
learning service, then the model updates can be validated.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
If data is protected due to privacy concerns and only the
model updates are shared, then it becomes considerably more
challenging to determine the validity of a given update.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
A
blockchain can provide part of the solution to this problem
through its consensus mechanisms.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
They have been shown to
outperform traditional consensus mechanisms in the presence
of erroneous or malicious data in other scenarios within the
robotics domain [24].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Ofﬂoading Services
Reliable connectivity and existence of MEC services in
a large area opens the doors to robots and vehicles relying
on network-enhanced intelligence for their operation.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Instead
of developing and building complex robotic systems able of
long-term self-supported autonomy, local organizations and
businesses can build simpler products with similar capabil-
ities, relying on computational ofﬂoading to achieve certain
functionalities.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Not only does this reduce the development and
production cost, it also potentially decreases time-to-market,
further boosting innovation.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We propose a separate slice for the ofﬂoading orchestrator
and services because the focus is on optimizing computing
power and reducing execution time when possible, compared
to the storage and mobility requirements of the streaming
slice.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Even if the underlying hardware is the same, a different
degree of reconﬁguration is expected in order to optimize the
ofﬂoading scheme.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
GPU-based and FPGA-based accelerators have been widely
used in sensor development and deep learning acceleration
over the past few decades, being a perfect match for the
requirements of edge computing [48].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
More recently, au-
tonomous navigation, localization and mapping algorithms
have started to use FPGA-based implementations for real-
time matching of HD maps or odometry [49].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Some of these
operations are inherently parallelizable, and therefore FPGA-
based accelerators have the potential for decreasing the latency
by several orders of magnitude.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In the proposed architecture,
we envision that dynamic reconﬁguration of FPGA-based
hardware accelerators will play an important role in optimizing
edge resources for computational ofﬂoading, increasing the
number of nodes that can be supported and reducing the
execution time of different processes.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
ROS services can be directly utilized in ofﬂoading schemes,
where third party services simply offer these to the network.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In addition, there has been a recent interest in developing
ROS-compliant accelerators to match the rising computational
needs [50].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Having reconﬁgurable hardware available on-
demand at the edge can help third-party service providers
integrate these solutions.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The reconﬁguration and provision-
ing of resources can then be made through smart contracts
executed in the MEC-hosted blockchain.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Hardware accelerator
models can be naturally abstracted in terms of the number of
processing units or resources required, and multiple models
can co-exist within a single chip.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Finally, data partitioning
schemes at the blockchain level and its modular architecture
with the aforementioned concepts put together an efﬁcient,
open and ﬂexible framework for offering ofﬂoading services.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Security Concerns
The blockchain is a key piece in the proposed architecture as
a source of trust.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
We consider that the main security concerns
in a MEC service framework is not the exposure of data
but instead its validity and reliability.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
This is exempliﬁed
by threats identiﬁed by ENISA such as the manipulation of
the network resources orchestrator (unreliable orchestration
or invalid data regarding the resource orchestration) [36].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
As we are discussing services that support the operation of
autonomous vehicles, we need to take into account that this is
a safety-critical application scenario where sending wrong data
to a connected vehicle or robot might put in danger pedestrians
and drivers.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
While the blockchain is not able to provide a
robust way to validate data by itself, a ranking of the different
identities offering services can be created and updater in real-
time.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Moreover, by implementing the resource orchestration
and management of edge resources with smart contracts, the
reliability of services providing mission-critical data can be
kept under tighter control.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Finally, the immutability of the
transaction record can be utilized as a posteriori to assign
liability and ensure accountability.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
DISCUSSION
The architecture and slicing strategy deﬁned in the previous
section are based on the characterization of different services
that support autonomous operation of connected robots and
vehicles.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
This characterization is illustrated in Table I from
the point of view of the data and network parameters.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Of-
ﬂoading services require low-latency and high-throughput data
transmission in order to ensure full operational safety and
high levels of performance.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Latency is not so critical in the
streaming of high-deﬁnition maps, however, if this is done
such that a map of a large enough area around the vehicle
is sent at a time.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Finally, in distributed learning the amount
of data is not critical (as raw data is not shared).
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Moreover,
low-latency is not required because new data provided to
vehicles is not critical to their operation (only improves their
performance) and the learning process is long.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Nonetheless,
identity management and trustability are key parameters as
erroneous or malicious updates to a model could have a
signiﬁcant impact on performance and operational safety.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The rest of this section describes the main challenges that
emerge from the integration of blockchain for real-time ser-
vices thar require large amount of data exchanges: scalability
and storage.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Nonetheless, one key point in the proposed
architecture is that not all data goes through the blockchain.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
The purpose of the blockchain is to offer a transparent and
reliable resource orchestrator, and as such service requests
from connected vehicles are managed by the blockchain.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
However, once edge resources have been provisioned for a
service and a request validated and accepted, the service
is provided outside of the blockchain.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Therefore, the data
that supports the autonomous operation is not stored in the
blockchain.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In summary, it would not be very different from
keeping a distributed database with all service requests.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Scalability
Recent advances in blockchain technology show promising
results and potential for scalable and low-latency blockchain
networks.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
presented Elastico, where sharding in a
permissionless blockchains was explored [51].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Sharding is a
technique that allows for distributed consensus in a network
where nodes are divided in subnetworks or committees.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Rather
than processing and conﬁrming all transactions globally across
the network (for example through a majority consensus),
each committee is in charge of processing a disjoint set of
transactions, also denominated shard.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In Elastico, researchers
demonstrated the ﬁrst sharding protocol that is secure in the
presence of byzantine adversaries.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
introduced
OmniLedger [52], a decentralized and secure ledger that scales
linearly with the size of the network and supports transaction
conﬁrmation times of under two seconds, potentially being
able to match credit card standards in terms of transaction
conﬁrmation response time with a large enough network,
compared to an average transaction conﬁrmation time (block
validation) of around ten minutes in the case of Bitcoin.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
While
Elastico scales almost linearly with the available computation
power,OmniLedger does so with the number of validators.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Regarding the scalability of Hyperledger and its channel
model, the initial versions did not have a truly scalable
performance.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
However, this has improved considerably sinve
Hyperledger Fabric v1.1.0 [53].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In terms of scaling the number
of channels, this has shown little performance impact with low
to no degradation so far [53].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Storage
One of the key concerns when utilizing a blockchain as
a service management framework is the exponential storage
that will be required along time.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
While this is a signiﬁcant
factor to take into account with early networks such as
Bitcoin or Ethereum, next-generation blockchains have tack-
led this issue.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Omniledger introduced state-blocks decreasing
storage costs [52].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
More recently, RapidChain achieved a
storage saving factor of over 5x when compared to Om-
niledger, and 16x when compared with Elastico and Bitcoin-
like blockchains [54].
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In any case, the storage needs of a
blockchain and its impact on performance can be controlled
by truncating it or deﬁning a ﬁxed lifecycle.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
While this is a
challenge in permissionless open blockchains, a strategy can
be deﬁned by public authorities for a permissioned blockchain
such as Hyperledger if the infrastructure being used to validate
transactions depends on the same public authorities.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
CONCLUSION
We have presented a system architecture for offering auton-
omy support services at the MEC layer in 5G and beyond
networks.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
Our architecture combines network slicing with
blockchain technology and distributed robotic systems.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In
particular, we envision a future of connected vehicles and
robots where higher degrees of autonomy will be achieved
through third-party services at the MEC layer.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
These services
and the provisioning of MEC resources can be managed
with permissioned blockchain networks such as Hyperledger,
where ofﬂoading orchestrators and streaming orchestrators are
implemented through smart contracts.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020

text:
In future work, we will utilize ROS2 and Hyperledger to
provide a proof-of-concept for the proposed architecture, and
the bottlenecks and limitations will be analyzed.
title: arXiv:2007.01156v1  [cs.DC]  1 Jul 2020
