Los Alamos National Laboratory, Theoretical Division T-2, Los Alamos, NM87545, USA
LANL-SWME Collaboration
We present updated results for εK determined directly from the standard model (SM) with lattice
QCD inputs such as ˆBK, |Vcb|, |Vus|, ξ0, ξ2, ξLD, fK, and mc.
title: arXiv:1912.03024v2  [hep-lat]  11 Dec 2019

text:
We ﬁnd that the standard model with
exclusive |Vcb| and other lattice QCD inputs describes only 65% of the experimental value of |εK|
and does not explain its remaining 35%, which leads to a strong tension in |εK| at the 4.6σ ∼4.2σ
level between the SM theory and experiment.
title: arXiv:1912.03024v2  [hep-lat]  11 Dec 2019

text:
We also ﬁnd that this tension disappears when we
use the inclusive value of |Vcb| obtained using the heavy quark expansion based on QCD sum
rules.

In
2017 when Bigi, Gambino, and Schacht [8, 11] ﬁrst raised a claim that there might be an incon-
sistency in exclusive |Vcb| between the CLN and BGL analyses on the BELLE-2017 tagged data
set of the ¯B →D∗ℓ¯ν decays, the BGL results seemed to be superﬁcially consistent with those for
inclusive |Vcb|.

text:
However, the 2019 analyses of both BELLE [6] (on the untagged data) and BABAR
[7] show that the results of the BGL analysis might be consistent with those of the CLN analysis,
which denies the previous claim of Refs.

The pink dashed line with label FLAG-19 repre-
sents preliminary results of BELLE-18 which the FLAG 2019 report took over to do their analysis
on |Vcb|.
title: arXiv:1912.03024v2  [hep-lat]  11 Dec 2019

text:

Abstract—The computing continuum extends the high-performance cloud data centers with
energy-efﬁcient and low-latency devices close to the data sources located at the edge of the
network.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
However, the heterogeneity of the computing continuum raises multiple challenges
related to application management.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
These include where to ofﬂoad an application – from the
cloud to the edge – to meet its computation and communication requirements.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
To support these
decisions, we provide in this article a detailed performance and carbon footprint analysis of a
selection of use case applications with complementary resource requirements across the
computing continuum over a real-life evaluation testbed.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
1 Introduction
The advent of fog and edge computing
has prompted predictions that they will take
over the traditional cloud for information pro-
cessing and knowledge extraction at a large
scale.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Notwithstanding the fact that fog and
edge computing have undoubtedly large po-
tential, these predictions are probably over-
simpliﬁed and wrongly portray the relations
between fog, edge and cloud computing.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Concretely, fog and edge computing have
been introduced as an extension of the cloud
services towards the data sources, thus form-
ing the computing continuum.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The computing continuum enables the
creation of a new type of services, span-
ning across distributed infrastructures, for au-
tonomous vehicles, smart cities, and content
delivery, among other applications.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
These
services have a large spectrum of require-
ments, burdensome to meet with “distant”
cloud data centers.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
For instance, they may
need low-latency connections for fast deci-
sion making close to the data sources and
substantial computing resources for complex
data analysis.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The computing continuum pro-
vides a vast heterogeneity of computational
and communication resources, which have
the potential to meet these demands.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The heterogeneity of the computing con-
tinuum raises multiple application manage-
ment challenges, such as where to ofﬂoad
an application from the cloud to the fog or
to the edge.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
These issues primarily concern
the large diversity of the devices, which range
from single-board computers such as Rasp-
berry Pis to powerful multi-processor servers.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
This poses the following dilemma of many
practitioners and researchers:
Should we use devices accessi-
ble with low latency and with lim-
ited resource availability, or a high-
IEEE Internet Computing
Published by the IEEE Computer Society
© 2021 IEEE
1
arXiv:2101.10417v1  [cs.DC]  25 Jan 2021


performance cloud at the expense of
high communication delay?
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
To answer this question it is essential
to characterize the performance of the re-
sources.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Existing literature [1], [2], including
the DeFog benchmark suite, addresses this
problem by conducting performance analy-
sis of cloud services and to some extent
of edge infrastructures.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Nevertheless, these
approaches (i) consider the edge and the
cloud resources in isolation, (ii) provide only
quantitative analysis of the performance with-
out ofﬂoading recommendations, (iii) evaluate
a limited number of devices, and (iv) do not
consider the environmental impact in terms of
CO2 emissions for executing the applications.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We present in this article a performance
characterization and an analysis of the CO2
emissions of the resources across the com-
puting continuum.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Our main goal is to support
the decision process for ofﬂoading an appli-
cation to fog or edge resources by consid-
ering the application characteristics.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
For this
purpose, we deployed a real testbed named
Carinthian Computing Continuum (C3) that
aggregates a large set of heterogeneous
resources.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We base the analysis on three
complementary applications widely utilized by
industry and research: video encoding, ma-
chine learning and in-memory data analytics.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We conclude by providing recommendations
on where to compute applications across the
computing continuum.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
2 Carinthian Computing Continuum
Figure 1 depicts the top-level view of
the Carinthian Computing Continuum.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The
C3 testbed includes a heterogeneous set of
resources, distributed across different con-
trol domains, including public providers such
as Exoscale Cloud1 and Amazon Web Ser-
vices (AWS), and research institutions such
as University of Klagenfurt2.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We utilize the
ASKALON cloud application computing en-
vironment [6] with the MAPO resource pro-
visioning algorithm [5] to deploy the appli-
cations across the C3 testbed.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Furthermore,
1https://www.exoscale.com
2https://itec.aau.at
Figure 1: The C3 testbed.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
we employ a bootstrapping script that au-
tomatically conﬁgures the resources in the
testbed 3.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Table 1 summarizes the resource
characteristics of the C3 testbed.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We classify the resources in the C3
testbed into three layers: cloud layer, fog layer
and edge layer.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
2.1 Cloud layer
The cloud layer is the uppermost layer of
the C3 testbed.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
It contains high-performance
resources consolidated in vast data-centers,
provisioned on-demand as virtual machine
instances.

title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We carefully selected three instance types
based on the x86-64 architecture that of-
fer to the C3 testbed a balance of com-
pute, memory, and networking resources for
a broad set of applications: general pur-
pose (t2.micro), and compute-optimized
(c5.large and m5a.xlarge).
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
2.2 Fog layer
The fog layer comprises computing infras-
tructures consolidated in small data-centers
in close vicinity to the data sources.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
This layer
comprises resources from two providers in
the C3 testbed [4]: Exoscale and University of
Klagenfurt.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We allocate these providers in the
fog layer as a result of the low round-trip com-
munication latency (≤7 ms) and high band-
width (≤10 Gbps).
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The Exoscale cloud com-
prises data centers in Vienna and Klagenfurt
(Austria).
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We selected three computing opti-
mized x86-64 instances from the Exoscale
cloud offering: Tiny, Medium and Large.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
University of Klagenfurt provides a private
cloud infrastructure operated by OpenStack
v13.0 and Ceph v12.2 with one computing
optimized instance type described in Table 1.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
2.3 Edge layer
This layer encompasses edge resources,
such as single-board computers, directly con-
nected to the IoT devices and sensors.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
An
Edge Gateway System (EGS) controls the
edge layer, and is the entry point to the
other resources available on this level.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The
EGS supports 10 Gbps Ethernet, dual band
PCIe WiFi 5 (802.11ac) and a 150 Mbps LTE
2600 MHz connection.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
A layer-3 HP Aruba
switch with 48 1 Gbps ports connects the
EGS to the single-board computers with a
latency of 3.8 µs and an aggregate data
transfer rate of 104 Gbps.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The edge layer
also contains 35 physical nodes based on
either Raspberry Pi 3B or Pi 4B.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Besides, the
testbed contains ﬁve Jetson Nano devices,
each equipped with a general purpose GPU.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The edge layer has 1 Gbps Ethernet, Wi-Fi
and LTE network connection interfaces.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
3 Benchmark applications
We selected three representative appli-
cation classes with complementary require-
ments to evaluate the computational perfor-
mance and the CO2 emissions of the com-
puting continuum.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
3.1 Video encoding
Video encoding allows transmission of
video content with different qualities over
limited and heterogeneous communication
channels.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
It compresses an original raw video
to reduce its effective bandwidth consump-
tion, while maintaining a subjective high qual-
ity for viewers.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Video encoding has wide ﬁelds
of applications, including content delivery (live
and on-demand video streams), trafﬁc control
and surveillance.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The video encoding appli-
cations have high processing and throughput
requirements.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
3.2 Machine learning
Machine learning is a branch of artiﬁcial
intelligence that explores approaches for en-
abling systems to learn from data, identify
patterns and make decisions.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Its vast ﬁeld
of application includes automated control in
manufacturing, adaptive trafﬁc planning and
smart health-care diagnosis, among others.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Machine learning, in general, has high pro-
cessing and operating memory requirements.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:

3.3 In-memory analytic
In-memory analytic is essential for efﬁ-
cient low-latency decisions on devices with
limited resources.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
It explores data manipula-
tion such as inspecting, ﬁltering and trans-
forming, and enables efﬁcient extraction of
knowledge and non-biased decision-making.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Its ﬁelds of application include smart cities,
healthcare and recommender systems.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The
in-memory analytic applications require large
memory capacity and strict communication
latency.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
4 Performance evaluation
4.1 Video encoding
We evaluate the encoding performance
of the computing continuum using FFm-
peg version 3.4.6 with the most popular
H.264/MPEG-4 video encoder4 deployed by
more than 90% of the video industry5.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We
perform the encoding on a raw video seg-
ment with length of 4 s and size of 514 MB,
available in the Sintel6 video-set.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The video
segment is encoded in three resolutions (HD-
ready, Full HD and Quad HD) with data rates
of 1500, 3000, and 6500 kbps.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Figure 2 depicts the average encoding
time and transfer time, from the video source
(located at the University of Klagenfurt) to
the encoding device or instance, for a single
raw video segment in the three resolutions.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The standard deviation ranges from 1.3%
for the AWS m5a.xlarge instance to 3.6%
for the Raspberry Pi 3B devices.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We ob-
serve that the older generation single-board
computers (Raspberry Pi 3B) have a signif-
icantly higher encoding time than the other
resources.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
However, the Raspberry Pi 3B
devices provide lower transfer times than the
cloud instances and are suitable for video-on-
demand services employing ofﬂine encoding.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The Raspberry Pi 4 and the Jetson Nano de-
vices efﬁciently perform video encoding and
provide low transfer times.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
In some cases,
Jetson Nano was capable of encoding up to
20% faster than the AWS t2.micro instance

The

range between 0.5 s to 1.3 s.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Nevertheless,
the cloud and fog resources have limited
effective throughput causing higher raw video
transfer times.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
However, the cloud resources
are suitable for live video streaming due to
the low encoding times.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Overall, the EGS
achieved the lowest encoding and transfer
time due to the low utilization rate and its high
computing and networking capabilities.

4.2 Machine learning
We use TensorFlow Core version 2.3.0 to
evaluate machine learning performance.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We
created two training and validation scenarios
for feature identiﬁcation in a set of images:
• A
quantum
neural
network
using
the
MNIST data-set7 limited to 20000 samples
with a size of 3.3 MB.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The scenario cre-
ates a neural network with two layers and
128 outputs from the previous layer to the
next.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We conduct ﬁve iterations to reach a
feature identiﬁcation accuracy of 90%.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
• A convolutional neural network using the
Kaggle data-set8 with a size of 218 MB.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The convolutional network has three layers
with a kernel size of three.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Each layer uses
increasingly higher ﬁlter sizes in the range
[32, 64, 128].
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
After each layer, we use
a max-pooling sample-based discretization
process to reduce the spatial dimensions.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Figure 3 analyzes the average execu-
tion time for training the two neural network
types and the transfer times of the train-
ing data from centralized storage to the de-
vice or instance that performs the training.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The standard deviation ranges from 1.2%
for the Raspberry Pi 4 devices to 5.4% for
the AWS t2.micro instance.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The evaluation
shows that the less complex quantum neural
network requires a relatively lower training
time across all resources.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The old generation
single-board computers show again a lower
performance, and their suitability for training
heavily depends on the size of the training
data and the model.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The other fog and edge
devices provide similar performance to the
cloud resources.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The single-board computers
7http://yann.lecun.com/exdb/mnist/
8https://www.kaggle.com/tags/animals
provide lower training performance for the
convolutional network.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The only exception are
the Jetson Nano devices able to train the
convolutional network up to four times faster
than the Raspberry Pi devices.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
In general,
the EGS provides the lowest training time
among all devices.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The training data trans-
fer time has limited inﬂuence on the training
process, especially for the quantum neural
network.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
While the training data transfer time
is signiﬁcantly higher for the convolutional
neural network, the cloud and fog resources
outperform the edge devices, except EGS.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We
recommend
the
model
training
with
large
data-sets
and
multiple layers in the cloud or on dedicated
systems (such as EGS), whenever possible.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We recommend ofﬂoading to the edge only
when the training data is of limited size, or
when the neural network has few layers.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
4.3 In-memory data analytics
The in-memory data analytics evaluation
explores two scenarios using Apache Spark
version 2.4.6:
• Collaborative data ﬁltering aims to ﬁll miss-
ing entries for improved recommendation
of movies to consumers.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
The model uses
the alternating least squares algorithm and
a data-set9 of movie preferences with a
size of 31.6 kB.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
We trained the model over
the available data-set with a cold start
strategy that randomly divides the data into
training and validation sets.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
• π estimation is a memory and computa-
tionally intensive task that estimates the
value of π by distributing the work among
multiple Spark executors.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
This enables us
to evaluate the computational and mem-
ory performance of the distributed memory
computing continuum for complex tasks.
title: Cloud, Fog or Edge: Where to Compute?

text:
Figure 4 shows the average execution
time of the in-memory collaborative data ﬁl-
tering and the π estimation.

deviation ranges from 1.3% for the AWS

sources are most suitable for applications that
generate frequent input and output requests
with larger data sizes.

LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware
Fog Computing Environments
Philipp Wiesner and Lauritz Thamsen
Technische Universit¨at Berlin, Germany
{wiesner, lauritz.thamsen}@tu-berlin.de
Abstract—Despite constant improvements in efﬁciency, today’s
data centers and networks consume enormous amounts of energy
and this demand is expected to rise even further.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
An important
research question is whether and how fog computing can curb
this trend.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
As real-life deployments of fog infrastructure are still
rare, a signiﬁcant part of research relies on simulations.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
However,
existing power models usually only target particular components
such as compute nodes or battery-constrained edge devices.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Combining analytical and discrete-event modeling, we develop
a holistic but granular energy consumption model that can
determine the power usage of compute nodes as well as network
trafﬁc and applications over time.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Simulations can incorporate
thousands of devices that execute complex application graphs
on a distributed, heterogeneous, and resource-constrained infras-
tructure.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
We evaluated our publicly available prototype LEAF
within a smart city trafﬁc scenario, demonstrating that it enables
research on energy-conserving fog computing architectures and
can be used to assess dynamic task placement strategies and
other energy-saving mechanisms.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Index Terms—Simulation, Modeling, Fog Computing, Edge
Computing, Energy Consumption
I.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
INTRODUCTION
With the rise of the internet of things and the beginning
of the fourth industrial revolution, many sectors and environ-
ments are expected to become interspersed with connected
sensors.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
As these sensors produce an ever-increasing amount
of data, the classical cloud computing approach of sending
all information directly to a few powerful data centers, often
far away from the data source, is not feasible anymore.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
One
attempt to solve these emerging problems is to deploy a
distributed layer of compute nodes close to the edge of the
network that ﬁlters, aggregates, and preprocesses the raw data
generated by end devices and sensors.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
This new paradigm,
called fog computing, promises to save large amounts of
bandwidth, reduce latencies for time-sensitive applications,
and increase end-user privacy as the fog nodes can take care
of aggregating and anonymizing data [1].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
However, due to
their distributed and heterogeneous nature, fog computing
environments are much more challenging to manage than
centralized data centers [2].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
At the same time, energy consumption of information and
communications technology is already accounting for more
than 10 % of global energy consumption and is expected to
exceed the 20 % mark by 2030 [3].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
An open research question
is whether fog computing will be able to reduce the overall
energy consumption of future computing infrastructure or if it
may even be responsible for a further increase [1], [4], [5].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Although the general trend of concentrating computing re-
sources into hyper-scale data centers continues [6], research
has shown that distributed architectures could save between
14 % to more than 80 % of total energy consumption compared
to fully centralized architectures [7], [8].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
A major part of today’s fog computing research is centered
around modeling and simulations.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Nevertheless, to the best
of our knowledge, there exists no tool that is suitable to
explore the overall power usage of large-scale fog deployments
and enables research on energy-conserving architectures and
algorithms in this domain.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Major existing fog computing
simulators provide no energy modeling at all [9]–[11] or only
focus on speciﬁc components of fog infrastructures [12], [13].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Furthermore, many simulators fail to realistically model fog
environments by leaving out substantial aspects like mobil-
ity [10], [12].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Existing analytical approaches on the other hand
provide only a high level of abstraction and cannot represent
change over time, prohibiting the modeling of mobility and
evaluation of online decision making algorithms [4], [7], [14].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
We present LEAF1, a new simulator for modeling Large
Energy-Aware Fog computing environments.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
In contrast to the
related work, our model was designed with the following four
requirements in mind:
(1) Realistic Fog Computing Environment: Enable the sim-
ulation of applications with complex task graphs in
distributed, heterogeneous, and resource-constrained fog
computing environments.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Nodes can be mobile and they
can join or leave the topology at any time.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
(2) Holistic Energy Consumption Model: Enable the sepa-
rate assessment of power usage of compute nodes, net-
work trafﬁc, and applications, allowing for the creation
of load proﬁles for individual parts of fog computing
environments.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
(3) Energy-Aware Online Decision Making: Enable research
on task placement strategies, routing policies, and
energy-saving mechanisms that dynamically adapt their
behavior based on the power usage of infrastructure and
applications.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
(4) Performance and Scalability: Enable the simulation of
complex scenarios with thousands of devices and ap-
plications at least two orders of magnitude faster than
real-time on commodity hardware.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
1 Java implementation available at https://github.com/dos-group/leaf-java
Python implementation available at https://github.com/dos-group/leaf

Our model combines analytical and discrete-event modeling
to enable easy-to-analyze large-scale experiments.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Speciﬁcally,
we model infrastructures and applications as variable graphs
that can change throughout the simulation and do not rely on
representing individual packets.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
This way, the model enables
research on novel task placement strategies or energy-saving
mechanisms that must be evaluated in large settings.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
We expect
LEAF to help both researchers and practitioners assess the
power usage characteristics of different cloud, fog, and edge
computing architectures, which can lead to more well-founded
decisions when planning future infrastructures.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text: The remainder of the paper is structured as follows.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Section III introduces
our infrastructure and application model for fog computing
environments.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Section IV explains the different kinds of power
models that can be applied.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Section V evaluates our model on
a smart city scenario.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
RELATED WORK
Energy-efﬁcient data centers have been a research area for
years as electricity costs account for a signiﬁcant part of a
data center’s operating expenditure.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
In fog or edge computing,
however, most research on power usage only concerns speciﬁc
components such as battery-constrained edge devices [13]
or fog nodes [12].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The bigger picture, namely the potential
impact of fog computing on the overall energy consumption
of information and communications technology, has retrieved
comparably little attention.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
One approach to assess the estimated consumption of fog
computing environments is analytical modeling.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
These mod-
els are usually suitable for examining large-scale scenarios
since they are fast to execute and convenient to experiment
with.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
[14] compare service latency and energy
consumption of fog and cloud computing by performing a
high-level examination of different architectures.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The authors
focus on infrastructure only and incorporate no concept for ap-
plications.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Furthermore, they do not distinguish between static
and dynamic energy consumption, which limits the informative
value of the analyses.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
[4] model energy usage by
using a ﬂow-based model for highly shared equipment such
as core routers and switches, and a time-based model for end-
user equipment that is usually not shared among many clients.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Their ﬁndings show that the power impact of fog computing
depends on many factors such as the type of attached access
network.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
However their scenario is a relatively speciﬁc use
case and not suitable as a general purpose model.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
[7] propose a model that differentiates between static
and dynamic power usage and incorporates the consumption
of network devices and cooling.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Even though their model
is relatively comprehensive, it incorporates several critical
simpliﬁcations such as an even distribution of VMs among
data centers and the assumption that all fog nodes connect to
the same number of devices.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Moreover, there exists no concept
of applications or tasks, nor is there a way to calculate the
relative power requirements of VMs.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
All presented analytical
approaches suffer from the fact that they model at a high level
of abstraction and, for example, make the invalid assumption
that fog nodes are homogeneous [7], [14].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Moreover, they
cannot represent change over time, prohibiting the assessment
of mobility and online decision making algorithms.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Besides analytical models, a large number of discrete-event
simulators has been developed in recent years.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Although there
exist cloud computing simulators that feature comprehensive
power models like GreenCloud [15], these tools are not
designed to model highly heterogeneous and variable envi-
ronments like those encountered in fog computing.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Many popular simulators in the domain of fog and edge
computing such as EdgeCloudSim [9] or IOTSim [10] com-
prise no power modeling at all.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Others, like YAFS [11],
allow users to specify custom attributes related to node power
usage but do not feature any power modeling at runtime.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The
simulators that do are either overly simplistic or focus only
on speciﬁc components of the infrastructure.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
For example,
iFogSim [12] inherits some power modeling capabilities from
CloudSim and can model the power consumption of data
centers and fog nodes.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Nevertheless, there is currently no
way to simulate the power usage of edge devices, networks,
or applications.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
PureEdgeSim [13] features a comprehensive
energy consumption model for edge devices, including Wi-
Fi trafﬁc, to simulate battery-constrained devices.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
However,
the consumption of data centers, fog nodes or wide area
network (WAN) trafﬁc cannot be modeled.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
FogNetSim++ [16]
is the only fog computing simulator to our knowledge that
features an energy model for applications.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Albeit the focus
on performance, the detailed modeling of network trafﬁc on
a per packet basis inevitably results in worse scalability than
our model.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Furthermore, due to our analytical approach, it is
a lot easier to set up experiments in LEAF, explore different
conﬁgurations, and analyze results.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
FOG ENVIRONMENT MODEL
The way LEAF models fog computing environments is in-
spired by analytical modeling.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Infrastructure and applications
are represented as graphs and power models as functions that
operate on these graphs.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Together, these components deﬁne
the state of the simulation at a certain time step, which we

text:
1: LEAF uses discrete events to update the state (con-
ﬁguration) of the simulation.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
In this example, an additional
compute node (a car) was added to the infrastructure graph
and a new application was placed on this infrastructure.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
In contrast to purely analytical models,
the state of network and applications can change over time
through the use of events, as illustrated in Figure 1.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
LEAF uses
events only in two cases: To read and to update conﬁgurations.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Read events can, for example, be emitted by an algorithm
that performs power measurements at a certain time step to
adapt its behavior.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Examples of update events are changes
to the current application placements or the infrastructure
graph like adapting the latency of a network link or adding
a new compute node.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
LEAF does not use events to simulate
individual network packets.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Every conﬁguration contains all information necessary for a
deeper analysis and can be inspected without any knowledge
about future or past events.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Modeling fog computing environ-
ments in this way enables easy-to-analyze experiments that can
execute scenarios with thousands of devices and applications.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Yet, our approach also has decisive advantages over purely
analytical models: First, by allowing the model to change over
time, heterogeneous environments with dynamically changing
network topologies, mobility of edge devices, and varying
workloads can be represented.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Second, LEAF allows for online
decision making, enabling research on dynamic energy-aware
task placement strategies, scheduling algorithms, or trafﬁc
routing policies.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Infrastructure Model
As depicted in Figure 2, the network and computing infras-
tructure are represented as a weighted, directed multigraph
I = (N, L), where
N is the set of compute nodes.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
A compute node N i ∈N
may be resource-constrained, can have a location, and
may be mobile.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
It can represent an entire cloud data
center as well as mobile sensors with limited or no
computing capacity.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text: L is the set of network links between nodes.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
A network
link Li ∈L can represent individual wired or wireless
connections as well as entire network routes such as WAN
connections.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Network links can be constrained by band-
width and may have additional properties like latency that
users can utilize for implementing routing policies.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Edges
are directed to allow modeling different constraints and
power models for uplink and downlink.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Multiple edges
between nodes are allowed and can represent different
available link types such as Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The infrastructure graph can change during the simulation,
as nodes are free to move around and can join or leave the
network.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Furthermore, any property, like the latency of a link,
can change.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Application Model
LEAF considers all applications to be streaming applica-
tions and, hence, regards all communication between different
application tasks as continuous data ﬂows.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Applications are
represented by directed acyclic graphs A = (T, F), where T
is the set of tasks in the application, and F is the set of data
ﬂows between tasks.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:

2: Infrastructure graph with resource constraints and
power usage characteristics (black), a placed application with

title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
In this conﬁguration,
the application’s combined power usage is 13.12 W.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Applications can be placed on the fog
by mapping their tasks to compute nodes, and their data ﬂows
to network links.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Application placements are described in more
detail below.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
A task T i ∈T demands certain resources from its compute
node.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
A compute node can host as many tasks as its resources
allow.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
There exist three different kinds of tasks that are
responsible for emitting, processing, and retrieving data:
1) Source tasks are bound to a speciﬁc compute node, for
example, a sensor-equipped or mobile device.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
They are
constantly emitting data and have at least one outgoing
edge and no incoming edges.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
2) Processing tasks can be freely placed on any compute
node N i ∈N that fulﬁlls their resource requirements.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Processing tasks have at least one incoming edge and at
least one outgoing edge.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
3) Sink tasks are again bound to a speciﬁc compute node
and have at least one incoming edge and no outgoing
edges.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Examples of data sinks are cloud storages or end-
user terminals.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
A data ﬂow F i ∈F represents a continuous stream of data
between two tasks, stated in bits/s.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Like any parameter, the
data rate can change during the simulation.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
A network link can
“host” as many data streams as its bandwidth allows.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Due to
its abstract network model, LEAF is not suitable to explicitly
model complex effects resulting from network congestion like
queuing delay or packet drops.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
When placing an application, its tasks have to be mapped
onto compute nodes, which is illustrated in orange in Fig-
ure 2.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Since the assignment of source and sink tasks is ﬁxed,
task placement strategies have to determine the placement of
processing tasks.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
After the placement, a user-deﬁned routing


policy searches for an optimal path in the network between
every pair of connected tasks.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
If there is no node that meets
the resource requirements or if no sufﬁcient path can be found,
the placement failed.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Typically, processing tasks aggregate and ﬁlter the data
stream in a way that outgoing data ﬂows require less band-
width than incoming data ﬂows.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Consequently, the placement
of processing tasks close to the source tasks generally reduces
network usage and, thus, energy consumption.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Finding optimal
placements in dynamic, resource-constrained, distributed, and
heterogeneous environments is a complicated problem and a
focus of research [17].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
LEAF enables application placement
strategies that take the infrastructure’s energy consumption
into account.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
POWER MODELS
We model infrastructure power usage by assigning each
compute node and network link its own power model.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
This
enables users to determine the power usage of data centers,
edge devices, and network links individually.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
A power model
P(t) is a function that returns the current power usage of
its corresponding entity at any point in time t during the
simulation.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Power usage is reported as the sum Pstatic+Pdyn,
where Pstatic is the static (load-independent) power usage and
Pdyn the dynamic (load-dependent) fraction.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Power models
may maintain a state which can be used to implement energy-
saving mechanisms (see Section IV-D).
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
To create load proﬁles of infrastructure components, their
power models can be called through periodic events.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Addi-
tionally, other simulated components can call power models
at runtime to adapt their behavior or update their state.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Ex-
amples of such components are energy-aware task placement
strategies or hardware like batteries that update the state of
charge.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Linear and Non-Linear Power Models
Research shows that the power usage of infrastructure can
often be modeled with sufﬁcient accuracy as a linear function
that is only based on the entity’s current load C(t) [18],
[19].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Linear power models are beneﬁcial since they are
computationally efﬁcient and easy to comprehend.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
They are
described as
P(t) = Pstatic + C(t) σ,
where C(t) σ represents Pdyn.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The variable σ determines
the incremental energy per load.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
For example, for network
equipment, σ represents the energy consumed per bit of
transferred data (J/bit).
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
When modeling resource-constrained
compute nodes or network links that have a maximum load
Cmax with power usage Pmax, σ can be expressed as:
σ = Pmax −Pstatic
Cmax
An example for more complex entities, where a simple,
linear function may not model the power usage well, are
compute nodes representing entire data centers.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Data centers
incorporate several different hosts and require additional power
for operational overhead like cooling and lighting.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
An exem-
plary approach for modeling this kind of compute node is to
deﬁne a power model PHi for each host Hi and to aggregate
their results to Pdc.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
To account for operational overhead, we
can multiply the result with the data center’s power usage
effectiveness (PUE):
Pdc(t) = PUE ·

Compute nodes and network links can also apply non-
linear power models and power models with multiple inputs
to improve the accuracy of the simulation.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
An example is the
power model for wireless network links of [20], which, in
addition to the load, also takes the distance of communicating
devices into account.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
However, more complex power models
will lead to more computationally intensive simulations, hence
longer runtimes.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Power Models for Shared Resources
When describing the power consumption of shared re-
sources such as cloud data centers, mobile base stations, or
entire WAN links, it is not meaningful to specify static power
usage.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
For example, it is impossible to know at which point an
externally operated data center will need to switch on or off a
new physical machine.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Many of these resources are assumed to
scale on demand, hence deﬁning a Pmax is not even possible.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
For these reasons, Pstatic = 0 for power models of shared
infrastructure.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Users must estimate a meaningful σ that directly
incorporates a fraction of the static consumption.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
By modeling shared resources without static power us-
age, we implicitly assume this infrastructure to be energy-
proportional.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Nevertheless, there are ways to incorporate inef-
ﬁciencies into the parameters.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
In practice, servers as well as
routers are rarely used to full capacity but are over-provisioned
to ensure performance and availability.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Equivalently to the en-
ergy model proposed by [4], users can estimate and incorporate
an operational capacity fraction U into a power model.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The
effect of U is illustrated in the staircase curve depicted in
Figure 3.

text:
Power Models for Network Links
Although we assign power models directly to edges in
the infrastructure graph, in reality, energy is not consumed
by the cable or wireless connection itself but by networking
equipment such as routers or wireless transmitters.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Network
link power models hence represent the aggregated power usage
of all networking equipment involved to transfer data from
one compute node to another, and σ describes the incremental
energy per bit (J/bit).
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Static power usage should be attributed
to the adjacent compute nodes, to assure it correctly drops to
zero when the node is shut off.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Intermediate routing devices
are considered shared infrastructure and their consumption
should be incorporated directly into the network link’s σ.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Table I depicts an exemplary parameterization of a WAN link
between a mobile device and a cloud server.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
For wireless connections, power usage characteristics of
uplink and downlink usually differ [21], [22].
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Since infras-
tructure is represented by a directed multigraph in LEAF, it
allows modeling asymmetrical power usage characteristics by
assigning different power models to the respective directions.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Energy-saving Mechanisms
Energy-saving mechanisms aim to reduce static power usage
of hardware during periods of low utilization by throttling or
powering off parts of the system.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
They can signiﬁcantly in-
ﬂuence overall energy consumption by pushing infrastructure
towards operating energy-proportionally.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Such load proﬁles
can be modeled in LEAF by making Pstatic, which usually
describes the load-independent power usage, indirectly load-
dependent.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
For example, a common strategy in data centers
is to consolidate workload on a few hosts and to power off
the remaining hosts.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Pstatic of such a data center could be
modeled as a step function, similar to the example in Figure 3.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Furthermore, to evaluate the impact of even more complex
energy-saving mechanisms, users can make use of the fact that
power models can maintain state.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
For example, [23] presented
a precise model for dynamic voltage and frequency scaling
(DVFS), which requires the current and past utilization of the
CPU to implement different strategies.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
LEAF’s power models
2 http://tools.cisco.com/cpc, accessed 2020-10-17
can store past utilization states of their assigned entity and take
them into account when computing the current power usage.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Tracing Back Power Usage to Applications
To support the implementation of energy-conserving appli-
cation placement strategies, LEAF allows tracing back the
infrastructure’s power usage to the responsible applications.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The power consumption of an application is deﬁned as the
sum of all power usage that its tasks and data ﬂows cause
on their allocated resources, see Figure 2.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Depending on the
scenario users may decide to only attribute dynamic power
usage, or dynamic and static power usage.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
For example, if the
underlying resource is powered on, regardless of its utilization,
the static energy consumption does not have to be attributed to
any applications since they have no inﬂuence on it.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
However,
if the resource can be powered off when it is idle, the placed
resources actually cause the energy usage.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
In this case, the
static energy should be attributed to all tasks that currently
run on the node depending on their fraction of the total load.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
EVALUATION
We created two open source implementations of LEAF
in Java and Python.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The respective GitHub repositories are
referenced in Section I.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The following evaluation uses the Java
implementation, based on the CloudSim Plus [24] simulator,
and simulates different fog architectures and application place-
ment strategies in a smart city trafﬁc scenario.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:

The urban environment of the experimental setup is inspired
by Manhattan, namely a rectangular street grid with blocks of
274 m by 80 m.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
It covers an area containing 16 crossings, each
equipped with a smart trafﬁc light (STL) that optionally has
a fog node attached.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Within this city center, we simulate 24
hours of taxi trafﬁc with time steps of one second.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Quantity
and speed of taxis were modeled according to a dataset
published for the 2015 DEBS Grand Challenge competition3,

The infrastructure graph consists of four kinds of compute
nodes: The cloud, fog nodes, STLs, and taxis.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The mapping of data ﬂows to network edges is updated
periodically as taxis move around.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
STLs communicate with
other close-by STLs via Wi-Fi too, effectively forming a
mesh network.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Additionally, they are equipped with 4G LTE
modules connecting them to the cloud node via WAN.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text: Table II shows the infrastructure parameterization.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Only
cloud and fog nodes have computing capacities stated in
millions of instructions per second (MIPS).
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Since the load
on STL and taxi nodes is the same in all experiments, their
power usage is not modeled in this evaluation.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
All other
compute nodes and network links have linear power models.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The cloud is considered shared infrastructure and has no
static but high dynamic power usage.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Energy per bit for
WAN links was conﬁgured as the example shown in Table I.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Direct Wi-Fi communication between STLs consumes less
energy than communication with taxis because they always
have a direct line of sight and deploy energy-efﬁcient, high-
throughput access points.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
We simulate a smart trafﬁc system comprising two kinds of
applications:
CCTV applications process data recorded by cameras de-
ployed at STLs.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The source task, located at the STL,
sends 10 Mbit/s of video data to a processing task
that requires 30 000 MIPS and is responsible for trafﬁc
monitoring, enforcing trafﬁc laws and automatic incident
detection.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The 200 kbit/s of resulting data are sent to
the sink task located in the cloud for further analysis
and storage.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
16 of these applications are running in our
scenario, one for each STL.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
V2I applications are vehicle-to-infrastructure, smart trafﬁc
management applications that control trafﬁc lights to
ensure maximum throughput of public transport.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Each
taxi on the map streams 100 kbit/s of sensor data to a
processing task which requires 7000 MIPS and forwards
50 kbit/s to all STLs on the way of the taxi.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The number
of applications running depends on the number of taxis
on the map.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:

that our model enables research on energy-efﬁcient fog archi-

anisms.

text:
Analysis
So far the evaluation has shown that we have successfully
met our Requirements (1), (2), and (3): LEAF was used
to model a realistic fog computing scenario with different
kinds of compute nodes, network links and applications.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
By


assigning individual power models to different parts of the
infrastructure, we were able to analyze the energy footprint
of different fog node deployments in order to ﬁnd the most
energy-conserving conﬁguration.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
In the last experiment, we
demonstrated how our model enables research on dynamic task
placement strategies and energy-saving mechanisms.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
To evaluate Requirement (4), Performance and Scalability,
we analyzed the runtimes of simulations.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Each presented
experiment simulates around 46 500 taxis executing around
330 000 tasks and ﬁnishes in less than 50 seconds on a
single core of a 1.4 GHz Intel Core i5.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
A series of further
experiments show that in the outlined scenario, the only
algorithmic component that shows non-linear growth is the
algorithm for ﬁnding shortest paths between tasks.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Even when
scaling experiments by factor 10, namely 465 000 taxis and
3 300 000 tasks, they had a median runtime of 613 seconds.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
Consequently, the presented model is suitable to simulate
large-scale experiments several magnitudes faster than real
time on commodity hardware.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
CONCLUSION
This paper presents LEAF, a simulator for modeling large
energy-aware fog computing environments.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
LEAF features a
holistic but granular energy consumption model that covers
data centers, edge devices, and network as well as applica-
tions which are running on this infrastructure.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
By combining
analytical and discrete-event modeling, the proposed model
enables the simulation of thousands of streaming applications
on a distributed, heterogeneous, and dynamic infrastructure.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
The publicly available implementation of LEAF was evaluated
within a realistic smart city trafﬁc scenario and proved to be a
valuable tool for research on energy-conserving fog computing
architectures, task placement strategies, and energy-saving
mechanisms.
title: LEAF: Simulating Large Energy-Aware Computing Environments

text:
In the future, we plan to extend our model to provide time-
based and location-based calculations of the carbon emissions

Applications: Survey and Research Challenges
YOSHITOMO MATSUBARA and MARCO LEVORATO, University of California, Irvine, USA
FRANCESCO RESTUCCIA, Northeastern University, USA
Mobile devices such as smartphones and autonomous vehicles increasingly rely on deep neural networks
(DNNs) to execute complex inference tasks such as image classification and speech recognition, among others.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: However, continuously executing the entire DNN on mobile devices can quickly deplete their battery.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Although
task offloading to cloud/edge servers may decrease the mobile device’s computational burden, erratic patterns
in channel quality, network, and edge server load can lead to a significant delay in task execution.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Recently,
approaches based on split computing (SC) have been proposed, where the DNN is split into a head and a
tail model, executed respectively on the mobile device and on the edge server.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Ultimately, this may reduce
bandwidth usage as well as energy consumption.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Another approach, called early exiting (EE), trains models
to embed multiple “exits” earlier in the architecture, each providing increasingly higher target accuracy.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Therefore, the trade-off between accuracy and delay can be tuned according to the current conditions or
application demands.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey of the state of the art in SC and EE
strategies by presenting a comparison of the most relevant approaches.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
We conclude the paper by providing a
set of compelling research challenges.

1
INTRODUCTION
The field of deep learning (DL) has evolved at an impressive pace over the last few years [68], with
new breakthroughs continuously appearing in domains such as computer vision (CV), natural
language processing (NLP), digital signal processing (DSP), and wireless networking [56, 118]
among others – we refer to [110] for a comprehensive survey on DL.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For example, today’s state
of the art deep neural networks (DNNs) can classify thousands of images with unprecedented
accuracy [51], while bleeding-edge advances in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have shown to
provide near-human capabilities in a multitude of complex optimization tasks, from playing dozens
of Atari video games [99] to winning games of Go against top-tier players [127].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
As DL-based classifiers improve their predictive accuracy, mobile applications such as speech
recognition in smartphones [20, 45], real-time unmanned navigation [105] and drone-based surveil-
lance [129, 170] are increasingly using DNNs to perform complex inference tasks.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
However, state-of-
the-art DNN models present computational requirements that cannot be satisfied by the majority of the
mobile devices available today.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In fact, many state-of-the-art DNN models for difficult tasks – such
as computer vision and natural language processing – are extremely complex.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For instance, the Effi-
cientDet [139] family offers the best performance for object detection tasks.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
While EfficientDet-D7
achieves a mean average precision (mAP) of 52.2%, it involves 52M parameters and will take seconds
to be executed on strong embedded devices equipped with GPUs such as the NVIDIA Jetson Nano
and Raspberry Pi.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Notably, the execution of such complex models significantly increases energy
consumption.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
While lightweight models specifically designed for mobile devices exist [122, 138], the

text: reduced computational burden usually comes to the detriment of the model accuracy.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For example,
compared to ResNet-152 [43], the networks MnasNet [138] and MobileNetV2 [122] present up to
6.4% accuracy loss on the ImageNet dataset.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
YOLO-Lite [116] achieves a frame rate of 22 frames per
second on some embedded devices but has a mean average precision (mAP) of 12.36% on the COCO
dataset [83].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
To achieve 33.8% mAP on the COCO dataset, even the simplest model in the Efficient-
Det family, EfficientDet-D0, requires 3 times more FLOPs (2.5B) 1 than SSD-MobileNetV2 [122]
(0.8B FLOPs).
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
While SSD-MobileNetV2 is a lower-performance DNN specifically designed for
mobile platforms and can process up to 6 fps, its mAP on COCO dataset is 20% and keeping the
model running on a mobile device significantly increases power consumption.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
On the other hand,
due to excessive end-to-end latency, cloud-based approaches are hardly applicable in most of the
latency-constrained applications where mobile devices usually operate.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Most of the techniques
we overview in the survey can be applied to both mobile device to edge server and edge server to
cloud offloading.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: For the sake of clarity, we primarily refer to the former to explain the frameworks.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Recently, edge computing (EC) approaches [10, 88] have attempted to address the “latency vs
computation” conundrum by completely offloading the DNN execution to servers located very close
to the mobile device, i.e., at the “edge” of the network.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
However, canonical EC does not consider
that the quality of wireless links – although providing high throughput on the average – can
suddenly fluctuate due to the presence of erratic noise and interference patterns, which may impair
performance in latency-bound applications.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For example, mobility and impaired propagation have
been shown to decrease throughput even in high-bandwidth wireless links [89, 169] while many
Internet of Things (IoT) systems are based on communication technologies such as Long Range
(LoRa) [121], which has a maximum data rate of 37.5 Kbps due to duty cycle limitations [1].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The severe offloading limitations of some mobile devices, coupled with the instability of the
wireless channel (e.g., UAV network [36]), imply that the amount of data offloaded to edge should be
decreased, while at the same time keep the model accuracy as close as possible to the original.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For
this reason, split computing (SC) [60] and early exiting (EE) strategies [140] have been proposed to
provide an intermediate option between EC and local computing.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The key intuition behind SC and
EE is similar to the one behind model pruning [38, 44, 74, 160] and knowledge distillation [46, 61, 98]
– since modern DNNs are heavily over-parameterized [165, 166], their accuracy can be preserved
even with substantial reduction in the number of weights and filters, and thus representing the
input with fewer parameters.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Specifically, SC divide a larger DNN into head and tail models, which
are respectively executed by the mobile device and edge server.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
EE, on the other hand, proposes the
introduction of “subbranches” into the early layers of DNN models, so that the full computation
of the model can be halted – and a prediction result provided – if the classifiers in the current
subbranches have high confidence with the specific model input.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The proliferation of DL-based mobile applications in
the IoT and 5G landscapes implies that techniques such as SC and EE are not simply “nice-to-have”
features, but will become fundamental computational components in the years to come.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Although
a significant amount of research work has been done in SC and EE, to the best of our knowledge, a
comprehensive survey of the state of the art has not been conducted yet.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Moreover, there are still a
series of research challenges that need to be addressed to take SC and EE to the next level.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For this
reason, this paper makes the following novel contributions:
• We summarize SC and EE studies with respect to approaches, tasks, and models.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
We first provide
an overview of local, edge, split computing, and early-exit models in Section 2, by highlighting
similarities and difference among them;

highlighting the training strategies and applications.

Since code availability is fundamental for
replicability/reproducibility [34]2, we provide for each work its corresponding code repository,

• We conclude the paper by discussing in Section 6 a compelling agenda of research challenges in

2
OVERVIEW OF LOCAL, EDGE, SPLIT COMPUTING AND EARLY-EXIT MODELS
In this section, we provide an overview of local, edge, split computing, and early-exit models, which
are the main computational paradigms that will be discussed in the paper.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Figure 1 provides a
graphical overview of the approaches.

title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
All these techniques operate on a DNN model M(·) whose task is to produce the inference output
y from an input x.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Typically, x is a high-dimensional variable, whereas the output y has significantly
lower dimensionality [143].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Split computing and early exit approaches are contextualized in a
setting where the system is composed of a mobile device and an edge server interconnected via a
wireless channel.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The overall goal of the system is to produce the inference output y from the input
x acquired by the mobile device, by means of the DNN y=M(x) under – possibly time varying –
constraints on:
