text:
Resources: (i) the computational capacity (roughly expressed as number operations per second)
𝐶md and 𝐶es of the mobile device and edge server, respectively, (ii) the capacity 𝜙, in bits per second,
of the wireless channel connecting the mobile device to the edge server;
Performance: (i) the absolute of average value of the time from the generation of x to the avail-
ability of y, (ii) the degradation of the “quality” of the output y.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Split, edge, local, and early-exiting strategies strive to find suitable operating points with respect
to accuracy, end-to-end delay, and energy consumption, which are inevitably influenced by the
characteristics of the underlying system.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
It is generally assumed that the computing and energy
capacities of the mobile device are smaller than that of the edge server.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
As a consequence, if
part of the workload is allocated to the mobile device, then the execution time increases while
battery lifetime decreases.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
However, as explained later, the workload executed by the mobile device
may result in a reduced amount of data to be transferred over the wireless channel, possibly
compensating for the larger execution time and leading to smaller end-to-end delays.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
2.1
Local and Edge Computing
We start with an overview of local and edge computing.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In local computing (LC), the function M(x)
is entirely executed by the mobile device.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
This approach eliminates the need to transfer data over
the wireless channel.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
However, the complexity of the best performing DNNs most likely exceeds
the computing capacity and energy consumption available at the mobile device.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Usually, simpler
models ˆ
M(x) are used, such as MobileNet [122] and MnasNet [138] which often have a degraded
accuracy performance.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Besides designing lightweight neural models executable on mobile devices,
the widely used techniques to reduce the complexity of models are knowledge distillation [46]
and model pruning/quantization [55, 73] – described in Section 3.2.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Some of the techniques are
also leveraged in SC studies to introduce bottlenecks without sacrificing model accuracy as will be
described in the following sections.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In EC, the input x is transferred to the edge server, which then executes the original model
M(x).
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In this approach, which preserves full accuracy, the mobile device is not allocated computing
workload, but the full input x needs to be transferred to the edge server.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
This may lead to an
excessive end-to-end delay in degraded channel conditions and erasure of the task in extreme
conditions.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
A possible approach to reduce the load imposed to the wireless channel, and thus
also transmission delay and erasure probability, is to compress the input x.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
We define, then, the
encoder and decoder models z=𝐹(x) and ˆx=𝐺(z), which are executed at the mobile device and
edge server, respectively.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The distance 𝑑(x, ˆx) defines the performance of the encoding-decoding
process ˆx=𝐺(𝐹(x)), a metric which is separate, but may influence, the accuracy loss of M(ˆx)
with respect to M(x), that is, of the model executed with the reconstructed input with respect
to the model executed with the original input.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Clearly, the encoding/decoding functions increase
the computing load both at the mobile device and edge server side.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
A broad range of different
compression approaches exists ranging from low-complexity traditional compression (e.g., JPEG
compression for images in EC [101]) to neural compression models [4, 5, 162].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
We remark that
while the compressed input data e.g., JPEG objects, can reduce the data transfer time in EC, those
representations are designed to allow the accurate reconstruction of the input signal.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Therefore,
these approaches may (i) decrease privacy as a “reconstructable” representation is transferred
to the edge server [147]; (ii) result in larger amount of data to be transmitted over the channel
compared to representation specifically designed for the computing task as in bottleneck-based SC
as explained in the following sections.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges
0:5
2.2
Split Computing and Early Exiting
Split computing (SC) aims at achieving the following goals: (i) the computing load is distributed
across the mobile device and edge server; and (ii) establishes a task-oriented compression to reduce
data transfer delays.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
We consider a neural model M(·) with 𝐿layers, and define zℓthe output of
the ℓ-th layer.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Early implementations of SC select a layer ℓand divide the model M(·) to define the
head and tail submodels zℓ=M𝐻(x) and ˆy=M𝑇(zℓ), executed at the mobile device and edge server,
respectively.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In early instances of SC, the architecture and weights of the head and tail model are
exactly the same as the first ℓlayers and last 𝐿−ℓlayers of M(·).
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
This simple approach preserves
accuracy but allocates part of the execution of M(·) to the mobile device, whose computing power
is expected to be smaller than that of the edge server, so that the total execution time may be larger.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The transmission time of zℓmay be larger or smaller compared to that of transmitting the input x,
depending on the size of the tensor zℓ.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
However, we note that in most relevant applications the
size of zℓbecomes smaller than that of x only in later layers, which would allocate most of the
computing load to the mobile device.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
More recent SC frameworks introduce the notion of bottleneck
to achieve in-model compression toward the global task [90].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
As formally described in the next
section, a bottleneck is a compression point at one layer in the model, which can be realized by
reducing the number of nodes of the target layer, and/or by quantizing its output.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
We note that as
SC realizes a task-oriented compression, it guarantees a higher degree of privacy compared to EC.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: In fact, the representation may lack information needed to fully reconstruct the original input data.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: Another approach to enable mobile computing is referred to early exiting (EE).
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The core idea is to
create models with multiple “exits” across the model, where each exit can produce the model output.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: Then, the first exit providing a target confidence on the output is selected.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
This approach tunes
the computational complexity, determined by the exit point, to the sample or to system conditions.

BACKGROUND OF DEEP LEARNING FOR MOBILE APPLICATIONS
In this section, we provide an overview of recent approaches to reduce the computational complexity
of DNN models for resource-constrained mobile devices.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
These approaches can be categorized into
two main classes: (i) approaches that attempt to directly design lightweight models and (ii) model
compression.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
3.1
Lightweight Models
From a conceptual perspective, The design of small deep learning models is one of the simplest
ways to reduce inference cost.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
However, there is a trade-off between model complexity and model
accuracy, which makes this approach practically challenging when aiming at high model perfor-
mance.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The MobileNet series [47, 48, 122] is one among the most popular lightweight models
for computer vision tasks, where Howard et al.

3.2
Model Compression
A different approach to produce small DNN models is to “compress” a large model.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Model pruning
and quantization [38, 39, 55, 79] are the dominant model compression approaches.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The former
removes parameters from the model, while the latter uses fewer bits to represent them.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In both
these approaches, a large model is trained first and then compressed, rather than directly designing
a lightweight model followed by training.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
[55], the authors empirically show that
their quantization technique leads to an improved tradeoff between inference time and accuracy
on MobileNet [48] for image classification tasks on Qualcomm Snapdragon 835 and 821 compared
to the original, float-only MobileNet.

text: For what concerns model pruning, Li et al.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
[86]
demonstrates that it is difficult for model pruning itself to accelerate inference while achieving
strong performance guarantees on general-purpose hardware due to the unstructured sparsity of
the pruned model and/or kernels in layers.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: Knowledge distillation [8, 46] is another popular model compression method.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
While model
pruning and quantization make trained models smaller, the concept of knowledge distillation is to
provide outputs extracted from the trained model (called “teacher”) as informative signals to train
smaller models (called “student”) in order to improve the accuracy of predesigned small models.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Thus, the goal of the process is that of distilling knowledge of a trained teacher model into a smaller
student model for boosting accuracy of the smaller model without increasing model complexity.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For instance, Ba and Caruana [3] proposes a method to train small neural networks by mimicking
the detailed behavior of larger models.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The experimental results show that models trained by this
mimic learning method achieve performance close to that of deeper neural networks on some
phoneme recognition and image recognition tasks.

The formulation of some knowledge distillation
methods will be described in Section 4.4.

4.2
The Need for Bottleneck Injection
While Kang et al.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
[60] empirically show that executing the whole model on either mobile device or
edge server would be best in terms of total inference and energy consumption for most of their
considered DNN models, their proposed approach find the best partitioning layers inside some of
their considered CV models (convolutional neural networks (CNNs)) to minimize the total inference
time.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
There are a few trends observed from their experimental results: (i) communication delay to
transfer data from mobile device to edge server is a key component in SC to reduce total inference
time; (ii) all the neural models they considered for NLP tasks are relatively small (consisting of only
a few layers), that potentially resulted in finding the output layer is the best partition point (i.e.,
local computing) according to their proposed approach; (iii) similarly, not only DNN models they
considered (except VGG [128]) but also the size of the input data to the models (See Table 2) are
relatively small, which gives more advantage to EC (fully offloading computation).
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In other words,
it highlights that complex CV tasks requiring large (high-resolution) images for models to achieve
high accuracy such as ImageNet and COCO datasets would be essential to discuss the trade-off
between accuracy and execution metrics to be minimized (e.g., total latency, energy consumption)
for SC studies.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: The key issue is that straightforward SC approaches like Kang et al.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
[60] rely on the
existence of natural bottlenecks – that is, intermediate layers whose output zℓtensor size is smaller
than the input – inside the model.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Without such natural bottlenecks in the model, straightforward
splitting approaches would fail to improve performance in most settings [6, 35].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: Some models, such as AlexNet [64], VGG [128] and DenseNet [51], possess such layers [90].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
However, recent DNN models such as ResNet [43], Inception-v3 [136], Faster R-CNN [117] and
Mask R-CNN [42] do not have natural bottlenecks in the early layers, that is, splitting the model
would result in compression only when assigning a large portion of the workload to the mobile
device.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
As discussed earlier, reducing the communication delay is a key to minimize total inference
time in SC.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For these reasons, introducing artificial bottlenecks to DNN models by modifying their
architecture is a recent trend and has been attracting attention from the research community.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Since
the main role of such encoders in SC is to compress intermediate features rather than to complete
inference, the encoders usually consist of only a few layers.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Also, the resulting encoders in SC to
be executed on constrained mobile devices are often much smaller (e.g., 10K parameters in the
encoder of ResNet-based SC model [94]), than lightweight models such as MobileNetV2 [122]

Matsubara et al.

text: (3.5M parameters) and MnasNet [138] (4.4M parameters).
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Thus, even if the model accuracy is
either degraded or comparable to such small models, SC models are still beneficial in terms of
computational burden and energy consumption at the mobile devices.

Split Computing with Bottleneck Injection
This class of models can be described as composed of 3 sections: M𝐸, M𝐷and M𝑇.

text:
We define
zℓ|x as the output of the ℓ-th layer of the original model given the input x.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The concatenation of
the M𝐸and M𝐷models is designed to produce a possibly noisy version ˆzℓ|x of zℓ|x, which is
taken as input by M𝑇to produce the output ˆy, on which the accuracy degradation with respect to
y is measured.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The models M𝐸, M𝐷function as specialized encoders and decoders in the form
ˆzℓ=M𝐷(M𝐸(x)), where M𝐸(x) produces the latent variable z.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In worlds, the two first sections
of the modified model transform the input x into a version of the output of the ℓ-th layer via the
intermediate representation z, thus functioning as encoder/decoder functions.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The model is split
after the first section, that is, M𝐸is the head model, and the concatenation of M𝐷and M𝑇is the
tail model.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: Then, the tensor z is transmitted over the channel.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The objective of the architecture is to
minimize the size of z to reduce the communication time while also minimizing the complexity of
M𝐸(that is, the part of the model executed at the – weaker – mobile device) and the discrepancy
between y and ˆy.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: The layer between M𝐸and M𝐷is the injected bottleneck.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: Table 3 summarizes SC studies with bottleneck injected strategies.

text:
To the best of our knowledge,
the papers in [26] and [90] were the first to propose altering existing DNN architectures to design
relatively small bottlenecks at early layers in DNN models, instead of introducing compression
techniques (e.g., quantization, autoencoder) to the models, so that communication delay (cost) and
total inference time can be further reduced.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Following these studies, Hu and Krishnamachari [49]
introduce bottlenecks to MobileNetV2 [122] (modified for CIFAR datasets) in a similar way for SC,
and discuss end-to-end performance evaluation.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
[14] combine multiple compression
techniques such as quantization and tiling besides convolution/deconvolution layers, and design
a feature compression approach for object detectors.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Similar to the concept of bottleneck injec-
tion, Shao and Zhang [126] find that over-compression of intermediate features and inaccurate
communication between computing devices can be tolerated unless the prediction performance of
the models are significantly degraded by them.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
[57] propose introducing a
reconstruction-based bottleneck to DNN models, which is similar to the concept of BottleNet [26].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: A comprehensive discussion on the delay/complexity/accuracy tradeoff can be found in [91, 164].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: These studies are all focused on image classification.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: Other CV tasks present further challenges.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For instance, state of the art object detectors such as R-CNN models have more narrow range
of layers that we can introduce bottlenecks due to the network architecture, which has multiple
forward paths to forward outputs from intermediate layers to feature pyramid network (FPN) [81].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The head network distillation training approach – discussed later in this section – was used
in Matsubara and Levorato [94] to address some of these challenges and reduce the amount of
data transmitted over the channel by 94% while degrading mAP (mean average precision) loss by
1 point.

EARLY EXITING: A SURVEY
This section presents a survey of the state of the art in EE strategies.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
We first provide a compendium
of work focused on CV and NLP applications in Sections 5.2 and 5.3, respectively.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Section 5.4
summarizes training methodologies used in the EE studies.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
5.1
Rationale behind EE
The core idea of EE, first proposed in Teerapittayanon et al.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
[140], is to circumvent the need to
make DNN models smaller by introducing early exits in the DNN, where execution is terminated
at the first exit achieving the desired confidence on the input sample.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For instance, some samples
in test datasets (and in real-world problems) will be easy for a DNN model, but others may not
be, depending on ML models we use.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Thus, EE ends the inference process with fewer transforms
(layers) for such easy samples so that the overall inference time and computation cost are reduced.

SPLIT COMPUTING AND EARLY EXITING: RESEARCH CHALLENGES
In this section, we describe some of the research challenges in the SC and EE domains.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Evaluation of SC and EE in more practical settings
Due to the cross-disciplinary nature of this research area, it is essential to design practical and
convincing evaluation settings to demonstrate the effectiveness of proposed approaches.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
As shown
in Tables 3 and 4, the techniques proposed in many of the recent related studies are validated only
on small-scale datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR datasets, which leads to some concerns on the
input data size in relation with compression.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Indeed, Table 2 suggests that the input data size in
many of such datasets is relatively small (e.g., smaller than 2 kilobytes per image with a resolution
of 32 × 32 pixels).
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The low-resolution of the input size may enable conventional EC, where the
mobile device fully offloads the computing task by transferring the input data to an edge server.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In
fact, the transmission of such a small amount of data would require a short time even in settings
with limited communication capacity.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
As a consequence, executing even small head models on a
resource-limited mobile device could lead to an overall delay increase.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Based on the above discussion, it becomes apparent that the models and datasets, in addition
to the wireless and computing environments, are of paramount importance when assessing the
performance of SC and EE schemes.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Of particular relevance is the evaluation of accuracy, which
is not provided in some of the early studies (e.g., [43, 122, 128]) and the consideration of state-
of-the-art models and datasets which are largely used in the machine learning community.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For
instance, the use of small models, such as MobileNetV2, ResNet-50, VGG-16, which are likely
overparameterized for simple classification tasks, could lead to wrong conclusions when injecting
bottlenecks.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Conversely, it was shown in [90] how challenging it is to inject bottlenecks when
considering complex vision tasks such as classification on the ImageNet dataset [120].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Optimization of bottleneck design and placement in SC
The study of the architecture and placement of the bottleneck in a DNN model is also of considerable
importance.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
As suggested in [96], important metrics include: (i) bottleneck data size (or compression
rate), (ii) complexity of head model executed on mobile device, and (iii) resulting model accuracy.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
As
a principle, the smaller the bottleneck representation is, the lower the communication cost between
mobile device and edge server will be.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In general, the objective of SC is to generate a bottleneck
whose data size is smaller than that of input data such as JPEG file size of input data, which is
in turn much smaller than data size of input tensor (32-bit floating point), as the communication
delay is a key component to reduce overall inference time [90, 91, 94, 158].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Secondly, since mobile
devices often have limited computing resources and may have other constraints such as energy
consumption due to their battery capacities, SC should aim at minimizing their computational load
by making head models as lightweight as possible.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For instance, designing a small bottleneck at
a very early stage of the DNN model enables a reduction in the computational complexity of the
head model [93, 94].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
On top of these two criteria, the resulting model accuracy by the bottleneck injection should not
be compromised as the introduced bottleneck removes more or less information at the placement
compared to the original model.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
A reasonable lower bound of the model accuracy in SC would
be that of widely recognized lightweight models e.g., MobileNetV2 [122] for ImageNet dataset,
considering a local computing system where such lightweight models can be efficiently executed.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In general, it is challenging to optimize bottleneck design and placement with respect to all the
three different metrics, and existing studies empirically design the bottlenecks and determine


0:22
Matsubara et al.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Thus, theoretical discussion on bottleneck design and placement should be an
interesting research topic for future work.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Dynamic control of exits in EE
In most of the recent studies, early exits are used when one of the introduced early classifiers (exits)
is confident enough in its prediction.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
However, users are required to determine a threshold for
each of the classifiers beforehand at least for one early classifier in the original model where we
introduce the early classifier to.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For example, if the first classifier’s prediction score is greater than
0.9 in range of 0.0 and 1.0, then the inference for the input is terminated.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
To achieve more efficient inference without significantly sacrificing the accuracy of the original
model, the system needs to find a balance between (early) classifiers.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
As recent studies introduce
multiple early exits to a model at different stages, such optimizations are challenging.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
In addition to
manually defining such a threshold for each of the classifiers based on empirical results, a possibly
interesting direction is the optimization of the decision-making process, that is, at which (early)
classifier we should terminate the inference for a given input, without a set of thresholds defined
beforehand based on system characteristics.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Expanding the Application Domain of SC and EE
The application domains of SC and (in minor part) EE remain primarily focused on image classifi-
cation.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
This focus may be explained by the size of the input, which makes compression a relevant
problem in many settings and the complexity of the models and tasks.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
However, there are many other
unexplored domains which SC would benefit.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Real-time health conditions monitoring via wearable
sensors is a notable example of application where a significant amount of data is transferred from
sensors to edge servers such as cellular phones and home hubs.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For instance, the detection and
monitoring of heart anomalies (e.g., arrhythmia) from (ECG) [30] require the processing of high-rate
samples (e.g., 100-1000 per heart cycle) using high complexity DNN models[41].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Health monitoring
applications pose different challenges compared to CV-based applications.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Indeed, in the former,
both the computing capacity and the bandwidth available to the system are often smaller compared
to the latter scenario, and conceptual advancements are required.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Toward an Information-Theoretic Perspective
The key intuition behind the success of SC and EE is similar to what has led to the success of
techniques such as model pruning [38, 44, 74, 160] and knowledge distillation [46, 61, 98]: most
state-of-the-art DNNs are significantly over-parameterized [165, 166].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
A possible approach to justify
SC and EE can be found in the study of information bottlenecks (IB), which were introduced in [142]
as a compression technique in which a random variable X is compressed while preserving relevant
information about another random variable Y.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The IB method has been applied in [143] to quantify
mutual information between the network layers and derive an information theory limit on DNN
efficiency.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
This has led to attempts at explaining the behavior of deep neural networks with the
information bottleneck formalism [123].
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Despite these early attempts, a strong connection between this relatively new perspective and
the techniques described in this paper is still elusive.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
Some of the approaches and architectures
discussed in this paper are meaningful attempts to efficiently extract a compressed representation
of the input and provide sufficient information toward a certain task early in the network layers.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
The emerging IB formalism is a promising approach to enable the first moves in the information
theoretic analysis of neural networks-based transformations.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
We believe that this interpretation
could serve as a foundation for an in-depth study of structural properties for both SC and EE.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

CONCLUSIONS
Mobile devices such as smartphones and drones have now become an integral part of our daily
lives.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
These devices increasingly utilize deep neural networks (DNNs) to execute complex inference
tasks such as image classification and speech recognition, among others.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
For this reason, in this
paper, we provided a comprehensive survey of the state of the art in split computing (SC) and
early exiting (EE) by presenting a thorough comparison of the most relevant approaches.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text:
We also
provided a set of compelling research challenges that need to be addressed to improve existing
work in the field.
title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges

text: We hope this survey will elicit further research in these emerging fields.

Ripple : Simpliﬁed Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with
Polymorphic Data Layout
Robert Clucas∗, Philip Blakely, Nikolaos Nikiforakis
Maxwell Centre, Cavendish Laboratory, JJ Thomson Avenue, Cambridge, CB3 0HE
Abstract
GPUs are now used for a wide range of problems within HPC.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
However, making eﬃcient use of the computational power
available with multiple GPUs is challenging.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The main challenges in achieving good performance are memory layout, aﬀecting
memory bandwidth, eﬀective use of the memory spaces with a GPU, inter-GPU communication, and synchronization.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We address
these problems with the Ripple library, which provides a uniﬁed view of the computational space across multiple dimensions and
multiple GPUs, allows polymorphic data layout, and provides a simple graph interface to describe an algorithm from which inter-
GPU data transfers can be optimally scheduled.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We describe the abstractions provided by Ripple to allow complex computations
to be described simply, and to execute eﬃciently across many GPUs with minimal overhead.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We show performance results for a
number of examples, from particle motion to ﬁnite-volume methods and the eikonal equation, as well as showing good strong and
weak scaling results across multiple GPUs.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Keywords: Parallel computing, GPU, High performance computing, Graph, Tensor, Heterogeneous architecture
1.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Introduction
The heterogeneous nature of compute servers containing
multiple many-core CPUs as well as a large number of
accelerators—usually GPUs—makes it diﬃcult to take full ad-
vantage of the available computational resources.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
CPU or GPU) eﬀectively requires ex-
pert knowledge of the respective hardware and associated tools,
but is especially true for GPU implementations, where the pro-
gramming model is signiﬁcantly diﬀerent from that required to
program many-core CPU-based systems.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
It is also typically
more diﬃcult to extract high levels of performance from accel-
erators due to the diﬀerence in hardware design between CPUs
and GPUs, which makes the performance of GPU code very de-
pendent on register use, lack of indirection, and regular memory
access patterns.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
These eﬀects are magniﬁed once multiple ac-
celerators are present in a system due to cost of data transfer
between them.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Most existing software frameworks separate the computa-
tional domains, or provide improvements in either programmer
productivity or performance, but not both.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Therefore, we iden-
tify two categories which need to be addressed to achieve good
performance on systems with many CPU cores as well as mul-
tiple accelerators: ﬁne-grained parallelism and coarse-grained
parallelism.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Within ﬁne-grained parallelism, there is the parallelisation of
data and the execution of the computation on the data.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
These are

usually the kernels which run on the accelerators, or across the
many CPU cores in the system.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Achieving good performance
in this area requires tuning the data layout, kernel execution
sizes, and use of speciﬁc memory regions on the computational
devices (i.e.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Coarse-grain parallelism involves the scheduling of kernels
which execute on the computational resources, partitioning of
work across the heterogeneous devices, and the reduction of
latency when data must be transferred or shared between the
diﬀerent devices.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
There is very little existing work which addresses both ar-
eas, and speciﬁcally all mentioned sections within each area,
eﬀectively.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Here we present Ripple1, a software library which
addresses the above problems, providing an interface for speci-
fying both coarse- and ﬁne-grained parallelism, as well as pro-
viding the user with a simple means for conﬁguring all aspects
of parallelism to allow good performance to be achieved for
their application with minimal eﬀort, and with limited knowl-
edge of GPUs or parallel and distributed systems.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The major
contributions of our work are the following:
• Polymorphic data layout for user-deﬁned types: Users
can specify data layouts for user-deﬁned classes as a tem-
plate parameter, which allows the class to be used as ei-
ther Array-of-Struct (AoS, contiguous layout) or Struct-
of-Array (SoA, strided layout).
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We provide interoper-
ability of the layouts so that they can be used seamlessly
throughout an application.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This allows users to determine
the best layout for the problem, and to use diﬀerent data
1https://robclu.github.io/ripple_docs/
Preprint submitted to Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing
April 20, 2021
arXiv:2104.08571v1  [cs.DC]  17 Apr 2021


layouts for each part of an application or execution do-
main.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
• Speciﬁcation of the memory space: The user can spec-
ify which memory space should be used for each block of
the data involved in a computational kernel (for example,
shared or global memory on the GPU).
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Achieving good
performance on GPUs requires testing all memory spaces
and data layouts for a problem, which is cumbersome for
large applications.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We allow the memory space to be spec-
iﬁed (in a single line) at the point of computation, allowing
the same data to be used in diﬀerent memory spaces for
diﬀerent parts of an algorithm.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
• N-dimensional tensor data type and iterators: We pro-
vide an N-dimensional tensor data type and an iterator in-
terface over the space.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This removes the need for error-
prone manual memory allocation and index computations.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Further, padding cells can be speciﬁed for the tensor, re-
quired for many stencil-type operations, and allow these
can be ﬁlled from neighbouring tensors where necessary.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
• Expressive graph model for the structure of a series of
kernels: Kernels, and the implicit and explicit dependen-
cies between them, can be speciﬁed at a high level as a
Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The memory and compu-
tational dependencies can then be determined by the li-
brary allowing optimisation of kernel-scheduling to min-
imise the overall latency of the computation.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
• Heterogeneous computation Kernel-execution can be
speciﬁed in a graph for execution on the CPU or GPU, en-
abling heterogeneous computation and making it possible
to fully utilise the available computational power of both
domains in a system.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
While our library allows general computation to execute on
heterogeneous nodes, our focus is on computations performed
on multi-dimensional tensor-like data partitioned across mul-
tiple GPU accelerators.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We take this approach due to mod-
ern GPUs providing signiﬁcantly more computational perfor-
mance than CPUs, and their ability to process regularly laid-out
data eﬃciently.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Despite their much higher theoretical compu-
tational throughput, attaining this on the GPU is more diﬃcult
than for the CPU, so simplifying programmer eﬀort for better
utilisation of GPU accelerators has the largest overall beneﬁt—
particularly for problems which require non-trivial data struc-
tures.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Ripple requires a compiler implementing the C++-17 stan-
dard and therefore supports Clang 9, 10, and 11, with CUDA
[1] versions 9.0 though 11.2, as the compiler for both host and
device code, or CUDA versions >= 11 with nvcc as the device
compiler with GCC versions ≥9.3.0 or Clang versions ≥9.0.0
as the host compiler, since CUDA 11.0 provided the ﬁrst nvcc
compiler with C++-17 support for device code.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: In Sec-
tion 2 we review existing work.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Section 3 gives an overview of
the abstractions in Ripple.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
These are described in more detail in
Section 4 where we describe the n-dimensional tensor data type,
polymorphic data layout functionality, a simpliﬁed method for
accessing elements in polymorphic data types, and the itera-
tor abstraction which allows eﬃcient accessing of tensor data
in kernels.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
At a higher level, Section 5 outlines heterogeneous
allocators in Ripple for improving the performance of work-
ﬂows with dynamic memory requirements, the graph interface
for computational workﬂow description, how constraints can be
placed on kernel data access to specify data dependencies be-
tween kernels in a graph, and how to schedule work between
the CPU and GPU computational domains.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
In Section 6 we
describe how work is scheduled on either CPU or GPU as ap-
propriate.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Then, in Section 7 we provide benchmarks for the
performance of the ﬁne-grained aspects of our library, while
Section 8 shows the scaling performance of the library across
multiple computational devices.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
In Section 9 we discuss the
main limitations of the library and directions of future work,
and Section 10 summarises the whole work.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Related Work
While most related work falls into either the ﬁne- or coarse-
grained categories, SYCL [2] does provide features for both.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The latest revision has support for kernels written in C++17,
which can be executed on a number of backends, allowing a
lot of ﬂexibility for supported hardware.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The framework also
allows for kernels to be executed across multiple devices if
available.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
However, a lot of the work has to be done manu-
ally by the user, such as the partitioning of data and transfer
of data between execution devices.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The main limitations of
SYCL are a lack of support for CUDA devices as a backend,
which likely results in less eﬃciency on CUDA supported de-
vices as OpenCL does not provide all the features available in
CUDA.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Additionally, a number of the abstractions we provide
to make programming simpler and more eﬃcient in a multi-
GPU context, such as polymorphic data layout, iterators, multi-
dimensional tensors, and the graph interface which handles data
transfer between devices, are not available in SYCL.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Fine-grained Parallelism
There are a number of existing frameworks which allow code
to be parallelised by the compiler following programmer direc-
tives.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
They are
simple to use, but are limited in the complexity of computa-
tion which they can parallelize eﬀectively.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
OmpSs [5] extends
OpenMP to allow heterogeneous computation, but still requires
a large amount of work from the programmer and does not pro-
vide cross-GPU functionality.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
These perform very well at par-
allelising simple loops, but are not able to handle more complex
computations.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
A good overview of the beneﬁts and limitations
of these types of programming models is provided by Lee and
Vetter [6].
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Kokkos [7] is a more sophisticated solution which has seen
signiﬁcant use, particularly in scientiﬁc applications.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
It pro-
vides data-layout ﬂexibility for simple data-types (not user-
deﬁned), and high-level constructs for oﬄoading computation
2


to one of the supported many-core backends.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
While the func-
tionality is vast, and performance is very good relative to raw
CUDA, the interface is quite involved, particularly for custom
data structures.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The main limitation of Kokkos is that it re-
quires the programmer to manage inter-GPU communication
and data transfer explicitly with another library, such as MPI,
thus requiring a good knowledge of the underlying hardware
and its API.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Additionally, it does not provide an interface for
shared memory use on the GPU or polymorphic data layout,
which can both provide signiﬁcant performance improvements
for some applications, as we show later.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Coarse-grained Parallelism
Task based programming models have recently become pop-
ular due to their ability to specify complex computational work-
ﬂows at a high level, and have them run eﬃciently in parallel.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
These are particularly suited to CPUs due to the dynamic and
irregular nature of the tasks in the computational ﬂow.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Early
works are StarPU [8], which provides a scheduling environ-
ment for tasks to run on heterogeneous architectures, exhibit-
ing good performance.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
HPX [9] is similar, but is C++ stan-
dard conforming and allows task-based work to be executed
on larger-scale heterogeneous architectures.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
It provides simi-
lar functionality to our graph interface for specifying a com-
putational ﬂow, but does not provide ﬁne-grained data-space
abstractions or polymorphic data-layout, which reduce devel-
opment complexity and improve performance.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
A more recent
work is Cpp-Taskﬂow v2 [10], which has seen signiﬁcant use
of late.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The second version extends the original implementation
to allow tasks to be executed heterogeneously on both the CPU
and GPU, but does not provide any GPU based abstractions for
data spaces or data transfer between GPUs.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
While all of these works provide good abstractions for task-
based parallelism, they oﬀer limited support for the ﬁne-grained
parallelism which is required to take advantage of the through-
put provided by GPU accelerators.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Once multiple accelerators are present in a system, most ap-
plications require data-transfer between the accelerators which
contributes signiﬁcantly to the overall computation time due to
the bandwidth and latency of the memory system, resulting in
under-utilization of the accelerators as they wait for data to pro-
cess.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Work addressing these issues includes CuMAS [11], which
looks at reducing the latency of data-transfer with respect to
GPUs, but for the multi-application space, rather than within a
single speciﬁc application.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
[12] provide a frame-
work for overlapping data transfers and compute on the GPU,
however, the overall use is limited by the requirement for ker-
nels to be written using OpenACC, which they show to produce
sub-optimal performance compared to CUDA.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Lastly, Daino
[13] is a framework for hiding memory-transfer latency, but
speciﬁcally for Adaptive Mesh Reﬁnement, which limits its
scope.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Abstractions
Modern computational environments contain multiple nodes
which communicate via an interconnect.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Ideally the system ar-
chitecture would be abstracted by the programming interface,
but this is challenging, especially when the data transfers cre-
ate dependencies between operations on diﬀerent devices in the
system.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Thus there is a separation into coarse- and ﬁne-grained
parallelism, for which we provide a number of abstractions to
allow the programmer to maximise performance in both areas.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The data abstractions we provide are tensors, polymorphic
data layout, accessors, and allocators, which target ﬁne-grained
parallelism, while the execution abstractions, which facilitate
coarse-grained parallelism, are iterators and graphs.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We de-
scribe these in more detail in the following sections.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Data Abstractions
Here we describe the abstractions that deal with data; gener-
ally improving ﬁne-grained parallelism.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Tensors
In Ripple, a tensor is an abstraction over a multi-dimensional
space.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
It contains a data type, which is stored for each point
in the multi-dimensional space, and the dimensionality of the
space, both provided at compile-time as template parameters.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text: Data types can be scalar, such as double,float,int, etc.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
When the type is user-deﬁned, the data-layout
data can be speciﬁed as polymorphic, allowing the storage of
the class data in the tensor to be SoA (elements are strided) or
AoS (elements are contiguous), as described in Section 4.2, and
shown in Figure 1.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
When initializing the tensor data, the layout
is inferred from the data type, and the size of each dimension in
the space is speciﬁed as a run-time parameter when the tensor
is created, which can be resized if necessary.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text: Many operations require the use of data within a stencil.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For
example, an approximation of the ﬁrst derivative of f using a
forward diﬀerence in the x dimension at index u is
∆x fu = fu+1 −fu
(1)
which requires access to the data point fu+1.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
If fu is at the
boundary of the domain, the data at fu+1 is invalid, so padding
data is required, which can be speciﬁed as a parameter when
a tensor is created.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Ripple provides a number of methods for
loading the padding for common cases—such as ﬁrst order and
constant extrapolation.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Padding becomes more complicated
when the tensor data is strided or exists on multiple devices,
potentially introducing a memory dependency in the DAG rep-
resenting the computation, and Ripple simpliﬁes the handling
of the padding data in such cases.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Through the graph inter-
face, options are provided for the strictness of the dependency
on operations which use or modify padding data, allowing the
computational graph to be optimized to minimise the latency of
memory operations as well as removing the need for the pro-
grammer to implement these themselves.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
These operations are
described fully in Section 5.3.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The tensor data can be partitioned across the system devices,
and also within each device.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This only requires changing a single parameter, making bench-
marking straightforward.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Partitioning across multiple dimen-
sions results in smaller blocks in each of the partitioned dimen-
sions.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
However, this requires data to be transferred between the
devices if neighbour data is accessed, introducing dependencies
in the DAG.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We suggest partitioning across a single dimension
for best performance.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For multi-dimensional tensors, partition-
ing the higher dimensions is likely the best strategy because it
results in a memory transfer of data which has a coalesced ac-
cess pattern (i.e.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
As shown in Listing 1, the tensor interface allows both the
number of partitions per dimension, as well as the number
of sub-partitions to be speciﬁed for each dimension.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Sub-
partitions exist on the same device so may introduce a memory
dependency where one might not be necessary.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
However, they
may also increase the overall opportunity for parallelism in an
application, or create partition sizes which are suitable for both
the CPU and GPU, leading to improved performance.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Polymorphic Data Layout
Tensor data layout is determined by the data type, which is
always contiguous, unless the data type is user-deﬁned and in-
herits from the PolymorphicLayout struct, which requires a
template parameter to specify the type of layout.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This allows
user-deﬁned types to have ﬂexible data layout, and therefore
the option to proﬁle which layout is the best for diﬀerent parts
of an application.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
In Ripple, the layout of the class data can
be deﬁned as contiguous or strided.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Contiguous data has the
elements of the struct laid out contiguously in memory, while
strided data is laid out with a stride equal to the size of the ﬁrst
dimension in the tensor.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Internally, strided data stores an array
of each of the components of the struct contiguously, with the
component arrays being stored successively.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Creating a polymorphic data layout requires a user-
deﬁned
class
to
specify
the
types
stored
using
the
StorageDescriptor
template
class,
which
takes
the
layout and a list of types to be stored, similar to std::tuple.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We provide a Vector<T, Size> class to specify that Size
elements of type T should be stored in a vector-like con-
tainer.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
There are existing solutions which allow polymorphic
layout within containers, but only for built-in types such
as double, float, int, etc.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Additionally, accessing the
elements is done through an index, which does not provide
the context that the name of a struct member does, and does
not allow the polymorphic data to be used as both an object
and within the tensor.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Both of these limitations are signiﬁcant
in the development of large software projects.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Ripple allows
heterogeneous types to be stored in the tensor, and class-data
to be accessed through the StorageDescriptor as if it
were a std::tuple.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The types must be deﬁned through the
StorageDescriptor interface rather than directly within in
the class, and to inherit from the PolymorphicLayout<T>
trait-class, allowing Ripple to determine that the user-deﬁned
type has a polymorphic memory layout with no runtime-
overhead.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The StorageDescriptor provides an alias for the
actual storage type, and the elements can be accessed though
the get template method which computes oﬀsets at compile
time.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
An example is shown in Listing 2 which deﬁnes a state
class with D elements of type T and a bool indicating whether
the state is valid.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
When used with a tensor, this will lay out
the data based on the type provided as the Layout template
parameter.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Accessors
For some use cases, it is more descriptive to deﬁne the mem-
bers of a class as public, rather than as member functions which
access the associated components from the storage, as shown
in Listing 2.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
One such example is that of a vector class, with
components for x,y,z, etc., which could be implemented with
x,y,z as public members that can be accessed directly.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
How-
ever, if the storage is a contiguous array, they would have to be
deﬁned as public member functions for getting and setting the
values, or would have to be stored as public members, which
would require specialization for each number of elements.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We provide an Accessor<ValueType, StorageType,
Index> abstraction to allow a given index in the storage to re-
turn a given value type, while still allowing the polymorphic
layout ﬂexibility.

The advantage of the accessor im-

text:
Execution abstractions
In this section we describe abstractions relating to the ﬂow
control; typically associated with coarse-grained parallelism.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Allocators
Often memory requirements are not known upfront, and
therefore require memory to be allocated dynamically.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
How-
ever, this signiﬁcantly reduces performance since cudaMalloc
and cudaFree require synchronization to ensure that the mem-
ory being allocated or freed is not touched before or after the
operation.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
These calls introduce signiﬁcant points in the exe-
cution pipeline of an application where no work is being per-
formed on either the CPU or the GPU.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
It is thus important to
avoid dynamic allocation during a computation.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For the Euler
example presented in Section 8, dynamic allocations, even ac-
counting for only 2% of the total memory requirement, caused
performance reductions of up to 30%.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We therefore provide an allocator, MultiarchAllocator,
which provides dynamic memory allocators for the CPU and
the GPU via the cpu_allocator() and gpu_allocator()
methods, respectively.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For the CPU, we allocate a buﬀer of
pinned host memory, since this is faster for transfer to the GPU
and is required for asynchronous copies between the CPU and
GPU.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For the GPU we allocate a buﬀer with cudaMalloc, from

We use the same allocation strat-

early from the buﬀer.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The CPU allocator has a buﬀer per thread,
while the GPU allocator has a buﬀer per GPU, and both are
thread safe to allow them to function correctly with the sched-
uler described in Section 6.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Since the linear allocation strategy
is relatively simple, we plan to extend the allocation strategy in
future.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For our use cases, however, the current implementation
signiﬁcantly improved overall performance in multiple appli-
cations.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This was also the case for performing an out of place
reduction across multiple devices, since the results buﬀers for
the the reduction of the individual devices did not need to be
allocated reducing the time for which the GPU was idle.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

We
also provide constructors for the tensor data type which allow
it to take a MultiarchAllocator from which it can allocate,
for tensors requiring dynamic creation or resizing.

When
a

and

parameter

either
an

or
a
BlockIterator<T, Space>, where T is the type of the
tensor data and Space is the multi-dimensional space of the
block within the tensor on which the iterator can iterate.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The
layout of the data iterated over is always the same as that of
the tensor, and includes padding data if present.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The iterator is
automatically oﬀset to the relevant cell in the tensor, avoiding
the need for the user to have to perform any oﬀsetting over
padding data.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The layout of the data is hidden by the iterator so
that it can iterate over both contiguous and strided data.
