text:
Indexed Iterator
The IndexedIterator carries with it indices which deﬁne
the location of its block within the tensor, as well as its indices
in the global iteration space, allowing the iterator to provide
thread, block, and global indices and sizes.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This allows the
multi-dimensional space, partitioned across multiple devices, to
appear as a single space.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The iterator, however, can only iterate
within a single block in the partitioned tensor space, due to the
tensor data for diﬀerent blocks potentially being on diﬀerent
devices.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This has an overhead per thread of 12 bytes per dimension in
the tensor and iterator.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
However, benchmarks have shown the
performance eﬀect to be small, and the increase in ease of use of
iterators compared to raw multi-dimensional indices is signiﬁ-
cant.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The performance implications of the iterator framework
are provided in Section 7.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
An additional beneﬁt of the iterator
is that the syntax for accessing data is consistent for diﬀerent
dimensions.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Most frameworks overload operator() to enable
indexing in multiple dimensions requiring separate specializa-
tions for each number of dimensions.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
While sometimes neces-
sary, other operations diﬀer only in the number of dimensions,
thus, the iterator provides a compile time trait for the number
of dimensions, and an unrolled_for<dims>(operation)
method is available to unroll an operation for a number of di-
mensions as shown in Listing 4.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We have benchmarked code
which uses unrolled_for against a regular loop with a run-
time value and have observed slightly better performance, and
lower register usage on the GPU, in almost all cases.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

The iterator is similar to that in the standard C++ library,
with extensions to support a multi-dimensional space.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
An it-
erator can be oﬀset in a given dimension, as shown in List-
ing 4, and de-referencing provides access to the underlying oﬀ-
set data.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Calls to the oﬀset method can be chained to oﬀset in
multiple dimensions.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
When a callable is executed, a check is
performed on the iterator’s index against the the bounds of the
multi-dimensional iteration space so that any out of range itera-
tors do not execute the callable, ensuring that iterators only run
on data valid within the tensor space.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Block Iterator
A
BlockIterator
is
a
lightweight
version
of
the
IndexedIterator, and used in more performance critical con-
texts.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
It iterates over a subspace of a tensor partition, and does
not contain index information for the global space so cannot de-
termine its global location.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
It can, however, provide the index
with the subspace it can iterate over.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
A BlockIterator can
be created over both statically and dynamically sized spaces.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
In the statically sized case, the size of the iterator is the size
of a pointer, while for a dynamically sized space an additional
four bytes are required per dimension to store the strides for it-
eration.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
An additional beneﬁt of statically sized spaces is that
the index computations are performed at compile time, as well
as the determination of the amount of memory required for the
space (shared memory on the GPU, or allocation from a pool
on the CPU).
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
In practice, these diﬀerences are minor compared
to the computation time of kernels, and the BlockIterator
over both static and dynamic spaces gives similar performance,
which is improved compared to the IndexedIterator in
contexts where memory is scarce, such as in shared mem-
ory.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The interface for BlockIterator is a subset of the
IndexedIterator interface, with the IndexedIterator pro-
viding additional functions which return information about the
global iteration space, and traits to determine the type of an it-
erator.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Graphs
Graphs in Ripple allow a complete workﬂow to be described
at a high level, from which the dependencies are determined
when the graph is built.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
While the overhead of determining
the graph-dependencies is minimal, we incur it at the time of
graph creation because a graph is typically built once but exe-
cuted many times.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The graph is then submitted to an executor,
which executes the nodes of the graph in parallel such that the
dependencies are met.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Operations are emplaced onto the graph,

text:
In this context, a graph is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG),
where nodes represent the computations (kernels) to be per-
formed and edges represent the dependencies between the com-
putations.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We deﬁne a level in the graph to contain all nodes
which have a dependency on a node in the previous level, with
all nodes having no dependencies being the ﬁrst level.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Nodes
on the same level may execute in parallel, as soon as their de-
pendencies are met.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The Graph constructor takes an argument
for the default type of execution space, which can also be over-
ridden for each operation, as either ExecutionKind::Cpu or
ExecutionKind::Gpu.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

A simple example of the levels in the
graph is illustrated in Figure 2

text:
Nodes
The nodes in a graph are deﬁned using a Node which stores
the callable deﬁning the node operation, as well as any ar-
guments which are required to invoke the callable.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
To allow
callables with any signature, type erasure is used to store a
generic executor in the node, which is diﬀerent from most exist-
ing solutions that require callables to have a speciﬁc signature.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
In addition to the callable object, the node stores information to
allow it to be accessed and modiﬁed after the graph has been
created.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Operations on non-tensor types
In some task-based models, nodes are added to the graph
and then the dependencies are speciﬁed.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
However, we take a
diﬀerent approach, where the graph is deﬁned more explicitly
and concisely.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We also provide functionality for modifying de-
pendencies between individual nodes after graph creation by
allowing nodes to be searched for by the node name.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The op-
erations which add non-tensor based operations to a graph are
emplace() and then().
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Emplace adds a node onto the graph, with the depen-
dencies of the node being any nodes in the previous level.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
To
allow multiple nodes to be placed in the same level (such that
they execute in parallel), emplace can be called multiple times,

The new node is added as a

text:
Operations on tensor types
For tensor operations, data may be spread across multiple
devices, and therefore a node which deﬁnes its operation on a
tensor will, in most cases, have the partitions of the tensor ex-
ecute in parallel.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
To reduce overall latency, the kernel must
ideally be submitted asynchronously to the device on which
the partition of the tensor data exists, so that it can begin ex-
ecution as soon as all dependencies are met.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
If a single node
were to deﬁne the operation on the tensor then the submission
of the kernel to the multiple devices would be sequential (since
if there is a single node running on a single thread, but multi-
ple kernels are required to be submitted for each partition, the
submissions must be serial).
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
To avoid this, when a kernel is
emplaced onto a graph which operates on a tensor, a node is
automatically created for each partition in the tensor, with each
node being on the same level.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This allows the kernel associated
with each node to be submitted to the device in parallel, using
any number of the available GPU cores in the system.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This is
more challenging to achieve when the tensor has padding, since
memory transfer nodes are required to copy the padding data
from another device, which may need to complete before the
node with the kernel is executed.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We provide utilities to allow
the user to achieve as much parallelism as possible by allowing
diﬀerent requirements for the padding data transfer to be speci-
ﬁed, described in detail in Section 5.4.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For adding nodes which
operate on tensors, the split() and then_split() methods
are provided, so named to indicate that the operation is split into
multiple nodes for each of the tensor partitions.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
On nodes emplaced for computations on tensor data,
split() has the same eﬀect as emplace() in that it will em-
place nodes onto the graph at the current level, with each of the
nodes having a dependency on the nodes in the previous level.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
If the tensor does not require any padding, split() creates a

The then_split() method allows dependencies
to be created between operations on previously emplaced nodes

text:
The method speciﬁes that the new operation on each parti-

title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

If the previous operation was a split()
or then_split() operation, then dependencies are only added
between nodes associated with the same partitions in the tensor.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This reduces the overall required connectivity of the resulting
graph by reducing the number of synchronization points.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

If a
then_split() operation is added after a non-tensor operation,
then each node generated depends on all operations in the previ-

The reduce() and then_reduce() operations
operate speciﬁcally on tensors, and reduce the data in the tensor
into a ReductionResult<T> type which stores the result of the
reduction as well as a ﬂag indicating whether the reduction is
complete.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The ﬂag is required because for tensors where data is
spread across multiple devices the reduction for each partition
of the tensor may happen asynchronously.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This design allows
each partition to perform the reduction of its data as soon as its
dependencies are met, so that the entire reduction across mul-
tiple devices ﬁnishes sooner than if the reduction was started
once all nodes in the previous level were complete.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
It also al-
lows subsequent nodes associated with the partition to continue
if they do not have any dependency on the result of the reduc-
tion.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Similarly to then_split(), for nodes in the previous
level that are associated with the same partitions on which the
reduction will be performed, there is only a dependency be-

on the dependencies of S0, if this graph were part of a larger graph.

For larger graphs, some paths may progress more quickly
than others, which may then need to be synchronized.

allow for all pending nodes to complete before any partition
continues, the sync() function, with the same signature as
emplace() and split(), can be used to emplace a node onto
the graph which synchronizes all work from both domains, and
then executes the callable for the sync() node.

text:
Subgraphs
To enable better separation of code, and overall ﬂexibility
in the graph creation API, we allow graphs to be added us-
ing the emplace() and then() operations, which adds the
graph passed to the operation as a subgraph in the current graph,
which will either execute in parallel with the nodes in the last
level (for emplace()) or after the nodes in the last level (for
then()).
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For complex graphs, this allows each of the sub-
graphs to be implemented separately, and then to be combined
in a ﬁnal step which deﬁnes the connectivity between the sub-
graphs.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
To ensure that the resulting graphs are correct, the nodes in
the last level of the graph onto which the subgraph is emplaced
need to be connected to the nodes in the ﬁrst level of the sub-
graph.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For nodes on non-tensor types the process is simple
since each node in the last level of the graph is connected to
each node in the ﬁrst level of the subgraph.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
However, as men-
tioned in Section 5.3.3, when the nodes in the levels operate on
the same tensor partition then the node in the subgraph should
only be connected to the node which corresponds to the same
partition in the tensor, as well as any other non-tensor nodes
in the previous level.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
If this is not the case, the operations on
the tensor partition will wait longer than necessary due to an
unnecessary dependency between the node and another tensor
node which operates on a diﬀerent partition.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Conditional execution
There is a trade-oﬀbetween static and dynamic speciﬁcation
of a graph; if a graph is speciﬁed statically then compile-time
optimizations can reduce its complexity so that the execution
is more eﬃcient, however, for most real-world applications,
graphs likely need some form of dynamic behaviour at runtime.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We provide dynamic behaviour through conditional operations
that can be emplaced onto a graph, which determine whether or
not the graph should be executed.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
A conditional node takes a
predicate which returns true if the graph should execute, and
false otherwise.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Along with the subgraph functionality de-
scribed in Section 5.3.5, this allows graphs of arbitrary com-
plexity to be created which have completely dynamic runtime
behaviour.

Tensor Data Dependencies
As described in Section 5.3, when nodes are added to the
graph for tensor operations it is important to reduce the con-
nectivity of the resulting graph.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This allows operations on in-
dependent partitions of the tensor to begin execution as soon
as possible, reducing synchronization during execution of the
graph.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The complexity of the graph, however, depends on the
how the kernel modiﬁes the partition data associated with a
node—whether the operation on the data requires concurrent or
exclusive access and whether the tensor has padding accessed
by the kernel.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The simplest case is a tensor operation requiring no padding,
since it cannot require data from neighbouring partitions.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This
does not cause any ordering dependency between the node and
any subsequent nodes which operate on the same data.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Thus,
when a tensor is passed to one of the methods for emplac-
ing nodes onto the graph we assume this is how the tensor is
accessed.

text:
For any other type of access, one of the methods
for specifying the access requirement when the operation uses
padding must be used, which ensures that the correct dependen-
cies are added to the graph to avoid race conditions.

text:
Scheduling
For scheduling, we use a modiﬁed form of the well-known
work stealing algorithm.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We provide an overview of the algo-
rithm, and our extensions of the algorithm to multiple domains
of execution—CPUs and GPUs.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Work Stealing
Work stealing is a common pattern for task-based parallelism
and has been used successfully in [15, 16, 10].
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
A group of
worker threads is spawned, each with its own queue of work
from which tasks can be executed.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
When a thread’s queue be-
comes empty, it steals work from the queues of other worker
threads [17, 18].
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Once a worker thread completes execution of
a task it looks to the successor of the completed task as the next
candidate for execution, which can be executed if all the depen-
dencies of the task are met [19].
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The pool of worker threads

text:
Most existing research on work stealing has focused on a sin-
gle domain, which has primarily been the CPU in the context
of large task-based systems which utilise hundreds to thousands
of CPU cores.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For heterogeneous domains, however, there is
little work on using work stealing to achieve good parallel eﬃ-
ciency across domains.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
In such a context, worker threads could
submit tasks for execution on either the CPU or the GPU, and
the scheduling algorithm needs to ensure that the dependencies
in the graph are met for the execution of both domains, while
still being eﬃcient.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The most recent work for heterogeneous
domains is that of [10].
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
However, their work focuses on the ex-
ecution of large graphs on the CPU.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
While it does allow nodes
to contain GPU work, it does not have knowledge of how data is
accessed by kernels, and therefore cannot allow for determining
data dependencies for GPU-based workﬂows, instead requiring
that the user write all GPU code within the graph nodes.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We
follow their heterogeneous scheduler approach, but modify it to
better support our higher-level GPU abstractions to allow good
performance for GPU-based workﬂows.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Design
We use the general work stealing idea, with a pool of worker
threads, however, we additionally give each worker thread a
domain priority for the type of work it primarily schedules—
as either CPU or GPU.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The worker threads in the algorithm are
adaptive, sleeping when there is not enough work for all threads
in the domain, and waking when the workload increases, which
is determined when nodes are scheduled for execution.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Each
worker thread stores state information to facilitate its suspen-
sion: the domain priority, the number of processed nodes, and
the queue of nodes.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The main loop for the worker threads in
our scheduler is shown in Algorithm 1.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
By default, we set the number of threads with GPU prior-
ity (GPUP) to be one more than the number of physical GPUs
in the system, and the number of threads with CPU priority
(CPUP) to be the number of remaining physical CPU cores
in the system.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
In all benchmarks, using both more or less
GPUP threads than this reduced performance due to either re-
quiring more CUDA context switching and stream synchroniza-
tion than necessary, when more threads were used, or too little
parallelism, when fewer were used.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

We must ensure that when multiple workers try to steal the
same task from the same queue, it is only possible for a single
worker to gain access to the task.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Thus the main data struc-
ture for the scheduler is a lock-free implementation of a work
stealing deque [20, 21], where the thread to which the queue be-
longs can push and pop from one end, while other threads can
steal from the other end.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
GPUP threads have queues for both
CPU (CDQ) and GPU (GDQ) work, and can push and pop onto
either of their own queues (prioritising GDQs) or steal from
the GDQ or CDQs (again prioritising the GDQs) of any other
threads.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
CPUP threads, however, have only a single work steal-
ing deque (CDQ) and can only push and pop from it, but can
steal from any other CDQ, regardless of the domain priority of
the thread to which the queue belongs.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This allows all CPU
cores to perform multi-threaded CPU work, but only a subset
to perform submission and synchronization of GPU work, al-
lowing an increase in the level of CPU parallelism when some
GPU kernels are signiﬁcantly longer executing than other CPU
kernels.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
In the work stealing deque for a worker thread, we encapsu-
late the work to be executed by the executor in a Node class—
which represents a node in a graph to be executed—and store
the nodes in the deque.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The node contains information about
its connectivity in the graph, via an atomic counter which
stores the number of dependents, and a pointer to its succes-
sor, whose dependents counter needs to be decremented when
the node completes its work, allowing the graph dependencies
to be maintained.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Within the execute_work function of Al-
gorithm 1, a worker pops a node oﬀone of its queues, tries to
execute it, and then either exits, upon success, or tries to steal
from another queue.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This is shown in Algorithm 2, while the
algorithm for attempting to execute a node’s work is shown in
Algorithm 3.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
When a node fails to execute due to unmet dependencies,
it is pushed back onto the queue of the worker which tried to
execute it, which is cheap due to there being no contention
with other threads for pushing and popping onto the one side
of the work stealing deque.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This allows other nodes to exe-
cute the node work if the dependencies are met while the node
is stealing from other threads.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
When a node attempts to steal
from other nodes, there are a number of strategies which can be
used, and any number of attempts can be made before giving up
and going back to a node’s own queues.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Three stealing strate-
gies are: the random strategy which randomly chooses a queue
from another thread, the round robin strategy which chooses a
queue by increasing index starting from one more than the steal-
ing thread’s index, wrapping around, the topological strategy
which chooses a queue based on the cache sharing properties
of the thread, trying to choose queues from threads which share
caches.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Currently, we employ both the random and round robin
strategies, however, we have seen that the performance of round
robin is far superior to random stealing, likely due to the lower
likelihood of two threads trying to steal from the same queue,
leading to less contention.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The stealing algorithm is shown in
Algorithm 4.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For a node whose work needs to be executed on the GPU, it is
important that the resulting graph is eﬃcient, i.e.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
not introduc-
ing points where the GPU is unnecessarily idle because of over
synchronization.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Thus, when calling the CUDA API we use the
asynchronous version of all memory related functions to en-
sure that threads are not blocked, and rely on atomic operations
in the work stealing deque and node execution function to en-
suring scheduling dependencies.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Lastly, we introduce stream
synchronization when a graph node requires that GPU work
completes before executing the node.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We use multiple streams
per GPU for copy and compute to allow memory transfer and
kernel execution to happen asynchronously where it is possi-
ble (for example concurrent_padded_access()), but place
operations onto the same compute stream when it is not, since
operations on the same stream are performed synchronously in
the order in which they are submitted.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This produces compact
GPU pipelines, resulting in low overall overhead and good scal-
ing performance, as illustrated in the results section.

Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

The Ripple NBC column is the
performance using Ripple without checking the boundary condition.

text:
Fine-grained Performance Evaluation
The performance tests in this section are all performed on
a single GPU to allow a comparison against implementations
of similar kernels using other frameworks or libraries designed
for ﬁne-grained parallelism, such as Kokkos [7].
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The hardware
conﬁgurations of the AWS compute nodes are shown in Table 1,
where we use the p3.2xlarge node for single GPU tests, and all
larger node types for the scaling tests in Section 8.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
When implementing the kernels in Kokkos we follow the ex-
amples presented in [7], as well as the examples in the Kokkos
repository.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The implementations of the kernel function objects
and structs for Kokkos and Ripple are very similar, with the
exception that for Ripple there is a template parameter for the
layout kind for any struct which is used in a benchmark.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
SAXPY
The ﬁrst benchmark is SAXPY which computes
y = a ∗x + y
Its minimal computational requirements make it a good exam-
ple for determining the overhead of the iterator functionality
provided by Ripple.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We compare the performance of Ripple
against both cuBLAS [1] and Kokkos, with the timings shown
in Table 2.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For 1 billion vector elements, Ripple takes 56% of
the time taken by Kokkos, and 99.2% of that taken by cuBLAS.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Proﬁling indicates that Ripple has a small amount of over-
head for the iterator abstractions, due to the checking of the
validity of the iterator.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The overhead is in the range of 3-4%,
but this is for a simple kernel which loads data into registers,
performs a single fused multiply-add (FMA), and loads the data
back to global memory.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This kernel uses a one dimensional iter-
ator, so the boundary check is only performed once.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For higher
dimensional data spaces the overhead would be higher, since
the validity of the iterator needs to be checked for each dimen-
sion.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For workloads which are more computationally intensive,
however, the overhead would be a smaller relative percentage.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

Additionally,
the position and velocity data require vector data types with
multiple components, which can either be stored contiguously
or strided.

For a three-dimensional update, the position and velocity re-

spectively.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We deﬁne a Particle class similar to the State
class shown in Listing 2, to hold the particle position and ve-
locity and use an update(dt) method to update the position
given ∆t.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This benchmark
is memory bound, since for both the position and the velocity,
each thread needs to read the six elements, perform an FMA
to update the position for each dimension, and then write the
results back to global memory.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For contiguous data, coalesced
access is not possible, so more than a single memory transac-
tion is required per element in each vector.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
However, when the
data is strided, only a single memory transaction is required per
element so the memory access is coalesced for each element,
which for this benchmark results in a 33% improvement over
the contiguously laid out implementation in Kokkos, and a 40%
improvement over the contiguous implementation in Ripple.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We also see that using shared memory is slower for this
benchmark, due to the increase in the instruction count of the
kernel.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For compute architectures prior to Ampere (such as the
Volta architecture used here), loading data into shared memory
goes through the register ﬁle, both increasing register usage,
which may reduce occupancy, as well as increasing the overall
instruction count of the kernel.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For a kernel with such a sim-
ple computation it is not necessary to use shared memory, since
accessing data from global memory already puts the data into a
register, so a load to and from shared memory reduces the per-
formance.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For the recent Ampere architecture, however, there
is new functionality for copying data from global memory to
shared memory asynchronously which bypasses the load into a
register.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This could improve performance of the shared memory
results presented here.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
There is also more ﬁne-grained control
of the synchronization for this type of asynchronous data load-
ing, which allows the compute cores to be utilised while waiting
for the load to complete.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We intend to investigate how to take
advantage of this for our iterator abstractions.

a special case of the nonlinear Hamilton–Jacobi partial diﬀeren-

For this benchmark we set f(x) = 1, which is the case for
reinitializing a signed-distance function.

The solution of the equation propagates information from
source nodes throughout the domain—for example, for levelset
reinitialization the source nodes would be the locations at which
the levelset value is zero.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Again, there are a number of meth-
ods which can be used to solve the Eikonal equation, such as
The Fast Marching Method [23], the Fast Sweeping Method
[24], [25] and the Fast Iterative Method [26] have been used for
parallel implementations.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

We choose to use the Fast Iterative
Method for this benchmark, and set a single source node at the
centre of the domain.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Varying the number of cells in the reini-
tialization band varies the computational expense of the prob-
lem, and we therefore perform the computation with diﬀerent
numbers of cells in the band around the source node, as well
as for diﬀerent levels of precision.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

With strided layout in shared memory, Ripple is 1.95
times faster than Kokkos for 5 cells in single precision, and 2.97
times faster for 10 cells in double precision.

Using shared memory gives up to 30% improvement in per-
formance compared to global when using strided data, while
compared to contiguous data the strided shared memory im-

fact that the computational component of the results contributes

previously.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

The combination of strided data layout and shared
memory gives a speedup of 2.2x and 2.88x when compared
to non-shared contiguous data for ﬂoat and double precision,
respectively.

When CUDA experience is limited, contiguous,
non-shared data would typically be used, and given that the
changes required by Ripple compared to such an implemen-

signiﬁcant.

Scaling Performance
Ideally, performance of Ripple would scale linearly with
an increase in computational resources, however, with multi-
ple GPUs additional data transfer is required which introduces
synchronization points, reducing the eﬀectiveness of the par-
allelism.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The benchmarks in this section are designed to de-
termine the eﬀectiveness of the framework to hide these costs.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
As a benchmark, we choose a solver for the 2D Euler equa-
tions since it requires many of the features of the framework
described previously and will form the basis of a future appli-
cation paper.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The speciﬁc problem we choose is a Mach 3.81 shock wave
impacting a low density air bubble.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This is a problem often
used to validate a solver in computational ﬂuid dynamics, so
provides a good example of how Ripple can be used to simplify
the implementation of a real-world problem.

Strong Scaling
Again we assign each GPU a partition of the domain and
split along the y dimension.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For this benchmark we keep the
problem size ﬁxed and use two problem sizes at resolutions of
6400 by 4000 cells (small), for a total of 25.6 million cells,
and 9600 by 6000 cells (large), for a total of 57.6 million cells.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Adding GPUs thus decreases the number of cells on which each
GPU performs computation.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For perfect scaling we would ex-
pect an increase in speedup which is linear in the number of
GPUs.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
However, since as the number of GPUs increases the
relative cost of the overhead for data transfer, synchronization,
and contention in the work stealing algorithm also increases,
linear scaling is not practically achievable.

The results are shown in Figure 13b, with the eﬃciency
shown in Figure 12.

GPUs at an eﬃciency of 87.5% for the small problem, and

We
see that for the small problem, the cost of the overhead is high
due to the small problem size, while for the larger problem the
overhead is minimal since each GPU still has enough work to
better hide communication costs.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
A signiﬁcant portion of this
reduction comes from the NUMA conﬁguration of the node.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

When the GPUs are connected via NVLINK, the padding data
transfers can be performed directly between the GPUs without
going through the CPU (which is the default for Ripple when

Limitations & Future Work
The main limitation of our library is the neighbouring region
for which data can be accessed.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
It is only possible to access
data which is on the same device as the data to which an iterator
points.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Therefore, if a domain is partitioned in two, one half of
the domain cannot access data from the other half.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
However,
this is true of any application which uses multiple devices, and
the data would have to be sorted so that any elements which
need to access each other are on the same device.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Future work
would add support for manipulation of the tensor data type to
provide support for these kinds of use cases.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Currently, while very close to providing a uniﬁed inter-
face for kernels which can be executed on both the CPU
and the GPU, Ripple has some limitations in this area.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
The
ﬁrst is in kernels which require synchronization of threads
on the GPU, through __syncthreads(), or our abstraction
ripple::syncthreads().
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
On the CPU, this would require
that a thread executes part of a function until the syncthreads
call, saves the state for the thread, does the same for all other
threads, and then resumes back at the ﬁrst thread after restoring
the state.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
This is challenging in C++; however, with the recent
introduction of coroutines, it is possible to suspend a function
which can later be resumed, and one area of future work is to
provide this support so that there is a uniﬁed interface for both
the CPU and the GPU.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

As mentioned in Section 7.2, NVIDIA’s latest Ampere archi-

and shared memory, with a more ﬁne-grained synchronization
model.

We intend to use this to improve the performance of our
library for shared memory, speciﬁcally to reduce the overhead
of checking the validity of the iterators.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Improving the functionality of the allocators and the ability
to create hierarchical tensor structures is another area of fu-
ture work.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Many applications have regions of interest within
a domain which are distributed sparsely within the global com-
putational domain, requiring adaptive, hierarchical data struc-
tures.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For optimal performance on the GPU, we have shown
that memory access patterns play a large role, and thus it would
be ideal to allow the same access patterns but have adaptive
resolution.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Our tensor data structure and iterator abstractions
could be extended to provide such functionality for other data
types such as k-d trees, octrees, adaptive meshes, and bounding
volume hierarchies, for example.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Lastly, our library is designed for single nodes with multi-
ple GPUs and CPUs.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
While modern compute nodes allow for
many GPUs and hundreds of CPU cores with hundreds of GB of
RAM for both the CPU and GPU, some problems require still
larger computational resources, and thus we could extend our
library to allow for computation across any number of nodes.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Conclusion
We have presented the abstractions and details of our library,
Ripple.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Our main contributions are the ability for user-deﬁned
types to have polymorphic layouts to achieve the best possible
performance on GPU accelerators, a multi-dimensional tensor
data type and iterator classes over the multi-dimensional space,
a graph interface for specifying the structure of a computation,
and an eﬃcient scheduler for execution of the computational
graph.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Lastly, our interface allows computations to scale across
all accelerators on a node, allowing high-performance computa-
tions over very large domains to be implemented with minimal
programmer eﬀort.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We have used micro benchmarks to illustrate the eﬀective-
ness of data layout polymorphism as well as the importance
of utilising diﬀerent physical memory spaces available in GPU
accelerators.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We also show how all these options are problem
dependent, and that our library exposes these through simple
interfaces which allow for rapid testing of the diﬀerent possible
conﬁgurations.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Results have been presented for strong and weak scaling
cases to illustrate the eﬀectiveness of our library on real world
problems, as well as to evaluate the overhead of the abstractions
provided by the library and its performance to existing frame-
works.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
For weak scaling we achieve around 95% for 8 GPUs,
while for strong scaling we achieve performance scaling of be-
tween 6.9 and 7.3x for 8 GPUs, for a common problem from
computational ﬂuid dynamics.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
Ripple is under constant development and we plan to fur-
ther investigate additional data structures, scheduling algo-
rithms, and allowing our tensor data type to increase resolu-
tion in sub-regions, dynamically, for applications where com-
putation is concentrated in certain regions.
title: Ripple : Simplified Large-Scale Computation on Heterogeneous Architectures with Polymorphic Data Layout

text:
We also intend to
extend the CPU interface to allow CUDA constructs such as
__syncthreads() to work in both computational spaces, and
lastly to scale to multiple nodes to allow even larger problems
with minimal knowledge of parallel and distributed systems.

ABSTRACT
Maintaining computational load balance is important to the perfor-
mant behavior of codes which operate under a distributed comput-
ing model.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
This is especially true for GPU architectures, which can
suffer from memory oversubscription if improperly load balanced.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
We present enhancements to traditional load balancing approaches
and explicitly target GPU architectures, exploring the resulting
performance.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
A key component of our enhancements is the intro-
duction of several GPU-amenable strategies for assessing compute
work.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
These strategies are implemented and benchmarked to find
the most optimal data collection methodology for in-situ assess-
ment of GPU compute work.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
For the fully kinetic particle-in-cell
code WarpX, which supports MPI+CUDA parallelism, we investi-
gate the performance of the improved dynamic load balancing via a
strong scaling-based performance model and show that, for a laser-
ion acceleration test problem run with up to 6144 GPUs on Summit,
the enhanced dynamic load balancing achieves from 62%–74% (88%
when running on 6 GPUs) of the theoretically predicted maximum
speedup; for the 96-GPU case, we find that dynamic load balancing
improves performance relative to baselines without load balancing
(3.8× speedup) and with static load balancing (1.2× speedup).
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Our
results provide important insights into dynamic load balancing
and performance assessment, and are particularly relevant in the
context of distributed memory applications ran on GPUs.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

INTRODUCTION
GPU-accelerated machines entered the TOP500 rankings just over
a decade ago [18].
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
GPUs offer an effective path to high computa-
tional throughput, and GPU accelerated machines are particularly
of interest, as they are central to the US Exascale, and EuroHPC
Pre-Exascale initiatives.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
HPC software must be adapted to take full
advantage of heterogeneous systems as parallelism continues to in-
crease and we approach an era of exascale computing in leadership-
class supercomputers.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Maintaining equal distribution of compu-
tational load (dynamic load balancing) is crucial for distributed
memory applications to make efficient use of hardware with con-
tinually increasing parallel-compute capabilities [10, 13, 19].
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
In this paper, we present and investigate GPU-targeted enhance-
ments for in-situ dynamic load balancing.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
These techniques are
demonstrated in the particle-in-cell (PIC) framework WarpX [21],
which, as a particle-mesh simulation code, models fields via an
Eulerian description and particles via a discretization in Lagrangian
markers.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
In WarpX, multi-node parallelism is achieved through
spatial domain decomposition, which is supported through the
block-structured framework AMReX [24].
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
WarpX’s particles are
used to model kinetic phenomena and often cause localized spikes
in memory consumption and compute demand.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
It is thus likely,
that herein studied scenarios exemplifying realistic geometries of
contemporary research, using highly mobile particles are applicable
to other distributed memory codes.

text:
In particular, WarpX models
plasma physics problems, including laser-plasma acceleration and
particle acceleration in astrophysical contexts [21].

load balancing algorithms used with these measurements.

challenges of load balancing in a GPU-based code and the GPU-

2.1
Overview of the Domain Decomposition in
Particle-Mesh Codes
A common motif in parallel particle-mesh codes is to partition the
simulation domain into separate sub-domains, typically contiguous
spatial sub-domains.

compute elements at runtime to achieve an even distribution of
compute work across computational resources.

A load-balancing
algorithm is implemented to achieve this even distribution.

Our study is designed as a general improvement in AMReX,

AMReX terminology, as it is consistent with our study and the nam-

In AMReX, a ‘sub-domain’ is
a rectilinear region of cells, defined by a box.

A distribution mapping
describes the current MPI process ownership of field and particle

This consists of a box-sized vector containing
the MPI rank (equivalently, GPU ID) to which each box is assigned.

Our load-balancing strategy is tested in WarpX, a particle-mesh
application, implemented on top of AMReX.

Cells are updated
in self-consistent, explicit time steps solving Maxwell’s equations.

Throughout all cells, representative particle markers (weighted par-
ticles) move according to the Lorentz-force and in turn modify fields
through deposited, charged currents [3].

When ran on systems with
accelerators, locally assigned boxes of particles and structured field
(cell) data are stored persistently in device memory.

Implementing
advanced, numerical schemes for those operations, single-source
kernels consistently accelerate the whole application.

and cell data in accordance with the new distribution mapping
(this is further discussed in the next section, Sec.

2.2
Load Balancing Strategy
A basic outline for dynamic load balancing in a distributed memory
particle-mesh code (representative of what we use in the present
work) is sketched in Lis.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
2.1; this resides within the main time-
stepping loop in WarpX.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
The frequency of the load balancing calculation is controlled by
a user-selected load balance interval (line 1).
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Computational costs
corresponding to each box are gathered from all GPUs to the root
process, so that the root process has a global view of the current
GPU ownership and cost for each box over the full simulation
domain.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
With this information, the root process computes a load
balanced distribution mapping and the corresponding load balance
efficiency 𝐸for the old and new mappings (lines 9–11).
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code
In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
The cost per GPU is taken as the sum of costs
over all boxes managed by it; an efficiency of 1 indicates a perfectly
balanced distribution.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
By default, the new distribution mapping will
not be broadcast to all GPUs (line 17), but if the proposed efficiency
exceeds the current efficiency by a user-selected amount (lines 18–
21), the new distribution is communicated to all GPUs and updated
(lines 23–31).
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Update of the distribution mapping includes shuffling
ownership of boxes as well as redistributing particles to GPUs (line
30), and when ran is the most expensive step of the load balancing
routine (this is the case for simulations we present in Sec.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
3.3; re-
distribution of box and particle data typically constitutes ≳99.7%
of the time required to load balance).
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Therefore, only redistribut-
ing in cases that will yield a substantial improvement is critical to
achieving an optimal load balancing implementation.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
We control
this with a hyperparameter for the required improvement to the
load balance efficiency 𝐸, i.e.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
a value that must be met or exceeded
in order for the proposed distribution mapping to be communicated
and updated (the performance impact of this hyperparameter is
discussed in Sec.

In distributing costs equally over all GPUs (i.e., computing a new
distribution mapping; Lis.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
2.1, lines 9–11), a variety of strategies
have been developed [2, 10, 13, 19].
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Two of the most common
algorithms are knapsack, which assigns sub-domains to GPUs such
that the corresponding computational costs are spread as equally
as possible over all GPUs, and space-filling curve, in which sub-
domains are enumerated with a Morton Z-order space-filling curve
and the resultant ordering is partitioned so that costs are distributed
as equally as possible among GPUs.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
For our simulations of laser-ion
acceleration, the performance impact of these algorithms when
running on GPUs is discussed in Sec.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Measuring computational cost offers a unique challenge with
GPUs, as GPUs leverage asynchronous compute [12].
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
For this rea-
son, timing sections of code with CPU timers will not yield a useful
load balancing metric [8].
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
To address this challenge, we imple-
mented three different GPU-amenable cost measurement strategies
to estimate the compute work associated with a box, (Heuristic,
GPU clock, and CUPTI), which we summarize below:
• Heuristic: Compute work is estimated as a weighted linear
sum of the number of particles and cells per box.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Note that
the optimal choice of weights may vary depending on hard-
ware, choice of field solver, and the interpolation order of
particle shapes.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
• GPU clock: The device clock() function is used to measure
thread execution time, which is accumulated using GPU
atomic add operations; the procedure is shown schematically
in Fig.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
To mitigate latency, thread times are accumulated
in shared memory before their sum is transferred to global
memory.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
With this GPU clock-based timer, we measure the
thread-summed execution time of a compute-intensive ker-
nel, which serves as a proxy for the compute work associated
with a box.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
For the laser-ion acceleration problem discussed
in Sec.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
3, current deposition typically accounts for 50% of
the total walltime, with the remaining walltime dominated
by communication routines, thus we take the time spent in
current deposition as representative of the compute work
that should be considered during load balance.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
• CUPTI: With the CUDA Profiling Tools Interface (CUPTI)
API [6], we constructed a timer capable of accessing kernel
execution times on-the-fly; the CUPTI-based timing strategy
is summarized in Fig.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
CUPTI enables collection
of kernel activity records— data structures that contain ker-
nel information including the absolute start and end times
of the kernel.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Registered callback functions, which handle
the request and delivery of buffers used to store activity
records, are activated by GPU activity; when the buffer re-
turn is complete, the activity records stored therein can be
used to compute kernel duration.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
With this CUPTI-based
kernel timer, we measure the duration of the current deposi-
tion kernel and use it as a proxy for the computational cost
associated with a box.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
The heuristic method has been used frequently in particle-mesh
codes which run on CPU [4, 7, 9, 13, 15, 17, 23], and transfers readily
to particle-mesh codes on GPU [5, 10, 19], given the user has tuned
appropriately the particle and cell weights.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
However, as mentioned
above, the optimal choice of weights can vary depending on algo-
rithmic choices and hardware, which limits the general applicability
of heuristic cost measurement.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
The need for careful tuning by the
user can be eliminated with an on-the-fly measurement technique
such as GPU clock or CUPTI mentioned above; to the authors’
knowledge, the present work represents the first implementation
and application of such techniques for dynamic load balancing in a
particle-mesh code running at scale on GPUs.

3.2
Load Balance: Time Evolution
As the ultrahigh-intensity laser pulse interacts with the dense par-
ticle target, electrons respond quickly relative to the more massive
hydrogen ions, and penetrate through the solid target.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
The different
response times of electrons and hydrogen ions to the incident laser
pulse generates strong electric fields, which can in turn accelerate
ions to high energies.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Throughout this process, a strong kick of the
target front by the incident laser results in substantial changes to
the spatial density profile as particles are transported through the
target; the time evolution for the range 3–147 fs of the spatial profile
of particles per cell is shown in Fig.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
The macro-
particle number is intentionally kept constant in the lower-density,
exponential plasma slope around the target, visible in later steps as
a ‘ring,’ for adequate modeling of laser-absorption.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Relative to the
initial number of particles per cell in the target (2 × 𝑛ppc0 = 1800

balance is maintained, without incurring a significant penalty to
walltime.

for load balance intervals ≳30 steps (this is due to the lower load
balance efficiency on average over the duration of the simulation).

SCALING OF LOAD BALANCING
In this section, we present a performance model, calibrated with
strong scaling measurements of our code, and use it to assess the
performance of our improvements to WarpX’s load balancing in
the laser-ion acceleration problem described in Sec.

For a given code, how much of a performance improvement
may be anticipated with load balancing?

text:
To answer this question,
we consider the load balancing operation in the context of strong
scaling, i.e.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text: increasing compute resources for a problem of fixed size.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
With measurements of strong scaling for a given code, one may
model the performance response as a function of available compute
resources; ideally, performance improves linearly with increasing
compute resources, and with a constant of proportionality equal to
unity.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
However, in realistic codes, factors such as communications
and overhead may modify the relationship and lead to less than
ideal scaling.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
A strong scaling model can capture these nonideal
effects and be used to predict the performance improvement that
would result from a given increase in compute resources.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
To apply strong scaling in understanding the performance im-
provement that is possible through load balancing, we consider a
simulation with a computational load that is initially imbalanced
(i.e., there is at least one compute element assigned a greater compu-
tational load than another); we call this initial maximum compute
work (over all compute elements)𝑐max0.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
The performance (e.g., wall-
time) of this hypothetical simulation is limited by the initial load
imbalance 𝑐max0, and may be improved by distributing compute
work evenly over available resources.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
After perfect load balanc-
ing, the compute work is equally distributed over all 𝑁compute
elements, 𝑐0 = 𝑐1 = · · · = 𝑐𝑁= 𝑐avg0, which becomes the new
performance limiter (we define 𝑐avg0 as the average at initialization
of 𝑐0,𝑐1, · · · ,𝑐𝑁).
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
Load balancing is similar to strong scaling: more
compute resources are assigned to the work 𝑐max0, and the work-
load of the compute element initially assigned that work decreases
from 𝑐max0 to 𝑐avg0; with strong scaling, increasing the compute
resources while holding the problem size fixed effectively decreases
the compute work assigned to each compute element.

RELATED WORK
State-of-the-art particle-in-cell codes [4, 5, 7, 9, 13, 17] typically
support either static load balancing or dynamic load balancing
targeting CPUs.

To the knowledge of the authors, those particle-
mesh codes that do support dynamic load balancing on GPUs rely
on cost functions based on node-local application data as a surrogate
for computing run time [10, 19].
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
The heuristic approach, however,
is not necessarily an accurate reflection of true computing run
time [22].
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

text:
To gain the full performance benefit of dynamic load
balancing, without excessive tuning of hyperparameters by the
user, computational costs can be measured accurately at runtime.
title: In-Situ Assessment of Device-Side Compute Work for Dynamic Load Balancing in a GPU-Accelerated PIC Code

An adoption of dynamic load balancing strategies for accelerator
hardware in exascale-workflows is therefore needed, including
a reduction of user-facing hyperparameters, which are hard and
expensive to tune in realistic scenarios.

[8] demonstrated instrumentation of CUDA ker-
nels as a way to measure kernel run times for post-run analysis.

One
of the herein presented implementations for cost assessment which
is free of user-facing hyperparameters, GPU clock, employs a similar
approach, yet provides measurement of costs in-situ as the applica-
tion is running, thus enabling on-the-fly load balancing based on
measured computational costs (see Sec.

Furthermore, the run-
time overhead introduced with this technique is small enough that
it does not negate the performance benefit of automatic runtime
load balancing [20].

The GPU clock strategy for cost measurement
is potentially portable, given the accelerator framework supports a
