2.1.1
CER Topics in Literature.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We start with an overview of how authors categorized topics in
CER publications.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The seminal book by Fincher and Petre [16] (2004) identiﬁed 10 core areas for CER and provided
an initial deﬁnition of the practices and methods of the ﬁeld [16].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Their work laid the foundation
for CER in the next 15 years.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[52] (2005) created a taxonomy of four key areas in CER
that builds on and groups Fincher’s and Petre’s [16] initial categorization.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021
arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[52] created a core CER literature
including inﬂuential, seminal, and synthesis work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[32] (2009) created a taxonomy to categorize the types of CER publications in 21 jour-
nals and 21 conference proceedings from either 2004 or 2005.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Their ﬁndings demonstrate that
conference venues tend to have a technical focus to their proceedings while journals have a peda-
gogical focus.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Some survey papers identiﬁed gaps in the topics covered by CER literature.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[33]
(2010) reviewed 67 ICER papers between 2005 and 2009.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Their categorization considered eight
categories based on a three-layered didactic structure including students, teachers, and goals/con-
text at a classroom, organization, and societal level.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Expanding their corpus of reviewed papers
by 13 and considering venues beyond ICER (e.g., ACE, SIGCSE TS, PPIG, ITiCSE, ITiCSE WGR,
CSE, Comput.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Small Coll.), they found papers reported results at the course-level and focused on
student characteristics and process.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Eight papers included additional focus areas of students’ con-
ceptions on and actions to achieve course goals and content.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The literature at that time did not
provide adequate coverage of categories around content/goals and teachers.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Simon and others (2007-2020) have conducted extensive classiﬁcation studies of computing ed-
ucation literature for ACE [64, 65], ICER [66], ITiCSE [67], Koli [63], and NACCQ [68].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The classi-
ﬁcation scheme considers the context (e.g., subject matter or course); theme (e.g., what the paper
is about like teaching technique); scope (e.g., extent of collaboration and work); and nature (e.g.,
distinction between research and practice) [62].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
A recent classiﬁcation of ITiCSE papers in 2020
found an increase in reported research over experience reports and that teaching and learning
techniques remain a common theme in published work [67].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[51] (2020) categorized papers from 15 years of ITiCSE, ITiCSE Working
Group Reports (WGR), and ICER using keywords and abstracts.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The main themes identiﬁed are
around introductory programming, assessments, and student performance.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The categorization of topics covered in the literature provides guidance to researchers and prac-
titioners about areas that are well studied and ripe for meta-review and gaps where additional
work is needed for a better understanding of computing education.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Empiricism in CER
7
a common categorization in many of the above surveys, however, they each have their own nu-
ance [16, 32, 33, 51, 62].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
While our work did not identify the context of the reviewed study (e.g.,
CS1, databases, etc.), we do consider the subject of the evaluation (e.g., curriculum or tool) which
has overlap with categorizations from related work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Several studies have classiﬁed CER literature by study type,
which could include high-level categories of quantitative and qualitative or more granular cate-
gories like experiments, quasi-experimental studies, and experience reports.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In one of the oldest CER surveys, Valentine [72] (2004) examined 444 CS1/CS2 papers from
SIGCSE TS between 1984 and 2003 and found that only 21% included experimental evaluation or
were experience reports.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Other categories considered were Marco Polo (“I went there and I saw
this”), Philosophy, Tools, and John Henry (“outrageously diﬃcult”) papers.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
There was an increase
in the number of experimental papers presented in the last 10 years of the study period.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[56] (2008) found that of 352 papers published in various CER venues between
2000 and 2005, 40% contained only anecdotal evidence and of the less than one-third of papers that
did have experimental or quasi-experimental designs, 54.8% of those papers used a weaker post-
test only design.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[56] categorized their sampled papers against Valentine [72]’s
categorization and found that 40.9% of sampled papers were experimental or experience reports.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[56] used their own categorization of research methodologies and found
that of the papers that reported human subject research (n = 144), 64.6% were experimental or quasi-
experimental, 26.4% were qualitative, 18.1% were causal comparative, 10.4% were co-relational, and
7.6% were survey research.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[40] (2010) identiﬁed two dimensions that described the type of research: purpose
and framework.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They found that 86% of papers had an evaluative purpose and that 79% of pa-
pers reported a research framework.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The most common research frameworks were survey (39%),
experimental (15%), constructive (14%), and grounded theory (13%).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[29] (2015) conducted a survey on educational data mining research published
at various venues between 2005 and 2015.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Of the 76 papers that met their inclusion criteria, 78%
described studies in a natural setting.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Only 14% reported on formal experimental research.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[5] (2016) found that 162 (70%) of the papers reviewed had some form of em-
pirical evaluation.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Their deﬁnition for empirical studies was broader than the deﬁnitions used
by Valentine [72] and Randolph et al.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, the detailed evaluation type numbers show
that 28% of the papers were experimental, suggesting some increase over earlier surveys.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[36] (2016) found that 71% of CSE and 87% of ICER papers between 2012 and
2015 reported empirical results and that 26% from CSE and 19% from ICER were experimental as
deﬁned by Randolph et al.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The percentages of experimental work were much lower when
considering the more speciﬁc deﬁnition of single group post-test only [36].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Early surveys of CER literature [56, 72] reported low rates of empirical work in the surveyed
papers.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
More recent surveys (e.g., the last 10 years) of CER literature have shown an increase of
empirical work published at a variety of CER venues.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
While two of the surveys reviewed litera-
ture from the CER-focused venues of ICER and CSE [36, 40], others surveys did consider other
venues [5, 29] suggesting the increase in empiricism is happening more broadly in the comput-
ing community.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, with diﬀerences in the deﬁnitions of empirical work between surveys,
direct comparisons cannot be made.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Many CER surveys discussed the use and creation of theory.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[40] (2010) found that 60% of the surveyed papers reported explicit use of theories,
models, frameworks, and instruments (TMFI) in their studies.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Additionally, they found a great
diversity of TMFI used during that time frame – 68 distinct resources out of 78 instances.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
8
Heckman, Carver, Sherriﬀ, and Al-Zubidy
Tenenberg’s [71] (2014) position paper argues for the importance of recognizing the theories and
theoretical frameworks that underlie CER research.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
His argument is that authors should recognize
the theoretical frameworks utilized when creating research questions because frameworks may
introduce limitations on the types of questions asked and the methods used to answer research
questions.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Including the theoretical stance of the authors is an important aspect of reported works
and serves as a foundation for future CER.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[39] (2014) conducted a deeper review of CER literature that considered additional
years and venues to identify the use of theories, models, and frameworks in the literature.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They
found that 51% of papers described at least one of 216 distinct theories, models, or frameworks.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The interdisciplinary nature of CER beneﬁts from the use of prior theoretical work, especially from
outside ﬁelds.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, the disparate usage of theory, models, and frameworks is a challenge for
creating a “stable theoretical base” for CER.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[36] (2016) reviewed CSE and ICER literature between 2012 and 2015 to identify
the use of outside educational and learning theory and the methodological quality of the research
using indicators that build on prior work (e.g., [39, 56]).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They identiﬁed an increase in the use of
theory to support research and in the reporting of empirical CER work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However they found many
studies utilized less rigorous methods.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Nelson and Ko [48] (2018) summarize the use of theory in CER and identify three areas of con-
cern in the community including tensions between explanation goals and design goals, lack of
work on domain-speciﬁc theories, and publication bias due to theoretical lens of the work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They
also provide concrete suggestions to move the community forward by focusing on design and us-
ing theory as a guide, investing in the creation of CER-speciﬁc theories, and reducing reviewer
bias in regards to manuscripts with novel designs where theory may not be appropriate.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[38] (2020) reviewed 50 papers with theoretical constructs around the topics of emo-
tions, attitudes, beliefs, and self-eﬃcacy of computing learners from a variety of venues between
2010 and 2019.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They found that three-quarters of the papers were published between 2014 and
2019 suggesting a maturation of the CER ﬁeld in using theory and validated instruments.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
More
recent papers on theoretical constructs relied on quantitative methods rather than qualitative.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
There are theoretical underpinnings to CER literature and authors utilize work from outside of
computing to support their research questions.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
More recent years have shown an increase in the
use of theory to support the increased empirical work in CER.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, the development of CER
theories is an open area of future work as the ﬁeld matures.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
While we do not consider theory in
our review of CER literature, there are enough surveys on the topic to include a discussion here
for completeness.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Other reviews examined the published literature to identify the type
of research methods and analysis techniques used in CER studies.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[56] (2008) found that of the 144 studies that utilized human participants, 107
(74.3%) used quantitative methods.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Only 15.3% of the studies used qualitative methods and 10.4% of
studies used mixed methods.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The authors found that 44 of the 352 papers reviewed used some form
of inferential statistics.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Additionally, 120 of the 123 of the behavioral, quantitative, and empirical
studies reported eﬀect size.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[61] (2009) conducted a review of papers on the teaching and learning of program-
ming, published in various CER venues between 2005 and 2008, which they classiﬁed as empirical.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Of the 164 papers reviewed, 37% reported quantitative results, 21% reported qualitative results, and
45% utilized mixed methods.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[40] studied ICER papers published between 2005 and 2009 found a variety of analy-
sis methods used.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
These methods included statistical analysis (42%), exploratory statistical analysis
ACM Trans.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Empiricism in CER
9
(17%), descriptive statistics (11%), interpretive qualitative analysis (35%), and interpretative classi-
ﬁcation or content analysis (26%).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[5] (2016) reported that 54% the papers with empirical results in SIGCSE TS
2014 and 2015 proceedings utilized surveys and 37% utilized experimental methods, which were
typically quantitative.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Very few papers utilized qualitative methods like observations.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[41] (2019) found 32% of papers published in TOCE, CSE, and ICER between 2013 and 2017
collected both qualitative and quantitative data and over half used multiple measures.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[58] reviewed the use of inferential statistics in ICER papers published between
2005 and 2018.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: They found that 51% of papers used inferential statistics.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, they noted that
the reporting associated with inferential statistics tended to lack precise test names, conﬁdence
levels, and p-values for results.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Other noted concerns with statistical test reporting included a lack
of detail about data preparation, missing discussion about the assumptions for statistical tests,
lack of explanation for “obscure” tests, lack of corrections for multiple statistical tests, and lack of
statistical signiﬁcance and eﬀect size discussions.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The literature suggests that published CER work tends to use quantitative methods, but there
is movement towards using multiple measures and appropriate statistical tests when answering
research questions.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Several reviews categorized how CER literature reports on the par-
ticipants of the research study and the context of the intervention(s).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[29] (2015) reported that 34% of the educational data mining studies in their survey
did not report any details about course context, which could include the course level, programming
language, and topics.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Additionally, 17% of the studies did not report the number of students in the
study, details about student level, or demographics.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[5] (2016) found that 11% of papers did not report the number of participants
in their study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Additionally, when trying to identify the number of participants from the papers,
there were discrepancies between reviewers due to inconsistent reporting.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[45] (2018) reviewed 92 papers from SIGCSE TS, ICER, and TOCE between 2012
and 2016 related to pre-college computing activities and how well papers reported key information
to support future replication.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
One area studied was the activity component data or information
about the activities and context of the intervention.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They found that papers infrequently reported
learning outcomes (25%), curriculum (33%), number of students in the activity (41.7%), and details
about the duration of the activity within the larger context (78.6%), but many did not list the
number of contact hours, which is important in K-12 work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They additionally found the reporting
of both instructor and student demographic data lacking.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The authors provided a checklist of
recommendations to support better, and more consistent, reporting of subject and context data to
support replication.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[37] (2018) found that a “large proportion” of publications related to intro-
ductory programming did not provide suﬃcient contextual details about the reported study, which
increases the diﬃculty for readers to determine transferability of the results.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They recommend that
authors report details about the population of students and teaching context.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[41] (2019) identiﬁed several empirical reporting best practices that are lacking
in CER, particularly related to the context of the study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
While 85% of papers reviewed reported the
number of participants only 49% reported additional participant characteristics (e.g., prior knowl-
edge and basic demographics).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Other contextual information that would be beneﬁcial to include
are details about the task and learning environment.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Literature surveys that considered the context and participants in reviewed research found gaps
or inconsistencies in reporting related to these items.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Several reviewed papers excluded contextual
ACM Trans.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
10
Heckman, Carver, Sherriﬀ, and Al-Zubidy
information about the classroom or environment of the study [29, 37, 41, 45].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Several studies found
that between 10-20% of papers did not report the number of participants [5, 29, 41].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Several studies reported on the source of the data collected, including the use
of validated and non-validated instruments.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[56] (2008) reported on the independent, dependent, and mediating/moderating
variables in 123 behavioral, quantitative, and empirical articles in their sample of CER literature.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: The most common independent variable was student instruction (98.9%).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The most common de-
pendent variables were attitudes (60.2%) and achievement in computer science (56.1%).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Only 29% of
papers used mediating or moderating variables, including gender, grade level, and learning styles.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The identiﬁcation of measures showed that questionnaires were the most commonly used (52.5%)
followed by grades (29.3%), teacher- or researcher-made tests (22.0%), and student work (17.9%).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[61] (2009) found that empirical papers from a variety of CER venues utilized formal
course assessments (42%), tasks students complete (38%), and questionnaires (33%) as the top three
data gathering techniques.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The authors note that the use of “established measurement instruments”
was low in reviewed studies and that publications lacked details about how the instruments were
used.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[40] (2010) classiﬁed the data sources from ICER papers as (1) naturally occurring,
(2) research speciﬁc data, (3) reﬂection, or (4) software.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The results showed 79% of those papers
used research speciﬁc data, i.e.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
data collected speciﬁcally for the needs of the research through
interviews, questionnaires, observational data, assignments, or tasks.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[5] (2016) found that most SIGCSE TS papers that used empirical evaluation
reported on pedagogical techniques followed by courses and curriculum.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Additionally, they found
that over 75% of authors reported on new subjects speciﬁc to the paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
There was little replication
or even reuse of data, even from the authors’ previous studies.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[29] (2016) found in their survey of educational data mining literature that 81% of
studies reported work from a single institution, 80% of studies did not consider longitudinal data,
and 66% of studies only considered a single course.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Additionally, they considered methods and
analysis from several perspectives including details about the tasks students performed as part
of the study, the type of data collected (e.g., logging, key-stroke), and the analysis methods.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They
found several gaps in reporting for each of these.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Decker and McGill [15] (2019) consider evaluation instruments as a key data source in CER liter-
ature.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They found 47 evaluation instruments that measured cognitive, non-cognitive, and program
evaluation constructs that are useful for CER researchers and would complement other quantita-
tive and qualitative measures.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They categorized the instruments based on number of items, type
of items, target demographic, reliability, and validity as reported in the literature.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The sources of data for CER work covers a variety of measures from student grades, attitudinal
surveys, key-logging, and other automated data collection.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
A variety of evaluation instruments are
available to measure various constructs [15].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Several of the literature surveys found that data was
created speciﬁcally for the research study [5, 40] and focused on a single class or institution [29].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Many surveys noted that reviewed literature lacked details in reporting on the data collected and
that reuse of data was low [5, 29].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Several recent papers consider the impact of reporting quality
on the possibility for comparisons between and replications of CER work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[29] (2015) identiﬁed 5 studies (7% of their selected papers) as replication studies
in the domain of educational data mining.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[5] (2016) found that 46% of papers
ACM Trans.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Empiricism in CER
11
reviewed had no comparison point as part of the study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The remaining papers either had a com-
parison to historical data or a comparison to a data set created speciﬁcally for the study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Addition-
ally, fewer than six papers each year of the review (2014 and 2015) reported replications of prior
work [5].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[4] (2016) surveyed 73 CER researchers about their perspectives on the value of
replication work in the community.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They found challenges related to the language used to describe
replication/reproducibility, bias and incentives towards original work, and a lack of community
value on replication work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
An example of a language challenge is related to the deﬁnitions we
use for replication.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
A survey quote suggests that replications are challenging due to the highly-
contextualized nature of the research environment.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The authors further suggest that terminology
is used inconsistently in the ﬁeld [4].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, a replication in a new environment is a conceptual
replication and can help generalize the work [19, 59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
McGill [42] (2019) summarizes current work on replication, reproducibility, and meta-analysis
in CER and provides a call to action on how to improve the ﬁeld.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The ﬁrst suggestion is to improve
individual studies because replication, reproducibility, and meta-analysis rely on high quality re-
porting.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Other suggested actions are to pre-register studies, support open science, invest in large-
scale collaborative research, report power analysis and eﬀect size, create systems to store data and
research tools, and incentivize replication through community support.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[41] (2019) found that while CER literature has adopted measurement instru-
ments outside of computing and has created computing-speciﬁc instruments, most papers do not
use standardized instruments to measure variables of interest.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Use of standardized and validated
instruments increases the reliability and validity of study results and will support meta-analysis
by providing a common measure to compare across studies.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[24] (2019) completed a systematic literature review on replications in the CER com-
munity (including SIGCSE TS, ICER, ITiCSE, TOCE, CSEJ) between 2009 and 2018.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Of the 2,269
articles, only 54 (2.38%) were considered a replication (as deﬁned by Schmidt [59]).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Of the 54 repli-
cations, 63% were successful replications.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: The others reported failures or mixed results.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Three-
quarters of the replications were conceptual (e.g., methods varied from the original study), while
the remaining replications were direct (e.g., methods were as similar as possible to the original
study).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
CER literature does contain replications and comparisons, but replication studies are a small
percentage of published CER work [24].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The CER community views direct replications as chal-
lenging, with most replication studies being conceptual replications [4, 19, 24, 59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Comparisons
and replications can be supported with the use of validated instruments [15, 41] and other open
science practices can support replications [42].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Many literature reviews included a discussion about gaps in reporting of
the literature surveyed.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
These gaps are places where the literature review was more challenging
because papers were missing key pieces of information.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[56] (2008) reviewed 352 papers randomly selected from all papers published
in several computing education venues between 2000 and 2005.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
As part of their methodological
review, they identiﬁed whether papers contained elements considered important by the American
Psychological Association [7], which include items like an abstract, research questions, and a de-
scription of participants.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They found that less than 50% of the sampled papers reported purpose/ra-
tionale (36.6%), research questions/hypotheses (22.0%), participants description (45.5%), procedures
(37.4%), and separate results and discussion (29.3%).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[61] (2009) report on a lack of connection between ﬁndings related to the process
of learning programming and relevant theories and models of learning.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
12
Heckman, Carver, Sherriﬀ, and Al-Zubidy
found it challenging to identify the theories, models, frameworks, and instruments utilized in the

title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[29] demonstrated the challenges to re-analysis, replication, and reproduction
resulting from a lack of context and details in existing literature through three case-studies.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Ad-
ditionally, their analysis of quality measures on reviewed papers found that reporting related to
confounding factors, threats to validity, and ethical issues were lacking.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[4]’s (2016) work suggests that replications can be diﬃcult due to gaps in the
reporting of a research study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[5] (2016) identiﬁed several areas where gaps in reporting lead to challenges
when reviewing the literature particularly with regard to lack of replication and inconsistent paper
organization.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In particular, they found that between 40% of 70% of papers in the years evaluated
from the SIGCSE TS were lacking threats to validity.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[36] (2016) found that 47% of CSE and 56% of ICER papers during their study
timeframe reported explicit research questions.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
While this level of reporting is an improvement
over the use of research questions as reported by Randolph et al.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[56], the lack of explicit research
questions in some empirical studies is a concern.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[36]’s ﬁnding about research
questions are lower than the 79% reported by Ihantola et al.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[29] possibly due to the focus on
educational data mining and learning analytics.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[45] (2018) found many gaps in reporting of pre-college activities related to the
study context and the demographics of instructors and students.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They provide a checklist with
recommendations that would also be useful for education researcher more broadly.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[37] (2018) found in their review of introductory programming that many
papers lacked details about the construct/intervention and its operationalization and eﬀect sizes,
which limits replication.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They suggest archiving course information including “syllabus, learning
outcomes, infrastructure, teaching approaches, and population demographics...”.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Prior work found several gaps in reporting quality [5, 29, 36, 56], lack of connection between
results and theories [40, 61], and lack of contextual information [29, 37, 45].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

Open science practices,
like archiving research study information, could supplement the details in the literature [37, 42].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
2.2
Guidelines for Reporting and Qality
Several organizations provide guidelines for reporting and assessing study quality.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We encour-
age interested readers to review these resources to consider additional quality expectations when
designing and reporting on empirical CER studies.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The What Works Clearinghouse (WWC) has developed a Standards Handbook [12] that provides
resources for a systematic review process, including the development of a quality rubric, to pro-
vide summary reports about empirical educational research that can be of use to policymakers.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: The structured review is intended to assess the internal validity of the study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
WWC focuses on
four types of research: randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental design, regression discon-
tinuity design, and single-case design.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Studies related to a particular area of interest and quality
rubric provide one of three labels: meets WWC Design Standards without reservations, meets
WWC Design Standards with reservations, does not meet WWC Design Standards.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For example,
quasi-experimental designs which lack randomization can only achieve the category “meets WWC
Design Standards with reservations” due to the lack of randomization in the process.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The WWC
Design Standards provide a deeper quality assessment, speciﬁcally around the methods, results,
and internal validity of educational research studies than our rubric on reporting norms.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Empiricism in CER
13
The CONSORT 2010 Statement [60] provides guidelines and a checklist for reporting parallel
group randomized trials.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
While the authors of CONSORT do not prescribe a speciﬁc article struc-
ture, they do suggest using subheadings to help readers ﬁnd information in the manuscript.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Ap-
propriate subheadings provide readers with guideposts on where to ﬁnd important information
and can be especially useful for supporting possible replications.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The American Psychological Association (APA) provides Journal Article Reporting Standards
(JARS) for researchers, reviewers, and editors [7].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The website provides guidelines for reporting
standards on quantitative, qualitative, and mixed research publications and study designs.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
It also
provides guidance on meta-analysis reporting standards.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The American Education Research Association (AERA) Standards for Reporting on Empirical So-
cial Science Research in AERA Publications provides guidance for reporting on empirical educational
research [6].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Guidance includes a clear statement of the problem, description of the study design,
overview of the data collection and sources of evidence, a description of key measurements and
how they are operationalized by the study, details of analysis procedures, scope, and ethics.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Within the computing education community, several articles provide guidance on high quality
reporting of CER work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Daniels and Pears [14] provide a framework for designing action research
to support answering research questions about “concrete teaching and learning challenges” in
computer science classrooms.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Their framework provides guidance on reporting the researcher’s
epistemology and theoretical perspective(s), describing the context of the research study, and de-
scribing the methodology and methods associated with the research question.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
McGill and Decker
[43] describe the challenges in creating a repository for K-12 CER research due to inconsistencies
in reporting standards and questions about study quality identiﬁed by a focus group gathered to
create repository requirements.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Some of the ﬁndings from the focus group suggest that report-
ing on basic technical components would support replication.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The www.csedresearch.org website
serves as a repository for instruments and guidelines for reporting on K-12 studies, which builds on
other work by McGill, Decker, and others [45].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
As part of their systematic literature review, Ihan-
tola et al.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[29] created a quality assessment rubric for selected studies that reported on educational
data mining and learning analytics.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Researchers in related ﬁelds which also consider human subjects, like software engineering,
have proposed reporting guidelines for empirical work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Runeson and Höst [57] describes guide-
lines for reporting case studies, including suggested headings and subsections.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The work [57] com-
pares case study reporting guidelines to experimental reporting guidelines created by Jedlitschka
and Pfahl [31] and reﬁned by Kitchenham et al.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[35] pro-
vides checklists that researchers, practitioners, meta-reviewers, replicators, and reviewers should
consider when reading experimental work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Carver [10] provides guidelines for reporting experi-
mental replications in software engineering that can also be useful as general reporting guidelines
for empirical work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
As part of reporting on a replication, the original study should be discussed,
including the research question(s), participants and their characteristics and context, experimental
design, artifacts or resources used in the study, context variables, and summary of the results as
general reporting guidelines for empirical work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
2.3
Guidelines for Replication
Our focus on reporting quality is in the goal of supporting replications, meta-analysis, and theory-
building in the CER community.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
This section describes key references on replications in CER and
more broadly.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Schmidt [59] provides a pragmatic and operational overview of replication, particularly in the
social sciences.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Their deﬁnitions of direct replication and conceptual replication form the foun-
dation of the discussion of replication and capture our views of replication.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
14
Heckman, Carver, Sherriﬀ, and Al-Zubidy
additional conﬁrmatory power about a research question.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Schmidt suggests ﬁve functions of repli-
cation: “to control for sampling error, to control for artifacts, to control for fraud, to generalize
results to a larger or to a diﬀerent population, and to verify the underlying hypothesis of the ear-
lier experiment.” While Schmidt [59] provides a framework for replications and reproductions, he
additionally provides a pragmatic reﬂection on practical publications of reﬂections given commu-
nity biases towards original work by using follow-up studies and systematic replications.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Follow-up
studies may include direct replication of earlier work and additional experimental conditions that
either provide generalizability or novelty beyond the replicative piece.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Systematic replications
provide a way of exploring the variation around a research replication modeled as a data ma-
trix.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Replications consider diﬀerent cases within the matrix to systematically explore the research
space.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Institute of Education Sciences (IES) issued joint
Companion Guidelines on Replication & Reproducibility in Education Research [19] as a supplement
to the Common Guidelines for Education Research and Development [18].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The Companion Guidelines
deﬁne reproducibility and replication and describe the importance of both in furthering theory in
education.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The guidelines for designing reproducible studies suggest that “Analyses should be
described in suﬃcient detail as to allow other researchers to reproduce the results using the same
dataset.” When reporting results, researchers should share data and analysis details, how results
compare to replicated or reproduced studies, and speciﬁc details about data that was excluded or
omitted [19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The deﬁnitions from the Companion Guidelines, which are similar to those provided
by Schmidt [59], are:
• reproducibility: “the ability to achieve the same ﬁndings as another investigator using extant
data from a prior study” [19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• replication: “involved collecting and analyzing data to determine if the new studies (in whole
or in part) yield the same ﬁndings as a previous study” [19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Replication studies are further
broken down into two categories:
– direct replication: “seek to replicate ﬁndings from a previous study using the same, or as
similar as possible, research methods and procedures as a previous study” [19, 59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
– conceptual replication: “seek to determine whether similar results are found when certain
aspects of a previous study’s method and/or procedures are systematically varied” [19, 59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Nosek and Lakens [49] describe the beneﬁts of direct replication as increasing the size of the data
that can help identify false positive results, help establish generalizability of results, and identify
the boundaries of results.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[21] explore the language and deﬁnitions of how other disciplines verify ﬁndings of
experimental research.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: A review of literature found 18 sources with classiﬁcations of replications.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Their synthesis identiﬁed three key groupings of deﬁnitions based on whether the authors use the
same methods for either operational replication of the methods or empirical generalization of the
results, diﬀerent methods for a conceptual replication to determine if the results around a given
hypothesis are reproducible, or existing data sets where the analysis is replicated for internal
replication or for a reanalysis of the data using diﬀerent methods.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[21] provide the
following terms and deﬁnitions:
• Re-analysis: uses the same or diﬀerent analysis on “the data of a previously run experiment
are used to verify the results rather than re-running the experiment.” [21]
• Replication: uses the same methods with diﬀerent data that “veriﬁes that the observed ﬁnd-
ings are stable enough to be discovered more than once.” [21]
• Reproduction: uses the same hypothesis, but diﬀerent methods and data to verify “that the
ﬁndings are not to be attributed to the experimental method.” [21]
ACM Trans.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[29] build on Gómez et al.’s [21] work to create a novel classiﬁcation of reproduc-
tion studies in the R.A.P.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
They consider three key criteria: researchers, data analysis,
and data production to identify seven classiﬁcations where one or more of the criteria are changed
for study reproduction.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
By considering the taxonomy, researchers can examine the state space of
possible study reproductions related to a speciﬁc hypothesis.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The seven categories and their deﬁni-
tions are:
• Re-Analysis: “a diﬀerent diﬀerent experimenter is following the same analysis done before
with the original data set for review purposes” [29]
• Extended Analysis: “an experimenter is extending the baseline study by looking at a previ-
ously analyzed data set, but using new analysis methods [29]
• Repetition: “an experimenter is repeating the same analysis with new data” [29]
• Veriﬁcation: “the same data set is looked into again by a diﬀerent experimenter and using a
diﬀerent analysis method to verify the conclusions” [29]
• Replication Study: “a diﬀerent experimenter is following the same analysis method as in the
baseline study, but using their own diﬀerent data set” [29]
• Triangulation: “an experimenter is collecting a new data set to be analyzed with a new
method” [29]
• Reproduction: “a diﬀerent experimenter is analyzing their own new data set and following a
new analysis method designed for the study in order to test the hypothesis in the baseline
study.” [29]
ACM updated their Artifact Review and Badging deﬁnitions [3] in 2020 to correspond to deﬁni-
tions used by the National Information Standards Organization (NISO).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
ACM uses the following
deﬁnitions:

We see our contribution as complementing the recent work of others [4, 5, 24, 29, 36,

text:
Speciﬁcally,
the current paper provides an advance over prior work in three dimensions:
• Scale - we considered the proceedings of ﬁve CER venues for a full two years, including the
SIGCSE TS;
• Scope - our study provides a broad snapshot that covers the full proceedings/issues of CER
venues compared with the more focused snapshots of prior work.

3
METHODOLOGY
Our goal is to describe the reporting of empiricism across the most common venues for computing
education research and practice.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We have identiﬁed elements of empiricism that should be included
in reports of research results, which parallel the key items needed during design of an educational
research study [8, 13, 16].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Our systematic literature review [34] will reveal the state of the practice
for reporting empirical research results and provide guidance to the CER community for how to
improve reporting to provide the basis the community needs to advance in a scientiﬁcally rigorous
manner.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Our study investigates the following research questions (RQs):
• RQ1: What percentage of papers in CER venues have some form of empirical evaluation?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• RQ2: Of the papers that have empirical evaluation, what are the characteristics of the empir-
ical evaluation?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• RQ3: Of the papers that have empirical evaluation, do they follow norms (both for inclusion
and for labeling of information needed for replication, meta-analysis, and, eventually, theory-
building) for reporting empirical work?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
3.1
Selection Criteria
Previous work done through 2008 [56, 72] showed a small increase in the presence of empirical
evaluation in papers in CER conferences in general.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Several more recent papers show an increase
in empirical work across a variety of venues [5, 29, 36, 40].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Our evaluation includes two years of
papers from ﬁve venues (SIGCSE TS, ICER, ITiCSE, TOCE, and CSE).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We included all papers from
the TOCE and CSE editions and two iterations of each conference during 2014 and 2015.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
3.2
CER Empiricism Assessment Rubric
We developed and piloted the ﬁrst version of the CER Empiricism Assessment Rubric in 2015 [5].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
This initial version of the rubric was based on the evaluation rubrics used in previous reviews of
CER literature [56, 72] and on items considered when designing empirical studies [8, 16].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Speciﬁ-
cally, the rubric was focused on aspects of a research paper that are essential for others to under-
stand and potentially replicate the experiment, as evidenced by prior work [56, 72] and supported
by guidelines in educational research [12, 19, 59, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Randolph et al.’s rubric, however, incorporated
more granular details in its categories.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For example, Randolph et al.’s rubric took into account the
computing domain from which the research intervention originated, including categories such
as “Visualization” and “Simulation” as discrete options [56].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Our rubric takes a more high-level
approach, focusing more on the general role of the intervention in how it relates to computing ed-
ucation.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In this example, instead of noting whether the intervention incorporated “Visualization”
or “Simulation,” we focused on whether the intervention was an assignment, a tool, a curricular
innovation, etc.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Empiricism in CER
17
After we applied the initial version of the rubric in our study of the SIGCSE TS proceedings, we
evolved both the rubric and the methodology for applying it to a large number of papers to arrive
at the current version of the rubric found in Appendix A.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In updating our rubric, we referenced
the evolving reviewing guidelines for ACM SIGCSE conferences and work in the scholarship of
teaching and learning (SoTL) space to ensure that our core rubric items were capturing current
best practices in CER work [8].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Further, we streamlined our evaluation methodology to make the
application of the rubric to a large set of papers more feasible, while still maintaining the quality
of our evaluation by examining the inter-rater reliability.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Finally, we discovered some papers that
exposed corner cases that we needed to address, such as papers that purported to be empirical
studies, but reported no number of actual participants in the study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The rubric is comprised of a Base Rubric that is applicable to all papers with some level of
empirical results and three additional rubrics for speciﬁc categories of research projects.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The Base Rubric contains a set of characteristics that captures the overall nature of the empirical
work including information such as the type of evaluation method, the evaluation subject, whether
there is any comparison, and the number of participants.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
These items provide a high-level charac-
terization of the empirical work presented, answering questions such as:
• What is the balance between quantitative and qualitative work?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • At what rate do researchers publish studies on curricula?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Are researchers performing replication studies or creating their own interventions?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • How many participants are in the typical CER study?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Depending upon the type of empirical study included in the paper, i.e.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
quantitative, qualitative,
survey, and/or descriptive, we then employed one or more additional rubrics.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Each of these rubrics
allowed us to characterize the presence and clarity of important information that CER papers
should include relative to each type of study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The items on these additional rubrics all use the
same categorization scale that identiﬁes whether a piece of information is present and how easy it
is for the reader to identify that piece of information.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The scale captures both types of information
as follows:
• Completeness - the level of completeness of presented information
– Complete - Answers/addresses all questions for a rubric category.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
There is no assessment
on the quality of the answer.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: – Partial - Answers/addresses some of the questions for a rubric category.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
There is no as-
sessment on the quality of the answer.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: – Not Present - Answers/addresses none of the questions for a rubric category.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: – Not Applicable - The rubric item is not applicable to the paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• Labeled - whether the presented information is clearly labeled
– Labeled - There is a heading appropriate for the rubric item or there is emphasis (bold/i-
talics) for the rubric item.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
– Not Labeled - There is no heading or emphasis for the rubric item to easily ﬁnd the item
in the paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Therefore each rubric item can take one of six labels:
• Complete and Labeled
• Complete and Not Labeled
• Partial and Labeled
• Partial and Not Labeled
• Not Present
• Not Applicable
ACM Trans.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
18
Heckman, Carver, Sherriﬀ, and Al-Zubidy
The items included on the rubric represents the type of information necessary to support repro-
ducibility and replication of research studies.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We use the deﬁnitions from the Companion Guide-
lines on Replication & Reproducibility in Education Research published jointly by the National Sci-
ence Foundation (NSF) and the Institute of Education Sciences (IES) [19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• reproducibility: “the ability to achieve the same ﬁndings as another investigator using extant
data from a prior study” [19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• replication: “involved collecting and analyzing data to determine if the new studies (in whole
or in part) yield the same ﬁndings as a previous study” [19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Replication studies are further
broken down into two categories:
– direct replication: “seek to replicate ﬁndings from a previous study using the same, or as
similar as possible, research methods and procedures as a previous study” [19, 59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
– conceptual replication: “seek to determine whether similar results are found when certain
aspects of a previous study’s method and/or procedures are systematically varied” [19, 59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• meta-analysis - is a quantitative, formal, systematic analysis of a number of related study
results in order to identify general patterns and draw overarching conclusions about the
entire body of research [23].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• theory-building - is the process of using replication, repetition, and meta-analysis to system-
atize knowledge.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Theories can drive the generation of hypotheses and produce predictive
theory through scientiﬁc enquiry [16].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Additionally, conceptual replications can produce
understanding and conﬁrm underlying theory [59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For the remainder of this paper, we use the term replication to cover any type of study design
that builds on prior study designs through replication in the same setting (i.e., direct replication)
or through systematic variance (i.e., conceptual replication).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Reporting commoninformation and using open science supports replications [19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Meta-analysis
can then utilize these common results, aggregate them, and increase overall generalizability of
ﬁndings to “gain a better understanding of what interventions improve (or do not improve) ed-
ucational outcomes, for whom, and under what conditions” [19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Because individual studies are
more prone to error or bias, meta-analysis or meta-studies provide the opportunity to synthesize
results around a research question to understand impacts on a broader set of learners [5, 19, 42, 59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
This process provides for a mechanism for theory, either conﬁrmatory of educational theory in a
computing context or the emergence of theory to support new phenomenon [16, 42, 59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For example, good practice is for a paper to provide an overview of the participants, including
demographics and the sampling or recruitment method [45].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
If a paper met all the criteria speciﬁed
in the rubric, the paper receives a label of “Complete” for that rubric item.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
If the paper meets at
least one, but not all, of the criteria, the paper receives a label of “Partial” for that rubric item.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
If
the paper meets none of the criteria in the rubric, the paper receives a label of “Not Present” for
the rubric item.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Finally, if this particular rubric item does not apply to the paper, the paper receives
the label of “Not Applicable” for that rubric item.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
To ease the replication, meta-analysis, or theory-building process, it is important for a paper to
not only contain the appropriate information but also to present that information in a way that
readers can easily locate it, similar to the checklists in CONSORT [60] and suggested information
for reporting in APA JARS [7].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We determined a rubric item to be easy to ﬁnd if there was a relevant
section heading in the paper for the item.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We also considered text that emphasized a speciﬁc item
through italics, bolding, or a bulleted list.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
These are common ways of noting research questions
rather than using a section header.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We assigned a value of either “Labeled” or “Not Labeled” for
each rubric item in each paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Empiricism in CER
19
To reiterate, the purpose of the CER Empiricism Assessment Rubric is to characterize the study
and the rigor in which a paper reports an empirical study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The goal is to comment on the eﬃcacy
of the reporting from the perspective of a reader who wishes to replicate, perform meta-analysis,
or build theories.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The rubric does not comment in any way on the quality of the study or reporting
itself, beyond the presence of the expected information.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We completed the Experimental Rubric for each paper that contained some form of empirical
evaluation.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
This rubric characterizes the rigor in which the paper reports and labels the key aspects
of an empirical study [8, 13, 16, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
These aspects include concepts and questions such as:
• Are the research objectives obvious and easy to ﬁnd?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Is the study design properly presented?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • How was the data gathered and analyzed for this work?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Are the results presented in a succinct, direct way?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In order for an empirical study to be replicated, a paper needs to thoroughly discuss and clearly
label these items so readers can easily ﬁnd them.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We completed the Survey Rubric for each paper that uses a survey as either the primary research
methodology or one of the data sources.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Within those topics, the rubric items examine whether the
paper describes the survey creation process, the rationale behind the questions, and the execution
of the survey, including its administration and the medium used.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We completed the Descriptive/Persuasive Rubric for papers that do not claim any cause/eﬀect re-
lationship.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: These papers are often presented as position papers.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
This rubric contains items focused
on the goal of the paper’s argument, the presence of related work, the soundness of the argument,
and whether supporting evidence is present.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
3.3
Gathering Data and Applying the Rubric
Because we included all papers from each venue in the chosen years, we manually extracted the
DOI entries for each paper from the digital library.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Then we downloaded the PDFs of the papers
to analyze locally.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: In an initial phase, we examined the ﬁrst 50 papers to reﬁne our methodology.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We randomly
assigned each paper to two researchers for initial categorization.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Each researcher independently
evaluated the paper using the rubric.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Then we met to discuss any discrepancies in the analysis.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
If
needed, we asked a third researcher to review a paper to resolve any discrepancies.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
At the end of
this process, all researchers agreed on the ﬁnal categorization of the paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Based on the experience with the ﬁrst 50 papers, we modiﬁed our methodologyfor the remaining
papers.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Overall, we found very few discrepancies in this ﬁrst set of papers.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We computed kappa
to measure the inter-rater reliability for each of the rubric items across the 50 papers.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Overall,
our level of agreement was very high, with the kappa values for each rubric item above 0.8 (p
<0.01).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Based on this high level of agreement, we decided it was not necessary for two reviewers
to complete the full rubric on each paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, we also did not want to fully rely on only one
reviewer for each paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
As a compromise, because the Base Rubric contains the information that
determines the type of research present in the paper and determines which other rubric(s) apply,
we had two researchers complete the Base Rubric for each paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
After resolving any discrepancies,
this process resulted in a consensus on the type of research present in each paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Based on the type
of research present, one researcher then reviewed the paper using one or more of the remaining
rubrics (Experimental, Survey, and Descriptive/Persuasive Rubrics).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Finally, we merged all results
into a single spreadsheet for analysis and calculations [27].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
An Observational study is performed in a natural setting in which
the researcher collects data via observation without manipulation of the situation.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Conversely, an
Interventional study is performed by assigning participants into groups (e.g., control and experi-
mental) and applying the treatment to the experimental group to measure its eﬀect.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Our use of
observational and interventional are not intended as a direct relationship to qualitative and quan-
titative methods, but are instead a way of describing the setting.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Observational studies are similar
to Fincher’s and Petre’s [16] deﬁnition on in situ – the normal or natural setting.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Interventional
studies correspond to Fincher’s and Petre’s [16] settings of under constraints and in a laboratory
where there is some direct intervention to the environment.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: There is a fairly even split between the two types of studies across all venues.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

This result indi-
cates a nice balance in CER work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

However, when looking at Quantitative work only, we do see
an increase in the proportion of Interventional studies.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

These results suggest that there is a gap in
using Qualitative methods to assess CER interventions.

4.3
RQ3: Norms of Empirical Evaluation
RQ3: Of the papers that have empirical evaluation, do they follow norms (both
inclusion and labeling of information needed for replication, meta-analysis, and,
eventually, theory-building) for reporting empirical work?
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For empirical papers, we expect a paper should contain a research objective, related work, an
overview of the research participants, an overview of the study design or methods, a description
of the data collection process, a description of the analysis procedures, a report of the results, and
a listing of the threats to validity for the research [8, 13, 16, 60] as deﬁned in the CER Empiricism
ACM Trans.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
26
Heckman, Carver, Sherriﬀ, and Al-Zubidy
Assessment – Experimental Rubric.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Any papers reporting the results of a Survey as a data source
should have information about how the survey was conducted and the survey questions asked
as deﬁned in the CER Empiricism Assessment – Survey Rubric.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Descriptive/Persuasive work should
include the goal of the argument, related work, at least three premises and a conclusion, all with
supporting evidence as deﬁned in the CER Empiricism Assessment – Descriptive/Persuasive Rubric.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, due to the small numbers of Descriptive/Persuasive papers in our analysis (e.g., 10), we
do not provide an analysis of that category in this section.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
To provide an overall characterization of the papers, we classiﬁed each paper into one of three
categories for each of the key elements listed above:
• Strongly Supports Replication - items that were “Complete and Labeled” provide all the
details necessary to support replication;
• Weakly Supports Replication - items that were “Complete and Not Labeled” or “Partial
and Labeled” provide some, but not all of the details required to support replication;
• Not Present - items that were “Not Present” are missing information necessary to support
replication.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Table 12 summarizes the results of our analysis of reporting norms.

Overall, the only two ele-
ments where more than 50% of papers reach the Strongly Supports Replication level are Related
Work and Results.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Looking across all elements, the papers published in ICER do a better job by
having more then 50% of papers reach the Strongly Supports Replication level for all elements
except for Threats to Validity.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, as the numbers in Table 12 show, there is still room for
improvement as a community to reach the Strongly Supports Replication level for all attributes
most (or all) of the time.

One of the most critical pieces of information in an empirical paper is the
research objective, goals, hypotheses, or other summative statement that provides the context of
the work reported in the paper.

text:
It is concerning that, across all venues, 18% of the papers lacked
a summative statement about the work (i.e.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[56] reported
only 22% of papers between 2000 and 2005 had research questions or hypotheses and Lishinski
et al.

[36] found that only 47% of CSE and 56% of ICER papers between 2012 and 2015 had explicit
research questions.

Our numbers for CSE (55%) and ICER (55.3%) for complete and labeled are
similar to Lishinski et al.

text:
[56] suggesting some improvement
in the reporting of research questions.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
A summative statement guides the reader to the main ideas of the study and is critical for de-
termining if the methods and analysis are appropriate for the statement and if the results answer
or address the statement.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
One or more research statements, objectives, or hypotheses are recom-
mended in standards like CONSORT [60], APA JARS [7], and AERA [6].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In addition, we found
over half of the papers reached only the Weakly Supports Replication level because they lacked
important information.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
These papers either did not highlight the summative statement in a mean-
ingful way, through text attributes (e.g., italics or bold), callouts (e.g., boxes or bullets), or clear
labeling (e.g., RQ1, Goal, etc.), or did not clearly label the goal of the paper, thereby requiring the
reader to infer the context of the paper through other statements in the paper.

Most papers reported and labeled related work demonstrating Strongly Supports
ACM Trans.

text:
The SIGCSE Board policy4 states that Program Chairs should “re-
quest that all paper submissions include a review of previous, related work.” This guidance demon-
strates the importance of establishing reporting norms for the community to ensure high quality
dissemination of empirical results.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The papers we rated as Weakly Supports Replication typi-
cally did not link the related work to the research objective or did not contain an explicitly labeled
related work or background section.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For those papers that lacked a related work section, the au-
thors typically discussed the related work or background information in the introduction.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Most papers did include information about the study participants.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, over
half of the papers fell into the Weakly Supports Replication category because they lacked either
full details about the participants or a clear label for the section of the paper describing the partici-
pants.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
A description of participants should contain demographic information to provide context for
the results [6, 7, 19, 45, 60].

We found a split between

There were a number of

By providing the study design information in a separate section, the authors help readers
more easily extract important information about the design to support replication.

In addition to
not being labeled, some study designs sections omitted key information.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

One key piece of informa-
tion is identiﬁcation of the dependent and independent variables [7, 60], which could be as simple
as identifying the key item under observation or providing overview of an intervention.

pers fell into the Weakly Supports Replication category.

Some of those papers did not include a
clearly deﬁned data collection section.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Sometimes, the papers integrated the discussion about data
collection into the discussion about the study design or methods.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Other times, papers integrated
the discussion about data collection into the results section.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
By providing a clear section or sub-
section around data collection [6, 7], authors can provide details to readers who may be interested
in using similar techniques in their own work.

Other Weakly Supports Replication papers omitted important information describing the
how, where, and who of the data collection.

For example, papers frequently lacked details about
survey administration, which is discussed further in Section 4.3.2.

Around 34% of papers demonstrated Strongly Supports Replication re-
lated to the reporting of analysis procedures.

papers were both incomplete and not properly labeled.

full description of how the authors worked with or processed that data after collection.

Addition-

appropriate for the analysis.

with Strongly Supports Replication in this space [58].

Standards support clear reporting on
analysis procedures and statistical tests used [6, 7]

and TOCE reached the level of Strongly Supports Replication.

If papers did discuss threats or limitations, the threats/limitations were typically unlabeled and
appeared in either a results or discussion section.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

Papers with a Weakly Supports Replication
may have listed the threats, but typically did not discuss how the authors addressed the threats.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
A threats to validity section provides context to the study design and provides details on how
readers should interpret the work in a broader context and potential biases that might impact
the result [5, 7, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Because CER is complex work, threats to validity describe how the authors
controlled that complexity (or not) [5, 29].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Replications help control for sampling error and artifacts
which identify potential weaknesses with internal validity of the original study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Clearly articulated
threats to validity can help identify key variables to vary in replications [59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Replications also
support increasing external validity through generalizability [59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We completed the Survey Rubric for any paper that contained a survey as
a data source.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021
