To provide replicable survey research, authors must provide details on the survey
design and survey execution.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The reuse and standardization of surveys would be a good starting
point for building a culture of replication [6, 41].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
If authors provide details about their surveys,
even as an un-reviewed supplement to the the paper, it would help build this culture.

5
DISCUSSION
The CER community has seen a growth in submissions and participation.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
As our community grows
we need to mature the norms of reporting empirical research so the broader community can beneﬁt
from the dissemination of high-quality results, that answer well-stated research questions, situated
in the appropriate literature, with a clear discussion of limitations and threats to validity.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Papers
should clearly document methods and analysis procedures to allow others to replicate studies in
their own contexts.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Reviewers should begin to expect paper authors to follow reporting norms and
use those norms as guidance when performing paper reviews.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In the following sections, we provide observations and recommendations from our review of re-
porting norms.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Where appropriate, we connect our recommendations to the broader literature and
guidelines, particularly APA JARS [7], CONSORT, [60], What Works Clearinghouse [12], AERA [6],
and the IES/NSF Guidelines [18, 19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
5.1
Observations and Recommendations from the Results
Based on the results described in the previous section, we make a number of observations and
recommendations for authors.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We note that these recommendations may not apply in all situations
and that the individual research questions and researcher context will impact the decisions that
are made during a study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The results showed that only ﬁve papers had used multiple evaluation
methods.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We encourage researchers to consider using mixed methods approaches more often in
study designs to utilize the complementary strengths of both Qualitative and Quantitative methods
(see Fincher and Petre [16], Bishop-Clark and Dietz-Uhler [8], APA JARS [7] for details on mixed
method studies).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, we acknowledge that it is not always possible or advisable to use mixed
methods approaches and that page limits often constrain the level of detail researchers can include
in their publications.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The results showed that more than half of the papers used evalua-
tion subjects developed for the speciﬁc study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: This result suggests that replication in CER is weak.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Replication provides a mechanism for generalizing ﬁndings about a research question or set of
research questions that can lead to the development of theory to support the computing education
community [29, 59].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We challenge the computing education community to consider using com-
mon methods, evaluation metrics, and data collection and reporting procedures to support the
comparison and aggregation of data to generalize CER ﬁndings.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Utilizing standards can support
this goal [6, 7, 12, 19, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: The results showed that a large number of papers utilized only one source of data.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We encourage researchers to utilize multiple data sources to provide more robust insight to the
phenomena under study and stronger answers to research questions.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In addition, 29% of the pa-
pers used surveys as the only data source.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
There are many situations where surveys are an ex-
cellent form of data collection (i.e., understanding a community); however, in classroom studies,
researchers should supplement surveys with additional information to provide stronger evidence
to answer a research question.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For example, a research question about how an intervention im-
pacts student learning should not rely solely on student’s self-report of their learning.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[41] argues that collecting both process (e.g., progress or experience) and product (e.g., perfor-
mance or outcome) data can increase the applicability of the results to a larger group of educators.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We observed a number of papers that lacked a clear study design or methods sec-
tion.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
A study design section should tie the observation or intervention to the research question(s)
and provide justiﬁcation that the observation or intervention will support answering the research
question(s).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The study design section should clearly describe the steps of the study so others could
replicate the study in their own environments.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For subjective measures, the paper should contain
a discussion of the coding process and the method for obtaining agreement or consensus among
multiple raters.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: These items are important for determining how to properly interpret the results.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In addition, citing seminal work and standards about the study methods strengthens the methods
discussion and can help build the community’s knowledge about CER methods [6–8, 12, 16, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We observed that most authors did not provide a justiﬁcation for the speciﬁc
survey questions included.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
While page restrictions can make it diﬃcult to provide the full survey,
authors can include the full survey as an un-reviewed supplemental content or on a website.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In
cases where an author does not want to make the survey publicly available because it may bias
future results, the author can include a statement to that eﬀect in the paper and provide contact
information for interested researchers to obtain a copy of the survey.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The use of standardized
survey instruments can support replication [41].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
5.2
Author Guidelines for Empirical Papers
Many CER researchers may not have any formal training in conducting human subject research
in educational environments.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Examples of high-quality literature and study frameworks for repli-
cation can help new researchers get started investigating interesting challenges in their own class-
rooms, departments, and communities.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We therefore propose the following guidelines for CER
authors when preparing their studies and writing up their work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
These guidelines are similar
to expectations when designing CER studies [8, 16] and have elements in common with stan-
dards [6, 7, 12, 19, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
CER Venues, like TOCE, are now recommending that authors utilize APA
JARS for future submissions.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
General Reporting Guidelines
• Clearly identify the evaluation method(s) and subject(s) under evaluation in the study [6, 7,
60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• Clearly identify what work is new to the study and where the study builds on prior work or
data [6, 7, 19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• Clearly identify any comparisons with prior work or with a control group, if appropriate [6,
7, 19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Provide information about participants, including demographics [6, 7, 45, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Identify the study as observational or interventional [7].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • For surveys, describe the administration process and provide the survey questions.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• Where possible, provide supplemental resources that would help others replicate the work,
e.g.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
code used to analyze data on a public version control system or anonymized, aggregate
data on a website [19, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• Utilize pre-registration and open science to strengthen research integrity and transparency [19,
42, 49, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
32
Heckman, Carver, Sherriﬀ, and Al-Zubidy
Research Question [6, 7, 60]
• The research goal or question is of upmost importance because it drives the rest of the work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Utilize resources on writing high quality and actionable research questions.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Highlight the research goal and questions in the text.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For example, italicize the goal state-
ments in the paper’s introduction.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: List and name more speciﬁc research questions (e.g.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
RQ1,
RQ2) in the introduction and revisit them in the results.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Related Work
• Report related work in its own section.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
It should situate the research question or goal in
the context of the broader literature.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Because most SIGCSE conferences now provide extra
pages for references, authors should be able to provide a robust discussion of related work
with suﬃcient citations of relevant literature.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• Provide a discussion that links the related work to the research goal, objectives, or questions
for the paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The section should also discuss how the related work informs the study and
how the study builds on previous work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The information about previous work is especially
important for replication papers [6, 7].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• Synthesize the key themes in the prior work to provide context and motivation for the cur-
rent study, which should not simply be an annotated bibliography.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Participants
• Report demographic information about the participant groups in the study.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For students,
minimally report numbers, ages, education levels, gender, race/ethnicity, prior computing
experience, and regional location for the students [6, 7, 45].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
[45] provide other
suggestions for reporting demographic information for other participant populations.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• If number of participants is too small that reporting demographics would become identifying
for those participants, clearly state this information in lieu of reporting speciﬁc demograph-
ics.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Describe the process for selecting participants.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
If the study uses multiple groups, the paper
should discuss the process for allocating participants to each group.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
If the authors exclude
participants from the study (e.g., minors in a university-level study), the paper should explain
the exclusion criteria [6, 7, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• Explain the process for obtaining consent from participants and any ethical considerations
associated with human subjects research.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Since ethical standards vary by country and insti-
tution, authors should clarify expectations in their context and assure reviewers and readers
that the human subjects study was handled in an appropriate manner for the author’s con-
text [6, 7].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Study Design
• Separate the study design or methods from the discussion of results.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
This separation will
allow readers to assess the quality of the study and to more easily see the steps needed for
replication.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Identify independent and dependent variables [7, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Describe each step in conducting the study [6, 7, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Data Collection
• Identify data collection procedures including mediums for data collection, who collected the
data, and how the data addresses or answers the research questions [6, 7, 19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Empiricism in CER
33
• Provide a rationale for why the data collected will help address the research question(s) [6, 7].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Analysis Procedures
• Describe the process for working with the collected data, including the process for cleaning
data, if necessary [6, 19].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• For qualitative analysis, describe the coding process and the process for evaluating the cor-
rectness of the coding (e.g., multiple raters, inter-rater reliability, etc.) [6, 7].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • For quantitative analysis, describe, and justify, the statistical tests, if appropriate.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For other
types of analysis, provide a justiﬁcation on how the analysis helps answer the research ques-
tion(s) [6, 7, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Results
• Ensure that results directly address the research question(s) [6, 7, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• For qualitative results, provide tables, descriptions, quotes, and arguments to answer the
research questions [6, 7].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• For quantitative results, provide summary or descriptive statistics to answer the research
questions [6, 7].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Threats to Validity
• Include a dedicated threats to validity section that lists internal, external, construct threats,
and biases as appropriate for the research question(s) and study design [6, 7, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Discuss how the study design addresses the threats.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Discuss any threats not addressed by the study design.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Explain and justify the unaddressed threats.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• Explain the potential impact on the interpretation of the study results due to the unaddressed
threats [6, 7, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
5.3
Reviewer Guidelines for Reviewing Empirical Papers
The responsibility for high-quality publications about CER work does not rest solely on authors.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Review guidelines over the past several years have clariﬁed expectations for reviewing empirical
work, both as CER and experience reports.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Reviewers have a responsibility to hold authors ac-
countable for following norms for reporting CER.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We recommend that reviewers use the author
guidelines and standards documents above as a checklist for things to provide feedback on during
peer review.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
These guidelines and standards echo guidelines and standards from education and
other ﬁelds about presentation of empirical work [6, 7, 12, 19, 60].
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
6
THREATS TO VALIDITY
In developing our rubric and applying it to the work described in this paper, we identiﬁed some
limitations and threats to validity we must address.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We have backgrounds in conducting human-
based empirical research in computing education, software engineering, and security, but do not
explicitly have research degrees in education.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, two of authors have been members of the
program committee of SIGCSE TS for multiple years, including years volunteering as program and
symposium chairs, so we believe that we do have the needed background.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
During the creation of the CER Empiricism Assessment Rubric, we did not explicitly review or
reference other validated rubrics.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Therefore, it is possible that we omitted some aspects of educa-
tional research project design.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
To address this threat to validity, after we completed our work, we
ACM Trans.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
34
Heckman, Carver, Sherriﬀ, and Al-Zubidy
compared our rubric to other guidelines for reporting and assessing empirical research study qual-
ity, such as APA JARS [7], the What Works Clearinghouse Standards Handbook [12] and CONSORT
[60], as discussed in Section 2.2.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We found that there was signiﬁcant overlap in the core concepts
of these other guidelines and rubrics with our own, indicating that our rubric captures many of
the same reporting values.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In choosing the years and venues for inclusion in this review, we selected the conferences and
journals that are widely considered to be the top tier for CER and only analyzed the proceedings or
issues from two years, 2014 and 2015.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We did not include more general education conferences that
have a computing track, such as ASEE or FIE, and we excluded some other venues (e.g., Koli Calling)
to make the review more feasible.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
While this choice means we could have missed a portion of the
community, we believe that the venues we chose cover the majority of the computing education
literature.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Further, some other venues accepted papers based solely on the abstract, rather than the
entire paper, which we believe does not accurately represent the current state of empiricism.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We
chose the particular set of years to create a baseline on empirical work before more recent changes
to paper tracks and reviewing guidelines at SIGCSE TS and other venues.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Also, we recognize that
the ﬁndings from 2014 and 2015 may not represent the current state of empiricism in 2021.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Future
work will consider a review of more recent publications.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Furthermore, we do not have the perspective of manuscripts that were not accepted into these
venues.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
As Fincher, et al., discussed in the conclusion of their book chapter [17], a weakness of
systematic literature reviews is that they focus on a quantitative analysis to characterize a body of
work through an author deﬁned lens and may miss the broader context of the timeframe in which
the work was published.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We do not consider the broader context of computing education during
2014 and 2015 and how that may impact the types of papers accepted.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, we minimize
this limitation by focusing on characterizing empirical elements independent of the speciﬁc topic
of the work (e.g., K-12 or CS1).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Our work provides value by suggesting how the community can
improve reporting standards independent of the broader community context for the acceptance
and publication of the reviewed literature.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: In our application of the rubric, we settled on a two-pass approach.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Two researchers evaluated
each paper using the Base Rubric - evaluation method, evaluation subject, evaluation subject source,
comparison, and number of participants.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We used this approach to better ensure proper overall
categorization of papers.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We calculated the inter-rater reliability among the research team working
on the categorization and determined only minor diﬀerences in the evaluations.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
After this initial
evaluation, one researcher then completed the remaining items in the CER Empiricism Assessment
Rubric sub-rubrics as appropriate for each paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We chose this approach because it gave us the
best balance between eﬃciency and accuracy.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
However, we recognize the possibility that individual researchers mischaracterized aspects of
individual papers.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
For example, one researcher might rate General Rubric: Research Objectives for
a paper as Partial and Not Labeled because she found a discussion of research objectives, but not
a dedicated section, while another reader could have missed the discussion altogether because
he read too quickly.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We have provided our dataset [27] for other researchers to consider when
utilizing our rubric.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
7
CONCLUSION
Our research goal was to characterize the reporting of empiricism in Computing Education Re-
search literature by identifying whether publications include content necessary for researchers to
perform replications, meta-analyses, and theory building.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
This systematic literature review sum-
marizes the type of papers and studies included during 2014 and 2015 in the SIGCSE TS, ICER,
ACM Trans.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Empiricism in CER
35
ITiCSE, TOCE, and CSE venues.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: A majority of the accepted papers report empirical work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
How-
ever those papers do not consistently follow reporting norms.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We have provided suggestions to
authors and reviewers to move the community forward in publishing high-quality empirical work
that can lead to meta-analysis and theory building.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: We did observe progress in reporting empirical work in recent years.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
With the creation of the
CS education research track at the SIGCSE TS for SIGCSE 2018 [54], the organizers updated the re-
view criteria to speciﬁcally request reviewers evaluate the items we include in our General Rubric.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Additionally, TOCE now recommends that authors utilize APA JARS when organizing their sub-
missions.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In future work, we will conduct a similar literature review on more recent publications to gauge
whether the community has made any progress.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
With improved reporting, our next review will
attempt to consider categorizing papers at a more granular level than survey, qualitative, and quan-
titative, which would provide the opportunity for more detailed rubrics.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We welcome feedback on
our rubric for possible revisions in this future review.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
As computing education is growing as a ﬁeld and community, we need to establish norms for
reporting empirical work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: By doing so, we will support replication and meta-analysis.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Increased
rigor in reporting expectations will increase the reputation of CER in the broader computing re-
search community, which will facilitate the growth and increased reputation of CER scholars and
the computing education ﬁeld.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
We all need to contribute: authors and researchers need to create
and report well-designed, high-quality research studies or well-documented and supported expe-
rience reports; reviewers need to provide feedback not only on the novelty of the idea, but the
quality of presentation; and the community needs to support replications and meta-analyses so
we can grow our understanding of how to share computing education with the world.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

9
APPENDIX A: CER EMPIRICISM ASSESSMENT RUBRIC
INTRODUCTION
The CER Empiricism Assessment Rubric was developed as a repeatable methodology for determin-
ing the degree and rigor in which empirical research principles are reported regarding research
activity in CER literature.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The rubric makes no judgement on the quality of the research or of the
research question of the reported project.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Instead, the rubric tries to establish the eﬀectiveness of
the paper at communicating the various aspects of the research activity to the reader such that it
could not only be understood, but possibly replicated for further investigation.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
RUBRIC QUESTION RESPONSE VALUES
For all sub-rubrics other than the Base Rubric, we only use values from the following scale, as
discussed in Section 3.2:
• Complete and Labeled
• Complete and Not labeled
• Partial and Labeled
• Partial and Not Labeled
• Not Present
• Not Applicable
The descriptive values address two key two parts of reporting CER work - the completeness of
the presentation of the information and whether the information is labeled in the paper or not.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Completeness - the level of completeness of presented information
• Complete - Answers/addresses all questions for a rubric category.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
There is no assessment
on the quality of the answer.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Partial - Answers/addresses some of the questions for a rubric category.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
There is no assess-
ment on the quality of the answer.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Not Present - Answers/addresses none of the questions for a rubric category.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: • Not Applicable - The rubric item is not applicable to the paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Labeled - whether the presented information is clearly labeled
• Labeled - There is a heading appropriate for the rubric item or there is emphasis (bold/italics)
for the rubric item.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
• Not Labeled - There is no heading or emphasis for the rubric item to easily ﬁnd the item in
the paper.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
RUBRIC STEPS
Follow the steps highlighted in the boxes.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Key sub-activities associated with each step in the rubric
are denoted by §.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Step 0: Read the research work you wish to evaluate.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: Step 1: Apply the Base Rubric to the research work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Empiricism in CER
41
BR) BASE RUBRIC
The Base Rubric consists of ﬁve high-level questions that provide basic information about a work,
including the primary methodology,the subject being studied, where the subject originated, whether
there is any comparison, and the size of the study as measured by the number of participants or
data instances.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
BR-1) Base Rubric: Evaluation Method
After reading the paper, the ﬁrst step is to determine the evaluation method used in the work.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The
evaluation method is a high-level categorization regarding the overall nature of the project that
is being reported.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
It is possible to select multiple options for the evaluation method, although any
more than two would be highly unusual.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
An example of this could be a project that examined both
student assessment scores and student survey responses when evaluating a new teaching method.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: In this case, the project could be categorized as Experimental, Survey.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
A work is categorized as a literature review if it is mainly focused on reporting
on the current state of the body of knowledge on a particular topic or research question.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The work
does not necessarily have to add to the body of knowledge, but it often will draw conclusions on
where the state of the research is heading.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
§: If the work is a literature review, complete item BR-2 (Evaluation Subject) from the Base Rubric
(BR) only and then continue with Descriptive/Persuasive Rubric (DR).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: An exploratory work is a research work-in-progress.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
An exploratory project could
originate from a model building exercise, observation without any predeﬁned research questions,
or building a framework or taxonomy.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text: §: If the work is exploratory, complete the Base Rubric (BR) and the Experimental Rubric (ER).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
A descriptive or persuasive work describes a current situation or paints a
picture but does not test predictions nor does it imply any cause-and-eﬀect relationships.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
This
type of work is diﬀerent than a literature review in that it is reporting on a research subject rather
than the current body of knowledge.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
§: If the work is descriptive/persuasive, complete the Base Rubric (BR) and the Descriptive/Persuasive
Rubric (DR).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Survey works use information gathered through forms or some other asynchronous query-
ing method as their primary data source.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
CER project often have surveys or similar instruments
(such as student evaluations) as a secondary data source even when there are other data sources
being used.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
§: If the work uses a survey as one of its evaluative methods, complete the Base Rubric (BR), the
Experimental Rubric (ER), and the Survey Data Source Rubric (SR).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
The primary indicator of an evaluative project with a qualitative evaluation method is
the presence of free form or free text answers from participants.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
These responses then have to be
individually coded or evaluated separately in order to draw any conclusions regarding the research
questions of the project.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
Qualitative data is common for projects with a small sample size, where
in-person interviews or focus groups are used, or if participants are audio or video recorded in any
way.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
In each of these cases, the data typically requires more time to evaluate, code, or process as
opposed to quantitative data.
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

text:
§: If the work uses qualitative data as one of its evaluative methods, complete the Base Rubric (BR)
and the Experimental Rubric (ER).
title: arXiv:2107.01984v1  [cs.CY]  2 Jul 2021

42

title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:

title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
of Computer Science, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA
‡ Computation Institute, University of Chicago and Argonne National Laboratory, Chicago, IL, USA
Abstract—Scripting languages such as Python and R have
been widely adopted as tools for the productive development
of scientiﬁc software because of the power and expressiveness
of the languages and available libraries.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
However, deploying
scripted applications on large-scale parallel computer systems
such as the IBM Blue Gene/Q or Cray XE6 is a challenge because
of issues including operating system limitations, interoperability
challenges, parallel ﬁlesystem overheads due to the small ﬁle
system accesses common in scripted approaches, and other
issues.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
We present here a new approach to these problems
in which the Swift scripting system is used to integrate high-
level scripts written in Python, R, and Tcl, with native code
developed in C, C++, and Fortran, by linking Swift to the library
interfaces to the script interpreters.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In this approach, Swift
handles data management, movement, and marshaling among
distributed-memory processes without direct user manipulation
of low-level communication libraries such as MPI.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
We present a
technique to efﬁciently launch scripted applications on large-scale
supercomputers using a hierarchical programming model.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
INTRODUCTION
An increasing number of modern scientiﬁc applications and
tools are built by using a variety of languages and libraries.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
These complex software products combine performance-
critical libraries implemented in native code (C, C++, Fortran)
with high-level functionality expressed in rapidly developed
and modiﬁed scripts.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Additional specialized language-speciﬁc
features may be used for concurrency, I/O, the use of accel-
erators, and so on.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
These development techniques have been
used in a wide range of application domains, from materials
science and protein analysis to power grid simulation.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Such applications and tools are commonly developed with
the following software development pattern.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
First, a native
code library is built or repurposed for the core processing.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Second, a collection of scripts is built up around the core
library or program to express the complex, often dynamic, but
less performance-critical coordination logic.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Such “wrapper
scripts” may be developed with shell, Python, Tcl, or other
tools.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Third, when additional scalability is required, native
code or additional scripts are developed to deploy the applica-
tion in some distributed computing model such as MPI, Swift,
some other grid workﬂow system, or with custom wrapper
scripts that submit jobs to a scheduler such as PBS.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Swift [1] is a programming language and runtime designed
to ease the software development methodology described
above.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Swift has a well-deﬁned concept of wrapper scripts,
the ability to coordinate calls to tools through its programming
model, and built-in support for many schedulers and data
movement protocols.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The latest implementation, Swift/T [2],
generates an MPI program from the Swift script and provides
tools to run that program on various scheduled resources.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
This
approach has allowed Swift/T to scale the execution of scripted
applications to hundreds of thousands of cores [3].
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The Swift/T framework supports direct calls to native code
through library loading and access.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
As described above, how-
ever, modern scientiﬁc applications are built not only with
native code, but also with scripts and scripting interfaces to
core libraries.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Thus, to ease the coordination of calls to tools in
the Swift programming model, we wish to support direct calls
to script code without calling external programs or forcing the
user to master complex linking techniques.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In this work, we report on new features in Swift that support
direct calls to Python, R, and Tcl.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
These features, which could
easily be extended to other scripting languages, allow Swift
scripts to orchestrate distributed execution of code written in a
wide variety of languages, currently including C, C++, Fortran,
Python, R, Tcl, and the shell.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Indeed, any external program
may be called through the shell-based technique.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The method presented here is a more approachable soft-
ware development technique for distributed-memory comput-
ing than are traditional techniques.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Using MPI, the developer
could write MPI code in C and call to an application compo-
nent script (say, in Python).
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In this technique, the user would
have to manage the call to the script, possibly using an internal
API speciﬁc to that language.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Application data would have to
be marshaled to and from the component and among processes
in a laborious manner.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The developer would have to build
signiﬁcant infrastructure to manage load balancing and other
distributed computing challenges.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Alternatively, the developer
could try a scripting language-speciﬁc MPI implementation,
which might ease some but not all of the described challenges.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Additionally, that approach would limit the number of lan-
guages that could be used; it is unlikely that communicating
among MPI processes in multiple languages would work as
desired.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In our method, the developer starts with a Swift script
that describes the calls to application components in a con-
venient syntax.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Swift data is passed among language-speciﬁc
components implicitly as the script progresses; no user data
arXiv:2107.02841v1  [cs.DC]  6 Jul 2021


marshaling is required.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
(MPI messaging is used internally
by the Swift/T runtime.) Multiple components written in
different languages may be brought together.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Progress and
load balancing are managed by the Swift runtime.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Overall,
the approach provides a coherent programming model, allows
for compatibility among multiple languages, provides high
scalability, and is compatible with advanced architectures such
as the Cray XE6 and Blue Gene/Q.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

In Section II we describe
the architecture of Swift/T, and in Section III we describe
the interlanguage features that are the focus of this paper.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

In Section IV we offer concluding remarks and a glimpse of
future work.

ARCHITECTURE
We next provide some background on the Swift language,
describe the Swift/T architecture, and discuss how Swift/T
calls application components.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Swift language
Swift is a scripting language with C-like syntax, with
pervasive, automatic concurrency built into the language.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Con-
currency is achieved through dataﬂow processing, in which
progress depends on the availability of input data, not state-
ment ordering.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing
Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Subsequent func-
tion calls to g() block until a value is stored in x.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
When f()
completes, both calls to g() are eligible to run concurrently
on different processors.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Massive concurrency can be achieved in Swift with rela-
tively little code.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing
Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Each execution of f() may be
run concurrently, but each g(t) is blocked on the correspond-
ing f(t).
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The code implies the dataﬂow dependencies shown
in Fig.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text: 1, where several parallel pipelines of tasks are present.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Swift will construct and execute these pipelines in parallel on
any available resources.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text: Diagram of implicit dataﬂow of Swift loop.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In the Swift model, bulk user computation is performed in
leaf tasks: user code outside of Swift, such as libraries or
external programs.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
These are load-balanced between available
processors by dispatching tasks on demand.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
If f() and g()
are compute-intensive functions with varying runtimes, the
asynchronous, load-balanced Swift model is an excellent ﬁt.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Swift/T runtime
Swift/T [2] is a reimplementation of the Swift/K [1] frame-
work for high-performance computing.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Swift/K excels at distributed, grid, and cloud computing,
and offers wide-ranging support for schedulers (PBS, LSF,
SLURM, SGE, Condor, Cobalt, SSH) and data transfer, fault
tolerance, and other features useful for that environment.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
K indicates that the language is implemented atop the Karajan
workﬂow engine.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Swift/T is designed for high-performance computing at the
largest scale.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
T indicates that the key features are implemented
by the Turbine dataﬂow engine [4].
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In this implementation of
Swift, the Swift script is translated into a runtime framework
based on the MPI-based Asynchronous Dynamic Load Bal-
ancer (ADLB) [5] and Turbine libraries, which evaluate Swift
semantics in a distributed manner (no bottleneck).
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Thus, at run
time, Swift/T programs are MPI programs.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text: The Swift/T architecture is diagrammed in Fig.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Each
MPI process operates as an engine, ADLB server, or worker.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text: Engines carry out Swift logic, creating leaf tasks for execution.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
ADLB servers, shown as an opaque subsystem, distribute
tasks to workers, which execute user work (such as f() and
g() in our example above).
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Typically the vast majority of
processes (99%+) are designated as workers.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The engine and
server processes are called control processes and collectively
orchestrate script execution.

text:
SWIFT INTERFACES TO VARIOUS LANGUAGES
Swift/T has multiple new methods not reported previously
for calling to user code .
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In this section, we consider these in
detail.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Calling Tcl
The Swift/T compiler (STC) translates user Swift code to
a representation (Turbine code) that uses the Turbine, ADLB,
MPI, and user libraries, all of which are written in C.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
While
STC could generate C code, we desired a compiler target
with the following properties: 1) A straightforward way to
ship code fragments through ADLB for load balancing and
2


evaluation elsewhere, 2) A textual, easily readable format, and
3) A runtime that did not require the user to run the C compiler
in order to avoid complexities on advanced systems.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Thus, we
chose Tcl to represent Turbine code, and made use of the ease
of calling C from Tcl in order to bind the system together.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Since Swift/T runs on Tcl, calling from Swift to Tcl is the
most advanced interlanguage feature in Swift/T.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Consider the
Swift code fragment
1
(int o) f(int i, int j)
2
"my_package" "1.0"
3
[ "set <<o>> [ f <<i>> <<j>> ]" ];
4
...
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
5
int x = f(2, 3);
In this code, Tcl procedure f is made available to Swift
with the given signature.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
When inputs i and j are avail-
able, the Tcl code (line 3) is executed.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The Tcl package
my_package 1.0 is loaded on the assumption that f will
be found in that package.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The Swift/T runtime supports user
additions to TCLLIBPATH so that arbitrary Tcl code may be
attached to a Swift/T run.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Interlanguage
operation
is
supported
by
1)
inserting
dataﬂow semantics to the interface between Swift/T and Tcl
and 2) automatic type conversion.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The Tcl code on line 3
cannot execute until inputs i and j are set and transmitted to
the worker on which the code will be executed, and storage
for output o has been allocated.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
This code is automatically
inserted into the compiler output by STC and is hidden from
the user (by default).
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The programmer provides a template
for the Tcl code.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Double angle brackets <<·>> indicate that a
variable should appear in that location.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Swift/T variables are
automatically converted to the appropriate Tcl types, which
are oriented toward string representations.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The ease of interlanguage operation here offers multiple
beneﬁcial features to Swift/T development and application
users.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
First, the ease of exposing simple Tcl snippets to Swift
allowed for the rapid development of Swift builtins such as
printf(), strcat(), etc.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Many Tcl features can easily be
brought into Swift this way.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Second, Swift users often express
a desire to mix dataﬂow programming with short fragments
of imperative code.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
This is easily done by extending the Tcl
fragment on line 3 to a multiline script snippet, using the
Swift multiline string syntax.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Certain arithmetical or string
expressions may be easier to perform in Tcl than in Swift,
especially for experienced Tcl or shell programmers.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Third,
existing components built in Tcl can easily be brought into
Swift by using Swift support for Tcl packages.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Fourth, the
strength of Tcl support for calling native code is easily brought
into Swift as well, as described in the following subsection.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Calling native code
A primary goal of Swift/T is to speed the development pro-
cess for scaling existing codes in compiled languages (C, C++,
Fortran) to high-performance systems.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Thus, good support
for calling these languages is paramount.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Tcl provides good
support for calling native code, and good tools such as SWIG
are available.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
This approach has demonstrated the ability to

text: SWIG providing Tcl bindings for C functions callable from Swift/T.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
successfully call native code in many applications, including
applications that may be expressed as MPI libraries [6].
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In order to call into an existing native code program from
Swift, the following steps must be followed.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
First, the user
identiﬁes the key functions to be called.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Simple types (num-
bers, strings) must be used to ensure compatibility with Swift.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Second, the program is compiled as a loadable library - any use
of main() must be removed through conditional compilation.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Third, the library headers are processed by SWIG to generate
Tcl bindings for the C/C++ functions; in the case of Fortran, a
C++-formatted header is ﬁrst created with FortWrap [7], then
processed by SWIG.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Fourth, the user writes Swift bindings
for the generated Tcl bindings as described in the previous
subsection.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Fifth, a Tcl package is constructed containing the
native code library and any additional Tcl scripts that the
user desires to include.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Figure 3 illustrates the process of
binding a C code with Tcl using SWIG.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The functions in object
afunc.o become callable from within Swift/T code.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The interlanguage complications here are more challenging
than that in the Tcl case because more language considera-
tions must be taken into account.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Our approach has been to
delegate complexities and conventions to SWIG, since it is a
general-purpose tool (i.e., learning SWIG has broader utility
than learning a Swift-speciﬁc tool).
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Thus, type conversion
conventions are delegated to SWIG conventions.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In addition to simple types, scientiﬁc users of native code
languages often desire to operate on bulk data in arrays.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The
Swift approach to these is to handle pointers to byte arrays
as a novel type: blob (binary large object).
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
The Swift/T
runtime handles blobs in a similar manner to strings, but with
appropriate handling for binary data.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
This approach allows
users to write dataﬂow scripts that operate on C-formatted
strings and arrays, contiguous binary data structures, and even
multidimensional Fortran arrays.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
SWIG supports operations functions that consume and pro-
duce pointers as represented by Tcl variables.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Thus, Swift/T
provides a small library called blobutils to handle trans-
mission
of the Swift/T blob type to raw pointers com-
patible with SWIG.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Type conversion routines are provided
to handle many common cases.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
For example, SWIG will
3


not automatically convert void∗to double∗– blobutils
provides tools to handle the simple but myriad interlanguage
complexities found when operating on binary data.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Calling Python or R
As described above, many modern scientiﬁc applications
have key components or interfaces built in Python, R, or
other high-level languages.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Previous workﬂow programming
systems call external languages by executing the external in-
terpreter executables.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
This strategy is undesirable for Swift/T,
however, because at large scale the ﬁlesystem overheads
are unacceptable.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Additionally, on specialized supercomputers
such as the Blue Gene/Q, launching external programs is not
possible at all.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Our approach, based in Swift/T, treats the external inter-
preters for Python and R as native code libraries.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Thus, the
complexity of calling them is reduced to the complexity of
calling a C library from Swift/T, which was addressed in
the previous section.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
First, a Tcl extension for each language
was constructed.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
(These could conceivably be reused by non-
Swift developers who simply desire to call Python or R from
Tcl.) Then, a Swift/T leaf function was written that evaluates
fragments of code.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Users interact only with the high-level
Swift/T leaf function, greatly reducing complexity.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In the Swift model, each task is started without state; only
the well-deﬁned Swift inputs are available.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
When calling into
an external interpreter, however, old state from the previous
task could be available and cause confusion or debugging
issues (this is not a security issue, since all of this state is
inside the Swift/T MPI run).
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
One approach is to ﬁnalize the
interpreter at the end of each task and reinitialize it when
the next task is started, thus clearing any state.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
This approach
raises concerns about performance and possible resource leaks.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Thus, we provide options to either retain the interpreter or
reinitialize it.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
(Old interpreter state can also be used to store
useful data if the programmer is careful.)
IV.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
CONCLUSION
Modern scientiﬁc application development is trending to-
ward greater software complexity and more demanding per-
formance requirements.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
These applications blend structured
and unstructured computing patterns, features for distributed
and parallel computing, and the use of specialized libraries
for everything from numerics to I/O.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
For continued progress
in scientiﬁc computing, tools must be developed and adopted
that enable rapid prototyping and development of complex,
large scale applications.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In this work, we provided a broad overview of relevant
scientiﬁc computing applications that combine computing pat-
terns and use multiple languages.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
We described the Swift/T
system for high-performance computing, highlighted its new
features to support scripting languages such as Python and R,
and showed how these can be combined to solve numerical
problems.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
We also described the rich shell interface retained
and extended from Swift/K.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
We described our use of em-
bedded script interpreters, making interlanguage programming
relatively easy while remaining compatible with systems hav-
ing restricted OS functionality such as the IBM Blue Gene/Q.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Additionally, we showed how the many small ﬁle problem
common in scripted solutions can be addressed with our static
packages.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
In future work, we intend to improve support for external
languages by improving support for automatically translating
more complex data types.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

text:
Future applications are sure to
challenge the current performance envelope, and we will
improve and apply our techniques to solve bigger problems
with more advanced tools on the largest scale machines.
title: Toward Interlanguage Parallel Scripting Distributed-Memory Scientiﬁc Computing

Abstract  
The advancements in the use of Internet of Things (IoT) devices is increasing continuously and 
generating huge amounts of data in a fast manner.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Cloud computing is an important paradigm 
which processes and manages user data effectively.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Further, fog and edge computing paradigms 
are introduced to improve user service by reducing latency and response time.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
This chapter 
presents a manifesto for modern fog and edge computing systems based on the current research 
trends.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text: Further, architectures and applications of fog and edge computing are explained.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Moreover, research opportunities and promising future directions are presented with respect to 
the new paradigms, which will be helpful for practitioners, researchers and academicians to 
continue their research.

Background: Fog and Edge Computing  
The concept of fog computing was emerged in the year 2009 and was adopted in the year 2011 
as an assistance to cloud computing [11] and manages the extensive data incoming from IoT 
devices continuously.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Fog computing servers are deployed among edge devices and CDCs to 
process the small jobs quickly instead of sending to the CDC [12].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Further, edge computing is 
emerged in the 2010 and adopted in the year 2012, which helps users to process their requests at 
their edge devices instead of sending to fog or cloud server [13].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Both fog and edge computing 
optimizes energy, execution cost and time while maintaining the quality of service at required 
level.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Figure 1 shows the basic model of fog and edge computing, which contains four main 
layers: cloud, fog, edge and IoT.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Cloud layer consist of data centers and process the user requests 
which needs large processing capability to manage big chunk of data.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Fog layer contains the fog 
devices (servers or nodes) to process the small user requests to reduce latency and response time 
and it needs less processing capability as compared to cloud computing.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Edge layer contains 
edge devices to process user request at edge device despite of sending it to fog or cloud server.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
IoT layer comprise of IoT devices related to the various applications such as healthcare, 
agriculture, traffic monitoring, weather forecasting or other sensors related to particular 
application.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

Type of Architectures  
Basically, there are three different types of architectures for fog and edge computing [23-25]: 
centralized, decentralized and hierarchical as shown in Figure 3.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
There is one chief controller in 
the centralized architecture, which controls all the internal activities such as task scheduling, 
provisioning of resources, scheduling of resources and its execution.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
There are two different 
levels of schedulers in hierarchical architecture: upper and lower level.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Upper level is a chief

broker which manages all the lower-level schedulers while lower level schedulers perform 
various internal activities independently.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Decentralized architecture allocates the resources to 
various user requests based on their specific necessities to complete their task, which also 
provides a high level of scalability.

scalability, cost and execution or response time [2].

5.2 Energy Efficiency and Sustainability 
There is a need to run the cloud data centers continually to deliver the cloud service in a 
proficient way, which uses enormous volume of energy for computation and cooling [30-31].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Further, the utilization of large amount of CDC and utilization of massive chunks of 
energy/power is making an impact on the environment, which leads to climate change by 
producing carbon footprints [32-33].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
To provide the sustainable and energy-efficient fog and 
edge service, there is a requirement to develop effective energy-efficient techniques for the 
management of fog/edge resources using machine learning, deep learning or Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) [34].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
5.3 Provisioning and Scheduling of Resources 
Resource management for fog and edge computing comprises of three main tasks such as 
provisioning, scheduling and execution of fog/edge resources [35-36].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Resource provisioning is 
defined as the filtering of best matched resources based on the QoS requirements of the requests 
[37].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Further, resource scheduler manages the provisioned resources using different scheduling 
policies based on optimization algorithms, machine learning or AI techniques to optimize the 
system performance [38].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Finally, resource manager executes the user workloads on scheduled 
resources.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
5.4 Fault Tolerance (Reliability)  
Fault tolerance is very important concept to maintain the reliability and performance of the 
system [39].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Fog and edge computing paradigms provide an effective fault tolerant service to run 
the system continually without any interruption by fixing the faults dynamically [40].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

text:
Further, 
there is a need to find out the software, network or hardware failure and their reasons and fixes to

Furthermore, effective fault tolerant techniques can help 
system to achieve required objective under predefined conditions in a particular time period.
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

5.5 Interlayer Communication  
Interlayer communication plays an important role for effective resource management to enable 
coordination amongst various tasks and subtasks going inside resource manager to perform 
resource provisioning and scheduling [42].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

In fog-edge computing model, there is a requirement 
of an effective communication among various layers such as cloud, fog, edge and IoT as shown 
in Figure 1, which can improve the quality of service in terms response time and latency [43].
title: A Manifesto for Modern Fog and Edge Computing: Vision, New Paradigms, Opportunities, and Future Directions

Security and privacy are two important challenges in computing system while delivering services 
to end users [44].

and probing [47] [48].

ABSTRACT
Serverless computing offers a pay-per-use model with high
elasticity and automatic scaling for a wide range of applica-
tions.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Since cloud providers abstract most of the underlying
infrastructure, these services work similarly to black-boxes.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
As a result, users can influence the resources allocated to their
functions, but might not be aware that they have to parallelize
them to profit from the additionally allocated virtual CPUs
(vCPUs).
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In this paper, we analyze the impact of paralleliza-
tion within a single function and container instance for AWS
Lambda, Google Cloud Functions (GCF), and Google Cloud
Run (GCR).
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
We focus on compute-intensive workloads since
they benefit greatly from parallelization.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Furthermore, we
investigate the correlation between the number of allocated
CPU cores and vCPUs in serverless environments.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Our results
show that the number of available cores to a function/con-
tainer instance does not always equal the number of allocated
vCPUs.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
By parallelizing serverless workloads, we observed
cost savings up to 81% for AWS Lambda, 49% for GCF, and
69.8% for GCR.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

INTRODUCTION
With the advent of Amazon Web Services (AWS) Lambda in
2014, serverless computing has gained popularity and more
adoption in different application domains such as machine
learning [6, 7, 15], scientific computing [9, 14, 16, 17], and
linear algebra [31].
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In serverless computing, developers do
not have to manage infrastructure themselves but completely
hand over this responsibility to a Function-as-a-Service Plat-
form.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Several open-source and commercial FaaS platforms
such as OpenWhisk, Google Cloud Functions (GCF), and
Lambda are currently available.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Applications are developed
as small units of code, called functions that are independently
packaged and uploaded to a FaaS platform and executed on
event triggers such as HTTP requests.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
On function invocation,
the FaaS platform creates an execution environment (instance)
which provides a secure and isolated runtime environment for
the function.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
The functions can be written using various lan-
guages such as Java, Go, or Nodejs and a language-specific
environment called as runtime is created in the function’s
execution environment.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
However, due to the limitations on
the available runtimes in commercial FaaS platforms such
as GCF, serverless Container-as-a-Service (CaaS) offerings
such as Google Cloud Run (GCR) [24] have been introduced.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text: GCR is a fully-managed service based on Knative [20].
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
CaaS
provides developers greater flexibility and allows them to
build custom container images for their functions.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
While most details about the backend infrastructure man-
agement are abstracted away from the user by commercial
FaaS and serverless CaaS platforms, they still allow develop-
ers to configure the amount of memory and number of vCPUs
(GCR) allocated to a function/container instance [25, 30].
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
As
a result, each function/container instance has a fixed number
of CPU cores and memory associated with it.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For commercial
