This is because these platforms increase
the amount of compute capacity available to a function by
increasing the number of vCPUs or the fraction of the CPU
time if more memory is configured [18].
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Serverless is adver-
tised as a pay-per-use model, where the users are billed based
on the execution time of the functions measured in 100ms
(GCR/GCF) and 1ms (Lambda) intervals.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
However, due to
the billing policies followed by cloud providers, increasing
the amount of memory often leads to an increase in costs
due to fees payment wrt GB-Second (and GHz-Second with
GCF/GCR [23, 26]).
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
The comparison between the average
execution time and cost [29] for the modified MVT bench-
mark [12] when deployed on Lambda is shown in Figure 1.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Although the average execution time decreases when more
memory is configured, the cost increases significantly.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Further-
more, after a certain memory configuration (>2048MB) allo-
cating more memory does not considerably affect the function
execution time.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Serverless FaaS/CaaS platforms launch the
function instances on the platform’s traditional Infrastructure-
as-a-Service (IaaS) virtual machines (VM) offerings [8, 18].
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
However, the provisioning of such VM’s is abstracted away
from the user.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
As a result, the user is not aware of the details
of the provisioned VMs such as the number of CPU cores
and the virtual CPUs (vCPUs).
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Figure 1 shows the number of
CPU cores available to the function for the different memory

title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

We obtain the number of avail-
able cores using the Linux proc filesystem.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Since the native
implementation of the MVT benchmark is single-threaded it
cannot utilize the underlying cores leading to resource under-
utilization.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
To this end, parallelization of functions can lead
to a significant reduction in execution time and thus reduced
costs.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Our key contributions are:
• Identification of #CPU cores and vCPU allocations:
We investigate the number of allocated CPU cores in
FaaS/CaaS platforms and how they are mapped to the
allocated vCPUs.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
• Intra-function parallel workloads: We modify and
parallelize three different compute-intensive serverless
workloads1, using C++, Java and Go.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
We execute these
workloads on AWS Lambda, GCF, and GCR, and ana-
lyze their execution times.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
• Cost analysis: We demonstrate the benefits of paral-
lelizing functions and discuss conditions when paral-
lelization can be beneficial.

2
RELATED WORK
The majority of previous work on parallelizing applications
via FaaS has focused on splitting the workload via separate
function instances, i.e., inter-function parallelism [4, 5, 31].
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
[31] showed that the elasticity provided by
serverless computing can be used to efficiently execute lin-
ear algebra algorithms, which are inherently parallel.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
They
implemented a system to split a linear algebra algorithm into
tasks which are then executed by AWS Lambda functions.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
The data between function instances is shared via a persistent
object-store.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
With their system, they achieved performance
within a factor of two, as compared to a server-centric Mes-
sage Passing Interface (MPI) [1] implementation.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
[4] analyzed the performance of fork/join workflows us-
ing existing services such as AWS Step Functions [2], Azure
Durable Functions [3], and OpenWhisk Composer [22].
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
They
found that, while OpenWhisk Composer offers the best per-
formance, all of the function orchestration solutions have
significant overhead for executing parallel workloads.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In [5],
the authors present a system called Crucial that allows devel-
opers to program highly-concurrent stateful applications with
serverless architectures.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Crucial ports multi-threaded applica-
tions to a serverless environment, by leveraging a distributed
shared memory layer.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For coordinating functions they used
shared objects.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
With Crucial, the authors achieved perfor-
mance results similar to that of an equivalent Spark cluster.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
While distributing workloads across function invocations can
be useful due to the high elasticity, results show that it can
still lead to significant communication and synchronization
overhead.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In contrast, we focus on intra-function parallelism
where we parallelize functions and execute them within a
single function instance.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text: 1We use the term serverless workload and function interchangeably.

Evaluating the general performance of FaaS platforms and
improving the performance of FaaS functions has also been
actively researched [8, 10].
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In [10], the authors present the
Serverless Application Analytics Framework (SAAF), to im-
prove observability on the performance of FaaS functions
on commercial FaaS platforms.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
SAAF currently supports
multiple FaaS platforms and several different programming
languages.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In our previous work [8], we examined the under-
lying processor architectures on GCF and demonstrated the
usage of Numba [21], a Just-in-Time (JIT) compiler based
on LLVM for optimizing and improving the performance of
compute-intensive Python based FaaS functions.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
We showed
that the optimization of FaaS functions can improve perfor-
mance by 18.2x and save costs by 76.8%.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
However, all of
the previous approaches evaluate the performance of single-
threaded FaaS functions.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In contrast, we evaluate and analyze
the performance of parallelized FaaS functions.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Furthermore,
we investigate different function configurations and evaluate
their respective parallel efficiency.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Moreover, we demonstrate
significant cost savings for parallelized functions as compared
to their sequential implementations.

4 which is used to estimate π.

4
EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
In this section, we describe our experimental setup and present
results wrt performance and costs for the parallelized server-
less workloads for the different services.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Finally, we discuss
the impact of cold starts in our experiments.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
4.1
Experimental Setup
For GCF and Lambda, we deployed the different workloads
(§3.1) using the memory profiles 512MB, 2048MB, 4096MB,
and 8192MB.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For Lambda, we also utilized the highest avail-
able memory configuration for a function, i.e., 10240MB.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In
Figure 3: Number of available CPU cores for the different

text:
contrast to GCF and Lambda, GCR allows developers to con-
figure the number of vCPUs allocated to a function along with
the memory.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For GCR, we used similar memory configura-
tions as GCF except for 2048MB.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In this case, we configured
the workloads with 2148MB of memory since that is the
minimum memory required to allocate 4vCPUs to a func-
tion.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
We allocate 4vCPUs for every memory configuration
in GCR except for 512MB where we allocate 2vCPUs.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
To
reduce variance in performance measurements for the server-
less workloads due to cold starts [10], we set the maximum
number of concurrent instances for all services to one.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Fur-
thermore, we set the maximum number of concurrent requests
that can be handled by a container in GCR to one.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
This is
done to prevent the sharing of vCPUs while handling multiple
simultaneous requests.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
We deploy all functions on GCR and
GCF in the us-central1 region.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For Lambda, all functions
are deployed in the us-east1 region.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
4.2
#CPU cores to vCPU mapping
For the different services, language runtimes (§3.2), and con-
figurations (§4.1), we identified the number of available CPU
cores.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
We obtained the number of available cores for the func-
tion/container instance using the Linux proc filesystem.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
The
number of available CPU cores for the different services at the
different memory profiles is shown in Figure 3.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For Lambda,
we observed at least two CPU cores for every memory config-
uration.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Lambda allocates one full vCPU per 1769MB of allo-
cated function memory [30].
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
This implies that the amount of
allocated vCPUs is not equal to the number of available CPU
cores.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For instance, for a memory configuration of 512MB
on Lambda, we observed two CPU cores while not getting
a full allocated vCPU.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Moreover, Lambda always rounds up
the number of available CPU cores as shown in Figure 3.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For
example, 4096MB translates to 2.3vCPUs, but we observed
three CPU cores for that specific configuration.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For GCF, we
always observed two CPU cores irrespective of the config-
ured function memory.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Similarly for GCR, we observed at
least two CPU cores for the different configurations (§4.1).
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

A possible explanation for observing two CPU cores at
lower memory configurations for the different services, i.e.,
AWS Lambda and GCF can be hyperthreading or Simulta-

As shown in previous
works [8, 18], these are the family of processors found in the

4.3
Comparing Performance
Figure 4 shows the average speedups obtained for the differ-
ent serverless workloads (§3.1) across the different memory
configurations (§4.1) for the different services.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For a particu-
lar memory configuration, we compute the speedup obtained
by dividing the mean execution time of the sequential server-
less workload by the mean execution time of the parallelized
version.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Note that, when executing a parallelized workload,
we use the maximum number of available CPU cores for a par-
ticular memory configuration (§4.2).
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For Lambda and GCF,
we don’t observe any significant speedup for lower memory
configurations, i.e., less than 2048MB.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
This is because, in
Lambda and GCF, each function instance has a fixed memory
and fraction of allocated CPU cycles.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Since both FaaS plat-
forms do not allocate complete two vCPUs for lower memory
configurations, utilizing the underlying two CPU cores does
not improve performance.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For Lambda, two vCPUs are al-
located for a memory configuration greater than 3538MB,
while for GCF they are allocated at a memory configuration
of 4096MB [23].
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
This is also apparent from the increase in
speedup observed for GCF when switching from 2048MB to
4096MB as shown in Figures 4d, 4e, and 4f.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For memory con-
figurations greater than 4096MB, we observed speedup close
to the number of available vCPUs for both GCF and Lambda.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
This shows that irrespective of the number of available CPU
cores to a function instance, the performance of a parallelized
function is limited by the allocated vCPUs.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

4.4
Comparing Costs
To calculate costs for the different serverless workloads (§3.1),
we use the obtained mean execution time across the differ-
ent memory configurations.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For Lambda, we round up the
execution time to the nearest 1ms increment, while for GCF
and GCR it is rounded up to the nearest 100ms increment.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Following this, we use the rounded up mean execution time
to calculate function compute time in terms of different units
defined by the providers [23, 26, 29].
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For Lambda, the com-
pute time depends on the amount of allocated memory, i.e.,
GB-Seconds, for GCF it depends on the configured mem-
ory and the allocated CPU clock cycles, i.e., GB-Seconds


Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing
WoSC ’21, December 6–10, 2021, Québec, Canada
and GHz-Seconds, and for GCR it depends on the config-
ured memory and the allocated vCPUs, i.e, GB-Seconds and
vCPU-Seconds.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
The different providers define a fixed price
for one second of compute time depending on the deploy-
ment region.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
We use the pre-defined price values specified by
all cloud providers for calculating the compute costs for the
serverless workloads.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In our calculations, we exclude costs for
free-tiers and networking.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Moreover, we calculate costs per
million function invocations.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
As a result, a fixed price of $0.2
and $0.4 is added for Lambda and GCF/GCR respectively.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Figure 5 shows the cost comparison for the sequential and
parallelized serverless workloads (§3.1) across the different
memory configurations on Lambda.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For Lambda, the differ-
ence in costs for the sequential and parallelized serverless
workloads is not significant for lower memory configurations,
i.e., less than 2048MB.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
However, for the sequential serverless
workloads the costs significantly increase for higher memory
configurations, while for the parallelized versions the increase
in cost is considerably less.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For instance, the increase in aver-
age cost from the lowest to the highest memory configuration
for the workloads parallelized using C++ is 30%, while for
the sequential versions it is 498%.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Therefore, by efficiently
parallelizing serverless workloads we can obtain improved
performance (§4.3) at approximately the same costs.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Over-
all, we observed that parallelizing functions with C++ leads
to minimum costs as shown in Figure 5.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For the sequential
workloads, Java is the cheapest, except for lower memory
configurations.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For Lambda, we obtained maximum cost sav-
ings of 81% for the Go implementation of the Monte Carlo
workload as shown in Figure 5h.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Due to space limitations, we do not present detailed cost
analysis results for GCF/GCR but summarize our findings
in Table 2.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
We obtain the maximum cost savings for GCF
with a memory allocation of at least 4096MB which also
corresponds to the highest obtained speedup values (§4.3).
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For GCR, the maximum cost savings are obtained for the
memory configuration of 2148MB with 4vCPUs.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
4.5
Impact of Cold Starts
From our experiments, we observed that the latency of cold
starts is equally long for the sequential and parallel implemen-
tations of the serverless workloads (§3.1).
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Since cold starts
constitute a fraction of the function execution time, if large
enough, they can potentially impact the speedup and cost
savings obtained from parallelizing serverless workloads.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
The
average billable cold start latency for the different services
and language runtimes (§3.2) is shown in Figure 6.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
While
AWS Lambda directly provides the billed cold start time in
function logs, for GCF and GCR, we compute the billed cold
start latency by subtracting the billed function execution time
Figure 6: Average billable cold start latency for the differ-
ent runtimes across the different services.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In our experiments, we did not ob-
serve a significant difference in the cold start latencies for the
different serverless workloads and function memory configu-
rations.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
However, the values shown in Figure 6 are averaged
across all benchmarks.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
We observed a significant cold start
latency for the Java runtime on GCR as compared to the C++
and Go runtimes.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
A possible explanation for this could be a
high amount of time required for the Java Virtual Machine
(JVM) to warm up.

5
CONCLUSION & FUTURE WORK
In this paper, we analyzed the effect of parallelizing compute-
intensive serverless workloads within a function/container
instance in terms of performance and costs for AWS Lambda,
Google Cloud Functions, and Google Cloud Run.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
We identi-
fied that for the different services the number of CPU cores
available to the function/container does not always equal the
number of allocated vCPUs.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Furthermore, we demonstrate
that parallelizing serverless workloads can significantly im-
prove performance and lead to cost savings.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
For Lambda, we
observed cost savings up to 81%, for GCF up to 49%, and for
GCR up to 79.8%.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
In the future, we plan to evaluate other serverless offerings
and language runtimes.
title: Towards Demystifying Intra-Function Parallelism in Serverless Computing

text:
Furthermore, investigating a hybrid
approach between inter and intra-function parallelism to re-
duce synchronization overhead is another future direction.

Molecular Dynamics Simulations on Cloud Computing and Machine Learning Platforms
Prateek Sharma1, ∗and Vikram Jadhao1, †
1Intelligent Systems Engineering, 700 N.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Woodlawn Avenue, Indiana University, Bloomington, Indiana 47408
Scientiﬁc computing applications have beneﬁted greatly from high performance computing infrastructure
such as supercomputers.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
However, we are seeing a paradigm shift in the computational structure, design, and
requirements of these applications.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Increasingly, data-driven and machine learning approaches are being used to
support, speed-up, and enhance scientiﬁc computing applications, especially molecular dynamics simulations.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Concurrently, cloud computing platforms are increasingly appealing for scientiﬁc computing, providing “inﬁ-
nite” computing powers, easier programming and deployment models, and access to computing accelerators
such as TPUs (Tensor Processing Units).
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
This conﬂuence of machine learning (ML) and cloud computing rep-
resents exciting opportunities for cloud and systems researchers.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
ML-assisted molecular dynamics simulations
are a new class of workload, and exhibit unique computational patterns.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
These simulations present new chal-
lenges for low-cost and high-performance execution.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
We argue that transient cloud resources, such as low-cost
preemptible cloud VMs, can be a viable platform for this new workload.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Finally, we present some low-hanging
fruits and long-term challenges in cloud resource management, and the integration of molecular dynamics sim-
ulations into ML platforms (such as TensorFlow).
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
INTRODUCTION
Scientiﬁc computing applications play an important
role in the analysis and understanding of a wide variety
of natural and synthetic processes.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
These applications
are typically implemented as large-scale parallel pro-
grams that use communication frameworks such as MPI,
and are largely deployed on high performance computing
(HPC) infrastructure such as supercomputers.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Molecular
dynamics (MD) simulations are among the most ubiq-
uitous scientiﬁc computing applications.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
These simula-
tions have been used extensively by materials scientists,
chemical engineers, and physicists to investigate the mi-
croscopic origins of the macroscopic behavior of mate-
rials such as self-assembled nanoparticles, viral capsids,
electrolytes, lubricants, and polymers [1–4].
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
A key goal for MD simulations is to explore the de-
sign space associated with the material attributes, and
establish the links between the design parameters and
the material response (generally, encoded in the struc-
tural and dynamical properties).
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
To this end, simulations
are deployed as a collection or “bag” of jobs.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Collec-
tively, a bag of jobs “sweeps” a multi-dimensional design
space and furnishes the links between the material design
parameters (inputs) and the material response (outputs).
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
These links provide a reliable guide to experiments for a
rational discovery of regions of the material design space
exhibiting interesting structural and dynamical proper-
ties.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
The bags of jobs approach is also central to the rapidly
developing area of using machine learning (ML) to en-
hance MD simulations and expedite the exploration of
the material design space [5–14].
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Large collections of
∗prateeks@iu.edu
† vjadhao@iu.edu
jobs with independent parameter sets are launched in or-
der to train and test the ML models designed to enhance
the predictive power or reduce the computational costs
of MD simulations.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
For example, artiﬁcial neural net-
work based regression models, trained on data from MD
simulations of soft materials, can successfully predict the
relationships between the input parameters and the sim-
ulation outcomes [12, 15].
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
These ML surrogates accu-
rately predicted the distributions of ions for a variety of
conﬁned electrolyte systems with 95% accuracy and an
inference time 10000× less than the corresponding MD
simulation runtime [12, 15].
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
As the utility of MD simula-
tions and their ML-enhanced versions in the rational de-
sign of materials is further demonstrated, it will be neces-
sary for accurate and fast simulations to be performed for
larger sets of parameters in order to efﬁciently explore
the material design space.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
To this end, it is important to
leverage diverse advanced cyberinfrastructure platforms
to perform low-cost simulations.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
MOLECULAR DYNAMICS ON CLOUD
PLATFORMS
Increasingly, cloud computing platforms have begun
to supplement and complement conventionalHPC infras-
tructure to meet the large computing and storage require-
ments of simulations [16].
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Public clouds offer many ben-
eﬁts: on-demand resource allocation, convenient pay-
as-you-go pricing models, and ease of deployment on
an “inﬁnite” resource pool.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
An important objective in
cloud deployments is to optimize for cost in addition to
performance.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Costs can be reduced through the use of
transient computing resources that can be unilaterally re-
voked and preempted by the cloud provider, but their pre-
emptible nature results in frequent job failures.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
The con-
siderations of cost, frequent job failures, and server con-
ﬁguration heterogeneity intrinsic to the system present


2
multiple challenges in deploying applications on cloud
platforms.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
These challenges are fundamentally different
from those that appear in using HPC clusters as the exe-
cution environment for simulations.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Systems such as SciSpot [17, 18], a framework that
uses a new reliability model for constrained preemptions
of Google Preemptible Virtual Machines (VMs), can op-
timize the deployment of scientiﬁc computing applica-
tions on transient cloud servers and enable low-cost MD
simulations.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
SciSpot uses an empirical and analytical
model of transient server availability to predict expected
running times and costs associated with jobs of different
types and durations.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Considering an entire bag of jobs
as an execution unit enables simple and powerful poli-
cies for optimizing cost, makespan, and ease of deploy-
ment.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
SciSpot’s cost-minimizing server selection and job
scheduling policies reduce costs by up to 5× compared
to conventional cloud deployments.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
MOLECULAR DYNAMICS ON ML SYSTEMS
The use of ML systems such as TensorFlow and Py-
Torch has been largely limited for designing ML-based
enhancements (e.g., surrogates, integrators, force ﬁelds)
for MD simulations [6, 12, 13].
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Some recent studies have
explored the utilization of ML platforms for “non-ML”
tasks related to MD simulations [19–23].
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
However, the
use of ML systems to develop and execute MD simula-
tions and integrate them with ML-based enhancements is
unexplored.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
In the following, we outline advantages of
ML systems as environments for executing MD simula-
tions and integrating them with data-driven models.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
We
also discuss the associated systems challenges.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
MD simulations are typically coded in C/C++ and par-
allelized using OpenMP and MPI [24].
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
However, more
modern MD software packages such as HOOMD-Blue
[25] have demonstrated that MD simulations can be eas-
ily written in high-level languages such as Python.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
ML
platforms such as TensorFlow are based on Python and
the associated high-level data-ﬂow abstraction can en-
able rapid prototyping of MD simulations.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
We highlight
a few key advantages of utilizing ML systems for execut-
ing MD simulations:
• High-performance simulations: ML systems offer
automatic parallelization of simulations and en-
able seamless use of next-generation cloud and
HPC hardware such as GPUs and TPUs.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
• One-stop platform: ML systems offer extensive
support for debugging, data analytics, and post-
processing tasks that can be leveraged to perform
all simulation-related tasks at a single platform.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
• Large ecosystem: Developers have access to a
much bigger data science and ML community.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
• Better software engineering: Associated tools are
richer and are actively developed and improved
(compared to, for example, MPI).
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
• Reproducibility and ease of sharing: Users and
developers can easily share all simulation models
and methods in one notebook that can be run on
ML system backends such as Google Colab (com-
pared to cumbersome conﬁguring of simulations
on different HPC systems).
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
• Integration with data-driven approaches: Data op-
erations in ML systems are ﬁrst-class operations,
instead of being a separate stage of the simulation
workﬂow aimed at exploring the material design
space.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
The seamless integration of simulations and data-
driven models on a single platform offers many oppor-
tunities for a rational and expedited exploration of the
material design space.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
We now illustrate a set of these
opportunities using ML surrogates as an example.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
An
ML surrogate is a model trained on data from MD sim-
ulations that is used to approximate the relationships be-
tween the input parameters and the simulation outcomes,
bypassing part or all of the explicit evolution of the simu-
lated components.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
For instance, the ML surrogate in [12]
can reduce the inference time from 30 minutes to 0.2
seconds—a 10, 000× speedup!
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
This surrogate model
was trained using a bag of jobs of size N = 6, 000, each
job representing a unique set of parameters discretizing
the high-dimensional input design space.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
In the conventional, un-integrated approach, the bag of
jobs (of size N) is run sequentially on HPC systems, with
a long wait time until a surrogate is trained.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
N is chosen
a priori (usually informed by domain expertise) such that
the generated data is sufﬁcient to train an ML model (typ-
ically a deep neural network).
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
In contrast, an integrated
approach utilizing ML systems for simulation facilitates
a rapid transition from simulation to surrogate.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
The sur-
rogate training can now begin with a smaller number n
of simulations and the training progress can be monitored
in a seamless fashion.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
When surrogates are designed in
an integrated manner on ML systems, a number of new
opportunities emerge:
• A uniﬁed approach to executing simulations and
training ML models to approximate input-output
relationships enables the development of the sur-
rogate during the exploration of the material de-
sign space with a bag of n < N jobs.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
ML systems
can facilitate the automation of the switch to de-
riving outputs using surrogates when the training
and testing errors become small and surrogate ac-
curacy reaches a high value.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
• On-the-ﬂy development of the surrogates enables
a principled approach to quantify the completion
of the material design space exploration.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
3
• Surrogate accuracy and inferences times can be
readily improved with minimal overhead associ-
ated with the one-stop platform that enables a
seamless accumulation of training data resulting
from more simulation executions.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
• The ease of designing surrogates in parallel with
the simulation-driven exploration of the material
design space enables efﬁcient new simulation code
development (e.g., writing new pair interaction
potentials).
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
The trained surrogates can be used
as benchmarks of existing understanding that can
guide code updates.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
OPEN QUESTIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
The conﬂuence of ML, MD simulations, and cloud
computing presents the broader cloud and HPC research
communities with several exciting challenges, and also
provides a unique opportunity to bring these commu-
nities together.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
ML-assisted MD simulations impose a
unique set of computational requirements which will re-
quire advances in cloud resource allocation, such as:
• Abstractions: Our bags-of-jobs abstraction is the
ﬁrst step towards a “cloud-native” abstraction for
ML-assisted MD workloads.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Easier ways to de-
ploy such applications on the cloud will lower
costs and will make it easier for domain scientists
to rapidly iterate.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
• Rethinking performance metrics: Conventional
metrics such as parallel speedups will be insufﬁ-
cient for ML-assisted workloads that use a combi-
nation of training and inference, where the answer
can be provided by a trained ML-model.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
We be-
lieve that cost will remain a ﬁrst-level metric in
the cloud, and must be a core part of performance
and resource optimizations.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
We also claim that ML platforms can provide a single,
uniﬁed framework for future applications that will inte-
grate ML and MD simulations in new ways.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Fundamen-
tally, we are proposing to use systems in ways that they
are not designed for, which leads to many natural per-
formance challenges.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
For instance, the dataﬂow model
used by TensorFlow provides suboptimal performance
for ﬁne-grained parallelism required for MD simulations
on GPU and TPU clusters, and new performance opti-
mizations and abstractions are necessary.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
Finally, bringing a “classic” HPC workload such as
MD simulations into an entirely new cloud+ML ecosys-
tem will require the HPC, cloud, and ML communities
to work together with domain scientists and engineers in
new ways.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
The conﬂuence will provide opportunities for
the next generation of domain scientists to be trained in
practical ML and cloud skills.
title: arXiv:2111.06466v1  [cs.DC]  11 Nov 2021

text:
At the same time, cloud
researchers should be more cognizant of this new class
of workload, which is radically different from the “en-
terprise” and “big-data” workloads that cloud platforms
have traditionally been optimized for.

Abstract—Quantum technologies available currently contain noise in general, often dubbed
noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) systems.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
We here present the veriﬁcation of noise in
measurement readout errors in cloud-based quantum computing services, IBMQ and Rigetti, by
directly performing quantum detector tomography, and show that there exist measurement
crosstalk errors.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
We provide the characterization and the quantiﬁcation of noise in a quantum
measurement of multiple qubits.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
We remark that entanglement is found as a source of crosstalk
errors in a measurement of three qubits.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
THE COMPUTATION based on the laws of
quantum mechanics makes it possible to achieve
the capability beyond the limitations of conven-
tional computing [1], [2], [3].
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
To understand the
existing gap between theory and implementation
in the realization of quantum computing, the
key is to ﬁnd how noise deteriorates the capa-
bility of quantum information processing.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
Noise
in a quantum system signiﬁes its transition to
a classical one.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
Once systems are governed by
classical physics, no quantum advantages can
be obtained.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
An ultimate solution to deal with
quantum noise may be obtained by quantum
error-correcting codes that can preserve quantum
states [4].
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
The quantum technologies available at
present, dubbed noisy intermediate-scale quantum
(NISQ) technologies [5], do not meet the level to
implement quantum error correction.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
Although the errors are present, NISQ tech-
nologies can be used to show advantages over
classical systems [6].
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
Much effort has been de-
voted to improving the capability of NISQ-based
information processing.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
Quantum algorithms ﬁt-
ted to NISQ technologies are devised, e.g., quan-
tum approximate optimization [7] or variational
quantum eigensolvers [8].
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
Strategies to mitigate
the errors in quantum dynamics have been pro-
posed while quantum error-correcting codes can-
not be realized [9], see also [10], [11], [12].
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
In
fact, industry vendors such as IBMQ, IonQ, or
Rigetti immediately provide cloud-based quantum
computing services.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
The main focus of the present article is mea-
surement readout errors, in particular, crosstalk
errors, appearing in a quantum measurement with
NISQ technologies.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
The signiﬁcance of measure-
ment errors is twofold.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
Firstly, no method is
known so far to generally clear measurement
errors.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

to deal with noise appearing in quantum dynam-

The step of QDT

For instance, crosstalk among detectors may

This means that one should not consider

Moreover, it is generally hard to verify the source
for measurement crosstalk errors, which may be
caused by interactions within systems but an
environment.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
All these make it even harder to deal
with measurement errors in general.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
In this work, we show that crosstalk errors in a
measurement of two and three qubits in fact exist
in the cloud-based quantum computing services,
IBMQ and Rigetti, by performing QDT directly
on the detectors for multiple qubits.

In particular,
entanglement is detected in the measurement op-
erators describing three-qubit detectors but two-
qubit ones.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
We introduce an operational method
to quantify measurement crosstalk errors and
provide the analysis.

text:
Our results can be used to
devise methods to mitigate measurement errors.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
We then introduce the
characterization and quantiﬁcation of crosstalk
errors in a quantum measurement.

Measurement
errors in IBMQ Yorktown and Rigetti Aspen-8
are analyzed.

Finally, we summarize the structure
of correlations appearing in a measurement of
multiple qubits.

Crosstalk Errors
Crosstalk errors in a quantum measurement
can be rephrased as correlations shared by detec-
tors.

text:
The correlations may be investigated at the
angle of entanglement theory that characterizes
quantum correlations which do not have a classi-
cal counterpart.

text:
In what follows, we apply entan-

multi-qubit POVM elements of IBMQ Yorktown
and Rigetti Aspen-8.

Two-qubit POVM elements
Two-qubit POVM elements correspond to 4×
4 non-negative operators.

text:
We call a normalized
two-qubit POVM element contains entanglement
if it cannot be decomposed into a probabilistic
mixture of local POVM elements.

text:
Otherwise, the
POVM element is called separable such that it
can be prepared by local operations and classical
communication:

For the two-qubit cases, a simple
condition can tell whether entanglement is con-
tained or not.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
A normalized two-qubit POVM is
entangled if it is non-positive under the partial
transpose (NPPT), where the partial transpose
may be taken either of the qubits [19].
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
Otherwise,
it contains correlations that can be prepared by
local operations and classical communication.

This shows that two-qubit
crosstalk errors are from classical correlations
shared by two detectors.

Correlations shared by three qubits can be
approached by bipartite splittings.

Negative eigenvalues conclude

applied to other bipartite splittings, B : CA and

Conclusion
In conclusion, we have analyzed measurement
readout errors in cloud-based quantum computing
services.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
A method of quantifying crosstalk errors
is introduced and applied to analyzing readout
errors in IBMQ Yorktown and Rigetti Aspen-8.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
Our results characterize and quantify measure-
ment crosstalk errors in quantum computing with
NISQ technologies, and pave a way to devise
a method of dealing with measurement readout
errors in multiple qubits, such as measurement
error correction or mitigation.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
Our results also
suggest that QDT may be performed before qubit
allocations so that the crosstalk errors are ana-
lyzed and those qubits having a large fraction
of crosstalk in a measurement are avoided by
the command of qubit allocations.
title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing

text:
It would be
interesting to investigate the relations of error
mitigation and the properties and the structure of
crosstalk errors in a quantum measurement.

were generated at the cloud-based quantum com-
puting services IBMQ and Rigetti.
